 Chapter VI. THE STRUGGLE FOR CONTROL OF NORTH AMERICA 

AFTER AMERICA had been discovered and explored by the European nations, it was considered by several of the most ambitious ones as worthy of being settled and claimed as a part of their empires. In this unit we shall see how an advanced civilization was transplanted to a primitive environment. The English, as rivals of powerful Spain, were interested in obtaining new lands and greater natural resources. Lands were considered desirable because of their precious metals and also because of crowded conditions at home. The English were successful in transplanting their institutions by reason of their control of the seas, and their ability in promoting and governing the colonies. From a small beginning in Virginia in 

1607, settlement continued, one colony after another being planted, until, after a period of 126 years, Georgia, the thirteenth colony, was founded. 

At first the pioneers built their homes along the river banks and the sea coast from Maine to Florida, but as the number increased, they began to penetrate the back country. The settlement of America was only another step in the westward movement of civilization. 45

Many of our present-day institutions had their origin in this period. 

The early immigrants strove for religious liberty, freedom of the press, and local self-government. From the small group of a hundred who settled at 

Jamestown they grew into a self-governing nation. We are interested in their home life, their ways of living, their problems, and their dangers. 

We respect and appreciate them, for they endured great hardships and overcame many obstacles in order to accomplish what they did; and today we enjoy the blessings made possible by their sacrifice. Their interest in schools and in churches attracts our attention, for these early people laid the foundations for our education and religion. Our cultural heritage is the result of their wisdom.

Settlements were made also by the French, Spanish, and Dutch, with the result that a struggle for the control of America was inevitable. This finally led to the French and Indian War, a part of a world embroilment which ended in 1763, with victory for the English, the outcome of which gave assurance that the institutions and ideals of America, built on the foundations laid by the English "sea dogs" of the sixteenth century, should remain English. However, French influences are still found in those sections in which French settlers predominated. 

An early colonial village green; from an old print 

Culver Service

CHAPTER III 

English Colonies in America

Why the English Settled in America. More than a century passed after Cabot explored the coast of North America before the English made a permanent settlement in the New World. Their rulers were concerned with domestic affairs, and felt that their country was financially unable to promote settlements across the Atlantic. However, as international rivalry increased, and as Spain became wealthy and powerful because of her colonial possessions, the English rulers became desirous of weakening the power of Spain and at the same time adding to the strength of their own country. One of England's statesmen at the time stated that nothing could add more to the greatness of the nation than the procuring of additional territory. Besides territory, there was a desire for gold and silver, which it was believed would add to the strength of the nation. The nations of Europe were purchasing many things from India and China. This eastern commerce was depleting their stock of silver and gold coins and they needed an increased supply of precious metals to continue their imports. 

The nations of Europe were also interested in finding a waterway through America to the Pacific and the East. The early English settlers were instructed to search for this "northwest passage." Finally, there was the important stimulant of economic pressure. Changes were taking place in the economic life of England; large tracts of land were turned into sheep pastures because of the growing demand for wool. This denied many farm laborers a chance for making a living. The increased amount of gold and silver advanced prices at a time when many were out of employment, and people unable to earn a livelihood often became beggars or thieves. From this came the belief that England was overpopulated, and colonies were needed to find a place for the surplus population. 

How Colonization Was Promoted. The experiences of Gilbert and 

Raleigh demonstrated to the English people that colonization was too great a task for individuals to attempt alone. The government, however, 47

was not willing to undertake this enterprise; therefore, English settlement was promoted by means of joint-stock companies. Such companies, composed of merchant adventurers, had already been organized in England and in Holland, France, Sweden, and Denmark. In the sixteenth century 

England had chartered several such companies. Outstanding among these was the East India Company. Following the custom established by these trading companies, James I in 1606 granted the Virginia charter which established two companies: one known as the London Company, which consisted mainly of men from London; and the other, known as the Plymouth Company, which consisted of men from Plymouth and other nearby towns. The London Company was authorized to settle in the region between 34 and 41 degrees north, and the Plymouth Company, between 38 and 45 degrees north. The region between 38 and 41 degrees, therefore, was open for settlement by either company, on the condition, however, that neither should settle within 100 miles of a settlement established by the other. The land to go with a settlement was to extend from it 50 miles each way along the coast, and 100 miles inland. (See map, p. 51.) 

The charter also provided that the settlers in the New World should have the same rights as the Englishmen at home. 

The Plymouth Company attempted a settlement at the mouth of the Kennebec River, in 1607, but after a winter of terrible suffering the attempt was abandoned and no further settlement was made by that company. 

The London Company, however, was more successful. It was composed of 659 persons, including peers, knights, gentlemen, merchants, and citizens. Its organization was similar to that of a corporation of our own day. It was organized for the purpose of making profit for the stockholders, but of course it was hoped that it would benefit England by supplying such products as she could not produce at home. It was further hoped that the settlers would carry Christianity to the Indians. There were two classes of stockholders: first, those known as adventurers, who invested their money but stayed at home in England; and second, those known as planters, who migrated to America. 

VIRGINIA 

The Settlement of Virginia. In December, 1606, the London Company sent out from London three small vessels, the Goodspeed (or Godspeed), the Discovery (or Discoverer), and the Sarah Constant (or Susan Constant). 

These ships were commanded by Christopher Newport, who was an experienced seaman. The three vessels left England for Virginia with 120 prospective settlers, of whom sixteen died on the voyage. The ships were

small, the voyage was long, and there was neither sufficient and proper food nor enough good drinking water. After a long and tedious voyage across the Atlantic they sailed up a river which they called the James, in honor of their king, and in the month of May landed on a peninsula and made a settlement which they called Jamestown. The settlers, consisting of boys and men, at once began to build a fort for protection. Then they built a storehouse, a church, and a number of log huts for homes. In this modest way the settlement of Virginia began. 

The Early Settlers Suffer Great Hardships. When the settlers landed, they were in high spirits, for they had come to a beautiful land, in the month of May. However, before long, many difficulties beset them. Their food supplies ran low and their native food crop had not been successful. 

Their surroundings turned out to be unhealthful. Fever and dysentery broke out, and many of the settlers died. With the approach of cooler weather, the others were able to survive, and during the winter they obtained food by trading with the Indians. In the second summer sickness and hardship came again. Thus in the early years the first English settlers suffered great privations. Many of the planters were known as "gentlemen," who were unaccustomed to manual labor. They also suffered attacks from hostile Indians. For some time the first English settlement hung on a very slender thread, but courage and determination finally prevailed. The leadership of Captain John Smith was of great importance. As president of the Council he secured harmony in the Council, obtained corn from the Indians, and demanded labor from the settlers. Thus the colony was saved from starvation. Great hardship was endured because Early view of Jamestown;

from an old print

of hope for better days, but in order to continue as a permanent settlement, economic prosperity was necessary. It was desirable that the colony should be not only self-supporting, but that it should produce supplies of value to England in order that the company could pay dividends. In 

1612 it was discovered that tobacco could be successfully grown, and John Rolfe learned the art of curing tobacco. This commodity soon became so valuable a product that it placed the struggling settlement on a better economic basis. The hostile attitude of the Indians also changed, at least for a time. John Rolfe fell in love with Pocahontas, the favorite daughter of the great Indian chief Powhatan, and married her in the English church at Jamestown (1614).

The Company Reorganized. The first settlers worked for the company rather than for their own individual interests. This plan was not very desirable, and in 1616 a reorganization took place by which each of the settlers received 100 acres of land for his own use. Later, each emigrant who paid his way across the Atlantic was promised a 50-acre tract, and each person was also given an additional 50 acres for every new settler that he brought over. This was known as the head-right system, which became the basis of the land system in Virginia. 

The first charter had limited the area granted to the company to a region 100 miles from the coast; but in 1609 the company obtained a new charter by which it received the land to the west and northwest from sea to sea. In 1612 the company received another charter, by which it became a self-governing corporation. The company held four meetings a year in London, called meetings of the General Court. At them the stockholders elected officers and made laws for the colony. The London Company now came to be known as the Virginia Company; its governing body was the General Court in London, which managed the business of the company, and appointed governors and councilors for Virginia. 

The Rise of Representative Government. Before long there developed different points of view concerning the government of the colony. There were those in the General Court who believed that a more liberal policy should be established. This group, led by Sir Edwin Sandys, urged that the settlers in Virginia be given more freedom in the government of their colony. This liberal group came into control of the company, and in 1619 

Governor George Yeardley was instructed to call on the free inhabitants of the colony to choose representatives to join with him and the Council in passing ordinances for the welfare of the colony. Thus there was established the first representative legislature ever to meet in America. This assembly, consisting of the governor and councilors appointed by the

Land grants by Virginia charters company, and the representatives, known as burgesses. chosen by the inhabitants, met in the little church in Jamestown on July 30, 1619. The inhabitants of the Virginia colony were grouped into eleven boroughs for the purpose of selecting representatives. 

Soon after the establishment of representative government, however, other problems confronted the new settlement. In 1622 an Indian massacre occurred. There was much suffering and loss of life from disease as well as from the Indians. A royal commission appointed to investigate the affairs of the company charged misgovernment and inefficiency, and recommended a reorganization by which Virginia became a crown colony in 1624. This did not mean the end of representative government, for after a brief period the settlers were again allowed to elect representatives to 41°

their assembly. However, the king, instead of the company, now appointed the governor and the councilors. The governor became an agent of the crown instead of an official of the company. At first the governor, councilors, and burgesses sat together in one house; but in time the government of the colony was modeled after the pattern of the English Parliament: the burgesses and councilors separated and became two houses. 

During the first few years under the royal government the population grew slowly. The settlers found it difficult to adjust themselves to the new conditions; but after the outbreak of the English civil war (16421649), and especially during the reign of Oliver Cromwell, many disappointed Cavaliers came across the sea and found refuge in Virginia. It is estimated that by 1652 there were as many as 20,000 people in the new province. Thus, beginning in a very small way, and facing almost insurmountable difficulties, the colony prospered. 

The Virginia Land System. One of the important factors which contributed to the growth of Virginia was the land system. The head-right system (p. 50) made it possible for large estates to be created. By the middle of the seventeenth century, the average size of a grant in Virginia was about 500 acres. These large tracts were called plantations. The holders of these large areas were required to pay annually to the king a quitrent, which was commonly paid in tobacco. Under this system many important plantations developed, such as those owned by William Fitzhugh, Abraham Wood, and William Byrd. By the end of the seventeenth century, the Virginia planters were an important group. The population had greatly increased under the plantation system, which became characteristic of the South. The planters became the real rulers of the Virginia colony-called "the Old Dominion"-and contributed a very important element to Virginia society. 

NEW ENGLAND 

The Separatists in England. The first permanent settlement in 

New England was made by the Pilgrims, or Separatists, who established a colony on the coast of Massachusetts in 1620. This settlement, like 

Jamestown, was promoted by a commercial company. These early settlers were interested in improving their economic condition, but there was another factor which played a very important part, namely, religion. In 

1534, Henry VIII of England, because of a quarrel with the Pope, demanded that the English Church be separated from the Church of Rome. 

This led to the establishment of the Anglican Church. The religious practices and beliefs which followed were the result of compromises between

Catholicism and Protestantism. There were many people in England who were dissatisfied with the doctrines and practices of the Anglican Church, or Church of England, because there were still vestiges of the Roman Church to be seen in it. The Catholics, however, were loyal to the Church of Rome and refused to accept the Church of England. The dissatisfied 

Protestants were called Puritans, and consisted of two groups. (1) The 

Nonconformists believed in an established church, and were willing to remain in the Church of England, but worked for changes in the form of worship. They were interested in securing simpler ceremonies. (2) The second group of Puritans, however, insisting on immediate changes, decided to withdraw from the Church of England, and were called Independents, or Separatists. Many of the Separatists believed in the doctrines of Robert Browne, who, in the latter part of the sixteenth century, had attacked the Church of England as an unchristian body. He maintained that the church is a community or number of believers who make a willing covenant with God and keep His laws. The fundamental idea with Browne was the willing covenant. This idea that men could make their own church was an important one; because if they could make their own church and elect their own church officers, then perhaps they could also make their own government and elect their own state officers. The Separatists who believed in these doctrines of Robert Browne were therefore very unpopular with the king. The preaching of such doctrines might lead to the overthrow of the established government. 

The Pilgrims Leave England. In cider to escape the persecution of the king, a group of Separatists, called Pilgrims, left their home at Scrooby, England, and fled to Holland, where they hoped to enjoy religious liberty. 

However, they were soon dissatisfied, because Holland was not a land in which they could carry on their English customs. They therefore decided to leave Holland for America. They secured permission from the 

Virginia Company to make a settlement, and finally also received the king's consent after they had pledged their loyalty to the crown. Most of these people, however, were without money, and in order to obtain transportation to America they made an agreement with a group of London businessmen. A joint-stock company was formed, as in the case of the 

Virginia Company. The shares in this case were divided between those who came to America and the merchants who remained in London. The agreement with the London merchants provided that for a period of seven years the settlers should work for the company, and that all of the land on which they settled and which they cultivated should be held by the company.

The Plymouth Colony. After these financial arrangements had been made, the Pilgrim settlers embarked on the Mayflower for a new land of hope. The Mayflower, however, ran out of her course and landed on the shores of Cape Cod Bay, which was beyond the bounds of the Virginia Company. The Pilgrims were, therefore, squatters on land to which they had no right. Browne, who believed that men should make their own government. They landed on the "bleak New England shores" in the cold month of December, and founded the town of Plymouth. During the first winter they suffered such hardships that nearly half their number were buried on that "stern and rock-bound coast." However, in the following spring, those surviving planted their crops and prepared to face the future. Friendly Indians taught them how to catch fish and plant corn. In addition to agriculture and fishing, they engaged in the fur trade, and with the products they obtained through these efforts they were able at the end of the seventh year to make an agreement by which they freed themselves from the 

London merchants.

At first the affairs of the group were carried on in a general meeting, at which they passed laws for the good of the colony. They chose a governor

and one or more assistants. As the settlement grew in size, however, and as the people scattered, it became more difficult for them to meet in general meetings. They therefore instructed each community to send delegates to a General Court. Thus representative government developed in New England as well as in Virginia.

The Settlement of the Massachusetts Bay Colony. The Massachusetts Bay Colony, which became the most populous and important of the New England communities, was founded almost ten years after the Pilgrims settled at 

Plymouth. The chief reason for its settlement was dissatisfaction with religious conditions at home. The 

Puritan party in England did not get along well with James I, and under his successor, Charles I, who came to power in 1625, the situation became worse. To get rid of the Puritan opposition, the king dissolved Parliament in 1629, and

did not summon another until 1640.CON SAMVEL 

During this period he ruled with the advice of Archbishop Laud, who had little consideration for the Puritans.

St. Gaudens statue of a Pilgrim 

The outlook for the Puritans was not bright; so they looked to America, where the Pilgrims had found a place to worship unmolested. Some of them soon formed the Massachusetts Bay Company and asked for a charter from the king. The charter was granted in 1629, and was very much like that of the Virginia Company in 1612. It created a corporation which was made the proprietor of the colonies founded under it and was given the right to govern these colonies according to English law. The company had received a patent from the Council for New England for the land from a point three miles north of the Merrimack River to a point three miles south of the Charles River, and westward from sea to sea. 

The Council for New England was composed of Sir Ferdinando Gorges, Captain John Mason, and others who had been interested in the old Plymouth Company and were anxious to make settlements in New England.

New England colonies

By a charter from the king this Council had been given the right to colonize and govern the vast area between the fortieth and forty-eighth parallels, stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. It was within this area that the settlement at Plymouth was made. It was also within the limits of this same area and from the same authority that the Massachusetts Bay 

Company received its patent.

The charter having been granted by the king, the next step was the organization of the government. The Puritan leaders conceived the plan of using this new trading corporation for the purpose of founding in the 

New World "a bulwark against the kingdom of Anti-Christ." To bring this about they decided that they themselves should go to America. For this purpose they signed the Cambridge Agreement, by which the stock-

holders who did not wish to go to America transferred their rights to the members of the company who wished to go. This was important. The company itself went to America, while the Virginia Company remained in London and sent settlers to the New World. 

The Massachusetts Government. The Massachusetts Company differed from the Plymouth group in that its members belonged to a somewhat wealthier class of English society. While the Pilgrims were made up largely of farmers, laborers, and artisans, in the group that came to Massachusetts Bay there were few of that class, while some possessed large landed estates. 

There were also some wealthy merchants and several of the professional classes; some were scholars from the English universities; however, the greater number came from the middle class of England. In the company were included such outstanding men as Sir Richard Saltonstall, John Endicott, and John Winthrop. The charter which they received was very much like the Virginia charter, but it was carried by the company to America, while the Virginia charter remained in England. Self-government, therefore, was set up in the New World. The stockholders of the 

Massachusetts Company were called "freemen of the company." They were to meet in a General Court to conduct the affairs of the company, and were to elect officers, consisting of a governor, deputy governor, and eighteen assistants.

The settlers came to the Massachusetts Bay Colony in order to find a place to worship free from interference, and because they felt that opportunities for economic advancement were better in America than in the Old World. Besides these reasons, it should be remembered that the contest between Parliament and the King led many to become dissatisfied with the political conditions, and they came to America for that reason. They came in large numbers. During the year 1630 seventeen vessels came to 

America, carrying about 2,000 people to Massachusetts Bay, where Boston was the town first settled. This migration was the beginning of what is referred to as "the Great Migration," which in the course of ten years brought no less than 16,000 people to Massachusetts. While these people set up a government of their own, they were not interested in setting up a democracy. In fact, Winthrop, who became the governor of the colony, pointed out that the best part of the population "is always the least, and of that least part the wiser is always the lesser." It was also pointed out that "among nations it [democracy] has always been accounted the meanest and worst form of government." This group, therefore, was by no means democratic. Of the 2,000 who came over in 1630 only the freemen of the company, that is, the signers of the Cambridge Agreement, of whom

there were only twelve, controlled the government. This was the entire body of stockholders, and all the privileges that the charter granted were in their hands. They composed the General Court, and had elected themselves officers in the government. With the exception of the governor, they were all assistants. They therefore had the right to govern the whole colony, and they exercised that privilege. Before long, there were those among the unprivileged 2,000 who began to object to this form of government. Because of the objections on the part of many who were not allowed the privilege of partaking in the government, the General Court decided to admit such of them as were members of the church, into the body politic, and give them the privilege of voting for assistants. However, they did not grant them legislative power- that is, power to make laws, nor the right to vote for governor. The government thus set up is sometimes referred to as a theocracy, a government in which only church members participated, and in which the clergy took the leading part. Governor Winthrop pointed out that those in authority intended to set up a government which was both civil and ecclesiastical. 

The New England Town. As the colony developed, the area was extended. The land, however, was not granted to individuals, but to groups, who incorporated new towns. The New England town thus developed, which in many respects corresponds to a township rather than to a village, was a unit for local government. The town soon gained the right to send representatives to the General Court. The town meeting became a means for giving the people an opportunity to take part in the government. 

At this meeting the people drew up laws relating to their local affairs, and elected officers to enforce them. Here they also chose their representatives, called deputies, to sit in the General Court. After the land had been granted to the town, much of it was laid out into woodland, pasture, and meadows, all of which were held in common, but close by were tracts given to heads of families to cultivate for their own benefit. Each family therefore had its own small tract as well as part in the common land. 

Connecticut Settled. As the population increased, some of the settlers moved out to other lands. A group of settlers, under the leadership of 

Thomas Hooker, in 1636 moved to the fertile Connecticut Valley. Hooker and his people had become dissatisfied with the Massachusetts type of government. Moreover, Hooker criticized the government for restricting participation to church membership, and felt that the government had set up too narrow limits for the right of voting. The people who followed 

Hooker therefore took their herds and household goods and settled at 

Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield.

New Haven Settled. While these settlements were being made in the 

Connecticut Valley, another was founded at New Haven, on Long Island Sound. Most of the settlers who went to New Haven had recently come from England, but they decided not to stay in Massachusetts. They hoped to establish an important trading center at New Haven, and also to build a Bible commonwealth similar to the one in Massachusetts. 

The Connecticut Valley settlements remained separate from New Haven for almost twenty-five years. In 1662, they obtained a charter from 

Charles II, by which New Haven and other towns were united as Connecticut.

The Settlement of Rhode Island. In Massachusetts religious controversies soon appeared. The central figure of one of these disputes was 

Roger Williams, while in another important one it was Mrs. Anne Hutchinson. Roger Williams attacked the narrow convictions of the Puritans. 

He urged the separation of church and state. He maintained that governmental authority should not be used to control a man's religious views; that one's duty toward God must be left to the individual conscience. He further incurred disfavor in Massachusetts because he maintained that the English government had no right to take the Indian lands and give them to the Massachusetts people. If that contention were granted, the very foundations on which Massachusetts was built would be destroyed, for the English grants did not consider the Indians' claim to the land. As a result of Roger Williams's views, the General Court ordered his expulsion from the colony, and in 1636 he left Massachusetts for Narragansett Bay, where he began a new settlement. A little later, Mrs. Hutchinson also was banished, and she and her followers established a settlement at Portsmouth. The religious ideas held by the Massachusetts leaders were not what we should today call liberal. We must remember, however, that these people had left their home country in order to set up a government in which they could work out their own ideas and their own religious views. They therefore felt that they should not be disturbed by those who disagreed with them. They were severe in their attitude toward 

Roger Williams and Anne Hutchinson, and later even more severe in their attitude toward the Quakers who came into their midst. We must also remember that the seventeenth century was not noted for liberalism in matters of religion. 

All of these New England colonies had the problem of defending themselves against their enemies. Among these enemies were the Indians, as well as the Dutch, who had by this time made settlements in America. In an attempt to solve these problems, four colonies in 1643 formed the

union called the New England Confederation. This confederation consisted of Massachusetts, Plymouth, Connecticut, and New Haven.

The Settlement of New Hampshire. As early as 1623, a settlement was made in New Hampshire. The region which now comprises Maine, New Hampshire, and Vermont was granted by the Council for New England to Sir Ferdinando Gorges and Captain John Mason and their associates. In 1629, Mason and Gorges divided their territory. Mason took the part to the south and west, which later became New Hampshire, while Gorges took the part to the east and north, which became Maine. Some of the early settlements were unsuccessful, but in time, settlers from Massachusetts, who became dissatisfied with religious conditions, moved into these regions. Later, most of these colonies were taken over by Massachusetts; but in 1679 the king made New Hampshire a separate royal province.

THE MIDDLE COLONIES New York Settled by the Dutch. The Dutch West India Company received from the Netherlands (often called Holland), in 1621, a charter which gave it the right to trade in America. The Dutch India Company, however, had been organized as early as 1602. It became actively interested in America in 1609, when it sent an Englishman, Henry Hudson, to America to explore the continent. He sailed up the Hudson River and claimed that region for the Dutch. These people early engaged in the fur trade and erected Fort Nassau, near the site of Albany, in 1614. They also established a trading station on Manhattan Island, at the mouth of the Hudson River. In 1623-1624 they started a settlement by bringing over about thirty families who were landed on Manhattan Island. Some of them went on to Albany, and some to the Connecticut River Valley, where they came in contact with the English who had settled there. 

1626 the Dutch, under their governor, Peter Minuit, made a settlement on Manhattan Island and named it New Amsterdam, which became the capital of the Dutch colony in America, known as New Netherland. In

As the fur trade developed, the Dutch West India Company became interested in permanent settlement, and gave every stockholder who would bring fifty families at his own expense, a portion of the land sixteen miles along one side of the river, or eight miles on both sides, and extending back an indefinite distance. These stockholders were known as patroons. They became the rulers as well as the owners of their estates. The patroon system, which was established in America by the Dutch, was not a success. 

Land was plentiful, and the settlers soon discovered that they could ob-

tain land of their own, and therefore refused to remain bound by an old medieval system.

The Settlement of Delaware. The Dutch West India Company also attempted the settlement of Delaware. In 1633, about thirty emigrants were brought over and settled, but the Indians destroyed the settlement before the end of the second year. A successful attempt to establish a colony in Delaware was made by the Swedes. In 1638, about fifty emigrants were brought over by a Swedish trading company, and a number of small settlements were made. The colony, however, did not prosper. 

The first attempt was made at Wilmington. It was called Fort Christiana, in honor of the Swedish queen. The Dutch protested against the settlement by the Swedes, but because Sweden, together with England and the Netherlands, were allies in the Thirty Years' War in Europe, no serious objections were raised. However, after the war was over, the Dutch were ready to assert their authority over the Swedish settlement in Delaware, called New Sweden, and in 1655 it became a part of New Netherland. 

Conquest of New Netherland. In 1647 Peter Stuyvesant became governor of New Netherland. He was unpopular because he was narrowminded and stubborn, and therefore did not have the support of the people. 

Many of his subjects became dissatisfied when they suffered religious persecution and were denied self-government, and they were therefore willing to see a different government established. The English claimed the territory held by the Dutch, because of the exploration of John Cabot. 

When war between England and the Netherlands broke out in 1652, the English in America were ready to attack New Netherland, but orders from England prohibited this because peace was soon restored in Europe. In 

1664, four years after Charles II came to the throne, he granted the New Netherland territory to his brother James, the Duke of York, who proceeded to conquer it. An expedition was sent out under Colonel Richard 

Nicholls, and the Dutch in America, being out of sympathy with their governor, surrendered; most of New Netherland became New York, and 

New Amsterdam also was renamed New York.

The Proprietary Middle Colonies. We have learned that New York and Delaware were settled by trading companies; they were therefore, at first, referred to as corporate colonies. New Jersey and Pennsylvania, on the other hand, were settled mainly by proprietors as individuals who received grants of land. New York and Delaware also, after the English conquest of New Netherland, became proprietary colonies.

A liberal policy was pursued by the proprietors, who granted religious freedom and gave the people a voice in the making of the laws. This encouraged further settlement from England and also from New England.

The Charter for Pennsylvania. The Quakers, who called themselves 

Friends, were a sect of Protestants that arose in England about the middle of the seventeenth century. This sect was founded by George 

Fox. Their doctrines maintained that every Christian should be taught by the Holy Spirit within him, and that it was therefore unnecessary to have trained preachers or paid ministers. In their meetings for worshiping God, the Quakers would sit together in quiet until some one was moved by the spirit within him. They felt no need for ceremony in their religion, and considered the ordinances of baptism and the Lord's Supper unnecessary. They held that war is wicked, and refused to serve as soldiers. This religious group was persecuted in England, as well as in some of the colonies. The Puritans in New England did not wish to have any of the Quakers settle in their midst, as such newcomers might disturb their own religion. 

William Penn, the son of Admiral Sir William Penn, while a student in college became interested in the Quakers. His father very seriously objected to their type of worship and did what he could to persuade his son. to give up this new form of religion. He sent him to Paris, hoping that by coming in contact with the life of that city, William might forget the Quaker religion. William Penn, however, retained his religious views, and

became intensely interested in other members of the church who were being persecuted for their religious ideas, and hoped to find a place where they all could worship without interference. 

Admiral Penn was a close friend of King Charles II and the Stuart family. The king had become personally indebted to Admiral Penn for an amount of about $80,000. On the death of Admiral Penn, William, who was then thirty-six years of age, fell heir to this claim against the crown. 

The king preferred to pay the obligation with a large grant of land in the New World. Such an arrangement was acceptable to William Penn, who was looking for a place to set up a government where he might try out his new ideas, and relieve his friends who were persecuted for their religious beliefs. Therefore, in March, 1681, Charles II gave Penn a charter by which he might rule over a large tract of land located west of the Delaware River. The royal charter which Penn received, however, was not as liberal as some charters which had been granted to other proprietors. It provided that the laws of the new province must be in harmony with those of England, and that they might be passed only with the consent of the majority of the freemen, or their representatives. The laws made in the colony were to be sent to England within five years for examination by the Privy Council, and all measures proposed could be vetoed by the home government.

Boundary Disputes. In order to be sure of free access from the sea to Pennsylvania, Penn bought Delaware (in 1682) from the Duke of York, but the boundary between it and Maryland was not settled till many years later. Penn's grant of Pennsylvania gave him lands, some of which had already been given to New York and to Maryland. This condition soon caused boundary disputes. The northern boundary was adjusted, however, by an agreement with New York, which established the parallel of 42° north latitude as the dividing line. But the conflict with Maryland was not so easily settled. The grant of Maryland to Lord Baltimore had been made earlier than Penn's, and the controversy between these two colonies continued until 1760, when an agreement was finally reached. A few years later two English surveyors, Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon, marked out the boundary thus agreed on. This line, the famous 

Mason and Dixon Line, the southern boundary of Pennsylvania, came to be considered the dividing line between the North and the South. 

Prosperity in Pennsylvania. The first colonists sent over by Penn came in 1681. During that year about a thousand persons settled in Pennsylvania. However, Penn himself did not arrive until the next year, when he brought over a hundred additional settlers. Philadelphia, the capital

of the province, was laid out by Penn's commissioners in 1682. This town was located at the junction of the Schuylkill and Delaware rivers, and was accessible to ocean vessels. The settlement grew rapidly as additional 

Quakers arrived, and prosperity followed because of the industry and thrift of the settlers. The climate was favorable, and the soil was fertile. There were many other natural advantages which contributed to the prosperity of the new colony. It was rich in natural resources, and Pennsylvania did not suffer many of the hardships which some of the other colonies were forced to endure.

One of the important reasons why Pennsylvania prospered steadily was her friendly relations with the Indians. From the very beginning, Penn maintained that the natives should be treated fairly. He entered into agreements with them by which he purchased their land at prices satisfactory to the Indians. This fairness was largely responsible for the friendly relations which existed between the early settlers in Pennsylvania and the Indians. However, this policy of fair dealing with the Indians was not continued by the sons of Penn. The result was that later the Indians turned against the settlers in Pennsylvania, and during the French and Indian War we find them on the side of the French, vigorously fighting the English.

THE SOUTHERN PROPRIETARY COLONIES 

Maryland. Maryland (chartered, 1632) was the first of the proprietary colonies. King Charles I granted to George Calvert, Lord Baltimore, the area from the Potomac River to the parallel of 40° north latitude. However, because George Calvert died before the grant was completed, the charter was issued to his son, Cecil Calvert, the second Lord Baltimore. 

This large area was given to Lord Baltimore and his heirs to rule as they should see fit. However, restrictions similar to those placed on Penn's grant provided that the laws of Maryland must be in harmony with those of England, and that the proprietor, in the making of laws, must have the "advice, assent, and approbation of the freemen . . . or their delegates or deputies." The settlement was made under the direction of the second Lord 

Baltimore, at a time when the Catholics in England were not permitted to worship as they pleased. They were fined for failing to attend services of the Church of England; the privilege of voting was denied them; and their priests were not allowed to remain in England. Lord Baltimore, a 

Catholic, was anxious to find a place where his people could worship without persecution. The charter which the king granted to Lord Baltimore was very liberal. Lord Baltimore was made absolute owner, but was to

Scale of Miles 0 25 50 75 100 acknowledge his allegiance to the king. His lands were to be free from taxation. Baltimore adopted a very liberal policy toward the settlers. 

From the very beginning he welcomed Christians of all kinds and granted them religious liberty as well as political equality. 

In 1634 a settlement was made at St. Marys. Because of the liberal religious policy, many Protestants settled in Maryland. In fact, within ten years after the settlement was made, the Protestants far outnumbered 34° 40

the Catholics. In 1649 the General Assembly passed an Act Concerning 

Religion (by some historians called the Toleration Act). Recent research shows that this law, while it was an advance over the generally accepted ideas of religious freedom of that day, was not as liberal as the actual practices of the founders and the first colonists. It provided that no person within the province who professed to believe in Jesus Christ should be troubled or molested for his religion so long as he was not unfaithful to the lord proprietor or the civil government. Maryland increased in population, though there were many difficulties to overcome. Finally, as a result of the English revolution of 1688, Lord Baltimore lost control of the colony, but it was restored to his family in 1715 and remained as the property of the Calvert family until the outbreak of the American Revolution. 

The dispute with Pennsylvania was settled as told on page 64 and as shown on the map, page 66. 

North Carolina. For the early attempts at settlement in North Carolina see page 40. Permanent settlement of North Carolina began in 1653 when settlers from Virginia entered the region north of the Roanoke River and began what is known as the Albemarle settlement. 

In 1663, King Charles II gave the territory known as the Carolinas to eight of his courtiers who had aided in his restoration. This area, however, far exceeded the present Carolinas. It extended from Virginia to the parallel of 31°; that is, to Florida. Westward it extended to the 

South Sea; that is, the Pacific Ocean. In this region were founded both 

North Carolina and South Carolina.

One of the proprietors, Lord Shaftesbury, together with the English philosopher John Locke, drew an elaborate plan of government for the Carolinas, known as the Grand Model, or the Fundamental Constitution. 

This plan provided for a division of classes, such as nobles, great land owners, and selectmen, as the laborers were to be called. The Grand 

Model, however, was a failure, because in America, where so much land was available, the people could not be placed in distinct classes and forced to remain there.

South Carolina. The first permanent settlement in South Carolina was made by the English in 1670. In that year William Sayle brought a number of Puritans from the Bermudas. This settlement on the Ashley 

River, made in 1670, was named Charles Town, but ten years later it was moved to the peninsula between the Cooper and Ashley rivers, and became in time the city of Charleston. Later in the seventeenth century many French Huguenots came to America and settled in South Carolina. 

For several years there was one governor for both North Carolina and

South Carolina. The proprietors, in the beginning, had not planned for two distinct colonies. However, as the colonies developed and increased in population, it became evident that the two settlements were too far apart for a single government. There was much friction between the colonists and the proprietors, and finally, in 1729, the region was divided into the two royal provinces of North Carolina and South Carolina. 

The Settlement of Georgia. Georgia, the last of the original thirteen colonies, was first settled in 1733. This was seventy years after the grant of the Carolinas. Virginia, the first colony to be settled, was already 126 old when the last of the thirteen was founded, and America had been years discovered by Columbus 241 years earlier.

We have learned that some of the settlers came to America because they were dissatisfied with political conditions in the Old World; others came in search of a place to worship their God according to the dictates of their own consciences; while still others hoped to improve their social and economic conditions. Georgia was founded by James Edward Oglethorpe, in an attempt to help worthy men who had been imprisoned for debt. 

Oglethorpe was a man of great influence. He had served with distinction in the British army, and as a member of Parliament had become interested in the deplorable conditions in English prisons. At this time the laws were exceedingly harsh. People were put in prison because they owed small amounts. Some who owed less than one dollar were placed behind prison bars. Many honest men who had met misfortune through no fault of their own might be obliged to spend the remainder of their days in jail. Oglethorpe saw the injustice of this condition and worked to give these unfortunate men an opportunity to escape from it. He conceived a plan of settling with the creditors of these men and then finding for them a home in the New World, where they might have an opportunity for a fresh start.

Oglethorpe had been a member of the House of Commons for ten years, and had been interested in the development of the English colonies in America. He knew that to the south of the English colonists the Spaniards had settled in Florida. He knew that many people realized the importance of the English having a buffer colony on the Spanish border. Oglethorpe was an able military leader, patriotic and in favor of an aggressive policy toward Spain. He was therefore a desirable leader for a colony in that section of the country. He wished also to establish a place of refuge for persecuted Protestants from Europe. This, together with his interest in the opposition to the Spaniards and relief for the unfortunate debtors, led him to press upon King George II the desirability of establishing a colony

in the New World. In 1732 Oglethorpe and a group of other philanthropists received a charter from King George. 

The territory granted lay between the Altamaha and the Savannah rivers. It was named Georgia in honor of the king. The charter provided that the proprietors should act as trustees for the colony. They should have control of the colony for twenty-one years, after which period it was to revert to the crown. In 1732, Oglethorpe, together with 120 men, women, and children, started for the New World, and early in 1733 made a settlement, named Savannah, at the mouth of the Savannah River. A few years later a settlement was made at Augusta, farther up the river. In 1734 a number of 

Germans, known as Salzburgers, came to Georgia and made a settlement at Ebenezer, about twenty-five miles above the mouth of the Savannah River.

These were Protestants who had been driven out of the principality of Salzburg because of bitter persecution by their Catholic ruler. 

Statue of Oglethorpe in Savannah  

The First Advance of the Frontier. While the colonists were learning to adjust themselves to their new life in America, they remained in groups along the great bays and navigable rivers. Because of the necessity for trade with Europe, very few settlers by 1660 were more than ten or twelve miles from deep water. But the settlements became crowded and the new immigrants were not content to take the less desirable lands. The intolerance of the men in authority became less bearable to the younger generation, who desired greater freedom. There was also the call of the frontier especially of cheap land and opportunity-which lured later generations of Americans across the entire continent. Many settlers began to go westward and to search for new and more fertile lands. Before the close of the seventeenth century, both sons of the original settlers and newcomers were, despite the dangers and hardships of the frontier, turning to it as a means of solving their social, economic, and religious problems. The colonies assisted the movement by granting lands for settlement.

In New England the expansion of population was regulated by the colonial governments. One of the first inland settlements in New England was that of Concord. The General Court of Massachusetts authorized the settlement in September, 1635, and several families moved to the frontier site that autumn. Springfield was founded in 1636. Rhode Island and 

Connecticut, settled the same year, are typical of the normal westward drift of the Americans. Although the purpose of these two settlements was ostensibly to obtain greater religious freedom, the colonists also needed more pasturage for their cattle. By the close of the seventeenth century, there was an officially drawn frontier line for New England and the inhabitants were forbidden to desert the frontier towns on penalty of im prisonment or loss of their lands. After 1715, when the forced concentration in Massachusetts had ceased, expansion began to the west and north because of the increase of population and the rise in the price of old lands. 

In New York hostility of the Indian tribes, especially that of the Iroquois, prevented westward expansion. In 1698 more than two thirds of the inhabitants were still on Long Island and near the mouth of the Hudson. However, Albany and Schenectady were established as outposts. 

In the eighteenth century, German immigrants moved into the Mohawk Valley and made the farthest advance in that province before the Revolution. German settlers were also among the leaders in this westward movement in Pennsylvania.

In the South, movement westward began almost as soon as settlement was made, since the Tidewater region afforded ample room for expansion. 

In August, 1650, Abraham Wood led an exploring expedition from Fort Henry at the falls of the Appomattox River southward as far as the falls of the Roanoke. The result of this expedition into the interior was put into a small pamphlet, The Discovery of New Brittaine, by Edward Bland, a member of the party. John Lederer, a German physician, led three expeditions, the first in 1669 and the other two the following year, across the Piedmont, and ascended the Blue Ridge. Lederer is the first white man whose ascent of the Blue Ridge is recorded. In 1671 a small party, among whom were Captain Thomas Batts, Thomas Wood, and Robert Fallan, set out for the country beyond the Blue Ridge and continued until they penetrated the watershed of the Ohio. Theirs was the first recorded journey of Englishmen into that section. In 1716 Governor 

Spotswood of Virginia led his famous company of men over the Blue Ridge into the valley of the Shenandoah. Such instances mark the beginning of the extension of the frontier which continually advanced westward until our country extended from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean.

King John signing the Magna Charta (p. 76), a great step in the development of the ideas and institutions which the English colonists brought with them to America 74

CHAPTER IV Colonial Contributions to Democracy 

Origin of Our Institutions. With the founding of Georgia, the last of the original thirteen colonies was settled. From 1607, when the first permanent English settlement was made at Jamestown, until the founding of Georgia, 126 years later, several important ideas were brought into our American life. During the remainder of the colonial period these colonies developed and afforded a place for still other ideas and institutions to originate, develop, and mature. 

The original thirteen colonies were a part of the British Empire, and many English ways of living were brought to America. While the English were making their settlements, the French, Dutch, Spanish, and Swedes were also making settlements, and some of their customs were brought to the parts in which they settled. 

It is important for us to study the history of the American colonies, for in doing so we find the beginning of many of our American institutions and ideals which we have come to value highly. Several hundred years ago representative government began in Virginia in a small way, but the development of self-government was one of the most important movements in modern history. Another important ideal which developed in this early period was that of freedom of religion. The idea of the separation of state and church as promoted by Cecil Calvert, Roger Williams, and William Penn, has become one of our fundamental American principles. 

The Origins of Self-Government. The early English settlers who came to America brought with them the ideas and institutions which they had developed at home, and here on American soil these ideas found opportunity for further growth. The first Virginia charter (page 48), granted by the king of England, provided that all persons who were to inhabit the several colonies, and their children who should be born within the limits of these colonies, should "have and enjoy all Liberties, Franchises, and Immunities, within any of our other Dominions, to all Intents and Purposes, as if they 75

had been abiding and born within this our Realm of England or any other of our said Dominions." From this we see that the Americans began with the heritage which the English had developed before they settled America. 

Let us, therefore, see what progress the English had already made toward governing themselves. Let us see what steps they had taken in the development of freedom before America was settled. 

Origin of the Grand Jury. In 1164 Henry II of England issued the 

Assize of Clarendon, the purpose of which was to introduce a reform in the punishment of crime. This assize provided for the establishment of a jury of indictment, or the grand jury of today. Its purpose was to take away the independence of the feudal court in criminal matters by providing that before people could be tried, they must be indicted by a grand jury. This custom continues in America to this day. Indeed, the Constitution of the 

United States provides that no one shall be tried in a Federal court, for a capital or otherwise infamous crime, without first being indicted by a grand jury.

Importance of Magna Charta. Another great step in the development of English liberty was the Magna Charta, which the barons at Runnymede forced King John to sign in 1215 (p. 74). This charter of English liberty guaranteed to each citizen the "writ of habeas corpus, * and the right of trial by his peers, and permitted taxation only by the consent of the council. It is an important document because it placed a limit on the powers of the king. This important document, sometimes referred to as the Great Charter of Liberty, contained many important provisions. One of the most interesting was Section 39, which provided that “no freeman shall be taken, or imprisoned, or dispossessed, or outlawed, or banished, or in any way destroyed, nor will we go upon him, nor send upon him, except by the legal judgment of his peers, or by the law of the land." Section 40 of the same document contained this important provision: "To no one will we sell,... deny, or delay right or justice." By this Magna Charta King 

John and later rulers of England promised important rights to feudal tenants or vassals. By it a baron was entitled to trial in a court by his peers.

The Model Parliament, 1295. The struggle for British liberty, however, was far from won. The barons continued their struggle with the king, and in 1265 Simon de Montfort called a national assembly (parliament), to which shires, cities, and boroughs as well as the nobility and the *A “writ of habeas corpus" is issued for the purpose of preventing unjust imprisonment without trial; by it a judge directs a person detaining another to produce the body of the son detained, for an inquiry to find out whether the person is held rightfully or wrongfully. per-

church were to send representatives. This was the beginning of representative government in England. In 1295 was held the meeting of the Model 

Parliament, which included as representatives, nobles, clergy, knights, and burgesses. 

Representative Government in America. These were some of the important ideas which the English brought with them to America. It is therefore not surprising that the English who settled in Virginia were interested in governing themselves. In 1619 they secured from the company in London the right to set up representative government; and when the 

House of Burgesses assembled in the little church in 1619, the English idea of self-government was being planted in America. The following year the Pilgrims drew up the Mayflower Compact, by which they created a "civil body politic" on democratic lines. That was the beginning of selfgovernment in New England. Later the town meeting developed. It was the most democratic institution which had been established anywhere at that time.

The Petition of Right. The struggle for self-government was not yet won. A good beginning had been made when the Virginia House of Burgesses met and when the Pilgrims drew up the Mayflower Compact, but in England political conditions seemed discouraging, especially to the Puritans. The members of the House of Commons quarreled with King 

Charles, and in 1628 forced him to accept the Petition of Right, by which he was prohibited from levying various forms of taxation without the consent of Parliament, and also was prohibited from arbitrarily imprisoning accused persons without due process of law. During this struggle between the King and Parliament many people left England and came to America. 

The Great Migration from 1630 to 1640 (page 57) brought thousands to America who were opposed to the arbitrary rule of the king. In America the settlers insisted on the same rights which an unwilling king had been forced to grant. In fact, in America the colonists were free to develop further their ideas of self-government. Many of those who came over were anxious to continue their opposition to the king and were therefore important factors in developing these ideas on American soil. 

The Fundamental Orders of Connecticut, 1639. Some of the Massachusetts settlers moved into the Connecticut River Valley and established Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield, under the leadership of Thomas Hooker, who maintained that the power of officials is subject to strict limitations because "the foundation of authority is laid firstly in the free consent of the people." In accordance with this idea, the representatives from these towns met at Hartford in 1639 and formed a constitution which

was called the Fundamental Orders. Here we have a government created by the people. It was an important step in the development of constitutional government. It was a further development of the English and the 

American idea of liberty. The government established under the Fundamental Orders was modeled after the Massachusetts government, with a governor, deputy governor, and assistants, all of whom were chosen annually by the freemen.

The Body of Liberties. The magistrates of Massachusetts in administering justice were guided by the English common law and also by the Bible. Yet some were not clear on the principles of common law, and demanded a codification of the laws so that everyone might know what the laws were. In response to this demand, a code of laws known as the Body of Liberties was drawn up in 1641. The government thus set up is sometimes referred to as a "Bible Commonwealth."

New England Confederation. Steps in the development of representative government were carried still further in 1643, when the colonies of Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut, and New Haven formed the New England Confederation, which was a federal union of these colonies for the purpose of protecting their common interests. Thus very early in the colonial period we see an attempt on the part of the colonists to unite, and here we have the germ of what later became the union of the states under our Constitution. Bicameral Government. One of the outstanding characteristics of our government today is that in the national government we have two houses of Congress—the House of Representatives and the Senate. Likewise, in all the forty-eight states, excepting Nebraska since 1935, there are two houses in the legislature. For the beginning of this system we must look to the early colonies. The General Court in Massachusetts was made up of the deputies and the assistants, who met as one body. It was called upon to decide a dispute which had arisen between a Mrs. Sherman, who claimed that her pig had been stolen, and a Mr. Keayne, who was wealthy shopkeeper in Boston. In rendering the decision, the majority of the deputies—that is, those who came later to be the lower house, and a few of the assistants, who later came to be the upper house, voted in favor of the poor woman, while the majority of the assistants voted for Mr. 

Keayne. Since in this case the two groups voted as a body, the deputies were able to outvote the assistants, and thus render a decision in favor of the woman. The assistants saw that if the two groups-that is, the deputies and the assistants-sat as separate houses, their influence would be greater because they then could not be outvoted by the deputies. After

considerable discussion it was finally decided that the General Court should thereafter consist of two chambers; and that while each had the right to introduce bills, laws could be enacted only if passed by a majority of both houses. So in 1644 we have the beginning of bicameral government in 

Massachusetts. Bicameral government later was adopted in the Virginia 

Assembly, and in the assemblies of the other colonies. It should be remembered, too, that the colonies had a precedent for bicameral govern ment, since the Parliament in England was made up of two houses. 

Relations Between America and England in the Struggle for Self- 

Government. England's supervision over the colonies was very close at times. However, at other times the American colonies were practically neglected by the English government and were permitted to attend to their own affairs. A period of neglect came with the struggle between 

Parliament and the King, known as the Puritan Revolution, which finally led to civil war in England, in which Charles I was deposed and finally beheaded and Oliver Cromwell came to rule. During this period the colonies were permitted to develop after their own fashion. The English people were too much absorbed in a struggle at home to pay much attention to developments on this side of the Atlantic. During the first half of the seventeenth century, therefore, the colonies developed without much interference from England. However, after the end of Cromwell's rule, when Charles II became King of England in 1660, a new colonial policy began. In accordance with this new policy, the crown became anxious to exercise closer supervision over the colonies. The charters granted after this time were not so liberal as they had been in the earlier period, but placed more restrictions on the colonies. The king was definitely interested in securing a more effective control over the colonies. 

The Struggle between the Governors and the Colonists. In order to carry out this policy more effectively, the home government became interested in converting all the colonies into royal provinces. Some of the colonies had been established by trading companies and had become selfgoverning. Some were founded and ruled by proprietors. These colonies were therefore not directly controlled by the home government; but after 

England developed her policy of greater imperial control during the years following 1660, she attempted to bring more and more colonies under the direct control of the royal government. It should be remembered that in the charter colonies the people elected their own governors; in the proprietary colonies, the proprietors appointed them; while in the royal colonies, the king appointed these officials. After 1660, when the king began to supervise his empire more closely, he learned that he could do it more

effectively through the governors whom he himself appointed. The royal governors would see to it that the trade laws were enforced, and that the laws passed by the colonial assemblies were in harmony with the idea of the mercantile system devised to benefit the empire rather than the colonies. The colonists, however, were interested in maintaining their own self-government, and engaged in many bitter quarrels with the colonial governors. One important question was whether a governor's salary should be paid by the colonists themselves, or whether the colonists should submit to taxation by the home government, which in turn would pay the governor. The colonists maintained that they themselves should pay the salaries of the governors, because they felt that they could then exercise more control and thereby force the governors to submit to the will of the people.

Opposition to the Government; Bacon's Rebellion. Following the Restoration which brought Charles II to power in 1660, much opposition to the government of the king developed. Many people felt that the king was treating the colonies as private estates, and that numerous privileges were being taken from the colonists. They objected to the Navigation Acts of 

1651 and 1660, which provided that only English- or American-owned ships should carry American products to the English dominions. They protested against the restrictions on suffrage, which gave only freeholders the right to vote. The colonists of Virginia furthermore became dissatisfied with the policies of Governor Berkeley. They felt that he left the people on the frontier without protection against the Indians because he was profiting by his private interest in the Indian fur trade. This opposition finally in 1676 led to an uprising headed by Nathaniel Bacon, who, with an armed force, marched on Jamestown, the capital, and compelled the governor to authorize him to lead a force against the Indians. Bacon went so far as to attack the governor's forces, and Berkeley was defeated and driven from the town. Very soon after this clash, however, Bacon became sick and died. Without their leader, his forces were defeated by 

Governor Berkeley's troops, and twenty-three were hanged and a number of others imprisoned. However, the rebellion was not without its contribution to democracy. It was an uprising against the autocratic 

Governor Berkeley, who was later recalled. It was also an expression of dissatisfaction on the part of the frontiersmen, who wanted more power in government through the extension of suffrage. The small farmers of the west objected to the rule of the planter aristocracy in the east. 

Sir Edmund Andros the Royal Governor of New England. Following the restoration of Charles II in 1660 friction developed between the gov-

Bacon's interview with Governor Berkeley at Jamestown. The Governor, at the left, at first angrily refused Bacon's request, but was soon forced to grant it (page 80). ernment in Massachusetts and the English government. The colonial governors had been rather lenient in their enforcement of the Navigation Acts. The result was that special collectors were appointed by the 

English government. This often resulted in violence between the collectors and the colonists. Special commissioners were sent to Massachusetts in 

1664 to investigate conditions. It had been reported that the power of the magistrates of Massachusetts was increasing and that they were not governing the colony according to the ideas of the English king. The commissioners' report on the colonists was unfavorable, and finally in 1684 the charter of Massachusetts was annulled. It was evident that the charters of the self-governing colonies and of the proprietary colonies stood in the way of imperial organization. Up to 1679, Virginia was the only royal colony, but after that there was a steady trend toward more royal colonies. In 1686 King James II united New York,

New Jersey, and Delaware, together with Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Rhode Island, under one government, known as the Dominion of New England, over which he appointed Sir Edmund Andros governor-general.

Andros appeared in Boston to take charge of his new work. New York and 

New Jersey were governed by deputy governors. Thus the whole region from Delaware Bay to Canada was under the rule of Andros. 

The new governor was harsh, narrow, and determined to carry out the instructions which he had received from the king. However, the more zealous he was in the performance of his duties, the more resistance he met from the colonists. The more opposition Andros encountered, the more severe became his rule. He required the landowners to obtain new deeds, and for this service fees were charged. He also required annual quitrents in order to impress upon the colonists that they had received their land from the king. He abolished the local assemblies. The towns were required to collect taxes, and when the people objected, town meetings were prohibited except for the purpose of electing officers. He denied the colonists fair trials, established a strict censorship of the press, and even introduced the services of the Anglican Church in Boston. Some of the Puritans of 

Boston especially resented the idea of having Anglican worship in their 

Puritan churches.

The Glorious Revolution. By the "Glorious Revolution" of 1688, 

James II was driven from the throne, and his daughter Mary and her husband, William of Orange, became joint rulers, and were known as William and Mary. When this change became known in America, the colonists at once seized Andros and put him in prison. With Andros in prison, the people again assumed control of the government and awaited the pleasure of the new king. Out of the Glorious Revolution in England came the famous Bill of Rights, which in 1689 brought to an end the unlimited powers of the king. William and Mary accepted the Bill of Rights, which provided for the supremacy of Parliament over the king, and gave impetus to the idea that government was founded on the consent of the governed. 

This was a great step in the development of British and American freedom. It brought an end to personal government and substituted for it a government based on law. In 1691 Massachusetts received a new charter by which she became a royal province, and to her territory were added all of Maine and the colony of Plymouth. Connecticut and Rhode 

Island now brought their charters out of hiding and went back to their early form of government. In the main, the revolution of 1688 and the 

Bill of Rights marked the end of tyrannical government in the colonies and restored political liberty to the people. 

Development of Religious Liberty. While the colonists were thus with great difficulty making steady progress in the direction of their political liberty, forces were also at work making for religious liberty. The first

Or settlers in New England, the Pilgrims, were rather generous in their toleration of other religions. However, the Puritan migration from England known as the Great Migration (1630-1640), brought in a group that was less liberal and less tolerant. This group, dissatisfied with religious and political conditions at home, left England in order to establish a theocracy—that is, a government based on church membership. This government of Massachusetts proved very narrow and intolerant. 

These people left home to establish a government in which their religious beliefs would be the only ones tolerated. They expelled those who did not conform, and finally in 1660 hanged several Quakers because they insisted on worshiping according to the "inner light," or according to "divine revelation."

This doctrine was contrary to that of the Puritan religion, which was not liberal enough to permit freedom of worship.

The government was so narrow, and the relation between church and state was so close, that Roger Williams rebelled against it, and insisted on the separation of church and state. He maintained that the government of Massachusetts should not interfere with religion-that government applied only to civil things. With this in mind, in 1636 he left Massachusetts and established a settlement in Rhode Island, in which church and state were separated, and in which complete religious freedom prevailed. 

Another colony in which religious toleration prevailed was Maryland. It was established, as we have seen, as a colony chiefly for Catholics; but 

Lord Baltimore was so liberal that both Catholics and Protestants settled there, and in the Act Concerning Religion (p. 67), the rights of all believers in Jesus, both Catholics and Protestants, were recognized. There was a further movement in the direction of religious freedom in the establishment of Penn's Holy Experiment in Pennsylvania. Yet progress toward enlightenment, tolerance, and religious freedom was slow, and occasionally there was a reaction. In 1692, nineteen persons were hanged in Salem, Massachusetts, for witchcraft. Most of these unfortunate people were women who were suspected of being witches in alliance with Satan. They were not given a fair trial but were convicted on insufficient evidence given by children and excited women. 

Freedom of the Press. In 1735 American liberty was advanced a step further by the famous Zenger case, in which a victory for freedom of the press was won. The governor of New York (William Crosby) had removed the chief justice of that colony because he objected to the governor's stand in a case in which the governor himself was personally interested. This brought sharp criticism of the governor in an article printed in the New- York Weekly Journal, which was published by John Peter Zenger. The governor then proceeded with the prosecution of Zenger for libel. The new

chief justice, being friendly to the governor, had a strong bias against Zenger. However, Zenger's supporters had an able lawyer in Andrew 

Hamilton, of Philadelphia. He made a strong appeal to the jury on behalf of the freedom of the press. Hamilton maintained that the jury had the right to decide whether the article in question was false, malicious, and, therefore, libelous, while the judge maintained that the jury merely had to decide whether or not Zenger had written the article. Hamilton, however, persuaded the jury that they must pass on all the facts in the case. The jury, following Hamilton's suggestion, acquitted Zenger, and thereby upheld the freedom of the press. Gouverneur Morris called this trial of 

Zenger "the morning star of the liberty which subsequently revolutionized America." This case was especially important because by this time newspapers were being printed in nearly all the colonies, and were becoming a valuable means for instructing the American colonists concerning their rights. It now became more difficult to suppress newspapers which attacked the colonial governors. In the struggle between Great Britain and 

America which soon followed it was of great importance that the freedom of the press had not been suppressed, for it would have been more difficult for the Americans to secure their freedom and ultimate independence without a free use of the press.

Further Efforts at Union. We have already learned about the New 

England Confederation of 1643. More than a hundred years later the 

Albany Plan of Union was proposed by Benjamin Franklin. This plan of union was put forth in the hope of uniting the colonies for the struggle which was impending between the British and the French in America. This plan, however, was not adopted, because the colonists felt that it involved the surrender of too much of their power. The proposed plan was also not entirely satisfactory to Great Britain. Franklin remarked that "the assemblies all thought that there was too much prerogative, and in England it was thought to have too much of the democratic." Time was not yet ripe for concerted action. The colonies, however, were again spurred to action for union because of the Stamp Act in 1765, when they felt that their liberties were being interfered with by this attempt on the part of Great Britain to tax them. Twenty-seven delegates from nine of the colonies met in New York in the same year to oppose the policy of Great Britain in the passage of the Stamp Act. The congress petitioned the king and Parliament and drew up a declaration of rights and privileges. 

They asserted in this declaration that no taxes should be imposed upon them without their consent. They held that no taxes could be consistently levied on them except by their respective colonial assemblies. The colonies

had over a long period of time acquired a consciousness of their freedom-freedom of Americans and freedom of Englishmen. We have seen how from the very early period-from the Magna Charta of 1215-they insisted on their rights as Englishmen. How they continued this argument, and how in 1765 and later they used it against the British government, by insisting that there should be no taxation without representation, will be shown in Unit Three.
