CHAPTER V 

Colonial Life and Culture 

The Colonial People; Immigration to America. Our ancestors in colonial America came from across the Atlantic, bringing with them their institutions, ideas, and ideals, which they planted on American soil, and which in this new environment were modified and adjusted to American conditions. The first of these immigrants to America, about 100 in number, came from England in 1607. From this small beginning our country grew into a great nation. Growth in population by natural increase and by immigration continued so that by 1790 the population of the United States had grown to nearly 4,000,000. 

During the first hundred years nearly all of those who came, except the negro slaves, were English, but by 1763 about 40 per cent of the population was composed of other groups, among which were the Germans, Irish, Scotch, "Scotch-Irish," French Huguenots, and Jews. In addition to these were the African negroes, who by 1776 numbered about 500,000. 

The immigration movement, which began with the settling of America, has continued throughout our history, and by 1935 had brought more than 37,000,000 people to our shores. Many nationalities and racial groups have contributed to our cultural heritage and have greatly influenced the development of our civilization. 

Family Life. The first English settlement in America, at Jamestown, was composed almost entirely of men, but those interested in the colonization of America soon realized the importance of women in establishing a permanent settlement. They knew that it was necessary to build homes in order to make the colony a success. In 1619, ninety young women were sent to Virginia to become the wives of the settlers. Many lonesome men gathered at the shore as the ship arrived, chose their wives, and after paying one hundred twenty pounds of tobacco, each, for the cost of transportation, happily took their brides to their new homes. 

The next year, when the Mayflower brought the Pilgrims to New Eng- 88

land, thirty-two of the settlers brought their wives, while others sent for their wives as soon as rude homes could be built and land could be cleared to furnish a means of supporting their families. In New England and in the South women were at a premium. Their work consisted not only of cooking the meals and making the clothes, but also of assisting in many other activities; and, like the men, they were often exposed to physical danger.

The rigors of frontier life took a heavy toll among the women, and it was not uncommon for some men to marry three or four times. Colonial widows were often remarried within a few weeks or months of the deaths of their husbands, and young girls rarely lacked numerous suitors. Although some freedom of choice was allowed young girls in the selection of their husbands, the important decision was often made by their parents. Courtship was carried on with difficulty, by the fireside, with all the family present, though in some localities the young couples made use of courting sticks-long reeds, through which they conversed in whispers. In some cases, in spite of the disapproval of Puritan ministers, young people courted as they strolled on the village green in the late afternoon. As population and wealth increased, the customs concerning courtship became less strict, and prospective husbands demanded dowries from their future fathers-in-law. In accordance with the rigid morality of the day, divorce was rare, and a divorced person was an object of pity or contempt.

The scarcity of laborers and money made large families desirable, and children were regarded as “an heritage of the Lord." It was not uncommon to find families in which there were twelve or fifteen children, although in the absence of skilled medical attention, and with the hardships of frontier life, the death rate was high. Strict obedience was exacted from the children, and corporal punishment was often inflicted; two precepts were generally held to be true: "Spare the rod and spoil the child," and "Children should be seen and not heard."

Clothing. The early colonists were poor in money and could not afford fancy clothes. Leather breeches and plain clothes of homespun were used in the early colonial period, but as wealth increased in the later period, silken hose, powdered wigs, and satin knee breeches were worn by the classes. The hardships of frontier life and the prevalent religious upper views both played their parts in making the clothing of the first colonists very simple. Gradually, the coarse homespun serges and linsey-woolsey gave place to imported cloth, and the families of the colonists dressed in the styles prevailing in England. Members of the poorest families usually

had one dress of the finer material, which was worn for attendance at church, funerals, and weddings. Such dresses were handed down from generation to generation, and recut and fashioned until the material was worn out. The extravagance of the wealthy consisted chiefly in the number of their changes of attire; and many families, reputedly wealthy, incurred heavy debts in England because of a love of costly dress.

Colonial Houses and Furni ture. Very often in picturing to ourselves the homes of colonial days we think of sideboards with gleaming glass and silver, beds with silk coverings, heavy mahogany furniture, and gilded mirrors.

Such furnishings were found in the homes of prosperous New 

England merchants and Southern planters, such as the Randolphs, the Carters, the Byrds, and the Lees, but the majority of the homes were simple, or even poor. In most homes the rough, home-made furniture was built for service rather than style. 

Courtesy of Essex Institute, Salem, Mass. 

Equipment of a colonial kitchen fireplace: andirons, crane, kettles, frying pans, etc.

Forks were rarely found on the tables before 1700; the fingers were used more freely than today. For this reason table napkins were greatly in demand, and the station of a wealthy family could often be determined by the number and kind of napkins owned. Kitchen utensils were scarce: wooden plates of the first colonists were gradually replaced by pewter, which was both cheap and unbreakable. Chinaware, glass, and silver were little used until the eighteenth century; and then they were found chiefly in the 

Styles of dress of

homes of the wealthy. The spinning wheel was a common article of furniture, as it was used in spinning the large amounts of thread necessary for the hand-woven cloth.

The homes of the early colonists were simple, one-room log structures, with huge fireplaces at one end, furnishing light, warmth, and heat for cooking. As prosperity increased, a room was built above or beside the original home, and the walls were whitened with a wash prepared from crushed shells. Few of these houses boasted of glass windows; instead, oiled paper let in the light. Heavy wooden shutters kept out wind and rain, and afforded protection at night. Gradually distinct types of architecture developed in New England and Virginia. In New England, where the livelihood of many was secured by manufacturing and from the sea, and where the climate was severe, the people lived in small settlements along narrow streets, and built compact houses with steep roofs sloping almost to the ground in the rear. The homes of prosperous merchants soon rivaled those of England. The monotony of sloping roofs was broken by gables; and carved staircases, paint, wallpaper, imported furniture, and brass knockers all proclaimed the prosperity of the owner. 

In the South, where agriculture was almost the only occupation, where nearly all the people lived on plantations, and where the climate was more moderate, the settlers lived farther apart and had less contact with their neighbors. In the absence of good roads, the planters built their homes near the rivers, so that they might have better access to markets. Those less successful were forced to live farther from the streams and rely on the use of their neighbors' wharves. The plantations often took on the appearance of a small village. Grouped around the great house, which was at first only a log structure, were the kitchen, smokehouse, springhouse, slave quarters, and shops for the making and repairing of implements. 

With prosperity, the log houses of the owners were replaced by wide, commodious, frame houses, often of two stories, with rooms opening into halls the English colonists

running the width of the building. During the summer, much of the social life of the plantation centered on the porches and balconies. 

Food and Drink. Except for a short time, in the early days, food was plentiful in colonial America. Even in Puritan New England, the tables groaned under the weight of steaming dishes, placed on the tables in great quantities. Today desserts follow the regular meal; in colonial days they preceded it, and it was not uncommon for several kinds of meat and several kinds of bread, pies, and puddings, as well as numerous vegetables, to be served at a single meal; and at dinner there were usually sweetmeats or nuts in addition. From the early colonial days, the streams and ocean furnished a never-failing supply of fish, oysters, and clams, while the forests yielded game in abundance. Many vegetables were cultivated from an early day. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, turnips, carrots, cucumbers, as well as herbs not eaten today, were found on the tables of the early Americans. 

Peaches, apples, cherries, and damsons were produced in abundance; and the thrifty housewives soon learned to preserve them in molasses or honey, or to dry them in the sun. Lack of refrigeration made it impossible to preserve fresh meats, but at "killing time," in the fall, the meat was salted down and later smoked. Only in the homes of the very poor were the necessities of life lacking in the winter. 

In the colonial period public conscience had not been aroused against the use of strong drink. The amount consumed is amazing to us today. 

Yet laws against drunkenness were rigidly enforced-—at least during the seventeenth century. Beer, apple and peach brandy, cherry fling, and rum were perhaps the commonest drinks sold at public taverns; but few homes lacked their cider presses. Some of the New England farmers put up from ten to twenty barrels of cider. In the homes of the wealthy, imported French wines and brandies were kept for important occasions, but cider and beer served all ordinary uses. The drinking of tea and coffee became popular in the eighteenth century. 

Medicine and Treatment of Disease. In colonial America health was not as carefully guarded as today. Superstition, ignorance of hygiene, lack of proper sanitation, together with incompetent medical assistance, were responsible for a high death rate. Disease and epidemics often took heavy toll, and the science of medicine was not sufficiently advanced to remove the causes or to perfect cures. Strange medicines were prescribed in addition to many home remedies. Various herbs, and earthworms, bugs, snakes, and toads, judiciously prepared with wines and spices, were remedies kept in the homes and given to the sick. Not only did doctors prescribe medicines, but a frequent treatment was bleeding or sweating-which in

some cases really cost a patient his last hold on life. The training of a doctor was not rigorous; there were no medical colleges and no government regulation. After accompanying another physician on his visits for a time, helping him prepare his medicines, and tending his office, the apprentice was ready to set out for himself-armed, perhaps, with a cookbook in which a section was devoted to preparing medicines. 

Punishments. At the time of the settlement of America, Europe showed little mercy in the punishment of criminals. In fact, many people were imprisoned because they refused to accept certain religious doctrines. 

Others were imprisoned for debt. A large number of offenses were punishable by death. In the colonies the criminal codes were not quite so severe, yet many cruel punishments were inflicted. Acts which today are settled within the family were then subject to public control. A scolding wife, if reported to a local official, was sentenced to be ducked in water, or to have a cleft stick placed upon her tongue for a portion of the day. Much the same punishment was meted out to gossips and disturbers of the peace, though the pillory and the public whipping post were on some occasions used instead.

Less formal types of punishment, but none the less effective, were those which required the offender to appear on the Sabbath day to confess his guilt before the congregation, or which required that the effigy of the offender, tarred and feathered, be drawn through the streets. For those guilty of more serious crimes, cruel punishments were devised; counterfeiters and runaway servants might be branded or have their ears cut off; and the gallows, standing in a public place, served as constant warning to murderers and pirates.

Sports and Amusements. Much time and energy were needed to earn a living, yet the colonists found time for various forms of amusement. 

Gambling, drinking, and smoking were not unknown, and in spite of the protests of Puritan clergy, flourished in the North as well as in the South. 

Horse racing was popular, and cockfighting contests between rival towns and plantations were often well attended. Fox hunting was popular in the South. Fishing was a sport enjoyed in all the colonies. In rural districts, fairs were held, at which livestock and other products were exhibited and offered for sale. These fairs were great social occasions. Various forms of entertainment were to be had-ranging from puppet shows to boxing matches. Wrestling matches and bearbaiting furnished lively amusement, but obstacle races and the catching of greased pigs were enjoyed by those who craved less excitement. Holidays, then as now, were often occasions of boisterous pleasure, except for Christmas in New Eng-

Colonial Capitol of Virginia, at Williamsburg: the authentic replica included in the restoration of colonial 

Williamsburg in the early 1930's land, where it was observed in a quieter fashion, and the New England Thanksgiving, which was a semireligious occasion. In the aristocratic families of the Southern and Middle colonies, elaborate balls were given, but Puritan New England frowned upon such "frivolities." 

The lack of good roads made riding in carriages for pleasure impracticable, but horseback riding was a source of prime enjoyment among old and young alike. Hunting and fishing became more a source of pleasure than of livelihood to the later colonists, and few men of property in the South failed to keep hunting dogs. On the village greens, football (not the game as we know it now, which developed after the War of 1861-1865) and cricket were played; and marbles, tops, tag, and dolls were sources of pleasure for negro children at their cabin doors as well as for the chil dren of the wealthiest New England merchant. 

Colonial Towns. The early towns in America were located on the seacoast or along rivers where boats could load and unload their cargoes. The lack of adequate land transportation prevented the growth of large inland cities, and those towns which grew up were usually country villages with houses built on a long, narrow street, unpaved and lined with trees. In

such communities were always found the village church, courthouse, and tavern, where the inhabitants from the surrounding country broke the monotony of the daily routine of life. In 1700 there were few large towns. 

Philadelphia then had a population of 12,000; and New York, about 5,000. 

By 1765, Philadelphia had a population of 25,000, while New York had 

12,500. Williamsburg and Fredericksburg, Virginia, were thriving villages and important social centers. At the time of the Revolution, these cities rivaled the commercial centers of England in bustling activity and fashions. 

In few of the towns or villages were the streets paved, and the absence of sanitation made diseases common. Except in Philadelphia, where most of the houses were of brick, hazards from fire were great, and every householder was required to have his own fire bucket and ladder in readiness for use at the cry of "Fire!" night or day. In spite of the lack of sanitation, unpaved roads, and danger from fire, the towns were centers of social life. 

In Charleston and Williamsburg, many Southern planters had their town houses, where they lived and enjoyed the social season during the meeting of the colonial assembly. In some Northern cities the streets were lined with the pretentious homes of the merchant princes. In the towns a distinct social order early developed, putting into distinct classes the rich merchants or planters, the lawyers and doctors, the shopkeepers, the artisans, and the servants or slaves. 

Organization of Society. In colonial America there were many opportunities for acquiring land and other forms of wealth. This equality of opportunity made for freedom, and tended to do away with a class system. 

Success in life depended largely upon a man's own efforts, and social standing was dependent upon personal achievement rather than upon birth. 

Yet a very definite aristocracy developed around the provincial governors and their councils, where the customs and traditions of England were preserved. Entrance into this upper group depended upon a person's success in acquiring property, usually land, and those families belonging to this favored group attempted to keep its number restricted by intermarriage within the group. Below this group was the middle class, composed of the large body of people in moderate circumstances, who derived their support from the land or from commerce, lived in comfort and often in luxury, and as their wealth increased, might become a part of the political and social aristocracy. 

The rise of a professional class was slow. Physicians usually followed several occupations, and combined quackery, ignorance, and common sense, to a remarkable degree. By 1750, however, a definite medical profession existed, particularly in the North, where settlements were closer

together. In comparison with the honor in which the legal profession was held at the time of the American Revolution, it is surprising that in the seventeenth century the name "lawyer" carried with it such implications of dishonesty that the profession was scarcely respectable. Nevertheless, with the disputes over property, and the drawing up of deeds and settlement of wills, lawyers had achieved by the middle of the eighteenth century a place of respect in their communities. 

From the earliest times, in the North, a definite merchant class was present, based upon fishing, slave trading, and commerce with England and the South. Throughout all the American colonies, the artisans made up an important class, which was constantly increasing in number, due to the apprentice system. Very often these artisans, by thrift or marriage, were able to enter the social group dominated by the successful merchants. 

But next to the aristocracy, the most honored class in the seventeenthcentury New England was that made up of the ministers and their families. 

The minister was the fearless mentor of morals, the guest of honor at social events, the confidant of those in trouble, and the adviser in all matters of politics. Until opportunities for trade began to interest the youths of ability, there was no more attractive calling than that of the ministry.

Laborers were so in demand that with economy they could in a short time acquire sufficient capital to become owners of land and livestock, and become prosperous farmers. In every colony were to be found the indigent, who were content with the bare necessities of life. Such free white men belonged to a lower social stratum than did indentured servants who, at the expiration of their terms of service, became independent landowners. 

Except for the condition of the slave, the organization of society was very elastic, but nowhere was social standing more important than in New England. College students were assigned living quarters, and seats in classrooms, dining halls, and chapel, according to the social positions of their families.

Industry and Commerce. The fertile soil and mild climate attracted many to agriculture. In early America fully 90 per cent of the people made their living by cultivating the soil. The lack of money and the difficulties of transportation caused each household, as far as possible, to be a selfsupporting unit. Each home supplied nearly all its own food, and most of its other needs; however, there were certain necessities, such as salt, millstones, iron implements, and some luxuries, such as coffee, tea, and sugar, which had to be purchased. As prosperity increased, demand arose for finished articles of such nature as could not be produced by the crude

methods of household manufacture; and since the colonists could not afford to import great quantities of manufactured articles, they built up their own industries. Thus products manufactured in one colony were in demand in the others; or members of one household might develop such skill in making certain articles-shoes, for example that the neighbors would prefer them to those made by their own efforts. Under these conditions, specialization gradually developed within and between the colonies, and industries appeared. This practice, however, was discouraged by English manufacturers, who had been accustomed to purchase raw materials from the colonies, at a cheap price, and after manufacturing these materials into finished products, to resell them to the colonies at an excessive profit. To the dissatisfaction of these industrialists of England was added that of the English merchants who had been engaged in the transporting of the raw and finished products. These moneyed classes protested vigorously to 

Parliament, and that body responded with a series of laws which prevented industry in the colonies from developing normally. These laws, however, led to dissatisfaction with British rule, and finally to revolution. 

An important colonial industry was shipbuilding. The forests of the 

New England hills provided fine timber for the construction of ships. Fine harbors were close to the timber supply, and the swiftly flowing rivers furnished power for sawmills. Many of the home-built ships were used by 

New Englanders in coastwise fishing and in the whaling industry, which was profitable because of the demand for whalebone, whale oil, and ambergris. 

Schools and Education. The idea of educating the children prevailed in the American colonies almost from the beginning. That idea has persisted and we still maintain that education is necessary for democracy. The first school in the English colonies was the College of Henrico, in Virginia, which was destroyed by the Indians in 1622. 

The New England group of colonies assumed an early lead in the matter of public support for education. Their plans, with modification, have been almost universally adopted throughout the United States. While it is true that in the beginning all education was under the control of the church authorities, a complete separation of the church and state was soon effected in matters of education. For the most part, this has become the general practice throughout the nation today. The New Englanders were anxious that their children should learn to read and write. In 1642 an act of the 

General Court of Massachusetts pointed out that there was "great neglect in many parents and masters in training up their children in learning and labor... especially of their ability to read and understand the principles of religion and the capital laws of the country." Before the establishment

of public schools, small children were sent to the homes of some of the village women, who taught them the alphabet and to read a few words. 

These early schools were known as "dame" schools. The regular schools later to be known as the public schools, had been voluntarily established in some communities before 1647. 

The early colonial legislatures for the most part assumed large responsibility for the establishment and maintenance of the schools. 

The Massachusetts General Assem bly took the lead in constructive educational legislation, and the law passed by that body in 1647 is regarded as the most important school law ever to be passed in American history. Known as the Old Deluder 

Satan Act, this law required every township having 50 householders to provide a teacher and a school building where the children were to be taught to read and write. The teacher's wages were to be paid either by the parents or by the masters of such children, or by the inhabitants in general. When a town grew to 100 families, a grammar school that would fit the youth for college was to be organized. The college later came to dominate the grammar school, and in many instances, to ignore entirely the desires and needs of the people. Early school equipment; reprint from Scholastic High 

School Weekly, by permission of the editors 1, Dunce's board, hung on the chest of stupid and lazy scholars. 2, Iron comb, with wooden handle, for treating itching scalps; cruel masters would strike with it. 

3. Plaks (Dutch), to slap naughty hands. 4, Hornbook. 5, Brush, to dust desk. 6, Stocks, where boys' feet were locked while the master whipped them. 7, Ink-well and quills. 8, Cup of sand for drying pages wet with ink. 

In these early public schools, the "hornbook" was the basis of the instruction given. It consisted of a small board with a handle, to which a sheet of paper was fastened, containing the alphabet, certain letter combinations such as ab, eb, ib, the Lord's Prayer, and the Roman numerals. 

Over this sheet of paper was placed a thin sheet of horn for the purpose of protecting the paper from the fingers of the children. Older pupils in the early public schools studied the New England Primer, which contained the alphabet, letter combinations, spelling lists, prayers, religious verses, and a collection of rhymes. Figuring, the catechism, and a little Latin were also taught in some of the schools. These schools were often taught by the local minister-or in the larger villages, by a regular schoolmaster.

The colonists were familiar with the Latin grammar schools of England, and it was therefore natural that they should model their higher schools after them. In 1635 the Boston Latin School was founded. This school, and others of its kind, taught chiefly the classical languages, with special stress upon Latin. Some reading and writing and arithmetic were taught in these Latin schools. This type of school spread slowly, and by 

1700 there were but 35 in all New England. However, the Latin grammar schools spread eventually to nearly all of the colonies. 

In New England the Latin grammar school was provided for by the town meeting. It was free to all boys, and was established for the purpose of extending learning and of preparing for the ministry. The curriculum was narrow and poorly adapted to meet the needs of many of the boys of the frontier communities. Such schools flourished in communities lying fairly near to Harvard College, which was chiefly a higher training school for ministers and lawyers. Girls were quite generally denied the privilege of attending the grammar schools, but sometimes they were given private lessons after school hours. While by law they were permitted to attend the elementary schools, records show that nearly two fifths of the women living in Massachusetts during the early part of the eighteenth century could not write their own names. 

The colonists early established several outstanding colleges. Eight of the oldest of these colleges that were founded before the Revolution were as follows: Harvard College, at Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1636; William and Mary, at Williamsburg, Virginia, 1693; Yale College, at New Haven, Connecticut, in 1701; College of New Jersey (now Princeton University, at Princeton, New Jersey), 1746; College of Philadelphia (University of 

Pennsylvania), at Philadelphia, 1749; King's College (Columbia University), at New York City, 1754; Rhode Island College (Brown), at Providence, Rhode Island, 1764; Dartmouth College, at Hanover, New Hampshire, 1769. These colleges, in the beginning, offered work of about the present high school level. They later developed into some of the finest educational institutions for higher learning in the country, and have produced many celebrated scholars. 

In Pennsylvania, New York, Maryland, New Jersey, and Delaware, the church maintained a stronger hold on education than in New England. 

Here the Germans, Quakers, Episcopalians, and other denominations operated their own schools in connection with their churches. In these "parochial" schools, few subjects were taught, church ritual was emphasized, and discipline was very strict, with corporal punishment quite commonly applied. In fairness to the Quakers, however, under the leadership

of William Penn, it must be said that theirs was probably the most practical education of any offered in the American colonies. In addition to learning to read and write, their children were taught some useful trade or skill, "that the poor may work to live, and the rich, if they become poor, may not want."

The Southern colonies represented a third distinct attitude toward education. These colonies followed more closely the English system of education; that is to say, they did not encourage a general plan of free elementary schooling for all of the children. They did favor private secondary schools and colleges under public patronage. A few scattered attempts were made to compel educational attendance, and to provide a tax-supported county system of schools. Free education was provided for the poor in the larger centers. These schools were known as "pauper" schools, and were, in many instances, taught by indentured white servants who were not particularly well trained for the work, nor greatly interested in the educational progress of their pupils. 

Many of the boys of the wealthier class in the South went to England to study. They aspired to the life of a country gentleman, such as that led by the cultured county squire of England. Because of this tradition of training for leadership, the South, for many generations before and after the Revolution, furnished many able statesmen and military leaders. 

The colonial schools as a whole represented the English tradition of severe discipline. Hot-tempered teachers resorted to all sorts of stratagems in order to punish the unruly youngsters. This, coupled with a narrow, uninteresting, subject-centered curriculum and an ill-adapted method of teaching, explains in large part the fact that the early writers nearly always referred to their school experience in very uncomplimentary terms. In fact their school experience was a happy one only while they were at play, at which time they were usually supervised by an indolent or disinterested instructor.

Colonial Literature. The early colonists had to spend most of their time in conquering the wilderness and in providing themselves and their families with food, shelter, and clothing. They did not have much time for study, and did not, in the early days, devote much time to writing. 

Literature of real importance because of its intrinsic aesthetic value, therefore, did not exist in colonial America. But there were some people who gave time to writing, and the books, sermons, speeches, pamphlets, and correspondence of the period are valuable contributions to the life and thought of the time. Many of the better-class immigrants to the Southern colonies in the early days were interested in bettering themselves in a

material way; but some, such as George Sandys, and John Smith, were skilled in literary expression. Their writing includes poetry and various works giving information about the country, the Indians, and the conditions of living. Some of the founders of New England were accustomed, before they left England, to the use of the pen. Many of them were college-trained. Before coming to America, they had engaged in theological and political matters. They kept diaries, wrote histories, and printed sermons and tracts. 

Historical Literature. The most important historians of the Southern colonies were Captain John Smith, William Strachey, and William Byrd.

Of several books by Smith dealing with the American colonies, the best are A True Relation, 1608, an account of the founding of Virginia; and 

A Map of Virginia, 1612, which is a description of the country, its physical features, climate, plants, animals, and inhabitants. It is possibly from the description of a storm and shipwreck off Bermuda, in A True Repertory of the Wracke and Redemption of Sir Thomas Gates, by William Strachey, that Shakespeare found material for The Tempest. William Byrd wrote of his experiences while acting as commissioner of a party which surveyed the boundary line between Virginia and North Carolina in a History of the Dividing Line. It contains humorous impressions of some of the early settlers.

William Bradford and John Winthrop were the chief writers of the history of the New England colonies. Bradford, in his History of Plymouth 

Plantation, begun in 1630, and continued for nearly twenty years, treats of the rise of the Separatist group, their flight to Holland, their experiences while there, their reasons for coming to America, and finally the voyage of the Mayflower. The latter part covers the period from 1620 to 1647. 

John Winthrop was the first governor and the first historian of the colony of Massachusetts Bay. His History of New England, in the form of a diary, includes, among accounts of weightier matters, little everyday occurrences that help to make the book more readable. 

Diaries. Among the diaries of the colonial period are those by Philip 

Fithian of Virginia, and William Eddis of Maryland. The most important diarist of the later colonial period was Samuel Sewall, of Boston. 

He played a prominent part in the persecutions for witchcraft at Salem, but later confessed publicly his error. Besides the Diary, he wrote The 

Selling of Joseph, usually considered the first antislavery tract in America. 

His Diary is the best authority extant on the details of colonial life and customs during the last part of the seventeenth century and the first part of the eighteenth.

Theological Writings. The most significant writings produced in early 

New England are those which deal with religion and theology. These were the work of the Puritan clergy. 

The foremost minister of the first half century in Massachusetts was John Cotton, whose best-known work, besides his controversy with Roger Williams, is the classic New England catechism known as Spiritual Milk for Boston Babes. Spiritual

Another representative of aristocratic conservatism in the New England church was Increase Mather.

He produced about a hundred works on theology, history, philosophy, politics, earthquakes, witchcraft, comets, fires, drunkenness, and smallpox. His son, Cotton Mather, is known for the 

Magnalia Christi Americana: or The 

Ecclesiastical History of New England, from its First Planting. It is an attempt at a general history of New England (1620-1698), containing classified material on the governors, magistrates, and preachers, a history of Harvard, a collection of reports of church transactions, an account of Indian wars, and a record of divine providences.

Title page of a book by John Cotton 

Jonathan Edwards, the most brilliant of the New England divines, wrote the Freedom of the Will, which holds to this day an important place in the philosophical literature of the world. 

One of the few works created in colonial literature which is still read is the Journal of John Woolman, written in 1756-1772, and published in 

1774. Woolman was a New Jersey Quaker who stressed "duties rather than doctrine."

Colonial Poetry. There was hardly any poetry, in the strict sense of the term, produced by the early colonists. Verses, especially epitaphs,

elegies, and memorial verses, were common. The Bay Psalm Book, published in 1640, the first whole volume printed in America, was a rendition of the Psalms into so-called meter, by three New England ministers, Richard Mather, Thomas Welde, and John Eliot. Michael Wigglesworth wrote a sort of rhymed sermon called The Day of Doom, which became the most popular of the American Puritan poems. 

Drama. The South led in the drama. The first known presentation was Ye Beare and Ye Cubb, given in Accomac County, Virginia, in 1665. 

In 1702 "a pastoral colloquy" was recited at William and Mary College. 

The first known professional actor in America was an Englishman, Tony Aston, who acted in Charles Town, South Carolina, in 1703. In 1716 a theater was built at Williamsburg, where in 1718 the governor of Virginia saw a play presented by Charles and Mary Stagg and their company. 

New York had a theater by 1732, while the first American drama to receive a professional production was The Prince of Parthia, a tragedy by Thomas Godfrey, produced at Philadelphia in 1767. Entries in Washington's diary indicate the popularity of the Annapolis Theater in 1773. 

The Revolutionary Period Stimulates Political Writing. During the early part of the Revolutionary period the most numerous and the most important writings were those that presented various phases of the questions of colonial rights-orations, pamphlets, newspaper articles, and Early American drama: St. John Street Theater, New York, in 1787; redrawn from an old print

state papers. The colonial interest in religion gave way to an interest in politics. The writing of the last part of the period deals with the organization of the new government. 

Such men as James Otis, Patrick Henry, and Samuel Adams stirred the people through their oratory, while John Dickinson and Thomas Paine published political pamphlets. St. Jean de Crevecoeur wrote twelve essays on colonial life, called Letters from an American Farmer, the final essay suggesting the devastating changes brought about by the Revolution. The book is one of the most readable in early American literature. 

Numerous ballads and songs of the Revolution appeared. "Yankee 

Doodle," is probably the best-known today, but "Hale in the Bush," by an unknown writer, is the most poetic. "The Battle of the Kegs, by Francis Hopkinson, a humorous ballad on the reputed alarm created among the British by some charged kegs set floating in the Delaware River, was a popular Revolutionary song.

An important group of writers was made up of a number of Connecticut men, mostly graduates of Yale, who came to be known as the Hartford Wits. The leading members of the group were John Trumbull, Timothy Dwight, and Joel Barlow. The oldest and probably the most talented was John Trumbull. He is known for his satire on modern education, called The Progress of Dulness; and M'Fingal, a burlesque epic on the Tory sympathizers. Dwight, the grandson of Jonathan Edwards, was a Congregational minister, and president of Yale 1795-1817. His Conquest of Canaan is a dull epic in eleven books. Barlow became famous for an epic, The Columbiad, but he is remembered now chiefly for a mock heroic poem, "Hasty Pudding."

The most representative poet of the Revolutionary period, and the most significant American poet before Bryant, was Philip Freneau. He was a teacher, political writer, sea captain, editor, and farmer in New Jersey. His early poems were satires and songs, but his really poetical works are his shorter lyrics on American outdoor nature and American tradition. Such poems as "The Indian Burying Ground," "To a Caty- 

Did," "The Wild Honey Suckle," and "On a Honey Bee," are almost the first verse produced in America on native subject matter and expressed in simple and direct form. Individual stanzas in several of his short lyrics are really artistic.

The influential work of the period was done by the statesmen. Benjamin Franklin found time from his scientific investigation, his educational reform, his civic improvement, and his diplomatic duties, to write two of the outstanding works in American literature, Poor Richard's Almanac

and his Autobiography, which ranks among the world's great autobiographies. Thomas Jefferson made a place for himself in the drafting of the 

Declaration of Independence and in his Notes on Virginia, written in 1782, at the request of the French government. Alexander Hamilton, James 

Madison, and John Jay attempted to acquaint the people with the principles back of the Constitution in The Federalist papers. George Washington wrote enough to fill fourteen volumes, but his style is at its best in the familiar First Inaugural, 1789, and the Farewell Address, 1796.

Colonial Libraries. While the colonists themselves were not producing a great literature, they read so many books brought in from England that colonial booksellers became prosperous. The Byrds and Carters, of Virginia, and Cotton Mather, of Massachusetts, boasted of libraries of several thousand volumes, composed largely of books on theology, poetry, history, essays, and a few books of fiction. For young people, Don Quixote, Gulliver's Travels, Robinson Crusoe, and Arabian Nights proved unending sources of delight. On the whole, novels during colonial days were frowned upon unless they contained a definite moral, as did The Power of Sympathy or the Triumph of Nature-A Novel Founded on Truth and Dedicated to the 

Young Ladies of America. 

In nearly every home were found a Bible, a cookbook, and an almanac. 

The almanac was the guide in secular affairs, as was the Bible in things spiritual. It was the encyclopedia to which the colonists turned for information about politics, economics, science, and agriculture. Few homes were too poor to buy it and none too rich to give it an honored place on their shelves.

Newspapers. The first newspaper to appear in America was the 

Boston News-Letter, published in 1704. For a long time newspapers were rarely seen except in the towns. By the middle of the eighteenth century there were only thirty or forty. They contained such items as advertisements, accounts of incoming boats, and letters written by travelers. Of the more than twenty magazines established in colonial America, the most interesting was the American Magazine, 1757-1758, published at Philadelphia under the direction of William Smith. The poor postal service made the little news contained in the newspapers out of date before they were received, except in the towns where they were published. The censorship of the press, by the royal governors, made the editors of the papers afraid to publish anything critical about the government; but with the 

Zenger case of 1735 (pp. 84-85) came a new era of freedom of the press. 

Religion. Of the many motives in colonizing, one of the strongest, particularly in the New England settlements, was that of religion. In New

England, religion and government were so closely allied that at times it was difficult to say where one ended and the other began. On the Sabbath day the meeting house was a place of worship; on other days it was the public gathering place where speeches were delivered and affairs of government were settled. The minister was not only the religious guide; he was also the social mentor and the civil adviser. Before 1689, in most colonies, suffrage depended on religious conformity. After that time, the 

Toleration Act, enacted by the English Parliament, tended to break down religious barriers, except against Catholics and Jews. 

In the South, the ministers were the companions of the people in pleasure and in sorrow. In both North and South, the position of the clergy was one of honor and responsibility. The contrast between Anglicanism and Puritanism was one of the distinct features of colonial life; not only was the Anglican ceremony more formal, and the churches more pretentious than those of the Puritans, but the length and type of sermons differed. In the former, the sermons, which usually lasted less than a half hour, dealt with accepted doctrines, and the prayers were read from the prayer book; whereas in the latter, sermons lasted several hours, dealt with weighty theological problems or the sins of the people, and were preceded or followed by prayers which were lengthy sermons in themselves. At noon those people who lived farthest away either visited in the homes of friends or gathered under the trees or around fires to discuss the sermon, politics, or family affairs. In the afternoon the people again assembled for another sermon. The absence of fires or lighting in the meeting houses offered no excuse for absence, and those who absented themselves without excuse were fined by the government officials. 

Nor were tiny infants who had reached the age for baptism excused from that sacrament, even though ice had to be broken from the bowl containing the water.

As the wealth of the colonies increased, the churches, too, were improved. The simple log house was replaced by a more pretentious edifice, with its tall steeple pointing the way to God, and its bell tolling the time for church, and announcing the deaths of citizens. Occasionally, after 

1700, musical instruments were imported from England-though the reverent Puritans were reluctant to make use of these innovations in the psalm singing.

Throughout the colonies religion was a powerful influence for good, and churches developed and increased in numbers as steady progress was made along material lines as well as along cultural lines. The leading denominations in colonial America included the Anglicans, Puritans,

Dutch Reformed, Presbyterians, Catholics, Quakers, Mennonites, Lutherans, and Baptists. All of these prospered during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. It was on the frontier that the less formal religious sects found their chief support, for a highly organized church could not adapt itself to the informality of frontier life. New German and Scotch- 

Irish immigrants settled in Pennsylvania, and from there went south into the valleys of the Appalachian system, including the Shenandoah Valley. 

In the western parts of New York, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and the Carolinas, there were introduced new racial and religious elements. The older colonies welcomed these new settlers, who improved the prosperity of the colonies and acted as buffers against Indian attacks. The new sects, together with their churches, built frontier schools for the promotion of education. 

As wealth increased, the colonists became dissatisfied with a religion which restrained them from spending their money for luxuries and amusements, and gradually the authority of the church began to diminish. Moreover, as opportunities for success in commerce grew, the ministry no longer offered the only opportunity of advancement to the young men. 

The Great Awakening. In the middle of the eighteenth century, however, a religious revival swept through the colonies-a revival which, because of its power and extent, has been called the Great Awakening. Under the persuasive preaching of George Whitefield, and the warning words of Jonathan Edwards, men were brought under a conviction of sin and a dread of death which helped to overcome denominational differences. Few were exempt—even practical-minded Benjamin Franklin paid his tribute to the persuasiveness of Whitefield. But reaction soon set in, and the revival had little lasting influence. Jonathan Edwards himself was removed from his parish, and after preaching to the Indians, became for a short time until his death-president of the College of New Jersey. A little later, however, Methodism was brought over from England, where John Wesley had begun it, and through its evangelistic message, which was carried by itinerant ministers to all parts of the colonies, drew many into its fold; and, unlike that of Whitefield, retained its gains because it had a permanent organization.

After 1760, however, in the older eastern sections, politics became the dominant interest of the day, and much of the enthusiasm previously devoted to religion was then diverted into political channels.

CHAPTER VI 

The Struggle for Control in 

North America

During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the nations of Europe became aware of the economic importance of colonies. They saw in colonial empire building an opportunity to increase their wealth and power as nations. The colonies in North America were a source of strength, and since the Spanish, English, French, and other nations had made settlements in the New World, the question would soon arise as to which power would gain ultimate control. 

On the Atlantic seaboard, by 1680, the English had an unbroken line of colonies from an uncertain boundary line between New England and New France, on the north, to another uncertain boundary line between the Carolinas and Spanish Florida on the south. 

English and French in America. In 1689 France and England began a long struggle for dominance in Europe and for the control of colonies in North America and elsewhere. The struggle ended in 1763, with England in control. Between those dates four wars were fought between the French and English in America, three of which began as overseas campaigns of wars in Europe.

The American conflict was due to many basic causes and fundamental differences. The real issue was the control of North America. From the viewpoint of the home governments, the colonies were valuable for supplies of fish, furs, naval stores, tobacco, dyestuffs, and sugar. The economic policy of the day was mercantilism, which meant profitable trade with the colonies. The colonies supplied the commodities the mother country could not produce, and bought most of their imports from the mother country. Ships were necessary for this commerce, and each country wanted to do its own "carrying trade," and, if possible, that of other nations 111

Courtesy Peabody Museum, Salem, Mass.

Early New England trading ships at the port of Mocha, Arabia also. Colonies and merchant vessels both required a navy for protection; thus sea power became important. 

Many English colonists had crossed the Atlantic to make a home in the New World because they were dissatisfied with the religious, economic, or political conditions in the mother country. These colonists had no dreams of vast empires, but were interested in local self-government. 

The French people who were dissatisfied with the government at home were not permitted to come to New France, and consequently the population in the French settlement increased slowly. The French government kept close supervision over New France. Protection was given, by the home government, and even food came year after year from France. No self-reliance was developed, and while New France was not lacking in men of ability, nevertheless French power in America was weak as compared with that of the English. While the French colonies were kept in close contact with the home government, the English colonies developed greater freedom and self-government. 

In 1689 the English settlements were still mostly along the Atlantic seaboard. In the west, the settlers were coming into contact with the claims of the French. About the upper Hudson River, Lake George, and 

Lake Champlain were regions in which the English and French were bidding against each other for the fur trade with the Indians. Farther west, in the region of Lake Erie and the upper Ohio River, a similar conflict was certain to develop. In fact, the whole Mississippi Valley was a great prize for a mighty conflict. As the French increased their control of the Great Lakes region, the colonists in Pennsylvania and Virginia were

THE STRUGGLE FOR CONTROL IN NORTH AMERICA 113 

pushing westward, and serious conflict was threatened. Farther to the south, the traders of the Carolinas, with their packhorses, were visiting the Indians living in the region of the present states of Alabama and Mississippi, among whom the French were attempting to establish control. 

The majority of the English who had come to America were or became farmers. The more restless element was to be found farthest west, where population was the scantiest and the brunt of displacing the Indians had to be borne. The French became agricultural to a less extent. Acadia and the St. Lawrence region were farming areas with feudal characteristics. 

New France's chief economic reason for being was the fur trade. The coureurs de bois (unlicensed forest rangers) penetrated the forests, and with a few trinkets they bartered with the Indians and secured valuable furs.

In addition to interest in the fur trade, the French were interested in converting the Indians to the Christian religion. French missionaries 

French fur trappers: mural painting by Allen True in the Capitol of Wyoming

Onondaga County Park 

Early French settlement (1656); restoration (1933) in a park on Onondaga Lake, near 

Syracuse, N. Y. often accompanied the fur traders and thus religion and the desire for gain went hand in hand in developing the French power in America. 

There were also religious differences between New France and New England. The French government permitted only Catholics to come to 

Canada, while the Puritans' objection to the Church of England applied also, of course, to the Catholic Church. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries the effects of the Protestant Reformation and the following religious conflicts were still important factors in producing hostility between groups of different religious faiths. The New Englanders, under the influence of zealous Puritan divines, and Canadians, under the influence of zealous Jesuits, were quite likely to look upon an invasion of the others' country in the light of a crusade. 

During the period of conflict the French were outnumbered by the English. The ratio of English colonists to French colonists in 1689 at the beginning of the struggle was probably as high as fifteen to one, with the French scattered over a much wider territory. This deficiency in numbers was in part counterbalanced by the military efficiency of the French government, and the outcome of the conflict was long uncertain. The French, in addition to their superior organization and support from the home government, usually had the support of the Spanish. 

The Indians. An important factor in the contest was the attitude of the Indians. Here the French had an advantage, as most of the Indians

THE STRUGGLE FOR CONTROL IN NORTH AMERICA 115 

were friendly to them. The English built compact settlements, and the fur trader was soon followed by the farmer, who cut down the forest and destroyed the hunting grounds. The French, on the other hand, had fewer settlements, scattered over a wider area. They did not destroy the hunting grounds, but rather came to live among the Indians and supplied them with the articles which they needed or wanted. The activities of the 

French missionaries were also powerful factors in gaining the support and friendship of the Indians.

King William's War. The first of four wars between England and 

France began in 1689, and is known in American history as King William's War, but in European history is called the War of the League of Augsburg. 

England, Austria, Holland, Spain, and Sweden were allied against France. 

In America there were French and Indian raids against the outlying settlements in New York, New Hampshire, and Maine. The English colonists, with the support of the Iroquois Indians, attacked the French in Canada, and an English expedition captured Port Royal, the French governor surrendering all Acadia with it. The war ended in 1697, with the Peace of 

Ryswick, by which Port Royal and Acadia were returned to the French. 

Queen Anne's War. In the five years of peace, 1697-1702, the French were active in building forts and missions, and in expanding the fur trade as far south as Louisiana. In 1702, the War of the Spanish Succession began. This conflict was known in America as Queen Anne's War. In spite of impressive plans for offensive campaigns, the French attacks were largely Indian raids. 

Port Royal had become a menace because privateers from there were interfering with Boston's shipping. The New England forces therefore captured it, in 1710.

The most important undertaking of the war in America was the effort to take Quebec, but it ended in failure. The war ended with the Treaty of 

Utrecht, in 1713, with neither side defeated. During the war England and 

Scotland had joined to form the United Kingdom of Great Britain. In the treaty of 1713 Great Britain acquired Newfoundland, but France retained fishing rights on part of the coast. France acknowledged the 

British claim to the Hudson Bay region, but its boundaries were not stated. Great Britain also acquired Acadia, and changed its name to 

Nova Scotia. France was weakened by the war but almost immediately began to rebuild her power. In the year in which the treaty was signed, France began to strengthen her hold in North America by building the fortress of Louisburg on Cape Breton Island. The French continued to extend and tighten their grip on the interior of the continent.

The French colonists at Quebec looked with concern upon the French activity in the south, for it meant a diversion of part of the fur trade from the St. Lawrence. In 1701 Louisiana was created a province, and Quebec's anxiety was increased. Its boundaries were not definite, but in general it included most of the area drained by the Mississippi, Missouri, and Ohio rivers. Efforts were made to secure the fur trade along the Missouri 

River, but the savage Indians and resentful Spanish prevented success. 

King George's War. In 1739 Great Britain went to war again. The conflict had opened with Spain, under the name of the "War of Jenkins's Ear," because the seaman Jenkins had told Parliament of how the Spanish had boarded his ship and very cruelly cut off his ear. He presented as evidence not only the scar on his head but also the ear, wrapped in cotton. 

The conflict between Spain and Great Britain broadened into the War of the Austrian Succession, 1740-1748, in which France came in on the side of Spain. The latter half of the war was known in America as King 

George's War, 1744-1748. The outstanding event of the Anglo-French struggle in America was the siege and capture of Louisburg, on Cape Breton Island. On the frontiers there was the usual dreary story of Indian raids, with their cruel scalpings and burnings. 

The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle closed the war in July, 1748. Neither 

France nor Great Britain was the victor. Each returned to the other captured possessions; hence Louisburg, which the colonists had taken, was returned. As far as America was concerned the war had accomplished nothing, and peace was felt to be but a truce. Parliament paid the colonies a sum of money to reimburse them for what they had spent. There was considerable feeling among the colonists, however, that their efforts and sacrifices in the capture of Louisburg had not been appreciated by the 

British rulers.

Causes of the French and Indian War. Three wars had been fought between the French and English in America and hardly anything had been accomplished. The question which had to be decided ultimately was who should be supreme in America. Friction continued in those regions where the trading interests overlapped. This conflict of interest was especially keen (1) in Nova Scotia, (2) in the region around Lake George and Lake Champlain, (3) in the Great Lakes region, and (4) at the forks of the Ohio. 

The latter two were especially important because they were gateways to the great Mississippi Valley, which was eagerly sought by both French and English. In 1749 the governor of New France sent Blainville (often called 

Bienville) into this country. He was anxious to claim the Ohio Valley for 

France, and buried there lead plates proclaiming French possession, and

THE STRUGGLE FOR CONTROL IN NORTH AMERICA 117 

to some trees he nailed tin plates bearing the arms of France. Blainville saw many signs of English traders in this region. 

In the same year King George II chartered the Ohio Company. It was made up of influential Virginia gentlemen, including George Washington's brothers, and important London merchants. This company was granted half a million acres of land in what is now West Virginia. The following year the company sent Christopher Gist to explore the region and to select sites for settlements. The Virginia assembly chartered another company and sent Dr. Thomas Walker to select its lands along the upper Cumberland River. These two companies were unable to accomplish their purpose because the French became too aggressive in maintaining their hold on the region.

In 1753 the French built Fort Le Boeuf on the upper waters which flow into the Ohio, and close enough to Lake Erie to receive aid from the French in Canada. Governor Dinwiddie, of Virginia, realized the value of the 

West and wished to hold it for the English. He selected George Washington to bear a message from the governor of Virginia to the commander at Fort Le Boeuf. In the message Governor Dinwiddie stated that the 

English could not allow an armed French force to invade this territory, and demanded French withdrawal at once. The French commander received the young Virginian courteously, but answered that he would stay there as long as his superiors ordered him to do so. Taking careful notice of the strength of the French, Washington returned with his discouraging message.

War Begins. In preparation for a contest for possession of this region, some Virginians had begun a fort at the forks of the Ohio. This site was taken by the French, who built there a larger fort, which they called Fort Duquesne, in honor of the governor of Canada. Washington was then sent out with an underpaid and poorly disciplined army, with instructions to build a fort on the Ohio. He encountered a French force and fighting resulted; the first shots of the final struggle for control of North America were thus fired in the wilderness of Virginia two years before war was declared. Washington won the skirmish but realized that he was in a country where there were more French than English and the loyalty of his Indian allies was uncertain. He built Fort Necessity (in what is now southwestern Pennsylvania), which was soon attacked by the French. He was forced to surrender but was allowed to march out with the honors of war and return home.

The home governments now began to take more interest in the affairs. of America, France sent an army to Canada. The British began to seize

French ships bound for North America, and General Braddock, with an army of British regulars, was sent to Virginia, even though war had not yet been declared.

Braddock called a conference of governors. The governors explained their inability to extract money from the colonial assemblies and urged that Parliament tax the colonies. General Braddock was a brave soldier, but lacked tact, and therefore irritated the colonists who served with him. He did not understand fully the Indian methods of warfare. He moved with his troops westward through Virginia, bound for Fort Duquesne, building a road for his army as he advanced. Washington served as one of his aides-de-camp. The advancing party was large and the reports the French scouts brought back to Fort Duquesne were discouraging. 

On the morning of July 9, 1755, a party from Fort Duquesne unexpectedly met Braddock's slowly advancing column. The French and Indians took cover under bushes and behind trees and began fighting in frontier fashion. Braddock's men began to do the same thing but he forced them into regular battle formation. When the colonial militia attempted to save the day by their own style of fighting they were caught by the fire of the British regulars. During the battle Washington showed great skill and personal bravery, and one after another three horses were shot from under him. Braddock was mortally wounded and died a few days later, while the defeated British and colonial forces were retreating. 

Attempt at Union. It soon became evident that a long and bitter war would follow, and the colonists felt the need of co-operation and organization. In June, 1754, commissioners from New Hampshire, Massachusetts, New York, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Rhode Island, and Connecticut met at Albany to confer with the Indian representatives and to discuss the formation of a colonial union for common defense. Several plans for such a union were presented. The best-known plan was presented by Benjamin 

Franklin. It provided for a Council, chosen by the colonial assemblies, with power to pass laws for all the colonies. It also provided for a President-General, to be appointed by the king, and to have executive and veto powers. The plan was favored by neither the king's advisers nor the colonists, and came to naught. The colonies were left to fight the war entirely unorganized and unable to co-operate effectively. 

Acadians Expelled from Canada. With the British in control of Acadia, in 1755 they tried to secure the loyalty of the French inhabitants. 

After a final offer to administer the oath of allegiance, which the Acadians did not accept, most of their property was confiscated and about half of their number loaded into ships and scattered among the English colonies. This

treatment aroused the sympathy of many people, and the event was made famous by Longfellow's popular poem "Evangeline."

British Defeats and the Final Victory. War was declared in 1756. The conflict was known in Europe as the Seven Years' War-because it lasted from 1756 to 1763-and in America as the French and Indian War. Early in the year the French sent to America Montcalm, one of the greatest men New France ever had in her service. Montcalm reorganized the French forces and made careful plans. In August he surprised the British at 

Oswego and captured the fort, taking 1,600 prisoners. The British lost their small hold on the Great Lakes region. 

A change was to come, however, in Great Britain's long list of defeats. 

A new cabinet rose to power, in which William Pitt became war minister. 

Pitt was an empire builder and knew how to co-operate with the American colonists instead of antagonizing them. He had not been in office long before the tide had turned and England was winning victories. Appointments and promotion in the fighting service came now as a result of merit and ability. Pitt realized the value of Louisburg and determined to take it. In July, 1758, the fortress was besieged and captured. The same month, Abercrombie, one of Pitt's few poor appointees, failed in his attempt to take Ticonderoga. In August, Fort Frontenac fell to Bradstreet. Bradstreet's victory was of strategic importance, for it broke the line of communication with Fort Niagara and Fort Duquesne. The French were forced to withdraw from Fort Duquesne. The British replaced it with 

Fort Pitt, the beginning of the present great city of Pittsburgh. 

The climax of the war was the siege of Quebec. Louisburg was the gathering place for the British forces under the able command of General James Wolfe. The fleet many miles long made its way up the St. Lawrence to Quebec. Montcalm had stationed his forces at Quebec and Montreal, he himself remaining at Quebec. Montreal could not be left unprotected, because Amherst was advancing toward it by way of Lake Champlain. 

Quebec, protected by cannon and by great cliffs, seemed safe from attack. 

From June 26, on through the summer, the British ships floated before Quebec. Wolfe knew that if he could reach the Plains of Abraham, back of Quebec, he could force Montcalm to fight. Montcalm knew that if 

Wolfe did not act soon, the early Canadian winter would drive him out of the St. Lawrence. After careful examination of every pathway and ravine, Wolfe found one which was not carefully guarded, and which his men could scale. During the early hours of September 16, the British left their ships and, two abreast, climbed up the steep pathway, overpowered the few sentinels on duty, and were drawn up in battle formation when Montcalm

arrived to see what the disturbance was about. Severe fighting followed. in which both Wolfe and Montcalm were wounded. Wolfe lived long enough to know the victory was his, and Montcalm lived until the next day. On a monument to these two heroes, in Quebec, there is a Latin inscription which, translated, reads: "Valor gave a united death, History a united fame, Posterity a united monument." 

The Peace of Paris was signed in February, 1763. By it France surrendered to Great Britain her claims to Canada, Cape Breton, and all of Louisiana east of the Mississippi River except the Isle of Orleans. New 

Orleans and the vast region between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains was ceded by France to Spain. Spain had aided France in the war, and in making peace with Great Britain was obliged to give up her possession of Florida. The British now held all of North America east of the Mississippi River, from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean, excepting Greenland, two tiny islands near Newfoundland, and the Isle of 

Orleans at the mouth of the Mississippi.

 Chapter VII.  Chapter VIII.  

SOON AFTER THE FRENCH AND INDIAN WAR, discontent with the British mercantile system was increased and the relations of the American colonies with the mother country were strained to the breaking point. As the 

American colonies grew in size and strength, and as they developed their institutions, they became more and more interested in self-government and therefore resisted the British idea of imperial control. This in time caused the leaders in the American colonies to challenge the British authority. The colonists, in their controversy with the mother country, put forth the argument of individual liberty. They resorted to the philosophy of John Locke, who had emphasized the idea of natural rights. 

As the British government tried to perfect its imperial organization by imposing new taxes on the American colonists, and by regulating their industries, the opposition to British rule became so bitter that it finally caused the colonists to resist all British attempts to govern them, and led to a complete separation. By the Declaration of Independence, written by Thomas Jefferson and adopted by the Continental Congress in 1776, the colonies declared themselves free and independent states. 

Following this declaration, the colonies adopted state constitutions and thereby were changed from dependent colonies to self-governing commonwealths. They united in their resistance to Great Britain, through the 127

Continental Congresses. The First Continental Congress met in 1774, while the Second was a continuous body holding sessions during the period from 1775 to 1781.

Even before independence was declared, the break with England resulted in open conflict. Under the capable leadership of George Washington the Americans organized armed forces which were able to defeat the British. The war, which began with the battle of Lexington in 1775, ended victoriously for the Americans with the defeat of the British at Yorktown in 1781. During the period of the war the American people were put to a severe test. They had to face the difficult problems of organizing and supplying an army; but with the help of France and with loans from other 

European nations, they successfully resisted the British and maintained their independence. The colonists then organized their own central government under the Articles of Confederation, which became the basis of our national government from 1781 to 1789. 

The American Revolution should be carefully studied in order that its political, economic, and social effects may be thoroughly understood.
