The War in the Carolinas. In an attempt to rally the Loyalists in the 

Carolinas to the support of the king, British fleets were sent to Wilmington and to Charleston. When some of the North Carolina Loyalists advanced toward Wilmington to co-operate, they were met by the patriots and were

defeated at Moore's Creek in February, 1776, before the arrival of the fleet. 

When Sir Henry Clinton reached Wilmington six weeks later he realized that there was no chance for success in North Carolina. He then moved to attack Charleston, South Carolina, which was defended by a band of six hundred patriots under the command of Colonel Moultrie, who had built a fort of palmetto logs on Sullivan's Island in the harbor of Charleston, and had collected a few cannon and a small amount of munitions. The fleet, under the command of Sir Peter Parker, could not withstand the fire of the fort and was forced to withdraw to New York-and the Carolinas were, for a time, saved to the American cause. 

New York Taken by the British. A few months after the British had left Boston for Halifax, General Howe with about twenty thousand troops sailed southward to New York, where he was joined by re-enforcements and where he was supported by a large fleet under the command of his brother, Admiral Richard Howe. Washington, with a force inferior in numbers, in experience, and in training, had stationed a part of his army on Long Island, where he was attacked and defeated. His army was in danger of being captured, but under the cover of fog and darkness he succeeded in evading the British and transported his entire army to Manhattan. Slowly he was driven back and up the Hudson. Fort after fort was lost to the superior British army, and more than 2,800 men and many guns were surrendered. Only the great ability of Washington saved his army from complete demoralization. Many of the militia deserted, thinking that the cause was lost. It was with great difficulty that Washington led a small remnant 

Statue of Washington at Newark, N. J. of his army across the Delaware into Pennsylvania and endeavored to protect them against an attack by taking all the boats which could be found for miles along the river-late in 1776. 

New Jersey Is Recovered. 

Enthusiasm for the American cause was now at a low ebb, but the genius of Washington soon revived the lagging spirit of the 

Americans. Cornwallis, who had been placed in command of the

British army, thinking that the war was practically over, entrusted the task of watching

Washington to a small army of hired Hessian troops at Trenton. 

About three weeks after Washington's hasty retreat from New York to Pennsylvania, he decided upon a bold move. On Christmas night he recrossed the Delaware, which was dangerous because of floating ice, and attacked the Hessians. Taken by surprise, several hundred Hessians, including their commander, Colonel Rahl, were killed, and about a thousand more were taken prisoners. Cornwallis, thoroughly alarmed, hastened from New York. Washington, however, outgeneraled him and defeated another British force at Princeton. Having reclaimed most of the state of New Jersey, Washington went into winter quarters at Morristown.

The Turning Point of the War. In the spring of 1777 the British entered upon a carefully worked-out plan for splitting the colonies into two groups. General Burgoyne's well-equipped army was to advance from 

Montreal along Lake Champlain to the Hudson Valley in New York. 

General St. Leger was to lead a force of British troops and Indians from 

Lake Ontario across New York and join Burgoyne near Albany. General

Howe was to move up the Hudson River to co-operate with Burgoyne and St. Leger. Many complications arose, however, and the British plan failed. 

Burgoyne's army, after minor successes, was so hindered in its march through swamps and forests that it was able to advance only twenty miles in twenty days. It was operating in a region where there was a strong patriotic sentiment, and was therefore vigorously attacked at every move. 

It was unable to get needed supplies. Detachments of troops which had been sent to Vermont to secure food and other supplies were defeated at Bennington by a force of militia under Colonel Stark. 

Meanwhile General St. Leger's advance across New York met with mishaps at Fort Stanwix and Oriskany, where he was defeated and forced to retreat. At this critical period in the campaign, instead of advancing up the Hudson to co-operate with Burgoyne, Howe decided that it would be a better plan to capture Philadelphia, the American capital. Thus 

Burgoyne, unassisted, was forced to meet a formidable American army under the command of General Horatio Gates. For several days the two armies struggled desperately near Saratoga, New York. The British were unable to advance or to retreat, and were forced to surrender on October 17, 1777. The surrender of Burgoyne's army was the turning point of the war; it saved New York state and New England. The plan of separating New England from the rest of the states had failed. Since there was now a chance for success, the Americans were able to make a treaty of alliance with France, for which purpose Benjamin Franklin, a very capable diplomat, had been sent to Paris.

The Philadelphia Campaign. When Burgoyne began his march from 

Canada, the British army at New York, under General Howe, was being watched by Washington. Instead of striking a sudden blow at Washington's greatly depleted army and then joining with Burgoyne, Howe waited until summer and then embarked an army of about 18,000 men on a fleet of over 200 vessels and set sail. His destination was unknown to Americans, but the cautious Washington was not to be taken by surprise. He moved his army toward Philadelphia as a matter of precaution. He soon learned that the British fleet had entered Chesapeake Bay and that Howe was planning an attack on Philadelphia. Washington took position on 

Brandywine Creek (at Chadds Ford) but was defeated in a hotly contested battle, after which the British entered Philadelphia. Several weeks later 

Washington attempted to surprise Howe's army which was encamped at Germantown, a suburb of Philadelphia. He was probably robbed of a victory by a fog which arose just as the battle began, and was so dense that one American brigade mistook another for the enemy and fired upon it with devastating effect. In the confusion which followed, Washington withdrew his men in surprisingly good order and went into winter quarters at Valley Forge, about twenty miles northwest of Philadelphia. 

Washington at Valley Forge. The winter following the victory at

Saratoga was the darkest period of the war for the Americans. Washington had been unsuccessful in several battles of major importance. The famous Conway "cabal" (that is, plot), participated in by prominent military officers and members of Congress, threatened to remove Washington from command. His "illy clad, badly fed, and worse paid" army spent a winter of intense suffering at Valley Forge. Some of the soldiers were without shoes and left bloody footprints in the snow, while others shivered in clothing which was fit only for summer wear. An epidemic of smallpox added to the suffering. Men deserted by the hundreds. At one time there were probably not more than two thousand men in the army who were fit for military service, and yet the cautious Howe failed to attack. 

The lack of supplies in the American army may be attributed in part to the poor system of transportation; but a more important factor was the indifference of the people around Philadelphia, as they preferred to sell their goods to the British, who paid them in gold, rather than to Americans, who were able to pay only with paper money of doubtful value. 

Even the buoyant spirit of Washington was depressed by the conduct of the American "profiteers," but, although he felt that the game was pretty nearly up, he never spoke of resigning nor dreamed of giving up the struggle. His courage and persistence won against great odds.

Washington at Valley Forge, where his "illy clad, badly fed, and worse paid" army endured intense suffering 161

The French Decide to Help. The Americans were heartened by the news of an alliance with France. For a long time the French had been hostile to the British. They remembered their defeat in 1763 whereby they lost their empire in America. Moreover many of the French people were interested in the liberal principles advocated by the Americans, and they had great respect and admiration for Benjamin Franklin, who had been sent to Paris to obtain help. Through the influence of Franklin, the 

French had been aiding secretly by sending money and supplies, but were unwilling to go to war with Great Britain unless they felt reasonably certain that the Americans would win and be able to maintain their independence.

When the news of Burgoyne's surrender reached Paris the French decided that they could risk an open alliance with the colonies. This not only cheered and encouraged the Americans, but also became a real help in that it forced Great Britain to use much of her strength against France in other parts of the world and thus prevented her from throwing full force against the Americans. Furthermore, the French were ready and willing to send a fleet to America. When this news reached General Henry Clinton, who now held the command of the British army, he decided to evacuate Philadelphia to prevent the possibility of a French blockade of the Delaware River. His army moved to New York (June, 1778). 

European Officers Come to America. The French alliance prompted many prominent European officers to volunteer their services in the cause of American independence. Even before the alliance had been consummated, Lafayette, a Frenchman of wealth and high social position, came to America in 1777, at the age of twenty years, and offered his services to Washington. He soon won the confidence and friendship of Washington, who appointed him to the rank of major general. Other Europeans who distinguished themselves during the war were DeKalb, the son of a German peasant, and Kosciusko and Pulaski, Polish officers schooled in the arts of war and able to render efficient service. Especially valuable was the work of the Prussian military officer Baron von Steuben. Trained in the army of Frederick the Great, he had had successful military experience in European wars, and was especially helpful in drilling recruits and in organizing the American army. He joined Washington at Valley Forge and served with great distinction throughout the war. 

Following the alliance with France, Spain also declared war on Great Britain, though she did not form an alliance with the United States. Later, Holland also entered the war against the British, while other European powers openly displayed a sympathetic attitude toward the Americans.

War in the Northwest. Soon after the outbreak of the war the Indians in the territory north of the Ohio River, who had been aroused against the colonists by British agents, were guilty of many cruel massacres. They were encouraged in their depredations by Hamilton, the British governor of the Northwest, who bought the scalps the Indians obtained. For that reason he was known as the "Hair-Buyer," and was bitterly hated by the colonists. Virginia claimed this territory, and in 1778 Patrick Henry, the governor, commissioned George Rogers Clark to carry the war into the Northwest. With a poorly equipped army of several hundred men he made his way down the Ohio River and on to Kaskaskia-in what is now southern Illinois-which was taken without resistance. He next captured 

Cahokia. These posts were inhabited by French people who, learning of the alliance that had been made, willingly took an oath of allegiance to the American cause and assisted Clark in the capture of Vincennes, in what is now Indiana. Clark's victories were very important. Not only did they reduce the menace of Indian warfare, but by giving the Americans actual possession of the region north of the Ohio they strengthened their claim to it when the treaty of peace was negotiated with Great Britain. 

The War Is Carried to the South. In 1778 the war was again transferred to the South. With the assistance of Loyalists, the British captured Savannah in December, 1778, and overran the state of Georgia in spite of the brave resistance of the patriots. With the aid of a French fleet the Americans attempted to retake Savannah in October, 1779, but were unsuccessful. In May of the next year the British attacked and captured Charleston, which was defended by an American force under the command of General Benjamin Lincoln.

South Carolina and Georgia were now in the hands of the British, but their possession was by no means secure, for the British forces were continually menaced by small detachments of men who went about their regular work one day and fought the British the next. Their most important leaders were Francis Marion, Thomas Sumter, Andrew Pickens, and Elijah Clark. Without risking open battle these small bands constantly harassed the British in guerilla warfare. Congress attempted to help the patriots in the South by sending to their aid General Gates, who had gained prominence because of his victory at Saratoga. But Gates did not live up to his reputation; he was severely defeated in the battle of Camden in August, 1780, and nearly two thirds of his army was destroyed. 

Arnold's Treason. After the defeat at Camden the Americans had good reason to feel discouraged because of the situation in the South. It was during this gloomy period, also, that the country was shocked by the

news of the treason of Benedict Arnold. After distinguishing himself by his bravery at Quebec and Saratoga, Arnold had been stationed at Philadelphia while recovering from wounds received in those battles. There he lived extravagantly and became involved in financial difficulties. He was associated with many people who had Loyalist sympathies, and he had married a lady who belonged to a Tory family. While stationed there, charges were brought against him and Congress ordered that he be reprimanded by Washington. This Washington did in a kindly manner by making the reprimand a eulogy, for he realized that Arnold had rendered great service to his country and had been falsely accused by his enemies. 

Arnold was then placed in command at West Point, an important position on the Hudson River. He soon negotiated with General Clinton, the British commander in New York, to betray his post in return for a sum of money and a brigadier general's commission in the British army. The negotiations would have been successfully completed but for the fact that Major André, who was conducting them, was captured, and papers revealing the plot were discovered on him. In September, 1780, Arnold made his escape and joined the British, while Major André was executed as a spy. 

Kings Mountain. Assistance came to the people of the South from an unexpected source the frontiersmen. Major Ferguson, who commanded a British force, sent a message to the frontiersmen on both sides of the Appalachians, saying that unless they remained quiet he would come over and punish them. The Westerners, however, were not intimidated by the threat. From Watauga and other settlements west of the mountains they collected for the purpose of attacking Ferguson. About nine hundred strong, they were led by William Campbell, John Sevier, and Isaac Shelby across the mountains into the Carolinas, where they were joined by about five hundred North Carolinians and four hundred South Carolinians. 

When Ferguson, with a force of a thousand men, found his way of retreat blocked, he took a position on Kings Mountain, a rocky eminence on the border of the two Carolinas. Because of the rough slope he felt that he would experience no difficulty in maintaining his position, but he had not reckoned with the expert marksmanship of his assailants and their skill in this type of warfare. The frontiersmen surrounded the base of the mountain and, taking shelter behind trees and boulders, slowly fought their way up the slope. Any foe who exposed himself became a target for their unerring aim. In the severe battle which followed, Ferguson and nearly half of his men were killed, while all of the survivors were captured. 

The battle of Kings Mountain (October 7, 1780) was the turning point of the war in the South and helped to revive hope for the success of the patriots.

The Battle of Cowpens. Weakened by the loss of Ferguson's army, Cornwallis, who was in general command of the British forces in the South, temporarily gave up the idea of conquering North Carolina and retreated southward. In the meantime General Nathanael Greene replaced General Gates and took command of the patriot army in the South. He sent part of his forces under the command of General Daniel 

Morgan to unite with the mountaineers in an attack upon the British. 

Cornwallis attempted to meet this attack by sending Colonel Banastre Tarleton against Morgan. In the battle of Cowpens, which was fought on January 17, 1781, the Americans won a complete victory, but because of the approach of the much stronger army of Cornwallis, Morgan and Greene retreated across North Carolina. By spring Greene had recruited his army sufficiently to risk a battle with Cornwallis at Guilford Courthouse, North Carolina, when he forced the British to withdraw to the coast. Feeling that his position in North Carolina was insecure because of the persistent attacks of the Americans, and deeming it unwise to go back into South Carolina, Cornwallis therefore advanced into Virginia. After some encounters with Lafayette, he retired to Yorktown, where he awaited re-enforcements from Clinton in New York. 

Cornwallis Surrenders at Yorktown. As soon as Washington received word that Cornwallis had stationed his army on the peninsula at Yorktown, he began to make plans for a movement which he hoped would end 

Washington at Yorktown, 1781 

Drawing by David Hendrickson

the war. He received assurance from Count de Grasse that the French fleet would come from the West Indies and would co-operate with him by preventing the escape of Cornwallis's army by sea and also by making it impossible for him to receive re-enforcements. Strengthened by French troops under the command of Rochambeau, Washington feigned a movement against New York in order to cause General Clinton to believe that he was about to be attacked, and then quickly moved his army southward. 

He was joined by Lafayette's army in Virginia, and the combined American and French forces began the siege of Yorktown September 2, 1781. Unable to escape, and with a force not strong enough to engage Washington and Lafayette in battle, Cornwallis surrendered on October 19, 1781, with his entire army of about 7,000. This brought the war in America to an end, though the treaty of peace was not signed until 1783. 

The War on the Sea. At the beginning of the war Great Britain was mistress of the seas. Her navy was 

Paul Jones, and the Bonhomme Richard and Serapis; facsimile of the frontispiece of a rare French Memoirs of Jones the strongest in the world. In spite of the efforts of the Continental Congress, the Americans were not able to produce a naval force strong enough to engage the British openly on the sea, though some daring exploits were performed. The most outstanding of these were by John Paul Jones, who, with only a few vessels at his command, did much to destroy British shipping. In 1779, in the Bonhomme 

Richard, he came upon the British warship Serapis off the coast of England, and after a desperate battle succeeded in capturing it. His own ship sank but he sailed away in the captured vessel. This feat is one of the most remarkable in the entire history of the war.

The weakness of the American navy was offset to some extent by the activity of the privateers. These were private commercial vessels that were authorized by Congress or by the states to prey upon the commerce of the enemy. The ships and

cargoes captured by them were sold, and the profits were usually divided between the owner and the crew, the owner usually receiving half of the plunder while the crew took the remainder. It has been estimated that during the war approximately two thousand such owners-also known as privateers were engaged in this type of warfare. Many British vessels were captured or destroyed, while numbers of the privateers became wealthy. Some of these were known to have captured prizes which sold for several million dollars.

Peace Negotiations. After the surrender of Cornwallis at Yorktown, the British statesmen, especially Lord North, the prime minister, felt that there was no use to continue the war; King George III, however, was not willing to admit defeat. He was anxious to prosecute the war further, and even threatened to abdicate the throne unless this were done. But the struggle in America was discontinued in spite of his objections, and Richard Oswald was sent by the British government to Paris to consult with Franklin concerning the terms of peace. The Americans had sent three commissioners, Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, and John Adams, to Paris with instructions to make peace with the consent of our ally, France; but when negotiations began, it soon developed that France stood in the way of immediate peace, and our commissioners therefore proceeded to make a preliminary treaty with Great Britain without consulting the French. 

This action on the part of the American commissioners greatly irritated Vergennes, the French minister, because the United States had agreed in the treaty of alliance that it would make no peace without the consent of France. Franklin admitted that the Americans had been guilty of bad manners, but hoped that they would be forgiven by their allies. That this was done is indicated by the fact that a few weeks later, at the request of Franklin, the French made another loan of six million livres (that is, about $1,146,000) to the United States.

The Terms of Peace. The terms of the final treaty, which was signed at Paris on September 3, 1783, provided: (1) that the independence of the 

United States be acknowledged by Great Britain; (2) that the territory as far west as the Mississippi River, and extending from Florida to Canada, should belong to the United States; (3) that the Americans should continue to have the right to fish on the Banks of Newfoundland; and (4) that the British should evacuate the territory which they had ceded to the United States without carrying off American property. On the other hand, the United States agreed: (1) that there should be no further persecution of the Loyalists; (2) that Congress would recommend to the state legislatures that the Loyalists' property should be restored; (3) that no lawful

attempts should be made to prohibit British creditors from collecting debts from the American debtors; and (4) that the Mississippi River, from its source to its mouth, should be "free and open to the subjects of Great Britain and the citizens of the United States." Only the succession of a Whig ministry into power in the British government made possible a treaty so favorable for America.

Money Cost of the War. The cost of the war, in money, has been variously estimated. It was perhaps more than a hundred million dollars. 

The problem of raising that amount was a very difficult one. The funds were derived mainly from four sources: (1) paper money, (2) requisitions on the states, (3) domestic loans, and (4) foreign loans. It is interesting to note that little or no effort was made to raise money by taxation. The 

Continental Congress did not have the power of taxation, but even more important was the fact that the colonies had rebelled against Great Britain partly because they were opposed to the paying of taxes, and they did not, therefore, look with favor upon the levying of taxes for the purpose of carrying on the war. 

The issuing of bills of credit was resorted to by Congress as early as 1775. In that year Congress authorized an issue of two million dollars in paper notes in denominations of from one to eight dollars. Later other denominations varying from a sixth of a dollar to sixty-five dollars were issued. Since Congress did not have power to levy taxes for the redemption of this paper currency, it recommended that each state should gradually pay off its proportionate share of these notes. As the war continued and additional money was needed, other issues of "Continental" currency were authorized, until, finally, more than $240,000,000 had been issued by Congress. In addition to this amount more than $200,000,000 was issued by the states. Depreciation was inevitable. As the purchasing power of money went down, prices of commodities went up. The paper money declined so far in value that it became almost worthless; hence the expression, "not worth a continental." Washington remarked that he needed a wagon- 

Colonial silver cups and pitchers

Metropolitan Museum of Art

load of money to buy a wagonload of supplies. Prices continued to go higher and higher. A bushel of corn in 1781 sold for $80, while a barrel of flour was worth $1500. Tea sold for $90 a pound, and shoes for $100 a pair. The method of financing the war by issuing paper money was highly undesirable, but it is difficult to see how Congress could have carried on the war without it. In all the states this Continental money was declared legal tender and creditors were required to accept it in payment of debts. 

This gave an opportunity for dishonest debtors to force their creditors to accept this worthless money, thus canceling their obligations. 

The method of obtaining money by requisitions on the states was not successful because the states did not readily respond to the requests; each state felt that it was contributing more than its share. The method of obtaining money by domestic loans was only partially successful. Bonds bearing interest at the rate of from four to six per cent were issued and sold through loan offices set up for this purpose in the states. Money was also raised by the use of certificates issued by the quartermaster and other officers for food, clothing, and other supplies needed for the army. It is estimated that more than $16,000,000 of these certificates were issued during the period of the war. Finally, there was the method of raising money by loans from foreign countries. The greatest amount, more than $6,000,000, was obtained from France. In addition to this, loans were secured from Holland and from Spain. 

Great service was rendered by Robert Morris, a merchant of Philadelphia, in raising money to meet the bills, thus saving the government from bankruptcy. From 1781 to 1784 he was superintendent of finance, and in 1781 he succeeded in getting Congress to charter the Bank of North America. This bank during the closing events of the war made several loans to the government.

Political Effects of the Revolution. The most outstanding political effect of the Revolution was the fact that the colonies declared and main- 

Colonial silver utensils

Metropolitan Museum of Art

tained their independence. Following the Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776, the colonies considered themselves free from Great Britain and began to organize independent commonwealths. The organization of state governments began even before the Declaration of Independence had been adopted. New constitutions were framed and adopted by all of the states with the exception of Rhode Island and Connecticut, whose charters served the purpose. In all of these constitutions provision was made for the three branches of government-the executive, the legislative, and the judicial. All of the states had had rather unpleasant experiences with the colonial governor; in their new constitutions, therefore, they limited the power of the executive. In many of the states the governor was chosen by the legislature. In several states his term was limited to one year, while in all but two of the states he had no power of veto. The state constitutions made provision for the protection of the rights of individuals through bills of rights. In these bills of rights were announced the doctrines which had been set forth in the Declaration of Independence. 

Social Effects of the Revolution. The American Revolution was far more than a political struggle; some of its most significant influences were social in their nature. Not only was it a fight for the rights of the colonies as political units, but it was also a struggle on the part of the underprivileged masses against the aristocratic form of society which had existed in the Tidewater sections. The right of suffrage was extended and many of the property requirements and other arbitrary restrictions on the right of voting were removed.

Another blow to aristocracy was the breaking up of many of the largest estates. Some of the most extensive estates had been owned by Loyalists, and many of them were confiscated by the state governments and sold in smaller units. Among the largest estates thus broken up were those of 

William Penn, which had been valued at about $5,000,000, and the Philipse manor in New York, which contained 192,000 acres of land. Landholding was made still more democratic by the abolition of quitrents, primogeniture, and entail.

The "leveling movement" also reached the church and disestablished the Episcopal Church. It also gave considerable impetus to the antislavery movement, the first antislavery society being organized at Philadelphia in 1775. (See page 346.) It seemed difficult to reconcile the institution of slavery with the doctrine of equality enunciated in the Declaration of Independence. During the Revolution and in the following decade several of the Northern states provided for the abolition of slavery, and in Virginia ten thousand slaves were freed in the period from 1782 to 1790.

A Central Government Organized. The Second Continental Congress, which directed the national affairs from 1775 until the Articles of Confederation went into effect in 1781, had served as the central government. 

In 1777 the Articles of Confederation were adopted, but they were not ratified until 1781. Their ratification, which required unanimous consent, was delayed by Maryland's refusal to concur until the states which had claims to western territory should agree to cede these lands to the central government. These feeble efforts at a central government paved the way for a stronger national government, which came with the adoption and ratification of the Constitution of the United States.

THE SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC CONDITIONS in America following the 

Revolution were important factors in the establishment of our government. 

The conditions were so chaotic during this critical period that they made strong government necessary. Following the Declaration of Independence the states set up governments based on constitutions, while the Articles of Confederation served as a basis of the central government. At that time the population of the United States was only about 3,500,000-that is, less than the present population of the one state of New Jersey. The new government under the Articles of Confederation did not have sufficient power to deal effectively with the many difficult problems which confronted it. A study of the conditions during this perplexing period will enable us to appreciate the work done by such great American leaders as George 

Washington, John Adams, Thomas Jefferson, Alexander Hamilton, and

James Madison, all of whom rendered great service in establishing our nation on a firm basis. 

The Convention which drafted the Constitution of the United States -the document which has been the basis of our national government 175

ever since 1789-deserves careful study. It established a central government in which the people are represented both by states and according to population. It set up three distinct departments of government-the executive, the legislative, and the judicial. The method of electing the 

President by an electoral college, his term of office, the qualifications of the United States Senators and Representatives, and many other details of our present national government were determined at this Convention. 

Following the adoption and ratification of the Constitution, the new government was promptly organized. The election of Washington as 

President and the selection of able statesmen for his cabinet are matters of great importance in our history. The financial situation was handled by Hamilton as Secretary of the Treasury; and the difficult foreign problems which arose as a result of the upheaval in Europe caused by the French Revolution, were the concern of Jefferson as Secretary of State. 

Political parties, which have been such a vital factor in our history, originated in Washington's administration as President. The present 

Democratic party was organized in 1793 under the leadership of Thomas Jefferson, but it was then called the Republican party. The Federalist party was in power during the eight years while Washington was President and the four years of Adams's term; but in 1801 the control of the government passed to the party headed by Thomas Jefferson.

CHAPTER IX Social and Economic Conditions 

Following the Revolution

The United States in 1783. The American people by 1783 had achieved their independence and set up their own government. The new nation had an area of 850,000 square miles and a total population of about 3,500,000 people, most of whom lived on or near the Atlantic coast. Of the total area claimed by the United States, less than one third was inhabited by the American people, while a large part of the remainder was still occupied by the Indians, and some of it was claimed by foreign powers. While the 

Americans had become independent, they had as yet no strong feeling of nationalism. There were thirteen separate states, with the people of the states more interested in their local welfare than in the welfare of the nation. The first great task for American statesmen, therefore, was to develop a stronger feeling of unity. This was difficult because of the many different nationalities in America. While most of the people were 

English, there were Dutch, Scotch-Irish, French, Germans, and others not bound together by common traditions. 

Transportation and communication had not been developed sufficiently to bring the people together, and since they lived far apart, and since the different sections of the country had different economic interests resulting from different physical conditions which tended to make for sectionalism, it was difficult to secure national unity. In fact differences in soil, climate, and other geographical factors have made sectionalism in the United States more or less permanent. 

But while there were these factors which made for sectionalism and lack of unity, there were also at work certain other factors which tended to bring the people together into one nationality. For example, most of them spoke the English language. Most of them were of the same great 177

branch of the white race, namely, Teutonic. They had had common political experiences; that is, they had worked together in their quarrel with the mother country, and finally united in the Revolution. Furthermore, they had common ideals of government; all of them were interested in self-government and had fought the British to realize these ideals. 

Economic Problems in 1783. Following the treaty of peace, there came a brief period of prosperity, but it soon gave way to a serious economic depression. By 1785 many of the American businessmen found. it difficult to continue their business. Farmers were unable to sell their surplus crops. During the war they had received high prices, but soon after the war was over, their foreign markets disappeared because the return of peace gave Europeans a chance to produce their own food supplies. The American manufacturers likewise suffered from the depression. 

Their domestic market was almost destroyed because English manufacturers sent cheap goods into this country, and Congress did not have the power to pass tariff laws. In the absence of tariff laws passed by Congress, many of the states passed such laws, not only against foreign goods but also against goods from the other states. 

In addition to manufacturers and farmers, the shippers also suffered. 

New Englanders, especially, had been engaged in shipbuilding and had carried on a lucrative shipping trade. Massachusetts, for example, had built as many as 125 ships a year. With the decline in foreign trade and destruction of trade with the West Indies, she could find a market for only 15 or 20. The American merchants suffered along with the farmer, manufacturer, and shipper, for not only did the British send goods to America, but they also sent agents to distribute and sell them in this country. This was a serious problem for the American merchant. The heavy imports from 

England and from some other countries presented also another problem. 

Since foreign goods were paid for by coin, the financial system of the country was greatly disorganized by the heavy drain on its specie (coin). 

Early industries

Government of the New States. Soon after the Declaration of Independence, most of the colonies took steps necessary to adopt state constitutions. Virginia led in this movement. Other states followed, and by the end of the Revolution all the states except two had adopted written constitutions. Connecticut and Rhode Island had such liberal charters that they used them as the framework for their state governments. 

The experience which the colonies had with the mother country led them to believe that they should have written constitutions which definitely stated what powers belonged to the government. Their constitutions were based on the idea that in all free governments the powers are limited. In all of these new state constitutions restrictions were placed on suffrage. Some required property qualifications, and several had religious qualifications. The time for universal manhood suffrage had not yet arrived.

Some of the constitutions provided that the governor should be elected by the legislature, while in others he was chosen by the qualified voters. 

His power was greatly restricted, for he did not have the right to veto laws passed by the assembly. The reason for this limitation of the governor's power was that the experience of the colonists with the royal governors had been rather unpleasant. The royal governors quarreled with the local legislatures, and were more interested in pleasing the British authorities than the colonists. But while the power of the governor was limited, the early state governments gave more power to the state legislatures, since the members of the legislatures were chosen by the people. 

The Articles of Confederation. Soon after the Declaration of Independence was adopted, the Continental Congress authorized a committee to draw up a plan for a central government. The committee drew up the 

Articles of Confederation, which became the basis of the central government during the period from the close of the Revolutionary War until 1789 when the new Constitution went into effect. of New England

This was not the first attempt to secure a union of the colonies. As early as 1643 the New England Confederation, a union of Plymouth, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Haven, was formed for protection against the Indians and the Dutch. In 1754 delegates from seven colonies attempted to form a union under the Albany Plan. Again, in 1765 delegates from nine of the colonies met in the Stamp Act Congress, in an attempt to resist the measures of taxation which the mother country was trying to impose on the colonies. After the struggle with Great Britain became more acute, twelve colonies met in the First Continental Congress (1774) and considered Galloway's plan of union, which was rejected. In 

1775 the Second Continental Congress met and for six years served as a central governing body for the colonies. Before 1781 there was no constitutional or legal basis for this Congress, but it served as a de facto government (a government in fact). It was somewhat in the nature of a diplomatic body, which could take no important action without instructions from the different states, and therefore was not a powerful central governing body. 

Shortly after Richard Henry Lee had introduced the resolution for independence, he proposed another resolution suggesting a permanent central government. In accordance with this resolution, a committee was appointed to consider the matter, and in 1777 it submitted to Congress the Articles of Confederation. Before these Articles could go into effect, it was necessary that they be ratified by all the states. Maryland refused to ratify because she felt that some of the larger states, which claimed western lands, should cede these lands to the central government. There were a number of other states which had no western lands, and they united with Maryland in this protest. But finally all the states ratified the Articles except Maryland, which steadily refused until the states claiming western lands should give up their claims and cede them to the central government with the recommendation that the central government sell these lands to actual settlers and use the money to pay its debts, and also that the lands thus ceded to the central government should in time be formed into new states to be admitted into the Union. As soon as the first state, New York, made its cession, in 1781, Maryland ratified the Articles and they became the basis for the central government. 

The Articles of Confederation declared that the government was to be a confederacy, or league of friendship, in which each state retained its sovereignty, freedom, and independence." The newly created states were jealous of giving up their power to a central government. They therefore refused to set up a government which might oppress them as the British government had done. The central government under the Articles

of Confederation was responsible to the states. It was felt that only matters of common concern, such as "power of determining on peace and war . . . entering into treaties and alliances," and a few others, should be left to the control of Congress. Such important powers as taxation and the regulation of trade, the states refused to give up. The result was that the government created under the Articles of Confederation was weak. 

Congress did not have enough power to overcome the main difficulties which arose.

Representation and Powers. Under the Articles of Confederation each state was represented in Congress by not less than two nor more than seven members. Each state, regardless of its size, population, or the number of representatives it sent, had one vote. The Articles of Confederation did not provide for a President, or any other chief executive. Congress had power to appoint civil officers, such as secretary of foreign affairs, superintendent of finance, and secretary of war. There was no provision for a national judiciary, but Congress had power to appoint courts to try piracies and felonies committed on the high seas, and likewise to establish courts of appeal in prize cases. Congress also had authority to provide, in a specified manner, for setting up a special court to settle disputes between states concerning their boundaries, or other controversies. 

The main difficulty of the government under the Articles was its weakness. Congress did not have sufficient power to pass laws. There was no executive officer to enforce the laws it did pass, and no regular federal courts to decide cases arising under them. In addition to these difficulties, it required unanimous consent to secure an amendment to the Articles. This was impossible to obtain, and no amendments were made. 

Under these conditions the new government faced many difficulties with which it was unable to cope, and the period during which it was in operation has been designated as the "Critical Period in American history." 

The Creation of a Public Domain. Seven of the thirteen colonies had claimed land west of the Appalachians-in most cases as a result of their charter grants. When independence had been won the disposition of this western land became a question of considerable importance. The six states which owned no western land did not wish to enter into a union in which they would be overshadowed by the states which were not only much larger in area but were in a position to secure much greater revenue through the sale of land. They argued that the Proclamation of 1763 had reduced the territory west of the mountains to "crown lands," and that they should now be given to the central government. Maryland, as we have seen, refused to ratify the Articles of Confederation unless the states

agreed to cede their lands to Congress. The question was further complicated by the fact that the claims of some of the states conflicted. New 

York, followed closely by Virginia, surrendered most of her claim in 1781, and by 1790 all of the other states had done so except Georgia, which did not fall into line until 1802. By this action of the states nearly all of the vast unoccupied area west of the mountains and east of the Mississippi -excepting what are now West Virginia and Kentucky-became the Public Domain from which new states were later formed. 

Congress Adopts a Land Policy. When Congress came into possession of the public domain it was confronted with the task of formulating a system by which the land might be distributed. In the earlier westward movement most of the pioneers had secured the title to land by the simple process of building a cabin and clearing a small amount of land. Since the land was not surveyed the early settlers experienced difficulty in getting a clear title to their land. This was one of the chief grievances of the frontiersmen. In 1785 Congress passed the Land Ordinance, establishing the public land policy which, with some modifications, was followed throughout the entire history of our frontier. This ordinance provided for a survey of the land in ranges divided into townships six miles square. 

Each township was divided into thirty-six sections one mile square. The land was to be sold in entire sections at a price of one dollar per acre. 

Hence the sum of $640 was required for the purchase of a western farm of a whole section. Another provision of the ordinance was that the sixteenth section of every township was to be reserved for the support of the public schools. The settlers who already were pouring into the country were warned that no land would be offered for sale until it had been surveyed. 

By 1787 seven ranges had been laid out and opened to settlement. 

Military Reservations. In making their cessions to Congress several of the states made reservations of land for the payment of their Revolutionary soldiers. Congress, too, had issued land certificates. Some of the soldiers were becoming impatient. In 1786 a group of Revolutionary offi.. cers at Boston organized the Ohio Company of Associates and delegated Dr. Manasseh Cutler, pastor of the Congregational church at Ipswich, Massachusetts, to appear before Congress for the purpose of securing a large tract of land which would be paid for with the certificates which Congress had given them for their services during the Revolution. He was successful not only in securing the desired land for his company, but also in purchasing an additional 5,000,000 acres for the Scioto Company. 

Another grant of 150,000 acres was made to George Rogers Clark and his followers as a reward for their services in conquering the territory. Virginia

reserved the ownership (but not government) of six thousand square miles of land which was known as the Virginia Military District, and Connecticut likewise retained the Western Reserve, one part of which, called the "Fire Lands," was set aside for those whose property had been No./

A Territorial Policy 

Is Adopted. It was a novel experience for the new Confederation, composed of the recently dissatisfied colonies in the British Empire, to be faced with the necessity of formulating a plan for the government of territories of its own. Thomas Jefferson was the chairman of a committee which had been appointed to draft an ordinance for this purpose. His report, which was adopted as the "Ordinance of 1784," provided for a territorial stage during which the inhabitants of the district would have a restricted form of self-government before it could be admitted to statehood. It also provided for the division of the entire public domain between the Appalachians and the Mississippi into eighteen districts, each of which was to enter the Union when its population was equal to that of the smallest state. A clause providing for the exclusion of slavery from the entire West failed to gain the approval of Congress. 

Before the conditions contemplated in the Ordinance of 1784 came about, a new plan was drafted in 1787 and was adopted almost as the "swan song" of the Confederation. It was known as the Northwest Ordinance or the Ordinance of 1787. This most important of the legislative acts of the Confederation Congress provided for the eventual organization of the territory north of the Ohio River into at least three and not more than five states. Until the districts were ready for statehood they were to have governments similar to that provided for in the Ordinance of 1784. 

At first each was to be governed by a governor, a secretary, and three judges, all of whom were to be appointed by Congress. As soon as the population reached 5,000 a territorial legislature was to be organized with the lower house elected by the people and the upper house appointed by Congress. A delegate without a vote was to have a seat in Congress. This

government was very similar to that of colonial Massachusetts. As soon as the population reached 60,000o the district was to be granted statehood on terms of equality with the original states. This was a great improvement over the British colonial system, which had held the colonies in permanent subordination. 

The ordinance also contained a bill of rights which guaranteed freedom of religion, trial by jury, property rights, and public education, and forbade slavery or involuntary servitude except as a punishment of crime. When the new Constitution was ratified the first Congress re-enacted the Ordinance of 1787 for the government of the Northwest Territory. Its greatest importance lies in the fact that it offered to the world a new principle of colonial government-the promise of statehood with democratic selfgovernment for new states on terms of equality with the original states. 

The Western Problem. One of the problems that the new government was called upon to deal with was the trade of the West. Since the close of the Revolution, and even earlier, many people had moved across the mountains and had settled in the West. These people had no outlet across the mountains to the east for their products, and so were obliged to send them down the Ohio River and the Mississippi River, and then to other parts of the world. They were therefore insisting upon the free navigation of the 

Mississippi River. However, Spain, which held the land west of the river as well as Florida, was in control of the Mississippi River at its mouth, and was not willing to permit the Westerners free use of the river. The 

Westerners, therefore, looked to the new government to secure satisfactory arrangements with Spain for the use of the river. Spain knew that unless these western settlers could secure an outlet they would not be loyal to the new government, and she even hoped that the people in the West might break away from the East and join the Spanish provinces. To prevent such an emergency, it became highly important that the problem of the western trade be satisfactorily solved. Washington realized its importance when he said that the West stood "upon a pivot; the touch of a feather would turn them any way."

The establishment of a stronger central government in 1789 quieted the movement for secession and raised the hopes of the Westerners for an early opening of the Mississippi. In 1795, as we shall see later (pp. 214215), their hopes were justified by the conclusion of the Pinckney Treaty. 

Foreign Problems. A further difficulty for the new government arose in securing satisfactory trade arrangements with European powers. Some of these, including Sweden, Prussia, France, and the Netherlands (Holland) made satisfactory treaties with the new government. However, the Ameri-

cans had long been accustomed to use the products imported from Great Britain and were therefore concerned about satisfactory commercial relations with the British. Great Britain, however, was not willing to make a favorable commercial treaty with the new government, and John Adams, who was sent as minister to England, failed to secure satisfactory relations. 

Great Britain excluded American shipping from the British West Indies, and the American government was for a time unable to obtain a favorable commercial treaty. The problem of securing favorable treaties was made more difficult because European powers were in doubt as to whether Congress had power to make treaties, or whether that power belonged to the thirteen independent and sovereign states. 

Financial Disorder. Perhaps one of the most perplexing problems before the new government was that of securing sufficient money to carry on the necessary functions of the government. The Continental Congress had issued vast sums of paper money which had been repudiated. But there was still a national debt of about $45,000,000, of which about $8,- 000,000 was due to foreign nations. In order to meet these obligations, the states were asked by Congress to pay certain sums of money. But the amount received from the states was never enough, and Congress had no power to levy taxes to meet its obligations. Congress asked the states for $10,000,000, but received less than $1,500,000. Because of the lack of revenue, it was suggested that the Articles of Confederation be amended so as to permit Congress to collect a duty of 5 per cent on the value of imports. This money was to be used for the payment of both the interest and the principal of the national debt. To secure an amendment to the 

Articles, it was necessary that all the states agree to it. But Rhode Island refused to agree to such an amendment, and the attempt failed. Congress later tried again to secure additional power by proposing a general revenue amendment, but this again was defeated. 

The state governments likewise were unable to deal successfully with their financial problems. Following the Revolution came a period of depression and economic distress because so much property had been destroyed by the war. To meet the obligations incurred in the war, heavy taxes were levied by some of the states, but the people had less money with which to pay the taxes. Hardship followed for persons who were unable to meet their obligations and they often found themselves confronted with foreclosures and lawsuits; and very often people who had contracted debts lost their property because they could not meet their obligations. Some were even placed in prison for failure to pay their debts. Bitter feeling existed between those who had property and those who had none. Many

of the small farmers came to hate the wealthier people, especially those who attempted to collect debts.

The paper money had been repudiated, and much of the specie (coin) had been drawn out of the country to pay for the goods imported during the years immediately following the war. The people in debt therefore demanded that more paper money be issued so as to make it easier to pay their debts. Before and during the Revolution the American people often resorted to issuing paper money to meet their financial obligations. Now, during the Critical Period, the people again demanded that paper money should be issued. In some states a Paper Money party came into power. Creditors, however, did not wish to be paid in this depreciated money, and very often they ran away from their debtors, refusing to take the money. As a result, laws were passed providing that if the creditors refused to take the money the debtor could deposit the money with the court and advertise the fact in the papers. These notices usually began with the words "Know Ye"; and in time the Paper Money party became known as the "Know Ye" party.

Shays's Rebellion. In Massachusetts the Paper Money party did not gain power, and therefore the debtor group, made up largely of farmers, mechanics, and laborers, rebelled. A mob formed and released those people who had been imprisoned because of their debts. Under the leadership of 

Captain Shays, in 1787, the insurrection spread in the western part of the state. The governor of Massachusetts sent troops to suppress the insurrection, but he became very unpopular because of that action, and in the following election he was defeated.

The inability of the government under the Articles of Confederation to work out a satisfactory solution for the economic and financial problems, together with the difficulty of dealing with foreign nations, produced a feeling of uncertainty. This uncertainty made a stronger government desirable, and many Americans looked toward a revision of the Articles as a possible remedy for a weak central government.

CHAPTER X The Work of the Constitutional 

Convention

Need of a Stronger Government. During the Critical Period many of the more conservative people felt that the central government was unable to cope with the difficult problems of the time, and therefore suggested a revision of the Articles of Confederation in order to secure a stronger government. Alexander Hamilton, as early as 1780, pointed out that the idea of an "uncontrollable sovereignty in each state... will defeat the other powers given to Congress, and make our Union feeble and precarious. 

Congress should have complete sovereignty in all that relates to war, peace, trade, finance." General Henry Knox, of Massachusetts, said, "Our government must be braced, changed, or altered to secure our lives and property." John Marshall, of Virginia, wrote, in 1787, “I fear ... that they have truth on their side who say that man is incapable of governing himself. I fear we may live to see another revolution." The Annapolis Convention (1786). Many American leaders felt that great difficulties might arise from a weak government, and thoughtful men came to believe that something must be done to secure a more efficient government. A beginning toward securing a stronger national government was made in the attempts to amend the Articles, but these attempts failed. 

The problem was finally solved by the calling of the Constitutional Convention in 1787. The first step leading to the calling of the convention was taken when commissioners from Virginia and Maryland met at Mount Vernon for the purpose of settling a dispute which had arisen over the navigation of the Potomac River. At the meeting, Virginia asked that another meeting be held, to which all the states were to send delegates for considering the problems of commerce in general. This meeting was held in 1786, at Annapolis, but delegates from only five states attended. 190

The Constitutional Convention. At the Annapolis meeting it was recommended that a convention be held at Philadelphia, in May of the following year, for the purpose of revising the Articles of Confederation. 

This proposal was submitted to Congress, and after some hesitation that body issued the call for the famous convention that opened on May 25, 1787. Sixty-five members were chosen by the different states, but only fifty-five attended, and of these only thirty-nine finally signed the new Constitution that was framed by this convention.

Part of the first few lines of the Constitution finally adopted and signed by members of the convention; from a photograph of the original document. For complete wording see Appendix, pages xxviii-xxxv. 

Of the thirty-nine who signed, six had signed the Declaration of Independence, and four had signed the Articles of Confederation. As a group, they were more conservative and more interested in securing order out of chaos, than was the Revolutionary group. Many of the Revolutionary leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Samuel Adams, Richard 

Henry Lee, and Patrick Henry, for example, did not attend; neither did John Hancock; nor Thomas Jefferson, who was in France; nor John

Adams, who was in England. A majority of those who attended were well educated. Many of them had known each other as students in American colleges, and some of them had studied law in England. Conspicuous among those who attended the convention were Edmund Randolph, James Madison, George Mason, and George Washington, of Virginia. 

From New York came Alexander Hamilton; from Pennsylvania, Benjamin 

Franklin, Robert Morris, and James Wilson. Oliver Ellsworth and Roger 

Sherman came from Connecticut. Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and

John Rutledge of South Carolina, Rufus King of Massachusetts, Luther 

Martin of Maryland, John Dickinson of Delaware, and William Paterson of New Jersey were among the many other prominent leaders.

George Washington was selected as the presiding officer. James 

Madison, of Virginia, a profound student of government, was one of the most influential members present and is sometimes referred to as the Father of the Constitution. He took a seat near the front of the room and kept careful notes of everything that took place. It is largely from his notes, published in 1840, fifty-three years after the convention met, that historians have learned what difficult problems were discussed at the convention.

Difficulties to be Faced. The convention held its meetings behind closed doors because it faced many serious problems. As soon as the delegates assembled, it became evident that it was difficult to revise the Articles and that a new structure of government was necessary. The important problem which was to be decided then was what form of government should be established. Should there be a government in which the states would exercise most power, in which the central government should be subordinate to the states; or should there be a strong central government, with the states subordinate? The experiences of the Confederation had taught the people that the central government must have sufficient power to act on important questions of a general nature. One of the greatest difficulties under the Confederation was that the states were selfish, and placed their own interests above the welfare of the nation. Another problem before the convention was to find a way of overcoming this selfishness. 

Two important plans for the organization of a government were suggested. One, known as the Virginia Plan, suggested a strong central government, one in which the states should be represented in proportion to their population; while a second plan, known as the Paterson Plan, or New 

Jersey Plan, suggested more power for the states and proposed that the states should be represented equally. The Virginia Plan is sometimes referred to as the Large State Plan because most of the larger states were in favor of it since it proposed representation according to population, which was an advantage to the large states. The smaller states objected to the Virginia Plan and supported the Paterson Plan, which was referred to as the Small State Plan. The supporters of the Paterson Plan wanted equal representation so that the small states might have the same influence in Congress as the large states. 

The Great Compromise. In order to overcome the difficulty, a compromise known as the Compromise on Representation was made, by which it was agreed to have two houses in Congress-the lower house, or House of Representatives, in which the states are represented in proportion to their population, and the upper house, or Senate, in which the states are

HB 

Arguing an important question in the Constitutional Convention at Philadelphia, 1787 193

represented equally. Following this compromise, a federal government was established. It was a government in which the states retained important powers, but in which much power was given to the central government. The central government, or Federal government, was given many powers that Congress did not enjoy under the Articles of Confederation. 

Other Compromises. After the question of representation had been settled, the question next arose as to whether the negro slaves should be counted as population in determining the number of representatives. The convention finally agreed that in apportioning both representation and direct taxes to the states according to population only three fifths of the number of slaves should be included. 

A serious discussion arose over the question of giving Congress power to regulate commerce. One of the difficulties under the Articles of 

Confederation was that Congress did not have this power. The commercial states were anxious that Congress should have power to pass navigation acts, while some of the states feared that this power might add to the freight rates, and that Congress might use this power to forbid the importation of slaves. A compromise was agreed to, which provided that Congress should have the power to pass navigation laws, but that Congress should not prohibit the importation of slaves for a period of twenty years.

A Government of Delegated and Limited Powers. The powers to be exercised by Congress are enumerated in the Constitution. For example, the Constitution provides that Congress shall have power to lay and collect taxes, to coin money, to declare war, and to raise and support armies, as well as a number of other powers which are for the general welfare of the states. Thus the Federal government is one of delegated or enumerated powers; and it is also one of limited powers. Some of the ideas which went into the Constitution of the United States were evolved by the colonies in their struggle with Great Britain. While the colonies were engaged in the argument with the mother country over the nature of the British Empire, they consistently maintained that Parliament had power to act only on matters of imperial or general concern, while the colonies themselves should manage their own internal affairs. They were arguing for a government in which there was distribution of power. Now, in the formation of the Constitution, they distributed power, giving to Congress such powers as they felt the central government should have because they were of general concern; while those powers relating to their own internal affairs were retained by the states.

In the struggle with Great Britain, the colonies also came to believe that the powers of government should be limited. Thus when James Otis made his speech against the writs of assistance (see pp. 134-135), he said that an act against the constitution was void. He maintained that there was an English or British constitution which (although not written) was really binding on the British government. The idea prevailed throughout America that government should be kept within certain limits, and that the limits should be set down in a written constitution. 

The Form of Government. The framers of the Constitution felt that some method should be provided whereby the central government should have more authority than it had under the Articles. A clause was therefore inserted in the Constitution, stating that "This Constitution, and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof; and all treaties made, or which shall be made, under the authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land; and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, anything in the Constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding." This statement, of course, does not say that the Federal government, established under the Constitution, shall be sovereign. The framers of the Constitution felt that in some respects the states should be sovereign, while in other respects the national government should be sovereign. Some believed that sovereignty was divided between the states and the nation, while others believed that all sovereignty remained in the states. 

The members of the convention decided that there should be a national government, consisting of legislative, executive, and judicial departments. 

The members of the convention were acquainted with the state constitutions which had been formed during the period of the Revolution, and which had provided for these three departments of government. 

Another important problem before the convention was to find a method for selecting the President of the United States. Some felt that the President should be chosen by Congress, but others argued that he should be independent of the legislative department. The convention therefore provided for the election of the President and of the Vice-President by the votes of electors, each state to choose as many presidential electors as it has members in Congress-counting both senators and representatives. 

Checks and Balances. The form of government provided that the executive department shall have a check on the legislative department in that laws passed by both houses of Congress may be vetoed by the President, but, if vetoed, may become laws after being passed by a two-thirds vote of both houses. Likewise, there was a check on the President, for the

Senate has the power to confirm or reject appointments made by the President, and to confirm or reject treaties proposed by the President. 

Finally, the Supreme Court, or the judicial department, has exercised the power to declare laws unconstitutional. 

Provision was made for amending the Constitution so that it can be revised to meet the needs of a growing nation. Amendments to the Constitution may be proposed by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress. 

Amendments thus proposed become part of the Constitution if they are ratified by three fourths of the states. Amendments may be ratified by three fourths of the state legislatures or by three fourths of the states through constitutional conventions called for that purpose. It is also provided that on application of the legislatures of two thirds of the states, Congress shall call a convention for the purpose of proposing amendments. 

Amendments thus proposed would become part of the Constitution if ratified by three fourths of the states. Many important amendments have been proposed by Congress, and those that have been ratified by the necessary number of states are now printed as part of the Constitution. 

The Ratification of the Constitution. The work of the Constitutional 

Convention was completed on September 17, 1787. That day has since been designated as Constitution Day, and appropriate exercises are held by many schools and civic and patriotic organizations in honor of that occasion. As soon as the Constitution was completed, it was submitted to 

Congress with the suggestion that Congress transmit the Constitution to the state legislatures for ratification by the states. The Constitution itself provided that it should go into effect as soon as it was ratified by the conventions of nine states.

The Constitution was thus placed before the people of the different states for ratification, and a lively contest ensued. Opposition developed and in many states a very important struggle took place between the group in favor of the Constitution and the group opposed to it. Those who favored its adoption were called Federalists, while the group opposed to ratification were known as Antifederalists. Some of those favoring the 

Constitution wrote a series of pamphlets, in which they discussed the advantages to be gained by its ratification. A number of these pamphlets, written by Hamilton, Madison, and Jay, were known as The Federalist. 

By September 13, 1788, the Constitution had been ratified by eleven states, and was ready to be put into operation. 

Elections were held and senators and representatives were chosen for the new government, which was to begin on the first Wednesday in March, 1789. in New York, which was then the capital of the United States,

Because that day was March 4, the terms of the members of Congress and of the President began and ended on March 4 until after 1933, when the 

Twentieth Amendment to the Constitution changed the date. This amendment, sometimes referred to as the Lame Duck Amendment, provides that the term of office for members of Congress shall begin on January 3 and the term of office for the President shall begin on January 20.

Many people had objected to the Constitution because they felt that their rights were not sufficiently guaranteed. They felt that there should be a bill of rights. Some states ratified the Constitution with the understanding that amendments should immediately be made to the Constitution, setting forth these rights of the people. The new government took up this matter, and on September 25, 1789, Congress proposed to the states the first ten amendments, constituting a Bill of Rights. Following the sub-
