CHAPTER XI The Organization of the New Government 

The Constitution in Operation. When the ninth state had ratified the 

Constitution, the Congress under the Articles of Confederation helped to put the new government into operation. The first Wednesday in January was set as the time for choosing presidential electors. These cast their ballots on the first Wednesday in February; and the first Wednesday in March was set for the beginning of the government. That was the day on which 

Congress should meet. However, on that day not enough members of 

Congress were present in New York to organize Congress, so the matter was delayed until April, when enough members of both houses were present to organize.

The House of Representatives chose as its presiding officer (Speaker), Frederick A. C. Muhlenberg, who had held a similar position in the state legislature of Pennsylvania. The Speaker was empowered to appoint committees and the chairman of each. He was also given the right to decide which of several members, desiring to speak, should be recognized, and in time he became a very powerful factor in the House. The Vice-President of the United States is the presiding officer of the Senate, according to the Constitution. However, when the Senate met in April, the Vice-President had not yet been elected, so the Senate chose as its presiding officer a president pro tempore, who presided until the Vice-President was elected. 

As soon as the preliminary steps had been taken and the Houses were organized, they proceeded to the important business of counting the electoral votes and deciding who had been chosen President and Vice-President. (It will be well at this point to read the original Section 1 of Article II of the Constitution.) After the presidential electors in each state had cast their votes, each voting for two men, lists of these votes were sent to Con- 200

Drawing by David Hendrickson 

Departure of Washington from Mount Vernon for his inauguration as President gress to be counted at a joint session of the two houses. The person having the highest number of votes, provided he had a majority, would be declared President. The person having the second highest number would be declared Vice-President. The electors did not designate one person for President and another for Vice-President. (This method of voting was changed in 1804 by the Twelfth Amendment, which provided that the electors should cast separate votes for President and for Vice-President.)

When the lists of votes were opened in Congress in April, 1789, it was found that George Washington's name was on the ballot of every elector. 

He was the unanimous choice for President. John Adams had more votes than any other candidate except Washington and was, therefore, declared Vice-President.

Method of Choosing the Electors. The presidential electors for each state are now chosen on a general state ticket. However, in the first election, this was not the case in all the states. In five of the states the legislature elected the presidential electors. This custom was continued in some states for a long time. In two of the states the electors were chosen from districts rather than from the state as a whole. Under that method it was possible to have electors from some districts for one party and from other districts for another party. In three states, in the first election, the electors were chosen by popular vote on a general state ticket as they are now. New York lost its vote in the first election (1789) because of an

unsettled contest as to the method of selecting electors. Rhode Island and North Carolina were not members of the Union in time for the first election.

Washington the First President. The fact that Washington was chosen by a unanimous vote showed that he had the confidence of the people. The service he had rendered during the American Revolution and in the Constitutional Convention, as well as his advice and counsel during the difficult times of the Critical Period, made him an outstanding leader, and the new government prospered under his wise guidance. The Constitution of the United States indicated merely in broad outline what the form of government should be. It was necessary for the President and Congress to work out many of the details, and for that reason it was highly important that the government from the beginning should be in the hands of those who were friendly toward the Constitution. In the first election, the Federalists who had supported the Constitution elected most of the members of Congress, though some of the members were Antifederalists. 

The President's Cabinet. The Constitution refers to "heads of departments," but contains no definite provision as to the number or nature of these departments. It was the duty of Congress to pass the necessary laws creating them. The first one created was the Department of Foreign 

Affairs, now called the Department of State; the second was the Department of War; and the third, the Department of the Treasury. In addition to the heads, or "secretaries," of these departments, there were also the offices of Attorney General and Postmaster General, not then called heads of departments. Washington selected capable men to fill these offices. For 

Secretary of State he appointed Thomas Jefferson, who was representing the United States in France at the time. For Secretary of War he selected Henry Knox; and for Secretary of the Treasury, Alexander Hamilton; while Edmund Randolph, of Virginia, was appointed Attorney 

General. The heads of the departments in time became known as the 

President's Cabinet, and their number has been increased until today the 

President has a cabinet of ten members.

The Judiciary. Congress was also called upon to enact laws giving form to the judicial system of the United States. The Constitution merely provides that the judicial power of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court and such inferior courts as Congress may from time to time establish, the judges thereof to hold office during good behavior. The 

Constitution also gives the President the power to appoint the judges of the Supreme Court, with the Senate's approval. It should be noted, however, that the Constitution does not designate the number of judges for

the Supreme Court, nor does it give details regarding its organization or functions. These were details to be worked out by the new government. 

Congress, therefore, passed the Judiciary Act of 1789, which provided for a Supreme Court made up of five associate justices and one chief justice. 

It also provided for other Federal courts. Later acts increased the number of justices in the Supreme Court until now there are nine. 

Financial Legislation. One of the first laws passed by Congress was for the purpose of raising revenue. Alexander Hamilton, the Secretary of the Treasury, suggested several means for raising revenue. One of the first measures he recommended was a tariff act, imposing a duty on imports. In the discussion of the tariff act in Congress some of the principles which have affected our later tariff acts were brought out. A member from 

Pennsylvania suggested that the duty should not be laid uniformly on all imports, but rather upon such as competed with our domestic industries. 

Scene in New York about 1800: mural painting by Ezra Winter 

Courtesy Manhattan Company

The idea there suggested was the protective principle, though the measure was devised largely for the purpose of raising revenue. The New England states opposed a tax on molasses, which was imported for the purpose of making rum, while other sections of the country felt that molasses should be taxed in order to raise revenue for the government. The act as it was finally passed, laid a duty averaging about 8 per cent of the value of the imports taxed. Following the tariff measure, Hamilton recommended that 

Congress pass a law providing for an excise tax on distilled liquor. The law was passed, but it did not produce much revenue; however, it did create a new body of officials, and so helped to increase the importance of the government.

Public Credit of the United States. One of the most pressing problems before the new government was that of providing for a sound financial system so as to establish the credit of the United States. During the war large debts had been contracted. These debts had to be paid if the credit of the government was to be sound. The total national debt, foreign and domestic, now amounted to about $54,000,000. In addition to this vast sum, the various states had incurred debts amounting to about $21,500,000. 

Many of these debts existed in the form of bonds which the government had issued. The bonds had declined in value because many of the holders doubted the government's ability to pay them in full. Hamilton proposed that this debt be funded; that is, he suggested that Congress should authorize the treasury to issue new bonds, bearing a uniform rate of interest. 

The old bonds, which were of varying denominations and different rates of interest, were to be paid at par by giving the new bonds in exchange. 

The taxing power of Congress made it possible for the government to pay the interest on the new bonds and thus stabilize their market value. 

A vigorous fight developed over the question of funding the public debt. Many of the outstanding bonds had been issued by the Continental 

Congress and were no longer in the hands of the original holders. Many original owners had sold their bonds to speculators, who had paid much less than the face value. In many cases speculators had bought bonds for as little as fifteen cents on the dollar. James Madison felt that if the government should now redeem these bonds at par, the speculators would make unduly large profits. He proposed that speculators be paid the market value, only, and that the difference between the market value and the original value be paid to those who originally bought the bonds. 

Such a plan, however, would be difficult to administer, and Hamilton objected to it even though it brought on disagreement between Madison and himself. Hamilton maintained that the government had pledged itself

to pay the debt in full, and in order to establish the credit of the government it was absolutely necessary that every cent of the debt be paid regardless of whether the bonds were held by the original purchasers or by speculators who had bought them at a much lower price. Madison was the leader of a group which opposed the funding of the debt, but the plan proposed by Hamilton was adopted and the debt was refunded. 

The Assumption of the State Debts. Hamilton next proposed that the Federal government take over the debts ($21,500,000) of the states. 

He felt that those debts had been incurred by the states in the defense of the nation—that is, for the common interest-and should be assumed by the general government. This suggestion brought on very serious opposition on the part of some of the Southern states which had already paid a large part of their debts and felt that it would be unfair to have the Federal government assume the debts of those states which had not paid as large a proportion of them. There was also political opposition to the assumption of the state debts. Hamilton was interested in strengthening the power of the central government, and felt that the assumption of the state debts would bring about that result, for the holders of bonds would then look to the central government for their interest and capital rather than to the states. This would strengthen the central government at the expense of the power of the states. A bitter controversy over the question of assumption followed when the matter was brought to a vote in Congress. 

It failed to carry by two votes.

Hamilton, however, was not satisfied with defeat that was so near to victory. There was at the time another problem before Congress—that of the location of the national capital. Several of the Southern states that were opposed to the assumption of state debts were anxious to have the capital located on the Potomac River. Hamilton felt that a bargain might be arranged whereby the Southerners would vote for the assumption of state debts in exchange for the location of the capital on the Potomac. 

With this compromise in mind, Jefferson, the Secretary of State, at the suggestion of Hamilton, gave a dinner at which it was agreed that two Southern members who had previously voted against the assumption of State debts should vote for it, while in exchange Hamilton would secure votes for the location of the capital on the Potomac. Both bills then passed Congress.

The First Bank of the United States. The next step in Hamilton's financial program was for the establishment of a Bank of the United States, which was to be privately owned but chartered by Congress. This bank, with a capital stock not to exceed $10,000,000, of which the government of

the United States should subscribe one fifth, was to receive a charter for a period of twenty years. Hamilton argued that the growing business of the 

United States made necessary additional banking facilities. The experience with paper money issued by the states and by the Continental Con- The first Bank of the United States, in Philadelphia gress had taught many people that a better-regulated system of money was needed. Hamilton argued that the establishment of a central bank which would issue notes and would redeem them on demand was a good way to provide a sound currency. There were, however, many friends of the state banks who were opposed to a central bank. They held that a United 

States Bank would be a great financial advantage to the moneyed class, and that it would not serve the general interests of the people. Madison's view was supported by Thomas Jefferson, who argued that Congress had only those powers which were enumerated in the Constitution, and no power to authorize a bank was listed in the Constitution. 

Strict versus Broad Interpretation of the Constitution. The law creating the bank passed Congress and was sent to President Washington for his signature. He asked members of his cabinet for their opinions as to the constitutionality of the proposed law. Hamilton recommended that the bill be signed, for the Constitution, he pointed out, gave to Congress, in addition to those powers specifically enumerated, also power "to make all

THE 

laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the government of the United States, or in any department or officer thereof." 

He maintained that the bank was necessary in order to facilitate the handling of money by the government. 

He argued further that the Constitution should be interpreted broadly to give Congress the powers that were necessary for establishing the bank. His doctrine of interpreting the Constitution broadly is sometimes called the doctrine of implied powers, and had as its object the strengthening of the central government.

"Shrine" in the Library of Congress, Washington, D. C., where the original draft of the Constitution is kept 

Thomas Jefferson, on the other hand, felt that Congress did not have these implied powers. He argued that Congress had only those powers which were definitely stated in the Constitution. He denied that the "necessary and proper" clause could be properly interpreted so as to grant to Congress the power to establish a bank. 

Washington, after considering the arguments of both Hamilton and Jefferson, was inclined to the broad construction of the Constitution. He accepted Hamilton's doctrine of implied powers, and signed the bill and committed his administration to the policy of broad construction. 

The Whisky Rebellion. Serious opposition had developed to some of 

Hamilton's financial measures. The most serious came as the result of the excise tax law. Many of the farmers on the frontier, because of poor transportation facilities and the high cost of transporting their grain to market, converted it into liquor, some of which was for domestic use. This whisky could be transported to market much more easily, and at a much smaller cost, than the grain from which it was made. When these western farmers learned of the excise measure, which would place a tax on whisky, they seriously objected. Many of them did not understand why they should be taxed for the benefit, as they said, of the propertied class. They felt that Great Britain had been resisted in the Revolution because of oppressive tax measures. Now they did not wish the new government to

oppress them in a like manner, and hence they refused to pay the tax, and government collectors became very unpopular in their midst. Finally, in 

1794, when the government attempted to serve warrants on those who had been indicted for refusing to pay the tax, a determined resistance arose, known as the Whisky Rebellion. Those in charge of the government felt that the people who objected to the tax were ignorant and unpatriotic, and Hamilton urged that the government "shall assert its strength and that law and order shall be enforced," and advised Washington to use force if necessary.

The militia was called out, and marched toward the scene of the revolt. 

The army moved slowly, however, and messengers had been sent ahead, trying to restore order and persuade the people to submit to the government. The revolt was thus easily put down without bloodshed. Several of the leaders were arrested and put in jail, but only two of them were convicted, and these were pardoned by the President. The importance of the Whisky Rebellion, however, lay in the fact that the government had shown itself strong enough to cope with the situation. The people learned now that there was a central government, with authority to lay taxes, and with sufficient force to suppress a rebellion against it. 

The Rise of Political Parties. Political parties appeared early in our history. During the Constitutional Convention, as already stated, there were two distinct groups. After the Constitution had been drafted and was submitted to the states for ratification, those who favored the ratification of the Constitution were known as the Federalists, while those who were opposed to ratification were known as Antifederalists. The Constitution itself made no provision for political parties, and Washington had hoped that it would be possible to have a government without parties or factions. However, soon after the new government was inaugurated, those who supported Hamilton's financial measures—the funding scheme, assumption of state debts, the tariff, the national bank, and the excise law -made up a distinct group, while those opposed to his measures composed an entirely different group. Those favoring Hamilton's program believed in a broad, or loose, construction of the Constitution, while his opponents believed in a strict or narrow construction. These groups also differed on the attitude that the government should take toward the French Revolution. Those favoring Hamilton's measures were in general opposed to the 

French Revolution, while those who opposed his measures were more sympathetic toward the French. 

After the disagreement over the chartering of the bank, Jefferson, who had opposed many of Hamilton's measures, resigned from the cabinet and

became the leader of a group which he called the Republican party. Many of the Antifederalist group who accepted his views of government joined this party. Hamilton and Jefferson represented two widely differing points of view. Hamilton favored a strong central government-a government which, in the main, was interested in preserving and promoting the economic welfare of the merchant class, or the wealthier, propertyholding, industrial group; while Jefferson believed in a less centralized government, and was more interested in local government. He had faith in the common man and his ability to vote wisely; he was especially interested in the small-farmer group, and may be said to have represented the agrarian interests. 

Foreign Affairs in Washington's Administration. During Washington's first term as President (1789-1793), problems concerning the organization of the government and domestic policies took most of his time; but after his re-election for a second term, foreign affairs came to the front. In the years following 1789 the French Revolution, a struggle between the privileged and underprivileged classes in France, had brought on many reforms in France. A large number of Americans were sympathetic with these reforms because they had themselves recently passed through a revolution, in which they secured reforms by overthrowing the control of the British government. Many Americans looked upon the French Revolution as a struggle in behalf of the rights of man, and rejoiced in its success. 

Liberty poles were erected, and people became interested in the slogan of the French Revolution, "Liberty, equality, and fraternity." The Hamiltonians, however, felt that there was too much democracy in the French Revolution, that it meant the overthrow of law and order, and the substitution for it of "government by the rabble." Many Democratic clubs were organized in America, but they were frowned upon by the Federalists, who considered them "hotbeds of treason."

In 1792 the French Revolution became more violent, and the revolutionists, after executing their king and queen, were involved in a war with Great Britain. The newly formed French government sent Edmond 

Charles Genest, or Genêt-usually called "Citizen Genêt"-to the United States as the representative of revolutionary France. The French were interested in securing the support of the Americans, and felt that they were entitled to it, for during our Revolution they had loaned money and sent troops to help overthrow the rule of the British. They pointed to the 

Treaty of Alliance made between France and the United States in 1778, by which the United States had agreed to help France in case she were attacked. As soon as France and Great Britain were at war, the French

גוי 

Many Americans who sympathized with the French Revolution raised "liberty poles" and wore "liberty caps." 210

reminded the United States of that alliance and looked for aid. The 

United States government was confronted with a difficult foreign problem, and President Washington asked the advice of his cabinet members. 

Alexander Hamilton, the Secretary of the Treasury, argued that the treaty of 1778 was no longer in force, since it was a treaty which had been made with the Bourbon monarchy, which had now been overthrown by the revolutionists. He further contended that the American republic was not required to come to the assistance of France, because the treaty had provided for help only in case of a defensive war, while the war in which France was engaged was offensive. Thomas Jefferson, the Secretary of 

State, on the other hand, maintained that the treaty had been made between two nations, and was binding even though the form of government of France had been changed. Washington had to make a decision, and accepted the point of view that the war which France was carrying on was an offensive war, and according to the treaty, the United States was bound only in case of a defensive war. In accordance with this view he issued a Proclamation of Neutrality, in which he announced that the United States would not be a party to the conflict. 

Genêt, however, felt that there were many people in America who were interested in helping the French; that Washington, though he was at the head of the government, was in reality not expressing the sentiments and wishes of the American people. He therefore attempted to organize expeditions in the United States against Louisiana and also against Florida. 

He proceeded to issue letters to privateers and encouraged Americans to fit out ships to attack British commerce. Jefferson, Secretary of State, in charge of foreign affairs, carried out Washington's Proclamation of Neutrality and protested against Genêt's activities, which had become so objectionable that Washington asked the French government to recall him. The new party in power in France was no longer interested in what 

Genêt was trying to accomplish, and recalled him. But Genêt feared that return to France would be dangerous, as many were being sent to the guillotine. He therefore decided to remain in America, though no longer in the service of France.

Disputes over Trade. New difficulties with foreign countries arose. In the war between Great Britain and France, the United States as a neutral nation suffered many disadvantages, for the British navy was in control of the sea. The Americans were anxious to carry on trade with the French 

West Indies, for much of the trade which had been carried by French ships was wiped out by the British navy. American shipowners wished to take over this trade, and the French were willing that they should, but Great

Britain maintained that trade which was limited in times of peace should not be open during war. The British felt that France should not have a monopoly of this trade in times of peace, and later in war, when she could not carry it on herself, be permitted to allow the Americans, under a neutral flag, to take it. The United States seriously objected to the British attitude toward neutral trade. 

The outbreak of the European war seemed beneficial to American commerce. Many articles produced in America were now in great demand in 

Europe. The planters were much interested in raising crops which could be sold to Europe, for American foodstuffs were in demand and our farmers were enjoying high prices. With this additional trade, American shipbuilding increased, American merchants became prosperous, labor received higher wages, and prosperity became general. But England embarked on a policy to cut off this neutral trade. She had for several centuries enjoyed the advantage of being the most important naval power, and so had developed a system of international law which was beneficial to her own interests.

The Americans maintained that since they were neutral, they should not be molested, and should have the freedom of the seas; they disputed the British position on several points of international law. The most important of these were the rules concerning contraband of war. 

The term "contraband of war" means articles that are necessary for war. 

The United States maintained that the foodstuffs which our farmers produced were not contraband of war, while Great Britain claimed the right to seize American vessels carrying foodstuffs on the ground that the foodstuffs should be classed as contraband because without them the war could not be carried on. Great Britain further declared many of the French ports blockaded, and the United States, on the other hand, maintained that a blockade, in order to be legal, must be effective. Our government maintained that the British did not have sufficient vessels to make the American ships of the 38

blockade effective, and therefore insisted on the right to send vessels to Europe, even to French ports. 

Another point of controversy between the British and the Americans was the question of the "right of search" and impressment. The British claimed the right to stop American vessels and examine their papers and their cargo. This the United States would not concede. Great Britain maintained that many of her citizens had left the British navy and were now on American ships. She therefore claimed the right to stop American ships and impress British citizens; that is, take them off and force them into the British navy. She further maintained that anyone who was 

English-born would always be an Englishman, while the United States held that English-born sailors who were naturalized Americans should not be claimed by England, and that it was the duty of the American government to protect its citizens, whether they were native-born or naturalized. 

The Jay Treaty. President Washington in 1794 sent John Jay, the

Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, to London on a diplomatic mission for the purpose of securing an agreement with the British government. 

John Jay was a capable diplomat, but he did not make the best of his opportunities, partly because of his timidity, and also because of the military weakness of the United States. The British drove a hard bargain with him, and the proposed treaty was considered unfavorable to the United States. In it, however, Great Britain agreed to evacuate the posts in the American Northwest which, contrary to the treaty of 1783, she had held since the Revolution. She also agreed to arbitrate the case of disputed boundaries, as well as the adjustment of injuries done to American shipping. The treaty did not mention the impressment of American seamen, and this omission was a great disappointment to the Americans, for they had greatly resented that British practice. The important question of British trade was also left unsatisfactory to the Americans. Our vessels early nineteenth century

The main house, in the foreground at the right, has been kept nearly as it was in Washington's time. were granted very restricted privileges in the British West Indies, and were not permitted to carry such of their products as molasses, sugar, coffee, cotton, or cocoa to any part of the world except to the United States. 

Washington submitted the treaty to the Senate for ratification even though he was not highly pleased with it. Many people referred to the treaty as a "plot against the liberty of the people." After much discussion the Senate approved of ratification only if the treaty should be modified by omitting the undesirable parts relating to trade with the West Indies. 

To this modification, however, Great Britain agreed, and the treaty, duly ratified, proved to be favorable to the United States. The evacuation of the British posts in the Northwest-the region between the Great Lakes and the Ohio River-led to the settlement of that section. 

The Pinckney Treaty (1795). Soon after the Jay treaty was concluded, Spain agreed to a treaty by which she admitted the American

claim to the parallel of 31 degrees north latitude as the southern boundary of the United States (map, p. 182), and granted the free navigation of the 

Mississippi River, also permitting New Orleans to be used as a place for deposit. This treaty,* negotiated for the United States by Thomas Pinckney, settled successfully one of the difficult problems in the West, namely, the opening of the Mississippi River.

Washington's Retirement. The many difficulties which had presented themselves during Washington's first term made him tired of public life and anxious to return to his home at Mount Vernon. However, his friends urged him to accept a second term because times were still critical, and the nation needed his counsel and guidance. He finally agreed to become a candidate, and was re-elected unanimously, while Adams was again chosen Vice-President. Four years later, however, Washington decided that he should retire, and by refusing to accept a third term he established a precedent which has been continued until this day, namely, that the President should not hold office for more than two terms. In his Farewell Address he cautioned the people of the United States against the danger of sectionalism, and warned them against the evils of party and factional strife. 

He also urged that the United States, in its foreign affairs, should preserve the policy of neutrality, and avoid permanent alliances with European nations.

The Election of John Adams. In 1796, as the time came for another election, John Adams and Thomas Pinckney were selected as the Federalist candidates for President and Vice-President, while Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr were chosen by the Republicans. Alexander Hamilton distrusted Adams and hoped to reverse the order of the candidates so that Pinckney might be elected President and Adams Vice-President. Each elector, you remember, at elections before 1804, simply cast votes for two men, without specifying which one was preferred for President and which one for Vice-President. Alexander Hamilton tried to influence some of the electors to vote for Pinckney and not for Adams, thereby giving Pinckney the largest vote, so that he would be elected President. However, his plan became known, and much to his surprise, the result was entirely different from what he expected. Some of Adams's friends were afraid that Pinckney would receive the largest number of votes, so they declined to vote for Pinckney, with the result that Adams was elected President; and the person having the second largest number of votes was Jefferson, the Republican candidate for President, who therefore was elected Vice-President. *Commonly called the Pinckney Treaty but sometimes known as the Treaty of San Lorenzo Real.

Foreign Problems During Adams's Administration. Foreign problems, which were so important while Washington was President, continued to come up during Adams's administration. France was disappointed because the United States had made the Jay Treaty. She felt that the sympathies of the United States were with England rather than with France. James 

Monroe, a friend of Jefferson, who was representing the United States in France, was so sympathetic with the French point of view that he was recalled, and President Adams appointed as his successor a Federalist, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney-brother of Thomas Pinckney. The French 

In government, however, refused to accept Pinckney as our minister. an attempt to satisfy the French, Adams sent John Marshall and Elbridge Gerry to join Pinckney in France. The French government was still reluctant to deal with this commission, but the French foreign minister, Talleyrand, sent his agents to inform the commissioners that the French government would negotiate if bribes were given to him and his associates, and if a large sum of money should be paid into the French treasury.

Our representatives being unwilling to compromise in this manner, and submit to bribery, broke off negotiations and reported the affair to President Adams. The Federalists had been pro-English and more or less anti-French, while the opposition, the Republicans, had been pro-French. 

President Adams realized that here was an opportunity to weaken the opposition, so in March, 1798, he reported the negotiations to Congress. 

He did not call the French agents by name, but merely referred to them as Mr. X, Mr. Y, and Mr. Z. The negotiations therefore came to be known in history as the XYZ affair. The American people were outraged by this attempt on the part of the French to extract bribes from the United States. 

There was a decided reaction against French sympathizers in this country, and many former Republicans who had been pro-French, now, because of this incident, went over to the Federalist party. 

President Adams declared that he would not send another minister to France without first having assurance that our minister would be received, respected, and honored as the representative of a free, powerful, and independent nation. Feeling against the French government ran high, and it looked as if war might result. The Federalists began to make preparations for war, and declared the French Treaty of Alliance of 1778 at an end. 

Congress passed an act providing for the raising of additional men for the army, and the officers in the navy were instructed to capture French ships which were interfering with our commerce. This resulted in naval engagements in the West Indies region, so that, though no war had been declared

on either side, war was actually being waged. The Supreme Court later ruled that a limited war existed. The war is referred to as the Naval War of 1798, during which period the Americans captured eighty-five armed vessels. Washington was again named commander in chief of the army, though Alexander Hamilton was appointed major general in command, but no fighting took place on land. 

It was soon discovered that France did not want war, and near the end of 1798 the United States received assurances that France was willing to receive a minister from the United States, and would respect him as the representative of a free nation. A treaty was negotiated whereby the 

United States was released from the Treaty of Alliance, and in return gave up its claim to damages for injuries inflicted upon our commerce. 

The Alien and Sedition Acts. While the feeling against the French government was developing, the Federalists, who were in power in Congress, took advantage of their opportunity and passed laws intended to curb liberalism and suppress any French citizens in this country who were taking an active part against the Federalist program. The first of these acts was known as the Naturalization Law. Foreigners had theretofore been permitted to become American citizens after five years of residence. The new law provided that before acquiring citizenship, a foreigner must reside in this country for a period of fourteen years.* A second bill, known as the Alien Act, was passed, which empowered the President to deport (send out of the country) any aliens (foreigners) whom he considered dangerous to the peace and safety of our country. A third law, known as the Alien Enemy Act, provided that the President could deport resident subjects of any country with which the United States might be at war, and place restraint on those who remained in the United States. 

The most objectionable of these acts was the fourth, known as the Sedition Act, which provided for severe punishment of any persons who "shall . . . unlawfully combine or conspire together, with intent to oppose any measure or measures of the government of the United States. . . 

It further forbade any person to ". . . write, print, utter or publish.. any false, scandalous, and malicious writing or writings against the government of the United States, or either house of the Congress of the United 

States or the President of the United States with intent to defame...."

The Alien Act was not enforced, but under the Sedition Act there were a number of convictions. *Under later laws the required period of residence was again made five years, as it is now for most aliens.

These acts were considered by the Republicans to be grossly unfair, for some of the members of their party were aliens. Under our political system, the party out of power often gets control of the government by criticizing the party in power. With a Sedition Act in force it was against the law to criticize the President or Congress, a fact which made it difficult for the party out of power (in this case the Republican) to defeat its opponents. 

The Republicans considered the act unjust, and felt that the acts of the Federalists went too far in the direction of centralization, and that the powers of the states had been interfered with. They pointed to the First 

Amendment to the Constitution of the United States, which provides that "Congress shall make no law . . . abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press. 

Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions. What would the Republicans do about the Alien and Sedition Laws? Would they sit by and see their progress checked by the passage of laws which would prevent their election to office? Such was not the plan of Jefferson and those associated with him. Jefferson felt that the best way to deal with the matter was to bring it to the attention of the voters, for he had confidence in the judgment of the people. Resolutions were drawn up, calling attention to these laws. 

Jefferson himself drew up the Kentucky Resolutions which were introduced in the Kentucky legislature by John Breckinridge. They stated that the Constitution of the United States was a compact, and that "the government created by this compact was not made the exclusive or final judge of the extent of the powers delegated to itself. . . but that . . . each party has an equal right to judge for itself, as well of infractions as of the mode and measure of redress."

James Madison drew up resolutions which were introduced in the Assembly of Virginia. These resolutions gave an interpretation of the 

Constitution similar to that of the Kentucky Resolutions. They stated "that in case of deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the States, who are the parties thereto, have the right and are in duty bound to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil, and for maintaining within their respective limits the authorities, rights, and liberties appertaining to them." 

These resolutions were sent by Kentucky and Virginia to a number of the other states, but the replies received were not very encouraging, as many did not accept the interpretation presented by Virginia and Kentucky. But the resolutions had the effect of calling the attention of the voters to the matter. There has been some doubt in the minds of historians as to what the authors of these resolutions intended to accomplish. The

resolutions were a protest against what the authors considered unfair laws passed by the Federalists. 

The Election of Thomas Jefferson. As the time approached for another presidential election, the Federalists nominated John Adams and 

Charles Cotesworth Pinckney as their candidates. Alexander

Hamilton again was not inclined to support John Adams for President. Dissension in the ranks of the Federalist party helped to elect the Republican candidates, namely, Thomas Jefferson of 

Virginia, and Aaron Burr of New 

York. It was clever political management on the part of the Republicans to have candidates from different sections, thereby making an appeal to the voters in the Middle States as well as in the South. The Republicans were victorious with seventythree electoral votes to sixtyfive for the Federalists. It was evident that the Republicans had been elected, but it was not yet decided who was elected President, for Jefferson and Burr had each received seventy-three votes, and the election was a tie. The Republicans had intended that Jefferson was to be President, and Burr, Vice-President; but according to the Constitution of the United States at that time, the person receiving the highest number of votes should be President if he had a majority, and the one receiving the second highest should be Vice-President. In this election, no one had the highest number, and the contest went to the House of Representatives, where the choice between Jefferson and Burr was to be decided by a majority vote of the states, each state voting as a unit and casting one vote. 

Statue of Thomas Jefferson in the University of Virginia In the House the Republicans controlled the votes of only eight of the sixteen states. The Federalists controlled six, while the representatives of two (Vermont and Maryland) were evenly divided. This resulted in a deadlock, for the Federalists cast their votes for Burr, and the vote was eight states for Jefferson, lacking one of being a majority. Some of the

Federalists appealed to Alexander Hamilton for advice, and he preferred 

Jefferson, whom he considered less dangerous than Burr. Burr had been his rival in both public and private life and was a bitter enemy. Following 

Hamilton's advice, enough Federalists changed their votes so that Jefferson was chosen President and Burr became Vice-President. This election called attention to the unsatisfactory method of selecting the President, and was responsible for the Twelfth Amendment to the Constitution, which requires distinct ballots for President and Vice-President, making such a deadlock in the future impossible. Burr felt that Hamilton was responsible for his loss of the presidency, and their enmity continued, and finally, in 1804, led to a duel between the two men, in which Hamilton was killed. 

The Record of the Federalists. The success of the Republicans in 1800 meant the decline of the Federalists, for they never regained control of the government. They had been in power for twelve years, and during that time had given the country a good government. The Constitution was put into operation by them, and in the early days, when many difficulties surrounded the government, the affairs of the nation were directed by capable and conservative men. The Federalists put the credit of the 

United States on a firm basis and preserved the neutrality of our country while Europe was at war. Finally, near the end of Adams's administration, he appointed, as Chief Justice of the 

Supreme Court, John Marshall, who later laid down constitutional principles which have served as a guide for many decisions of the Supreme Court. 

The Federalists lost control of the government because they were out of sympathy with the majority of the people, for, unlike the Jeffersonians, they did not have faith in the people's ability to govern themselves. One of their leaders in 1804 said, "I hold democracy in its natural operation to be the government of the worst." Some of them believed that "The best part of a community is always the least, and of that least part, the wiser is still less." Their principles of government had grown out of date by 1800, but at the time the government was founded, in 1789, the country had passed through a period of disorder which made law and order more desirable than democracy. After the 

John Marshall

government was firmly established, there was need for the more liberal ideas which Jefferson and his party supplied.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF AMERICAN NATIONALISM AND DEMOCRACY 

Chapter XII. JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY Chapter XIII.  Chapter XIV.  Chapter XV. JACKSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

POLITICAL CONDITIONS in the United States have in some periods of our history been greatly influenced by the ideals of men of strong character and personality. Their ideas have contributed to the welfare of the American people. One of these great Americans was Thomas Jefferson. He had faith in the people and was interested in the development and success of democratic government. He was a firm believer in those institutions which brought government closer to the people. He favored education, local government, majority control, and every other element that made for more complete democratic government. He emphasized equality of opportunity, economy, equal and exact justice, peace, commerce, and supremacy of the civil over the military authority, and he tried to put these ideals into actual operation. He came to power at a time when the Federalists preferred centralization of power in the hands of an aristocratic group. He succeeded in making some changes, and many of his ideas of government have persisted throughout our history. It is important that we understand and appreciate his contribution to American political ideals. 225

During Jefferson's administration as President the Louisiana territory was purchased, and by it the area of the United States was nearly doubled. 

He was interested in peace and made great efforts to prevent our government from becoming entangled in the political disturbances of Europe. 

Following the eight years of Jefferson's administration, James Madison, who was interested in promoting the ideas of Jefferson, succeeded him in office. During Madison's administration many difficult foreign problems persisted, and finally brought us into a war with Great Britain. During this war the most brilliant engagements were those fought on the sea, and the battle of New Orleans, in which Andrew Jackson and his Western frontiersmen defeated a strong British army. This war stimulated nationalism, helped American independence in the eyes of the world, and brought Andrew Jackson to the front as a great leader.

The spirit of nationalism, which was characteristic of the nineteenth century, developed in the United States following the second war with Great Britain. It expressed itself in the demand for the establishment of the second Bank of the United States, the insistence on a protective tariff, and the desire for a system of internal improvements. 

Along with the growth of nationalism came that of sectionalism. Following the War of 1812, manufacturing developed, and, as a result, an industrial section appeared in the northeastern part of the United States. 

In the South, on the plantations, staple crops such as tobacco, sugar, and cotton were produced. The West was a distinct section where grain and livestock were grown by farmers operating on a small scale. Each of these sections had its own economic interests, and each looked to its representatives in Congress to promote its sectional advantages. It was during the period following the War of 1812 that the American System, based on economic nationalism, was proposed by Henry Clay but later was opposed by Calhoun and other leaders in the South. In the struggle for economic advantage, the leaders of the various sections entered into a controversy which involved the nature of the Union. The spokesmen for the South put forth the idea of states' rights and state sovereignty, while the industrial section, under the leadership of Webster, pleaded for the nationalist theory, or for the sovereignty of the national government. 

With the election and inauguration of Andrew Jackson the West came to a position of increased power in national affairs. Since a Westerner was 

President, the democracy which had developed in the West asserted itself, and under Jackson's leadership this section assumed an important role in the affairs of the nation. A new alignment of parties came about, and for many years the Whigs and the Democrats dominated politics.

CHAPTER XII Jeffersonian Democracy 

A New Era in American Politics. With the inauguration of Thomas 

Jefferson, March 4, 1801, a new era in American politics began. Jefferson considered the events which brought him to power a revolution, for his ideas of government were very different from those of the Federalists, who, during the first twelve years of the nation's existence, had put their ideas into practice by building up a strong central government. Jefferson favored local government rather than a strong central government. He believed in democracy and felt that the people, if given an opportunity, would demonstrate that they were capable of governing themselves. He was the first 

President to be inaugurated at the new capital, Washington, to which the government had been moved the year before. The Capitol building and the White House had not been completed, and most of the city of 

Washington was still a wilderness.

In this new capital the inaugural ceremony was, in accordance with the President's wishes, made a very simple affair. Jefferson did not follow the custom of his predecessors by riding in a coach drawn by four or six horses, but instead he walked from his boarding place to the Capitol for the inauguration. John Marshall, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, administered the oath of office, after which Jefferson delivered his inaugural address, in which he announced many important principles of government. There was a conciliatory note in his inaugural address. He did not wish to offend the 

Federalists, but instead hoped to bring them to his support. He felt that many Republicans had left his party and had gone to the Federalists because of the feeling against French democracy which resulted from the Reign of Terror in the French Revolution, and from the naval war of 1798. In his inaugural address he said, "But every difference of opinion is not a difference of principle. We have called by different names brethren of the same principles. We are all Republicans, we are all Federalists." 

He pointed out that there should be less governmental interference in the 227

The first Capitol at Washington affairs of the people when he said, "A wise and frugal government, which shall restrain men from injuring one another, shall leave them otherwise free to regulate their own pursuits, of industry and improvement, and shall not take from the mouth of labor the bread it has earned. This is the sum of good government." .. the

Jefferson was a believer in democracy, and felt that economy was a necessary condition for democracy. Unnecessarily excessive taxation and extravagance in government are not consistent with a democratic government. Jefferson enumerated a number of other principles of government, such as "equal and exact justice to all men... ; peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations, entangling alliances with none; the support of the state governments in all their rights. ; preservation of the general government in its whole constitutional vigor. ... ; a jealous care of the right of election by the people... ; absolute acquiescence in the decisions of the majority ... ; a well-disciplined militia... ; the supremacy of the civil over the military authority; economy in public expense that labor may be lightly burdened; the honest payment of our debts and sacred preservation of public faith; encouragement of agriculture, and of commerce as its handmaid; freedom of religion, freedom of the press, and freedom of persons under the protection of the habeas corpus, and trial by jury impartially selected."

Democracy was put into practice, and much of the formality at the White House gave way to simplicity. The new President did not maintain some of the older and recognized formalities in receiving and entertaining

JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

229 diplomats from other nations, but instead applied the democratic principle by substituting the rule of pell-mell. This was at first so unsatisfactory that the British minister declined the President's invitation to dinner. 

Jefferson also wished to be more informal in dealing with Congress. 

Instead of delivering his annual address in person, he sent a written message and explained that it was for the convenience of the Congress. This manner of sending the presidential message to be read by the clerk of the House continued until the days of President Woodrow Wilson, who returned to the precedent which Washington and Adams had established, and delivered his message in person. 

Liberal Principles Adopted. The principles which Jefferson had announced and tried to carry out were what we designate as liberal. In 

1800 he had written, "I have sworn upon the altar of God eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man." He wanted freedom from every form of restraint, and did not believe in a government which was dominated by any one class, but had faith in the leadership of the agrarians, or small farmer group. He was the representative of the agrarian South and had confidence that the small farmer element was capable of carrying on the affairs of government. He felt that education was necessary for successful democratic government, and under his direction the University of Virginia was founded so that the youth of the state could be trained for leadership. His interest in education is revealed in his 

Early view of the University of Virginia; from an old print 

BRELO

statement that "We are not afraid to follow the truth"; and that "Error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it." FED GOVE G.WAS J.ADA 

Because of his liberal views, many of his opponents who believed in a strong central government, directed by the conservative and well-to-do, felt that Jefferson was a radical, and feared that grave consequences might result from his administration. Many 

New Englanders felt that there was too much democracy, for they had heard of the extreme democracy of the French 

Revolution. The Reign of Terror was still in their minds. They objected to some of the Jacobin Clubs which had been formed in this country by the believers in the democracy of the French 

Revolution. Theodore Dwight, in an oration delivered at New Haven, Connecticut, in 1801, declared, "The great object of Jacobinism, both in its political and moral revolution, is to destroy every trace of civilization in the world and to force mankind back into a savage state... That is, in plain English, the greatest villain in the community is the fittest person to make and execute the laws. . . . We have now reached the consummation of democratic blessedness. We have a country governed by blockheads and knaves; the ties of marriage with all its felicity are severed and destroyed; our wives and daughters are thrown into the streets; our children are cast into the world from the breast and are forgotten; filial piety is extinguished, and our surnames, the only mark of distinction among families, are abolished. Can imagination paint anything more dreadful on this side of hell?" Subsequent events show that these fears were not realized; that the democracy of Thomas Jefferson, with its liberal ideas, instead of an object of fear, proved to be a real blessing. 

MAD TOM in A RAGE 

A Federalist cartoon attacking Jefferson Removals from Office. With the election of Jefferson, a new political group came into control of the government, and the change from one party to another was the first in the history of our country. Since the party in control usually appoints its own members to fill the offices, the question naturally arose as to what the Republicans would do with the appointive offices held by the Federalists, for few Republicans had been appointed to

JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

231 office by Washington or Adams. Many of the Republicans now felt that the Federalists should be removed, but Jefferson did not wish to remove men from office for merely political reasons. He felt that the Federalists should be kept in office and even hoped that thereby they would be won over to his party. He maintained that the only questions to be asked of a man in office should be, "Is he honest? Is he capable? Is he faithful to the Constitution?" Jefferson tried to hold firmly to these principles, and made less than twenty removals for political purposes, even though there were at the time more than three hundred officials who were subject to removal by the President when he took office. Yet some Republicans had to be appointed to office, though, as Jefferson remarked, none of the Federalist office holders resigned, and few died. 

Jefferson removed some of the Federalists who had been appointed to office by Adams after his defeat in the election. In fact, some of the appointments by Adams had been made so late in his term that it was reported that he was busy until midnight on March 3, signing commissions. 

Since the appointments had been made so late, the commissions had not yet been delivered, but were found on the desk of the Secretary of State when the new administration came in. Such appointments seemed unfair to Jefferson, and he instructed James Madison, the Secretary of State, not to deliver the commissions to the late appointees. One of the late appointees, named Marbury, then asked the Supreme Court of the United States to issue a mandamus ordering the Secretary of State to deliver his commission. John Marshall, the Chief Justice of the United States, announced the court's decision in that case, known as Marbury versus

Madison, in which it ruled that Marbury was entitled to the commission but that the Supreme Court did not have the authority under the Constitution of the United States to force the issuing of the commission, and went on to say that a law which Congress had previously passed, giving the court that authority, was contrary to the Constitution. This case became important, because it was the first time that the Supreme Court declared a law of Congress unconstitutional. 

The Purchase of Louisiana. The most important achievement of 

Jefferson's first term as President was the purchase of Louisiana. By this act the area of the United States was nearly doubled, and complications with foreign nations over the navigation of the Mississippi River were removed. A vast part of the southern United States had been explored and settled by Spain. The French had explored the Mississippi Valley, established trading posts, and claimed the region as part of New France. 

The English colonies claimed much of this region because their charters

gave them the land from sea to sea. These rival claims were decided by the French and Indian War, which closed in 1763. France was defeated and forced to give up all claim to territory in the continent of North America. The territory west of the Mississippi, and the Isle of Orleans, east of the river, were ceded to Spain; thus Spain came into possession of land on both sides of the mouth of the Mississippi and so controlled the outlet to the Gulf of Mexico.

After our country obtained its independence from Great Britain, the territory east of the Mississippi River north of Florida belonged to the United States. The new nation feared that with the control of the mouth of the river and the region west of the Mississippi in the hands of a foreign power, difficulties might develop. Yet, so long as Spain held this region there were no great dangers, for she was not a powerful or aggressive nation. Our government felt, however, that the people of the West looked to the Mississippi as an outlet for their products; that the river must be kept open; and that unless the United States could keep it so, the West might be alienated and become a part of the power which controlled the river.

The United States, by a treaty made with Spain, had obtained the right to navigate the Mississippi, and had secured a place near the mouth of the river where goods might be deposited and reloaded for further shipment. In 1800, France and Spain signed a secret agreement known as the 

Treaty of San Ildefonso, by which Louisiana was transferred from Spain to France. When the United States learned that this area had been transferred to France, a strong power, there was much concern as to the future of the West. Napoleon, at the head of the French government, was at war with many nations, and had designs of building a world empire. 

For several years one of the most important possessions of the French in the New World had been the entire island of Hispaniola, often called Santo Domingo, or Haiti, the western part of which had been a French colony for over a hundred years. This island produced sugar and other tropical products, but not a sufficient supply of foodstuffs, and was therefore dependent on the United States for products and trade. Napoleon realized how important Santo Domingo was for his empire, and also realized that in order to be independent of the United States, Santo Domingo must get supplies of foodstuffs from other sources. Louisiana could supply what was needed, and would be especially desirable as a part of a French empire. 

President Jefferson looked with suspicion on the attempt of Napoleon to build up an empire in the New World, for he felt that Napoleon might even lay claim to part of the United States east of the river. Jefferson, a

JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

233 firm believer in peace, could see in Napoleon's plans serious complications, and hoped that something might be done to prevent a conflict. 

Jefferson, in his inaugural address, had pointed out that our country desired peace, commerce, and friendship with all nations, and entangling alliances with none; but now he felt that a new situation had arisen, and pointed out that if France should attempt to close the Mississippi River to the western part of the United States, we might have to look to the British fleet for protection and help. The affairs in the new republic were then, as always, closely tied up with what was taking place in the rest of the world, and no one knew this fact better than Jefferson. But fortunately a turn in the affairs of Europe and the West Indies forced Napoleon to change his foreign policy. Conditions developed which destroyed Napoleon's vision of an empire in the New World. A revolt in Santo Domingo, under the leadership of Toussaint L'Ouverture, was suppressed by French troops, but a new revolt broke out when the French tried to re-establish slavery in the island. Serious conflict arose, and because of unfavorable climatic conditions, and yellow fever, the French army was defeated by the negro soldiers in Santo Domingo, and Napoleon lost his hold on the French West Indies. Without the French West Indies, Louisiana became less important. 

At the same time, European conditions became even more complicated for Napoleon. It became more and more apparent that his armies might be defeated on the European continent, and his time, energy, and money were needed to bolster up his continental policy. Empire building in 

America became less important to him. Jefferson had instructed our minister to France, Robert R. Livingston, to try to buy land near the mouth of the Mississippi River to make certain that the United States would have a place of deposit. He hoped thereby to avoid complications arising out of the question of the control of the river by Napoleon. To facilitate these negotiations, he sent James Monroe as a special envoy to assist Livingston. Before Monroe arrived in Paris, the failure of Napoleon's plans in Santo Domingo, together with events in Europe already referred to, forced him to give up the idea of an empire in America; and when Livingston offered to buy a small tract near the mouth of the river, Napoleon's representative, Talleyrand, offered to sell him all of Louisiana. 

This was so great a surprise to Livingston that he did not know how to answer, but waited for Monroe, who favored the purchase of the entire area. On April 30, 1803, Monroe and Livingston signed the treaty whereby the United States bought all of Louisiana for $15,000,000, of which $3,750,000 was to be paid to United States citizens for their claims against the French government,
