JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

235 The Constitutionality of the Purchase. Jefferson believed in strict interpretation of the Constitution so that the central government could exercise only those powers which were specifically stated in the Constitution. 

The right to purchase territory is not one of the stated powers; hence 

Jefferson felt that even though XX it was desirable to purchase all of Louisiana, the Constitution should be obeyed until it was amended to give power to acquire the territory. His friends pointed out that this would mean considerable delay, for an amendment to the Constitution after being proposed by Congress does not go into effect until it has been ratified by three fourths of the states. His friends felt that in the meantime Napoleon might change his mind and withdraw the offer. They urged upon Jefferson that he accept the doctrine of implied powers, for, they argued, since the Constitution granted the power of making war and treaties, it thereby implies the power to acquire territory, because that is often one of the necessary results of war and treaties. Jefferson finally yielded, and accepted this interpretation, and submitted the treaty providing for the Purchase of Louisiana to the Senate for ratification. The treaty was ratified in 1803, and New 

Orleans and the rest of the Louisiana Purchase became a part of the territory of the United States. 

State Museum of Louisiana

Demonstration at the transfer of Louisiana to the U. S.; painting by Thulstrup

The Lewis and Clark Expedition. President Jefferson was a man of broad interests. In addition to his activities in government, he concerned himself with science, agriculture, philosophy, and many other pursuits. 

His interest in science led him to propose explorations in the vast region beyond the Mississippi River. As early as 1783 he suggested that an expedition for exploring that western country should be undertaken, and when he became President he secured funds from Congress for the expedition, which was led by two adventurous young men, Meriwether Lewis

and William Clark, a younger brother of George Rogers Clark. Even before the Louisiana Purchase treaty was made, these men were authorized to conduct this expedition, for Jefferson felt that there would be no objection to an undertaking of a scientific character, even if conducted on foreign soil. In 1804 the expedition, consisting of thirty-five men, went up the 

Missouri River, and into what is now North Dakota, where they spent the winter. The next spring they went on westward to the Columbia River and then downstream in canoes to the Pacific Ocean. They went beyond the territorial limits of the United States, exploring the Far Northwest and thus laying the basis for a claim to the Oregon country. 

Lieutenant Zebulon M. Pike also made journeys in the region west of the Mississippi River. In 1805 he ascended the Mississippi River in search of its source, and later he made his way up the Arkansas River toward the west, where finally he came to Pikes Peak, which is named in his honor.

The Dispute over West Florida. The acquisition of Louisiana involved the United States in a boundary dispute with Spain, for our treaty with France stated that the United States should receive Louisiana "with the same extent" that it had in the hands of Spain in 1800 (that is, by the treaty of 1763), "and that it had when France possessed it" (that is, before 1763). This statement did not make clear the exact boundary of Louisiana. 

The French, before 1763, had claimed the western part of Florida as far east as the Perdido River, while Spain had claimed that the boundary was the Isle of Orleans. In 1763 Great Britain had been given all the land east of the Mississippi River except the Isle of Orleans; but in 1783 Florida had been transferred back to Spain. The dispute over West Florida continued with both Spain and the United States claiming the area between the Mississippi River and the Perdido River. The dispute was finally settled in 1819 when the United States purchased all of Florida from Spain. 

War with Tripoli. Soon after Jefferson took office, Tripoli, one of the 

Barbary states of northern Africa, declared war on the United States, because we refused to submit to the injustice of paying further tribute to the Barbary pirates. In this war, of 1801-1805, our navy cleared the 

Mediterranean Sea of pirates, protected our commerce on the high seas, and gained the respect of other powers. 

The Dispute over Neutral Rights. Jefferson's first term was eminently successful, and in 1804 his party renominated him for a second term, but nominated Clinton for the vice-presidency in place of Aaron Burr. The 

Federalists nominated C. C. Pinckney and Rufus King. In the election that followed, Jefferson was chosen by an overwhelming majority (172 to

At the end of a portage past falls on a stream. Many such portages were used by traders and explorers in the early days. 237

14 electoral votes). One of the most important problems of Jefferson's second term was that concerning the rights of neutrals. The wars in Europe, in which England and France had taken an important part, were renewed after the Peace of Amiens in 1803, and waged on a larger scale than before. Nearly all of Europe was drawn into them, and the United 

States, with its policy of isolation and neutrality, found great difficulty in maintaining the rights of Americans. 

The conflict in Europe was responsible for renewed prosperity in the United States because the European powers, being at war, needed our products. Under these conditions our farmers prospered because of the higher prices they enjoyed, and American shipping increased many fold. 

This rapid growth in our neutral commerce alarmed the British mercantile interests, and British statesmen were called upon to frame a policy which would maintain the British mercantile and naval supremacy. Following the battle of Trafalgar, in 1805, Great Britain was in control of the seas, and with her naval supremacy established, she dictated the rules for international trade, which other nations were forced to accept. She decided that 

French goods were liable to seizure if carried by American vessels unless they had actually become the property of American merchants. She insisted that trade which was closed in time of peace should remain closed in time of war. This worked to the disadvantage of American shipping, for in time of peace the French did not permit the Americans to carry products from the French West Indies to Europe, since the French were interested in carrying on this trade themselves; but during the war with 

Great Britain, the British navy swept the French vessels off the seas and France was then willing to have the American neutral vessels carry on this trade. Great Britain protested, and maintained that the goods could not be carried to Europe in American vessels unless they were first brought to 

America and there paid duty.

Impressment of Sailors. Another source of difficulty arose over the question of impressment of our sailors. As the American carrying trade became more profitable, and the American merchant marine was built up, the wages paid our sailors rose from $8 to $24 a month. Food and living conditions also were better than in the British navy. Because of these conditions, some British sailors deserted the British navy and joined our merchant marine. British naval officers, in order to keep their vessels manned, insisted on taking from American vessels such British citizens as had deserted her vessels. British officers insisted on the right to stop vessels on the high seas, examine the papers of the ship to find out whether any members of the crew were men who had deserted the British navy,

JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

239 and take them off and force them back into her service. This was known as impressment. It was estimated that 2,500 sailors had deserted the 

British marine, public and private, every year, and impressments by the British amounted to about 1,000 a year. Many of the former British subjects had become American citizens, and the United States therefore felt that it was her duty to protect her citizens. 

Jefferson decided to come to an agreement with Great Britain on the matter of impressments, and sent William Pinckney, of Maryland, to assist Monroe with the negotiations for a new treaty. Monroe and Pinckney were unable to obtain a satisfactory treaty, for England insisted on the right of impressment. The British ministry, however, assured the United 

States that great caution would be taken to impress British seamen only, so that the rights of American citizens would be safeguarded. 

The Leopard-Chesapeake Affair. The question of impressment reached a climax when the United States warship Chesapeake was attacked by the British ship Leopard. The Chesapeake, commanded by Captain James 

Barron, in June, 1807, started for a voyage to the Mediterranean. She was not prepared for battle, for two of her guns had not yet been mounted, but her captain hoped to mount them during the voyage. The British ship 

Leopard, commanded by Admiral G. D. Berkeley, was informed that the 

Chesapeake had British deserters in her crew and was asked to intercept the Chesapeake and seize these seamen. Shortly after the Chesapeake had left our shores, the Leopard overtook her, and the commander sent an officer to ask for the surrender of the deserters, but Captain Barron reported that he knew of no deserters in his crew and that his crew would be mustered for inspection only by his own officers. Upon receiving this reply, the Leopard opened fire, and for fifteen minutes the Chesapeake was attacked, even though she was unable to return the fire. During this attack three men were killed and eighteen wounded. The British then came on board and found four deserters from the British navy and impressed them for their service. The Chesapeake was so crippled that she had to make her way back to Norfolk. This affair might have been cause for war, but 

Jefferson was not willing to plunge the country into war. Instead, he ordered that all British armed ships should leave our ports, while the Secretary of State demanded punishment of Admiral Berkeley, the British commander, and reparation for damages, and again insisted that the British must abandon the impressment of our seamen. The British minister 

Canning wrote a letter of regret. He promised reparation if the British officers were found guilty of crime. But England would not give up the impressment of our seamen,

Napoleon's Decrees and British Orders in Council. The European war had become even more serious, and the struggle between Napoleon and the British had reached a deadlock. Great Britain was in control of the seas, while France was almost invincible on land. On May, 6, 1806, Great Britain announced a blockade of the coast of Europe from Brest to the Elbe River. However, she permitted neutral ships not carrying goods to or from enemy ports to pass through the blockade. 

Napoleon retaliated with his Berlin Decree, November 21, 1806, which declared the British islands in a state of blockade. He felt that 

England's trade was necessary for English success in the war and determined to destroy British power by destroying British trade. Great Britain realized the danger of Napoleon's decree and on January 7, 1807, replied with an Order in Council which forbade coasting trade between neutrals and French ports. In November of the same year came an Order in Council blockading all ports in Europe from which the British flag was excluded. 

Napoleon replied with his Milan Decree of December 17, 1807, in which he declared that any ship which submitted to search by the British would be regarded as enemy property.

The result was that American commerce suffered because of these restrictions, and our exports fell to about one third of their former value. This was a difficult problem for President Jefferson to deal with, for he saw the United States shipping interests suffer great losses, with no immediate relief in sight. He saw how the products of American agriculture were being reduced in value as the foreign market disappeared, and yet felt that the only remedy to be applied was the slow and uncertain peaceable “coercion." He felt that reason would be more likely to solve these problems than an appeal to war.

His first effort was an appeal to Nonimportation, and a bill was introduced in Congress which provided for the exclusion of such British goods as could be replaced by goods from other nations, or as could be produced at home. This bill directed against Great Britain was passed in April, 1806, and was to go into effect on November 15 unless Great Britain came to terms before that date. The time was later extended to December 14, 1807. The bill was considered by many insufficient to meet the emergency, and some referred to it as a "milk and water bill." Shortly after it went into effect it was replaced by another measure known as the Embargo, which forbade any vessels to leave for foreign ports, and required that coasting vessels give bond to land their goods in American ports. The 

Embargo was not satisfactory, for it did not sufficiently punish Great Britain and France, against whom it was directed, while our own foreign

JEFFERSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

241 trade was virtually destroyed and our farmers were suffering great losses because they could not dispose of their surplus products. Bitter opposition developed against the Embargo, not only in New England, among the mercantile interests, but also among the planters of the South. So vigorous were the objections to the administration that the Embargo was repealed after it had been in operation a little longer than a year. #H Embargo Act cartoon. CHAPTER XIII Nentral Rights and Expansionists of 1812

The Election of 1808. While the United States was involved in the struggle over our neutral rights, and was attempting to find the solution for this difficult problem without going to war with Great Britain and France, the administration of Jefferson was drawing to a close, and the parties were preparing for another election. The Republicans nominated 

James Madison, of Virginia, who was Jefferson's choice, for President, and George Clinton, of New York, for Vice-President. The Federalists again nominated C. C. Pinckney and Rufus King. The Embargo was the main issue, and with the exception of Vermont, New England was solidly against it. Madison received 122 electoral votes and was chosen President over the Federalist candidate, who received 47.

Madison's Problems. The incoming administration inherited the difficult foreign problems with which Jefferson had struggled during his second term. The Embargo Act had been repealed, and in its place Congress passed the Nonintercourse Act, which provided that trade with Great Britain and France should be suspended, but allowed American ships to trade with the rest of the world. The act further provided that if Great 

Britain should withdraw her Orders in Council, or Napoleon revoke his decrees (page 240), then the trade would again be permitted with the power which changed its policy. In other words, if Great Britain would repeal her 

Orders in Council, then trade would be resumed with her; while if Napoleon should revoke his decrees, we should again establish trade with France. 

It seemed at first that Great Britain was willing to take advantage of the offer, for Erskine, the British minister to our country, informed our government that his country had changed its attitude in the matter. Madison then withdrew the prohibition against British commerce, and 1,200 ships 244

sailed for that country. There was a misunderstanding, however, for 

Great Britain maintained that Erskine had exceeded his authority, and nonintercourse was again restored. 

Jefferson had attempted to solve the problem first by nonimportation, then by the embargo; but both of these methods failed. Madison continued in the attempt to solve the difficulty by trying nonintercourse but it also failed. In the meantime there was a continued demand on the part of our citizens to secure better relations with these countries, so that our commerce would revive and agriculture might again prosper. Congress, in a fourth attempt to solve the problem, passed the Macon Bill No. 2, which provided that trade be opened with all nations, but proposed that if either France or Great Britain should change her policy toward the United States, and if the other should not follow by changing her policy also, within three months, then the Nonimportation Act should be put into effect again against the country which did not change her policy. The efforts of Madison at "peaceable coercion" were no more successful than those of Jefferson. The situation continued tense, the rights of our country as a neutral were ignored by both France and Great Britain, and the struggle was becoming more and more bitter. The United States, as we shall see, finally went to war with Great Britain. 

The "War Hawks." While this controversy over our neutral rights was taking place, a new generation was coming to power in American politics. Many of the men who took their seats in the Twelfth Congress in 1811 were young in years as well as in political experience. They had great confidence in the future of their country, and were less willing to compromise than the older men who had previously directed our policy. 

Among them were some outstanding leaders from the West. The frontier had produced a new generation which was ready and eager for war, for they saw that years of compromise had failed to bring about satisfactory results. One of their leaders was Henry Clay, of Kentucky, a young man of great ability, who was chosen Speaker of the House. Other men of ability who worked with Clay were Peter D. Porter, of New York; Felix 

Grundy, of Tennessee; John C. Calhoun, and Langdon Cheves, both of 

South Carolina.

One of the first matters to engage the attention of these men was the unsettled state of affairs in West Florida, which was claimed by both Spain and the United States. West Florida was important to the region west of 

Georgia because some of its rivers flowed through the disputed section. The country which had control of that section could close their outlet to the Gulf. Moreover, Henry Clay and others felt that the British were inter-

ested in obtaining West Florida, and felt that the matter should be dis- Posed of as soon as possible by adding it to the United States. 

These men were expansionists whose view was stated by Felix Grundy hen he said, "I am anxious not only to add the Floridas to the south but Canada to the north of this empire." The expansionists, being in control of Congress, saw many reasons for expanding not only to the south but also to the northwest. They were suspicious of the British traders in the Northwest, who they felt had stirred up the Indians against the people, for everywhere in the Northwest the frontiersman was confronted by the red man. 

The British were interested in the fur trade of the Northwestern frontier and came in conflict with the American frontiersmen. This trade was valued at about a half million dollars annually. The desire for expansion and the control of the fur trade, as well as our defense of neutral rights, were what finally brought us to war with Great Britain. Henry Clay, in a speech, said, "The conquest of Canada is in your power. . . . Is it nothing to extinguish the torch that lights up savage warfare? Is it nothing to acquire the entire fur trade connected with this country and to destroy the temptation and opportunity of violating our revenue and other laws?" 

Felix Grundy, another Westerner, also could see why the Indians in the Northwest should be subdued. Three of his brothers had been killed by the 

Indians. This new generation had a strong feeling of nationalism and patriotism, and felt that they would not submit to further insults by foreign powers. Because of the activities of these "war hawks," more and more pressure was brought on the President to declare war against Great Britain. Declaration of War on Great Britain. It became evident to Madison that if he wished to be re-elected for a second term it was necessary for him to have the support of this powerful group which was interested in declaring war. His party renominated him for the presidency on May 18, 1812, and on

June 1 he sent a message to Congress in which he mentioned the many usurpations and wrongs committed by the British, and suggested that Congress must decide "whether the United States shall continue pas sive." He called attention, first, to the impressment of American sailors on the high seas; second, to the attacks on our commerce by British cruisers; third, to the fact that the British government had a "sweeping system of blockade under the name of Orders in Council." Following this message to Congress, a bill was introduced, declaring war against Great Britain; on June 4 the bill passed the lower House, and about two weeks later it passed the Senate and was signed by the President. Since Madison, in his message to Congress, had emphasized the impressment of seamen,

attacks made on our vessels, and the blockade, historians have long emphasized them rather than the desire for expansion as the causes of the war.

Before war actually began, the presidential campaign of 1812 was well under way. The Federalists had nominated DeWitt Clinton as a peace candidate for the presidency. The Federalist stronghold was still in 

New England. In the campaign which followed, the main issue was war or peace. In the thirteen original states, 90 electoral votes were cast for 

Madison, the war candidate, while 89 went to Clinton, the peace candidate. 

The five new states gave all their 38 votes to Madison. Of the thirteen original states, New England gave 43 votes for peace, while 59 votes south of the Potomac were for war. The Middle States were divided -31 for war, and 46 for peace. From this we see that the New England states, in which most of the shipping interests were located, were almost solid against the war, while the Western states, with no shipping interests, were solid for war. This leads us to the conclusion that there were other factors, besides impressment of our seamen, which were causes of the war; and historians recently have pointed out that one of the important reasons for the war, especially in the West, was the desire of the frontiersmen to acquire additional territory. By 1811, the westward movement of the people had brought enough population into the region beyond the Appalachian Mountains to make that section a powerful influence in American politics. Indeed, it was powerful enough to plunge the nation into war. 

War Strength and Weakness of the United States. The War of 1812 was between the United States and Great Britain only, but many other powers were involved in the European conflict between Great Britain and France. Russia had entered the war on the side of the British against 

France; Napoleon invaded Russia shortly before our country declared war on Great Britain. The United States was poorly prepared to wage war against a powerful enemy. During the eight years of Jefferson's administration, economy was stressed, and since he had been opposed to war, neither the army nor the navy was greatly strengthened during his term of office, though the navy won the war with Tripoli (page 236). The country, however, was rich and prosperous, with a population of about 7,500,ooo, and a possible military strength of about 1,000,000 men. Our position was weakened by the fact that the people of the United States were not united behind a war program, as some sections bitterly opposed the war. 

In the matter of raising money, there were serious handicaps, for the Bank of the United States, which had been chartered in 1791, for a twentyyear period, had not been rechartered in 1811, because many people were

opposed to it. Albert Gallatin, the Secretary of the Treasury, had recommended the renewal of the bank's charter, but his advice was not followed. 

A strong United States bank would have been of great value in financing the war.

Another serious handicap in conducting the war was the fact that the mercantile class, with its financial resources, was hostile to the war, and did not make loans or render other financial assistance. A further difficulty resulted from the loss of foreign trade, because so much of our revenue had been derived from the tariff, and as fast as the foreign trade was destroyed, the revenue from that source was likewise reduced. Albert Gallatin pointed out that the duties collected had fallen from about $12,000,000 in 1806 to $6,000,000 in 1811, and that a deficit was certain to result from its decline. To find additional revenue, the Republicans in 1813 again made use of a direct tax and resorted again to an excise tax. The total income of the government from all sources in 1813 amounted to about $10,000,000, while the annual expenses were estimated at twice that amount. The Secretary of the Treasury was forced to resort to treasury notes and to permanent loans. Before the war was over, $98,000,000 was obtained through loans, for which a rate of interest as high as 72 per cent had to be paid, and even then the bonds could not always be sold at par. 

The War Begins. If our modern methods of communication had existed in 1812, the war could perhaps have been prevented, for two days The battle of Lake Erie, a great American victory, September 10, 1813

before war was declared, Great Britain withdrew her Orders in Council. 

Once war was declared, the expansionists cried, "On to Canada." Great 

Britain was then using most of her army in Europe against Napoleon. 

The war began in August, 1812, with an attempt to invade Canada by way of Detroit, but because of the surrender of the American general William Hull, the expedition failed, and American territory west of Lake Erie was occupied by the British. Two other attempts in the same year to take Canada also failed; but a year later, under the leadership of General 

William Henry Harrison, assisted by Captain Oliver H. Perry's victory on 

Lake Erie, the early losses were retrieved. Canada was invaded and Queenstown was burned. A last attempt to invade Canada, in the summer of 

1814, ended in failure after General Winfield Scott had met the British in a hard-fought but indecisive battle at Lundy's Lane, near Niagara Falls. 

The British Offensive. After Napoleon's overthrow in 1814, the British were able to send more troops to America. One army invaded New York by way of Canada, and at the same time a force of about 4,500 British regulars made an attack on Washington. The Capitol, the White House, and other public buildings there were burned. The British forces next advanced up Chesapeake Bay, but were defeated in the battle of Baltimore. On 

September 12 the American militia at Baltimore withstood the attack of a larger force of British veterans, and on the following days the defenders of Fort McHenry withstood long hours of bombardment, and repulsed a landing party of the British. During the bombardment the United States flag continued to wave over the fort and inspired Francis Scott Key to write "The Star-Spangled Banner," which in 1931 was officially declared our national anthem.

War on the Sea. The navy of the United States consisted of only sixteen ships, but they made a brilliant record in their attacks on the British. 

Five capable naval leaders-Commodore John Rodgers, Commodore

Stephen Decatur, Captain Hull, Captain David Porter, and Captain Oliver Hazard Perry-were in a large measure responsible for the naval victories. The American ship Constitution (“Old Ironsides") forced the

Guerrière to surrender after a severe encounter. The frigate Essex, commanded by Captain David Porter, in the first year of the war, captured ten prizes and 423 men. Oliver Hazard Perry directed the construction of the ships with which he defeated the British on Lake Erie, and sent General Harrison the message, "We have met the enemy and they are ours. 

Two ships, two brigs, one schooner, and one sloop." Most of the American victories were single-ship combats but they were so effective that 254 enemy naval and merchant ships were destroyed or captured. In addition

to the navy, about 500 privateers were commissioned, which, during the course of the war, captured about 1300 prizes, valued at $39,000,000. 

But the British navy, with its thousand ships, was too powerful for a small though daring navy, and before the end of the war the American navy and merchant ships were either destroyed, captured, or blockaded, and American commerce practically ruined. Exports of the United States dropped from $61,000,000 in 1811 to less than $7,000,000 in 1814, and imports declined from $53,000,000 to $13,000,000. 

The Campaign in the South. In the South the Creek Indians attacked 

Fort Mims, in Alabama, in August, 1813, and massacred several hundred people. Andrew Jackson, of Tennessee, with a small force, was sent against them and thoroughly defeated them in the battle of Horseshoe Bend, in March, 1814. The Creeks then withdrew into Florida, and sought refuge with the Seminoles. West Florida, the ownership of which had been disputed for some time, was annexed by the United States in 1810, but East Florida was still held by Spain. Great Britain was the ally of Spain, and during the war it was feared that Florida might be used by the British as a base of operations against the United States. Madison had received authority from Congress, in January, 1811, to take temporary possession not only of West Florida, but of East Florida as well. At that very time British agents were operating from Mobile in West Florida, and from Pensacola in East Florida, in directing hostilities against the United States. They had incited the Creek Indians. Jackson therefore went into Florida and captured Pensacola and succeeded in defeating the Indians. 

The Battle of New Orleans. The military exploits of Jackson were so successful that he was put in command of the United States troops in the South, where he proved himself to be a capable soldier, and a trusted, resourceful, and energetic leader. When he heard that a large British force under General Pakenham was planning to attack New Orleans, he collected his army of about 4,500 men and prepared to defend the city. This he did very successfully by thoroughly defeating the 8,000 British soldiers. 

This was one of the most brilliant victories of the entire war, and it came at a critical time in the history of our country. The Americans were weary of the war in which they had enjoyed few great victories. The battle was fought on January 8, 1815, though the treaty of peace had been signed on December 24, 1814. News of the treaty, however, had not yet reached our country, as there were then no telegraphs or cables and no steamships. 

The treaty provided that "All hostilities, both by sea and land, shall cease as soon as this treaty shall have been ratified by both parties... "" The treaty was ratified by the United States on February 17, 1815.

This battle was considered of great importance because it saved not only New Orleans but all of Louisiana, to which the British might have laid claim. It demonstrated that American soldiers were a match for the best British troops. It raised American prestige in the eyes of the world and intensified the spirit of American nationalism by restoring confidence and self-respect.

The Hartford Convention. During the gloomy days of 1814, the Federalists controlled all of New England, and were hostile to the continuance of the war. The legislature of Massachusetts therefore elected delegates, who joined with delegates from Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire, and 

Vermont, in a convention at Hartford, Connecticut, on December 15, 1814, and remained in secret session until January 5, 1815. They formulated demands in the form of suggested amendments to the United States Constitution. Some of the amendments proposed that the power of Congress to declare war, and to admit new states into the Union, should be restricted. 

Other amendments proposed that the President should serve only one term, and that no two successive Presidents should come from the same state. By this proposal they were trying to put an end to Southern domination, since so many Presidents had come from Virginia. They also suggested that the Southern states should not have representation based on slave population. Before the delegates had an opportunity to present their demands to the government, peace was declared and the war was brought to an end.

The Peace Negotiations. Since the war was not decisively won by either party, the problems before the peace conference could not be settled without great difficulty. Peace discussions had begun almost as soon as war was declared. Russia, which had entered the European war on the side of Great Britain, offered mediation in September, 1812. The United 

States accepted this offer in the spring of 1813, and sent John Quincy Adams, Albert Gallatin, and James A. Bayard abroad to enter into negotiations for peace. Great Britain, however, refused at the time to negotiate, but the American representatives remained abroad. In 1814, Henry 

Clay and Jonathan Russell were added to the group of peace commissioners. They met the British commissioners and began their discussions at Ghent, in 1814. Great Britain's chief statesmen were not at this conference, since she was more concerned with the European affairs which were being discussed at the Congress of Vienna, following Napoleon's defeat. The British statesmen who negotiated with the Americans were not very capable diplomats, and they committed some blunders, of which the American delegates took advantage. The English industrial and commer-

cial classes were anxious for peace and the restoration of normal trade relations. This was an advantage to the American delegates. 

The British delegates demanded the adjustment of boundary disputes and the establishment of an independent Indian buffer state between the Ohio River and the Great Lakes. To this the Americans objected, for they refused to establish another independent state on American soil. They were at the time unwilling to adjust boundary disputes, but preferred to take that matter up later. The Americans, on the other hand, demanded that the British abandon the right of impressing American seamen. This the British would not do, nor would they agree to modify their rules concerning blockade. The British asked for the right to navigate the Mississippi River. This the Americans were unwilling to grant, while the British were not willing to renew the fishing rights of Americans in Canadian waters. Since the negotiators were unable to reach an agreement on the latter two points, they were left for a convention to consider at a later time. While the Americans did not obtain some of the concessions most desired, they were able to resist the demands of the British. The peace terms were finally signed on a basis of status quo ante bellum, which means a return to conditions before the war. 

It will be remembered that we went to war in order to obtain our neutral rights, and yet nothing was said about this matter in the peace treaty. 

Conditions had changed, for since the war in Europe had come to an end, our neutral rights were no longer violated. In both the Northwest and the 

South, where the United States had charged that the British were responsible for the Indian hostilities, peace and quiet prevailed, for the Indians had been thoroughly defeated, and the problem was no longer a matter for diplomatic controversy.

The Effects of the War of 1812. One of the important effects of the 

War of 1812 was that it helped American independence in the eyes of the world. The United States had for the second time engaged in war with an important world power and had come out of it undefeated. General 

Andrew Jackson's brilliant victory at New Orleans demonstrated to the world that the Americans could defeat some of the best soldiers of the world. Perry's victory on Lake Erie and the other naval exploits were very creditable achievements for our small navy, and were a source of pride to the American people.

CHAPTER XIV 

The Spirit of Nationalism 

A New Era. Following the War of 1812, a new era in American history began. During the period from 1763 to 1815, the two most important problems before the American people were (1) our relations with foreign countries, and (2) the organization of the government. After the War of 1812, American statesmen were concerned more largely with domestic affairs. 

The period following 1815 was one in which men were concerned with practical problems rather than with philosophic discussions; the price of corn, for example, was of more concern than the "rights of man." It was, moreover, a period of great change, and is referred to by historians as the period of transition in American history. It was a period of nationalization, for people became interested in our national development. Statesmen of an earlier period had said much about liberty; now they added the word "union," and used the slogan "union and liberty." Before the war, political conflict had been between the Federalists and the Republicans. This conflict now disappeared, for the Federalist party was discredited by the Hartford Convention, overwhelmingly defeated in the election of 1816, and practically ceased to exist as a factor in American politics after that date.

Era of Good Feeling. By 1817 there was beginning an era without the usual party politics, an era in which there was only one party, namely, the Republican. This has often been referred to as the "Era of Good Feeling," but that term does not accurately describe the existing conditions, for as soon as one of the parties disappeared, it became an all-important question as to who should control the remaining party. Different factions struggled for the control of the Republican party, and a period of factional politics ensued, which has sometimes been referred to by historians as an "era of hard feeling."

The older Republicans were still in control, but they had made considerable changes in their policies. Beginning with the purchase of Louisi- 255

Major political parties from 1789 to 1869. ana, they had undergone a process of nationalization. The war intensified this nationalism, for it brought to the attention of the party in power the fact that the central government must be in a position to defend itself in time of war. The opposition of the New England Federalists during the war showed that there was grave danger from weakened political authority in time of war.

Nationalism in Action. The spirit of nationalism began to take definite form in the minds of many of the Republicans as they attacked some of the practical problems of government. In the first place, they provided for an army and a navy on a peace basis, for now they felt that the nation should not be without adequate national defense. A second problem concerned the national currency. In 1811 the Republicans refused to recharter the Bank of the United States, which had been established during Washington's administration on the recommendation of Alexander Hamilton. 

This bank had been opposed by the Republicans because they were afraid of too much centralization in the government. In 1815, however, President Madison, in his message to Congress, suggested that the national bank be re-established to create a better currency. Following this suggestion, John C. Calhoun secured the passage of a law providing for a second 

Bank of the United States, with a capital of $35,000,000, one fifth of which was subscribed by the government. It was chartered for twenty years, during which period it issued paper money redeemable in specie, and for this privilege it paid the government a bonus of $1,500,000. Henry Clay, who in 1811 had opposed the rechartering of the first Bank of the United States, now came to its support. 

President Madison further recommended that there should be a protective tariff. The war had impressed the Republicans with the idea that the nation should be self-sufficing. England had by this time developed the factory system, and attempted to keep the inventions which produced it a secret, so that she could maintain a monopoly of her manufactured goods. After the war was over she sent goods to the United States and sold them so cheaply that American manufacturers had difficulty in com-

Under these circumstances many Republicans who had earlier objected to the protective tariff now felt that the tariff was desirable because of the changed conditions. Even Thomas Jefferson pointed out that in order to be really independent now, we must manufacture things for ourselves. He said that we must now place the manufacturer by the side of the farmer, and that those who were opposed to the domestic manufacturers must either be in favor of reducing the country to dependence on others, or in favor of being clothed in skins and in living like wild beasts in dens and caverns. The result of this agitation was the Tariff Act of 1816, which provided for a duty of about 25 per cent on imports. 

A System of Highways. To strengthen the national system further, President Madison favored a system of roads and canals. Among the 

Travel on a corduroy road; a stagecoach of early days and an ox-drawn wagon HRT

powers of Congress listed in the Constitution of the United States, there is none which grants the right to build roads and canals. Thomas Jefferson favored an amendment to the Constitution, to give Congress this right. 

He pointed out that as new states were being admitted into the Union, there was more need of a system of adequate transportation, and in 1806 he had signed a bill for a survey for a national road. In 1811 the construction of this road, known as the Cumberland Road, extending westward from Cumberland on the Potomac River, was begun; but with the coming of the war, the work ceased. The war revealed the need of such a road as a matter of self-protection, and Madison, in 1816, in a message to Congress, argued for internal improvements. He favored "the expediency of exercising existing powers, and, where necessary, to resort to the prescribed mode of enlarging them, in order to effectuate a comprehensive system of roads and canals." John C. Calhoun favored the building of roads and canals, and introduced the "Bonus Bill," which provided that the bonus of $1,500,000, paid by the second Bank of the United States, should be used for the construction of roads and canals. 

Division of the Republicans. It is evident that the Republican party, after the War of 1812, became interested in strengthening the national government, for they built a stronger army and navy, authorized a Bank of the United States, enacted a protective tariff act, and favored the development of internal improvements. All of these projects had been a part of the Federalist program. The early Republicans were opposed to most of them, but after the war it was different. 

Historians have pointed out that, following the War of 1812, many Republicans out-federalized the Federalists, by which they mean to say that those Republicans began to favor a stronger national government. 

The Republicans, however, were not all agreed on these measures making for a stronger national government. There was a group known as the Old-School Republicans who were opposed to these nationalizing tendencies. Outstanding among them was John Randolph, of Virginia. 

He was more concerned about sectional interests. He was opposed to the tariff of 1816 because he felt that it was a tax on the planters to enable another section to build up manufacturing. He stated that he would buy where he could get products cheapest, and that he would not agree to lay a duty on the cultivators of the soil in order to build up manufactures, for it would mean, he maintained, that thereby the consumer would have to pay higher prices. 

In addition to the Old-School Republicans, there were many Republicans-like President Madison and President Monroe-who felt that the

Constitution did not permit the expansion of these national policies, even though they in themselves might be desirable. President Madison had been in favor of protection and internal improvements as a means of strengthening the nation, but doubted their constitutionality. President 

Monroe likewise felt that the letter of the Constitution should be obeyed. 

In his first message to Congress, in 1817, he pointed out the desirability of internal improvements, but stated that a constitutional amendment was necessary in order to authorize Congress to establish them. 

We find, therefore, distinct differences of opinion on the question of national development. 

The Supreme Court and Nationalism. In 1801, before the Federalists turned the government over to the Republicans, President John Adams had appointed John Marshall, of Virginia, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. John Marshall believed in the power of the central government. He was in sympathy with the doctrine of implied powers as it had been developed by the Federalists. In a series of important decisions the Supreme Court lent its influence to the development of this national power. One of the outstanding cases brought before the court, in which Marshall rendered opinions, was the Marbury vs. Madison case (1803) in which the Supreme Court held an act of Congress unconstitutional. In 1810 the court, in the case of Fletcher vs. Peck, held an act of the Georgia legislature void. In 1819, in the case of Dartmouth 

College vs. Woodward, the Supreme Court held void certain acts of the 

New Hampshire legislature for amending the charter of Dartmouth College, declaring them to be in conflict with the clause of the Constitution which forbids a state to pass any "law impairing the obligation of contracts." In the case of McCulloch vs. Maryland, the Supreme Court upheld the right of Congress to incorporate a bank, and denied the state the right to tax the bank. By these decisions and others there was a steady growth of the power of the central government. 

The Growth of Sectionalism. The spirit of nationalism which swept the country after the War of 1812 soon gave way to sectional interests. 

During this later period the interests of sections, in many respects, became more important to their people than national interests. At least three important sections appeared: the Eastern, or Industrial Section, in which manufacturing developed; the Plantation Section, in the South, where cotton and tobacco were the chief products; the West, in which grain, livestock, and other products predominated. Each of these sections was dominated by its own economic interests, but being under the same national government, the same national laws applied to all and some of those

laws, such as the tariff, did not benefit all alike. Each section looked after its own interests, and its representatives in Congress worked to secure sectional advantages.

Early Growth of Manufacturing. When Washington became President, the United States was not a manufacturing nation. Throughout the colonial period, most of the people were farmers, and though some were engaged in shipping and commerce, very little manufacturing was done. 

Most of our manufactured goods were received from England and other foreign countries. In 1790, however, Alexander Hamilton, as Secretary of the Treasury, made his report on manufactures, in which he pointed out that already there were many distinct lines of manufacturing carried on in the United States, and he hoped to encourage this industry by means of a protective tariff. 

In England an industrial revolution had taken place in the middle of the eighteenth century, which made England a manufacturing nation. 

Machinery for the manufacture of textiles had been invented, and the steam engine was used to drive the machinery. Transportation was improved. Many farms were converted into sheep ranches to supply wool for the factories, and England was sending her manufactured products to many parts of the world. She attempted to monopolize her industrial machinery by keeping secret the processes by which manufacturing was carried on. During the American Revolution, when restrictions were placed on importing manufactured goods into the United States, interest in manufacture at home was forced upon the people; and in 1789 Samuel 

Slater, father of the American factory system, came to the United States and set up machinery for the manufacture of cotton goods. 

Slater had worked in English factories and was familiar with the inventions of Hargreaves, Arkwright, and others. With the help of an American carpenter and blacksmith, he reproduced machinery which he had seen in England, and in December, 1790, he opened the first successful cotton factory in the United States. Following this small beginning, other factories were established in our country. During the period of the Embargo, Nonimportation, and Nonintercourse acts, which restricted importation to the United States, the manufacture of articles in the United States became more and more important. American manufacturing was stimulated thereby until, in 1810, Albert Gallatin, Secretary of the Treasury, reported that the United States was manufacturing many articles and, in some lines, could supply the needs of the entire population of the country. He estimated that the total value of our manufactured products was $120,000,000 a year.

Spread of the Factory System. The effect of the Embargo and Nonintercourse acts may be seen clearly in the growth of cotton mills. In 1809 there were only sixty-two cotton mills in the country, while in 1810 the number had increased to 269. Once manufacturing had begun, it made 

An early manufacturing town: Lowell, Massachusetts, in 1838; from an old print steady progress. Americans made improvements on some of the machinery in use. The accomplishments of the American inventors may be seen by the number of patents registered in the Patent Office, which from 1790 to 1810 averaged 77 annually, but twenty years later averaged 544; while in 

Great Britain the annual number was only 145. 

The growth of manufacturing brought new groups into our American life-the business men, and the manufacturers who were especially concerned about profits. Captains of industry took part in politics, so that they might secure laws enabling them to make greater profits. Heretofore the commercial and landed interests had been dominant, but now industry came to challenge the older order. The American manufacturer became interested in promoting his own economic advantage through the protective tariff. He became a firm believer in the policies which Alexander 

Hamilton had put forth in his report on manufactures. The industrialists believed that manufacturing was desirable because it promoted greater division of labor than did agriculture. They felt that manufacturing would help to make the nation self-sufficient; that the manufacturing people would be able to consume the products of the farm, and would therefore create a home market. In short, the manufacturing interests promoted economic nationalism. The industrialists believed that, in addition to furthering their own economic welfare, they were serving the whole nation. They thought that the blessings of the tariff were for the best national advantage.

The Tariff Question. In the New England section there were still many who were concerned about the commercial interests. New England had been a shipbuilding and shipping section, and as such was concerned about carrying on trade. A protective tariff would tend to restrict commerce, and those engaged in commerce were opposed to the tariff. In this section there were two groups struggling for control--the manufacturing groups on the one hand, and the shipping interests on the other. Daniel 

Webster was the spokesman for Massachusetts in 1816. He favored the shipping interests and was against the tariff. He argued against legislative interference with the natural course of trade. He felt that legislative enactments were artificial efforts to stimulate manufacturing. The other sections stood as follows: The West was for the tariff. The South was divided, with the larger number against the tariff; the Southerners' vote in the lower house of Congress was twenty-three for, and thirty-four against. The Middle States were divided, with the greater proportion for the tariff-forty-four for, and ten against.

Soon after the tariff of 1816 became a law, following the peace in Europe after the downfall of Napoleon, European soldiers turned to farming and manufacturing, and the market for our products in Europe was almost destroyed. English and European factories produced goods to supply their own needs, and their farms produced their own food, so there was a great decline in trade. The British manufacturer, with a large supply of goods on hand, continued to sell in our markets, and began to dump his surplus in America, so that the American manufacturer found it impossible to compete. The tariff of 1816 failed to protect. British manufacturers by various means were able to undersell the American producer. That fact, together with the economic depression which came in 1819, led the American manufacturers to appeal for protection in the form of a higher tariff. Through their efforts the House of Representatives in 1820 passed a new tariff bill which raised the duty, but the bill was defeated in the Senate. This did not discourage the American manufacturers, who continued their fight for protection. Daniel Webster opposed the tariff of 

1820, and stated that he did not wish to push American capital into manufacturing faster than general progress propelled it. He said that he was not anxious to see a Sheffield and a Birmingham in America. Webster, in 

1820, was still speaking for the shipping interests of New England, but by 1828 he spoke for the industrialists, in behalf of a protective tariff. 

The American System. The New England manufacturers secured the support of the new West. The westward movement (which will be studied in later chapters) had carried millions of people across the mountains in a

short period of time and added a new element to American politics. By 

1800, when Jefferson was elected President, already 1,000,000 settlers had gone beyond the mountains. Kentucky and Tennessee had been admitted into the Union, and settlement farther west continued. By 1820, more than 3,000,000 people had gone across the mountains and settled in the West. Henry Clay, representative from Kentucky, was the spokesman for these people in the West who were interested in a market for their farm products. During the period of the war in Europe, Western farmers enjoyed high prices for their products, but as soon as the war was over, and the foreign markets disappeared, the surplus of the farms could not be consumed at home and prices of farm products were low. The farmers believed that protection would be to their benefit by creating a home market for their products; and Henry Clay, as their spokesman, joined hands with the manufacturers in advocating the American System, which proposed a high protective tariff, in order to encourage manufacture. It was argued that the manufacturing centers would require the products of the farm in large quantities.

In order to facilitate trade between the East and the West, so that manufactured products could be sent west, and products from the farms sent east, internal improvements were necessary. A second part of Henry 

Clay's American System therefore included the building of highways and other internal improvements. The money necessary for this would be derived from the tariff. High tariff and internal improvements, it was argued, would make for greater security at home, for they would build up a national economic system known as economic nationalism. To his program 

Clay added also the sale of western land. He proposed that the money derived from the sale of western lands should be given to the states in which the lands were located, to help them finance their internal improvements.

Henry Clay was not opposed to foreign markets, but felt that the home market was of the greatest importance, as the foreign market could not be depended on. He professed to speak not only for the West, but for all sections. He felt that while his American System would help the manufacturers in the East, it would also help the farmers in the West, and the planters in the South.

Opposition to the American System. The planters of the South and the shipping interests of New England, however, were not in favor of the American System, for they considered it a scheme to serve the selfish interests of the industrial group. Senator Robert Y. Hayne, of South Carolina, protested against it, and maintained that it would mean only high

prices for goods bought by the South. John Randolph, as we have seen (p. 258) likewise opposed it. He maintained that it was taxing the 

South to make profits for the manufacturing section. He sarcastically attacked the West by saying that men in hunting shirts, with moccasins 

John C. Calhoun on their feet, were asking for protection of manufacturers. John C. Calhoun had been in favor of the tariff in 1816 and in 1820, because he felt at that time that the protective tariff would be beneficial to the nation. As the tariff continued to mount, he failed to see the benefits derived from it, and when the protectionists sought further increases by the Woolens Bill, in 1827, Calhoun, as Vice-President, cast the deciding vote against it in the Senate and prevented it from becoming a law. 

John C. Calhoun, who had been an ardent nationalist, had hoped that a few years of protection would establish manufacturers so that our industries could compete with foreign manufacturers. He saw, however, that manufacturers, after they had once tasted the high profits which resulted from protection, were unwilling to assume their own burdens and attempt to compete with foreign manufacturers on an equal basis, but instead asked for increased protection so that they could have even greater profits. Calhoun, like many other Southerners, felt that the profits enjoyed by the industrial section as a result of the high tariffs were extracted largely from the other sections, which were forced to bear the burden of increased prices.

The Tariff of 1828. After the defeat of the Woolens Bill, the friends of protection sponsored a new bill, the Tariff of 1828. John C. Calhoun was now the leading opponent of the protective tariff. In New England the manufacturers' interests were gaining power, while the shipping interests were declining. These shipping interests formerly had joined hands with the planters of the South in opposing the tariff, but with their influence on the decline, the burden of opposing the tariff was left to the leaders in the South. Daniel Webster, who had opposed the tariffs of 1816 and 1820, because he represented the shipping interests of New England,

by 1828 had completely shifted his position and was now speaking in behalf of the industrialists in favor of the protective tariff. The tariff of 1828 was tied up with politics, and was so unsatisfactory that it was referred to as the Tariff of Abominations. President John Quincy Adams, a New 

Englander, was a candidate for re-election. He favored the tariff and the 

American System as proposed by Henry Clay, and was expecting the support of the West as well as of New England. 

Andrew Jackson, also a candidate for the presidency, was looked upon as the standard bearer for those people who were opposed to the tariff. 

There were also Northern Democrats under the leadership of Van Buren, who championed the American System and yet supported Jackson. The tariff of 1828 provided for high duties, not only on manufactured goods, but also on raw material, which the industrial section imported. The tariff of 1828 therefore had some features which were objectionable to the industrial section; yet that section supported it, while the South opposed it. 

The South Carolina Exposition. In opposition to the tariff of 1828, John C. Calhoun prepared his South Carolina Exposition and had it introduced in the state legislature as a committee report. In it the tariff was attacked as unconstitutional, as sectional, and as destructive to the liberty and prosperity of the people. The South Carolina Exposition was based on the contract theory of the Constitution. Calhoun maintained that the 

United States Constitution was a contract into which the states had willingly entered. He held that the states were completely sovereign, and did not agree with the theory of divided sovereignty, which some of the framers of the Constitution had proposed. He insisted that the United 

States government was merely an agent of the states, and if Congress exceeded its authority and encroached upon the powers of the states, the states then had a right to resist. 

Calhoun denied that the Supreme Court had the power to say whether a law was constitutional or not, for the court, he declared, was an agent of the Federal government. He maintained, on the other hand, that the states had the right to judge whether an act of Congress encroached upon their rights. Calhoun held that the constitutionality of acts of Congress should be decided by state conventions held for that purpose, and if such a convention declared that an act of Congress was not in accordance with the Constitution, that act became null and void within the borders of the state. He further maintained that such nullification would not be final, because the final authority rested on the judgment of three fourths of the states. Three fourths of the states had the right to amend the Constitution. 

Calhoun insisted, therefore, on these three claims: (1) If a law was declared

null and void by the convention of a state, it merely suspended that law until the other states could pass on the issue. (2) If three fourths of all the states declared through their conventions that the law was constitutional, it would be in effect everywhere, but the state which objected to it would have the right to withdraw from the Union. (3) If, on the other hand, the conventions of more than one fourth of the states objected to the act, then the law would be null and void. 

The Webster-Hayne Debate. While the different sections were thus engaged in arguments over the tariff, and were struggling for economic advantage, another element appeared to add to the controversy. On December 29, 1828, a resolution was introduced in Congress by Senator Samuel A. Foot, of Connecticut, which proposed that it might be desirable to stop further surveys of public lands and to restrict their sale, for the time being, to those already surveyed. The resolution aroused the Westerners, who did not want the survey and sale of Western lands discontinued. The 

West and New England sharply disagreed on the question of the sale of public lands, but on the tariff, the New England states and the West were in accord. Closing public lands to further sale would stop the migration into the West. This was desirable for the Northeast, but not for the West. 

On the question of public lands, the two sections were therefore hostile, and the Foot Resolution was at once attacked by Senator Thomas H. Benton, of Missouri, who spoke in behalf of the West. He pointed out that it was necessary for the growth of the West to open the lands to settlement. He asserted that the Foot Resolution was the result of jealousy on the part of the self-seeking manufacturers of the East, who wished to stop migration to the West in order that their low-paid employees would remain in the industrial section.

New England and the West had been following the leadership of John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay, but by 1828 the West and the South both looked to Andrew Jackson for leadership. These sections were brought into a closer political union by the Western land question. The political alliance between the agricultural West and the industrial East, based on the protective tariff policy, was endangered by the New England opposition to the sale of Western lands. Then was heard, in the Senate, the famous Webster- 

Hayne debate, which therefore took on the nature of a sectional controversy between the Northeast and the South. The spokesman for the South was Senator Robert Y. Hayne, of South Carolina, who put forth many of the political ideas of Calhoun, for Calhoun was the Vice-President of the United States, and the presiding officer in the Senate was not permitted to take part in the debate. The spokesman for New England was Senator

Daniel Webster, of Massachusetts, a very capable lawyer and a convincing orator.

SPEECH OF DANIEL WEBSTER, 1 BEPLY TO MR. HAYNE, OF SOUTH CAROLINA: 

The Webster-Hayne debate lasted from January 19 to January 27, 1830. It was one of the greatest debates in the history of our country, during which the galleries of the Senate were crowded with eager listeners. 

Senator Hayne objected to the steady growth of the national power which had been used to secure financial advantages for the industrial section. He pointed out that restriction of land sales would further the interests of that particular section, and while it would build up the manufacturing section, it would hinder the growth and development of the agricultural states. He then elaborated the arguments which had been put forth in the South Carolina Exposition, that the Union is a compact of the states, and argued that the states must resist the encroachment of the national authority.

Speech in reply to Hayne

Webster made his chief arguments against Hayne's interpretation of the Constitution. He denied that the 

Union was a compact of the states, and maintained that the Constitution was formed by the people of the entire country. He was opposed to the doctrine of nullification, which he held to be unconstitutional. He felt that if each state could interpret for itself whether a law should be obeyed, there would be many interpretations of the Constitution and that it would be reduced to a "collection of topics of everlasting controversy." 

Modification of the Tariff of 1828. The Tariff of 1828 was unsatisfactory to the Northern industrial section as well as to the Southern planters. 

The Southerners hoped that Andrew Jackson, who was to be inaugurated President in 1829, would secure a revision of the tariff; but in his first message to Congress he referred to the tariff without proposing any definite action. Southern leaders felt that he would try to secure a reduction.

Jackson, however, was not interested in the constitutional argument about the nature of the union which had been raised by the Webster-Hayne debate. He was opposed to the theory of nullification as set forth by Calhoun, and was ready to enforce the laws of the Union. He definitely expressed himself on that subject at a dinner in celebration of Jefferson's birthday, on April 15, 1830. While responding to a toast, he made his famous statement, "Our Federal Union; it must be preserved.' 

In 1832 a new tariff act was passed which did away with some of the most objectionable features of the Tariff of 1828. The Tariff of 1832 was still a protective tariff, and was not satisfactory to South Carolina leaders, who now turned to nullification as the only remedy. The legislature of 

South Carolina called a convention which, on November 24, 1832, passed an ordinance which declared the new tariff law unconstitutional, and null and void after February 1, 1833. It was further provided that no appeal should be carried to the United States Supreme Court, and if an attempt were made to use force, that the state would secede from the Union. State officers were required to take an oath to support the ordinance. When 

President Jackson learned of the action of South Carolina, he stated that he would have the leaders arrested and tried for treason. He called upon 

Congress to pass a "Force Bill," which gave him power to use the army and navy to collect the tariff duties in South Carolina. 

Yet, at the same time, many people felt that the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 were too high, and that South Carolina did have a just grievance, and that the tariff should be lowered. Henry Clay introduced a compromise bill, which Congress passed in 1833. It provided for a gradual reduction of all duties over twenty per cent. South Carolina nullification leaders were satisfied with the new tariff, and on March 11 the South Carolina convention reassembled and withdrew the nullification ordinance.

CHAPTER XV Jacksonian Democracy Summary of Politics, 1800-1820. During Washington's administra tion, differences of opinion developed from the philosophy of government held by Alexander Hamilton, and that proposed by Thomas Jefferson. In 

1793, Jefferson withdrew from Washington's cabinet and organized a party of opposition, then known as the Republican party. The Federalists continued in power until 1800, when they were defeated by the newly organized party which elected Jefferson President. The Federalists made several attempts to regain power in later elections, but were always defeated. In 1804 Jefferson was elected for a second term, and was followed by James Madison, who was elected by the Republicans in 1808, and reelected in 1812. The Federalist party had become the party of opposition and became rather unpopular because of its refusal to support the War of 1812. Madison was in 1817 succeeded by James Monroe, of Virginia, who was chosen by the Republican party. In Monroe's first term the affairs of the government were so successfully conducted that he was re-elected in 1820, with only one elector casting his vote against him, in order to reserve for Washington alone the honor of a unanimous vote. The Federalist party had now passed off the scene and only one party-the Republican-remained. American politics entered upon an "Era of Good Feeling," but since there was only one party, it is evident that the person who was nominated for the presidency would be elected, and the contests then came over the nomination. This soon led to factions in the Republican party, and resulted in an era of factional politics. 

While Monroe in 1820 was chosen without opposition, many rivalries developed during his second term. Many of these may be traced to the selfish interest of the sections already discussed (pp. 259-260). The Republican party divided into groups, which retained the party name. group of Young Republicans had their main support in the West. Another group, known as Old-School Republicans, had most of their support The 271

in the planter section. The industrial section leaned toward the Young 

Republicans, and favored national developments and a protective tariff, while the shipping interests in New England were more in sympathy with the planters of the South. The Young Republicans, after a short time, were known as National Republicans. 

The Death of King Caucus. The earlier candidates had been nominated by a Congressional caucus, but as the campaign of 1824 approached there were so many internal differences that this method of nomination led to many serious conflicts. Many of the party became dissatisfied with the caucus and nominated their favorite sons by state legislatures. As early as 

1821, the South Carolina state legislature placed the name of William Lowndes, and the Tennessee state legislature in 1822 chose Andrew Jackson as their nominee. The Kentucky legislature declared for Henry Clay, and 

Massachusetts for John Quincy Adams. The regular caucus, which had lost its importance, nominated William H. Crawford, of Georgia. 

Election of 1824. In the election of 1824, the most important candidates in the field were Adams, Jackson, Crawford, and Clay, none of 

John Quincy Adams

Henry Clay whom received a majority of the electoral vote. Jackson, with the greatest number, led with ninety-nine votes; Adams was second, with eighty-four; and Crawford third, with forty-one; while Clay received only thirty-seven. 

According to the United States Constitution, if no Presidential candidate has a majority of the electoral vote, the selection must be made by the

JACKSONIAN DEMOCRACY 

273 House of Representatives, where each state, regardless of size or population, has one vote. The House is required to select one of the three having the largest number of votes. Henry Clay, thus eliminated, assumed the role of kingmaker, and threw his support, which came from the Western states— Kentucky, Ohio, and Missouri—to Adams. Crawford had suffered a stroke of paralysis, and being physically disabled, was not a serious contender. 

The election in the House then narrowed itself to a contest between Jackson and Adams. Henry Clay did not consider Jackson properly qualified for the office of President. He regarded him merely as a military leader who had no special training in government and politics. Adams, on the other hand, he regarded as a practical statesman, one who supported the national policies advocated by himself. With the support of Clay, Adams was chosen by the House, but because Jackson had a greater number of electoral votes, many of his friends felt that he had been cheated, and that corruption had entered into the selection of the President. The friends of 

Jackson charged that a bargain had been made between Clay and Adams, whereby Clay threw his influence to Adams and in return for it Clay was to be named Secretary of State. It now appears that no such bargain was made, but Adams did appoint Clay Secretary of State, and many of Jackson's friends insisted that such an agreement had been made, and referred to it as "a corrupt bargain." Jackson and his friends at once began preparations for the election of 1828. (6 Opposition to Adams developed soon after he entered the presidency. 

His administration was accused of being corrupt, for the charges of the corrupt bargain" continued. Adams hoped that animosities would disappear and that good feeling might prevail. He refused to remove people from office for political reasons. The desire of the West for markets kept the question of internal improvements before the people. Besides this question, foreign affairs, Indian problems, and the tariff demanded the attention of the Adams administration. 

Election of 1828. In 1828 John Quincy Adams was a candidate for re-election, and Andrew Jackson again was the opposition candidate. The issues of the campaign were few. The main question to be decided was who should run the offices and control the government. The campaign was largely confined to personalities, and much bitterness was created on both sides. The election resulted in the choice of Andrew Jackson, who received 

178 electoral votes, while Adams had 83.

The Westward movement, which had brought millions of people across the mountains, and which was responsible for bringing new states into the Union, built up a large following for Andrew Jackson, who was himself a

product of the West. The new frontier states cast their entire electoral vote for him. Besides the frontier, Jackson also had the support of the 

South. The Southern planters were opposed to the centralizing policy which the government had pursued under the Adams administration. In addition to the South and the West, there was also the Northern democracy, which cast its vote for Jackson. The Northern faction of the Democratic party contributed forty-nine electoral votes for Jackson, only one of which came from New England, which was almost solid for John Quincy Adams.

With the coming of Andrew Jackson to the presidency on March 4, 1829, a new era in American political history began. The people west of the mountains who were interested in democracy came into control of the government, and Andrew Jackson was the first President to be chosen from the region west of the Alleghenies. 

Early Life of Jackson. Andrew Jackson, seventh President of the 

United States, was born in 1767, at the Waxhaw Settlements, near the boundary line between North and South Carolina. In this frontier community, from early childhood, Jackson came in contact with the problems of the West. He had only a few years of formal education, and in 1784 took up the study of law. He was admitted to the bar in 1787, and the next year went west to Nashville, where he had been appointed prosecuting attorney of the western district of North Carolina. In 1791 he married Rachel Donelson, the daughter of Captain Donelson. He took an active part in the affairs of the new community, and in 1796 assisted in framing a constitution for the state of Tennessee, after which he was elected to represent the state in the House of Representatives. In 1797 he was appointed United States 

Senator, but resigned the following year in order to devote his time to private business. He invested his money in a fine tract of land about twelve miles east of Nashville, where he became a successful planter. Shortly before the War of 1812 he became known as a successful Indian fighter, Andrew Jackson about 1815, when he was a general in the U. S. Army
