CHAPTER XVII 

Expansion to the Southwest and the 

Pacific Northwest 

Introduction. The Americans seemed to be a land-hungry people and the quest for more and better lands continued to draw them westward. 

Louisiana and Missouri had been admitted into the Union before the first quarter of the nineteenth century was over and the idea prevailed that it was the "Manifest Destiny" of the American nation to inhabit and control the continent to the Pacific. UNDER MY 

WINGS EVERY ATHING 

PROSPERS 

Early view of New Orleans Expansion into Texas. The purchase of Louisiana was the first step in a migration into the country across the Mississippi. The United States claimed that Texas was included in the purchase, but in the Treaty of 1819, by which Florida was acquired, we surrendered our somewhat doubtful claims to Texas, which was kept by Spain as a part of her great colony 312

of Mexico. Many people were disappointed because we withdrew our claims, for the westward movement was rapidly gaining momentum and the fertile lands of Texas were well adapted to the raising of cotton. The prospective immigrants were encouraged by the fact that the coveted lands were in the hands of Spain, a weak power. 

In less than a year after the surrender of our claims to Texas, Moses Austin had secured permission from the Spanish authorities to bring three hundred American settlers there. He died before he could complete his plans, but the work was carried on by his son Stephen F. Austin. Soon after the arrival of these first American settlers in Texas, Mexico rebelled against Spanish rule and gained her independence. The Mexican government quickly formulated a very liberal land policy by which land could be distributed either directly to settlers or through "empresarios" who would be granted large tracts of land on the condition that they would bring at least two hundred families of settlers into the state. The "empresarios made a charge of twelve and a half cents per acre for the land in order to meet their expenses. At that time no land in the United States could be bought for less than $1.25 per acre. Thousands of Americans poured into the country, most of whom came from the Southern states and were usually accompanied by their slaves. 

The Texas Revolution. Soon the inevitable friction between the American settlers and the Mexican government arose. It was hastened by the known desire of the United States to acquire Texas. In 1827 the United 

States offered Mexico a million dollars for the country between the Sabine and the Rio Grande. In 1829 President Jackson offered five million dollars for the territory. But each offer was declined. The Mexicans, too, suspected Jackson of encouraging a revolutionary attitude of the American settlers. So in 1830 the Mexican government refused to admit any more immigrants from the United States, forbade slavery, and passed other acts equally offensive to the Americans. Conditions grew steadily worse until in 1835 a revolution broke out. On March 2, 1836, Texas declared its independence.

In the Texas War, already begun, one hundred fifty Texans had taken refuge in a walled mission called the Alamo, and were surrounded by a force of about three thousand Mexicans under the command of Santa Anna, the president of Mexico. The defense of the Alamo is one of the most heroic episodes in our history. Every defender was killed. Among the victims were the famous pioneers David Crockett, James Bowie, and William B. Travis. "Remember the Alamo" became the slogan of the 

Texans, who soon took a terrible revenge in the battle of San Jacinto,

April 21, 1836, in which the Texans under the command of General Sam Houston almost annihilated Santa Anna's army. Only about thirty men escaped; the rest were killed or were taken as prisoners. Santa Anna himself fell into the hands of the Texans, who forced him to sign a treaty recognizing the independence of Texas. The new republic was soon recognized by the United States, Great Britain, and France. Fort Worth, Texas, in the early days; from an old print 

The Annexation of Texas, 1845. Soon after the republic of Texas had set up an independent government a petition was sent to Washington asking for the annexation of Texas to the United States. The slavery issue was immediately brought into the question. Martin Van Buren, who was elected to the presidency in 1836, was opposed to the extension of slavery and showed no interest in the annexation of Texas, which expected to enter the Union as a slaveholding state, That was the attitude also of

his successor, William H. Harrison. But John Tyler, who succeeded to the presidency in 1841, was interested in expansion and immediately took steps to revive the question of annexation. Furthermore, the American people were becoming alarmed because of the interest Great Britain was taking in Texas affairs. In 1844 Secretary of State Calhoun negotiated a treaty of annexation, but it was not ratified because of the antislavery opposition in the Senate. The presidential election of 1844, however, was won by 

James K. Polk of Tennessee (map, p. 370) on a platform which called for the "reannexation of Texas and the reoccupation of Oregon"-expansion into the Southwest and the Northwest. President Tyler regarded the election as a referendum on the Texas question and immediately urged that Texas be offered admission into the Union by a joint resolution of Congress. The resolution was adopted (early in March, 1845) as one of the closing acts of the Tyler administration. The Texans presently accepted the offer and cast their lot with their kinsmen in the United States. 

Difficulties with Mexico. When Texas was annexed by the 

United States the Mexican government promptly withdrew the Mexican minister from Washington and severed diplomatic relations. Mexican officials claimed that the treaty recognizing the independence of Texas was not binding since it had been signed by Santa Anna under duress and had not been ratified by the Mexican Senate. Texas was still claimed by 

Mexico in 1845 in spite of the fact that the republic of Texas had maintained its independence for nine years. Its annexation by the United 

States, therefore, was interpreted by Mexico as a direct violation of her territorial integrity.

There were other questions under dispute. American citizens held claims against Mexico which that country had failed to satisfy, either because of inability or unwillingness to pay. More serious was the dispute over the boundary between Texas and Mexico, a controversy which the United States inherited with the annexation of Texas. The Mexicans claimed that the Nueces River was the boundary between the two nations, but the United States supported the Texas claim to all territory north of the Rio Grande, in spite of the fact that the Nueces River had been the southern boundary of Texas while it was a state in the Mexican republic, and that the United States had practically admitted the Mexican claim by offering to purchase the disputed land. 

The Mexican War. In the spring of 1846 President Polk ordered Gen eral Zachary Taylor to occupy the disputed territory between the Nueces and the Rio Grande and to resist any attempt by a Mexican military force to enter the territory. On April 25 a detachment of Mexican troops crossed

the Rio Grande, and met in a skirmish a small force of American cavalry; several Americans were killed. Soon after this incident Polk sent his war message to Congress, in which he stated that the Mexicans had invaded our territory and had "shed American blood upon American soil." "War exists," he added, "by the act of Mexico alone." In view of the fact that the blood had been shed upon disputed soil Polk's arguments seem unconvincing; but they were sufficient to cause Congress to declare war. 

Campaigns of the War. General Taylor promptly crossed the Rio 

Grande and began the invasion of northern Mexico. After a series of military victories he occupied Monterey and then pushed more deeply into Mexican territory. At Buena Vista he gained a brilliant victory over an army several times as large as his own. Meanwhile, Colonel Stephen 

Kearney had been ordered to occupy New Mexico and California. This country was very sparsely settled, and its occupation by American troops had little influence in determining the final outcome of the war, but it added weight to our demand for the cession of this territory in the treaty of peace. New Mexico was quickly conquered, but before Kearney could reach California that state had been occupied by an American fleet under Commodore Stockton and a small force under John C. Frémont. American authorities decided that the quickest way to bring Mexico to terms would be by a direct attack upon Mexico City. General Winfield Scott was placed in command of the expedition, which captured Veracruz after a short siege and then advanced against the Mexican capital. After a series of sharp engagements Mexico City was captured and the Mexican government asked for peace.

Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 1848. When General Scott began his advance upon Mexico City he was accompanied by Nicholas Trist, the personal agent of the President to negotiate peace. Before the American army reached Mexico City the crafty Santa Anna asked for an armistice. The armistice was granted upon the advice of Trist, but it soon became apparent that the Mexicans were merely playing for time. Polk was so displeased by the failure of the armistice that he recalled Trist. Ignoring the President's orders, Trist remained in Mexico and negotiated the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. When Polk received a copy of the treaty he was enraged at the presumption of his discredited agent, but since the treaty contained most of the provisions he desired he sent it to the Senate for approval. The treaty provided for the recognition of the Rio Grande as the boundary between Texas and Mexico. Mexico also ceded to the United 

States the vast block of territory, over 500,000 square miles, including California and land east of it, for which the United States paid Mexico

$15,000,000 and assumed liability for payment of claims of American citizens against Mexico amounting to over $3,000,000. 

The war with Mexico has been described by earlier historians as a war of aggression on the part of the United States for the purpose of acquiring territory for the extension of the institution of slavery. This view, however, in the light of recent investigations, does not seem to be the correct one, for our government tried to remain neutral during the Texas Revolution. Furthermore, since Texas had maintained her independence for nine years, and since she wished to come into the Union, we had a right to annex her without offense to Mexico. Moreover, the war that followed was not fought for the purpose of extending the institution of slavery. While there were many Westerners who believed in the ideal of "manifest destiny," and hence favored expansion, it should be noted that such were found in the free states (that is, free-labor states) of the West as well as in the slaveholding states in the Southwest. 

The Discovery of Gold, 1848. Americans knew little about California at the time of its cession to the United States. It had a sparse population composed of Mexicans and a number of Spanish priests who in their zeal to convert the Indian inhabitants had established missions there. Some reports had come back to the East about its sunny climate and big trees, but there was a question in the minds of many as to whether it was worth the price we had paid for it. 

A few Americans had made their way to California while it was still Mexican territory. John Sutter, a Swiss immigrant, had received a concession from the Mexican government and had erected a fort. It was his intention to set up a sort of feudal domain. In January, 1848, two weeks before the conclusion of peace with Mexico, James Marshall, a New Jersey immigrant, while digging a race for a sawmill near Sutter's Fort, discovered gold. Fearing that the news of the discovery might cause the agricultural work on his estate to be disrupted, Sutter attempted to keep the discovery a secret, but it finally leaked out and the rush to California began. San 

Francisco lost three fourths of its population within four months, as men hurried to the gold fields. Sailors abandoned their ships and soldiers deserted the army in order to try their luck in the hunt for gold. Before the close of the year six thousand men were in the gold fields, and had sent out six million dollars worth of the precious metal. During the early months of 1849 eight thousand men sailed for California from Atlantic ports in 137 vessels, and one traveler said he counted 459 covered wagons in ten miles along one cross-country trail. During the year 35,000 "forty-niners," as the gold seekers were called, arrived by sea and 42,000 more by land.

Early mining of gold in California; from an old print 

Congress had not yet organized a government in California. A reign of chaos, accompanied by all the lawlessness of a frontier community, was checked only by the organization of Vigilante committees who took matters into their own hands. California, as we shall see later, was granted statehood in 1850 after a bitter political struggle (p. 362). 

The Gadsden Purchase, 1853. The discovery of gold and the admission of California into the Union created a demand for better transportation to the Far West. In 1849 a railroad was begun across the Isthmus of 

Panama, but a more direct and an all-American route was desired. Agitation was begun for a railroad across the southern part of the United States. 

Engineers decided that the most feasible route for the proposed road lay through a strip of Mexican territory near the American border. James 

Gadsden, a railway president of South Carolina, was appointed minister to Mexico for the purpose of negotiating the purchase of this territory. 

In 1853, during the administration of President Franklin Pierce, the so-called Gadsden Purchase was made at a cost of $10,000,000; by it an area of 29,670 square miles was added to our territory, in what are now southern Arizona and New Mexico.

Expansion into the Pacific Northwest. American interest in the Oregon country dates back to 1788, when Captains Gray and Kendrick sailed to that region in search of furs. On a second voyage in 1792, Captain Gray discovered the river which he named after his ship, the Columbia. Soon after the purchase of Louisiana, President Jefferson sent Meriwether Lewis and William Clark to explore the Louisiana territory and push on to the

Pacific. They ascended the Missouri River to its source, and with an Indian woman as guide they made their way across the Rockies and the Cascades to the Pacific. American claims to the Oregon country were still further strengthened by the founding of Astoria, at the mouth of the Columbia River, by John Jacob Astor. But the Americans were not the only nation to claim this valuable land which stretched from California to Alaska. Great Britain claimed the whole region on the basis of the voyage of Drake along the Oregon coast in 1579 and the exploration of Cook in 1778. Spain and Russia also, for a time, laid claims to the country, but in 

1819 Spain surrendered her claims to the United States, and Russia withdrew in 1824.

At first our chief interest in the Northwest was in the control of the valuable fur trade, but later we were concerned in acquiring additional territory. After the expedition of Lewis and Clark both British and American trappers and fur traders began to pour into the region. The rivalry between the competing fur trading companies became very bitter. In 1818 the United States and Great Britain agreed to a joint occupation of the territory for a period of ten years; in 1828 the agreement was renewed indefinitely with the understanding that if either nation should desire to terminate the agreement, it should give the other nation a year's notice of its intention to do so.

The Oregon Trail. For a time the British traders seemed to be more interested in the Oregon country than the Americans. During the administration of President Jackson, however, some of the American churches became interested in missionary work among the Indians in the Far West. 

Attention was called to the Oregon country by the reports of these missionaries, and interest was stimulated. A financial panic in 1837 caused a sudden increase in the number of immigrants to this region. The "prairie schooner" soon became a common sight upon the western plains. Early in the forties Marcus Whitman, the best-known of the missionaries, led a great train of covered wagons with about one thousand settlers along the famous "Oregon Trail" into this attractive country. In 1843 the Americans in Oregon organized a government to preserve order until Congress could make provision for them.

Oregon is "Reoccupied." In the election of 1844 Polk not only advocated the "Reannexation of Texas and the Reoccupation of Oregon" but he also adopted the more militant slogan of "Fifty-four Forty or Fight."

By this he indicated that he was willing to fight if necessary for the entire region as far north as Alaska. His strong stand on the Oregon question won for Polk the votes of many people who were not in sympathy with his

proposal to annex Texas but favored expansion into the Northwest. After he had gained the presidency he became somewhat milder in his demands. 

The one year's notice to terminate the agreement which had provided for the joint occupancy of Oregon was duly served upon Great Britain. In the negotiations which followed, Polk readily accepted the British proposal to compromise. Oregon was "reoccupied," but with the parallel of 

49° as our northern boundary rather than that of 54° 40′.

The Mormons and the "State of Deseret." Soon after the settlement of the Oregon question an interesting migration to the West was begun by a religious sect named the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, but commonly known as the Mormons. Their leader, Joseph Smith, claimed to have discovered at Palmyra, New York, inscribed plates revealing the sacred Book of Mormon, which contained many of the teachings of the new sect. He and his converts made a settlement in Missouri and then moved back to Nauvoo, Illinois. There they suffered persecution because of their religious views; their leader was killed and they were ordered to leave the state.

In 1846, under their new leader, Brigham Young, they began a great trek to the Far West, where they sought a home for their church in the unsettled region beyond the Rocky Mountains. While the main party spent the winter at the "Camp of Israel" near Council Bluffs, Iowa, Brigham Young pushed on with a small band and selected a site for the new home on Great Salt Lake, in what is now Utah. The main body of 

Mormons followed, to begin farming on lands they skillfully irrigated, and to build a beautiful city as their capital. A government called the "State of Deseret" was organized, but Utah was made a territory of the United States in 1850. Its admission as a state, however, was delayed by contests over polygamy, which was authorized by Mormon leaders (from 1843 till 1890) and was practiced by some of the Mormons. 

Sale of the Public Lands. During the entire westward movement the desire for cheap land was the motive that prompted most of the settlers to seek new homes in the West. As a rule the pioneers were poor and were able to pay only a nominal price for the public land. In fact many of them believed that the land should be free. Migration into the West, therefore, depended to a great extent upon the generosity of the government's land policy.

The Land Ordinance of 1785 (p. 183) provided for the sale of the land at auction in tracts of 640 acres at a cash price of not less than one dollar an acre. Under this plan no settler could obtain western land unless he had six hundred forty dollars in cash, a sum considerably in excess of the

means of the average settler. In 1800 Congress passed an act, sponsored by William Henry Harrison,* which reduced the minimum amount of land which could be purchased to 320 acres. The price per acre was increased to two dollars, but only one fourth of the purchase price had to be paid in cash, the remainder being paid in three annual installments. 

Four years later the law was changed to provide for the sale of tracts of only 160 acres.

Thereafter it was possible for a settler to purchase a good farm even if he had only eighty dollars in cash. But it was difficult to meet the annual payments, since so much had to be spent in making improvements during the first few years that profits were out of the question. Practically every settler in the West became indebted to the government with little chance of meeting the payments when due. The fact that many settlers who did not meet their payments were not forced to give up their land made those who had paid for theirs angry with the government. In 1820 the situation was remedied by a law which provided for the sale of 80 acres of land at a cash price of $1.25 an acre. Under this law a farm could be purchased for a hundred dollars without the strain of having to make future payments. 

Pre-emption. Before the creation of the national domain most of the states permitted the occupation of western land upon the condition of building a cabin and clearing a small amount of land. Even after the government had begun its survey system and the sale of the land many of the bolder and perhaps more lawless pioneers moved out beyond the surveyors and occupied land which they expected the government to permit them to hold after the land was offered for sale. Indeed, the government from the beginning made it a practice to protect these squatters in their holdings. 

In 1841 Daniel Webster estimated that in the region west of Wisconsin there was a population of from 30,000 to 50,000 inhabitants, although the land had not been offered for sale. In that year Congress passed an act which gave permanency to its policy of pre-emption. A head of a family who had settled upon land was given the right, when the land was opened for sale, to purchase as much as one hundred sixty acres of the land he held at the minimum price of $1.25 an acre, provided a house had been built and the land was actually under cultivation. 

The Homestead Act, 1862. Many of the Westerners were not satisfied with the reductions in the price of the public lands. They felt that the government should make no effort to secure a profit from the sale of the land but should open it to settlers free of charge. Andrew Johnson favored *Then in Congress as a delegate from the Northwest Territory; later a President of the 

United States.

such a policy and in 1845 had introduced in Congress a bill to that effect. 

In 1860 a similar bill was passed by both houses of Congress only to be vetoed by President Buchanan. Two years later, while President Lincoln was leading the Union through the trials of the War between the North and the South, he approved a Homestead Act which had been passed by Congress. This law made it possible for the head of a family to acquire a quarter-section of land-160 acres provided he lived on it and cultivated it for a period of five years. The only charge was a registration fee of ten dollars. If foreigners availed themselves of the opportunity they were exempted from military service, and if a soldier took up land the time of his military service might be deducted from the period of five years. In 

1912 the residence requirement was reduced to three years and it was made possible for settlers to get larger blocks of land. The Homestead Law did much to hasten the settlement of the West and the passing of the frontier. 

The Mining Frontier. The last American frontier was overthrown by three successive waves of immigration which came rolling over the Far West during the last half of the nineteenth century. The first wave was composed of the miners who were attracted by rich mineral deposits in the Rocky Mountains and the Sierra Nevada; then came the ranchers who found in the vast grassy plains a region well adapted to the raising of cattle; and finally the farmers or homeseekers came in search of the fertile lands which, after the passage of the Homestead Act, were open to them almost without cost.

In 1858 silver was discovered on the side of Mount Davidson in Nevada, and the next year the rich Comstock Lode, a deposit of gold and silver near the western border of Nevada, was discovered and its fame spread to the limits of the nation. Many who felt the pinch of the panic of 1857 made the rush to Nevada. Nevada was organized as a territory in 1861 and was admitted as a state three years later. Almost simultaneous with the rush to Nevada was the discovery of gold in the Pikes Peak region of 

Colorado. With the slogan "Pikes Peak or Bust" about a hundred thousand "fifty-niners" reached Colorado in one year. But the gold deposits there were not as rich as they were in California and could be mined successfully only by the use of expensive machinery. Many disappointed miners returned home or drifted into the prairies which they had passed on their westward trek. Colorado was organized as a territory in 1861 and was admitted as a state in 1876. Gold was discovered also in Idaho, Montana, Arizona, and Wyoming. As late as 1875 there was a gold rush into the Black Hills of the Dakotas in spite of the fact that the land had been set aside as a reservation of the Sioux Indians.

Courtesy First National Bank, St. Joseph, Mo.

Holding up a stagecoach; painting by Edward Holzlag 

The lure of gold affected all classes of men. Among these were many desperadoes who tolerated no kind of restraint. They held up and robbed stagecoaches and the Pony Express riders, and no one's life was safe. 

Gradually, however, the better class of men took matters into their own hands by organizing the Vigilantes, who administered justice in a typical frontier style. Law and order were soon restored. 

The Cow Country. The plains from Mexico to Canada and from the 

Missouri River to the Rockies, over which the wave of miners was rolling, had long been considered as unsuitable for farming, and in the northern part of this district it was believed that cattle could not stand the severe winters. Over these plains roamed numerous tribes of Indians who depended for their food supply on the vast herds of buffaloes which fed on the short grass of the prairies. In 1866 it was discovered that cattle would thrive in this region, even in the severe northern climate. Consequently, there was a great influx of ranchers into the region and for about two decades the cowboy reigned supreme. The "longhorn" cattle of Texas proved to be best adapted to the western ranch, and were raised as far north as the Dakotas.

The "Long Trail." Before the construction of the transcontinental railways the markets for the western cattle were to be found at the army posts and the Indian reservations in the North. The government found it necessary to feed the Indians who were now its wards, and cattle were needed to replace the rapidly vanishing buffaloes. Every spring the cattle

were rounded up, branded, and then driven slowly, grazing along the way, to the Northern markets. Six hundred thousand cattle took the "Long 

Trail" in 1871. With the advent of the railroads into the West the "Long Trail" was considerably shortened. Dodge City in Kansas, Ogallala in Nebraska, and Miles City in Montana became famous as centers of the cattle industry. The great ranching frontier soon gave way to farming. The railroads brought into the West many farmers who took up the land and enclosed it with barbed-wire fences, greatly impeding.the long drives.

The Homesteader. The last wave of settlers into the West were the farmers, and with their coming the frontier passed into history. The settlement of the prairie land began in Kansas after the passage of the Kansas- Nebraska Act (p. 366). Slaveholders and free-state forces contended for the control of the territory. After the rush into Kansas had subsided settlers began to stake out claims in Nebraska. Remnants of many a train of covered wagons, tiring of the long journey to Oregon or California and attracted by the fertility of the soil, stopped to make their homes on the prairie. Likewise when many gold-seekers had been disappointed in their get-rich-quick schemes they returned to Kansas and Nebraska and exchanged the pick for the plow. The Homestead Act of 1862 attracted many immigrants through the lure of free land. The demand for food supplies during the War between the North and the South, with its resulting increase in prices, was a further incentive to the settlement of the Western plains. In the period between 1862 and 1880 nearly 470,000 settlers filed applications for homesteads and about one third of that number received land. Waving fields of wheat and corn displaced the pastures, and the recently constructed railroads transported millions of dollars worth of foodstuffs to the Eastern markets. In 1886 an unusual land boom caused a second migration into Kansas. European immigrants poured into the country.

Removal of the Indians. The Indians were the unfortunate victims of the westward movement. Acting upon the principle that there were "no good Indians but dead Indians," the frontiersmen forced them from their hunting grounds and homes with little regard for property rights and often with great cruelty. During the presidency of Andrew Jackson many of the Indians east of the Mississippi were removed to new homes in the West, which the government promised should belong to them permanently. 

With the discovery of gold and the resulting migration into the West many of the Indians who resented the incursions of the whites removed to reservations. Even then it was difficult to protect the property of the Indians

against the greed of the white men, especially if the land on the reservation was very fertile or if it contained valuable minerals. The first two decades following the War between the North and the South were marked by almost constant warfare with the Indians on the Western frontier. Frequently the battles resulted disastrously for the whites, but by 1885 most of the Indians had been restricted to reservations or had been driven into Canada or Mexico.

Change in the Indian Policy. The publication of Helen Hunt Jackson's A Century of Dishonor aroused the sympathy of the Easterners for the Indians and led to a strong humanitarian protest against the treatment of the Indians by the frontiersmen and the government. President Cleveland, deeply affected by Mrs. Jackson's portrayal of the mistreatment of the Indians, recommended legislation to Congress which resulted in the passage of the Dawes Severalty Act of 1887. The purpose of the act was to break up the tribal government and the community life of the Indians. 

The reservations, which had been held in common by the tribes, were divided into farms which were distributed among the individual members of the tribes. The Indian could not mortgage or dispose of his farm for twenty-five years, but after the expiration of that period of time he was free to do with his land as he pleased. 

As a result of the Dawes Act the Indians made considerable progress toward civilization. It soon became apparent, however, that in some respects the act was unwise, and in 1906 it was amended by the Burke Act. 

By this law the 25-year period was abolished and individual Indians were to be given full management of their property as soon as they were able to secure a certificate of competence testifying to their ability to manage their own affairs. Those who were considered incompetent were held in an indefinite period of dependence. On June 2, 1924, Congress passed an act which conferred citizenship upon all Indians born within the boundaries of the United States.

The passage of the Wheeler-Howard Act by Congress on June 15, 1934, was believed by the Commissioner of the Office of Indian Affairs, John Collier, to be "the most important piece of Indian legislation since the eighties." It authorized Indian organizations along tribal lines for the purpose of buying lands, preventing their sale, and carrying on general business.

Indian Health. The government has done much to promote health and education among the Indians. Hospitals have been erected and instruction has been given in sanitation and in the prevention and treatment of disease. Since 1911 annual appropriations have been made for this purpose.

In 1926 the medical work was reorganized, with a surgeon of the Public Health Service in charge of the four districts into which the Indian settlements are divided. Disease, which had been increasing because of the confinement of the Indians on reservations, is being gradually checked, and the "vanishing American" is no longer declining in numbers; in fact, according to the United States Census Reports, there has been an increase of about 90,000 within a decade.

Nearly all the Indians live in twenty-two states, with 61 per cent of the total number within the four states of Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico, and South Dakota. In Oklahoma there are more than 90,000 descendants of the Five Civilized Nations-Cherokees, Creeks, Choctaws, Chickasaws, and Seminoles. Arizona ranks next to Oklahoma in the number of its 

Indian inhabitants, most of whom are Apaches, Navajos, and Hopis, on reservations. New Mexico has about 30,000 Indians on reservations. 

In South Dakota the four Indian reservations of Cheyenne River, the 

Rosebud, Pine Ridge, and the Lower

Brule, cover a large area. There are many reservations, large or small, in other states also; seven in 

New York, for example, with a total area of less than 140 square miles. 

Indian Education. Until the beginning of the nineteenth century the policy of the government toward education of the Indians was inherited from colonial times. In 

1819 Congress provided an annual appropriation of $10,000 for this purpose and steady progress toward a more efficient educational program has been made. By 1848 there were reported in operation sixteen manual training schools and eightyseven boarding schools. The establishment of strictly government schools was stressed after 1873.

The Passing of the Frontier. The two main factors in the hastening of the destruction of the frontier were the Homestead Act already discussed and the extension of railroads into the section west of the Mississippi. With the completion of the Union Pacific Railroad in 1869 the continental frontier was doomed, and by 1884 it was possible to cross the continent along six different railroad lines. There was also a network of railroads extending in every direction, which made possible the colonization of all portions of the far West.

The railroad builders were anxious not only to dispose of the large tracts of land granted them by the government, but to see the free government lands taken. The financial panic of 1873 caused many of the railroads to promote the development of the West on a large scale. Advertising campaigns were organized and the farmers of both the Eastern states and Europe were told of the wonderful opportunities in the new section. The steamship lines aided by distributing literature and by making immigration attractive. Excursions were arranged and trainloads of prospective settlers were taken to the lands. 

The passing of the frontier was marked by one of the most spectacular rushes in our history. The United States government had bought from the 

Indians an unoccupied section of Indian Territory, later known as Oklahoma, and it was announced that a tract of over a million acres would be W-2x

thrown open for settlement at noon, April 22, 1889. Before the arrival of the appointed hour thousands of settlers waited to claim the land. When the signal was given they rushed across the border, some on foot, some on horseback, and others in many different kinds of vehicles. By night, Guthrie was a tented city with a population of about ten thousand. The next year the territory was formally organized, and Oklahoma was started toward ultimate admission as a state. 

Admission of New States. As the western lands became populated the territories, one after another, asked for admission as states. Because of the political influence they would exercise, the question became at times an important issue in Congress; but in most cases each territory was admitted to the Union soon after it had acquired a fairly large population. 

Under the Omnibus Bill of 1889 four new states-North Dakota, South Dakota, Washington, and Montana, were admitted. Wyoming and Idaho were added in 1890. Utah became a state in 1896, after adopting a constitution which forbade polygamy. There then remained only the territories of New Mexico, Arizona, and Oklahoma. Oklahoma was admitted in 1907, but because Arizona refused to unite with New Mexico in 1906, these territories did not become states until 1912. Arizona was the last to be admitted, since it had aroused the opposition of President Taft by providing in its constitution for the recall of judges. It was admitted only

The Influence of the West on American Political Institutions. No factor has been more potent in molding the character of the American people than the frontier. The first colonists were Europeans and they brought with them their European culture, institutions, and customs. They held on to much of their European culture as long as they remained in the Tidewater section, where they had easy access to the sea and to the mother country. But when the westward movement began new traits were developed and some of the old traits were accentuated. The frontier, removed as it was from the protection or assistance of the colonial government, developed among the settlers the spirit of self-reliance almost to the point of lawlessness. The necessity of providing for their own needs developed the initiative of the Westerners to such an extent that it has become a marked characteristic of present-day Americans. The long list of American inventions during the past century is ample evidence of the presence of this trait. Still other traits which Americans owe to the frontier are energy, ambition, pride, and unconventionality. 

The West and Democracy. In the West, where the family was a selfsufficing economic unit, and where there were no class distinctions based on birth or wealth, democracy was almost a religion. Many of the democratic innovations in our government are the direct result of the frontier influence. Almost from the beginning of the first American frontier in the 

Piedmont there was a sharp conflict with the more aristocratic and conservative Tidewater. Westerners demanded a more democratic system of representation in the legislature, manhood suffrage, cheap money for the benefit of the debtor classes, and the complete separation of church and state. It was the demand for these principles that led to Bacon's Rebellion, the Regulator movement, Shays's Rebellion, and the Whisky Insurrection. 

The American Revolution was fought for some of the same principles and was brought on and supported largely by the frontier section. 

In the 1830's the Tidewater aristocracy was defeated by the Jacksonian democracy with its glorification of the rights of the common man. A more liberal suffrage, rotation in office, an increase in the number of elective offices, and the adoption of the convention system of nominations were democratic innovations of the Western states. The Granger, Populist, Insurgent, Progressive, Farmers' Bloc, and Greenback movements are modern manifestations of the frontier influence. It is significant that most of the democratic innovations of recent years, such as the referendum,

initiative, recall, and woman suffrage made early and rapid progress in the 

Western states. 

Nationalism. An outstanding characteristic of the frontier people was their strong feeling of nationalism. Coming from many different states, and even from some European nations, these Western immigrants were influenced but slightly by a sense of loyalty to any particular state. Far more important to them was the national government, from which they secured their land upon easy terms and to which they looked for protection and maintenance of order until they were ready for statehood. But even after their admission into the Union as states, their dependence upon the national government did not cease. The aid of the entire nation was needed in solving the problem of transportation, for Western states were too poor to build the long lines of highways, railroads, and canals that were required to connect them with the Eastern markets. 

The West in Politics; Internal Improvements. One of the greatest problems the frontiersmen had to face was that of transportation. Land was almost the only form of wealth possessed, and this was frequently mortgaged. The new states, therefore, were unable to secure by taxation the great sums necessary for the construction of highways and canals. 

The question was further complicated by the fact that the transportation routes often passed through several states, and it was difficult to get all of the states concerned to co-operate in the enterprise. For these reasons the West looked to the national government for assistance, and throughout our history the voice of the Westerners has been insistent in demanding internal improvements which were to be paid for from the national treasury. The Cumberland Road (p. 258) was the first national undertaking of this kind. During the era of the railroad builders the construction of the transcontinental lines was made possible by extensive grants of public land to the railroad companies. In our own day the Federal government is rendering financial assistance in the construction of improved highways. 

The Tariff. Westerners who strongly urged government aid in internal improvements lent a sympathetic ear to the demands of the industrialists for protection, and they usually gave their support to the protective tariff policy of the central government. Such a policy was not lacking in benefits to the West, for the industrialization of the East meant an increased demand for the raw products and foodstuffs of the West. With the rise of the sugar-beet industry and sheep ranching, the West had a more direct reason for favoring a protective tariff. This common interest in a protective tariff helped to bring about the alignment of the East and the West in the sectional struggle against the South. (See also Chapter XXIV, pages 465-476.)

The Influence of the West on American Social and Economic Condi tions. From the time that the first American settlers established themselves along the Atlantic coast, there has been a continual movement westward in search of better lands and greater opportunity. For nearly three centuries the influence of the frontier was interwoven into all aspects of our political, social, and economic life. From colonial days the West provided an outlet for the crowded conditions of the East and for the influx of new immigrants from Europe by offering opportunity not only to farmers and prospectors, but also to lawyers, merchants, carpenters, printers, and others in the new towns that sprang up. It acted as a safety valve for laborers who hoped to find in government homesteads relief from the grinding toil of the mills. It furnished a spirit of optimism that characterized the American mind. It aided in the resistance to foreign cultures, thereby keeping the American a distinct individual. It was especially valuable in a time of stress, or after a war, in giving the unadjusted a chance to find again their economic place in society. In other words, the 

West, until about the end of the nineteenth century, kept us free from many of the difficulties experienced by the more crowded countries of Europe. 

The passing of the frontier had an important effect upon American life. 

It brought new problems of social adjustment. Depressions could no longer be solved by letting the unemployed go west. Agriculture, which had been the primary economic interest of the nation, had to yield first place to other interests. Some manufacturers, realizing that their workmen could no longer migrate to the West, began to lower wages, and this in turn stimulated the growth of labor unions. Since there were no longer any enormous, unexploited natural resources (excepting oil) after about 1900, interest was aroused in conservation, in the irrigation of arid lands, and in the drainage of swamps. The national problem was no longer how to cut down and burn away the vast forests, but to save and wisely use the remaining timber. Conservation rather than exploitation now became more important. 

Irrigation Projects in the West. Several Indian tribes in the Southwest had little irrigated garden plots before the coming of white men to our land. In 1847 the Mormons (p. 320) began extensive use of irrigation near the Great Salt Lake. They soon demonstrated that arid Western lands yield fine crops when supplied with enough water. Many large projects were undertaken later, and by 1933 nearly 20,000,000 acres in the arid parts of the West had been brought under irrigation. 

Early projects were the result of private initiative, and in 1894 Congress passed the Carey Act, granting a million acres of public land to each of certain states, to be used by them for promoting irrigation projects under

companies that would sell the land to the users; but the results were disappointing. In 1902, therefore, Congress passed the Newlands Act, or 

Federal Reclamation Act, which gave the Department of the Interior power to undertake irrigation projects in sixteen western states. The necessary funds were secured first by the sale of public lands and later by the "revolving fund" derived from the sale on the installment plan-of the irrigated lands to the settlers using them. Among the irrigation dams constructed by the Reclamation Service are the Arrowrock Dam in Idaho, the Elephant Butte Dam in New Mexico, the Roosevelt Dam in Arizona, the Shoshone Dam in Wyoming, the Owyhee Dam in Oregon, and, the Boulder Dam-730 feet high, the largest dam in the worldbuilt in 1930-1935 on the Colorado River in Nevada and Arizona. 

A Substitute for the Old Frontier. The full shock of the passing of the frontier was postponed by the World War and by the era of speculation which followed. Only in the last few years has it registered with increasing force. One of the great problems confronting us today is that of finding a proper substitute for the frontier with its free lands. This the administration of Franklin D. Roosevelt tried to do in the building of "synthetic frontiers" by the opening of new lands for settlement through several additional irrigation projects in Western states, and by the development of the Tennessee Valley in the South (pp. 761-762). The Tennessee Valley project was intended to serve as a laboratory to show what planned colonization could do as compared with the haphazard settlement of the Old West. 

The Resettlement Administration in 1935, according to R. G. Tugwell, was concerned with four important purposes: the retirement of substandard land from production, and the removal of the people to areas where they can become economically independent; the relocation of standard rural groups in self-help agricultural-industrial communities; the resettlement of industrial population in suburban communities to improve the housing conditions of low-income groups; and the rehabilitation of farm families, chiefly by loans necessary for livestock, seeds, and equipment. 

Colonization Project in Alaska. One of the chief colonization projects of the government in 1935 was that of the transplanting of one hundred ninety-one families (about one thousand persons) from the droughtstricken areas of Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan, to the Matanuska Valley, about a hundred miles north of Seward, Alaska. There the 

Federal Emergency Relief Administration was sponsoring a new type of subsistence-colonization project. Each family was provided with a 40-acre tract, a log cabin with built-in furniture and running water, livestock, farm machinery, and some cash. A physician, a dentist, and a Red Cross

Wide World 

Steamship landing at Seward, Alaska, in the summer of 1935. The men are on their way to aid in the settlement of the Matanuska Valley. nurse were in attendance. Each family was given thirty years to pay the government $3,000, with 3 per cent interest, the first payment due in four years. It was expected that within three years they would be able to support themselves and to begin to repay the loans. Crop control, soil management, processing, marketing, and distribution were centered in the official hands of the Alaska Rural Rehabilitation Corporation. 

When completed and in successful operation, it was hoped that the project would offer to the citizens of the United States a new frontier, for it is estimated that about 100,000 square miles in Alaska are suitable for farming and grazing. In 1930 there was a total population of 59,278. 

Fishing and mining were then the most important industries. There were in 1930 only 500 farms with a total area of 525,942 acres of which only 8,825 acres was improved land. With such a sparse agricultural population and with a vast area of tillable land still uncultivated there is in Alaska an agricultural frontier not yet exhausted. In the Matanuska Valley, which is thirty-five miles wide and seventy miles long, are large areas of virgin forests and fertile soil still untouched by plows. There is plenty of water for crops and cattle. The soil, rainfall, and many hours of summer sunlight combine to make the production of large crops possible. There is also an abundance of fish and game. The winds from the warm Japanese Cur-

rent modify the otherwise harsh climate so that the average winter temperature is about the same as that of Kansas City. 

In May, 1935, a newspaper in Seward printed an editorial welcoming the arrival of the families. It said: "You are one of us now. The last wave of American westward migration has in Alaskan parlance gone 'inside.""

Chapter XX. 

Chapter XXI. 

 RECONSTRUCTION 

BECAUSE OF DIFFERENCES in climate, soil, and other natural resources sectionalism developed in the United States. The South became a distinctly agrarian region in which large plantations produced staple crops. 

It differed from the other sections in its economic organization, since the negro slave was well adapted to plantation labor. 

Negroes were brought to one of the American colonies and sold as early as 1619. Because of the need of labor, especially in the South where the plantation system predominated, and where such staples as tobacco, rice, indigo, sugar, and later cotton, were produced on a large scale, slave labor became profitable. On the other hand, it was not profitable on the small farms in the West nor in the factories and mills in the East. In time, rivalry developed between the sections. The institution of slavery was criticized and those who opposed it became active in organizing antislavery societies to urge its abolition. This agitation for abolition caused the Southern planters, under the leadership of Thomas R. Dew, John C. Calhoun, and others, to formulate a philosophy for the defense of their institution. 339

The North and the South sought to protect their different economic interests, as well as their social institutions, through control of the national government. Each section wanted to extend its own economic system. 

Many differences appeared between the two groups, but compromises were sometimes able to smooth over the difficulties. In 1820, the Missouri 

Compromise settled for a time the status of slavery in the territory purchased from France; but as the country expanded, the question arose in the newly acquired territory. The opponents of slavery tried to exclude it from the new area, while the friends of slavery, that is, the representatives from the slaveholding states, insisted that the institution be permitted to grow there. The contest was adjusted only temporarily by the Compromise of 1850.

The breaking of the Union was the culmination of the long controversy for political power by the two sections with opposing economic interests. 

Each was bent upon making its policy that of the government. The contest for control became more and more bitter, and eventually resulted in the secession of the Southern states and in the organization of the Confederacy. The war which followed came to an end in 1865, and was in turn succeeded by another period of strife over the question of reconstruction. 

Radical leaders in Congress assumed control and proceeded to reconstruct the South along pro-negro lines. Before many years, however, the control of the Southern states was regained by the white men.

CHAPTER XVIII The Origin of the Controversy The Beginnings of American Slavery. The settlers in the New World were handicapped by an inadequate supply of laborers. The Spaniards, who had come to America principally for the purpose of exploitation, were not inclined to engage in hard manual labor, and almost immediately resorted to slavery as a solution of their labor problem. It was natural that they should do this, for the institution of slavery had existed in the Old World from remote antiquity, and, at the time when America was settled, was generally approved. The early Spanish colonists made extensive use of the Indians as slaves in their mines and on their sugar plantations in the West Indies, but the Indians were not accustomed to this kind of labor, and failed to make satisfactory slaves. They were unable to resist the white man's diseases, and died in great numbers. Las Casas, the famous 'Apostle of the Indians," suggested bringing negroes to the New World in order to alleviate the lot of the Indians. In 1563 and later Sir John 

Hawkins, the famous English seaman, brought many African negroes to the West Indies and sold them to the planters. The negroes proved to be much better adapted to hard manual labor than the Indians, and soon were in demand not only in the West Indies, but on the American mainland as well. 86 Negroes are Brought to Virginia. The English settlers at Jamestown at first depended upon white indentured servants for the solution of their labor problem, but the huge profits derived from the sale of slaves in the West Indies prompted a search for additional markets by those engaged in the trade. In 1619 a vessel came to Jamestown with twenty negroes, who were sold or indentured to Virginia planters. Negroes did not displace the white indentured servants; in fact, in 1650, thirty years after the first arrival of negroes, there were only three hundred of them in Virginia. 

It was tobacco, not cotton, that first made slavery profitable in the South. The tobacco crop, which required much hard labor in the broiling 341

sun, during its growing season of about six months, offered a type of work to which the African negro was well adapted. The growth of slavery in colonial Virginia very closely parallels the expansion of the tobacco industry. Tobacco exports increased from 500,000 pounds in 1627, to more than 

7,000,000 pounds in 1663, and to 15,000,000 pounds in 1700; while (during the greater part of the same period) the number of slaves in Virginia increased from 300 in 1650, to 2000 in 1671, and to 6000 in 1700. 

Slavery Spreads to Other Colonies. Maryland, like Virginia, found the production of tobacco profitable, and soon came to depend upon negro slaves to perform the great amount of work that was required for its culture. Many planters in the Carolinas were very successful in the cultivation of rice and indigo. These crops also offered much work for which the negroes were well suited, and slavery soon became firmly established in North and South Carolina. Georgia at first prohibited slavery, but competition with her slaveholding neighbors soon led to the removal of all restrictions against slavery in that colony. 

Slavery was not confined to the Southern colonies, but extended into all of the thirteen colonies. It was not very profitable in the Northern

Postboy, December 22, 1746 colonies, however, because of the severe climate, the small farms, and the soil which was unsuitable for raising staple crops. When the New England colonists turned to commerce and manufacturing as their principal occupations, the negroes were found unsatisfactory for that kind of labor. 

Although slavery was not profitable in New England, Northern shipowners found the slave trade very lucrative. They built up a "triangular" trade with Africa and the West Indies, in which rum was the main currency. Vessels would leave Boston and other Northern ports for Africa,

loaded with rum which was to be exchanged for slaves. The slaves would then be taken to the Southern states and to the West Indies and exchanged for money and for molasses, which would be brought to New England and distilled into rum, thus completing the triangle with huge profits. So zealously did the slave traders ply their trade that some of the Southern planters complained that the New Englanders were ruining them by forcing the blacks upon them for the sake of double profits from the negroes and the rum. The first census, in 1790, showed about 700,000 slaves in the United States, of whom all except about 40,000 were in the Southern states.

The Colonies Attempt to Restrict Slavery. It appears that the Virginia planters who bought the first negroes in 1619 believed that they were setting up a system which would be temporary. Many other planters also believed that the negroes would serve only a limited period. Few were in favor of a permanent system of slavery. Excepting Quakers, however, few 

Americans attacked slavery on moral grounds; the chief objections to it were social and economic. Massachusetts and Rhode Island passed restrictive statutes against negro slavery, but these laws were not enforced, and slavery was continued there as in other New England states. Some of the Southern colonists became alarmed at the steadily increasing number of negroes, and in 1710 Virginia attempted to check the slave trade by placing a duty of £5 on every slave imported. The bill was vetoed by the royal governor, who acted in the interest of the British slave traders. Other 

Southern colonies attempted to restrict the traffic, but they were always frustrated by the royal veto. The first Continental Congress, in 1774, agreed that no slaves should be imported into any of the thirteen colonies after December 1, 1774, and the first draft of the Declaration of Independence styled the slave trade as a "cruel war against human nature itself, violating its most sacred rights of life and liberty," and severely indicted the king for "suppressing every legislative attempt to prohibit or to restrain this commerce." Those clauses, however, were omitted before the 

Declaration was adopted.

Slavery Declines during the Period of the Confederation. The blessings of independence were tempered with certain disadvantages. While the Navigation Laws were in operation, Great Britain had purchased nearly all of her tobacco and much of her indigo and rice from the Southern colonies, but after the Revolution the British merchants shifted their trade to other colonies which had remained loyal to the king. This led to a marked decline in the price of the three staple crops, the cultivation of which had made slavery profitable. Had it not been for the difficult prob- W-23

lem of dealing with more than a half million negroes, most of them with little or no training in self-support, and the fear of race war and Africanization, it is very probable that all of the states would have been willing to emancipate their slaves.

In the Northern states, where the number of negroes was not great, and where slavery on a large scale had never been profitable, emancipation made considerable progress. By 1787 Massachusetts had abolished slavery, and Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, and Connecticut had provided for gradual emancipation. New Hampshire, New York, and New Jersey soon followed the example of these states. The question of slavery in the territories belonging to the national government, which was destined to become the subject of many bitter sectional controversies, first arose in 1787. 

In that year, Congress, under the Articles of Confederation, adopted a plan of government for the Northwest Territory, in which it declared that slavery should forever be excluded from that territory. 

The Constitution Recognizes Slavery. During the Constitutional Con vention in 1787, the question of slavery was frequently discussed. The system was attacked upon both economic and moral grounds. South 

Carolina and Georgia stood almost alone in its defense. These states upheld slavery, not as a positive good, but rather as a necessary evil. So strong was their determination not to enter a union in which the slave trade would be prohibited, that other states which desired a cessation of the traffic agreed to a compromise which provided that the importation of slaves should not be prohibited for twenty years, and that no import duty exceeding ten dollars a head should be levied upon them. This compromise was faithfully observed, but on January 1, 1808, the earliest date permissible under the Constitution, the slave trade was prohibited. 

The Constitution also provided for the return of fugitive slaves to their masters.

The Industrial Revolution Fastens Slavery upon the South. Few people in 1790, however, expected for slavery more than a brief existence in the United States. Not only was the system becoming unprofitable, but it was being widely attacked upon moral grounds. The antislavery movement in both sections was rapidly gaining momentum. Many Southerners condemned slavery as an evil. Washington provided in his will for the emancipation of his own slaves after the death of his wife, and Jefferson, in writing on the subject of slavery, said: "I tremble for my country when 

I reflect that God is just; that His justice cannot sleep forever." 

It was the Industrial Revolution which gave the slave system new life. 

A series of inventions in England had completely revolutionized the tex-

Slaves who worked in a cotton field getting food rations; from an old print 

Culver Service tile industry. The speed with which cotton and wool could be spun and woven into cloth was limited only by the supply of raw materials. Because of the extremely laborious task of separating the fiber from the seed, cotton had never been grown on an extensive scale. Eli Whitney, a New England schoolteacher, became interested in the problem, and in 1793 invented the cotton "gin" (a contraction of the word "engine"), which separated the fiber from the seed three hundred times as rapidly as it could be done by hand. It now became profitable to grow cotton upon an extensive scale. 

The amount of cotton produced in the South increased from 2,000,000 pounds in 1791, to 40,000,000 pounds in 1801, to 80,000,000 pounds in 1811, and to 177,000,000 pounds in 1821. Since slave labor was well suited to the cotton field, slavery again was placed upon a profitable basis, and was definitely fastened upon that portion of the United States which was adapted to the cultivation of cotton. 

Cotton and the Westward Movement. So great was the demand for cotton that from 1793 to 1810 the price never fell below sixteen cents a pound, and in 1818 it rose to thirty-four cents. Naturally the Southern planters could not resist the temptation to specialize in the production of this money-making crop. But the increased production of cotton meant a corresponding increase in the demand for slaves, and the average price of negro slaves in our country in 1820 was somewhere between $700 and $1100. The methods of cultivation under the slave labor system were extremely primitive. It was the general practice to cultivate the same land until the cotton produced no longer paid for the cost of production. Few planters thought of attempting to restore the fertility of the soil, and when the yield from a portion of a plantation became unprofitable, the owner simply allowed that land to lie fallow for several years, and sought in-

creased production in new and more fertile land. In this way, the size of the plantations constantly grew larger, and the system pressed farther and farther toward the southwest, where the land and climate seemed most favorable to the production of cotton. 

This westward expansion was facilitated by the cheapness of the land, the price of which as late as 1842 averaged only about ten dollars an acre. 

The cost of the land in a thousand-acre plantation did not exceed $10,000, but it was estimated that the cost of the slaves required to do the work on such a plantation was about $50,000. A few years later it was estimated that slaves valued at $600,000,000 were employed on land valued at $45,000,000. The slave, rather than the land, became the investment. 

The land came to be regarded as a part of the current expenses-something to be worn out, not improved.

The Quakers Lead the Antislavery Movement. During the colonial era, slavery was not regarded as permanent or as wholly desirable, and most of the opposition to it was based upon economic rather than moral grounds. There were some, however, who vigorously attacked the ethics and morality of the system, and prominent among these were the Quakers, or the Society of Friends. Under the leadership of John Woolman and 

Anthony Benezet, this sect denounced slavery as contrary to Christianity, and made the holding of slaves a cause of expulsion from the society. In 

1688 the Quakers made the first formal protest in America against slavery, and did not relent in their attacks until the Thirteenth Amendment brought an end to the institution. 

Antislavery Societies. The forces opposed to slavery began to organize about the time of the Revolution. The first antislavery society was organized at Philadelphia, April 14, 1775. The society very promptly memorialized the legislature of Pennsylvania to emancipate the slaves. By 1808, societies had appeared in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Kentucky, and New York; and by 1830 more than one hundred antislavery societies had been established. These societies were found in all the states except in New 

England, in the extreme South, and in Indiana. They formed a national organization to promote antislavery sentiment as early as 1794. 

The Churches Attack Slavery. Probably no single force was more effective in mobilizing public opinion against slavery than the churches, through their state and national bodies. The work of the Quakers has already been mentioned. In 1812 the Methodist General Conference voted that no slaveholder could continue as an elder. Three years later, the 

Presbyterian General Assembly urged that the slaves be educated as a preparation for emancipation; and in 1818 adopted a resolution condemning

slavery as "a gross violation of the most precious and moral rights of human nature, as utterly inconsistent with the law of God . . . and as totally irreconcilable with the spirit and principles of the Gospel of Christ." The 

Baptists were lacking in a national organization, and each congregation was permitted to establish its own policy with respect to slavery. Some churches refused to admit slaveholders into membership, while others took no action whatever upon the question. 

The American Colonization Society. One of the greatest obstacles to the emancipation of the slaves was the problem of disposing of the freed negroes. Had it not been for this problem, it is probable that emancipation in the South would have been carried out on a much more extensive scale. 

Jefferson, who opposed slavery (p. 344), proposed, in 1784, that the negroes be sent out of the country. In 1816 there was formed "The American 

Society for the Colonization of the Free People of Color of the United States." Bushrod Washington and Henry Clay served as presidents of the society. Liberia, in Africa, was selected as the site for the colony. Although the society had the support of many influential men, and of Congress, which appropriated $100,000 to be used in the movement, the society was not a success; in the period from 1820 to 1830, only 1162 negroes were transported to Liberia by the Colonization Society. 

Antislavery Arguments. The chief arguments against slavery were that it was contrary to the principles of the Declaration of Independence, uneconomical, and unchristian. Liberty was one of the "inalienable" rights of man. Slavery, therefore, could not be justified unless the negro was looked upon as something else than man. To exclude men from the blessings of free government because they were inferior to other men seemed to strike at the very foundation of democracy. 

Perhaps the most telling argument against slavery was that it did not pay. Abundant evidence pointed to the fact that the South was lagging far behind the North in wealth, industry, roads, population, and intellectual growth. The antislavery people were sure that slavery was the only explanation for this. 

The Rise of the Abolitionists. Before 1830, the antislavery leaders had, on the whole, been moderate in their criticisms, and seemed to be content to seek the gradual elimination of an undesirable institution; but now a new and more violent group of agitators, known as abolitionists, became active. They urged immediate, unconditional, and universal emancipation, without any compensation to the slaveholder, whom they regarded as a sinner in the sight of God. One of the pioneers of the abolition movement was Elihu Embree, who had been a slaveholder in Tennessee, and about

1812, at the age of thirty, joined the Society of Friends. Later he specified that his slaves should be "legally emancipated as soon as they can." He aligned himself with the Manumission Society of Tennessee, and in 1819 he published, at Jonesboro, Tennessee, the Manumission Intelligencer, a weekly newspaper soon to be succeeded by The Emancipator, a monthly publication appearing in April, 1820. In this paper he attacked slavery and announced that "one of the leading tenets of my creed is universal and equal liberty. . . and another tenet of my creed . . . Endeavor to know what is right, and do it, dreading no consequences." Embree died in December, 1820, and another pioneer, Benjamin Lundy, who had organized a number of antislavery societies, carried on the work. Lundy founded an abolitionist paper, The Genius of Universal Emancipation, and in his zeal to spread his message, traveled more than sixteen hundred miles on foot, preaching his doctrines. 

Another outstanding pioneer in the abolitionist movement was Theodore Weld. In 1834 he conducted an active antislavery campaign in Ohio, then carried the fight into Vermont, western Pennsylvania, and New York. 

He preached with great zeal, and, in the manner and spirit of an evangelist in a protracted revival meeting, moved his audiences to action with his remarkable eloquence. His opponents often resorted to violence; so bitter was the opposition that usually a bodyguard of young men was required to insure his safety. Often stones crashed through the windows of the churches where he spoke, but he continued in the face of violence and converted to the cause hundreds in his audiences. Many of his hearers became leaders in the movement and organized abolition societies. SLAVE.
