Facsimile of the heading of The Liberator 

William Lloyd Garrison is perhaps the best-known of the various abolition leaders. Without any particular literary training, he established the celebrated paper The Liberator. Garrison set the type for the first issue

with his own hands, and printed it on paper which he had bought on credit. 

This issue carried the startling announcement: "I shall strenuously contend for immediate enfranchisement of our slave population. . . . I will be harsh as truth and as uncompromising as justice on this subject. . . . I do not wish to think, or speak, or write with moderation. . . . I am in earnest -I will not equivocate-I will not excuse-I will not retreat a single inchand I will be heard!" He opposed the Constitution because it protected slavery, and in 1843 he placed at the head of his paper the words: "The compact which exists between the North and the South is a covenant with death and an agreement with hell. . . and should be annulled." 

Garrison soon won other converts to the cause. Among these were three New England poets, Whittier, Lowell, and Longfellow; the two 

Grimké sisters from South Carolina; Theodore Parker, James G. Birney,

Cassius M. Clay, and Wendell Phillips. All of these were pitiless in their attitude toward the slaveholders. Sometimes the abolitionists went so far as to send papers, pamphlets, and other forms of incendiary literature into the South, calling upon the slaves to revolt against their masters. 

Nat Turner's Insurrection. The fear of a slave uprising had hovered like a specter over the South for many years. In 1831, the same year that 

The Liberator appeared, this specter became reality when Nat Turner, a negro religious fanatic, led an insurrection against the whites in Southampton County, Virginia. Sixty white people were killed. Excitement and lawlessness continued for many days. Many people of the South believed that the insurrection was the result of the abolition propaganda, and demanded that all abolitionist literature be suppressed. Fearing the influence of abolition agents, Southern state legislatures passed laws restricting the education and religious worship of the slaves, but these laws were not rigidly enforced.

Northern Attitude toward Abolition. At the beginning of the movement, the abolitionists were almost as unpopular in the North as in the South. A mob in Boston destroyed the office of The Liberator and dragged 

Garrison through the streets. In 1835 a purse of one hundred dollars was offered the individual who would first lay violent hands upon an abolition leader who, it was rumored, would address an antislavery society at Boston. Two years later, Elijah P. Lovejoy, an abolitionist editor, was killed by a mob at Alton, Illinois, and his press was destroyed. 

Many of the Northern states had enacted "black codes," by which the rights of the negroes were restricted as much as they were in the South. 

Many of the Northern states did not allow negroes to serve on juries or in the militia, and in Ohio a negro was not admitted into the state unless two

white men gave a bond guaranteeing his good behavior. Few of the Northern states made any provision for the education of the negroes, and in some states they were not permitted to attend white schools. In New 

Hampshire three hundred men, with a hundred yoke of oxen, pulled a negro schoolhouse into a neighboring swamp; and in Connecticut Miss 

Prudence Crandall was forced to close her school because she admitted colored girls.

The succession of outbreaks in the North merely advertised the cause of the abolitionists, who gradually increased in numbers and resources. The aggressive policies of the slaveholders also strengthened the support of the abolitionists throughout the North. 

The Southern Attitude Toward Slavery Changed. The increasing profits from slavery brought about a decided change in the attitude of the Southern planters toward the system which was rapidly coming to be regarded in the South as a permanent institution. Before the Revolution, slavery was rather generally condemned, even in the South; but for several decades after the invention of the cotton gin, the Southern attitude gradually changed to a justification of the system, not on moral grounds, but on the claim that it had become a necessary evil. Proslavery leaders insisted that the warm climate of the South required slavery, and that emancipation could be accomplished only by seriously endangering the safety of the white race, an argument which was more readily accepted now that a slave had come to be valued at a thousand dollars rather than a few hundred dollars. Yet there were many Southern people who continued their opposition to slavery, and abolition societies in the South continued to increase in number.

The Proslavery Philosophy. With the growing attack of the abolitionists on the institution of slavery, the leaders in the South felt called upon to defend their social and economic system. Soon after 1831 the attitude advanced from that of justification to one of open praise: no longer was slavery regarded by Southerners as a necessary evil, but rather as a positive good. Leaders who were largely responsible for this change in Southern thought were John C. Calhoun, Thomas R. Dew, Chancellor 

William Harper, and John Henry Hopkins. These leaders openly repudiated the Jeffersonian dogma that all men are created equal, and substituted for it the Greek doctrine of inequality. 

Some men, they said, were fit only for hard toil; others, for the work of managers. They denied the existence of natural rights, and asserted that rights came as a result of service to society. Since property owners had a large stake in society, they should be the virtual rulers; while slaves had

the right of protection against violence, cold, and hunger, in return for their labor. Such a social system was regarded as ideal. Calhoun even went so far as to assert that there had never been a wealthy or civilized society in which one portion did not live on the labor of the other. According to this doctrine, slavery had become the actual "cornerstone of our 

Republican edifice."

So great was the influence of these leaders that the South readily accepted the theories. Even Biblical arguments were offered to uphold the new doctrine. Many believed not only that slavery was not a sin, but that it was especially commanded by God through Moses, and approved by Christ through his apostles. The South believed that it would become a model civilization, with no poverty, and therefore little crime, to which white men of the North would flee like runaway slaves.

A Southern Plantation. Not all of the people in the South lived on plantations. In fact, in 1850, only about 350,000 white families, out of a total of 1,800,000, held slaves. Fully two thirds of the white population of the South had no direct connection with slavery. The plantations varied considerably in size, but a thousand acres of land and a hundred slaves were regarded as the most productive unit. Many plantations, however, were smaller than this, while some were much larger. 

The plantation home was usually an imposing structure of ten or twelve rooms, with long porches and white columns, which added to its grandeur. Trees and shrubs increased its beauty. Graveled walks led to the slave cabins in the rear, and to the numerous other outer buildings. 

The negro cabins were in decided contrast to the palatial home of the master. They were small, dilapidated log houses, daubed with clay. The interior of the cabin was dingy and black with smoke, and the furniture was simple and rude, consisting of beds and mats for sleeping, a chest, a wooden stool, and cooking apparatus. The cooking was usually done at the open fireplace, but on the large plantations the main meals were cooked frequently in a central kitchen like an army mess hall. 

Food and Dress of the Slaves. The ordinary food of the field slaves was corn bread, bacon, sweet potatoes, and other vegetables. These articles, together with sugar, salt, and other necessities, were furnished by the masters. Frequently the slaves cultivated their own gardens, and many of them raised their own pigs and chickens. Wild game added variety to the diet. Household servants usually enjoyed the same foods that were served on the master's table. 

The dress varied according to the kind of work done by the slaves. The mistress usually took considerable pride in the appearance of the house-

IB, MINI  

Slaves at home, after the day's work was over. Negroes always have been fond of singing and dancing; and the banjo has been a favorite musical instrument with them, 352

hold servants, who were clothed in the garments recently cast aside by members of the master's family. The field hands, however, were not so fortunate, and often presented a ragged appearance. The pickaninnies wore little more than a long shirt, and sometimes, indeed, they played around the cabin without any clothing. 

The total annual cost of feeding and clothing a slave varied from fifteen to fifty dollars-in a period when these sums would buy much more food and clothing than they would in recent times. 

Treatment of the Slaves. Slavery, on the whole, was characterized by many objectionable features. The labor usually was hard, especially during the busy summer season, when the slaves frequently were required to work fifteen hours a day. Families sometimes were separated through sales, but in the main it was to the master's advantage to keep his slaves happy and contented. Punishments at times were severe; the common method of chastisement was whipping with a cowhide or "blacksnake" whip, a form of punishment which was in practice also in disciplining white sailors in the navy and merchant marine. Brutal treatment of the negroes was uncommon except on some of the largest plantations where the overseers often were more heartless than the masters, and where the large number of slaves made strict discipline necessary. 

Negroes also were punished in the courts more severely than whites who were guilty of the same offenses. Because of the fear of insurrection, negroes were denied the right to carry weapons, or even to assemble, except under certain restrictions, and it was considered a serious offense for a slave to be absent from the plantation without the written permission of his master or overseer. Patrols were organized in most of the states to enforce these restrictions.

Slavery, however, had a brighter side. The planter's family often displayed a sympathetic interest in the servants. When slaves were sick they were attended by the family physician, and sometimes were nursed by the mistress. In case of death the slave was given a simple but decent burial in the "God's acre" of the plantation. Amusements among the negroes were encouraged so long as they were conducted in an orderly manner. 

Kind treatment was the rule where the slaves were not very numerous, and was not uncommon even on the largest plantations. The characteristic loyalty of the slaves during the War between the States is strong evidence of the gratitude of servants for the sympathetic treatment of kind and generous masters, some of whom, upon entering the service of the Confederacy, left the management of their plantations in the hands of trusted slaves, without any fears or misgivings. Under such masters, slavery was

a patriarchal system in which master and slave felt themselves members of one family. 

Education of the Slaves. Most of the slaveholders were not greatly concerned about the education of their servants, and, except in the case of a few masters and mistresses who personally instructed the negroes in reading and writing, this kind of negro training was almost entirely neglected; in fact, some of the Southern states as early as 1740 had passed laws making it illegal to teach the slaves to read or write. After Nat 

Turner's Insurrection in 1831, there was a wave of such legislation designed to protect the institution against the incendiary literature of the abolitionists. These laws, however, were not rigidly enforced. Some schools for negroes continued to operate openly, and only in very rare cases were the instructors of slaves arrested. It has been estimated that in 1860 from ten to twenty per cent of the slaves could read.

Religious Instruction. The belief that no Christian could hold another in servitude discouraged all attempts to convert the slaves to Christianity during the first century of American slavery; but the influence of the Great 

Awakening and the Revolution tended to arouse an interest in the religious instruction of the colored race. Separate negro congregations were formed, sometimes with colored pastors, and in the first quarter of the nineteenth century two independent negro churches were organized. The movement was retarded by a series of slave insurrections from 1800 to 1831, most of which were planned by negro religious leaders; but when the abolition influence was removed from the churches in the South by the schisms in the Baptist and Methodist churches, in 1844 and 1845, the interest in the religious instruction of the slaves grew very rapidly. Church bodies, planters' associations for the instruction of the slaves, and plantation missions conducted a great missionary movement. In 1860 over 500,000 negroes were members of white or colored churches. This was about one fourth of the total number of negroes in the South above eighteen years of age.

CHAPTER XIX Slavery in Politics 

Geographical Bases of Sectionalism. The real causes of the War between the North and the South may be found in the conflicting economic interests of the two sections,-interests which, in turn, grew out of their divergent geographical conditions. Cold winters and poor, rocky soil made most of the area of the Northeast unsuited to agriculture, but abundant water power, proximity to the raw products of the West, and a large population which provided an adequate supply of skilled labor, gave that section great industrial and commercial advantages. After the War of 1812, aided by a protective tariff, the industrial development of the Northeast was great and rapid. The cost of production was relatively high, and competition with foreign manufactures, without special governmental protection, was considered impossible. The North, therefore, demanded a protective tariff, which raised the prices of manufactured goods sold in America; internal improvements, which rendered the raw products of the West more accessible; subsidies, which increased the tonnage of Northern ships; and a Bank of the United States, which added to the money power of the North. 

On the other hand, geographical conditions in the South were most favorable to the development of agriculture. Long summers, heavy rainfall, and rich virgin soil encouraged the Southern planters in the production of rice, indigo, tobacco, and cotton. The fact that these crops could be cultivated by cheap slave labor added to the profits, and caused the institution of slavery to be widely adopted throughout the South. 

Conflicting Economic Interests. The agricultural interests of the 

South were irreconcilably opposed to the industrial interests of the North. 

The protective tariff merely raised the prices of manufactured articles purchased by the Southerners without increasing the prices of the raw products which were for sale in the South. It was a common complaint that the tariff restricted the foreign trade of the South as much as the Navigation Acts had restricted the colonies under the rule of Great Britain. In like 357

Slaves at work in a cotton field Gendreau manner, legislation favoring shipping subsidies, internal improvements, and the national bank, was regarded as further evidence of an industrial despotism. As British oppression had justified a war for independence, so now, in the opinion of many Southerners, industrial oppression could justify another struggle for liberty. Such a struggle seemed imminent during the South Carolina tariff controversy (pp. 265-268). 

The Sections Eager for Political Power. The two sections differing in economic interests stood opposed to each other. To protect its welfare, each section sought control of the national government. New states meant additional senators and representatives in Congress, and consequently each section was vitally interested in the spread of its own economic system into the territories from which the new states would be formed. Since slavery was the cornerstone of the Southern economic system, while the industrial section relied upon free labor, the issue between these two systems of labor became the leading controversy at the admission of every new state.

In 1812 the states were equally divided between the sections-nine were free and nine were slaveholding. This equal division of states meant also an equal division in the number of senators, but the North, because of its greater population, had begun to forge ahead in the number of repre-

sentatives. Chief interest, therefore, centered in the control of the Senate. 

In 1816-1819 four new states were admitted, two from each section, so that in 1820 there were eleven free and eleven slaveholding states; but in the lower house the North had 105 representatives to 81 for the South. 

Missouri Applies for Admission. The question of slavery in the territory west of the Mississippi River and north of the state of Louisiana was brought up in Congress for the first time by the application of Missouri for statehood. The westward movement had brought a steady migration of settlers into the territory of Missouri, and by 1819 more than sixty thousand settlers, with about ten thousand slaves, had established themselves there. Soon after the introduction of a bill for the admission of Missouri as a state, James Tallmadge, of New York, proposed an amendment which declared that the further introduction of slavery into Missouri should be prohibited, and that all children born within the state after its admission should be free at the age of twenty-five years.

The Tallmadge amendment was the occasion of several bitter debates. 

Henry Clay favored the admission of Missouri as a slaveholding state, for he believed that the evils of slavery would be "mitigated by diffusion." 

Many Southern representatives and senators said the amendment was unconstitutional, for a clause in the Louisiana Purchase treaty with France had guaranteed the inhabitants of the territory the "protection of their liberties, property, and religion." Senator Rufus King, however, took the position that the power of Congress to admit new states necessarily implied the power to refuse to admit, and hence the power to make conditions on which a new state should be admitted. He said that the Northwest 

Ordinance (pp. 184-185) was evidence of the power of Congress to exclude slavery from territories, even after their admission to statehood. The 

Tallmadge amendment passed the House of Representatives but was defeated in the Senate, on February 27, 1819, by a vote of twenty-two to sixteen. A few days later, Congress adjourned without having disposed of the Missouri question.

The Missouri Compromise. In the next session of Congress, Maine, which was a part of Massachusetts, applied for admission to the Union as a free state. This new development offered a solution to the Missouri question, and after a long and bitter debate a compromise was obtained. 

Maine was permitted to enter the Union as a free state and Missouri as a slaveholding state, but in order to prevent the slavery question from arising every time a new state applied for admission, it was agreed that in the remainder of the territory purchased from France (the Louisiana Purchase), north of 36° 30' north latitude-the line of most of the southern 

W. 24

boundary of Missouri-slavery should forever be prohibited. It was presumed that slavery would be permitted in the small part of the Purchase south of this line (p. 234). Throughout the nation the Missouri Compromise was hailed as a permanent solution of the very perplexing question of slavery in the territories. That question, which Jefferson had likened to a "fire bell in the night that filled with terror," was actually retired into the background of national politics for nearly three decades. 

The Gag Resolutions. The slavery question, however, could not be kept entirely out of politics, and it soon reappeared in Congress in an unexpected way. The abolitionists kept the slavery question always before the people. So bitter became their criticism of the slaveholders, and sc insidious their propaganda, that their opponents determined to put an end to their activities, even at the price of freedom of speech and of the press. President Jackson recommended that "incendiary publications" be excluded from the mail. But who would be the judge as to the character of the publications sent through the mail? 

The abolitionists soon began to carry their propaganda into the very halls of Congress through antislavery petitions which were read by ex- President John Quincy Adams, who had been elected to the House of Representatives. In order to suppress these petitions, the Southern representatives, together with some from other sections, passed a series of resolutions known as the "Gag Resolutions," which provided that all petitions relating to the abolition of slavery were to be laid on the table without discussion. The indomitable Adams considered the resolutions as unconstitutional, charging that they violated the right of freedom of petition. Many other people who had not been in sympathy with the abolitionists held a view similar to that of Adams, and some of them enlisted in the abolition cause. The Gag Resolutions were repealed in 1844, but the fight over the right of petition had kept the question of slavery before the people and had added to the bitterness that existed between the sections.

Westward Extension. The slavery interests soon discovered that the 

Missouri Compromise was a distinct victory for the North, for by far the greater part of the national domain lay north of the compromise line, and very little territory in the Union was left open to slavery. Southern expansionists, therefore, began a search for new territory which might be brought into the Union as slaveholding states; for new states meant more senators, and control of Congress was the only protection against legislation which might be hostile to the economic interests of the agricultural South. Texas was well adapted to the production of cotton, and slavery would readily

be extended into this vast region. With the help of the Americans in 

Texas, as we have seen, she won her independence from Mexico in 1836, and applied for admission into the Union. The annexation of Texas was opposed in the North by the antislavery forces, who feared that a number of slaveholding states would be carved from it; and it was not until 1845 that President Tyler, regarding the election of 1844 as a referendum on the question, approved the act of Congress which admitted Texas into the Union as a slaveholding state. The next year saw the beginning of a war between Mexico and the United States (p. 315). It soon became apparent that the war would result in further territorial gains by the United States -in fact, many people believed that we had entered the war for the purpose of securing more slaveholding territory. 

The Wilmot Proviso. It so happened, however, that these events, which were expected to strengthen the position of the slaveholding interests, called forth a storm of opposition. Soon after the war began, President Polk asked Congress to appropriate $2,000,000 to enable him to negotiate to advantage with Mexico. David Wilmot, a Pennsylvania Democrat, introduced an amendment to the bill, which provided "That as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico by the United States, . . . neither slavery nor involuntary servitude shall ever exist in any part of said territory except for crime." 

The amendment was lost, but not until it had rekindled the flame which brought on bitter discussion between the two sections. 

The California Question. The Mexican War brought to the United 

States new territory nearly two and one half times the area of France. 

The question whether new territory should be slaveholding or free arose again, for the Missouri Compromise had applied only to the region acquired from France. There was a considerable difference of opinion as to how the new territory should be organized with reference to the question of slavery. The group which had supported the Wilmot Proviso wanted to exclude slavery from the entire territory. Another group, led by John 

C. Calhoun, proclaimed the doctrine that since territories belonged to all the states in common, Congress had no power to forbid citizens of any state, with their property, from settling in that territory. They insisted that the entire Mexican cession should be open to slavery. A third group proposed the extension of the Missouri Compromise line of 36° 30' through the new territory. There was still another group which held that the question should be decided by the territorial legislatures. 

While this question was under discussion, gold was discovered in California. Immediately there was a great rush to the new country, and in

1849 about eighty thousand "forty-niners" reached California. So large a population necessitated the immediate organization of a government. 

While Congress helplessly debated the slavery question, the settlers took the law into their own hands and drew up a constitution which excluded slavery, and demanded admission into the Union. 

The Compromise of 1850. When Congress convened in December, 1849, the Union was threatened with disruption, for at that time it included fifteen free states and fifteen slaveholding states, and Southern leaders were openly advocating secession if a new free state were added to the Union. In this critical situation, the personnel of Congress was most able and brilliant. For the last time, the voices of Thomas H. Benton and of that incomparable triumvirate of American orators, Calhoun, Clay, and Webster, sounded in the halls of the Senate. Almost as capable were a number of younger men who were just becoming prominent in national affairs-Stephen A. Douglas, William H. Seward, Jefferson 

Davis, Salmon P. Chase, and John Bell.

At a time when it seemed that the slavery question would wreck the nation, the "Great Pacificator," the aged Clay, proposed a series of measures which were calculated to reconcile the opposing sections. On account of the large number of provisions which it contained, Clay's compromise was known as the "Omnibus Bill." After a series of debates extending over a period of more than seven months, Clay's measures were finally adopted. They became known as the Compromise of 1850. The following were the most important provisions: (1) California was to be admitted as a free state (although a large part of it lay south of 36° 30′); (2) the remainder of the Mexican cession was to be organized into two territories without mention of slavery; (3) the slave trade (but not slavery) was to be prohibited in the District of Columbia; (4) a more stringent fugitive slave law was to be enacted; (5) Texas was to be paid $10,000,000 for her claim to part of New Mexico, and that territory was to be surrendered to the Federal government. While these provisions were being considered 

President Zachary Taylor died and was succeeded by the Vice-President 

Millard Fillmore, who was inaugurated as President July 10, 1850.

The chief gain for the North in the Compromise of 1850 was the admission of California as a free state, for it broke the balance between the free and the slaveholding states and gave the North a majority in the Senate. 

The South now lost control of both branches of Congress. The prohibition of the slave trade in the District of Columbia was also a victory for the North, but it did not satisfy the abolitionists, who had demanded the emancipation of all slaves in the national capital. On the other hand, the

South had expected to find compensation for the loss of California in the fact that slaves could be taken into the remainder of the Mexican cession. 

This gain, however, proved to be unimportant, for although slavery was not forbidden in this territory by law, it was forbidden by geography, because the economic system in which slavery was profitable could not flourish there. In like manner, the South was disappointed in the results of the fugitive slave law, for it soon became evident that attempts to enforce the law in the Northern states merely mobilized public opinion against the slavery system. The Texas question was unimportant so far as the question of slavery was concerned. If the territory in dispute had been given 

Culver Service

View of the parade in celebration of the admission of California as a state to Texas, it would have been definitely assigned to the slavocracy; whereas, as a result of the Compromise of 1850, its status was unsettled. As a matter of fact, as in the case of the remainder of the Mexican cession, nature had settled the question, for the territory was not adapted to the extension of slavery.

Calhoun and the Compromise. Calhoun made his last appearance in national politics on March 4, 1850, with a determined attack upon the compromise. Emaciated by disease, he was too weak to deliver the speech which he had prepared so carefully. He was carried up the steps of the 

Capitol to his desk in the Senate chamber, where he sat, his eyes flashing the fire which disease could not quench, while his colleague, Senator Mason, read his speech. He placed the blame for the crisis upon the North in attempting to interfere with the institutions of the South when its own institutions were not endangered. He insisted that slavery should be ad-

Uncle Tom's Cabin mitted into the new territory, and that the fugitive slave laws should be rigidly enforced. He also advocated an amendment to the Constitution, providing for two Presidents-one from each section, each having a veto upon the acts of the other.

Webster Defends the Compromise. 

On March 7, Webster delivered his famous speech in answer to Calhoun. He stated that the North and the South were equally responsible for the existence of slavery in the United States, and that the slavery question was not a moral issue. He also took issue with the antislavery societies by declaring that the fugitive slave law should be enforced, and that Congress had no right to interfere with slavery in the states where it already existed. Webster's one aim was to save the Union, and his logical arguments had much to do with the final adoption of the Compromise of 1850.

The antislavery men of New England, by whom Webster had been greatly admired, were sadly disappointed by his speech in favor of the compromise, and now in bitterness they accused him of treason to his state, and burned him in effigy. Their feelings were well expressed by the New England poet Whittier, in his poem "Ichabod," in which he compared Webster to a fallen angel.

Uncle Tom's Cabin and The Impend ing Crisis. The peace which followed the Compromise of 1850 was of short duration. In 1852 there appeared in the literary field a volume which fanned the flame of abolition to new heights. Harriet Beecher Stowe, of Cincinnati, used some of the stories which had been told her by runaway slaves as a background for the famous

Uncle Tom's Cabin. The book was an exaggerated account of the evils of the slavery system, but it was accepted by most of its readers in the North as a true picture of the Southern institution. Whittier offered up "thanks for the fugitive slave law; for it gave occasion for Uncle Tom's 

Cabin." The book was translated into twenty-three languages and was successfully dramatized. It was widely read in the North and more than a million copies were sold in the British Empire. It is difficult to appreciate fully the importance of this book in marshaling public opinion in the North against slavery.

Five years later, Hinton Rowan Helper, who belonged to a slaveholding family from North Carolina, wrote The Impending Crisis, in which he championed the cause of the "poor whites" of the South. Very forcefully he presented the unfavorable economic effects of slavery upon the South. 

The book was widely circulated by the Republican party as campaign material. 

Proposed Acquisition of Cuba. Soon after the Compromise of 1850 it became apparent that there was little possibility of a new slaveholding state being formed from the Mexican cession which would restore the balance of power in the Senate. Those interested in slavery therefore began to look around for new territory which might be organized into slaveholding states. Cuba seemed to offer the best opportunity. After attempts to purchase the island from Spain had failed, some impetuous Southerners resorted to more violent measures. In 1851 some American citizens from 

New Orleans, under the leadership of a noted adventurer, Lopez, attempted to seize Cuba. When they were captured and promptly executed by the 

Spanish government, the Spanish flag was torn down from the consulate at New Orleans, and the portrait of Queen Isabella was defaced. 

Three years later, Soulé, Mason, and Buchanan, our ministers to Spain, France, and Great Britain, respectively, met at Ostend, Belgium, and drafted the famous Ostend Manifesto, which declared that "if Spain, dead to the voice of her own interest and actuated by ... a false sense of honor, should refuse to sell Cuba, then... we shall be justified in wresting it from Spain if we possess the power." It seemed that Spain's seizure of the 

American steamer Black Warrior would furnish the necessary pretext for war, but hostilities were averted by Spain's apology and willingness to make all necessary restitutions. 

The Kansas-Nebraska Act. Having been barred from the greater portion of the Louisiana Purchase by the Missouri Compromise, the slaveholders, as we have observed, earnestly sought the acquisition of additional territory which might be brought into the Union as slaveholding states.

Up till 1854 they were thwarted in their efforts, except in the case of Texas, and the advantage derived from the annexation of that slaveholding state was lost in 1850 when California was admitted as a state without slavery. 

The compromises, however, had not definitely settled the slavery issue. In 

1854 Stephen A. Douglas, a senator from Illinois, introduced in the United 

States Senate a bill which provided for the organization of the two territories of Kansas and Nebraska. The bill ended the prohibition of slavery in those territories by act of Congress, and left the settlers in each territory free to decide for themselves whether slavery there should be permitted or excluded.

Douglas labeled this new principle with the pleasing name of "popular sovereignty," or "squatter sovereignty." He claimed two outstanding merits for the proposed policy: (1) it was thoroughly democratic, and (2) in view of the fact that the question of slavery would be decided directly by the settlers, popular sovereignty would remove that obnoxious problem from national politics. Enough congressmen were influenced by these arguments to secure the passage of the measure, after a series of debates which rivaled in eloquence and spirit those on the Compromise of 1850, only four years earlier. The Missouri Compromise was thus definitely repealed and the question of slavery in the territories entered upon a new phase. 

Northern Reaction to the Kansas-Nebraska Act. The passage of the act meant the end of compromise on the slavery question in the territories. 

The North now came to believe that it must fight for the protection of its free soil against the spread of the slavery institution all over the West. A still greater question was involved: Shall the plantation South or the industrial North govern the nation?

The country resounded with a cry of rage from the antislavery men of the North, many of whom believed that the action of Douglas was intended as a friendly gesture to the South in order to secure the support of that section in his effort to win the presidency. He was called the "Benedict 

Arnold of 1854," and in many cities his former supporters now burned him in effigy. Thousands of Whigs and Free-Soil Democrats, who regarded the repeal of the Missouri Compromise as the violation of a sacred pledge, made common cause with the antislavery forces. The birth of the Republican party came as a direct result of the passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act. (The map on page 370 shows how quickly it grew in strength, securing more than a third of the electoral votes in the presidential election of 1856.)

Bleeding Kansas. There was an immediate rush into Kansas by men from both sections. Many slaveholders from Missouri pre-empted land

without actually settling it. They maintained two homes-one in Missouri for actual residence, and the other in Kansas, for voting or fighting. Georgia sent many "Sons of the South," who were religiously dedicated to the cause of slavery. The antislavery men were quick to accept the challenge. 

The Emigrant Aid Society was organized in New England for the purpose of encouraging men who were hostile to slavery to settle in the new territory. In August, 1854, the first party arrived and founded the town of 

Lawrence. All of the members were fully armed. 

Kansas was not well adapted to slavery, and the free-labor settlers were soon in a majority. According to the census taken just before the election of the first legislature, there were only 2,905 legal voters in the territory, but the fraudulent votes of 5,000 Missourians elected a proslavery legislature. This legislature made it a penitentiary offense to deny, by speaking or writing, the right of a person to hold slaves in the territory, and excluded from jury service any person who was conscientiously opposed to slavery. The free-state men refused to recognize this legislature and drew up a government of their own. Guerilla warfare soon broke out between the two groups; Lawrence was sacked, and John Brown, an abolitionist, retaliated with a raid upon his proslavery neighbors, five of whom were killed. During the period of violence about two hundred men were killed and two million dollars worth of property was destroyed. 

Popular sovereignty was a failure in Kansas; it also failed to keep the slavery question out of national politics, as Douglas had claimed that it would do, for Congress was forced to choose between two constitutions, which were drawn up by the two rival factions in Kansas. Arguments were very bitter. A few days after the sack of Lawrence, Senator Sumner, in a speech called "The Crime against Kansas," was so scathing in his denunciation of the proslavery men that two days later, while seated at his desk, he was struck on the head with a cane by Preston Brooks, a representative from South Carolina. Senator Sumner did not resume his duties for nearly six months. The temper of South Carolina is reflected in the re-election of Brooks with only a few dissenting votes. Agreement on the Kansas question was impossible.

The Personal Liberty Laws. One of the chief causes of the increasing bitterness between the North and the South was the fugitive slave law of 1850. Perhaps this was due to the fact that almost all of the contacts of the people of the North with slavery were through the runaway slaves. 

After the passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act, public sentiment in the North became even more bitter toward the fugitive slave law. Ten states evaded the law by passing "personal liberty laws," which provided that

state officers were not to assist in the recapture of runaway slaves; state jails were not to be used by Federal officers to imprison escaped slaves; and the state courts were to give a fugitive slave a trial by jury-a provision which made the return of a slave to his master almost impossible because of the public sentiment in the North on this question. 

Riots often occurred in Northern cities when attempts were made to return escaped slaves to their masters, and many antislavery people united with the abolitionists in organizing "underground railroads" to help the runaway slaves to escape to Canada. Their acts not only irritated the slaveholders, but gave them a real cause for complaint.

The Dred Scott Decision. Congress was not the only department of our Federal government that was forced to consider the question of slavery in the territories; in 1857 the question was brought before the United 

States Supreme Court in the famous Dred Scott case. Dred Scott was a slave who, in 1834, had been taken by his master, a military officer, to an army post in Illinois, and then into what is now Minnesota, which, under the provisions of the Missouri Compromise, was free territory; from Minnesota he was taken back to his home state of Missouri. Prompted by some abolitionists who both managed and financed his case, Scott brought suit (1852) against the widow of his former master, on the ground that residence in a free territory had automatically entitled him to freedom. 

The courts of Missouri denied his plea on the ground that he was not a citizen and had no right to bring suit. Meanwhile, Scott had become the property of a citizen of New York. Since a suit may not be brought in a state court against a citizen of another state, Scott's abolitionist sponsors had the case transferred to, the Federal courts. The question had no practical interest for Scott, for he had been promised his freedom by his New York master, regardless of the outcome of the suit; but his friends were determined to force the question to a settlement. 

The Supreme Court might have evaded a direct decision on the question by simply upholding the action of the inferior court which had declared that Scott had no right to bring suit, or by stating that, regardless of whether Scott was free in Minnesota, he became a slave again when he returned to Missouri; but the question was faced squarely. The following were the most important points in the decision: (1) a slave was not a citizen and could not bring suit in a Federal court; (2) the Constitution recognized property in slaves and therefore a slave would not become free if taken into free territory; (3) neither Congress nor a territorial legislature could prohibit slavery in a territory belonging to the Union, and consequently the Missouri Compromise had been unconstitutional.

The decision was a decided victory for the South, which rejoiced to see the principles of Calhoun incorporated into the decision. The South might be criticized on moral or economic grounds for her defense of slavery, but there could no longer be any doubt about the legality of her position. 

Slavery in territories could be forbidden only by an amendment to the Constitution, which required the approval of threefourths of the states. This was out of the question. Since the majority of the members of the Supreme Court were from the South, the Republicans refused to accept its decision as permanently binding, and still insisted that slavery must not be permitted to be extended into new territory. It was their announced purpose to reform the court and thus secure the revocation of the distasteful decision.

A Lincoln and Douglas debate

The Lincoln- Douglas De bates. In 1858 the election of a state legislature in Illinois, which was to choose a United States senator, was a matter of wide interest and far-reaching significance. Stephen A. Douglas, a

Democrat, the author of the Kansas-Nebraska Act, was a candidate for reelection to the Senate. He was opposed by Abraham Lincoln, a comparatively unknown Republican opponent. Each of these men "stumped" the state in behalf of his party candidates for the state legislature, and finally agreed to a series of seven joint debates, in which they met each other face to face upon the same platform. Interest was soon at fever heat, and farmers and their wives rode for miles to applaud "Honest Abe" or to cheer the "Little Giant." 

In one of the debates Lincoln asked Douglas the following question: "Can the people of a territory in any lawful way, against the wishes of any citizen of the United States, exclude slavery from their limits prior to the formation of a state constitution?" If Douglas held steadfastly to his pet

Douglas evaded the issue rather skillfully by declaring that while slavery had the constitutional right to enter any territory, the territorial legislature could effectually prohibit slavery by withholding the laws which would provide the police regulations which were necessary to the existence of that institution; that is, by passing unfriendly local legislation. Douglas's answer, which became known as the "Freeport Doctrine," was a compromise between the apparently contradictory principles set forth in the Kansas-Nebraska Act and the Dred. 

Scott decision, and it won for him the seat in the Senate, but it was far from pleasing to the people of the South. 

John Brown's Raid. In 1859 John Brown, who had acquired a national reputation by his activities during the fighting in Kansas (p. 367), decided that the time had come for the slaves to strike for their own freedom by revolting against their masters. Supported by some of the most radical abolitionists, he led an armed band of determined followers into the South. 

It was their plan to seize the Federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, arm the slaves, and then assist them in the insurrection. They were successful in their attack upon the arsenal, but as a result of the prompt arrival of Lieutenant Colonel Robert E. Lee with a band of United States marines, Brown was captured, found guilty of treason, and was hanged. For many years the South had lived in mortal fear of a slave insurrection, and now they were horrified at the action of Brown and his friends, and they criticized severely the people of the North, although a large majority of the Northerners condemned Brown's raid. The friction between the two sections became more intense than ever before. 

The Election of 1860. The real significance of the Lincoln-Douglas debates became apparent in 1860, when the national Democratic convention convened at Charleston, South Carolina. Many of the Democrats in most of the South were displeased with Douglas's "Freeport Doctrine," which admitted the right of a territorial legislature to render the existence of slavery impossible by hostile legislation, and insisted that it was the duty of the Federal government to protect all property, including slavery, within a territory. The Democrats split on this issue in the convention, the Northern Democrats nominating Douglas for the presidency, and the 

Southern Democrats nominating John C. Breckenridge, of Kentucky.

Thus the united front of the Democratic party was broken at the most critical time in its history.

When the Republican party convention met at Chicago, William H. 

Seward was the acknowledged party leader; Lincoln was almost unknown outside of Illinois. Lincoln, however, was nominated on the third ballot on a platform which asserted that Congress had no right to interfere with the institution of slavery in the states where it already existed; and that 

Congress should exclude slavery from all of the territories of the United States. This statement on the slavery question suggested no immediate danger to the Southern institution, but many slaveholders had been disturbed by an earlier speech, in which Lincoln had said: "A house divided against itself can not stand. I believe this government can not endure permanently half slave and half free. . . . It will become all one thing or all the other." They interpreted this statement to mean that Lincoln would do all in his power to exclude slavery from the entire Union, besides having it governed by the industrial North; consequently they were alarmed over the prospect of Lincoln's election to the presidency. 

Still another candidate entered the race. Conservatives of the Whig and "Know Nothing" parties, believing that the preservation of the Union was more important than the slavery issue, organized the Constitutional Union party, which nominated John Bell, of Tennessee, for President. 

Abraham Lincoln, the candidate of the Republican party, was elected. 

He received 180 electoral votes to 123 for all three of his opponents (p. 370), yet his popular vote was only about forty per cent of the total vote cast. 

It is significant that while the slaveholders were divided as to their preference for the presidency, and scattered their votes for three of the candidates, yet votes for Lincoln in the South were almost non-existent. 

The House Is Divided. Southern reaction to the election of Lincoln was immediate. The governor of South Carolina, believing that the election of Lincoln would mean the destruction of the balance of power in the Union, and the rule of the South by a despotic majority "hostile to our institutions and fatally bent upon our ruin," requested that the legislature, which had met for the purpose of selecting presidential electors, remain in session until the results of the election were known. Soon the news of the election of the "Black Republican" candidate sped over the wires to South Carolina, and the legislature on November 10 appropriated money for arms and called a state convention to consider the question of secession. 

The convention met on December 17, and three days later it unanimously rescinded the ratification of the Federal Constitution and, amid the shouting of the populace, the waving of banners, the display of "liberty poles," and the thunder of cannon, the world was notified that South Carolina "resumed her place among the nations of the world." Appeals

were made to her sister states in the South to follow her example. Within six weeks after the secession of South Carolina, Georgia and the five Gulf states, in spite of formidable opposition, had severed their connection with the Union.

Why Did the South Secede? The question of the justification of secession by the Southern states has been debated, pro and con, by historians for many years. It is a mistaken conception that slavery was the sole cause of secession, for the abolition or the preservation of that institution was not a political issue in 1860. The Republican platform stated that that party was opposed to any interference by the Federal government with any institution existing in the states, and after the beginning of the secession movement, Lincoln declared that his object. was to preserve the Union "with or without slavery."

Secession was the culmination of a long struggle for political power by two sections with opposing economic interests, each section being bent upon making its own policy that of the 

Federal government. New England had opposed the Louisiana Purchase

Soon, however, the political balance shifted in favor of the North, and a series of protective tariffs called forth indignant protests from the South. 

Nullification and possible secession in South Carolina was staved off by a compromise, but the economic and political grievances persisted. In 1860, the industrial North found the Union profitable, while the Southern leaders declared that their section was carrying a burden of taxation in excess of any imposed by the British government prior to the Revolution. It is

significant to note that when the South formed a new government in 1861, a clause prohibiting protective tariffs was included in the Constitution of the Confederacy. The triumph, in 1860, of the Republican party, pledged as it was to the exclusion of slavery from the territories, seemed to Southerners to preclude the possibility of any further extension of Southern economic interests, and to guarantee the perpetual control of the government by the industrial forces of the North. Such a situation was unbearable to the people of the South, and secession seemed to offer the only escape. 

The Theory of Secession. The right of secession depended upon the nature of the Union. Nearly all of the people in the South believed that each state was a sovereign power. They stated that the thirteen colonies had been recognized by Great Britain as thirteen independent states, and that the sovereignty of the states had been expressly stated in the Articles of Confederation. They called attention to the fact that during the Constitutional Convention in 1787, a proposal to give Congress power to use force to compel a state to obey Federal laws was defeated. The Constitution, they held, was merely a compact entered into voluntarily by the states, from which a state could voluntarily withdraw. If it had not been so regarded, the Constitution would not have been ratified by the states. Furthermore, waiving all constitutional interpretations, the South defended secession on the ground that it was in accord with the right of revolution, a right that was regarded by all nations as sacred, and the exercise of which had made possible the birth of the Union. 

This theory was in the early days of the republic acceptable to most of the people in the Northern states, several of which had more than once proposed secession; but by 1860 an evolution in the thinking of the North had taken place. As the Federal government had come more and more to favor the industrial interests, those who profited from such a policy were willing to see the powers of the government enlarged, and asserted the supremacy of the nation over "states' rights." Webster was the spokesman of this group. He had stated that the Union was older than the states; that it began with the Continental Congress; that it was strengthened by the 

Declaration of Independence and the Articles of Confederation, and was sealed by the Constitution. The latter document, he said, established a "people's government, made for the people, made by the people, answerable to the people"-the people were sovereign rather than the states. 

Lincoln enlarged upon Webster's ideas by declaring in his inaugural address that the Union was perpetual and that the Constitution contained no provision for its own destruction, and could be destroyed only by an insurrectionary action. Many people in the North, however, agreed with

the statement of Horace Greeley, that "the South has as good a right to secede from the Union as the colonies had to secede from Great Britain," and were perfectly willing to let the "erring sisters go in peace. 

The Formation of a New Nation. 

On February 4, 1861, representatives from Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina met in a convention at Montgomery, Alabama, and founded a new government-the "Confederate States of 

America." They were joined a little later by delegates from Texas. A provisional government was set up, with 

Jefferson Davis as President, and Alexander H. Stephens as Vice-President. 

In March, a permanent Constitution was drawn up and submitted to the states for ratification. The general plan of the government of the Confederacy was very similar to that of the United States, but there was a difference 

Jefferson Davis

Montgomery, where the Confederate Convention met February 4, 1861; from an old print 

Culver Service

in the distribution of powers. It was stated that the states were not deprived of their sovereignty by joining the Confederacy, and the powers of the central government were greatly restricted. No protective tariff could be levied; the people could not be taxed for internal improvements; and the central government did not have the power to prohibit slavery. The 

Constitution was promptly ratified by each of the seceded states, and Davis and Stephens were regularly elected to their respective offices. 

Montgomery was the capital of the Confederacy until after the secession of Virginia, when it was changed to Richmond. 

Peaceful Settlements Fail. Many people in the North were reluctant to use force upon the seceded states, and earnestly desired to preserve the Union by peaceful means if possible. Likewise, the great majority of the 

Southern people loved the Union and would have welcomed the opportunity to remain in it if this could have been done without too great a cost. Several compromises were proposed. Thurlow Weed proposed the extension of the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific, but the proposal was defeated because of the opposition of Lincoln, who was unwilling to permit the expansion of slavery into any new territory. Perhaps the most important of the proposed compromises was that of Senator J. J. Crittenden, of Kentucky, whose home was divided by the war, one son becoming a major general in the Union army and another holding a similar position in the Confederate army. He proposed an "unamendable amendment,' by which the Missouri Compromise line would have been extended and Congress would have been forbidden to interfere with slavery in the states where it then existed. This compromise, too, was defeated through the influence of Lincoln, who was unwilling to surrender the principle upon which the Republican party had been founded and the platform on which its candidates had been elected. 

Another attempt at peaceable settlement was made by the Virginia legislature, which invited the other states to send delegates to a "Peace Convention." On February 4, 1861, the same day on which the representatives of the seceded states were meeting in Montgomery, delegates from twenty-one states met in Washington, with former President Tyler presiding. The labors of the convention, however, were fruitless because of the refusal of Congress to accept its recommendations. 

The Problem of Southern Forts. The states which had withdrawn from the Union promptly seized the Federal forts and arsenals within their bounds, that could be taken without violence, and sent commissioners to Washington to arrange compensation. They hesitated to take any action which might precipitate bloodshed, and consequently permitted Fort

Sumter, in Charleston harbor, and three other forts, to remain in the hands of the Federal government. It was evident that if the Southern states established their independence, these forts would eventually fall into their hands. What should be the policy of the Union government with regard to this delicate question? Although Lincoln had been elected in November, his term of office would not begin until March 4, and in the meantime President Buchanan had to deal with the problem. He did not believe in secession, yet he believed that the United States Constitution did not give the right to employ force to prevent secession. When the commissioners from the seceded states came to Washington to negotiate on the question of the forts, Buchanan refused to treat with them. 

Fort Sumter was then held by a small force under the command of Major Anderson. The supplies soon became exhausted, and Major Anderson appealed to the President for provisions and reinforcements. Early in 

January, Buchanan sent the merchant vessel Star of the West to the relief of the fort, but it was fired upon by the batteries located on Morris Island, and returned to New York without accomplishing its mission.

The Die Is Cast. When 

Lincoln took office on March 

4, 1861, he faced a critical situation. Seven Southern states had already seceded from the Union and had set up a separate government. 

Whether these states should be allowed to depart in peace, or whether the Union should be preserved at the cost of a terrific fratricidal war, depended upon the fateful deci sion of Lincoln. The entire country anxiously awaited the decision of the new President. 

In his inaugural address,

Lincoln left no room for doubt as to the policy he had determined upon. 

While he expressed a kindly feeling for the South, he also denied the right of secession, and declared that his oath of office required that he should "preserve, protect, and defend" the Union. He also announced that he 

Courtesy Baltimore and Ohio Railroad

would "hold, occupy, and possess the property and places belonging to the government, and collect the duties on imports." A month later he notified the governor of South Carolina that he would attempt to send a supply of provisions to Fort Sumter. The Confederate government at 

Montgomery regarded this announcement of Lincoln's policy as equivalent to a declaration of war, and President Davis ordered General Beauregard, who commanded a force of about seven thousand troops, to demand the immediate surrender of the fort.

CHAPTER XX 

The War Between the North and the South

The Appeal to Arms. Major Anderson and his little band of less than a hundred men courageously refused the demand to surrender, and made preparations for a stubborn defense of Fort Sumter. It was before dawn, April 12, 1861, that the thunder of a cannon at Fort Johnson announced that war had begun. This was followed by a heavy bombardment of Fort Sumter from three sides, and a spirited reply from the guns of the fort. For two days Anderson and his men stuck to their posts, while the Federal relief ships were waiting outside the harbor, unable to enter because of the heavy seas. Finally, when the fort had been set on fire by the bombardment, Anderson surrendered and was permitted to retire with the honors of war. Not a man on either side was killed or seriously wounded in the battle, which had begun a long and bloody conflict. 

Cannons in Fort Sumter

The Nation Is Aroused. Many people of the North who had been only lukewarm in their support of Lincoln's policies now came to the defense of their flag. President Lincoln issued a call for seventy-five thousand volunteers for a three months' term of service. The response was instantaneous, but it is evident that Lincoln was not fully aware of the seriousness of the conflict upon which the country was entering. 

The South was elated at the news of the fall of Fort Sumter, and President Davis's call to arms was answered by thousands of volunteers. 381
