Free States www DI *** www States of the North and the South in 1863 Four more slaveholding states-Virginia, North Carolina, Arkansas, and Tennessee-joined the Confederacy within two months after Lincoln's call for troops April 15, 1861.

People in the northwestern portion of Virginia refused to abide by the decision of the rest of the state; they "seceded" from Virginia and set up a loyal state which was received into the Union in 1863 as the state of West Virginia, in spite of the section in the Constitution which forbids the division of a state without its own consent. The slaveholding states of 

Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri were divided in their allegiance. They furnished a large number of troops to both armies, but because of prompt action on the part of the Northern government, headed by Lincoln, these states were kept in the Union. 

Advantages of the North. Two of the most vital factors in any war are man power and economic resources. In both of these the North had a decided advantage. The nineteen free-labor states of the North had a population in 1860 of about 19,000,000, and the four slave-labor states which were divided in their sympathies and support but remained in the Union, had another 3,000,000. The population of the states which joined the Confederacy was slightly in excess of 9,000,000, over one third of whom were slaves. There were about 5,000,000 white men of military age in the

North, as compared with about 1,500,000 in the South. It is not fair, however, to leave out of consideration the more than 3,000,000 slaves in the South. Although they were of little military value, they were used effectively on the plantations in the production of agricultural products, and thus made it possible for nearly every white man of military age to join the Confederate army; while in the North many of the men had to be kept at home for such work. Then, too, the Northern advantage in numbers was not so apparent during the first two years of the war, when the opposing armies were almost equal in size; but during the last stages of the war the 

Northern preponderance in numbers was overwhelming.

In economic resources the North was much stronger than the South. 

The industrial North possessed factories which were capable of supplying sufficient quantities of munitions, clothing, and other supplies necessary for military purposes. The fertile plains of the Middle West produced a large quantity of foodstuffs, and the reaper, which was just coming into general use, made possible the production of grain on a large scale. The invention of the sewing machine facilitated the manufacture of clothing and shoes for the soldiers. On the other hand, there was only one foundry. in the South for the manufacture of cannon, and only two powder mills. 

There was a similar shortage in factories for the manufacture of clothing and other supplies. Cotton was the main crop on the plantations, and the 

South had entered the war with the vain expectation of being able to exchange cotton for all necessary supplies. But again the advantage of the 

North in economic resources had little weight until after the first two years of the war, when the blockade of Southern ports became more effective. 

Still another advantage of the North was the control of the sea. The entire United States navy remained in the hands of the Federal government. Small though it was at the beginning of the war, it was quickly built up to a strength which made possible the blockade of the Southern ports. The South had very few ships. The Confederate government had hoped that an alliance with Great Britain would bring the powerful British fleet to her assistance. Several ships were built for the South in British shipyards, but they were no match for the Northern navy and were used mainly as commerce raiders. 

Southern Advantages. How could the South hope to fight successfully against such odds? As a matter of fact, the men from Dixie suffered from no inferiority complex, but entered the war with a confident buoyancy which in part contributed to their defeat. Several factors promoted 

Southern confidence. In the first place, the South was fighting a defensive war. This was a great advantage. Familiarity with the topography of the

country made it possible for the defending forces to choose battlefields to their own liking, and to keep in close proximity to their source of supplies. 

Furthermore, the fact that they were fighting in defense of their homes was of great psychological value to the Southerners. On the other hand, the invading armies were forced to use many troops in order to keep open lines of communication and to protect the trains of supplies. This condithe tion helped to offset part of the Northern superiority in numbers. 

The Confederacy also enjoyed an advantage in the fact that many of the experienced soldiers and officers in the United States army in 1860 were from the South, and had served through the Mexican War. When the states seceded, these men resigned and cast their lot with their native states. The South entered the war with such experienced leaders as 

Robert E. Lee, Joseph E. Johnston, P. G. T. Beauregard, T. J. Jackson, and Albert S. Johnston; while Lincoln, after offering the command of the Federal armies to Robert E. Lee, followed the costly method of trial and error in an effort to find a satisfactory leader. Seven experienced commanders were tried out with the Federal armies in the East during the first two years of the war, without success. before Lincoln had discovered his best generals-U. S. Grant (picture on 

The war was half over page 711), William T. Sherman, Philip Sheridan, and George H. Thomas. 

A Southern planter's home

Confederate Memorial Institute, and Wide World 

Robert E. Lee and other Confederate generals; from a mural painting by Charles Hofbauer in 

Battle Abbey, Richmond

Although the Confederate government was disappointed in its expectation of receiving open assistance from European nations, the secret aid of Great Britain and France was of considerable value. Before the tightening of the blockade, the citizens of these countries sold and shipped to the Confederacy great quantities of munitions, arms, surgical supplies, and other war materials, and gave considerable financial assistance through the purchase of Confederate bonds.

Many of the leisure hours on plantations were spent in shooting and horseback riding; and, partly for this reason, Southern cavalry forces showed a marked superiority over those of the North. 

Robert E. Lee

A review of the comparative advantages of the two sections reveals the fact that the Southern advantages were important only during the early part of the war, while those of the North were most telling during the later stages. It is not surprising, therefore, that during the first two years the South was almost uniformly successful; while in the end the North was triumphant.

Southern Disappointments. The seven states which organized the 

Confederacy believed that all of the other eight slaveholding states would join them. We have seen how the prompt action of President Lincoln prevented this. The Southern leaders also found much encouragement in the fact that Lincoln had secured only about half of the votes cast by the free states in the election of 1860. They believed that the North would be paralyzed by political divisions. Much to their disappointment, most of the Northern Democrats rallied to the support of the administration, and the abolitionists were won to its support by the Emancipation Proclamation announced in September, 1862.

The South was also severely disappointed in "King Cotton." It was generally believed in the Confederacy that the industrial nations of Europe were dependent upon Southern raw cotton. Great Britain, especially, it was thought, would intervene in the war rather than permit herself to be cut off from the Southern staple. As a matter of fact, though, there was, in 1861, a surplus of cotton in the English warehouses; and the announcement of the Emancipation Proclamation stopped any further consideration by the British government of intervention on the side of the Confederacy.

Curiously enough, one of the reasons for the defeat of the Confederacy was the very principle upon which the government had been foundedstates' rights. Each state was jealous of any unusual display of central authority. The suspension, by President Davis, of the writ of habeas corpus, the levy of a tax in kind, and the passage of the conscript acts, were special subjects of friction. Governor Joseph E. Brown, of Georgia, stated that "No act of the government of the United States prior to the secession of Georgia struck a blow at constitutional liberty so fell as has been stricken by the conscript acts." Several of the state governors objected to the removal of local troops beyond the state borders and the appointment of officers over them from "distant states." Southern hopes were greatly impaired by this serious lack of co-operation.

Arenas of War. The Appalachian Mountains, about one hundred fifty miles wide, divided the South into two distinct sections between which, in 1860, communication was very poor. The narrow section east of these mountains became an important arena of war, most of the fighting there centering around the Confederate capital, Richmond. The fighting in the 

West was largely independent of that around Richmond, and had as its chief object the control of the Mississippi River. This river was important from the standpoint of transportation and communication, but far more important was the fact that its control by the North would split the Confederacy into two isolated sections. A third field of activity was the Confederate coast. 

War in the East; First Battle of Bull Run. In the enthusiasm which followed Lincoln's call for volunteers, a Federal army of about thirty thousand men was speedily organized and ordered into Virginia under the command of General Irvin McDowell, who confidently expected to capture Richmond and suppress the "rebellion" with one blow. Twenty-five miles south of Washington this army found its way blocked by forces under General Beauregard. The two armies met on Sunday, July 21, 1861, along the creek called Bull Run, near Manassas, Virginia. For a while the Union forces were successful, but the Confederates under General 

T. J. Jackson held firm whence his nickname "Stonewall," — and a counterattack by those under General Joseph E. Johnston, at a critical time, caused the Northern troops to give way and to flee to Washington in a panic. The most important results of the battle were psychological. 

The North learned that the South could not easily be conquered, and began to prepare for a long struggle; while the South, believing that a few more easy victories would bring the enemy to terms, made no serious preparations for a protracted war. 

The Struggle for Richmond. The rout at Bull Run brought an end to the first phase of the struggle for the possession of Richmond. General 

George B. McClellan succeeded McDowell in command of the "Army of

the Potomac " and for nearly a year he carefully drilled his troops. Fearing to make a direct advance upon Richmond, he landed his forces near Fort Monroe, and cautiously fought his way up the peninsula toward his objective. He was strongly opposed by the Confederate army under the command of General Joseph E. Johnston; but in the severe fighting near Richmond (June 25 to July 1, 1862) Johnston was wounded and

General Robert E. Lee succeeded to the command. A month later, McClellan's army was withdrawn. The successful defense of Richmond was due largely to General "Stonewall" Jackson, who, by a marvelous campaign in the Shenandoah Valley, defeated three Union armies, each larger than his own, feigned an attack upon Washington, prevented McDowell from joining McClellan with a force of 40,000 men, and then joined his army with that of Lee. Here and in later campaigns, also, Lee was greatly aided by the cavalry corps under the brilliant leadership of General J. E. B. Stuart. 

Other Confederate Successes in the East. McClellan was succeeded by General John Pope, who soon met defeat at the second battle of Bull Run, or Manassas. Lee then decided to carry the war into the North, hoping to break the Federal hold upon Maryland and thus secure needed re-enforcements and supplies. He was followed into Maryland by the 

Federal army under McClellan, who had been restored to the command after the failure of Pope. After the bloody but indecisive battle of Antietam, Lee was forced to give up the invasion and retire to Virginia. 

Believing that the failure of McClellan to pursue Lee had deprived the North of a great victory, Lincoln again relieved McClellan of his command and entrusted the army to General Ambrose E. Burnside, who proved to be as bold as McClellan had been cautious. He foolishly attacked Lee in a strong position at Fredericksburg and was defeated with terrific losses. His successor, General Joseph Hooker, had no better fortune in the battle of Chancellorsville (May 2-4, 1863), but in this battle the South suffered a tremendous loss in the death of "Stonewall" Jackson, who was mortally wounded by his own men who fired upon him by mistake. The second year of the war in the East ended with the Northern army no nearer Richmond than it had been at the beginning. 

War on the Sea. One week after the firing of the first shot, President

Lincoln declared a blockade of the Southern ports. There were only twelve ships with which to enforce a blockade of some three thousand miles of coast. Of course it could not be effective. But soon many other ships had been built and the "paper blockade" became effective. For defense of the James River, the Confederates raised the Merrimac, a wooden

Battle between the Monitor and the Merrimac 

Culver Service frigate which the Federal authorities had sunk when they abandoned the navy yard at Norfolk, and converted it into an ironclad vessel. It boldly attacked the Federal fleet at Hampton Roads (near Fort Monroe) and might have destroyed it but for the arrival of the Monitor, also an ironclad, and but for the great strength of Fort Monroe. The battle between the Monitor and the Merrimac, or Virginia, as it had been renamed by the Confederates, is famous as the first in which ironclad vessels met. 

The result was indecisive. The Virginia, however, for a time kept control of the James River. The North quickly built many more ironclads. 

The most famous of the Confederate ships was the Alabama, a cruiser which had been built in Great Britain and delivered to the Confederacy. 

For several years, under the command of Captain (later Rear Admiral) Semmes, it preyed upon Northern commerce. In 1864 it was sunk in a battle with the Kearsarge off the coast of France. 

The work of the Federal navy was not restricted to the enforcement of the blockade. Fleets of gunboats co-operated effectively with the land forces in the capture of Fort Henry and Fort Donelson, on the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers, and New Orleans, Memphis, and Vicksburg on the Mississippi.

War in the West. While the Federals were failing in their attempts to take Richmond, their comrades in the West were meeting with a greater degree of success. Early in 1862 General U. S. Grant, commanding a strong Federal army, captured Fort Henry on the Tennessee River, and a few days later took Fort Donelson, the key to the Cumberland and middle Tennessee. Advancing up the Tennessee River, he engaged the Confed-

erate army under the command of General Albert S. Johnston, in the bloody two days' battle of Shiloh, or Pittsburg Landing. Johnston was killed the first day, when it seemed that a Confederate victory was certain; but during the night General Buell arrived with Union re-enforcements, and the Confederates were forced to retire to Corinth, Mississippi. Nathan 

Bedford Forrest was among the wounded, but later, as a general, became famous through his brilliant cavalry raiding against Union communications.

The chief objective of the Federals in the West was the control of the Mississippi. Soon after the battle of Shiloh, Commodore David G. Farragut entered the mouth of the Mississippi with a Federal fleet and occupied New Orleans, the largest city in the Confederacy. Meanwhile, a fleet of gunboats advanced down the Mississippi and captured Memphis. Only 

Vicksburg, which the South was determined to hold at all costs, kept the Federals from immediately realizing their objective. But Grant, after failing in two assaults upon the fortifications, laid siege to Vicksburg. 

The Turn of the Tide: Gettysburg and Vicksburg. While Grant was advancing into the heart of the Confederacy, Lee believed that he might be able to relieve the pressure upon the South by making an invasion of Pennsylvania. On July 1, 1863, he met the Federal army, then under the command of General George G. Meade, at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania. For three days the battle raged. On the third day there occurred one of the most heroic episodes of the entire war. Fifteen thousand Confederates, directed by General Pickett, attempted to drive a strong force of Federals from their position on Cemetery Hill. For nearly a mile they advanced under terrific fire. Thousands were mowed down by the shot and shell, but the others did not falter, and even succeeded in driving back the first line of the Federals. Their courage was matched by that of the men of the North, and the great charge failed. On the morning of July 4, Lee began the retreat to Virginia, with a greatly weakened army. 

On the same day that Lee began his retreat from Gettysburg, the Confederates suffered another disaster in the fall of Vicksburg. By excellent strategy, Grant had succeeded in completely surrounding the city and had begun the slow process of starving the soldiers and the population into submission. Despairing of receiving relief, General Pemberton, after a valiant defense, in which his men and the civilians had suffered from hunger, surrendered his force of thirty thousand men. 

The battles of Gettysburg and Vicksburg marked the beginning of the end for the Confederacy. With the Confederacy cut in two by the loss of the control of the Mississippi, and her already almost exhausted man

power sapped by the loss of fifty thousand men who could not be replaced, there could be little doubt as to the final outcome of the war. 

The Federals Gain Middle Tennessee. In the autumn of 1862, General William S. Rosecrans assumed command of the Union Army of the 

Cumberland, at Bowling Green, Kentucky. Almost immediately he advanced to Nashville, and then attacked General Braxton Bragg, whose army had gone into winter quarters at Murfreesboro. Here was fought one of the greatest battles of the war. After three days of indecisive fighting, Bragg was forced to fall back upon Chattanooga, which later became the chief battleground of the war in the West. The Confederates enjoyed their last great victory in the battle of Chickamauga, although the Federal General George H. Thomas held his part of the ground there, earning the title "the Rock of Chickamauga"; but the arrival of Grant and his victorious troops from Vicksburg turned the tide against the Southerners, and after a series of battles at Chattanooga, Lookout Mountain, and Missionary Ridge, they were forced to retreat into Georgia. 

The "March to the Sea." Grant was now placed in supreme command of all of the Federal armies. Having decided to direct the campaign against 

Lee, he placed General William T. Sherman in charge of the army in the 

West. With a vastly superior army, Sherman pursued the Confederates, The battle of Lookout Mountain 

Culver Service W-26

then under the command of General Joseph E. Johnston, toward Atlanta. 

Johnston's conduct of the campaign did not please the Confederate authorities and he was removed in favor of General John B. Hood, who, after being defeated in the battle of Atlanta, conceived the plan of cutting Sherman off from his base of supplies by returning to Tennessee, and thus forcing him to withdraw from Georgia.

Sherman, however, was not disturbed by Hood's strategy. Having destroyed the railroad to Chattanooga, and the machine shops in Atlanta, he began his famous march toward Savannah through country where there was no army to oppose him. Advancing in four columns, the Federals laid waste a strip of country sixty miles in width, extending from Atlanta to the sea. A series of "Sherman's sentinels," or blackened chimneys, marked the route of the invaders. Sherman estimated the amount of the damage as one hundred million dollars, and, unfortunately, much of the plundered property was not needed for military purposes. Savannah was taken on December 21, and in a report to the President, Sherman offered him the city as a Christmas gift.

Closing Events in the East. While Sherman was cutting through the 

Confederacy, Grant was launching the drive which he hoped would end the war. He was enough of a soldier to know that his best strategy would be to make full use of his greatest advantage overwhelming numbers. Consequently, with his much larger army he made a series of direct frontal attacks upon Lee. His losses were terrific, but they were easily replaced from his ample supply of reserves. On the other hand, the gaps in the Confederate army remained unfilled, and Lee was gradually pushed back upon Richmond. Grant then repeated the strategy he had used so successfully at Vicksburg by attempting to outflank the enemy and cut him off from any possible relief.

Appomattox. Lee was now in a desperate situation. Realizing that his little band of ragged and hungry men were unequal to the task of preventing Grant's encircling movement, he determined to stake everything upon one last desperate move. If he could escape Grant and join with Johnston, who had an army in North Carolina, it might be possible for their combined forces to defeat Sherman and then in turn drive Grant from Richmond. But his rival could not be caught napping. When the Confederates began their movement toward the west the Federals in hot pursuit forged ahead and completely blocked the line of retreat. Lee now submitted to the inevitable and on April 9, 1865, surrendered at Appomattox Courthouse, Virginia. Grant was generous in the treatment of his vanquished opponent. Not only were the Confederate officers allowed to keep their

side arms, but also the men who owned horses were allowed to keep them for "the spring plowing." Rations were issued to the half-starved men. 

Two weeks later, Johnston's army surrendered to Sherman, and the war was brought to an end with the surrender of a Confederate army west of the Mississippi, on May 26, 1865.

The War and Slavery. Slavery was not the issue of the war in 1861. 

Lincoln had been elected on a platform which insisted that Congress had no right to interfere with state institutions, and Lincoln repeatedly asserted the same principle. The border slaveholding states-Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky, and Missouri-had been kept in the Union with the understanding that slavery was not the issue between the North and South. Congress pledged itself to the same principle, a pledge which was renewed the day after the first battle of Bull Run, by a vote of 107 to 2. It is significant that the abolitionists who were uncompromising on the question of immediate emancipation, refused to support the Republican administration during the first two years of the war. In the summer of 1861, General 

Butler in Virginia declared that the slaves were contraband of war and ordered that they should be confiscated. His position was approved by the War Department and by Congress, but when General Frémont and General Hunter attempted to extend the policy by declaring the emancipation of the slaves of all disloyal citizens, Lincoln intervened and revoked the orders.

However, it was difficult for Lincoln to keep his personal dislike of slavery in the background, and furthermore it was evident that the slaves were of considerable aid to the South in the prosecution of the war. In 

1862 the administration's policy concerning slavery underwent a considerable change. In April Congress declared itself willing to co-operate with the border states in a policy of gradual compensated emancipation, by which the Federal government would purchase the slaves from their owners. This announcement did not meet with a cordial reception. June 

19, 1862, Congress abolished slavery in the territories, in spite of the 

Dred Scott decision.

The Emancipation Proclamation. For some time Lincoln had been considering the advisability of liberating the slaves in the Confederacy as a war measure, through his authority as commander in chief of the United States army. At a secret meeting of his cabinet on July 22, 1862, he made such a proposal, but at the suggestion of Seward he decided to postpone the announcement until after a military victory, so the proclamation might not be regarded as "our last shriek on the retreat." The battle of Antietam offered the desired opportunity, and on September 22 Lincoln made the

announcement that on January 1, 1863, the slaves would be declared free in all parts of the Confederacy that should still be engaged in rebellion. It did not apply to the border states nor to those parts of the Confederacy which had been occupied by the Federal armies. On January 1 the Emancipation 

Proclamation was adopted as the definite policy of the Federal government. 

Lincoln had three objects in issuing the proclamation. One object was to weaken the South through the loss of the slaves. This was only partly accomplished. Of course no slaves would be liberated until the district had been occupied by Federal troops, but in the later stages of the war when most of the South was in the hands of the invaders, many slaves took advantage of the opportunity to gain their freedom. The Northern armies were increased by 104,387 negroes enlisted from Confederate territory. 

Another of Lincoln's objects was to gain the support of the abolitionists. 

This was accomplished, but, in view of the fact that many Northern people who did not wish to be involved in a war to secure abolition were alienated, the net gain was extremely small. 

Lincoln's third object was perhaps the most important. The British government, welcoming the prospect of a divided Union and a lucrative free trade with the South, was known to be friendly toward the Confederacy; while the masses of the British population, interested primarily in the universal emancipation of slaves, were willing to support the government's friendly policy toward the South only so long as the slavery issue was not involved. When the Emancipation Proclamation was announced it was interpreted by the English people as meaning that the war had been converted into a crusade against slavery. Public sentiment immediately shifted in favor of the North, and the British government was forced to abandon its pro-Southern attitude. No longer was there any danger of foreign intervention.

The Thirteenth Amendment. The Emancipation Proclamation was only a war measure; many people doubted whether it would remain operative when peace should be restored. At the best, it reached only a small number of the slaves. Permanent and complete emancipation could be secured only by the voluntary action of the slaveholding states or by an amendment to the Federal Constitution. Lincoln's action, however, added a mighty impetus to the abolition movement, and by the early part of 1865 emancipation had been ordered by state conventions in Missouri, Maryland, Virginia, Arkansas, Louisiana, and Tennessee.

In the meantime public opinion was mobilizing in favor of universal emancipation by a constitutional amendment. Such an amendment was submitted to Congress in February, 1864, but it failed to receive the neces-

sary two-thirds majority in the House. In January, 1865, it was acted upon favorably and was submitted to the states for ratification. On December 18, 1865, it was incorporated into the Constitution as the Thirteenth Amendment. Its only direct effect was to grant immediate freedom to the slaves in Kentucky, Delaware, and West Virginia, which had previously adopted gradual emancipation, but it confirmed the action of conventions and of governments in other states. 

Diplomacy and the War. The South had entered the war with the expectation that Great Britain, France, and probably other European nations would come to her assistance. It was her belief that these nations would be forced into this course because of their dependence upon Southern cotton. However, in this the South was disappointed, for there was an increased amount of cotton from India which supplied the reduced English demand. But there were other reasons why England, in particular, might be expected to intervene in behalf of the Confederacy. The division of a nation which was rapidly developing into a formidable rival was not entirely unwelcome from the British standpoint, and furthermore, the aristocracy of Great Britain would be pleased at the failure of the American experiment with democracy. Another matter which caused some Englishmen to look with favor upon Southern independence was the Confederate policy of virtually free trade, which would open up new markets for the products of the British factories. But England did not intervene, partly because many Englishmen were making enormous war profits and were therefore willing to let the struggle go on without interruption. 

Shortly after the fall of Fort Sumter, and before the South had fought a single battle for independence, Queen Victoria issued a proclamation of neutrality. This was a distinct advantage to the Confederacy because it meant that the Southerners would be regarded as belligerents rather than as rebels, and therefore would be entitled to a greater freedom in their relations with foreign countries. The queen's act was entirely consistent with the policy Lincoln himself had followed by declaring the blockade of the Southern ports and by treating captured Confederates as prisoners of war; yet the act gave the impression of unnecessary and unfriendly haste, and it is not surprising that ill feeling toward England developed in the North, although the British government remained officially friendly. 

The Trent Affair. Six months after the announcement of the proclamation of neutrality, relations between the North and Great Britain were brought almost to the breaking point by an unexpected incident. President Davis had appointed James M. Mason and John Slidell as commissioners to Great Britain and France, respectively, to conduct negotiations

for the recognition of the independence of the Confederacy. They made their way to Havana, a neutral port, and boarded the British mail steamer Trent, a neutral vessel, for Southampton. The Trent was stopped on the high seas by the American warship San Jacinto, and the two Southerners were forcibly removed as prisoners of war and taken to Fort Warren, in Boston Harbor. This act was clearly a violation of the very principles for which the United States had fought in the War of 1812. The British government sent a vigorous demand for the release of the two commissioners, and added emphasis to it by dispatching eight thousand troops to Canada. 

Realizing the seriousness of the situation, Lincoln disavowed the act, made suitable apologies to the British government, and released the prisoners.

President Lincoln (seen in the foreground) had to face many social and diplomatic questions as well as military problems. 

The Confederate Cruisers. The United States had been guilty of a violation of the rights of a neutral, but Great Britain, too, was guilty of a very lax enforcement of her neutral duties. Although an act of Parliament prohibited the equipping by a British subject of any ship for the use of a foreign power against a nation at peace with Great Britain, the government violated the spirit if not the letter of the law by permitting vessels to be constructed in the British shipyards and then sent out to the high seas where they were armed and delivered to Confederate officers. Most famous among the ships thus built for the Confederacy was the Alabama, which inflicted very heavy losses upon Northern commerce until it was finally sunk in 1864. A few years after the close of the war, $15,500,000 was

awarded to the United States by an international court, which held that Great Britain was responsible for the damages to American shipping during the war because of her laxity in enforcing her international obligations (p. 629). Early in 1863 it became known that two other ships were under construction in England, and it was rumored that they were to follow in the path of the Alabama and be delivered to the Confederacy. But conditions had changed since the building of the Alabama. The Emancipation 

Proclamation had so completely won the support of the masses of people in England for the North, that when Charles Francis Adams, the American minister, reminded the British officials that the delivery of these ships to the Confederacy would mean war, the government was forced to yield. 

From that time to the close of the war, Great Britain rigidly enforced her neutrality obligations.

Strained Relations with France. Napoleon III of France was as friendly to the South as were the British leaders, but he hesitated to intervene without the co-operation of Great Britain. He consented to the construction of Confederate commerce destroyers in the French shipyards, and aided in floating a large Confederate loan in Europe. 

Financing the War: the North. The war cost the country, North and 

South, about $8,000,000,000. This placed an enormous burden upon a people unaccustomed to heavy taxation. The responsibility for meeting the expense for the North fell upon the Secretary of the Treasury, Salmon P. Chase. The financial policy which he enforced provided for several methods of increasing the Federal income. The most important of these was the sale of bonds. In order to facilitate the sale of the bonds, high rates of interest were paid, and the National Banking Act, which made the purchase of Federal bonds by the national banks obligatory (see p. 490), was enacted. Short-term loans were effected by the issuing of treasury notes bearing interest rates as high as 7.3 per cent. By such means the government raised a revenue of more than $2,500,000,000. 

Increased taxation offered another means of producing more revenue. 

The tariff on imported goods was increased to an average rate of fortyseven per cent, the highest rate that had been known; and internal revenue duties were placed upon such luxuries as tobacco and whisky, and upon such necessities as foods and clothing. The first income tax in the United 

States was authorized in 1861, and was increased twice during the war, until in 1865 incomes between $600 and $5,000 were taxed at the rate of five per cent, and above $5,000 at ten per cent. A total of approximately $357,000,000 was raised by the internal revenue and income taxes during the war.

The North also secured additional funds by issuing paper money, or "greenbacks," which were supported only by the promise of the government to redeem them as soon as it was able. In order to insure the circulation of these notes as money, the government declared them legal tender for the payment of all debts except import duties and interest on bonds. 

So much paper money was issued that faith in the government's ability to redeem it began to wane, and the exchange value of the greenback declined until at one time it was only thirty-nine cents on the dollar. In 1865, greenbacks with a face value of $431,000,000 were in circulation. 

Secretary Chase also increased the Federal revenue by the indirect method of building up the wealth of the country. Bounties were offered for the increased production of necessary goods and products; also for the construction of railroads. The settlement of new land was encouraged. In 

1862 Congress passed the Homestead Act, by the terms of which a citizen of the United States could acquire a farm of 160 acres without cost (except a small fee), simply by living on a tract of unsettled land for a period of five years. The wisdom of these methods was soon demonstrated by the rapidly increasing wealth of the nation. 

Financing the War: the South. Great as was the financial problem of the North, that of the South was immeasurably greater. The North had the financial machinery of the United States government through which to work; the South had to build from the ground up. The methods of raising revenue used by the Confederacy were similar to those of the North. A tariff was resorted to, but, because of the blockade, it produced very little revenue. Disappointed at the results of a request that each state levy a property tax for the benefit of the central government, the Confederate Congress enacted an internal revenue measure comparable to that of the North, including not only excise duties, but also taxes on incomes and licenses upon occupations. The collection of taxes, however, was difficult because of the scarcity of specie. To meet this difficulty the 

Congress levied a ten-per-cent tax on farm produce, payable in kind. This tax aroused much bitterness toward the Confederate government. The 

Confederacy also issued bonds, but again the results were disappointing because of the scarcity of specie. The efforts to sell Confederate bonds in 

Europe met with some success. Neither could the South resist the temptation to issue paper money redeemable only after the conclusion of a favorable treaty with the Union. Nearly one billion dollars was issued in this currency, with an inevitable depreciation as hopes of a Confederate victory waned. The Fourteenth Amendment to the Federal Constitution, after the war, forbade payment of any part of the Confederate debt.

The War-Time North: Industry and Labor. The outbreak of the war created a demand for a huge supply of cotton, wool, leather, and iron products. New factories sprang up throughout the North in response to this demand. The high prices paid for these products made it possible for some of the manufacturers to become wealthy, and laid the foundations for "big business." The concentration of capital led to the organization of labor, a step which was facilitated by the scarcity of laborers resulting from the departure of so many men from the various industries to the army. Many unscrupulous manufacturers and merchants could not resist the temptation to profiteer. Lucrative contracts with the government, some of them obtained by dishonest practices and orders, were filled by supplying paper-soled shoes and shoddy blankets; and the spoils of corruption were shared with the government representatives who had written the contracts and accepted the inferior goods. 

The War-Time North: Works of Charity. Those who wished to profit from the war at the expense of the government were, however, only a small minority of the population. Most of the people of the North firmly believed in the principles for which the war was fought, and were willing to make the sacrifices which might be required of them. Never before had relief work been so well organized or conducted on so vast a scale. Soon after the first soldiers left for the front, the women all over the North met in Ladies' Aid Societies to prepare bandages, towels, shirts, and other supplies, in much the same way that it was done a half century later, during the World War. 

This work was soon expanded into the wider service of the "Sanitary Commission," which undertook the task of caring for the sick and wounded soldiers and their dependent families. The work of the Sanitary Commission was supplemented by the newly organized Young Men's Christian Association, which provided the soldiers with diet kitchens and free reading rooms, besides promoting religious services for the men in the camps. The overtaxed Medical Department of the army was assisted by women who volunteered their services as nurses. Most famous among these was Clara 

Barton, who, nearly twenty years later, took the lead in the organization of the American Red Cross.

Life in the Confederacy: Sacrifices Demanded by the War. Social and economic conditions were incomparably worse for the Southern people than for the Northern. With their cotton and grain fields serving as battlefields, their homes, barns, and other property destroyed by the ravages of war, and even many of the necessities of life denied to them because of the strangling blockade, the Southerners were called upon to suffer untold

privations. Starvation itself threatened those who were left in the trail of the invaders. It is said that after Sherman's march to the sea, many 

Georgia families supported life on the scattered grains swept up from abandoned feeding places. Many soldiers at the front were constantly haunted by the fear that their own loved ones might be the victims of dire need, and some of them, for this reason, deserted from the Confederate army in the later stages of the war, in order to go to the aid of their families. 

The Scarcity of Necessities. The lack of an adequate supply of necessary commodities was due to three causes-the blockade, the inadequate system of transportation, and the speculators who demanded fabulous profits for their goods. The shortage of medicine and surgical supplies was keenly felt. Iron was in great demand for war purposes but it was so scarce in the South that church and plantation bells were melted and cast into cannon. Whenever iron implements for the farm or cooking utensils were worn out or broken, they could not be replaced. One lady, who had been accustomed to plenty, hired a skillet from a negro woman, for one dollar a month. Leather was so difficult to obtain that shoes were often made from wood. Usually the entire shoe was made from this material, but sometimes only the soles were made of wood; while buggy tops, carriage curtains, saddlecloths, or anything bearing a resemblance to leather, was used for the uppers. Paper became so scarce that newspapers were printed on a single sheet, and letters were written on the back of sheets already used on one side, pages from an old account book, and even pieces of wall paper; pokeberries, oak balls, and green persimmons furnished the ink. ";

Southern women soon became adept in the use of substitutes. "Coffee' was made by boiling parched wheat, rye, or okra seeds; sometimes sweet potatoes were dried in the sun, parched, and then boiled. "Tea" was made from raspberry or sassafras leaves, or from corn fodder; it was sweetened with sorghum, which took the place of sugar. The ashes of corn cobs were substituted for soda. There was no good substitute for salt. Families living near the sea obtained this commodity by boiling the sea water; those living inland sometimes took up the floors of their smoke houses, removed the dirt, and boiled it for the salt it contained. 

High Prices. Two factors were responsible for the extremely high prices of goods in the Confederacy—the scarcity of the supply, and the depreciated paper currency. The currency steadily declined in value as the Southern cause became more and more hopeless. Finally it became so worthless as to inspire the witticism that one should take money to market in a basket and bring provisions home in one's pocketbook. Coffee cost $4 a pound; tea, $35 a pound; milk, $4 a quart; butter, $2 a pound; corn, $15

a barrel; flour, $300 a barrel; muslin, $8 a yard; calico, $1.75 a yard; and a pair of shoes cost $150.

Heroism of the Women. The women of the South were perhaps no braver than those in the North, but the sacrifices they were called upon to make were much greater, for a larger proportion of men were at the front. When a husband answered the call of his country, he frequently left to his wife the management of his plantation and the supervision of his slaves, a difficult task, which was rendered somewhat easier by the almost universal loyalty of the negroes. Many of these proud, aristocratic women were reduced to plain, hard living. 

They brought into use the old spinning wheels and hand looms in order to make clothing for the soldiers; they made their woolen dresses into shirts, and the carpets into blankets. But hard work and privations were not the greatest tests of courage of the Southern women. Much harder to endure was the constant anxiety over the fathers, husbands, brothers, and sons who were bravely holding the last lines of defense; the solicitude for their children; the grief for the dead. Then there was the dread of ruthless bands of unprincipled men who roved over the South, defiant of both civil and military authority. A most tragic aspect of Southern life was the household composed of the women and children of several families huddled together without even a half-grown lad to support or protect them. 

Women of the Confederacy Memorial, Baltimore, Maryland

Results of the War. The War between the North and the South is called the "Civil War" in many histories; it is also often called the "War between the States." Since it was not ended by two independent nations, there was no treaty of peace at its close, to which we might turn to interpret the results. Nevertheless, the results of the war were momentous. 

First in importance was the fact that the supremacy of the Union was definitely established; never again would the peace be disturbed by questions of nullification or secession, and for a time states' rights were forced

to the background of our political issues. Although this question had been settled by the ancient method of trial by combat, yet it was given a legal setting soon after the close of the struggle in the case of Texas vs. White, in which the Supreme Court read into the Constitution, by interpretation, that the United States was an "indestructible Union of indestructible states."

The war also put an end to slavery in the United States. Few are the people today, in either section, who will deny that the abolition of slavery was a benefit to the South as well as to the nation as a whole. The overthrow of the slavery system removed a dangerous question from politics, but it substituted another problem almost as difficult—the race question. 

The fall of the slave power was accompanied by the overthrow of the planting system in the South, and the triumph of the industrial system in the North. Between 1860 and 1870, the number of factories in the United 

States increased 79.6 per cent, while the number of persons employed in them almost doubled. The triumph of industrialism meant the adoption of its habiliments-protective tariff, a liberal immigration policy, and government aid for the construction of railroads and internal improvements. 

There was no doubt about the future of industry in the United States.

CHAPTER XXI 

Reconstruction

Post-War Problems. When General Lee surrendered on the morning of April 9, 1865, the country was brought face to face with several difficult problems. The Union, indeed, had been preserved, but it was a very different Union from that of 1860; many readjustments were necessary. 

The most immediate problem was economic-disbanding the opposing armies and returning about 1,250,000 soldiers to their places in industrial and civil life. A million men in blue were carried back in triumph to their homes on special trains provided by an appreciative government. So great had been the stimulation of industry in the North that by November 15 most of the soldiers had laid aside the trappings of war with little more than a ripple upon the surface of industrial life. With the Confederate soldiers it was different. Many of them trudged for miles to their homes only to find their property in ruins. Having no capital, labor supply, or currency, their problem was that of existence. 

There was also a social problem. The question of slavery, which had disturbed the nation for so long a time, had been settled, but now there was the problem, no less perplexing, of disposing of about 3,500,000 negroes who had to learn the first lessons of liberty. How could this orphaned race, with little property, less inclination to work, and no conception of the responsibilities of citizenship, be so adjusted as to fill a useful place in the social, economic, and political life of the South? 

Great as were the economic and social problems, they were soon overshadowed by, and to a great extent merged into, the political problem. 

What was the status of the eleven states which had attempted secession? 

One group of extreme radicals, urged on by their bitter animosity toward the South, proclaimed that "Traitors must be punished," and took the position that the "rebellious" states had forfeited all rights in the Union and should be treated as "conquered provinces." Another group, somewhat less extreme, stated that the seceded states had been reduced to the 405

status of territories. Still another and much larger group took the more moderate and logical view that, inasmuch as secession was unconstitutional, the states had never really been out of the Union, but merely not in proper relation to it, and should be restored to their full rights as states as soon as this could safely be done. There was also a question as to whether the method of dealing with these states should be determined by the President or by Congress.

Lincoln Planned Immediate Restoration. President Lincoln was one of the moderates who believed that the Southern states were still states, but not in proper relation with the Union. Free from a spirit of vindictiveness toward a fallen foe, he desired to restore the states to their former position as quickly and as easily as possible. He had long believed that there was a strong loyal element in each state which might serve as a nucleus around which a loyal state government might be maintained during the war, and then, with the coming of peace, be quietly extended to include those who had been in arms. In this way the states would be restored to the Union with no disturbance, and without even considering whether they had ever been out of the Union.

As early as December 8, 1863, Lincoln announced his plan of reconstruction. To most of those who had aided the Confederacy, complete pardon and restoration of property was offered if they would take a prescribed oath of allegiance to the Federal Constitution. Only those who had held high civil or military offices in the Confederacy, and those who had resigned from similar positions in the United States government and army, were excluded from the benefits of this provision. Whenever the number of citizens of a state who had taken the oath equaled one tenth of the number who voted in the election of 1860, these loyal citizens would be permitted to re-establish the state government. Lincoln cautiously stated, however, that "whether members sent to Congress from any state shall be admitted to seats, constitutionally rests exclusively with the respective houses, and not to any extent with the executive." 

Many members of Congress thought that Lincoln's plan was too lenient, and refused to recognize representatives from Tennessee, Louisiana, and Arkansas, which had been reconstructed in accordance with Lincoln's proclamation. In 1864, Congress passed the Wade-Davis bill, which would have increased the ten per cent feature of Lincoln's plan to fifty per cent, and would have excluded more from the privilege of participating in the government. Lincoln defeated the bill with a pocket veto, but in a new proclamation he attempted to retain the good will of Congress by proposing the bill as a possible substitute for his own plan. Although

RECONSTRUCTION 

407 Lincoln wished to maintain harmony with Congress, yet he sincerely hoped that he would be permitted to carry out his program without any interference from that body. In a cabinet meeting the day of his assassination, he expressed his joy that Congress was not in session when the war came to an end; he rejoiced in the opportunity of restoring the states to their proper place in the Union without submitting them to the hatred and vindictiveness that characterized so many members of the national lawmaking body. 

Almost his last public words were: "I hope there will be no persecution, no bloody work after the war is over.... 

We must extinguish our resentment if we expect harmony of the Union." 

Ewing Galloway

Statue of Lincoln in the Lincoln Memorial Building, 

Washington, D. C.

The Death of Lincoln. 

Whether Lincoln could have carried out his program of reconstruction in the face of 

Congressional opposition is a matter of conjecture. He was not given the opportunity. On the evening of April 14, the fourth anniversary of the surrender of Fort Sumter, while attending a drama at Ford's Theater in Washington, he was shot by a half-crazed fanatic, John Wilkes Booth. He died early the next morning. A few hours later, the presidential oath of office was taken by Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Democrat who had been elected as Vice-President on the Union ticket in 1864, in an effort to preserve the Union by wiping out all party lines. His position was extremely difficult. Since his antecedents were all Southern and Democratic, he was distrusted by the Republicans; and because of his loyalty to the Union, and his dislike for slaveholders, he was distrusted by the Southern Democrats. He was untactful and stubborn to a degree that permitted no compromise with his opponents, and his real ability has been underestimated by many of the earlier historians; but even his severest critics testify to his integrity of purpose in all of his acts as President. His recent biographers emphasize

his great ability, honesty, and sincere devotion to the cause of justice and service to his country.

Johnson's Plan of Reconstruction. When Johnson became President there was much speculation concerning his attitude toward the South. The assassination of Lincoln by a Southern sympathizer played into the hands of the extreme radicals, who were bent upon a policy of revenge and punishment. Prominent among these radical leaders were Thaddeus Stevens, who was intensely bitter in his attitude toward Southern secessionists, and who advocated social and political equality of the two races; Charles 

Sumner, who fought constantly and uncompromisingly for the extension of suffrage to the freedmen; and Edwin M. Stanton, who as Secretary of 

War was a member of the President's official family. When Johnson began his administration by ordering the arrest of Jefferson Davis, Alexander H. 

Stephens, several state governors, and other high officials in the Confederacy, the radicals had reason to believe that they could rely on the support of the new President.

It was not long, however, before Johnson made known his determination to continue, in a large measure, the policy of Lincoln. On May 29, 1865, a new amnesty proclamation was announced, which followed Lincoln's example in granting pardon to those who had borne arms against the Union. More, however, were excluded from the benefits of the proclamation than under the plan of the former President. Most important among those now excluded were persons who owned property valued at twenty thousand dollars or more; but they were not a large group. Johnson also gave assurance that he would be generous in pardoning the members of the excluded groups who made application to him. 

By July 13, 1865, provisional governments had been set up in all of the Confederate states under a plan very similar to that proposed by Lincoln. 

These governments were to call constitutional conventions and take such other steps as were necessary for the establishment of permanent state governments. The conventions were expected to ratify the Thirteenth 

Amendment, which provided for the immediate emancipation of all of the slaves; declare secession invalid; and repudiate all debts contracted by the seceded states for the prosecution of the war. When these conditions had been met and the new state constitution had been approved, elections were to be held for representatives in the state legislature and in Congress. The negroes were not permitted to vote in these elections. By the end of the year all of the Southern states except Texas had organized new state governments and had elected their representatives to Congress. Texas took the same step a few months later.

409 

The Radicals Reject Johnson's Program. If Congress had been willing to receive the representatives elected by the reconstructed state governments, and thus give their approval to the President's program, the uncertainty concerning the status of the Southern states would have been at an end; but the radicals in Congress had no such intention. Several reasons may be given for the opposition of Congress to Johnson's plan of reconstruction. In the first place, many members of Congress thought that for several years the President had been extending his authority at the expense of the legislative department. They had yielded to the great increase in the powers of Lincoln only to preserve harmony during the struggle to maintain the Union. Now the time had come for Congress to assert itself. 

They believed that the problem of reconstruction came within their own jurisdiction rather than that of the executive, and consequently they were in no mood to approve the President's policy. Johnson was just as determined not to yield to what he considered the usurpation of the rightful prerogatives of the executive by Congress. 

Another reason for the opposition of Congress to Johnson's plan of reconstruction was the belief that it was too liberal. Many of the extreme radicals declared that the "rebel” states should not be restored to their former place in the national government without having been properly chastised for their disloyalty. Several unfortunate and grossly misinterpreted occurrences caused this belief to be more widely accepted in the North than at the end of the war. The assassination of Lincoln was regarded by many as the result of a widespread Southern conspiracy to overthrow the national government. Then, too, some of the reconstructed states had elected some of the highest officials in the Confederate government and army as their representatives in Congress. This was the result of a sincere desire to be represented by their most able men, but it was misunderstood by many of the people in the North. 

A still more unfortunate occurrence was the passage of the so-called "black codes" by most of the states which had complied with Johnson's program of reconstruction. Many of the negro freedmen positively refused to work, and became a burden as well as a source of annoyance to the whites. Laws were passed compelling the freedmen to work under certain conditions. Laws also restricted the negro's right to carry weapons, and would not permit him to testify in court against a white person. Although many of the Northern states had "black codes" similar to these, the acts of the Southern legislatures were regarded as a deliberate attempt to nullify the results of the war. These were used by the Northern radicals as grounds for demanding the punishment of the "traitors."

There was another factor which influenced the radicals as well as many of the moderate Republicans. The Republican party had gained control of the government in 1860; and retained control in 1864 in the guise of a Union party. With the Democratic Southern states back in the Union, there was a strong probability that the next election might see the return of the Democrats to power. Especially alarming was the fact that the 

Thirteenth Amendment, by superseding the three-fifths clause in the Constitution, would bring about an increase in the number of representatives from the former slaveholding states. The surest plan for the Republicans to keep in power seemed to be to enfranchise the negroes and thus shift some of the Southern states into the Republican column. The leaders in Congress were determined, therefore, not to recognize the governments of the Southern states unless negro suffrage was adopted. 

The First Congressional Plan. As the radicals knew that the support of their policies by the Northern electorate was very uncertain, they at first merely put off the acceptance of Johnson's plan by appointing a committee of fifteen members to study the condition of the Southern states. 

While the committee was making its investigation, Congress contented itself with the passage of several bills intended to protect the freedmen against the "black codes." In February, 1866, a second Freedman's 

Bureau Bill was passed and sent to the President for his approval. This bureau had been created by an act of March 3, 1865, for a period of one year. Its purpose was to look after the economic and social condition of the freedmen. Although the intentions of the higher officials of the bureau were entirely commendable, yet many of the local agents pursued a policy so unwise and discriminatory that they won for the bureau the ill will of the white people of the South. It was the purpose of the bill passed by 

Congress in 1866 to extend the life and the powers of the bureau. Although the bill was not in direct opposition to Johnson's policy, he vetoed it and was sustained by the Senate-his last victory over Congress. 

A few weeks later Congress passed over the President's veto the Civil Rights Act, which declared that the freedmen were citizens and were entitled to the same rights and privileges as the whites. Violators of the act were to be punished by fines or imprisonment, or both, and the military forces of the United States could be called upon for the enforcement of its provisions. On April 30, the committee which had been investigating conditions in the South made its report and recommended a course of procedure relative to the reconstruction of the states. 

The Fourteenth Amendment. The recommendations of the committee were incorporated into an amendment to the Constitution, which was

RECONSTRUCTION 

411 approved by Congress and submitted to the states for ratification on June 13, 1866. This amendment conferred citizenship upon the negroes and guaranteed them equal protection with the whites, thus removing doubts about the constitutionality of the Civil Rights Act. In an effort to induce the states to extend the right of suffrage to the negroes, one clause in the amendment provided for the reduction of the number of representatives in Congress from any state which denied that right. If all the Southern states gave the negroes the right to vote, their representation would be increased to seventy; if they refused, it would be reduced to forty-five. 

Even more obnoxious to the South was the third clause, which disqualified a large number of Confederates from holding office. Finally, the amendment guaranteed the validity of all debts of the national government, but declared all debts incurred in aid of rebellion and all claims for the loss or emancipation of slaves illegal and void. Tennessee promptly ratified the amendment and was restored to its full rights as a state, but all of the other Southern states defeated ratification by overwhelming majorities. 

Radical Reconstruction. The radicals were fortified by an overwhelming victory in the election of 1866, which gave them more than a two-thirds majority in Congress, and as they resented the attitude of the recalcitrant states toward the Fourteenth Amendment, they decided to discard the former plan of reconstruction and launch upon an entirely new program. 

In a series of reconstruction acts passed in 1867, the state governments organized under the earlier plan were not recognized as legal. The ten unreconstructed states were divided into five military districts, each under the command of a major general of the United States army. Military rule was set up in spite of the fact that the President, the courts, and Congress itself had concurred in recognizing the war as ended. It was the duty of the generals to preserve order and supervise the registration of voters who would elect delegates to a constitutional convention. For the first time, the negroes were to have the right to vote, and in view of the fact that all whites who had aided the Confederacy were excluded from registration, the negroes controlled the elections. The recognition of each new state government would depend upon (1) the ratification, by the qualified black and white voters, of a state constitution establishing negro suffrage; (2) the ratification of the Fourteenth Amendment by the new legislature; and (3) the final approval, by Congress, of the new state government thus established.

Under this plan, state governments dominated by the negroes were organized in North Carolina, South Carolina, Florida, Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, and Arkansas; and during the year 1868 these seven states were

readmitted to their places in the Union and participated in the election of 

1868. The ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment, which established negro suffrage in all the states of the Union, was then imposed as an additional condition to the restoration of the three remaining states, Virginia, Texas, and Mississippi. Early in 1870 those three were restored; and 

Georgia, which had been returned to military rule after expelling the negro members of her legislature, was restored in July of the same year. 

The Union again was complete. 

Johnson's Struggle with Congress. Meanwhile, the contest between the President and Congress had reached an acute stage. Johnson had vetoed all of the radical reconstruction measures, only to see his vetoes overridden by huge majorities. The radicals, moreover, were not content with reducing the President's power, but sought a pretext for removing Johnson from office. In order to prevent the removal of Stanton, the radical Secretary of War, upon whom would fall the supervision of the military governments in the South, Congress passed over the President's veto the Tenure of Office Act, which made it a "high misdemeanor" to dismiss from office, without the consent of the Senate, any official who had been appointed with the Senate's approval. Several months later, when Stanton had become intolerable to the President, Johnson asked for his resignation. Stanton refused to resign, but was suspended, and General 

Grant was appointed to serve ad interim. When Congress convened in 

December, 1867, the Senate refused to concur in the suspension of Stanton, whereupon Grant surrendered the office. In doing this, Grant thwarted the President's plan to test the constitutionality of the Tenure of Office Act by forcing Stanton into litigation for the possession of the office. On 

February 21, 1868, Johnson dismissed Stanton.

The Impeachment of Johnson. Johnson's act in dismissing Stanton gave the radicals a pretext for which they had been seeking, and three days later the House of Representatives passed a resolution impeaching him for "high crimes and misdemeanors." In accordance with the constitutional provision which outlines the course of procedure when a President is impeached, Johnson was brought to trial before the Senate, which acted as a jury, with Chief Justice Chase presiding. There followed one of the most farcical and deplorable episodes in American history. The radicals had intended to base their charges against Johnson upon the violation of the Tenure of Office Act, but there was a question as to whether Johnson, after all, had actually violated the law, for its provisions were intended to protect a cabinet officer only during the term of the President who had appointed him and for one month thereafter; and Stanton had been

RECONSTRUCTION 

413 appointed by Lincoln, whose term of office had ended with his death nearly three years previous. Consequently the radicals decided that they would have a better chance of success if they tried Johnson first on some general charges, drawn up by Thaddeus Stevens, which would not require specific proof, or involve constitutional controversies. 

The evidence proved conclusively that Johnson, though untactful, had been faithful to his oath of office and the precedents established by his predecessors. In spite of desperate efforts on the part of the President's enemies to secure by bribery and intimidation the two-thirds majority necessary for removal from office, the final vote was thirty-five to nineteen in favor of conviction. Had only one Senator who voted for acquittal, cast his vote with the radicals, Johnson would have been removed from office. It is fortunate that the country was spared the precedent of a powerful majority in Congress removing from office, for purely political reasons, a President who dared to oppose its policies. 

Radical Rule in the South. Immediately after the passage of the reconstruction acts, Northern adventurers, seeing the opportunity of

securing for themselves the higher offices in the reconstructed state governments through the control of the negro voters, began their invasion of the South. They were called "carpetbaggers" because they were said to have brought all of their possessions with them in carpetbags; but many of them returned a few years later loaded with the wealth they had extorted from their former enemies. Even more despised by the white people in the South were the "scalawags," 

Southerners who joined the "carpetbaggers," either in the hope of sharing in the booty or else in the belief that it was the best way to protect their people against misgovernment. Their success is indicated by the fact that in 1868, in the seven states that had just been restored, ten of the fourteen Federal senators, twenty of the thirty-five Federal representatives, and four of the seven governors, were "carpetbaggers." Most of the lesser offices were held by negroes and "scalawags."
