In the legislature of South Carolina, in 1868, there were eighty-eight negroes and only sixty-seven whites, and many of the negro members could neither read nor write. These colored legislators were ignorant and inexperienced in matters relating to the conduct of government, but it 

Culver Service

A session of the South Carolina Legislature of 1873; drawing by W. R. Leigh in a contemporary magazine was in the management of the financial affairs of the state that they made the most pitiful showing. Accustomed to the handling of only very small sums of money, they now attempted to administer funds amounting to millions. Nor did the responsibility rest heavily upon their shoulders, for they did not have to pay the taxes resulting from their extravagance. The same was practically true of the "carpetbagger" and "scalawag" members. The entire membership of the South Carolina legislature in 1868 paid annual taxes amounting to only $635.23, and ninety-one of the members paid no tax at all. Extravagant sums were appropriated from the public funds for fine desks, upon which the negroes put their feet; French mirrors; china spittoons; and the most lavish furnishings for the Capitol and the quarters of some of the members. When Moses, the Speaker, lost a thousand-dollar bet on a horse race, he was graciously reimbursed by his colleagues, who voted him a gratuity of a thousand dollars for the efficient way in which he had presided over the House. The cost of printing during the eight years of the radical government in South Carolina was nearly twice as much as it had been during the seventy-eight previous years. Even more extravagant were the grants to the railroads. Similar conditions, to some extent, were found also in other Southern states during the time when their governments were dominated by "carpetbaggers," "scalawags," and negroes. With regiments of Northern military forces on hand to enforce the acts of these governments, the white people of the South were powerless to stop such extravagance and corruption.

RECONSTRUCTION 

415 The Union Leagues. Almost as exasperating to the Southern whites were the activities of the Union Leagues. These had been organized during the war as agencies for the promotion of the Union cause in the South, but by the time the radicals had adopted their program of reconstruction, the membership had become predominantly negro. These organizations therefore became ideal agencies for the propagation of the radical policies in the South, and were extended into practically every community. Their meetings were held at night, and new members were initiated with pompous ritualistic ceremonies-factors which were well calculated to appeal to the emotional nature of the negro. At these meetings, the white "carpetbagger" leaders lectured the blacks on their obligations to the Republican party, and encouraged them to demand the social, as well as the political, equality of the races—a principle which was put into practice by the 'carpetbaggers" by fraternizing with the negroes on terms of racial equality. Some of these leagues adopted violent methods. In extreme cases, Democratic white leaders were robbed and even murdered, or their houses and barns were burned. The Southern whites, in desperation, sought some means of retaliation and protection. 

The Ku Klux Klan. Unable to offer open resistance to the Union 

Leagues because of the presence of United States troops throughout the South, the Southern whites, too, formed secret societies for their own protection. The most famous of these societies was the Ku Klux Klan, the name being derived from the Greek word "kuklos," meaning a band, or circle. It was first organized at Pulaski, Tennessee, as a social club, but, when it was found that the superstitious negroes were frightened by the white masks and robes which had been adopted as the official garb of the society, it was soon used as a means for maintaining order by the intimidation of the blacks. Other Ku Klux Klan clubs were formed throughout 

Tennessee and the other Southern states, and at a secret meeting in Nashville, in the spring of 1867, these clubs were brought together into the "Invisible Empire of the South," with General Nathan Bedford Forrest at its head.

Although the original purpose of the order was merely to discipline the criminally inclined negroes and "carpetbaggers," it was not long until a baser element had crept into the Klan, and, under the cover of the mask, had been guilty of conduct which was a discredit to the organization. In 

1869, therefore, General Forrest ordered that the Klan be disbanded. 

Some of the "dens," however, in which the lawless element were in the majority, refused to disband and continued their programs of violence. 

The disorders which resulted led to the enactment by Congress of a series

of laws which were intended to suppress the order. In spite of the fact that the essential features of these acts were later declared unconstitutional, they were rigidly enforced by the Federal troops, and by the end of 1872 the Ku Klux Klan had virtually disappeared.

Very similar in their organization and activities were the Knights of the White Camelia, who were especially active throughout the Gulf states. 

The Restoration of Home Rule. Many of the Northern people were becoming disgusted with the highhanded methods employed in the "reconstruction" of the South. Liberal Republicans joined with the 

Democrats in a movement which threatened to break the power of the radicals. Although the liberal movement was temporarily unsuccessful, it helped to mitigate the conditions in the South. In 1871 the "ironclad oath," which had disfranchised the Confederate soldiers, was repealed, and thus a large number of whites were allowed to have a voice in the government. By the end of the year the whites had regained control of the state governments in Virginia, North Carolina, and Georgia. The next year 

Congress passed a general amnesty act, which restored to all but about 750 Southerners the right to hold office. While the number of white voters was rapidly increasing, more and more of the negroes absented themselves from the polls; in most cases, probably, because of intimidation by the whites.

In 1874 the tide definitely turned in favor of the liberals. Disgusted by the corruption of the Republican administration, the voters came to the support of the Democratic nominees in the Congressional election, and for the first time since the war the Democrats secured a majority in the House of Representatives. The reign of the radicals had finally ended. 

By the time of the election of 1876, "alien" rule had collapsed in all of the Southern states except Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina, and there it held on only because of the presence of troops. Southerners were disappointed because of the defeat of Tilden in the contested election of 1876 (pp. 715-717), but it soon was clear that they had no reason to fear a continuation of the policies of the preceding administrations, for President Hayes very promptly ordered the withdrawal of the troops from the South. Deprived of the protection of the military forces, the remaining "carpetbagger" governments immediately collapsed.

The Fruits of Reconstruction. The South emerged from the war without any special resentment toward its conquerors, and was fully resigned to the resumption of its former place in the Union; but the excesses of reconstruction aroused a sectional bitterness which has not yet entirely disappeared. Not until the close of the century was there a marked

RECONSTRUCTION 

417 tendency in either section to forget the mistakes of the past and bring about a Union which would be united in spirit as well as in form. 

The three amendments adopted during the period of reconstruction unloosed the fetters from the slaves, but they did not solve the racial problem, which now became more serious. It was soon evident that the difficult question of racial adjustments would have to be worked out by the peoples who were most directly concerned. In spite of the constitutional amendments, the negroes have not been given their full civic rights. 

Most of the Southern states have evaded the Fifteenth Amendment by adopting suffrage laws which disfranchised a much larger proportion of negroes than whites; and the "Jim Crow" laws have given legal sanction in the South to the social barrier existing between the two races. One clause of the Fourteenth Amendment, calling for a reduction in a state's representation in Congress in proportion to the part of its population excluded from voting, has never been enforced; some hold that it was superseded by the Fifteenth Amendment and so is not now applicable. 

The racial problem, too, is no longer strictly Southern. The great exodus of negroes to the North early in the twentieth century was followed by race riots in St. Louis and Chicago. The North, too, must undertake the solution of the riddle of racial compatibility. 

A political result of reconstruction was the "solid South." Memories of the corruption and misgovernment under the reign of the radicals strengthened the loyalty of the South to the Democratic party to such an extent that it was not until 1920 that an electoral vote was given by one of the former seceded states to a Republican candidate for President; in that year Tennessee gave her vote to Harding. But with the mellowing of sectionalism, the party lines have become less distinct, and in 1928 the "solidity" of the South was broken when several Southern states gave popular and electoral majorities to Herbert Hoover.  Chapter XXII.  Chapter XXIII. LABOR AND THE MACHINE Age Chapter XXIV.  Chapter XXV. 

 Chapter XXVI.  THE MOST IMPORTANT PHASE of the development of the United States following the War between the North and the South was the process of industrialization which revolutionized manufacturing, agriculture, transportation, and mining. It was, in part, a continuation of the Industrial 

Revolution of the eighteenth century, which, through inventions such as that of the steam engine, made England a manufacturing center. These inventions were brought to the United States, improved, and used in the creation of new industries which made possible the rapid development of our natural resources. With the growth of industry and the improvement in transportation, large cities were built, and the leading occupation of the United States was changed from agriculture to manufacturing. 

During the Machine Age the economic and social life of America was transformed. The power supplied by man's own muscle or by that of his domestic animals was supplemented by that of falling water, steam, electricity, and gasoline. The use of this power aided in the production of great 423

quantities of goods and, in a degree, was responsible for the unequal distribution of wealth. Manufacturing plants grew in size and were consolidated into larger industries. Trusts were organized; and, because of their tendency to monopolize the industries, the government found it necessary to attempt regulation. This control was exercised especially during the administrations of Theodore Roosevelt, William H. Taft, Woodrow Wilson, and

Franklin D. Roosevelt.* 

In the large factories thousands of laborers were employed, each of whom was engaged in some detailed process of production in which expensive machinery was used. This was in sharp contrast to the early days when the laborer owned the tools with which he worked. In the factory system the machinery was owned by capitalists. This caused the control of industry to pass from the hands of the worker, and led labor to organize. 

Organized labor sought to increase wages, reduce the hours of employment, and secure more sanitary working conditions. So successful was it that by the 1830's the hours had been reduced to ten; later they were decreased to eight; and within recent years a demand for a six-hour working day has been made. In 1869 the Knights of Labor was organized by Uriah S. 

Stephens. This in time was superseded by the American Federation of 

Labor, which, under the leadership of Samuel Gompers, made much progress toward better working conditions. 

Labor has also sought to improve its status by means of strikes and boycotts. The National Industrial Recovery Act of 1933 recognized the right of labor to organize, and the National Labor Board was created for the purpose of securing co-operation between labor and industry. 

Industry in America has from the earliest days sought protection against foreign competition by the enactment of protective tariffs. Following the War between the North and the South, high tariffs enabled great industrial corporations to develop more rapidly. 

Another important problem which has commanded attention throughout our entire history is that of money. Even in colonial times the American settlers felt the need of some system of money to avoid the necessity of directly exchanging their goods. They resorted to paper money, but this soon became worthless because it was issued in large quantities; however, with the founding of our new government under the Constitution, a sound system of coinage was established with the dollar as the standard. Both gold and silver dollars were coined and provision was made for the issuing of a limited amount of paper money. The question of coinage and of the *The chart of administrations since 1869, on pages 708-709, shows not only the term and the party of each President, but also the parties in control of Congress.

issuing of paper money has been an important subject of controversy throughout our history, especially in the election of 1896. In 1933 and later the financial policy of the American government received much atten tion from Franklin D. Roosevelt and his advisers. 

Along with a system of currency, a system of banking and credit also was established. Soon after the national government was founded the first Bank of the United States was created. This was followed in 18161836 by a second Bank of the United States. In 1863 a system of national banks was provided for, and during the administration of Woodrow Wilson the Federal Reserve Bank system was added. Our banking system was modified by the Franklin D. Roosevelt administration to provide for the insurance of deposits in most banks, and for more centralized control. 

The great industrial changes brought on by the development of machinery have greatly affected American agriculture. The American farmer has been an important factor in the history of our country. In the early days our population was composed almost entirely of farmers; but as other forms of industry developed, a smaller proportion of our people devoted their energies to tilling the soil. During the colonial period, the farmer produced largely for home markets and his farm was usually a self-sufficient unit. After 1865 agriculture became more commercialized, and the farmer produced most of his crops for sale and bought many of the things he needed from manufacturing centers. The farm area greatly increased, and prior to 1914 farm products were the most important part of the export trade. This was true especially in the period of the 1880's and 1890's, when farm surpluses were sent abroad to pay for our imports. 

Since the World War America has become a creditor nation and is buying less from abroad, and therefore farm surpluses are no longer in demand as a means for paying for our imports. In the meantime machinery has made farms more productive and great surpluses have appeared. With the reduction of the demand, increased production has brought great agricultural distress. The farmer has sought various means for overcoming these difficulties, and in recent years farm relief has been one of the important problems of the national government. The Roosevelt administration attempted to deal with that problem through the Agricultural Adjustment Act, which had for its purpose the reduction of these vast surpluses and the raising of prices. In 1933-1935, through the operation of this act, the number of livestock and the amount of wheat, tobacco, cotton, and other farm products, were reduced. This reduction helped to increase prices and to restore the purchasing power of the farmer. Early in 1936, however, the 

Supreme Court declared the AAA to be unconstitutional.

CHAPTER XXII The Consolidation of Industry The United States Becomes Industrialized. The mechanical inventions which brought about the Industrial Revolution in England in the eighteenth century soon found their way to other countries. In 1790 Samuel Slater set up a cotton mill in New England and thus began on a small scale the development of machine industry in America. The War of 1812 provided an impetus to manufacturing, but it was not until after 1865 that the United States became a highly industrialized nation. Before that time we were largely agrarian, with nearly four fifths of the people living on farms or in small communities. In the thirty-year period from 1860 to 1890 American inventive genius brought about rapid changes which have continued to the present time. Before 1860 less than 42,000 patents had been issued by the Patent Office, while since that date there have been over 2,000,000. 

Samuel Slater's first cotton mill, in Pawtucket, Rhode Island-the building in the foreground 【藏​】 427

Coincident with the development of industry was the exploitation of our mineral resources-especially coal, iron, oil, and gas, which before that time had remained practically untouched. 

New Inventions Modify Life. There were comparatively few changes in the methods of living from the days of Washington to the middle of the nineteenth century, but since that time American life has been revolutionized. Electric lights, motion pictures, cement sidewalks, streetcars, bicycles, automobiles, sanitary plumbing, telephones, typewriters, steel rails, steel bridges, artificial ice, rural free delivery, repeating rifles, dynamite, submarines, electric sweepers, gas and electric stoves, sewing machines, airplanes, radios, and many other important inventions have come to change our ways of living. Different means of communication keep us in touch daily with every civilized nation. 

These inventions have also complicated our existence, and have made it more difficult for us to understand the social, political, and economic problems. They have brought about greater differences in the economic status of individuals. Before 1860 the material things of life were rather equally distributed; only a few people lived in poverty and a smaller number lived in luxury. Since that time improved machinery has made great production possible and has enabled men to amass large fortunes. 

Before 1860 there were only a few millionaires, but our industrial development has produced not only millionaires but multimillionaires. In 1928 there were, according to the Income Tax Bureau of the United States. 

Treasury Department, 513 persons who were receiving incomes of more than $1,000,000 a year, and eleven of these had incomes of $5,000,000 or more. The effect of machine industry on laborers will be discussed in 

Chapter XXIII. 

The changes in industry also affected our political life, for they influenced many of our domestic and foreign policies. Political leadership came to men of a practical turn of mind, who were concerned with the development of industry because they believed that the growth of great manufacturing enterprises was best for the American people. They favored a protective tariff and a foreign policy which would enable industry to secure more and better markets for its products. They wanted a stable financial system which would allow business to be transacted in foreign countries with more certainty. The increasing political control of wealth was pointed out as early as 1871 by Henry Ward Beecher when he stated that "We are in more danger from overgrown pecuniary interests [that is, from organized money] than we ever were from slavery." He also said that the battle of the future "will be one of gold and silver." His pre-

Culver Service

A peddler in 1868, as pictured in a contemporary magazine. Peddlers were very important when farmers' wives could seldom go to town. diction came true. In later chapters we shall see how our industrial life and the money question are related and how they became important in politics in 1892, 1896, 1907, 1913, and also during the administration of 

Franklin D. Roosevelt. 

Important Social Effects of Consolidation. One important effect of the industrial changes was the disappearance of most of the one-man shops where the owner was also a worker, perhaps employed one or two apprentices, and produced articles for a local market. Instead of the old-fashioned cobbler, who took orders for shoes to supply the local community, factories run by machinery produced shoes in great quantities. The market was no longer the local community, but instead the whole country, and even other parts of the world. This was possible because of the development of rapid and cheap transportation furnished by our railroad system. Soon the factories were consolidated into larger and larger establishments. 

Partnerships were replaced by corporations which in turn were consolidated in trusts or mergers. The worker who had relied on his own muscle, or on the use of water to turn his machinery, found his output greatly increased by the use of steam and electricity. 

During the War between the North and the South, there was an increased demand for products of the factory such as shoes, clothing, and

munitions of war. This demand stimulated consolidation, for the larger industries in many cases could be operated more efficiently. A further stimulus was supplied by the protective tariff, which made it possible for the manufacturers in the North to secure a greater profit. The policy of protection was continued after 1865, and industry, aided by our natural resources and an increasing domestic market, continued to expand and prosper. So great were the changes in this industrial development that an important economist pointed out in 1891 that there never had been another place or another time in the history of civilization where science and invention had produced such material progress as in the United States. 

Growth of Manufacturing. The number of manufacturing establishments increased rapidly. In 1859, for example, there were in America about 140,000 manufacturing plants, while ten years later there were about 252,000.

While the total number of manufacturing establishments was increasing, within particular types of industries the tendency on the whole was toward fewer and larger plants. In 1850 there were 1,333 factories making farm implements, but by 1910 there were only 640. Yet the value of the goods made by these factories had grown from $6,000,000 to $246,000,000. 

The same condition existed in some other lines of industry. In 1860 even many small towns had at least one slaughterhouse, while a large city, such as New York, had 200. The invention of artificial refrigeration made it possible to send carloads of meat from the western packing houses to New York and other cities in the East. This brought about the establishment of large slaughterhouses in the West. Meat-packing houses appeared in Kansas City, Chicago, and a few other places near the supply of raw materials. These tended to do away with the butcher shops and the slaughtering of animals on a small scale. In the meat-packing business the growth was so great that by 1905 it was reported that seventeen men, comprising the heads of five corporations, had monopolized the beefpacking industry of the whole country. In other industries a similar change took place. In 1880 there were nearly 2,000 woolen mills, but ten years later, only 1,300. During the same period, the number of iron and steel mills decreased by one third, but the products increased by one half. 

In the leather industry, the change was even more outstanding. Three fourths of the establishments were closed, but the products increased fivefold.

A similar development took place in the steel industry. In 1856 the 

Bessemer process was invented. By 1875 there were only twelve important 

Bessemer plants in the United States, producing 375,000 tons of steel

annually; but by 1880 nearly 1,000,000 tons were produced. The greatest part of this output went into steel rails for railroads. In the milling industry the same tendency was at work. Nearly all gristmills, which had existed by the thousands throughout the nation, disappeared, and were replaced by large flour mills. 

Manufacturers had discovered that large-scale production made for greater economy. By such production, machinery could be used more economically. Work was divided into such simple processes that machinery replaced men, and mass production resulted. There were many other economies, notably that of the utilization of by-products. In the small butcher shop or slaughterhouse much waste resulted, while in the larger ones waste was converted into profits. A modern packing house, in addition to furnishing meat, utilizes what small concerns would discard; and as by-products, manufactures fertilizer, soap, gelatin, buttons, tennis strings, knife handles, and many other articles. 

The Growth of the Oil-Refining Industry. Nowhere is the growth of industry better illustrated than in the production and refining of oil. 

Petroleum, in the few places where it was found, had long been considered a menace because it polluted the water and made it unfit for drinking. It was used as a medicine, under the name of Rock Oil, or Seneca Oil. About 

1840, it was put up in eight-ounce bottles and sold as the great American medicine, which could cure almost any ailment. In 1859, Colonel E. L. 

Drake sank an oil well in western Pennsylvania. A few years before that, a professor of chemistry at Yale University had analyzed oil and had come to the conclusion that by very simple and inexpensive processes many Pithole City, Pennsylvania, in one of the important early oil-producing regions Healey

Visual Education Society 

Oil refinery at Fort Worth, Texas valuable products could be manufactured from it. By 1864 large-scale production of oil had begun, and in less than a year's time more than 2,000,000 barrels were sent to the refinery. 

The oil industry was developed largely by John D. Rockefeller, who in 

1862 invested his first earnings in the oil-refining business. Three years later, he organized the firm of Rockefeller and Andrews. Very early he saw the advantage of large-scale operations and, together with H. M. 

Flagler, worked to secure more effective consolidation. In 1870 he organized the Standard Oil Company of Ohio, with a capital stock of $1,000,000. 

The company issued 10,000 shares, at $100 each, which were held by 

Rockefeller, his brother William, and other associates.

To secure economy of operation and avoid wasteful competition, he conceived a plan which he called "co-operation and conservation." He felt that under one leadership many industries could be combined, and the less economical ones eliminated. Their combined interest could be used to secure more improvement and economy. He saw the danger of overproduction, with a resulting poor market. He felt that oil should be kept off the market at times of oversupply, to stabilize prices. In 1872 was organized the South Improvement Company, which made a contract with railroads carrying oil. By this device the South Improvement Company received special advantages from the Pennsylvania Railroad, in the form of rebates, through which from twenty-five to fifty per cent of the money paid as freight charges was returned to the Standard Oil Company. This gave the South Improvement Company a great advantage over its com-

petitors. In addition to securing rebates, the South Improvement Company also obtained drawbacks, which meant that on the oil which was shipped by competitors, the South Improvement Company would secure a percentage of the freight charges, ranging from one fourth to one half of the amount paid by their competitors. In 1872 the capitalization was increased to $2,000,000, and Rockefeller bought the property of many other refineries in Cleveland. Later, the South Improvement Company was dissolved, and its place taken by an organization known as the Central 

Association of Refiners, with John D. Rockefeller as president. This organization, however, was not satisfactory and Rockefeller continued his process of consolidation, so that by the 80's, the Standard Oil Company controlled about ninety per cent of the refining business of the country. 

Trusts Organized. In order to effect a better organization, the company, in 1882, organized a trust, which was a type of organization theretofore unknown in business. The thirty-nine corporations which, with the Rockefeller interests, were engaged in the refining of oil, turned over their business affairs to the new organization, called a trust. The stockholders in the thirty-nine corporations gave their stock certificates to a group of nine trustees, among whom were John D. Rockefeller and his brother. These trustees had complete control. They managed the company and divided the profits among the stockholders of the thirty-nine companies according to the amount of stock they held. In other words, for each share of stock held in the original company, a stockholder received a proportional share of returns from the trust. Other monopolies followed this type of organization, and many trusts were organized. Among them were the Distillers' and Cattle Feeders' Trust (the whisky trust) and the Sugar Trust, both formed in 1887.

One result of the organization of trusts was higher prices. The American Sugar Refining Trust secured control of eighteen refineries, but operated only eleven of them, and raised the price of sugar. By 1888 many other commodities were controlled by the various trusts. Among them were copper, coal, glass, lead, flour, steel mills, stoves, and farm machinery. 

As the prices of commodities went up, and the trusts were reaping monopoly profits, many complaints came from consumers who objected to monopoly prices and demanded investigation and control of the trusts. 

During the years 1883-1891 investigations were made by some of the state legislatures, and were followed by state laws and provisions in state constitutions for the regulation of trusts. By 1890 no less than twenty-five states had passed laws against the trusts, and fifteen states had incorporated provisions in their constitutions, designed to prevent monopolies.

Political parties took notice of the sentiment against trusts, and in 1884 a third party, known as the Anti-Monopoly party, appeared. In 

1888 the Republican party declared itself in opposition to "combinations of capital, organized as trusts or otherwise," and the Democratic party platform said, "the interests of the people are betrayed when trusts and combinations are permitted to exist.” 

President Harrison, in his message of December, 1889, pointed out that trusts in the nature of conspiracies should be made a subject of study by Congress; and on July 2, 1890, Congress, under the authority given it by the interstate commerce clause of the Constitution, enacted the Sherman Antitrust Law. This law provided that combinations and conspiracies "in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations" are declared illegal and punishable by fine or imprisonment. The following year, the state of Ohio brought suit against the 

Standard Oil Company, and the court decided, in 1892, that the act of incorporation was illegal in that state. A similar suit was brought against the Standard Oil Company in the state of New York. Because of state and Federal laws against the trusts, the Standard Oil Trust was dissolved in 1892.

Organization of Holding Companies. Many trusts and large corporations often called "big business"-found it necessary to reorganize and to conform to law. Combinations, however, did not cease to exist; they merely changed their form. They obeyed the letter but not the spirit of the law. In place of trusts, big business now became organized as holding companies. In 1889, the state of New Jersey passed a law legalizing holding companies by permitting them to incorporate in that state. Many of the companies then changed their form and moved their home offices to New Jersey. 

There were two types of holding companies. In one form, the holding company purchased a bare majority, merely 51% of the capital stock of the companies concerned, so that it could control the policies of the companies. The second type owned the entire stock outright, and in reality formed a supercorporation. An outstanding example of this type of holding company is the United States Steel Corporation, which was organized by J. P. Morgan, who began to purchase stock in eleven large companies which controlled three fourths of the steel industry in the United States. 

The United States Steel Corporation was chartered in New Jersey in 1901, and was capitalized at $1,400,000,000.

Thus the consolidation of industrial establishments, which began in the period following the war between the North and the South, continued with

great rapidity after the passage of the Sherman Antitrust Law. In the thirty-year period from 1860 to 1890, 24 industrial companies were organized, with a total capital of $436,000,000; but in the next decade. 

157 such companies were organized, with a total capital of $3,158,000,000. 

Prior to January 1, 1898, only 82 combinations were formed, with a total capital of a little more than one million dollars; while from January 1, 1898, to January 1, 1904, 236 such combinations were established, with a total of more than six billion dollars. Consolidation of industry was becoming more and more complete. Greater and more powerful organizations were incorporated, and greater profits were made by the companies, and higher prices extracted from the public. During the years from 1899 to 1905, the annual profit of the Standard Oil Company ranged from $34,000,000 to $67,000,000 a year. The United States Steel Corporation controlled about seventy per cent of the iron and steel production, while the Amalgamated Copper Company controlled sixty per cent of all the copper produced. 

In the field of banking and finance it was said that by 1900 the Morgan and Rockefeller groups dominated to such an extent that it was almost impossible to begin any big business enterprise without the help of one or the other of these groups. It became evident that consolidation of industry was becoming more complete. Economy of production, regulation of output, and division of markets helped to maintain high prices. Cutthroat competition had been eliminated, but the public felt that the prices of commodities were too high. Consolidation continued in spite of the 

Sherman Antitrust Law, which was not vigorously enforced. During 

President Harrison's administration only three indictments were brought against big business, while in Cleveland's administration there were only two, and during McKinley's administration there was none. Big business, by changing its form from trusts to holding companies, tended to conform to the legal requirements but maintained the same economic principles in effect.

Social and Economic Effects of Industrialization. The development of industry brought the United States to the front as a leading manufacturing nation. Until 1880, the products of the farm continued to be our chief source of wealth; but by 1890 manufactured products were more valuable than those of agriculture; and by 1900 the value of our industrial output was worth more than twice that of agriculture. The United States had become a great industrial nation. While in 1860 it ranked fourth among the countries of the world in industry, by 1892 it led them all. From 

1860 to 1890 the number of factory hands had increased threefold, but the total value of the products had increased fivefold. Some sections of the

United States stood out as leading manufacturing centers. New England led in textiles, though after 1880 a movement began to move the mills to the cotton-growing region. By 1900 half of the cotton mills were located in the South, which has since then become the leading cotton textile center. 

Pennsylvania led in iron and steel products, but again, during the 80's, and since that time, blast furnaces have been erected in Alabama, Tennessee, and Virginia. So great was the development in iron production from 1860 to 1890, that pig iron production increased elevenfold. New 

Jersey became famous for its silk products, while New York and Chicago became important manufacturing centers for products of various kinds. 

As early as 1880 Chicago had nearly 800 woodworking establishments. 

Great quantities of minerals were produced in the Western states, as well as in the Lake Superior region. In 1860 the annual output of silver was worth $157,000; but by 1873 it had risen to $36,000,000; and in 1930 it was only $19,538,029.

Political Effects of Industrialization. This great development in industry had its effect on politics. Many of the statesmen of the period after 1865 became interested in the development of big business. Some of them felt that the best interests of the nation could be served by permitting wealth to be concentrated in the hands of a few. This was the view held by William McKinley, whose campaign for election as President in 1896 was directed by "Mark" Hanna (Marcus A. Hanna), himself a man of wealth and the spokesman of big business in politics. In this campaign the business interests of the country contributed more than $4,000,000 to the Republican campaign fund; the Standard Oil Company alone contributed $250,000. During McKinley's administration big business considered that it was free from government interference, since McKinley permitted the Sherman Antitrust Law to go unenforced. During his administration, the United States Supreme Court, in the case of the 

United States vs. E. V. Knight Company, ruled that the purchase of stock in other companies was not a violation of the Sherman Antitrust Law. 

This gave considerable encouragement to big business, and consolidations proceeded even more rapidly. 

Theodore Roosevelt and Big Business. Theodore Roosevelt, in 1901, in his first message to Congress, turned his attention to this important problem, and pointed out that while industrial concentration could not be prevented, industry must submit to regulation. He maintained that a distinction must be made between business which engaged in fair practices and that which resorted to illegal methods. He proposed that Congress provide for supervision and regulation of corporations doing interstate

business. As a result of his proposal, Congress passed an act which created the Department of Commerce and Labor. This act also provided for a 

Bureau of Corporations, headed by à commissioner who was authorized to make investigations of corporations engaged in interstate and foreign commerce, and to supply useful information concerning them. 

Roosevelt outlined a program for government regulation of industry. 

He did not believe in destroying business because it was big, but felt that big business was the outcome of natural economic forces. He felt that LAI

President Theodore Roosevelt halted by hostile amendments in Congress destructive competition had compelled industry to combine and cooperate to avoid destruction. He also felt that the growth of markets on a national and even international scale necessitated vast accumulations of capital, and that more economical management was possible by these means. Yet he saw that evils had arisen from such organization, and that they must be controlled, and that wrongdoing of any kind should be prohibited. In an address in Cincinnati, Ohio, he pointed out that the biggest corporation, like the humblest private citizen, must be held to strict compliance with the will of the people. 

Northern Securities Case. President Theodore Roosevelt, in accord ance with his policy of regulation and control, instructed his Attorney General to bring suit against the Northern Securities Company, a holding company, capitalized at $400,000,000, organized by James J. Hill, J. P. 

Morgan, and E. H. Harriman, for the purpose of controlling the stock of the Northern Pacific, the Great Northern, and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy railroads. The court rendered a decision against the Northern 

Securities Company and ordered the corporation dissolved. This verdict (1904) was a great victory for the government, for by this action against a large corporation Roosevelt demonstrated that no group is more powerful than the government. Other suits were instituted by Roosevelt, and before his administration closed, no less than forty-four antitrust suits were under way.

Big Business under Taft and Wilson. Roosevelt's successor, William

Howard Taft, continued the prosecution of trusts, while Woodrow Wilson not only continued the prosecution of trusts for violating the Sherman Law, but secured new trust legislation which more effectively checked the evils which had arisen. Consolidation had become so widespread that when Woodrow Wilson took office in 1913, it was estimated that five sixths of all the bank deposits were located in the Eastern industrial section. 

Industry was largely controlled from New York. President Wilson felt that great monopolies should be crushed, and that the tariff, which he considered the mother of trusts, should be reduced. Under his guidance, the Underwood Tariff Act-which greatly lowered the tariff rates—and the Clayton Antitrust Act were put on the statute books. The Clayton 

Antitrust Act forbade local price fixing, abolished interlocking directorates, and established a Federal Board of Trade for the purpose of studying the conduct of interstate business.

Big Business under the Postwar Administrations. Theodore Roose velt, Taft, and Wilson were able for a time to regulate monopolies and check their growth, but in the period following the World War there was a renewed trend toward consolidation, on an unprecedented scale. During this period many mergers—that is, combinations of several corporations into one-were formed, not primarily for the purpose of securing monopolies, but rather for obtaining more capital, finding more and better markets, and for bringing about more economy through the organization of sales agencies. The Machine Age made possible more production and brought about keener competition. Along with the Machine Age came standardization, uniform quality, and replaceable parts, noticeable especially in the manufacture of automobiles. The method of extensive mass production and standardization was one of the important developments of the 1920's. 

In the Department of Commerce, headed by Herbert Hoover (19211928), standardizing techniques were developed. Industry followed the model set by the Department of Commerce. Instead of greater variety of goods, a few standardized types were developed, as in the case of paving brick, where the number of forms was reduced from sixty-six to four. 

Invoice and purchase order forms were reduced from 4,500 to three. It was estimated by the Department of Commerce that under its direction, more than a hundred plans for standardization had been adopted, with the result of a great saving to industry. Large industrial establishments spent great sums on scientific research, with a view of further perfecting their methods of production.

These postwar developments made for large-scale production, and supercorporations were again becoming important in American industrial life. According to information compiled by Mr. J. T. Flynn, in The New 

Republic,* many mergers had taken place by 1929. In the iron and steel industry there were twenty-five mergers, which controlled 217 companies, with a capital of $2,114,115,000. In the automobile industry there were twenty-three mergers, controlling 187 companies, with a capital of $2,630,- 359,000. In electrical equipment there were eleven mergers, which controlled 71 companies. The market value of securities was $2,319,000,000.

The telephone and telegraph had three mergers, which controlled 627 companies, whose securities were worth $4,433,643,000. In food products there were fifteen mergers, controlling 119 companies, with a capital stock

Part of an automobile factory, where the finishing touches are put on the cars as they roll past different workmen of $1,471,142,000. The total of all mergers was 217, controlling 2,621 companies, with a market value of securities at $21,655,468,929. 

In the second decade of the twentieth century, industries were co-operating through trade associations; that is, they exchanged prices and other trade information openly. The Supreme Court on July 1, 1925, in an important decision, upheld the legality of these trade associations. 

During the postwar period, the Supreme Court was friendly in its attitude toward monopolies. The Federal 

Trade Commission and the 

Department of Justice also became more friendly toward big business. Yet during this period many suits were instituted against business practices which were considered unfair. The Department of Justice did not prosecute corporations because of their size. The Federal Trade 

Commission did not attack interlocking directorates, even though they had been prohibited by the Clayton Act, but devoted its energies to the enforce- *July 2, 1930.

ment of that part of the act dealing with unfair methods of competition. 

It did not interfere with the practice of issuing nonvoting stock, nor with the poor methods of reporting facts about corporations, nor with the development of holding companies, by which a few persons on the inside were able to acquire large interests in the properties of utilities companies and other corporations. Holding companies, under these conditions, took advantage of the public through stock manipulations, stock watering, and various forms of speculation. 

The Federal government, through its various agencies, was exercising very few restraints on business during the period 1920 to 1930. By 1930, the Sherman Law, as well as the Clayton Antitrust Act, was considered bad for business. It was felt that they created uncertainty and encouraged needless competition, and prevented industries from systematic production according to planned economy. Uncontrolled industry developed, and some resulting abuses were partly responsible for the depression which came in 1929.

Government and Industry. President Hoover appointed a Committee to study the Social Trends. This committee made a two-volume report on Recent Social Trends in the United States (1933),* in which it said that "The increasing complexity and interdependence of social life precipitate more sharply than ever the problem of the interrelations between the industrial and political forms of organization and control, and this has been accentuated by the rise of large-scale industrial units resembling in form while rivaling in magnitude some of the governmental units to which they are technically subordinate." It further stated that "Demands are now being made for more effective control over banking, investment trusts, holding companies, stock speculation, electric power industries, railroads, chain stores, and many other activities. The new forms of corporate structure raise many problems of legal control for the protection of the minority interests and of the community itself. . . . Under such circumstances the problem of interrelation between government and industry is of grave importance. Shall business men become actual rulers; or shall rulers become industrialists; or shall labor and science rule the old rulers? ... Observers of social change may look here for appearance of new types of politico-economic organization, new constellations of government, industry and technology, forms now only dimly discerned. . . . We may look for important developments alike in the concentration and in the devolution of social control, experiments perhaps in the direction of self- *The following quotations from this report are included here by permission of the publishers, the McGraw-Hill Book Company, Inc.

government of the various industries under central guidance, experiments in co-operation and accommodation between industry and government, especially as the larger units of industrial organization, co-operative and otherwise, become more like government in personnel and budgets, and as governments become agencies of general welfare as well as of coercion." 

Franklin D. Roosevelt and Big Business. While these problems were being considered by the Committee on Social Trends, the problems of industry became greater and greater, for, with the continuance of the depression that began late in 1929, many important industrial establishments were having serious financial difficulties. Millions of laborers were unemployed and the condition of industry became an important problem for the administration of Franklin D. Roosevelt. 

Soon after his inauguration (March 4, 1933) Roosevelt called a special session of Congress, at which one of the important pieces of legislation was the National Industrial Recovery Act (NIRA), which became a law on June 16, 1933, and was to remain in force only two years. One important object of the law was to put men back to work. President Roosevelt spoke of this act as “a great spontaneous co-operation to put millions of men back in their regular jobs this summer. The idea is simply for employers to hire more men to do the existing work by reducing the work hours of each man each week and at the same time pay a living wage for the shorter week." Industry had long insisted that it should be free from many of the restrictions placed by the government, which prohibited successful cooperation. Roosevelt pointed out this fact and stated that industry now was given the right to act in unison for the general good-now that the restrictions of the antitrust laws were relaxed. 

To carry out the provisions of the NIRA, elaborate machinery was set up. A Labor Advisory Board was appointed by the Secretary of Labor, to represent labor, and to see that its interests were adequately protected. 

The Industrial Advisory Board, appointed by the Secretary of Commerce, represented the industry, while the public was represented by a Consumers' 

Advisory Board. The National Recovery Administration (NRA) was set up with General Hugh S. Johnson, a man of wide experience, vigorous personality, and great ability, as administrator. The National Recovery 

Administration was instructed to secure from the various industries, codes which would set forth the rules for operating the industry. These codes were drawn up by industry, and after hearings, at which interested parties could express their approval or objections, the codes were approved by the President and put in operation. In less than two years nearly 600 codes were submitted and received the President's approval.

NRA MEMBER

The first code to be submitted was that of the cotton textile industry. 

It was presented to General Johnson on June 19, 1933. It stated the minimum wages to be paid in the industry, and the hours of work to be performed by each worker during any week. It encouraged fair competition by having the same requirements in all branches of the industry. In the Southern mills the minimum wage scale was $12 a week, while in the Northern states it was $13 per week. Children under sixteen years of age were prohibited from working in the mills. U.S.

WE DO OUR PART The Blue Eagle 

The industries which complied with the provisions of the codes displayed an emblem with a "Blue Eagle" as evidence of their co-operation with the efforts of the NRA. 

The Supreme Court Kills the Blue Eagle. Opposition to the NRA 

developed and many codes were ignored and numerous cases were brought to the courts. From the very beginning of the NRA, much doubt had been expressed as to the constitutionality of the act which established it. In 

May, 1935, the Supreme Court of the United States, in the Schechter case, unanimously declared the act establishing the NRA unconstitutional. 

As the nearly 600 codes could no longer be enforced, the NRA ceased to function. Many businessmen, however, voluntarily continued to live up to the provisions of the codes. For later legislation, see pages 461-462.
