CHAPTER XXIII Labor and the Machine Age 

The Changed Position of the Worker. With the changes that came in industry through corporate organization and consolidation, the position of labor became more precarious. To protect their own interests, the laborers organized, so that they might be more powerful in dealing with their employers. In the early days, with only small industrial establishments engaged in manufacturing, the owner of a shop located in a village was oftentimes a worker in it. He had associated with him one or two laborers who were personally known to him. With the coming of the large corporation, however, the owners of the industry no longer worked in the factory, but instead entrusted its direction to overseers or managers. The laborers now usually do not know the owners; while the owners or the stockholders often do not know the problems of the laborers or the conditions under which they work. 

The Industrial Revolution changed the status of the laborer, for the concentration of industry took the workingmen from the small shops in the villages and crowded them into large factories located in large towns and cities. Another important change was the development of expensive machinery, which became the property of the factory owner, instead of simple tools owned by the worker. The change of ownership of tools made the worker more dependent on the factory owner. The type of work also changed. The early workman was a skilled artisan, who with the aid of his own tools made complete articles; but with the change in industry he became an operator of machines driven by steam or electricity, each workman and each machine doing only a small part of the work done in making the complete article.

The Factory System. Before 1860 many of the factory workers were farmers. Their sons and daughters, too, worked in the factories during the winter months and on farms in the summer. A large number of children, ranging from six to sixteen years of age, were employed. In Samuel 448

Culver Service

A scene in a large department store in New York City, showing a dressmaking department before the days of the sewing machine

Slater's mill, the first nine employees were seven boys and two girls, all under twelve years of age. During the period from 1800 to 1860, about half of the total number of workers in factories were children. A large number were women who were employed because they accepted lower wages than men. A Committee on Manufacturing reported in 1828 that in the woolen mills about forty per cent of the employees were women, while in the cotton mills the proportion was even greater. 

Working Conditions. In these early factories the life of the worker was hard. He was required to work from twelve to fifteen hours a day, for wages ranging from $1 to $6 a week.* Often the machinery with which he worked was exposed and dangerous, while unsanitary conditions impaired his health. With low wages and long hours of work, there was little opportunity for self-improvement and advancement. The laborer enjoyed few privileges and pleasures, for his work was dull and filled with drudgery. 

The Mechanic's Free Press, in reporting the conditions of the Philadelphia factories, declared that "the principal part of the help in cotton factories consists of boys and girls . . . from six to seventeen years of age. . . confined to steady employment during the longest days of the year from *Prices in general, however, were then much lower than now. One dollar might then buy several times as much food, for example, as a dollar would buy in 1920-1930.

daylight until dark, allowing at the outside one hour and a half for meals ... and that too with a small sum that is hardly sufficient to support nature. We are confident that not more than one sixth of the boys and girls employed in such factories are capable of reading or writing their own names." The lot of the common laborer was a difficult one, for the wages paid him were low; his food was coarse and without variety; and if in the course of his existence he ran into debt without being able to pay it, he might be imprisoned. In 1830, it was estimated that 75,000 persons a year in the United States were imprisoned for debt. In Philadelphia 817 debtors were imprisoned in 1829, eighty of whom were in debt less than $1; while a report of 1830 shows that from thirty-two prisons, 2,841 persons were imprisoned for owing less than $20. The lot of labor was hard and difficult to improve.

Labor Attempts to Organize. In the face of these conditions, labor attempted to organize in order to improve its status. As early as 1648 the coopers and shoemakers of Boston organized guilds for the purpose of limiting the number in these trades. However, these guilds were not like the trade unions of today. Only a few present-day labor unions may be traced back as far as 1700. During the early days, labor unions made very little progress toward improving the conditions of labor, for at that time there was considerable prejudice against them. The English common law maintained that any combination of workingmen for the purpose of raising wages was illegal; and labor organizations were charged with conspiracy, and brought to court and prosecuted. The laborers appealed to public opinion, which, in the early days, was not in sympathy with the efforts to improve the condition of the workingman. When the laborers asked for freedom to organize and promote better working conditions, it was usually pointed out that higher wages would mean higher prices for the goods produced, and that the burden would become greater for the consumer. As manufacturing developed, and the number of laborers increased, the insistence on the right to organize also increased. By 1825 it was estimated that there were in our country 2,000,000 workers employed in industry. Laborers then sought to improve their condition by more active participation in politics. During the Jackson period, with its increased faith in democracy and in the common man, many of the workers felt that there should be greater opportunity for advancement for those who toiled in the factories.

Labor Demands Public Schools. During Jackson's administration, there was much interest in education and the organization of schools, but the children of laboring people were sent to pauper schools. Workers felt

Courtesy Butler Art Institute, Youngstown, Ohio 

Snapping the whip, in the yard of an early school: painting by Winslow Homer that many of the laws made by the ruling class had been enacted for the benefit of the rich, and that labor was not treated fairly. A Workingman's 

Party was organized in Philadelphia in 1828. It demanded opportunity for education; the abolition of imprisonment for debt; a just taxation law; and the abolition or the modification of the militia system, which had provided that all men supply their own equipment for military defense. 

This party also demanded direct election of public school officials. While this Workingman's Party was organized in Philadelphia, another one with similar views was organized in New York, in 1829, where it succeeded in electing candidates for the local government as well as a member of the state legislature. Workingmen also succeeded in electing candidates in 

New England, New Jersey, and Delaware.

Failure of Labor in Politics. Labor did not accomplish much in politics during this period, partly because the depression in the 1820's and 1830's made the lot of the laborer even more difficult. In the second place, the labor leaders could not agree on their demands, but split into factions, and wasted their energy; and in the third place, some of the reforms demanded by labor were advocated by political parties. For example, the large number of illiterate children, which in 1833 was estimated at 1,000,000, brought the problem of education to the attention of other leaders, who championed the cause of education and demanded a system of free, tax-supported schools, open to the children of all the people, which was soon established.

Following the business depression of the early 1830's, which destroyed workingmen's parties, prices rose, and the cost of living increased, while wages remained low. The manufacturer often tried to increase his profits by demanding of the laborer longer hours of work. During the period from 

1834 to 1837, when labor felt the pinch of high prices, another effort was made to organize trade unions, both local and national. 

Early Labor Strikes. Labor organizations tried to obtain their demands by means of the strike. 

In 1833, in New York City, the carpenters demanded an increase in wages from $1.37% to $1.50 a day, and secured their demands by a strike in which other workers supported them. In 18341837 there were a number of strikes for the purpose of securing a ten-hour working day. In 1835 laborers petitioned Congress for a ten-hour day for government employees. Congress refused, but other requests were made, and in 1840 President Van Buren issued an order establishing the ten-hour day for all government employees. During the years 1833 to 1837, there were no less than 173 strikes, of which 103 were for the purpose of obtaining higher wages, 26 to secure a ten-hour day, and the remainder to secure other demands. Violence sometimes accompanied strikes in those early days. In 1835 the cabinetmakers of New York, during their strike, smashed thousands of dollars' worth of chairs and tables. 

The panic of 1837, however, worked great hardship on the labor organizations, and many of them were unable to survive that period of depression. 

Culver Service 

Strikers being dispersed by mounted men in an early labor strike

The ten-hour day for workers in the service of the government gave impetus to the movement for a shorter working day. The state of New 

Hampshire soon provided for a ten-hour day. In the next few years Pennsylvania, Maine, Rhode Island, and Ohio passed laws providing for a tenhour day for factory labor. The demand for shorter hours continued, and in 1842 the carpenters in the Charleston Navy Yard received an eighthour day. It was not until after the War between the States that more considerable progress was made toward an eight-hour day. In 1867, laws

were passed in Illinois, Missouri, New York, and Wisconsin, providing for an eight-hour day for women and children. The next year Congress established an eight-hour day for public works. In 1916, in the face of a threatening railroad strike, President Wilson recommended and Congress passed the Adamson law, which provided for an eight-hour day for railroad workers. The railroad companies attacked this law as unconstitutional, but in 1917 the Supreme Court of the United States upheld the law. The demand for shorter hours and better working conditions on the part of labor came as a part of a humanitarian program, which included also the extension of suffrage, abolition of slavery, prison reform, and the extension of woman's rights.

Co-operative Stores Conducted by Labor Organizations. As early as 

1828, some of the labor organizations in Philadelphia and Cincinnati launched co-operative stores. These did not survive competition more than a few months, but in 1845 the New England Workingmen's Association attempted a similar project by organizing a protective union to save the retailer's profit for the workers. Their leaders said, "We must proceed from combined stores to combined shops, from combined shops to combined homes, to joint ownership in God's earth, the foundation that our edifice must stand upon." From a small beginning in 1845 the movement grew so that by 1852 it had 157 branches, and did an annual business of nearly $2,000,000. Other attempts at co-operative stores were made, many of which failed because of inefficient management. 

Organization of Labor on a National Scale. In 1846 the carpet weavers held a national meeting in New York City. Four years later the national convention of journeymen printers met, and out of it grew an organization known as the National Typographical Union. In 1855 the Journeymen Stone Cutters' Association organized. They were followed by the 

Potters, and later, in 1859, by the Iron Moulders' Union. Like some of the earlier local organizations which suffered during periods of panic and depression, these national labor organizations suffered during the panic of 1857. In that trying period, many industrial establishments closed, and a large number of laborers were out of employment. Instead of higher wages and shorter hours, many of the workers then asked merely for work. 

It is evident that the welfare of labor, like that of many other groups, was closely tied up with periods of prosperity and depression. 

Organized Labor Since 1865. During the great industrial expansion following the War between the North and South, factories and mills increased in size and number, and created a demand for labor. While manufacturing plants were being consolidated and the captains of industry were

struggling for more profit, the methods of competition became ruthless. 

The laissez-faire theory prevailed. Under those conditions the worker felt that it was highly important to secure a better organization to protect his own interests.

The Knights of Labor. In 1869 Uriah S. Stephens, a Philadelphia garment cutter, organized the secret society called the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor. Stephens was an earnest worker and skilled mechanic, as well as a lover of books. He was interested in promoting the interests of labor, and felt that all branches of honorable toil should be included in the new society. The organization, however, provided that "no one who either sells or makes a living, or any part of it, by the sale of intoxicating drinks, either as manufacturer, dealer, or agent, or through any member of his family, can be admitted to membership in this order; and no lawyer, banker, professional gambler, or stock broker can be admitted." As the organization was a secret society, many people became suspicious. It was founded, however, in the interest of high idealism. Its founder wanted justice, and he discouraged the use of violence. The successor to Stephens was Terence V. Powderly, who became Grand Master in 1879. He also was a great conservative and an idealistic leader. Under his guidance the order grew in numbers.

The Knights of Labor tried to impress on their members that “Labor is noble and holy. To defend it from degradation; to divest it of the evils of body, mind, and estate which ignorance and greed have imposed; to rescue the toiler from the grasp of the selfish-is a work worthy of the noblest and best of our race." In their obligations on members, they further said, "We mean no conflict with legitimate enterprise, no antagonism to necessary capital; but men in their haste and greed, blinded by self-interests, overlook the interests of others and sometimes violate the rights of those they deem helpless. We mean to uphold the dignity of labor, to affirm the nobility of all who earn their bread by the sweat of their brows. We mean to create a healthy public opinion on the subject of labor..."

This organization grew rapidly. From a membership of eleven, in 1869, it grew to a total membership of 1,000,000 working men in the United States and Canada, by 1886. A series of strikes which came in 1886, however, meant many defeats for the Knights of Labor, for some of the failures in the strikes were charged to the organization by the workers. The laboring men began to lose faith in the order, while public opinion was turned against it because of the violence which had taken place in connection with the numerous strikes.

The American Federation of Labor. Many of the labor leaders felt that the strikes had failed because the laborers had not been properly organized. They began, therefore, organization on a different basis. 

The organization of the American Federation of Labor was planned by a labor convention held in Terre Haute, Indiana, in August, 1881. At this meeting, plans were made for a second convention, which met at Pittsburgh in November, 1881, at which time the new association was organized under the name of Federation of Organized Trade and Labor Unions of the United States of America and Canada. The Federation met in 

Columbus, Ohio, in December, 1886, and united with the independent trade unions, which represented twenty-five organizations. At this meeting, the new organization took the name of the American Federation of Labor. A few years later, however, it was decided that the date to be. recognized as the beginning of the American Federation of Labor was 1881. 

For some time after its organization, the American Federation of Labor grew in numbers, due largely to the skillful organization and management of Samuel Gompers, who was elected president in 1886, and continued to hold that office, with the exception of one year, until his death in 1924. 

The American Federation of Labor is a national federation of selfgoverning trade bodies. It is composed of over 100 national and international unions. There are four departments, representing important groups of labor, namely, building trades, metal trades, railroad employees, and union label trades. There are forty-nine state branches (one for each state and Puerto Rico), with a total membership in 1935 of about 3,153,000. 

The basis of membership is the national union, though other labor bodies are admitted. The most important function of the officers of the American Federation of Labor is to strengthen existing labor organizations, to help organize new ones, to act in an advisory capacity during industrial conflicts, and to work for better labor laws at all times. 

One important difference between the Knights of Labor and the American Federation of Labor is that the Knights of Labor emphasized the central labor body, while the American Federation is loosely organized, working through the local and state organizations. Any group of wage earners may organize and establish a local union and be eligible for affiliation with the American Federation of Labor. 

Leadership of Gompers. Samuel Gompers exerted an important and capable leadership through the early years of the American Federation of Labor. He was the son of a cigar maker, and at an early age became a member of the Cigar Makers' Union. In this union he learned important principles of organization, and it was here that he got his early training

which developed in him qualities for leadership. Gompers believed in democratic rule for labor. He believed that the individual union should be the important part of the Federation. He believed in economy in money matters, and for a time he received no salary and very little money for 

Samuel Gompers Keystone expenses. In the early days he received a salary of only $1,000 a year. He insisted on free discussion of principles and the use of the referendum in reaching important decisions. He kept labor from entering into politics, and exerted a conservative influence. He was one of the earliest champions of the eight-hour day, and worked for Federal child labor laws. He advocated a Federal 

Department of Labor and secured many other advantages for labor.

One of the important services he rendered was that of serving as a national lobbyist for the American 

Federation of Labor. When the 

World War broke out, Gompers at once took a very vigorous part in supporting the government. He maintained that this was labor's war, and through his influence the American Federation of Labor co-operated in supplying labor for American activities. 

Labor Disputes. In order to obtain the demands of labor, which usually consist of shorter hours, higher wages, and better working conditions, labor unions often resort to strikes, picketing, and boycotting. In order to have the strike successful from the point of view of labor, it is necessary not only that the workers in a particular industry stop working, but that others be prohibited from taking their places. To prevent others, known as strikebreakers, from replacing them, the strikers establish pickets. The boycott is used by laborers and others in sympathy with labor for the purpose of enforcing their demands on industries or other business organizations which are considered unfair to labor. The most common method of boycotting is for trade unions to prohibit their members from patronizing such industries.

Historic Strikes. An important strike took place among the railroad workers in 1877. Soon after the panic of 1873, many railroad companies

Culver Service

Strike of railroad workers on the Baltimore and Ohio in 1877; from a contemporary magazine reduced wages ten per cent. In July, 1877, the Pennsylvania, New York

Central, and Baltimore and Ohio ordered another ten per cent reduction, and the workers ordered a strike, in which violence and disorder resulted. 

President Hayes was called upon to send troops, and at Pittsburgh a battle was fought between the rioters and the soldiers, in which twenty of the rioters were killed. Much property was destroyed. It is estimated that 

1,600 cars, 126 locomotives, and several railway shops were destroyed. 

The total damage was estimated at $5,000,000. 

In the years 1884-1886 occurred a number of important strikes-so many that the period is referred to as "the great upheaval." The Gould railroad system in the Southwest ordered a ten per cent reduction in wages for March, 1885. This brought on a strike of the railroad workers. In order to call the attention of the public to the matter, and to prevent further reduction, the American Federation of Labor, on May 1, 1886, ordered a general strike in favor of the eight-hour day. In the year 1886, 1,572 strikes and lockouts occurred, involving 610,024 workers and a loss in wages of $19,273,000.

In July, 1892, an important strike took place in the Carnegie Steel Company's plant at Homestead, Pennsylvania. A wage scale and recognition of the union were demanded by the workers, and when the company refused to grant them, the union ordered a strike. Carnegie attempted to

operate his plant with nonunion men, and in order to protect them he employed 300 armed detectives to stand guard. This resulted in a battle between the strikers and the detectives, in which ten were killed and sixty wounded. Eight thousand members of the state militia were then brought in, and the plant was operated with nonunion workers until the strike was called off in November without granting the demands of the union. 

In the year 1894, again following a panic, there was an important strike in the Pullman Palace Car Company, which had ordered a wage cut from twenty to twenty-five per cent. As a result of it, the American Railway 

Union refused to handle Pullman cars unless the Pullman Company agreed to submit the matter in dispute to arbitration. This the Pullman Company would not do, and the twenty-three railroads radiating out of Chicago into twenty-seven or more states were seriously handicapped. Disorder and violence followed, with the destruction of property. The damages, direct and indirect, amounted to more than $80,000,000. The governor of the state of Illinois refused to interfere, but President Cleveland felt that the railroad strike prevented the carrying of the United States mail, and sent troops to prevent the strikers from interfering with the operation of the railroads. A United States court issued an injunction which forbade anyone to interfere with the operation of trains carrying mail. Thus with the intervention of the Federal government through an injunction and the use of troops, the unions were forced to abandon the strike. Organized labor bitterly denounced the injunction as judicial tyranny. In 1914 the 

Clayton Antitrust Law exempted from antitrust prosecution all labor and agricultural organizations, and with some exceptions prohibited the use of the injunction in labor disputes. 

During the period from 1881 to 1900, about 24,000 strikes and lockouts occurred, which involved nearly 128,000 business establishments and 6,610,001 workers. This proved to be an expensive matter. A great cost, directly and indirectly, was placed on the American people for their inability to deal with this problem. It is estimated that the money loss resulting from labor difficulties during this period was more than $500,- 000,000. In addition to this, there was the great inconvenience and hardship of the people, as well as the bitterness and hatred brought on by acts of violence, which often resulted in loss of life. 

The Coal Strike, 1902. In 1902 the country was faced with an anthracite coal strike in northeastern Pennsylvania, where anthracite is mined in large quantities. In this section of the country companies had gained a monopoly of both the transportation and the mining of coal. The United 

Mine Workers, under the leadership of their president, John Mitchell, on

May 12 called a strike for the purpose of reducing hours from ten to nine, of obtaining a twenty per cent increase in wages, and recognition of the union. The operators of the coal mines, which were controlled by a few of the strongest capitalists in the country, refused to consider these demands of the union. Mitchell offered to submit the controversy to arbitration, and pledged that the miners would accept the decision. The operators, however, would not arbitrate. As coal became scarce, and the price went up with the approach of winter, the public became rather unsympathetic with the attitude of the operators, who were not willing to submit to arbitration.

President Theodore Roosevelt, while he felt that he had no constitutional authority, as President, to interfere, nevertheless, acting as a private citizen, called a conference of operators and miners to meet at Washington. 

Mitchell at this meeting offered to arbitrate, but the operators refused. 

Roosevelt finally secured consent to appoint a commission to investigate, and threatened that if the operators refused to arbitrate after the commission had investigated and reported, he might use troops to work the mines until a settlement had been reached. The operators agreed, and the miners went back to work. When the commission reported, it suggested that the miners be given a ten per cent increase and a shorter day, and that all future disputes were to be referred to a board of conciliation, composed of three representatives from the operators and three representatives from the miners. The union was recognized and the miners were given the right of collective bargaining. 

Interest of the Public. Throughout the 70's and 80's, it was generally accepted that strikes were to be settled by labor and capital; that it was not for the government to intervene except in cases where the government's interests were directly affected, as in interference with the carrying of the mail. Within more recent years many people have taken a different attitude, and are beginning to feel that the public also has a part which needs to be considered. Following the labor difficulties in the 80's, President 

Cleveland suggested that the government find better ways of settling labor disputes. In 1888, therefore, Congress passed a law which provided for voluntary arbitration of disputes between railroads and their employees. 

This law provided for arbitration between railroads engaged in interstate commerce and their employees. The act was not very effective, and ten years later the Erdman Act was passed, which provided that in disputes between railroads and their employees, either side might ask that the chairman of the Interstate Commerce Commission and the United States Commissioner of Labor act as mediators. This was not compulsory, and

during a period of about twenty years, only one effort was made to call it into use. The act itself was weak, but the people favored the principle embodied in it. It was thought desirable that there should be some way of securing industrial peace through mediation. In 1913 the Newlands 

Act was passed, which authorized the President, with the consent of the Senate, to appoint a board of mediation and conciliation for the purpose of settling disputes. The board did not have the right, however, to administer compulsory arbitration. 

Federal Legislation. The Federal government in 1884 established a 

Bureau of Labor; in 1903 a Department of Commerce and Labor; and finally, in 1913, a separate Department of Labor, with the Secretary of Labor becoming a member of the President's cabinet. During President 

Wilson's administration, the Clayton Antitrust Act of 1914 specifically exempted labor unions from the antitrust laws; and in 1916 Congress by law established an eight-hour day for railroad employees. In 1915 the 

Seaman's Act, sponsored by Senator La Follette, set up machinery to secure better living conditions for American seamen. In 1916 a child labor bill was passed which prohibited products manufactured in factories where children were employed, from being used in interstate commerce; but this act was presently declared unconstitutional. In 1919 an attempt was made to impose a tax of ten per cent on the net profit of factories that employed children under ten years of age, and whose products entered interstate commerce; but this also was declared unconstitutional. As a part of the New Deal, in 1933, child labor was prohibited, for two years, under the National Industrial Recovery Act passed by Congress during 

Franklin D. Roosevelt's administration. 

Labor since the World War. The conditions created by the outbreak of the World War were highly favorable to the growth of organized labor. 

Immigration was stopped; many men were withdrawn from the ranks of labor to enter the army; and demands for labor increased very rapidly, with the result that wages rose. The membership in trade unions was greatly increased. In 1916 it is estimated that the membership was 

2,808,000. By 1917, it had increased to 3,104,600. It increased a half million the next year, and continued to increase until it reached a new height of more than 5,100,000 in 1920. During this period of boom in business brought on by the war, trade unionism was extended to the unskilled as well as to the skilled laborers. Following the World War, there was a reaction, and membership in trade unions declined. 

The Transportation Act of 1920 created a Railway Labor Board made up of nine members, three to represent labor, three capital, and three the

public. This board was established for the purpose of settling labor questions which could not be settled by conferences between interested parties or by labor boards of adjustment. In 1926 it was replaced by the Federal 

Board of Mediation, composed of five members; and that board, in 1934, was replaced by the National Mediation Board, of three members. 

Labor and the Depression. Within recent years the hours of labor have been decreased. The normal working week in American industry has during the past fifty years decreased by twenty hours. From 1890 to 1926, the hours of labor in manufacturing industries had decreased from sixty to fifty hours a week. The first decades of the twentieth century, with the exception of a few minor business depressions, enjoyed continued prosperity, in which labor shared by a rise in wages and by the shortening of hours. During that period there was a decline in labor disputes. In the years from 1916 to 1921, there were, on an average, 3,503 labor disputes a year, involving an average of 1,798,805 workers a year. In the period from 

1922 to 1925, there were only 1,304 labor disputes a year, involving 853,051 persons annually, while the period from 1926 to 1930 was marked by only 791 labor disputes per year, involving 224,949 workers. It is believed that the decline was due partly to the general prosperity of the period as well as to efforts of the employers to handle industrial relations more intelligently. 

During the depression following the stock market crash in 1929, unemployment increased rapidly. Mr. William Green, president of the American 

Federation of Labor, estimated that by April, 1930, there were 2,954,000 persons out of work; and in 1933 the number was about 13,000,000. 

Labor and the New Deal. When Franklin D. Roosevelt took office on March 4, 1933, one great problem for the administration was to find employment for millions of people out of work. The National Industrial 

Recovery Act (pp. 442-443), in force nearly two years, worked toward this end. Section 7-A of the act stated "That employees shall have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing." The Wagner-Connery bill, passed July 5, 1935, and known as the National Labor Relations Act, replaces Section 7-A of the NIRA 

invalidated by the Supreme Court. It also created the National Labor 

Relations Board, a body of three members, with power to guarantee the right of collective bargaining, and to prevent employers from engaging in unfair labor practices. The Board's powers were upheld in a decision of the U. S. Supreme Court early in 1938. During the fiscal year ending 

June 30, 1938, the board received 10,425 cases, involving 2,139,566 workers. During that year, also, the board received severe criticism from both labor and capital.

The Seventy-fifth Congress passed the Fair Labor Standards Act of 

1938. Its purpose is to protect workers' health, efficiency, and general welfare. The act sets a minimum wage rate and a maximum number of hours of labor per week.

The C. I. O., and Sit-Down Strikes. Late in 1935 the Committee on 

Industrial Organization, headed by John L. Lewis, began a movement to set up labor unions for entire industries instead of for different crafts. 

Ten of the unions in the American Federation of Labor were suspended because they supported the C. I. O. The resulting contest split organized labor into two groups: one, the A. F. of L. headed by William Green, and the other, the C. I. O. unions under the leadership of Lewis. In January, 1937, the United Automobile Workers demanded (1) recognition of their

C. I. O. industrial union as the sole collective-bargaining agency of all automobile workers, (2) a new minimum rate of pay, (3) a 34-hour week, and other changes. In some automobile factories there were "sit-down" strikes with C. I. O. workers quitting their work but holding possession of the plants. After more or less lengthy delays and conferences, compromises were usually reached and work resumed. However, "sit-down" strikes also occurred in various other industries, and even in some stores. 

In November, 1938, the Committee on Industrial Organization became the Congress of Industrial Organizations, which then adopted a constitution and set up a national organization. Its roster, early in 1939, included 35 affiliated unions and a membership of about 4,000,000.

CHAPTER XXIV 

Industry and the Tariff

Importance of the Tariff. The tariff has been an important problem throughout our entire history. It had its beginning in colonial days. 

According to the mercantile theory-the prevailing economic view in the seventeenth century, not only in England but also in other European countries-colonies were established for the benefit of the mother country and were expected to furnish those products which the mother country was unable to secure from other sources. The English government and (after 1707) the British government applied this theory to the American colonies before the American Revolution. Their statesmen assumed that they had the right to impose duties on commodities sent to or from the colonies. They also made numerous other attempts to regulate colonial trade and industry. Bounties were sometimes provided in order to stimulate industry along certain lines. This was a protective idea, and like a protective tariff, fostered the growth of certain industries. Tariffs were also levied in order to raise revenue. The two important purposes of the tariff, namely, for protection and for revenue, thus appeared early in 

American history.

As early as 1704 Pennsylvania placed a tax on imported hops for the purpose of protecting the hop-growing industry. Tariffs were laid by other colonies, both for protection and for revenue. Very often the colonies placed duties on their exports in order to raise revenue, while some of them collected tariffs on the products imported from neighboring colonies. 

After the American Revolution, in the period from 1780 to 1788, the different states passed a number of tariff acts which resulted in tariff wars. 

These led the Constitutional Convention to insert in the Constitution a clause which forbids any state, without the consent of Congress, to levy any duties on imports or exports, and another clause which forbids Congress to levy duties on exports, and another which gives Congress the power to levy "taxes, duties, imposts, and excises, to pay the debts and 465

STORIC 

STOR MSKIBBIN&C Foreign trade: clipper ships at an East Side water front in New York City; from an old print provide for the common defense and general welfare of the United States; but all duties, imposts, and excises shall be uniform throughout the United States."

In accordance with this authority the first Congress of the United States, under the leadership of Alexander Hamilton, the Secretary of the Treasury, passed the first tariff act in 1789. This act was primarily for the purpose of raising revenue, but its duties were laid not uniformly on all goods imported, but mainly on such as competed with domestic industry. 

The protective principle, therefore, was embodied in this first measure. 

Two years later Alexander Hamilton made his famous report on manufactures, in which he argued for protection. However, most of the people were engaged in agriculture or in shipping and were therefore not primarily interested in protecting manufactures. As soon as manufacturing increased, however, the protective idea received more encouragement. 

The Tariff of 1816. As a result of the War of 1812, as well as of the embargo preceding it, manufacturing developed in America to a greater extent than ever before. The industrial revolution which had begun in 

England about the middle of the eighteenth century and had made headway in Europe was now extended to America. Many manufacturing plants were established. After the war, European countries sent manufactured products to America and undersold our American manufacturers.

It was then that the question of protection again appeared. The War of 

1812 had stimulated American patriotism and nationalism. There was a demand for self-sufficiency, and this idea made a stronger appeal to the leaders in America. They felt that our country would be stronger if it were economically independent. Thus a protective measure, the Tariff of 1816, supported by some of the New England manufacturing interests as well as the leaders from the South and the West, was enacted. 

Henry Clay and the Tariff of 1824. In the period under the embargo and during the War of 1812 the American farmers, unable to sell their products abroad, suffered from a decline in prices, while the shipping interests also were seriously impaired. Henry Clay, of Kentucky, representing an agricultural section, therefore became interested in the idea of the home market. He developed this idea in a speech in 1824 in which he pointed out that the European market had been destroyed and could not be relied upon. He maintained that a new market must be found. This he contended could be done if manufacturing were built up. The industrial class, thus created, would produce a market at home for American agricultural products. But in order to bring the products from the Western farm to the manufacturing centers of the East, transportation facilities needed to be developed. Hence Henry Clay maintained that a system of roads, canals, and railroads should be built in order to transport the farmers' products to the industrial centers. To secure revenue for this purpose a higher tariff should be enacted. In addition, Clay maintained that the public land in the West should be sold, thus creating more revenue and also making available additional land for the farmers. Clay's "American System" therefore demanded a protective tariff, internal improvements, and the sale of public lands. 

Because of these arguments, there was enacted the Tariff of 1824, which increased the list of protected products. The West as well as the 

Middle section supported this tariff. New England, however, was divided, because the shipping interests were still strong. The South opposed it because it was felt that the agricultural interests of the South would not profit by the protection. The leading product of the South was cotton, the chief market for which was in Europe. The home market did not appeal to the 

Southern farmer as it did to the Western farmer. When the Southern leaders had supported the Tariff of 1816 they felt that manufacturing might develop in the South. By 1824, however, it was evident that manufacturing would develop more rapidly in the Northern and Middle sections. 

The Tariff of Abominations (1828). A new tariff act, passed in 1828, established duties that had been proposed for political purposes. Some

of the Western congressmen, who were opposed to John Quincy Adams, voted a high tariff on raw products used in the New England factories in the hope that Adams and his supporters might reject it. The tariff bill, however, was passed, although there were many objectionable features in it; and it became known as the "Tariff of Abominations." It provided for the highest rates which had been established up to that time. 

South Carolina and the Tariff. In the period of the 1820's Alabama, Mississippi, and other cotton-growing states were being settled and were MO

OL Shipping cotton at Mobile, Alabama; from a recent photograph 

Ewing Galloway producing great quantities of cotton, which caused the price to go down. 

Cotton sold for thirty cents a pound in 1816, but for only nine cents in 1827. The economic prosperity of South Carolina was closely tied up with the price of this staple. The people of South Carolina felt that the economic depression was due to the tariff, which they thought beneficial to the Middle and Northern sections, while the South was obliged to pay higher prices for commodities bought without receiving the advantage of higher prices for what it sold. Under those conditions serious opposition developed. The South Carolina leaders declared the tariff unconstitutional; and in 1828 John C. Calhoun prepared "The South Carolina Exposition," in which he pointed out the effects of the tariff on his state, and proposed nullification.

Because of the serious protest against the Tariff of Abominations, a new tariff act was passed in 1832 which removed some of the most objectionable features. However, it still maintained the protective idea, and was unsatisfactory to South Carolina. The legislature of that state, in November, 1832, therefore passed the Nullification Ordinance, which declared that the tariff was null and void and was not binding on the people of South Carolina (see p. 268). Under those conditions the tariff was revised under the leadership of Henry Clay, resulting in the Compromise Tariff of 1833. This new tariff act placed many articles on the free list and provided for a gradual reduction of all other duties until they should reach the general level of twenty per cent by 1842. 

However, during the panic of 1837 revenues declined, and in order to secure more revenue the tariff was revised in 1842, under the direction of the Whig party, so that duties were restored to the higher level of the tariff of 1832.

The Walker Tariff of 1846. In 1845 the Democratic party came into power under the presidency of James K. Polk. His Secretary of the Treasury, Robert J. Walker, was interested in tariff revision. A new bill was drawn up along the idea of a tariff for revenue. It provided for definite classified schedules, such as Schedule A, Schedule B, and so on. Articles thus classified were taxed, most of them at much lower rates than before. 

This tariff remained in force until 1857, when still further reductions were made. Under the Walker Tariff the American people enjoyed a prolonged period of prosperity. The low rates did not seriously injure the manufacturing interests of the country, and also yielded considerable revenue. 

The receipts from the tariff advanced from $26,000,000 under the Tariff of 1842 to $46,000,000 under the Walker Tariff. In the main, the period from 1833 until 1861, when the tariff duties were raised again, was a period of relatively low tariff duties. The period from 1816 to 1833 had been one during which protection was emphasized. 

It is interesting to notice that at this time there was a struggle between the industrial section and the agrarian or agricultural section. 

The agricultural section, especially the South, objected to the high tariff rates which protected the industrial section and made for higher prices of the articles which the agricultural section bought. The New England section, throughout this period, was divided into the shipping and the manufacturing interests; but as manufacturing developed and shipping declined, this section supported protection. In the days of Henry Clay, the West was for protection, but later it found that the greater part of its market was not in the industrial section but in the agricultural section of

the South. Therefore, the West combined with the South in working for lower tariff rates.

Tariff and the War between the North and the South. When the war broke out between the North and the South, there was a definite return to high tariff. This was due in the first place to the fact that the industrial section dominated the nation after the Southern states withdrew. The 

Republican party in 1860 in its platform advocated a high protective tariff, and before the inauguration of Lincoln the Morrill Tariff Act of 1861 was passed. This was an indication to many in the South that the control of the Federal government was in the hands of the industrial section, and is considered by some historians an important factor in promoting secession of the South. A second reason for the high tariff act was the raising of revenue for carrying on the war. Other tariff acts were passed, which, by 1864, had brought the tariff to the high average level of fortyseven per cent.

After the war the high tariff remained a part of our American financial system. The industrial section had gained the upper hand during the war; and as industry developed, this section became powerful enough to maintain the high rates. However, by 1872, because of the influence of the liberal Republican movement, and because of an annual surplus of $100,000,000, a reduction of ten per cent was secured. Shortly afterwards the panic of 1873 came, and with it a decline in the revenue, which reduced the surplus to a deficit. Again demands arose for a higher tariff; and in 

1875 the tariff was restored to its previous level, where it remained until 1883. 

High Tariff Continued. In 1882 President Arthur, again confronted with a surplus of $100,000,000 a year, recommended a reduction of the tariff. He appointed a commission to investigate the matter. This commission recommended a downward revision of from twenty to twenty-five per cent, but Congress, composed mainly of protectionists, reduced it by only five per cent. In 1885 began the term of President Cleveland, a 

Democrat. Cleveland believed in the reduction of the tariff and in 1887 devoted his entire message to Congress to that question, and to arguments for the revision downward. He felt that the tariff should be reduced because it was an unnecessary source of taxation, and because it increased the cost of living without benefiting the wage earner. He pointed out that only fifteen per cent of the wage earners were engaged in protected industries. 

He feared that, with a surplus of $100,000,000 a year in the treasury, Congress would be tempted to spend money unwisely. The reduction of tariff was clearly necessary because of the great surplus. In this connection

he made the famous statement, "This is a condition which confronts us, not a theory."

Following the suggestion of the President, the House of Representatives proposed the Mills Bill, which provided for a reduction. However, the bill was defeated in the Republican Senate. The tariff question therefore became a leading issue in the campaign of 1888. The Republican party nominated Benjamin Harrison, while the Democrats renominated Cleveland. Harrison was elected (map, p. 716). With the Republican party in power, the tariff was again taken up in Congress and revised according to Republican principles. The McKinley Bill of 1890 was the result. William 

McKinley, of Ohio, felt that American prosperity depended on a high protective tariff. He said, "We lead all nations in agriculture, we lead all nations in mining, and we lead all nations in manufacturing. These are the trophies we bring after twenty-nine years of a protective tariff. Can any other system furnish evidences of prosperity?" McKinley maintained that a high protective tariff assured steady employment and higher wages to the laboring men. However, Cleveland had pointed out in his message of 

1887 that only fifteen per cent of the wage earners were engaged in protected industries. By the new tariff bill, rates were raised to an average of about forty-nine per cent. The protective idea was extended. However, a way was found for reducing the surplus. The duty on sugar was removed, and for the protection of the American producer a bounty of two cents a pound was provided for the domestic product. 

The new high tariff brought higher prices. There was much objection to the rising cost of living. People blamed the Republican party for these conditions; and in the fall election of 1890 many of the Republicans were defeated, and the Democrats gained control of the lower house, where several bills for the reduction of the tariff were passed; however, in the Senate, which had a majority composed of a protectionist group, the measures failed to carry. These bills were sometimes referred to as "popgun bills." 

The Wilson-Gorman Tariff (1894). In 1892 Grover Cleveland was elected President for the second time. The Congressional election of two years previous had returned Democratic members to the lower house of Congress. This trend continued, and by the election of 1892 the Democrats gained control of the Senate also. With both the legislative and the executive branches of the Federal government Democratic, it would be possible for the party to undertake such tariff legislation as it wished. Before the President was inaugurated, however, a severe panic set in. By 

May, 1893, more than 15,000 business establishments had failed. Many banks closed, and many railroad companies went into bankruptcy. Con-

gress passed a new tariff bill, the Wilson-Gorman Act, which did not become a law until August, 1894, although the panic began in the spring of 1893. 

It was argued, however, by many Republicans that the panic was brought on because of lack of confidence in the pending tariff legislation. 

The Wilson-Gorman Tariff was a disappointment to the friends of a lower tariff. The bill contained many of the protective features, though it transferred some articles to the free list. The bill was introduced by 

William L. Wilson in the House of Representatives. In the Senate, under the leadership of Senator Gorman, some 654 amendments were made to the bill. The bill was referred to a conference committee, where other adjustments were made. Wool and lumber were placed on the free list, but the general average rate of the bill was about forty-one per cent. The President was disappointed, as he did not feel that it was a genuine tariff reform measure; but he permitted the bill to become a law without his signature.

Cartoon of 1896, "Farmer McKinley Takes off his Coat"; that is, drops the tariff question for attention to other problems The Dingley Tariff. In the election of 1896 the Democrats nominated William Jennings 

Bryan, and the Republicans 

William McKinley. The main issue of the election was the currency question - the free coinage of silver at the ratio of 

16 to 1. The tariff was a minor issue. But as soon as the 

Republicans came to power they decided that the tariff should be revised, since many felt that the panic of 1893 had been the result of a Democratic tariff. The result was the 

Dingley Tariff of July, 1897.

It was a thoroughgoing protective measure and reached the highest level of protection up to that time. It provided for duties at a general average of approximately fifty-seven per cent. 

The years following were marked by remarkable prosperity. One reason for this was the fact that gold was discovered in and near Alaska and in Africa. Also the cyanide process of extracting gold from the ore made more gold available, and the supply of money was increased. The tariff then

disappeared as the leading public issue for about ten years, because in 1898 war with Spain brought our attention to foreign problems, and immediately after the war, the questions of expansion and of imperialism divided the parties. Another question, too, that demanded attention was that of regulating trusts. In this connection, however, the tariff was again brought into notice because it was referred to as the "mother of trusts." 

The Payne-Aldrich Tariff of 1909. The Dingley Tariff had made for higher prices, and attention was called to the rising cost of living. This had brought dissatisfaction to the grain-growing section of the Middle West as early as 1900. Many of the agriculturists called attention to the tariff and blamed the Eastern manufacturers for making large profits. In the Republican platform of 1908 the party promised a revision of the tariff. 

It said, "The Republican Party declares unequivocally for a revision of the tariff." This was interpreted by many to mean a revision of the tariff downward. William H. Taft, the Republican candidate for President, in his speech of acceptance at Cincinnati, September 2, 1908, referred to it as "a revision which shall reduce excessive rates." And in a campaign speech in Milwaukee, September 24, he referred to "the necessity of maintaining the tariff at the former rate of peace; the tariff . . . should be reduced."

When the question came up in Congress, after the Republicans had won the election, there was considerable opposition to a downward revision of the tariff. Some of the standpat Republican leaders pointed to the platform and said that it provided for revision but not necessarily revision downward. However, a number of progressive Republicans from states in the Middle West, often referred to as insurgents, began a fight for reduction of the tariff. Thus a struggle came within the Republican party for revision of the tariff. The "standpatters" were led by Senator Nelson 

Aldrich, Senator Lodge, and others; while on the progressive side were 

Senator Robert La Follette, of Wisconsin; Senator Dolliver and Senator 

Cummins of Iowa; Senator Bristow, of Kansas; and Senator Albert

Beveridge, of Indiana. The insurgent wing of the Republican party included from ten to fourteen senators from Wisconsin, Indiana, Minnesota, Kansas, Nebraska, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Iowa.

A tariff bill was introduced in the House by Representative Payne. It provided for downward revision. In the Senate, serious attacks were made upon it. Eight hundred forty-seven amendments were made, many of which provided for increased rates. The resulting Payne-Aldrich Act was finally signed by the President on August 5, 1909. It was estimated that this act, instead of revising the tariff downward, provided for a slight

increase. President Taft, on a speaking tour of the Middle West, attempted to defend the tariff in the section from which the insurgent senators came, and which advocated reduction. Speaking at Winona, Minnesota, Taft referred to the Payne-Aldrich Tariff as "the best the country had ever had." The division of the Republicans on the tariff question was largely responsible for the organization of the Progressive party, which took an active part in the election of 1912. Because of the split in the Republican party, the Democratic party was able to elect the President. 

The Underwood Tariff Act of 1913. As soon as the Democrats came to power, President Wilson called a special session of Congress (April 7, 1913). 

One of the first problems under consideration was a revision of the tariff. 

A tariff bill introduced by Underwood of Alabama was, after some amendments, duly passed. It provided for substantial reductions, especially reductions on raw materials and foodstuffs. It abolished tariff rates on more than a hundred items. It was a bill devised primarily for revenue. 

Raw wool, iron ore, pig iron, steel rails, agricultural implements, and other commodities were placed on the free list. The average level was reduced to about twenty-seven per cent. In the meantime, the Sixteenth Amendment to the Constitution had been adopted, making an income tax legal. 

Congress therefore passed a law placing a tax on incomes in excess of $3,000. Because of the World War this tariff act can not be judged on its merits. Trade relations with European countries were disturbed. The 

United States exports to Europe increased greatly because of the war demands. On account of the declining revenue, considerable pressure was put on Congress to raise the tariff. Congress, however, refused to change it.

Tariff Acts of 1921 and 1922. With the return of the Republicans to power in 1921, President Harding called a special session of Congress to take up the question of the tariff. The country was in the midst of an agricultural depression, and efforts were made to help the farmer. The emergency tariff act of May 21, 1921, was the result. This tariff imposed high duties on wheat, corn, meat, wool, sugar, and other farm products. 

In September of the following year (1922) the Fordney-McCumber Act was passed which provided protection for the manufacturing interests as well as the agricultural interests. It was the highest protective measure which had yet been passed by Congress. The act, however, provided for a Tariff Commission, on whose advice the President might raise or lower duties as much as fifty per cent in order to equalize the cost of production with competing countries. President Harding made use of this flexible provision, usually for the purpose of raising rates. From 1922 to June,

1928, thirty-seven changes in the tariff rates were made by Presidents Harding and Coolidge. Of these thirty-seven changes, thirty-two provided for higher duties. 

The Hawley-Smoot Tariff, June, 1930. By 1928 there was again dissatisfaction with the existing tariff. President Hoover called a special session of the Seventy-first Congress to examine the protective system. 

During his campaign speeches, President Hoover had promised a limited. revision with special attention to the needs of agriculture. While the emergency tariff of 1921 was designed to aid the farmers, it was evident that near the close of the decade they were worse off than they were at the beginning. In other words, seven or eight years of a higher tariff, a tariff designed to protect the farmer, found him in a worse plight than ever. 

When the tariff question was taken up, there were a good many opponents of high protection, especially those who were interested in creating a healthy foreign trade. Importers, investment bankers, and automobile manufacturers objected to a high tariff. They believed that the tariff wall should be lowered so as to make exchange with European countries easier. 

They hoped that President Hoover, because of his interest in foreign trade, would be sympathetic toward such a revision of the tariff. 

The new tariff bill became a law in June, 1930. It was the highest protective tariff that the country had ever known; but it embodied a flexible provision which gave the President the right to change the rate fifty per cent. The opponents of high tariff protested and pointed out that foreign nations might raise their tariff measures against the United States. This was evident by 1931, for fully twenty-five countries had made extensive tariff revisions and increased their duties, or else threatened to do so. They used as their argument the necessity of fighting the United States with her own weapon. It is difficult to say exactly how much the tariff was advanced over the previous tariff; but of the 1,022 changes, 878 were revisions upward. 

This as a whole provided for an average rate of about forty-one per cent ad valorem, an increase of 6.8 per cent over the previous one. 

President Hoover had desired to limit the tariff to revisions of agricultural schedules; but a general revision, providing higher protection, was made. Shortly before the bill was presented to President Hoover for his signature, he received a petition signed by about 1,500 economists from 179 colleges and universities of the country, urging him to veto the bill. 

However, he ignored their advice and signed it. One result of the law was the reprisal of foreign governments. By the spring of 1932 more than twenty had raised their tariffs and explained that it was for the purpose of retaliating against America. Our foreign trade, which had steadily increased

through the years 1922-1929, soon began to decline. The law provides for a Tariff Commission of six members, appointed for a term of six years, at salaries of $11,000 each. It is composed of men who are students of the problem and who are experts on this particular subject. 

Reciprocal Tariff of 1934. The Roosevelt administration did not suggest a general reduction in the tariff even though the high protective tariff stood in the way of a revival of foreign trade. In June, 1934, the Reciprocal 

Tariff Act was approved. It authorized the President, without consulting the Senate, to raise or lower tariff rates by not more than 50 per cent, in negotiating trade agreements with foreign countries. By 1939, agreements had accordingly been made with eighteen foreign countries, lowering some of the rates, and our trade with those countries had increased.

CHAPTER XXV Our Financial System 

Money and Our Industrial System. Money, which is so important in our industrial life today, has played an important part throughout our entire history. Our whole financial system is based on a money economy. 

It is therefore necessary that we understand how money has influenced the action of people and how it has affected our history. We must understand at the very beginning that no one except a miser is interested in money as such; but that people are interested in the things which money will buy. The laborer who works for his wages is not so much concerned about the money wages he receives as about the things which that money will buy. He thinks of his wages in terms of food, clothing, shelter, and other articles he desires. Likewise, the farmer, the business man, and the professional man are interested in the things that his money will buy rather than in the money itself. 

Some of the Purposes of Money. (1) Money serves as a medium of exchange. People must have food, clothing, shelter, and other articles, but do not receive them directly; they buy them with money which they receive in exchange for their goods and for their services. The farmer does not exchange his products directly, but sells them for money which, in turn, he uses to purchase other articles. (2) Money also serves as a standard for deferred payments. A debt may be contracted but payment delayed for several years. Money is usually the standard in such a case. (3) Money also serves as a common denominator; that is, in exchanging apples for coffee and sugar, for example, a farmer does not give a bushel of wheat in direct exchange for sugar and coffee, but estimates that the wheat is worth so much money and the coffee and sugar are worth a certain amount of money. So in exchanges of labor, professional services, and all forms of commodities, their values are determined in money, which serves as the common denominator of values. 478

Money in Colonial Times. The early colonists who came to America were poor in money. They did not bring money with them. In fact, it would have been of little value to them, as here in the wilderness of America there was little need of money. The Indians would not have recognized the value of money in trading with the colonists. The early settlers resorted to barter, and traded articles, such as cloth, beads, and other trinkets, with the Indians, in exchange for corn and other food products. Also among themselves, the early colonists traded products directly, and developed a system of barter. Under this system, substitutes for money were used. 

Corn, cattle, and furs served as money in New England, while in the South tobacco and rice were employed. In the absence of money, college students paid their bills with products of the farm. The records show that at 

Harvard College, in the early years, students paid tuition with livestock, feed, and other produce. During 1933 and 1934, in the time of depression, with money scarce in many communities, many people again resorted to barter. Some college students, like the students at Harvard in the seventeenth century, paid tuition and other bills with commodities instead of money.

Inconvenience of Barter. One can easily understand the inconvenience of barter. Products which are exchanged are not always of the same value. 

If the farmer exchanges a cow for shoes, the shoemaker might not wish to have a whole cow, and the farmer would want only one pair of shoes, while the cow might be worth ten or twelve pairs of shoes. Inconvenience would be experienced in determining the values and making the right exchange. 

Likewise, it would be difficult to handle the produce. In colonial days it was found to be inconvenient to carry the tobacco used in exchange, so it was stored, and warehouse receipts circulated instead. This arrangement was very similar to our present-day silver certificates. Silver money is stored in the United States Treasury, and against it there are issued silver certificates (paper money), which circulate.

Paper Money. The colonists early realized the inconvenience of barter, and sought a satisfactory medium of exchange. There were then no gold or silver mines in our country, and little metallic money came into the colonies from the outside. Though some came in through trade, there was usually an unfavorable balance of trade which took money out of the colonies. The colonists therefore early resorted to paper money as a medium of exchange. The first paper money in America was issued by 

Massachusetts, in 1690, to pay the soldiers who had taken part in a war against the French at Quebec. This paper soon depreciated, but was brought up to par by being made receivable for taxes, and the government

of Massachusetts promised to redeem it in coin within twelve months. 

Because this first issue of paper money was successful, Massachusetts in 1709 put out a second issue of 40,000 pounds (about $200,000). The 22
