The Depreciation of the Paper Money. With the issuance of so much paper money, its value depreciated. By January, 1779, one silver dollar bought as much as eight paper dollars; in November of the same year, one silver dollar bought as much as thirty-eight paper dollars; and by January, 1781, one silver dollar bought the equivalent of a hundred paper dollars. Finally the value was reduced until the silver dollar bought as much as a thousand paper dollars. With this depreciation of money, prices rose to unprecedented heights. In 1781, a pair of shoes cost 

A Continental paper note

$100 in paper money; a pound of seed, $90; and a barrel of flour, $1,575. 

In time paper money became almost worthless. Indeed, in some communities, barber shops were papered with bills; and soon the expression "not worth a continental" signified "it is worthless."

The Establishment of Our National Coinage System. With the found ing of the new government under the Constitution, the problem of establishing a sound monetary system came before the government. Because of the unsatisfactory money provided by the Continental Congress and the colonies during the colonial period, the new Constitution forbade the issuance of bills of credit by the states. The task of providing for a system of money was placed on the national government, and Thomas Jefferson proposed that money be coined according to the decimal system. His suggestion was accepted, and in 1792 a system of national coinage was adopted, providing for the coinage of both silver and gold at the ratio of 15 to 1; that is, the weight of the silver dollar was to be fifteen times that of the gold dollar. The gold dollar was to contain 24.75 grains of pure gold, and the silver dollar fifteen times as many grains of pure silver, or 

371.25 grains. Both silver coinage and gold coinage were to be free and unlimited. This means that any person would be permitted to bring silver or gold in unlimited amounts to the mint and have it coined into money, free of charge-except a possible very small charge, called seigniorage, for United States mint in Philadelphia, in the nineteenth century

the expense of coinage. By this coinage act of 1792, both gold and silver were made standards for our money. We were said, therefore, to have a bimetallic standard. The law provided for the establishment of a mint at 

Philadelphia, where money should be coined. In 1792, however, the market value of silver and gold were such that one ounce of gold was worth more than fifteen ounces of silver. Silver was slightly overvalued at the mint, and therefore not much gold was brought to be coined. Between 1804 and 

1834, only about $9,000,000 in the form of eagles ($10 gold coins), and a small number of half eagles ($5 gold coins) were coined. The country soon was practically on a silver standard, because it was the only metal coined. Silver dollars, which were coined also in small numbers, were sent out of the country in payment for imports, while many Spanish silver dollars came in in payment for exports; and in 1806, President Jefferson ordered the discontinuance of coining silver dollars. Our currency then consisted chiefly of small coins, foreign money, and banknotes. 

Paper Money after 1789. The banknotes which have constituted much of our paper money since 1789 were for many years issued mainly by banks chartered by the states; but since 1863 only by banks chartered by the Federal government. This study of our financial system will continue next with the rest of the story of our coinage, and then finally will take up the whole account of our paper money. 

The Coinage Acts of 1834 and 1837. Since the original coinage ratio was unsatisfactory, Congress studied the question, and after considerable deliberation a new coinage act was passed, on June 28, 1834, and was slightly amended in 1837. By this law, the weight of gold in the dollar was reduced from 24.75 grains to 23.22 grains. It then weighed only one sixteenth as much as the silver in the silver dollar. The ratio was therefore said to be 16 to 1. Under this new ratio, gold was slightly overvalued at the mint, and therefore was brought to the mint again for coinage, and came into circulation, while silver disappeared from circulation. Shortly after silver thus passed out of circulation, gold was discovered in California (1848), and large supplies were brought to the mint. During the War between the North and the South, the government issued paper money called 'greenbacks" (to be explained later), and also suspended the payment of specie, that is, coin, so that we were on a paper basis until 1879, when specie payment was resumed. "( The "Crime of 1873." In 1873 silver was demonetized, for Congress in that year passed a coinage act by which it dropped the silver dollar from the list of coins to be made in free coinage. Because silver had been undervalued, no silver dollars were in circulation, and no serious objection was

raised against the passage of the act. There was little interest in the question of demonetization of silver, in Congress or outside. No important debates on the question took place. It was almost unknown that a change had been made.

Shortly before and immediately after 1873 the quantity of silver in the country was increased by newly discovered Western silver mines. In the one year 1872 more than 22,000,000 ounces were mined. This was more than was produced in the total ten-year period before that date. Production of silver continued to increase; and as the price went down, the producers brought their metal to the mint to have it coined, and discovered that there was no authorization for having it coined. At once a demand arose for free and unlimited coinage of silver, and the advocates of silver referred to the act demonetizing silver as "the crime of 1873." 

Silver Demonetized in Europe. Several European countries, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway, demonetized silver at about that time, melted their coin, and sold silver on the market. This, together with the discovery of new silver mines in the United States, which produced large quantities of silver, reduced the price. Following the panic of 1873, the 

United States entered upon a five-year period of hard times, during which many people were unemployed, and prices were falling. A demand for the restoration of the silver dollar arose. There were three groups favoring it -the silver-mine owners in the Far West, many farmers of the West and South, and many of the wage-earning laborers in the East. They demanded the remonetization and free coinage of silver in the hope that it would bring prices to higher levels. The demand for recoinage, then, took on an inflation aspect; that is, people favored the restoration of silver as money because it would put more money into circulation, so that prices would rise. 

The Bland-Allison Act. Richard P. Bland, of Missouri, known as "Silver Dick," introduced a bill providing for free and unlimited coinage of silver. It passed the House of Representatives, but in the upper house, under the leadership of Senator Allison, the bill was changed to limit the amount of silver coined. The result was a compromise bill known as the 

Bland-Allison Act, which became a law in 1878. According to this law, the 

Secretary of the Treasury was authorized to purchase from $2,000,000 to $4,000,000 worth of silver bullion at the market price each month and have it coined into dollars. It was also provided that silver certificates should be issued to circulate on the deposit of the silver dollars in the United States Treasury. President Hayes vetoed the Bland-Allison Act, but it was passed over his veto. The Secretary of the Treasury purchased nearly

the minimum amount of silver specified, namely, $2,000,000 per month, a total of $24,000,000 a year. The silver thus purchased was converted into about 31,000,000 silver dollars per year. The act was in operation until 

1890. During this period of about twelve years 378,166,000 silver dollars were coined. The silver certificates issued were used as paper money, and 

Grover Cleveland were redeemed in gold coin when demanded, so that all our money was kept on the single gold standard. 

The Silver Purchase Act. The 

Bland-Allison Act was followed by the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, passed July 14, 1890. This authorized the Secretary of the Treasury to buy 4,500,000 ounces of silver bullion each month. This silver bullion was to be paid for by treasury notes, which became legal tender. 

These treasury notes were to be redeemed either in silver or in gold coin, at the discretion of the Secretary of the Treasury. 

Repeal of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act. In 1893 Grover Cleveland came to the presidency for a second time. The panic of 1893 brought low prices and hard times. Our gold supply in the treasury was low, and many people feared that the government would be forced to abandon the gold standard. The purchase of large quantities of silver put a strain on the treasury, in which the supply of gold was being rapidly reduced. It became evident that if this continued, the government would be unable to maintain gold payment, since the silver was purchased with treasury notes which were redeemable in gold or silver. Congress therefore at the recommendation of President Cleveland repealed the Sherman Silver Purchase

Act. During the three years the act was in operation, the currency was increased by $156,000,000. With the panic of 1893 there again came low prices, unemployment, and business failures. Again there were demands for more currency, especially in the West, where silver was being mined and where farmers were in debt. 

In fact a national People's party had been formed in 1892 partly to demand the free and unlimited coinage of silver. This party was made up largely of farmers, and a full account of their movement will be given in the next chapter (pp. 508-511).

The Campaign of 1896. As the election of 1896 approached, the Republican party nominated William McKinley of Ohio for President, and stood for gold as a single standard. Its platform read: "We are unalterably opposed to every measure calculated to debase our currency or impair the credit of our country. We are, therefore, opposed to the free coinage of silver except by international agreement with the leading commercial nations of the earth, which agreement we pledge ourselves to promote; and until such agreement can be obtained, the existing gold standard must be maintained." 

The Democratic party nominated William Jennings Bryan, a Westerner from Nebraska, after he had delivered the famous "Cross of Gold speech," in which he pleaded for a cheaper money as a means of relief for the workingman. He said, "Having behind us the producing masses of this nation and the world, the labor interests, and the toilers everywhere, we will answer the demand for a gold standard by saying to them: 'You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns-you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold!"" The Democratic platform stated, "We are unalterably opposed to monometallism," and further, "We demand the free and unlimited coinage of both silver and gold at the present legal ratio of 16 to 1 without waiting for the aid or consent of any other nation." 

The People's party, commonly called the Populists, approved of the nomination of Bryan and chose him for their candidate also. 

The campaign resulted in the election of McKinley, who received 271 electoral votes to Bryan's 176 (map, p. 730). With the defeat of Bryan the silver question, for the time at least, sank into the background. 

The Currency Act of 1900. In 1900 the Currency Act was passed, which provided that the gold dollar weighing 25.8 grains (23.22 grains of pure gold) be the standard of value, and that other forms of currency be maintained at a parity with it. By this act a monometallic (one-metal) standard was set up. The United States, which had been practically on a gold standard since 1873, now legally adopted it. The act of 1900 provided that the Secretary of the Treasury shall maintain a gold reserve of $150,- 000,000 for the purpose of keeping other forms of money at par with gold. 

The gold standard remained the standard of our monetary system until April 19, 1933, when the United States officially abandoned it and no longer offered to exchange gold for other forms of money.

Monetary Policy of Franklin D. Roosevelt. With the United States officially off the gold standard, the President was empowered to regulate and even prohibit the exporting of gold for foreign transactions. Hoarding of gold was prohibited by an order from the President requiring all gold to

be brought to the banks and exchanged for other forms of money. The banks in turn sent this gold to the United States Treasury. The President was empowered to revalue the gold dollar by changing the gold content by as much as fifty per cent of its former weight. He was also empowered to change the weight of the silver dollar and establish a new ratio. 

The dollar was revalued by the Treasury's policy of fixing the price of gold. While we were on the gold standard, before 1933, an ounce of gold (480 grains) was worth $20.67, because it could be made into that number of gold dollars each containing 23.22 grains of pure gold.* (480÷23.22= 

20.67). After we abandoned the gold standard and no gold was in circulation, the price of an ounce of gold was fixed by the Treasury, in 1934, at $35.00. One dollar then bought 1/35 of an ounce of gold, or 13.71 grains (1/35 of 480 grains = 13.71 grains). The former dollar contained 23.22 grains of pure gold, while the later dollar contained only 13.71 grains, and in terms of gold was worth only 13.71/23.22, or 59+ per cent of its former value (13.71/23.22.5906). In terms of the former standard the value of the former gold dollar was 100 cents, while the later dollar, measured by that former standard, was valued at 59.06 cents. And in terms of the later standard the former dollar was worth 100/59.06 of $1, or $1.69.

The Supreme Court and the Gold Clause. Many private corporations, for the purpose of raising money, had issued and sold bonds which contained a clause promising to pay the principal and interest in gold coin of standard content. A similar clause was found in United States government bonds. On June 5, 1933, by a joint resolution Congress abrogated (set aside) these clauses. Many people questioned the constitutionality of this act, and after 1934 suits were brought demanding that these obligations be paid in the equivalent of gold of the earlier standard contentthat is, at the rate of $1.69 of the later money for each $1 of interest or principal. The Supreme Court of the United States held that Congress had the power to set aside the gold clause in private bonds, and that although it had no right to do so in government bonds, their owners could not enforce the clause. This decision was of great importance because about $100,000,000,000 worth of bonds had been issued by private corporations and the amount involved was therefore an additional $69,000,000,000. 

The Silver Purchase Act of 1934. While the new administration was reorganizing our monetary policy, there again appeared the request to "do something for silver." In December, 1933, President Roosevelt authorized *The weight of the gold dollar was 25.8 grains. It was 10 pure gold. 10 of 25.8 grains = 23.22 grains. the Treasury to buy newly mined domestic silver at 64½ cents an ounce. 

This did not satisfy the silverites, who asked for more coinage of silver. 

Again the demand came from the West, as in the period following the panics of 1873 and 1893. Senator Key Pittman, of silver-producing 

Nevada; Senator Elmer Thomas, inflationist of Oklahoma; and Senator

William E. Borah, of Idaho, led the fight for silver, and finally, in 1934, secured the passage of an act which provided that the United States increase the amount of silver in our monetary stocks until it ultimately reaches the 25-75 ratio between silver and gold; that is, until 25 per cent of our metallic money is silver and 75 per cent of it is gold. 

The Nationalization of Silver, August, 1934. The Silver Purchase Act of 1934 did not specify the time within which silver must be bought. In 

August the President issued an order requiring all stores of silver in bulk to be paid in to the government within ninety days, for which the government paid $.5001 an ounce. It was estimated that silver in bulk amounted to about 150,000,000 ounces. At the same time the government continued to buy newly-mined silver at 642 cents per ounce.

Paper Money after 1861. The silver certificates of 1878 and later (p. 483), and the treasury notes of 1890 and later (p. 484) have already been described, in connection with the account of metal money. Our paper money has included also gold certificates, similar in character to the silver certificates, but retired from circulation when gold was called in (p. 486); banknotes of various kinds, to be described in the later pages of this chapter (pp. 488-492); and the United States notes called "greenbacks," which were issued during the War between the North and the South. 

Greenbacks. The greenbacks are "fiat money," mere promises to pay, issued by the United States government, but were made legal tender so that creditors must accept them. During the war, Congress authorized $450,000,000 of greenbacks, and an additional $50,000,000 in fractional currency, issued in denominations as low as three cents, and referred to as shin plasters.'

Since the greenbacks were issued on the credit of the government, their value depended on the faith of people in the government's ability to redeem them. During the war, the value of the greenbacks went up or down according to the success of the Union army, and according to the new amounts issued. In 1864 a greenback was worth only thirty-nine cents; that is, it took $100 of greenbacks to buy as much as could be bought with $39 in gold. After the war was over, the business interests in the East demanded the withdrawal of this "cheap money." In 1866 Congress authorized the reduction of the currency by gradually withdrawing greenbacks from

circulation. But this withdrawal contributed to a decline in prices, and caused much opposition among the farmers of the Middle West. Because of this opposition, Congress in 1878 decided that the amount of greenbacks then outstanding, a total of $346,681,000, should remain a permanent part of our currency. Three years before this, on January 14, 1875, Congress had passed the Resumption Act, which provided that on and after January 1, 1879, any greenbacks presented to the Treasury should be redeemed in gold. For this purpose a fund of $100,000,000 in gold coin was set aside and was to be kept available in the Treasury. 

Importance of Banks. Our financial system does not rest on money alone, but on credit as well. Banks are important as institutions which furnish credit, and also for issuing various forms of money known as banknotes. Colonial banks were established as early as 1730. Some of them issued paper money and thus added to the vast amount of paper money already in circulation. The best-known of these colonial banks was the 

Land Bank of Massachusetts, which was established in 1740 to supply paper money, because the British government in 1737 ordered that the colony of Massachusetts issue no more paper money. This bank issued banknotes upon the security of land or of commodities-banknotes that could be redeemed after twenty years, and that might be paid in commodities. It had no capital stock, but proposed to issue paper notes to the amount of 150,000 pounds (more than $500,000) to be secured by land. 

The Land Bank was finally suppressed by the British government. 

Banks during the Revolution. During the period of the American 

Revolution, several banks were established. In July, 1780, the Bank of 

Pennsylvania was established for the purpose of raising funds to carry on the war. In 1781 the Continental Congress, following the suggestion of 

Robert Morris, the financier of the American Revolution, created the Bank of North America.

The First Bank of the United States. After the founding of the government under the Constitution, Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury, recommended the establishment of a Bank of the United States. He argued that such a bank would increase the currency by issuing notes for circulation. It would also make it easier for the government to obtain loans, and would enable the people to pay their taxes. After considerable debate, Congress voted to establish such a bank, with a capital stock of $10,000,000, one fifth of which was subscribed by the government; the remainder was subscribed by the public. The bank was permitted to issue notes which were to be receivable for payments due the United States. The bank opened at Philadelphia in December, 1791, and subsequently estab-

lished eight branches. The bank had a charter for twenty years, which expired in 1811, and was not renewed because of the opposition to it which developed on the part of a large number of state banks. In 1800 there were only twenty-eight state banks, but by 1811 the number had grown to eighty-eight, with a capital stock of $42,600,000. The Bank of the United 

States was also unpopular because much of its stock was held in foreign countries.

Growth of State Banks. With the refusal of Congress to recharter the 

United States Bank, state banking became more important. During the years from 1811 to 1815, the number of state banks increased from 88 to 246. Many of these were organized without proper restriction and therefore issued notes beyond their power to redeem. The loose credit system of selling public lands in the West led to inflation. Disorder followed because many of the state banks were not properly supervised. The government received for the sale of its land, during the period from 1814 to 1817, worthless banknotes which amounted to more than $4,000,000. The banknote circulation had increased during the years 1812 to 1817, from $45,000,000 to $100,000,000. Some of these notes were sound, while others were not. 

The value of the notes depended upon the reliability of the bank which had issued them.

The Second Bank of the United States. This financial condition led to the organization in 1816 of the second Bank of the United States, chartered for a period of twenty years, with a capital of $35,000,000. As was the case in the first Bank of the United States, one fifth of the capital was subscribed by the Federal government. The bank was permitted to issue notes to the amount of its capital. These notes were to be payable in specie on demand and were receivable in payments due the United States. During the first three years of its existence, the bank readily extended its credit; but with the panic of 1819 the bank was in hard circumstances and was forced to contract some of its loans. This put an end to speculation, especially in Western lands, and made the crisis more acute. Because the bank called in many of its loans, it became very unpopular; later, it was accused of being in politics; and finally, in the election of 1832, the question of rechartering the second national bank was an important issue. President 

Jackson refused to charter the bank; and after the election of 1832 he ordered the withdrawal of the government deposits, and the second Bank of the United States went out of existence as a United States bank, in 1836. 

It then received a charter from the state of Pennsylvania. United States funds were then deposited in state banks, which became known as "pet banks," because a special favor was bestowed upon them.

Undue expansion led to speculation, which, together with crop failures in the West, and with failures of British business houses, brought on the panic of 1837. Northern factories were shut down and Southern cotton merchants failed. Bankruptcies became general, and 618 banks failed in a single year.

To safeguard public funds, President Van Buren proposed the "Independent Treasury," also called the "Subtreasury." In 1840, Congress passed a law providing for an Independent Treasury, with depositories for government money in several cities.

National Banks Established. The National Banking Act of 1863 

(amended in 1864) provided for banks under the direction of the United States government. When the War between the North and the South broke out, there were from 1,500 to 1,600 state banks which issued banknotes. These banks had been chartered by the different states, under different restrictions, and their notes were of different values. Some of them were near par, while others were nearly worthless. The system of currency was exceedingly complex and unsatisfactory. It is estimated that about 7,000 different kinds of banknotes were in circulation. With so large a number of notes of different value, counterfeiting became easy, and many worthless notes were in circulation. It was desirable to have some system of Federal regulation. The new banking law provided for the organization of banks according to Federal law. Each national bank was required to buy United States bonds to the extent of one third of its capital stock. 

These bonds were deposited with the government, and with such security, the bank was then permitted to issue notes up to ninety per cent of the value of the bonds thus deposited. Other measures were passed to safeguard the interests of the depositors. The banks were required to keep a certain cash fund on hand and were subject to periodical examination by 

Federal inspectors.

A large number of state banks continued to operate, but in March, 1865, Congress passed a law providing for a ten per cent tax on their banknotes. This made it practically impossible for the state banks to continue issuing banknotes, though many of them continued in the banking business; and note issue became a monopoly of the national banks. 

The Federal Reserve System. In time, many defects of the national bank system came to the attention of the American people. It was evident that the system was not elastic enough. There was no satisfactory method of expanding the currency at a time when more money was needed. During the season of the year when crops are marketed, more money is needed than at other times, but the national banks did not provide for such an

expansion and contraction. It was also felt that the financial power was concentrated in certain large cities. These defects of our national banking system came to the attention of the people during the financial panic in 1907. A committee was appointed by Congress to investigate the charge that a "money trust" existed, which controlled our banks. In 1908 Congress passed the Aldrich-Vreeland Act, which gave the national banks power to issue additional notes in time of emergency, and provided for a Monetary Commission to investigate the whole problem of money and credit. In 1912 this commission submitted its report and made recommendations which proposed a complete change of our banking laws. 

In 1913 Carter Glass introduced the bill, soon passed, creating the Federal Reserve system, by which the country was divided into twelve districts, with a central bank in the principal city of each district. These banks were known as Regional Federal Reserve Banks. All national banks were required to become members of the system, and state banks were invited to join. Each Federal Reserve Bank does business with banks only. 

All member banks are required to subscribe to the stock of the Federal Reserve Bank. This system provides for an elastic currency, because, when money is needed, the Regional Federal Reserve Bank can issue banknotes by rediscounting the commercial paper of the member banks upon which they have made loans to merchants. Federal Reserve notes are then issued in response to business activity; and they are further protected by a

The Federal Reserve system was placed under the direction of a Federal Reserve Board at Washington, which consisted of eight members, including the Secretary of the Treasury, the Comptroller of the Currency, and six members appointed by the President, for a term of twelve years. In February, 1936, however, the membership of this board was changed to consist only of seven members appointed by the President. 

The Federal Reserve system has been successful in providing a more elastic currency. It was able during the World War to aid the government in the enormous task of raising money to carry on the war. It is also claimed by many that financial panics are averted or lessened because of the Federal Reserve system. However, within recent years, the system has not been considered satisfactory, particularly in its relation to industry, and some further reforms have been proposed. 

The Federal Land Bank. In 1916 Congress passed the Federal Farm 

Loan Act, which provided for twelve districts, in each of which a Federal Land Bank was located, for the purpose of granting long-term loans to farmers. These loans were to be repaid in not less than five or more than thirty-five years.

Home Loan Discount Banks. In 1932 President Hoover attempted to secure help for distressed home owners, and recommended that a system of Home Loan Discount Banks be put in operation. These banks made long-term loans on mortgages to home owners, at a low rate of interest. 

The Home Loan Discount Banks were to help the small home owners in Interior of a modern bank 

Ewing Galloway

the same manner in which the Federal Land Banks helped the farmers. 

One important purpose of both of these acts was to prevent high rates of interest and renewal commissions which are often imposed on home owners. 

The Banking Act of 1932. During the depression Congress passed, and President Hoover signed, the Glass-Steagall Act of 1932. This act was for the purpose of making it easier for banks to borrow money from the Federal Reserve Bank. It was also for the purpose of creating more paper money and, indirectly, for bringing hoarded money back into circulation. None of the provisions, however, were drastic enough to accomplish the desired results. The weakness of our banking system became more and more evident as the economic depression continued. Its weakness had already been pointed out, because a large number of banks had failed and were forced to close their doors. 

The Banking Crisis. During the years 1920 to 1932, more than 10,000 banks failed, with losses to depositors estimated at over $5,000,000,000. 

This situation led many people to lose confidence in some of the provisions of our banking system. In the last few days of February, 1933, and the early days of March, the banking system collapsed. To prevent bank failure by wholesale withdrawal of deposits, many states declared banking holidays; and finally, on March 6, President Roosevelt by executive proclamation ordered all national and state banks closed until the confidence of the people could be restored and the Federal government could suggest remedies to make the system more efficient. During this period of about a week, only limited banking operations were carried on, under the regulations of the Secretary of the Treasury. Banks were authorized to open their doors for a few necessary transactions, such as did not involve the withdrawing of deposits. Congress in the meantime passed an Emergency 

Banking Act, which became a law on March 9. 

The Emergency Bank Act of March 9, 1933. The great majority of the banks were reopened within a few days, and others were placed in the hands of conservators; that is, persons appointed by the government to take charge of the banks and conserve their resources. The Emergency 

Bank Act gave the President power to prohibit the hoarding of silver and gold. In accordance with this power, he demanded that all gold be delivered to the Treasury. The act empowered the Reconstruction Finance Corporation to subscribe to preferred stock of banks and to make loans secured by this stock, to both national and state banks. It further authorized the issuance of emergency Federal Reserve Bank notes. 

Banking Act of 1933. The emergency banking legislation was followed by the Glass-Steagall Banking Act of June 16, 1933, which made several

important changes in our banking system. One of its provisions ordered a separation of commercial banking from investment banking. Commercial banks were no longer permitted to engage in speculative activities. Of great importance was the provision for insurance of deposits. For this purpose the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created. All banks which participated in this Deposit Insurance plan were required to contribute one half of one per cent of their deposits to a fund used to guarantee deposits. All member banks of the Federal Reserve system were required to participate, and other banks were invited to do so. Deposits in these banks were then, to a large extent, insured against loss. Full insurance was guaranteed, temporarily, to small accounts, and partial insurance to large accounts.

The Banking Act of 1935. In August, 1935, a new banking act went into effect. The act established a permanent system of Federal deposit insurance, providing full insurance to accounts of $5,000 or less. It increased the power and independence of the Reserve Board, now called the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. This board composed of seven members, serving fourteen years, at a salary of $15,000, is appointed by the President and is ineligible for reappointment. These seven members, together with five representatives of regional banks, are authorized to fix the policy for expanding and contracting the currency and credit.

V. Comparisons and Contrasts

CHAPTER XXVI The Machine Age and Agriculture 

The Farmers in Revolt. The Machine Age brought such great changes in agriculture that many people became alarmed. On August 8, 1932, the 

Iowa Farmers' Union started a thirty-day strike with the battle cry, "Stay at home. Sell nothing." In order to enforce their demands, they tried to close the main roads leading into cities. In the attempt to bring farm products into the cities, contrary to this order, "windshields were smashed and headlights put out." Milk trucks were returned to farms, and those who attempted to ignore the orders were roughly treated by the farmers, who were armed with picks, ax handles, pitchforks, and other crude weapons. The highways were blocked with chains and logs, and in some of the cities there was danger of a shortage of food. The farmers in the 

Middle West had organized a National Farm Holiday Association, and hoped to spread the strike to seven or eight different states. 

In a Middle Western state, in 1933, a mob of 1,000 farmers seized the attorney for an insurance company and threatened him with violence by dangling a rope before his eyes, if he proceeded with the foreclosure of a mortgage on a farm. After the farmers had prevented this foreclosure they held the judge of the district court a prisoner until he agreed that no more foreclosures would be ordered.

A Middle Western newspaper, sympathetic with the farmers, said, "The farmers are acting in good faith. Theirs is a righteous cause. They are not sporadic Reds or professional malcontents. They live in the best farming country in the world and are not content to be denied sustenance and security for investments without a struggle. They have an inherent right to fight for home and family."

On April 20, 1934, the Associated Press reported that "20,000 men in a Northwestern agricultural state are attempting to prevent foreclosures on mortgages." The report predicted actual battles by farmers to defend their land. They asked the governor to declare martial law for a period of 497

An early pioneer's home. In the foreground, the pioneer is plowing with a team of oxen. In the yard the pioneer's wife and children are making soap. 498

thirty days to prevent interference with the operation of the mortgage foreclosure moratorium.

In another state in the Northwest, it was planned to hold wheat off the market until the price rose to a certain level. The governor of this state ordered an embargo on wheat and would not permit it to be sent out of the state. A New York paper, in commenting on the situation, said, “The chief sufferer from a farmers' strike usually is the farmer himself. After a crop is made, the average farmer must sell it in order to live, and sales at any price that cover the cost of getting commodities to market are better than destruction of the product or ignorant gambling on the chances of future improvement. The farmer must institute production strikes, not sale strikes, if he wants permanently to improve his condition." Some of the farmers who picketed the highways to prevent the farm products from being transported to the cities were arrested, but the newspapers reported that 1,000 angry farmers threatened to storm the jail where the men were held pending their release on bail. The president of the National Farmers' 

Holiday Association declared that "until the buying power of the farmer is restored-which can be done only by acceding him the right to cost of production based on an American standard of existence-business institutions, whether great or small, important or humble, must suffer." 

Thus we find in 1933 and 1934 great disorder in the agricultural section of the Middle West and Northwest. Farmers were dissatisfied because of low prices received for their commodities, which made it impossible for them to pay the mortgages on their farms, and threatened to cause many of them to lose their homes. 

Farming in the Early Days. With this recent deplorable condition of farmers in mind, let us look at the history of the American farmer. In the colonial days, ninety-five per cent of the American people lived on farms. 

The new nation was built by the farmer. He cleared the land and made a place for the great American civilization to develop. In the early days of the republic the farmer was usually prosperous because he sold abundant crops to European nations, at high prices. In the period following 1815, the industrial system in America developed, under protection of the tariff. 

The American farmer, led by Henry Clay and others, secured some benefits through the American System, but high tariffs which followed were more beneficial to the industrial sections than to the agricultural regions; and by 1828 many farmers objected to the Tariff of Abominations (p. 467). 

With the coming of the War between the North and the South, the farmers of the Northwest again became prosperous, because labor-saving machinery had made it possible to produce large crops, and farm prices

were high, partly because of the war and partly because the grain harvests failed in some of the European countries. The price of wheat in 1865 rose to $2.50 a bushel. Following the war, however, came deflation and low prices, and the farmer again suffered because of these low prices and the changed conditions of agriculture.

The New Agriculture. Following the War between the North and the 

South, agriculture had to undergo considerable change. The farmer, during the colonial period, produced largely for a home market, and the farm was usually a self-sufficient unit. Nearly all of the food, wearing apparel, and other materials needed by the farmer and his family were produced either on the farm or in the local community. After the war, however, the farmer produced more crops to be sold in other parts of the nation and in foreign countries. Farming had become more of a commercial enterprise. The farmer harvested his crop and produced his products not for himself alone, but also for the rest of the world. 

This change came about largely because of the rise of the industrial system, which built up factories in large cities whose population had to get most of its food supply from the farmer, while the manufacturing centers produced machinery and other products which the farmer bought. 

The Homestead Act. The Homestead Act, passed by Congress in 

1862, provided for the opening of public lands. By the provisions of this act, one could obtain from the government 160 acres of land practically An early farm in 1840; from a Currier and Ives print 

Culver Service

Culver Service

A homestead on the Mississippi River free of charge. Many people took advantage of this act, and thereby the farming area of America was greatly increased. Most of these lands in the 

West were settled by farmers who produced more wheat, and soon large surpluses of wheat, corn, and other products were offered on the markets of the world. In the foreign markets the American farmer had to compete with the farmers of Russia, Australia, Argentina, Canada, and other farming regions, and so was unable to control the price. If the wheat fields throughout the world produced great crops, the farmer of the United States was in distress because of low prices, while on the other hand if crop failures were reported in other parts of the world, the American farmer was prosperous.

Increase in Farm Acreage. In 1860 there were about 407,000,000 acres of land held by American farmers; but because of the vast amount of land acquired by farmers under the provisions of the Homestead Act, and because other land was put under cultivation, the farm lands increased until in 1900 there were about 841,000,000 acres in farms. With this vast increase in acreage, the value of farm property also increased. In 1860, the value of land, buildings, implements, and livestock was about $8,000,000,000, and by 1900 it was worth more than $20,000,000,000. With the great increase in acreage, also, greater amounts of farm crops were pro-

duced, with the result that prices went down. The average price of wheat during the years from 1866 to 1875 was $1.05 per bushel, but in 1900 it was only $.62. Hence, while the annual yield of wheat by 1900 was two and one half times as great as in 1866, the total value of the crop was less than one and one half times as large. Thus most farmers experienced a reduction in the value of their crops even though they were producing greater quantities than before.

American Exports in Farm Products. During the 1890's farm products exported by the United States reached the total value of $663,500,000 annually, and were largely responsible for giving us a favorable balance of trade. The 1890's were an era of great American farm surpluses. These surpluses were sold abroad and in our international trade they paid for a large share of our imports. However, a great change soon took place, for while in 1900 the United States wheat growers exported forty per cent of their crop, only four years later they exported only eight per cent of the crop. Other farm products, such as livestock, beef products, butter, and cheese, were also declining, because by the twentieth century European and South American countries were producing more agricultural products for the world market. Besides the competition from European and South 

American farm products, the American farmer, in our export trade, had to compete with American manufactured articles. By the twentieth century, the United States had become an industrial nation, and great quantities of our manufactured goods were being exported to settle balances with foreign countries. Manufactured products were protected against foreign competition by a tariff, and were therefore able to build up powerful industrial establishments. The protected manufacturing interests steadily prospered, while the farming communities began to decline. 

Importance of Cotton. Following the War between the North and the 

South, a great change took place in Southern agriculture. The Southern plantation was transformed into smaller holdings, and the free negro in many cases became a renter of Southern farms, where he grew cotton and other staple crops. The free negro did not wish to work for wages, but preferred to rent on a crop-sharing basis. The cotton farmers of the 

South, like the wheat farmers of the Northwest, increased in number. 

During the years 1866 to 1877 the cotton-producing area was about 8,000,000 acres, but that amount increased to about 24,900,000 acres by 1900. This meant a greater and greater output of cotton. In 1859 the 

United States produced about 4,300,000 bales of cotton, and twenty years later, 5,750,000 bales. By the end of the nineteenth century, about 9,400,000 bales a year were produced; in 1919, 11,400,000; and in 1929, 14,800,000

bales. As more cotton was produced, however, a smaller proportion of it was exported. In 1860 seventy-six per cent of the total cotton yield was exported. In 1900 only sixty-six per cent was exported. With a larger amount produced came a lower price and a reduction in the income of the Southern farmer, who, like the farmer of the West and Northwest, was in distress because of overproduction. 

The Machine Age and the Farmer. During the colonial period, farming in America, as elsewhere, was in a rather primitive stage. Not much machinery was available. Seed was sown by hand, the grain was harvested with sickles or cradles, and threshed with a flail. However, with the coming of machinery, great changes took place. In the 1850's, the Deere plow with its steel moldboard was invented to supplant the old wooden plow, or the brittle iron plow. This early steel plow went through many stages of development, until today we have the gang plow, drawn by a tractor. 

Auris spleno

An early McCormick reaper on demonstration; from an old print. The reaper is seen at the right; crowds of observers in the foreground. 

The reaper, invented by Cyrus H. McCormick of Virginia in 1831, replaced the cradle. Further progress was made with the invention of the combined harvester and thresher. The modern plow was combined with the harrow and seeder, so that wheat could be sown more rapidly. So great were the improvements in labor-saving farm machinery that by 1900 the labor to produce a bushel of wheat required only 10 minutes, as compared with 183 minutes in 1830.

Large-Scale Agriculture. Since the use of machinery made it possible to farm on a larger scale, the size of some farms was greatly increased. The

state of Montana, from 1915 to 1917, had about 35,000 wheat farmers operating small farms; by 1929 there were in that state only 14,000 wheat farmers, who cultivated more acres and produced more wheat than the 35,000 did in 1915. In some of the Western states large farms, known as bonanza farms, developed. These farms usually contained 4,000 to 6,000 acres, and were planted with a single crop. On some of these farms dozens of plows, harrows, and reaping machines, a large number of tractors, and more than 100 head of farm animals were used. 

Science Helps the Farmer to Increase Production. The Federal gov ernment granted land to the states for the establishment of agricultural colleges. The Morrill Act of 1862 provided for at least one college in each state, to teach agriculture and the mechanical arts. In these colleges young men and women are taught the science of agriculture, and farmers in service are given short courses or extension demonstration courses, which help to make them more efficient producers of agricultural crops. In 1887 the Hatch Act provided for the establishment of experiment stations in those states where land-grant colleges existed. 

In 1862 the Federal government established a Department of Agriculture, headed by a Commissioner, who, in 1886, was made Secretary and became a member of the President's cabinet. The Department of Agriculture has done much through its various bureaus to stimulate scientific Agricultural regions of the United States. Each region is named for the dominance of a certain crop or a certain kind of farming, or for the extensive use of the land for grazing. 127 121°

agriculture. The work of the Federal government, together with that of the state agricultural colleges and experiment stations, has taught the farmer to become more efficient. Single cropping has been followed by crop rotation. More attention has been given to the use of fertilizers as a means of restoring soil fertility. Better types of farm animals have been selected, better varieties of plants are being cultivated. All these activities have improved methods of production and made possible even larger crops. 

Agricultural Distress. But although the farmer produced more and better crops, agricultural prosperity failed to come, and during the 70's, 80's, and 90's the farmer was forced to operate his business at a small profit, and in many cases at a loss. Farm machinery was expensive. The railroads which transported his products charged high rates, while prices of crops went down. Many a farmer was able to keep going only by borrowing money and giving a mortgage on his farm as security for payment. 

With the coming of the panic of 1873, which brought a shortage of money, hardships greater than ever before were imposed on the farming population. 

The farmers felt that the railroad companies were charging too high transportation rates, and therefore considered them their enemies. They also felt that manufacturers who were protected by high tariffs were charging too high prices for the goods the farmer bought, that bankers and moneylenders were taking advantage of them, and that a too-large number of government officials was largely responsible for the great burden of taxation.

The Granger Movement. Discontented with the prevailing economic system, agricultural leaders looked for remedies. As early as 1867, a movement known as the Patrons of Husbandry, but better known as the Grange, had been organized among the farmers by Oliver H. Kelley, a clerk in the 

Post Office Department at Washington. Kelley, who had been a farmer in 

Minnesota, together with William Saunders, a government employee in the Department of Agriculture, organized a secret order for the purpose of promoting better social life among the men and women in the agricultural regions. The Grange was composed of local organizations which in turn formed state organizations, and the leaders of the state organizations were known as the national Grange. These organizations were found in all the agricultural states, and the total membership, following the hard times of 1873, grew to 2,500,000. Farmers and their families gathered through their local granges for the purpose of amusement as well as for social and educational meetings, and for the purpose of listening to patriotic addresses. Independence Day, 1873, has been referred to as the Farmers'

Fourth of July. On that day, in a declaration of independence, they denounced the railroads and Congress for the plight in which the farmers found themselves. Even though they were organized as a non-political group, the Grangers in time became active in politics, and in some of the agricultural states were successful in electing to the legislature members who were interested in promoting their program. These legislators secured the passage of laws to regulate rates charged by the railroads and grain elevators.

The Farmers Initiate Co-operative Organization. The Grangers tried to improve their economic condition by setting up central agencies for the sale of farm products, hoping thereby to secure higher prices. In some states they set up co-operative creameries and grain elevators. They also ordered machinery and other products in wholesale lots, directly from the manufacturers. In Iowa the state Grange operated its own factory for manufacturing plows and harvesters. Most of these co-operative activities failed because they were not skillfully handled, or because of the competition of their opponents. Yet the idea of co-operation spread and played an important part in eliminating excessive profits formerly made by middlemen. The Grange was also responsible, in part at least, for the development of mail-order houses, which sold directly to the farmers.

Toward the middle of the 1870's, the Granger movement, the first great farmer movement in America, began to decline. The farmers had made an effort to improve their conditions, but failed. They next turned to inflation. 

The Farmer and Inflation. Inflation may be defined as an arbitrary means of increasing the amount of money put into circulation without cost to the government except the cost of printing. Such money is sometimes issued by a government unable to secure income in other ways; and sometimes one object of inflation is to raise the general level of prices. Many farmers, in seeking higher prices for their products, felt that the government should inflate the currency by printing more paper money. 

The issuance of greenbacks during the War between the North and the South (p. 398) had caused some inflation and higher prices; and when they were partly withdrawn from circulation the farmers of the Middle West objected to the withdrawal, and maintained that the contraction of the currency was the chief cause of low farm prices in the 70's. Since these farmers were mainly of the debtor class, they thought that a contracting currency would work a hardship on them. Many of the farm debts had been contracted when greenbacks were below 100 cents on the dollar as compared with gold. If these debts were later to be paid with a 100-cent dollar, the debtor would have to pay back more than he had borrowed. 

Let us assume that a farmer contracted a debt of $1,000 during the war, at a time when the dollar was worth fifty cents in gold, and a bushel of wheat sold for $2 in greenbacks. He borrowed the equivalent of 500 bushels of wheat. If the greenbacks were contracted, and money made scarcer, and the price of crops should fall until wheat sold for $1 a bushel, it would be more difficult for him to pay his debt of $1,000, since he would have to return the equivalent of 1000 bushels of wheat, or twice as much as he had borrowed.

The Greenback Party. With this idea in mind, many Westerners organized the Greenback party, which opposed the contraction of the greenbacks and also opposed the Resumption Act of 1875 (p. 488). In its national convention at Indianapolis in 1876, this party nominated Peter Cooper, of New York, for President, and Samuel S. Cary for Vice-President. In the election it cast 81,737 votes, most of which came from the agricultural states. However, two years later, in the congressional election of 1878, the Greenback party polled about 1,000,000 votes and elected fifteen members in the lower house of Congress. One of the most outstanding of these members was General James B. Weaver, of Iowa, who became the presidential candidate of the party in 1880. Weaver made an extended campaign but received less than 310,000 votes. It seemed that many

people subscribed to his principles, but failed to vote for him because they felt he would not be elected. In 1884 the party nominated Benjamin F. 

Butler, who polled less than 175,000 votes. The movement declined, but the important principles sponsored by it were incorporated by other parties. 

Other Agricultural Organizations. After the decline of the Grange (p. 507) other agricultural organizations such as the Farmers' League, the 

Farmers' Union, the Agricultural Wheel, the Farmers' Alliance, and the Farmers' Mutual Benefit Association appeared, each trying to promote the cause of the farmer. Among the demands of these various organizations were reduction of the tariff to a revenue basis, a graduated income tax, the promotion of industrial and agricultural education, the popular election of United States senators, the regulation of interstate commerce, the reform of the patent laws, and the reduction of salaries of officials. Most of these organizations disappeared after a brief existence, but several of the important reforms proposed by them have since been carried out. Some of these organizations undertook co-operative buying and selling, but most of their business enterprises failed, usually because of mismanagement. 

The Populist Movement. The Granger movement had spent itself, but the problems of the farmer remained. Agriculture in the South and in the 

West suffered because of crop failures and low prices. During the 1880's, many farmers had acquired land in the Dakotas and other Western states, and had heavily mortgaged their farms to secure the necessary machinery with which to cultivate the land. In the years following 1887, a severe drought swept over these Western states, bringing great hardships. 

In 1885, Kansas produced 158,000,000 bushels of corn, but two years later she produced less than half that amount, and in 1889 still less-only 55,269,000 bushels. In the meantime, a heavy burden of mortgages rested on many of the Western farms. In 1898 it was estimated that the farms of the Dakotas were mortgaged for a total of $50,000,000. The farms of 

Kansas and Nebraska were likewise heavily mortgaged. The Western farmers had borrowed money from Eastern cities which, it was reported, were reaping profits through foreclosures on mortgages. Philadelphia was reported to have absorbed $15,000,000 annually. During these troublesome times for the farmer, the price of corn dropped to twenty-eight cents a bushel, while cotton sold for six cents a pound. 

The farmers felt that the government, both state and Federal, could remedy these economic conditions, and insisted on political action. In 

December, 1889, the Southern Alliance held its annual convention in St. 

Louis. At this convention were representatives from other farm and labor organizations. Here plans were made for organization and resolutions were

adopted favoring the free coinage of silver, the abolition of national banks, the issuing of more money, government ownership of railroads, prohibition of speculation in grain, and limitation of taxes for the states and the nation. They endorsed a subtreasury plan which was presented by C. W. 

Macune, editor of The National Economist. This subtreasury plan was a scheme for lending money on farm products. It recommended that the national government establish warehouses and elevators where the farmer might store his wheat, corn, cotton, tobacco, and other non-perishable products, and receive a certificate of deposit upon which he would be entitled to a loan in legal-tender notes up to eighty per cent of the market price of these products.*

The movement started by the Southern Alliance at St. Louis received considerable impetus. The farmers in the West were thoroughly aroused because of their financial difficulties, and public gatherings were held in schoolhouses, churches, town and Granger halls. One important leader in this movement was Mary E. Lease, who went up and down the state of 

Kansas and said to the farmers, "What you farmers need is to raise less corn and more hell." Other outstanding characters were "sockless" Jerry

Simpson, and Senator W. A. Peffer, of Kansas, famous for his large whiskers. So aroused were the people in Kansas that in the election of 

1890 they chose five Populist congressmen and a majority in the state legislature. The state legislature then selected W. A. Peffer to represent 

Kansas in the United States Senate. The Populists were successful in several other states in the South and the West. In South Carolina they elected Benjamin Tillman governor. In Georgia the Farmers' Alliance chose the governor and elected a majority of the state legislature, as well as a number of Congressmen. Virginia, Kentucky, North Carolina, Mississippi, and Missouri likewise selected Populist congressmen to represent them in Washington.

The movement continued and became more important as time went on. 

In May, 1891, at Cincinnati, the Populists decided to form a national party. The farmers contended that there was need of such a party because the old parties refused to face the issue. They maintained that during the past year the people had grown poorer and the burden of indebtedness had grown larger. The issues were kept before the people, and at a meeting held in St. Louis on February 22, 1892, 860 persons, representing almost every agricultural society in the country, met and organized the People's 

Party. Ignatius Donnelly of Minnesota, Senator W. A. Peffer and Jerry *A plan similar to this was adopted in 1923 by the Federal government through the establishment of the intermediate loan banks.

Simpson of Kansas, J. B. Weaver of Iowa, and Thomas F. Watson of

Georgia were important leaders in this movement. Donnelly wrote the preamble to the platform, in which he stated: "The conditions which surround us best justify our co-operation; we meet in the midst of a nation brought to the verge of moral, political, and material ruin. Corruption dominates the ballot-box, the legislatures, the 

Congress, and touches even the ermine of the bench. The people are demoralized; most of the states have been compelled to isolate the voters at the polling places to prevent universal intimidation and bribery. The newspapers are largely subsidized or muzzled, public opinion silenced, business prostrated, homes covered with mortgages, labor impoverished, and the land concentrating in the hands of capitalists. The urban workmen are denied the right to organize for self-protection; imported pauperized labor beats down their wages; a hireling standing army, unrecognized by our laws, is established to shoot them down; and they are rapidly degenerating into European conditions. The fruits of the toil of millions are boldly stolen to build up colossal fortunes for a few, unprecedented in the history of mankind; and the possessors of these in turn despise the Republic and endanger liberty. From the same prolific womb of governmental injustice we breed the two great classes—tramps and millionaires. "The national power to create money is appropriated to enrich bondholders; a vast public debt payable in legal tender currency has been funded into gold-bearing bonds, thereby adding millions to the burdens of the people. "Silver, which has been accepted as coin since the dawn of history, has been demonetized to add to the purchasing power of gold by decreasing the value of all forms of property as well as human labor, and the supply of currency is purposely abridged to fatten usurers, bankrupt enterprise, and enslave industry. A vast conspiracy against mankind has been organized on two continents, and it is rapidly taking possession of the world. If not met and overthrown at once, it forebodes terrible social convulsions, the destruction of civilization, or the establishment of an absolute despotism." 

On the Fourth of July, 1892, the People's Party announced its Omaha platform. It asked for reforms in finance, transportation, and land ownership. Among the specific financial reforms, they demanded: (a) free and unlimited coinage of silver and gold at the present legal ratio 16 to 1; (b) that the amount of circulating media be speedily increased to not less than $50 per capita; (c) a graduated income tax; (d) that money of the country should be kept as much as possible in the hands of the people, and hence that state and national revenues be limited to the necessary expenses

of the government, economically and honestly administered; (e) that postal savings banks be established by the government for the safe deposit of the earnings of the people and to facilitate exchange. 

It also demanded changes in the means of transportation so that "the government should own and operate the railroads in the interests of the people." 

A third reform applied to land. The platform stated, "The land... should not be monopolized for speculative purposes, and alien ownership of land should be prohibited."

James B. Weaver was nominated as the standard-bearer of the Populist party, and in the election of 1892 received 1,041,600 popular votes, and 22 electoral votes. With the party defeated, many of the Populist issues were taken over by other parties, and in the election of 1896 the demand for free coinage of silver was an important issue.

The Campaign of 1896. In 1896 the Republican party nominated 

William McKinley as its standard-bearer on a platform which opposed the free and unlimited coinage of silver except by international agreement. 

The Democratic party nominated William Jennings Bryan of Nebraska, who championed the free-silver cause (see p. 485). The Populist party likewise supported Bryan for President, and he carried on an extensive campaign but lost the election. With his defeat the issue of free coinage of silver at the ratio of 16 to 1 declined, and so too did the Populist party. 

The attempt of the debtor class, many of whom were farmers, to improve their economic situation through inflation thus ended in failure. 

The Return of Prosperity. Soon after the election of McKinley, prosperity returned, probably due to an increase in the output of gold. The farmers enjoyed bounteous harvests and higher prices for their products. 

With agriculture profitable again, the farmers became content. They also received benefits from the government, such as rural free delivery, and better roads. New gold mines were discovered in Alaska and in South Africa, and a process of extracting gold from less profitable ores was invented so that the gold supply of the world increased. More money was put into circulation, because the government issued bonds to finance the war with Spain, in 1898. These bonds were purchased by the national banks, and this in turn gave them the right to issue more banknotes. Thus the return of higher prices led to the collapse of the inflation movement. In 1900 the 

Gold Standard Act was passed, by which we definitely went on a gold basis. The act provided for a single standard, namely, gold; and other forms of money were to be redeemable in gold. For this purpose, as we have seen (p. 485), a gold fund of $150,000,000 was set aside.

A large modern Western farm; from an airplane photograph 

The Condition of Agriculture from 1900 to 1915. The condition of agriculture from 1900 to 1915 may be characterized as one of prosperity. 

The farms became more productive, and the market for farm products was increased by our growing urban population and expanding foreign trade. 

Farm prosperity was reflected by better farm homes, improved rural schools, and a happier farm population. Wholesale prices of products, other than agricultural, increased during this period about thirty per cent, while the prices of farm products increased sixty per cent. 

The Period from 1915 to 1920. During the years from 1915 to 1920, the farmer became even more prosperous because of high prices caused by the World War. American agriculture expanded in an attempt to supply the fighting armies with food products. In 1913 wheat was selling in 

Chicago for $.93 a bushel; the price in 1919 was $2.76. In the year before the opening of the World War, corn was selling in Chicago for $.70, and in 1919 the price was $1.59. In New York, cotton sold in 1913 for thirteen cents a pound, while in 1919 it had risen to thirty-eight cents. These increased farm prices were reflected in the price of land. Agricultural land which in 1910 sold for $82 an acre, in 1920 sold for $200. The farmer enjoyed not only higher prices for his commodities, but an increase in value of his property. Encouraged by these high prices, farmers borrowed money to buy more land, to put up expensive and modern buildings on their farms, and to equip their farms with better and more expensive machinery.

Deflation Follows Prosperity. The period of prosperity, however, was soon over. The armies of Europe ceased fighting, were demobilized, and

their men returned to the pursuits of peace. Millions of European farms again began to produce as much food as before the war. In 1920 there was an abundance, and a period of deflation for agriculture as well as for industry began. Industry, however, soon began to recover. Agriculture did not. Farm prices continued to go down, and land values likewise continued to decline. Many of our farmers were burdened with heavy debts, and the vast acreage put under cultivation during the war days was beginning to produce an ever-increasing surplus, while the demand in foreign markets was steadily declining. The farmer once again faced low prices, high taxes, and mortgages on his property. Farm mortgages of all kinds, according to the Department of Agriculture, increased from about $3,300,- 000,000 in 1910 to $9,500,000,000 in 1920. Taxes increased one and a half times over the prewar period. Because of the expansion of agriculture during the World War, 40,000,000 acres had been added to productive farm land in the decade from 1910 to 1920. 

Power Machinery Replaces Farm Animals. Not only had acreage been increased, but the methods of agriculture had become more efficient. 

Power machinery, especially tractors, had been employed and helped to make agriculture more efficient and more productive. The development of machinery in the years following 1900 revolutionized agriculture. The number of horses and mules on farms was reduced by 10,000,000 from 1918 Estimated distribution of gasoline-driven tractors on farms in 1930 www.
