to 1932, while tractors increased by nearly 800,000 from 1918 to 1929. 

Farming on a large scale was becoming more general. Because of the decline in the number of farm animals employed, the acreage needed for producing food for these animals was reduced by 30,000,000 acres, most of which were added to the area producing crops for sale. 

Overproduction Brings Low Prices. The use of fertilizers, better selection of seed, the application of scientific principles to agriculture, and the aid of governmental agencies all tended to make for greater production at the very time when the market for the products of the farm was decreasing. 

The improvement of animal husbandry had added the equivalent of 25,- 000,000 acres to the crop area. During the early part of the twentieth century, by the use of mineral fertilizers, the yield per acre was in some cases increased from fifty to seventy-five per cent. Farmers in other parts of the world also were producing larger crops than before. The surpluses of Canada, Australia, Russia, and Argentina were competing with the farm products of our country. This meant a further decline in the prices of farm commodities. Cotton, which in 1919 was selling for $.38 a pound, sold in August, 1931, for less than $.07; and wheat, which in 1919 sold for $2.76, dropped in July, 1931, to $.57 a bushel. 

Farm Legislation, 1921-1931. This condition in agriculture forced to the front the question of relief for the farmer. During President Harding's administration, in 1921, Congress passed the Packers and Stockyard Act in an attempt to aid farmers producing livestock. In 1922 the Capper- 

Volstead Co-operative Act became a law. This law exempted agricultural associations from the operation of antitrust laws. In March, 1923, Congress passed the Federal Intermediate Credit Act for the purpose of extending credit to farmers through a system of Federal Intermediate Credit Banks. By this act the Federal Farm Loan Board was authorized to set up twelve banks, known as Federal Intermediate Credit Banks, which extended credit directly to agricultural co-operatives on notes secured by warehouse receipts. Thus the farmer, through a loan on his produce, was given an opportunity, with the help of the government, to hold his products off the market. In accordance with this act, agricultural credit corporations were established. More than 10,000 such co-operatives, with a membership of 1,800,000 individuals, were formed, doing an annual business of $2,400,000,000.

The farm problem, however, was not easily solved. In February, 1927, the McNary-Haugen Bill, which was to offer relief to farmers, was passed by both houses of Congress, but was vetoed by President Coolidge. During 

President Hoover's administration, an Agricultural Marketing Act was

passed, which established a Farm Board composed of eight members to be appointed by the President. The purpose of this board was to encourage the organization of agricultural co-operatives. The board was also to aid in preventing and "controlling surpluses in many agricultural commodities." To carry out this provision of the act, the Farm Board created a grain stabilizing corporation, which bought 330,000,000 bushels of wheat in an attempt to hold the surplus off the market and keep it from depressing the price. A cotton stabilization corporation was established, which bought 1,319,800 bales of cotton for the same reason. These two organizations expended $377,737,000, and at the end of two years reported a loss of $185,000,000 because the price of the commodities which they had bought refused to advance, but declined instead. The Agricultural Marketing Act failed to provide relief for the farmer, because farmers continued to produce more agricultural products than could be consumed at home, and there was a poor market abroad. 

Farm Relief a Campaign Issue. It became evident that the program for farm relief in 1931 employed by the Hoover administration had failed to provide adequate help for the farmer. In the coming campaign of 1932, farm relief was one of the important issues before the American people. 

The plight of the farmer was intensified by the severe depression which 

Harvesting rice in Arkansas

Courtesy Case Mfg. Co.

affected all forms of industry in the country. With prices already low, the farmer, who had been suffering a depression since 1920, was in a desperate financial condition when the crash of 1929 came. His purchasing power had been greatly reduced. As the depression wore on, this purchasing power was still further reduced. When millions of people were thrown out of employment because of the failure of many industrial establishments, farm prices hit the lowest levels, and help for the farmer became even more necessary. 

Farm Relief under the New Deal. President Roosevelt realized the seriousness of the farm situation, and, before he was inaugurated, he pointed out that nearly one third of the population of the United States was dependent upon the products of the farm for livelihood and purchasing power. He said that no single factor would be able to bring back immediate prosperity to the agricultural population of our country, but that it was necessary to have a program of national agricultural planning. He held that a definite policy, looking toward the planned use of land, was necessary. He realized the importance of farm prosperity because of its relation to industrial and financial institutions in our country. The relationship between agricultural prosperity and other business enterprises was shown to be very close, for during the depression in agriculture, from 1920 to 1930 more than 6,000 rural banks failed. 

With the farmer's purchasing power reduced, he was unable to buy the products of industry, and the merchants and manufacturers suffered great losses. This relation of agriculture to other industries was clearly pointed out by George M. Peek, the administrator of the Farm Act, when he said, "Agriculture must be restored to its proper place in the nation's life, not only for the sake of the farmer, but also for the general welfare." Its importance was also shown by a committee of the United States Chamber of Commerce, which reported that "this country cannot be permanently prosperous until it has a reasonably prosperous agricultural population. 

Ten million workers and 30,000,000 people are dependent upon the farm for their support. A large proportion, perhaps the majority, are receiving meager returns for long and arduous labor." Our past history had shown that it was difficult to obtain relief for the farmer. Several administrations had tried, but had failed to give adequate aid. Many people were convinced that some kind of large-scale control by the Federal government would be the only way to remedy the situation. Drastic action was con sidered necessary. When President Franklin D. Roosevelt called the 

Seventy-third Congress in special session, one of the important problems before it was that of helping the farmer.

Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933. On May 12, the Agricultural 

Adjustment Act, also known as the Farm Act of 1933, was passed. It contained three important provisions: (1) The administration was given power to adjust farm production by reducing the output of the farms and by eliminating some of the waste in distribution. (2) The law provided for refinancing and readjustment of farm mortgage payments. (3) The President was given power to inflate the currency as a means of raising prices. 

The main purpose of the act was to increase the purchasing power of the farmer. The Secretary of Agriculture was given power to arrange for acreage or crop reduction by dealing with individual farmers. He was given power to pay them, either directly or through rent, for land which they took out of production. For reducing the acreage devoted to wheat, farmers were paid, in one year, benefits of some $95,000,000. 

To obtain the money, the government put a "processing tax" of thirty cents a bushel on wheat bought by flour mills. The plan of reducing production by benefit payments was applied also to producers of cotton, hogs, beef and dairy cattle, barley, flax, grain sorghum, peanuts, rye, beet sugar, and sugar cane.

The AAA Is Declared Unconstitutional. The AAA program was financed by money obtained by various processing taxes. During 1934 and 1935, a number of suits were brought to recover such taxes paid to the government. 

The 74th Congress, therefore, amended the Agricultural Adjustment Act so as to permit processing tax recovery suits only when the processor could prove that he paid the tax without making a corresponding increase in the prices charged for his product or for his work. In spite of the amendment the Supreme Court on January 6, 1936, declared the act unconstitutional. 

By that time, however, the crisis in agriculture had passed and the buying power of the farmers had to a large extent been restored. 

The drought of 1934, together with the AAA operations, reduced the supply of cotton, wheat, oats, barley, and other farm products and thereby stimulated higher prices. The total farm cash income for the year 1934, including government payments, was about $6,100,000,000. This was a billion dollars more than the farmers received in 1933. Farmers' income continued to increase also in 1935-1937. 

Acts of 1936 and 1937. Congress felt that the benefits of a planned agricultural program should be preserved in a manner satisfactory to the Supreme Court. On March 1, 1936, therefore, the Soil Conservation Act of 1935 was amended so as to give the Secretary of Agriculture power for a two-year period to pay farmers for preventing erosion and for conserving fertility of the soil by planting soil-conserving crops, such as clover and

other legumes, instead of cotton, corn, and wheat. This, it was expected, would cut down the supply of the latter crops, as desired. 

By the Farm Tenancy and Rural Rehabilitation Act of July 22, 1937, the Secretary of Agriculture was authorized to make loans to farm tenants, farm laborers, and sharecroppers. The purpose of the act is to relieve and eliminate the worst forms of tenancy, retire from agriculture submarginal land, promote rural rehabilitation and proper land utilization. 

For this purpose the use of $10,000,000 was authorized for the year ending June 30, 1938; $25,000,000 for the year ending June 30, 1939; and $50,- 

000,000 for the year ending June 30, 1940. 

The Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1938. In February, 1938, Congress passed a new AAA, the constitutionality of which rests on the powers of Congress to regulate interstate commerce and to promote the general welfare. The purpose of the act is to regulate the production and prices of some of the major farm crops such as wheat, cotton, corn, tobacco, and rice. The act empowers the Secretary of Agriculture (1) to set national acreage allotments for each crop, this allotment to be based on production during preceding years; (2) to make loans to farmers who co-operate with the acreage allotment program, whenever the price of their crop falls below a certain level; and (3) to establish compulsory marketing quotas subject to a referendum of the growers. The act also created a Federal Crop 

Insurance Corporation, through which to insure farmers against crop disaster; and provided for establishing four regional research laboratories to investigate new uses, markets, and by-products for farm commodities. 

Later acts appropriated large sums for aiding farmers in accordance with the new AAA and earlier acts.

HOW THE INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION CHANGED  Chapter XXVII.  Chapter XXVIII.  Chapter XXIX. 

A COUNTRY can not be molded into a strongly unified nation unless its people have easy means of exchanging their goods and ideas. Many great nations of the world have recognized this fact. The conquest of a new province by the Persian or the Roman empire was promptly followed by the construction of highways, which made the conquest not merely one of arms but one of culture as well. Had it not been for the rapid extension of the means of transportation and communication, it is probable that the vast area comprising the United States, instead of being the home of one great national people, would have been divided into several smaller nations, such as there are in Europe or in Central America. 

Transportation and communication are important also for other reasons. The standard of living may be raised through the exchange of commodities; famines are averted, in districts where drought or floods have destroyed the crops, by the importation of food from more fortunate sections; and the level of culture is raised by the exchange of ideas. In fact it is often said that the progress of civilization may be measured by the progress of transportation and communication. 523

In the early days travel was largely by water and on horseback. The 

American people settled along the river banks and learned to use canoes as the Indians had done. As the country became more thickly populated and the importance of transportation increased, a system of highways was developed. These followed the trails of the Indians and the wild animals, and were first used to accommodate horsemen and pack animals. In time simple wagons and coaches were constructed, and highways were improved. 

Overland transportation of freight became important, and more attention was devoted to improving highways. Turnpikes, which were often financed by means of tolls, were built. The Conestoga wagon, carrying grain to the markets or settlers to the West, was often seen on these highways. Because transportation by water was cheap, the American people early began to improve the water systems by the construction of canals. After 1807 a vast improvement was made in transportation by the perfecting of steamboats, which were used on the rivers, the canals, and finally in ocean travel. 

The era of canal building was superseded by that of railroad building. 

The first American railroads were not very successful, and many people doubted the value of this means of transportation. In 1828 the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad laid its first rails, and soon after demonstrated the practicability of railway service. Other railroads followed, and in time the country was spanned by a vast network of rails. 

A transcontinental railroad was suggested as early as 1832, but it was not completed until 1869. At the close of the War between the North and the South approximately 35,000 miles of railroad had been built; but with the industrial development of the United States, there was a rapid increase in the construction of railroads, and large systems were the result. By 

1920 more than 250,000 miles of railroads had been built. These have rendered valuable service not only in passenger transportation but also in the hauling of freight. Flatcars have been devised for transporting heavy machinery; refrigerator cars for the transportation of fruits, perishable vegetables, and meats; and Pullman sleeping cars provide special accommodation for the traveling public. Within the last few years a new type of railroad train, known as the streamline train, which travels with safety at the rate of about two miles per minute, has been perfected. 

In addition to railway transportation the American people have favored the automobile. It first appeared near the close of the nineteenth century, and has developed in such numbers that today there are enough for the people of the entire country to ride at one time. Great speed has been attained, and millions of dollars have been expended on highways so that now one can travel from coast to coast over hard-surfaced roads.

Another important means of transportation is the airplane, which had its experimental stage early in the twentieth century. The plane has been so improved that it can now travel at a speed of more than 400 miles per hour, and has been able to remain in the air for days at a time. Flights have also been made around the world. 

Greatly improved methods of communication have also been developed. 

In 1860 the pony express carried mail across the western part of the United States, and covered the region from St. Joseph, Missouri, to California in about ten days. At present, however, we have a modern postal system which, by the use of fast trains and airplanes, is able to deliver a letter to any part of the United States in a very short time. The telegraph, invented in 1837 and put into successful operation in 1844, was an important addition to means of communication. By 1866 the Atlantic Ocean was successfully spanned by telegraph cable. The next step was the development of the telephone (1876), of which, by 1930, there were more than 20,000,000 in operation in America. A further advancement was the radio, over which messages and programs were broadcast as early as 1920. Today there are more than 21,000,000 radio sets in American homes. Other methods of communication are the teletype, by which messages are sent automatically; and television, with which inventors are now experimenting, though as yet it is not used commercially to any great extent. CHAPTER XXVII Early Means of Transportation 

Colonial Waterways. Travel in colonial America was a matter of necessity, not of pleasure. When the first English settlers reached their new homes in America, they found themselves cut off from the great interior of the continent by vast forests which today would be considered a natural resource of great value; but to our forefathers they were a barrier, and often a shelter for hostile Indian tribes. The first colonists, therefore, traveled more by water than by land. Settlements usually were made near the mouths of navigable streams, and as the colonies prospered, expansion into the interior naturally followed the course of the river, which soon was used by a procession of sloops, shallops, and "bateaux" carrying products from the outlying plantations to the market at the main settlement. The colonists at first did not like the Indian canoe, but as they pushed farther inland, where the streams were shallow, they came to appreciate its value. It was easily managed in the swift currents and could be carried without difficulty around falls and rapids or from the upper part of one stream across the watershed to another stream. These portages were so important in early trade that they were frequently protected by forts.

Some of the colonists, especially those in New England, turned to the sea for their living. Blessed with excellent timber and other facilities for shipbuilding, and protected by the Navigation Acts, which restricted the British carrying trade to ships built in Great Britain or her colonies, the New Englanders became known throughout the world for their fine seamanship and their superior ships. Yankee ingenuity constructed the schooner, which, having two masts instead of one, was more than a match for the heavier and clumsier vessels in use at that time. 

The Beginnings of Our Highway Systems. Troubles with the Indians soon convinced the colonists that they needed some other transportation routes besides the rivers, for when a section of a river between two settle- 526

Keystone 

An old wooden highway bridge ments was held by the Indians, all communication was cut off. The first overland travel was on foot along the trails formed by the Indians and the wild animals. Soon the trails were widened into bridle paths to accommodate the horsemen and the drivers of packhorses. Later these paths were widened still more for oxcarts, wagons, and coaches. The construction of such a road was a simple matter. It meant merely the widening of a path by clearing away the brush and small trees, the laying of logs or saplings across marshy places (such roads were called corduroy roads; see p. 257), and the construction of an occasional wooden bridge, over which a roof usually was built to protect the wood from the weather. Many streams were without bridges or ferries, and had to be forded, which meant that during the rainy season the roads were often blocked by the high water. 

Some of the larger streams were crossed by means of toll ferries. Sometimes the roads became so muddy that they were almost impassable. In the North, travel was much better in the winter, when the ground was frozen and often covered with snow, at which time sleighs offered an easy means of travel.

The first trunk line road, known as the Common Road, from Boston to Providence was completed in 1654, and later was extended to New York under the name of the Shore Road. The King's Path, from New York to 

Philadelphia, was completed a little later. These were the only roads before 

1763 which offered a regular schedule of travel by public conveyance. 

Early Means of Travel. During the seventeenth century almost the only method of overland travel was by horseback, and both men and women made use of this mode of transportation. About the close of the century, when the roads were being improved, the stagecoach came into

use and became the most common method of travel by land until the coming of the railroad. The first coach line was operated on a regular schedule between Boston and Rhode Island, in 1718. About the middle of the eighteenth century, the trip from Boston to New York could be made in four days, and in three days more the traveler could go from New York to Philadelphia.

The Transportation of Freight. The first agents of overland freight transportation, besides man himself, were packhorses, which carried heavy loads of goods in large packs suspended on both sides of the animal. Some of the planters solved the problem of getting their tobacco to market by packing it in large barrels, known as hogsheads, through which an axle had been run, and then rolling it to market by horsepower. Such bulky products as hay and grain were fed to cattle, and these were later driven to market, for it was much easier to transport the cattle than the crop of grain and hay. In the course of time, carts and rough wagons came into use. That such vehicles were not in common use during the seventeenth century is indicated by the fact that Philadelphia in 1697 could proudly boast of but thirty wheeled vehicles of all descriptions. 

The Turnpikes. The great westward movement, which began on a large scale after the cession by Great Britain (in 1783) of the land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi River, created a need for better roads. 

Shortly before the Revolution, Daniel Boone blazed his famous trail through Cumberland Gap and thence along a buffalo trail to Boonesborough. This trail was gradually developed into the Wilderness Road, which for a time after the Revolution, became the main artery to the West. 

The greatest problem in the construction of roads during this period was a financial one. Naturally the poor and sparsely settled communities in the West were unable to pay the cost of building long roads to the East, and the state and national governments hesitated to undertake such projects. The right of the national government to promote internal improvements at public expense became one of the great political questions of the day. The construction of roads by private capital was a partial solution of the problem. In 1792 a charter was granted for the construction of a privately owned road between Philadelphia and Lancaster, Pennsylvania. 

At intervals, long poles with sharp spikes were lowered across the road to force the traveler to stop and pay toll for the use of the road-hence the name "turnpike." This enterprise was such a success that it was imitated in all sections of the country. In the course of time, most of the turnpikes were absorbed into the state highway systems, but a few survived until the twentieth century.

Western Roads. The national government in 1811 began the construction of a road to the West from Cumberland, Maryland, and by 1817 it was completed to Wheeling, Virginia. It was known as the Cumberland Road or National Road. Political bickering interfered with the extension of the road, and its western terminus at Vandalia, Illinois, was not reached until 1852. The eastern portion of the road was eighty feet wide, with a thirtyfoot strip in the center constructed of crushed rocks covered with gravel, while the western part was not so highly improved. This road was the most important route to the West during the period of westward migration, and nearly every day it was used by a constant stream of cattle and hogs, packhorses loaded with freight, immigrants on foot or on horseback, stagecoaches, and Conestoga wagons.

Other important roads in the West were the Michigan Road from St. 

Joseph, Michigan, to Madison, Indiana, on the Ohio River; and the 

Natchez Road from Nashville to New Orleans. 

The Stagecoach. Although the stagecoach had appeared in many places in colonial times, it did not come into general use before the Revolution. There were only thirty-eight privately owned coaches in Pennsylvania in 1761, but with the construction of better roads it became the common method of travel. Regular stagecoach lines connected all of the important towns in the East; other lines to the West ran along the Cumberland Road; and still others carried passengers to Cleveland, Cincinnati, and other points north and south. HELCK Stagecoach arriving at an inn on the Cumberland Road Travel by stagecoach offered none of the comforts to which the modern traveler is accustomed. The roads were rough, and the earliest coaches were without springs. It was not unusual to request passengers to walk over a steep or dangerous part of the road, or to ask their assistance in lifting the wheels out of a rut. The first coaches had open panels, which in wet or cold weather were covered with leather curtains attached to buttons.

These curtains, however, were not a good protection against the wind, rain, or snow, and we can readily understand the satisfaction of the driver and passengers when they reached the cheerful fire of an inn after a cold. day of travel.

Inns and Taverns. Necessary accompaniments of the stagecoach days were the inns or taverns. They were the common gathering places of the community for the exchange of news, opinions, and drinks. The better inns offered many comforts to the travelers, such as warm fires, good food and drink, and comfortable beds. The wagon taverns for the drivers and poorer passengers were not so attractive, for in these were no private bedrooms, and the guests provided their own bedding, which they spread on the floor of the large common room which served as a bar room by day and a bedroom by night. Little sleep was possible because of the boisterous conduct of some of the guests.

The Conestoga Wagon. The freight car of the turnpikes was the 

Conestoga wagon. It is said to have been used for the first time when 

General Braddock made his expedition against Fort Duquesne, in 1755, and it became the chief means of travel and transportation by the pioneers as they moved into the Mississippi Valley, and still later, into California and Oregon. In the settlement of the Far West it was usually known as the "prairie schooner," or the "covered wagon." It did not entirely disappear from use until the latter part of the nineteenth century. 

The Conestoga wagon got its name from the Conestoga Valley, in Pennsylvania, where it originated. It was especially constructed for rough roads; the wheels were broad to prevent miring in the soft earth; the body 

Covered wagons crossing a Western prairie; from the moving picture "The Covered Wagon" Paramount

was built high above the ground and was made water tight so that it would float when crossing deep streams; and the bottom of the wagon bed was curved so that on steep hills the wagon load would not slip on the floor to either end. The wagon was covered with canvas supported by hoop-shaped slats. It could carry a load of from four to six tons and was drawn by from four to six horses. (For a picture of a Conestoga wagon, see page 

301.) It is interesting to note that the use of this wagon for commercial purposes was at first protested by the packhorse drivers, who considered it an infringement upon their rights.

The Canal Era. Hauling products to market over long distances in wagons was too expensive, and cheaper means of transportation were sought. Americans were acquainted with the cheapness of water transportation, but there were no through water routes connecting the East and the West. On some of the rivers there were navigable portions separated by rapids and waterfalls. Canals around these obstructions were needed. 

The first canal of importance in America, authorized by the legislature of Virginia in 1785, was one of this type between Richmond and Westham. 

It was only seven miles in length. A number of the other early canals were constructed to connect different navigable waters not far apart. The 

Dismal Swamp Canal, connecting Chesapeake Bay and Albemarle Sound, was completed in 1794, and the Middlesex Canal, between Boston and the Merrimac River, was begun in 1795 and completed in 1808. 

Soon after the close of the War of 1812 Governor DeWitt Clinton, of New York, became convinced of the practicability of building a canal between Albany and Buffalo. The Mohawk River and small lakes and streams farther west suggested a feasible route between the Hudson River and Lake Erie, and of course it would be a simple matter to move goods on the Hudson River between Albany and New York City. Failing to interest the national government in the project, Clinton persuaded his state to undertake it alone. The digging began in 1817 and eight years later the canal, forty feet wide and over 360 miles in length, had been completed at a cost of about $8,000,000. The advantages of this route were immediately apparent. It was discovered that the cost of shipping goods through the canal was only about one thirtieth of what it had cost to transport them by wagon; and the time required was reduced from twenty days to eight days. The canal soon became crowded with traffic, and in 1835 it was enlarged. By 1837 it had paid for itself, in the tolls paid for its use. Of course New York City profited most from the construction of the canal, for it now became the outlet for most of the western products. Its growth was very rapid.

Other cities, envious of the good fortune of New York, began to consider the feasibility of other canals to the West which would give them a part of the Western trade. In spite of the high mountains, Philadelphia undertook the construction of a canal to Pittsburgh. However, a large number of locks were necessary on that route, and the boats had to be pulled over one mountain range by cables operated by steam engines. 

Courtesy New York Public Library 

Canalboat on the Erie Canal, about 1830. In the foreground is a highway bridge crossing the canal.

Naturally the cost of transportation was greater than on the Erie Canal, and the traffic was never heavy. The construction of the Baltimore and 

Ohio Railroad* in the 1830's put an end to such projects in the East, but in the West several successful canals were constructed between Lake Erie and the Ohio River and between Lake Michigan and the Mississippi River. 

River Transportation. Before the completion of the Erie Canal the main outlet of the West was the Mississippi River. In the early days, farm products were loaded on rafts and floated down the river to New Orleans, where they were transferred to ocean-going vessels and carried to foreign countries. Improvements were made in the raft by building sides and a cabin upon it; later the entire structure was enclosed under a roof. 

These flatboats, which were from forty to ninety feet long, and from ten to twenty feet wide, were driven by the current and guided by one or more long sweeps. Since it was almost impossible to push the boat upstream it *The account of the earliest railroads is given in the following chapter, pages 539-543, so as to include it as part of the complete story of railroad development.

was usually broken up when it had completed its trip, and the lumber in it was sold. With the coming of the steamboat, the flatboats quickly lost their importance. More than 2,000 flatboats arrived in New Orleans in 

1846, but in 1855 there were only 718, and by 1860 they had almost disappeared. 

The First Steamboats. Although Robert Fulton is given the credit for building the first successful steamboat, we should remember that he was not the first man to apply steam power to boats; for before the Clermont was launched, in 1807, several Americans had made steamboats that were operated by their own power. Probably the most important of the predecessors of Robert Fulton was the inventor John Fitch, who in 1787 built a steamboat that could travel at the rate of three miles an hour. He built several other boats that were propelled by steam, one of which, in 1790, traveled more than a thousand miles on the Delaware River, in regular trips between Philadelphia and Trenton, at an average speed of seven or eight miles an hour. His engine, however, did not have enough power to propel a heavily loaded boat, and so the invention was not a commercial success. Fitch also experimented with a screw propeller, but he could not raise enough funds to complete the experiment. Reduced to poverty, and broken in spirit, he retired to his home at Bardstown, Kentucky, where he died in 1798. Other Americans who made important contributions to early steam navigation were John Stevens, James Rumsey, and Robert Livingston.

Fulton employed no new ideas in the construction of the first successful steamboat; he merely assembled ideas he had received from Fitch, Rumsey, and Livingston, and with scientific precision worked them into a boat which revolutionized water transportation. The crowd which had gathered at New York City to jeer at the attempt to move "Fulton's Folly" up the Hudson changed their jeers to cheers when the Clermont successfully began its trip to Albany. The 150-mile trip upstream was completed in thirty-two hours, and the return trip in thirty hours. Two weeks later under the management of Fulton and his partner, Livingston, the Clermont began regular scheduled trips between New York and Albany, and the practicability of the steamboat was definitely established. 

The Extension of Steamboat Traffic. The rapid development of the steamboat was hindered for a time by a monopoly over steamboat operation granted to Fulton and Livingston, in New York, and also on the lower Mississippi. In 1824 the monopoly was broken by a decision of the Supreme Court, and steamboats began to appear in considerable numbers on all of the important rivers and lakes. Although many dangers were

involved in the early navigation of the Mississippi, yet in 1839 the steamboat tonnage on "Ole Man River" exceeded the steamboat tonnage of the British Empire. Improvements in the river steamboats were extremely rapid, for not only were they increased in size and tonnage capacity, but the speed increased as well. In 1817 over twenty-five days were required to make the trip from New Orleans to Louisville; but by 1853 the distance was covered in less than four and one half days. The rapid development of the West caused the traffic on the Mississippi and Ohio rivers to increase by leaps and bounds until about 1860, when the extension of railroads into the Mississippi Valley caused a decline in the importance of the steamboat. 

Steam navigation on the Great Lakes did not show such a rapid growth because of the competition of sailing vessels which could operate more cheaply than the steamboats on the lake waters. 

Our Early Merchant Marine. Under the protection of the Navigation 

Acts the colonies had built up a respectable merchant marine; but when 

Great Britain recognized their independence in 1783 she regarded her former colonies as a foreign power and closed her markets to them. The industrious Yankee sailors sought recompense for the loss of the British markets by turning to the Baltic and the Mediterranean countries for new commercial adventures, and in 1784 a new field was opened when the 

Empress of China sailed for Canton. Boston and Salem, in Massachusetts, soon became the rival centers of a lucrative Chinese trade. Early in the nineteenth century, packet lines were established; that is, lines on which ships sailed between two or more ports on a regular schedule. The first of the American packet lines across the Atlantic was the 

Black Ball Line, which was operated for the first time, in 1816, between New York and Liverpool. So comfortably fitted and so fast were the American packet line ships that they succeeded in getting a large part of the transatlantic trade.

The Yankee Clippers. The keen competition which developed after the War of 1812

Courtesy N. Y. Museum of Natural History 

A clipper ship-the Flying Cloud made the speed factor almost decisive in the struggle for the world's carrying trade. The American packet liner Emerald established a remarkable record for that day when it made the western passage

from Liverpool to New York in seventeen days; but American ingenuity scored its greatest triumph with the development of the "clipper," or fast sailing ship with tall slanting masts and large sails. The first clipper ship, the Ann McKim, was built at Baltimore in 1832, and was followed by others made by the shipbuilders of that city. John Willis Griffiths, of New York, suggested some changes in design, and in 1843 began the construction of the Rainbow, which was launched in 1845. This clipper, on a voyage to China, made the round trip in less time than any other ship could make the trip one way from Canton to New York. Later the voyage from Canton to New York was made in seventy-three days. 

The most famous of all of the clippers was the Flying Cloud, which made the trip from New York around Cape Horn to San Francisco in eighty-

With the discovery of gold and the resulting rush to California, and the abandonment of the Navigation Acts by the British government in 1854, enthusiasm for the clipper ships still further increased. 

Great Britain, for a time, even feared the loss of her marine supremacy. 

Decline of the American Merchant Marine. Many changes were brought about by the War between the States. For some time before the beginning of the war a shift had been in progress from sail to steam. American steamship owners had devoted most of their energies to the development of the river and coastwise traffic, but some attention was given to ocean navigation. In 1819 the Savannah was the first steamship to cross the Atlantic, but not with her steam power alone; she used sails also during

part of the voyage. With the construction of the British ship Great Western, which made the trip across the Atlantic without refueling and without the use of sails, the supremacy in steam navigation of the ocean gradually passed to Great Britain, but for a time the American clipper ships more than held their own. Soon, however, the British shipbuilders gained another advantage over their rivals when they began the construction of vessels built of iron. During the War between the States the risks to 

American shipping became so great because of the activities of the Confederate commerce raiders, the Alabama and the Florida, and marine insurance rates were so prohibitive, that many American shipowners sold or transferred their vessels to foreign flags. A factor which encouraged them to do this was the opportunity for more lucrative investments in the rapidly expanding American industries. After 1860 the American merchant marine declined to a position of relative unimportance among the commercial nations of the world.

CHAPTER XXVIII Transportation in the Machine Age 

Antecedents of the Railroad. The cities along the Atlantic seaboard were not content to see New York practically monopolize the western trade as a result of the construction of the Erie Canal. Their efforts to retaliate by the construction of other canals having met with little success, they sought other means of commerce with the West. The railroad suggested a possible solution to the problem. For some time men in England and America had been experimenting with the operation of cars on specially constructed tracks and had met with some success, but the greatest problem was that of power. Some Americans had tried the inclined plane, on which gravity was the propelling force; others tried tramways, on which cars were pulled by horse power. Such a tramway was in operation in 1826 from Quincy, Massachusetts, to Neponset River, a distance of three miles. 

Over this road was hauled the granite used in the construction of the Bunker Hill monument. 

Ever since James Watt had built the first successful steam engine scientists had been attempting to discover some means by which it could be made to move under its own power and pull a load after it. Steam engines had indeed been made to move under their own power before 1825, but they had not been able to develop enough power to move with any practicable speed or pulling force. In 1829 George Stephenson, an English inventor, assembled the ideas of several other men into the Rocket, which really proved to be practicable. Thus Stephenson did for the locomotive what Fulton, twenty-two years earlier, had done for the steamboat. 

The First American Railroads. The first railroad in America, constructed specifically for the purpose of carrying freight and passengers, was the Baltimore and Ohio, chartered in 1827. The first rail was laid 

July 4, 1828. The operators, having tried unsuccessfully treadmills run by horse power and even sails for power, fell back upon the use of cars pulled by horses; but Peter Cooper, who was interested in the road, attempted to 539

PETER COOPERS TOM TALIM 629-30 BALTINORE & OHIO R. R. 

Courtesy Baltimore and Ohio R. R.

The first American locomotive, the Tom Thumb, with one of the earliest passenger cars convince them of the practicability of the steam locomotive by constructing the Tom Thumb, so named because of its midget size. In 1830, when the trial was made, the little locomotive pushed a car loaded with twentyfour passengers, at the rate of four miles per hour; and it did better in later trials. In 1831, too, Phineas Davis built the York, which was able to make a speed of fifteen miles per hour, and to pull on the level a load of fifteen tons.

The second railroad in America, and the first constructed specifically for the use of steam power, was the Charleston and Hamburg, chartered in 1829. In November, 1830, the locomotive named The Best Friend, which had been built for this road by a New York concern, attained the remarkable speed of thirty miles per hour. The next year the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad Company constructed a seventeen-mile line between Schenectady and Albany, the first link in the great New York Central system which was developed two decades later. By 1835 the railroads were rapidly gaining acceptance with the American public. In that year the Baltimore and Ohio alone carried a hundred thousand passengers over its road, which was then completed and in operation for only about seventy miles of its length.

Difficulties of Early Railroad Travel. The first locomotives were by no means safe, and accidents were common. Little was known about the use of steam, and some of the lessons learned by the trial-and-error method were very expensive. For instance, the boiler of The Best Friend was blown up when the negro fireman, who did not like the sound of the escaping steam, sat on the safety valve. The rails, too, were unsafe. The earliest rails were made of timber or stone. A little later, iron strips were

laid on the rails, and it was a common accident for the ends of the strips to become loose under the jar of the traffic and be driven through the floor of a car. Defects in the rails and sharp curves in the tracks frequently caused the derailment of the trains. Gradually cast-iron rails came into use, but, although a great improvement, they were brittle and unequal to the task of carrying the constantly increasing weight of the traffic. The inefficient couplers and brakes were another hazard. The coaches in the first trains were connected with chains of three links which allowed a considerable amount of play between them. When the slack was taken up in starting the train, passengers often were jerked from their seats. The results were equally unpleasant when attempts were made to stop, for when the brakes were applied on the engine each coach bumped into the one in front of it in a way that must have been very disconcerting to the passengers; really there was sometimes danger of the fragile coaches being wrecked.

The first American passenger trains followed the British idea of a number of stagecoaches pulled on a track by a locomotive. Often the passengers sat in the open, fully exposed to a constant shower of sparks from the puffing, wood-burning engine. The next improvement was a passenger car divided into compartments, carrying out the idea of several stagecoaches combined into one. This type of car is still in use in Great Britain. But gradually a distinctive American passenger car evolved. Showing the influence of the canal era, it was more like a boat on wheels-an enclosed room having two parallel rows of seats with an aisle between them. The

Railroads of the United States in 1860 

seats were nothing more than wooden benches. There was no provision for ventilation except the windows on each side, and in cold weather when the windows were kept closed on a long trip the air might become extremely foul.

In spite of all of these dangers and discomforts the railroads became more and more popular and their construction went on with great rapidity. 

In 1830 there were only 23 miles of railroad in the United States; by 

1840 the railroad mileage had increased to 2,818; and by 1860 it was 

30,626. Among the important roads that were built within thirty years

after the Baltimore and Ohio were the Pennsylvania, the New York Central, the New York and Erie, the Michigan Central, the Western and Atlantic, the Nashville and Chattanooga, the Mobile and Ohio, the 

Illinois Central, and the Rock Island.

A Transcontinental Railroad Is Envisioned. As early as 1832 a railroad to the Pacific coast had been suggested; after the acquisition of Oregon in 

1846, and California in 1848, the agitation became more enthusiastic. Not only would such a road bind together the extreme limits of the nation, but it was claimed that it would secure for us the lucrative and much-soughtafter trade with China. Some men, such as Thomas H. Benton, wanted a road to the Pacific in order to develop a portion of the Middle West in which they were especially interested. There were several suggested eastern termini for the road: Chicago, St. Louis, Memphis, New Orleans, and even 

Charleston. The choice of a terminus became a sectional issue which remained unsolved until the consideration of a southern city was eliminated by the secession of the Southern states. The competition was then narrowed to the adherents of Chicago and St. Louis. In 1862 these groups compromised their differences and Congress passed the Pacific Railroad Act, authorizing the construction of a transcontinental railroad with its terminus near Ft. Kearney, in Nebraska, from which point branch lines were to be extended to the near-by cities. Both St. Louis and Chicago would thus profit from the construction of the road. The act was passed as a war measure to protect the Pacific coast and to hold the Far West within the Union.

The Transcontinental Railroad Is Completed. Two companies were to build the railroad. The Central Pacific was to begin at Sacramento and build toward the east; and the Union Pacific was to begin at the eastern terminus and work westward. At first it was agreed that the juncture of the two companies should be near the California line, but later it was decided to let each company build as far as it could. Since the land bounties and bond subsidies offered by the government depended upon the number of miles laid by each of the rival companies, the construction of the road became a race. The Union Pacific had the advantage of a comparatively level roadway for most of the distance and an ample labor supply of Irish workers and war veterans, but it was handicapped by hostile Indians and by the unprincipled conduct of the Credit Mobilier (see p. 713). The roadbed was poorly constructed, little thought being given to anything but the completion of as many miles as possible. The 

Central Pacific was better organized and its work was better done, but it had to face greater obstacles than its rival. The route across the Sierra

Nevada was extremely difficult and much of the material had to be brought from the East around Cape Horn. Chinese coolies furnished most of the labor.

On May 10, 1869, the road was completed at Promontory, Utah, north of Great Salt Lake, with elaborate ceremonies. The last spike, which was of gold, was driven into a polished California laurel tie with a silver sledge hammer. The driving of the last blows was reported to all of the Eastern cities by telegraph, and everywhere the event was hailed as being almost as important in bringing the sections of the country together as the triumph of the Union at Appomattox. 

Era of Railroad Building. The completion of the transcontinental railroad was the beginning of an era of unparalleled railway construction. 

Everywhere the enthusiasm for more railroads was unbounded. At the close of the War between the States there were about 35,000 miles of railroad in the United States; seven years later, the mileage was doubled; by 

1880 it was over 93,000; and in 1920 it was more than 250,000. During this period of half a century an average of more than 4,000 miles of new railroads were constructed each year. At the close of the period the United 

States had more railway mileage than all of the European countries combined, and about one third of the total mileage of the world. In 1860 there was one mile of railroad to every 1,087 people in the United

States, but in 1920 there was one mile to every 418. Some of the larger systems that came into existence during this period were the 

Northern Pacific, the Santa Fe, the Great Northern, and the Southern Pacific. Men whose names are most closely associated with the development of the railroads are 

Cornelius Vanderbilt, E. H. Harriman, James J. Hill, Jay Gould, and 

J. P. Morgan. About 1916 railway mileage seems to have reached a maximum, and since that time it has been slightly reduced. Improved highways, with an ever-increasing number of privately owned automobiles and truck lines, have made the railroads less profitable, but part of the shrinkage has been due to the abandonment of unprofitable parallel lines which were constructed in 

Traveling at night on an early railroad car

the days of cutthroat competition but now are rendered useless as a result of consolidations. 

Consolidation of the Railroads. The tendency in recent years has been to grant monopolies to the utilities that serve the public-but with some governmental control over the rates to be charged. This principle was not observed in the early history of the railroad. Competition has never been keener or more unscrupulous than it was between the giants of the railroad world who were striving for the lion's share of the transportation business. 

Soon these leaders began to seek methods by which competition could be eliminated. Various forms of consolidations, too complicated for discussion here, were the result. In 1906 it was estimated that of the 224,000 miles of railroad in the United States, about 176,000 were controlled by seventeen systems, and about half of the total mileage was in the hands of six systems. It was even worse in 1921, when Senator Robert M. 

La Follette charged that 82 per cent of the country's transportation system was linked together by twenty-five common directors. 

Improvements in Service. The improvements in the safety and comforts of railway service have kept pace with the growth of the roads. Soon after 1860, steel rails replaced those made of iron; steel passenger cars took the place of the old wooden ones; and steel and concrete bridges came into use. Still other improvements which have added to the safety of railway travel are the automatic coupler; the Westinghouse air brake, by which the brakes on every car can be applied almost instantly; the block system of signals; and the interlocking switch systems. The adoption of the standard gauge (distance between the rails) of 4 feet 8½ inches has made it possible for goods to be sent from one side of the continent to the other without any transfers such as would be necessary if the gauge of the various roads were not the same. The importance of this improvement will be appreciated when we find that in 1866 twelve different gauges were in use on different railroad lines.

One of the greatest conveniences in railway travel is the Pullman car, first built in 1864 by George M. Pullman. The first Pullman, which was known as the Pioneer, was wider and higher than the other cars then in use and could not be used without some changes in the bridges and station platforms. When it was desired in 1865 to use the Pioneer in the funeral train of President Lincoln, the necessary changes were made in the road; the same thing happened a few years later on another road when President Grant wanted to take a trip in the Pullman. Still other railroads made the changes for the accommodation of the Pullmans, which immediately became immensely popular.

Courtesy N. Y. Central R. R.

Courtesy Pullman Co. 

On an early Pullman car

On a Pullman car of today As the number of Pullman cars increased, their designer introduced many luxuries. The standard Pullman was followed by the drawing-room or "palace" car, and this was followed by the "hotel" car which soon developed into the dining car. Since it frequently was necessary for the passengers, in order to reach the dining car, to pass from car to car while the train was moving, vestibule cars were brought into use. Some of the ultra-modern trains have their cars so articulated that the vestibuled connections between cars are no longer necessary. Another feature of modern trains is air conditioning, by which pure air is supplied at a comfortable temperature, thus eliminating many of the discomforts of travel. Many improvements have been made also in the railway stations and lunch rooms.

Freight service, too, has been improved. The first freight cars were flat, the goods being held in place upon them by ropes. Then sides and cloth covers-not unlike those of the Conestoga wagons-were used to protect the goods from the weather. Soon the boxcar was developed, and now we have freight cars adapted to almost every type of commerce-cars especially constructed for hauling coal; flatcars for heavy machinery and logs; furniture cars; refrigerators for the transportation of fruits, perishable vegetables, and meats; and specially constructed oil tanks.

Modern Locomotives. Perhaps the most striking difference between a locomotive in use today and that of a century ago is in the size. The Best 

Friend or the York would be a pygmy indeed in comparison with one of the great compound locomotives now in use on some of our roads. There are many other improvements too technical for discussion here. The old wood-burners were long ago replaced by coal-burners, and on many of our

Western roads oil has replaced coal as fuel. A still more recent introduction is the electric locomotive. As early as 1895 the Baltimore and Ohio used electric locomotives to pull trains through tunnels. Since then they have been put into use in the railroad yards and subways of our largest cities because of their freedom from smoke and cinders, and on some of the mountain roads where great power is required. Two of the most important roads that have been electrified are the New York, New Haven, and Hartford Railroad in the East, and more than six hundred miles of the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul, and Pacific Railroad through the Rockies. Perhaps the main reason why the steam locomotives have not been much more extensively replaced has been the great cost of installing the electrical equipment. The competition of the motor truck and motor bus has forced the railway companies to make many changes, especially on their branch lines. Some companies have abandoned their branch lines for truck and

Streamline Trains. The roads have made important changes to meet the new conditions and the increased competition. Speed and safety are two important factors in transportation. A new kind of passenger train, which travels at a speed of nearly two miles a minute, has been developed. 

Such trains are Diesel-engined and streamlined, and are comparatively light in weight. On May 26, 1934, such a train established a new nonstop world's record in running 1,015 miles in 785 minutes, from Denver to Chicago, for the reopening of the Century of Progress Exposition. Various streamline trains are now in actual service and more are being built. 

Government Aid to Railroads. Few, if any, of the problems of our early railroad companies were more pressing than the financial. This was especially true of the long transcontinental lines which extended for hundreds of miles through uninhabited or sparsely settled sections of the country, with no immediate prospect of dividends for the stockholders. 

But the national government, which had given up the principle of government ownership of roads and canals, was tremendously interested in the construction of the railroads, and came to the assistance of the promoters in such a way as almost to guarantee the financial success of the venture. 

This aid was extended in several forms. Sometimes it was given in the form of cash subsidies; often it was extended through the purchase of railroad bonds; but the most common method of aiding was by making grants of public land. When the Union Pacific was constructed the government loaned each of the companies engaged in its construction from $16,000 to $48,000 for each mile of road, and granted the alternate sections of public

land in a belt along the road, twenty miles in width. Similarly, the Santa 

Fe was given a grant of 6,400 acres of land for each mile of the road. By 

1871 the national government had granted nearly 200,000,000 acres to the railroad companies, but the amount of land actually delivered to them was reduced to about 137,000,000 acres by forfeitures resulting from the failure of some of the companies to meet the terms of the grants. 

The states also gave assistance to the railroad builders, especially in the early period of construction when sectional rivalry was very keen for the control of Western commerce. State aid also was frequently given through grants of land, but sometimes the states purchased the bonds and also the stock of the railroad companies. Some of the earlier charters given by the states granted exemption from the payment of taxes, sometimes permanently, but more often for a specified number of years or until the dividends had reached a percentage named in the charter. The right of eminent domain, which gave the company authority to purchase land for the right of way by condemnation proceedings, was always given to the railroads.

Corrupt Practices of the Railroads. In order to profit from the government's generosity, some of the railroad owners were tempted to extend lines into unprofitable areas, or even to build them parallel to other lines. 

In the bitter competition that resulted, rates were reduced so low that it was impossible to conduct the business on a profitable basis. This competition between the roads led to many kinds of unfair practices. Discriminations were made between shippers. Of course it was the desire of each of the competitive companies to secure the patronage of the big shippers; and they attempted to do this by means of lower rates than were charged to others, or by rebates; that is, by secretly refunding to the favored shipper a part of the freight charges. For instance, the Pennsylvania Railroad 

Company granted to the leading oil company rebates amounting to from 25 to 50 per cent of the freight charges on the oil it shipped on their lines; and in addition to this they gave it a similar percentage of the freight charges collected from competing companies that had to pay the regular rates. Discriminations were also made between places. A city served by several competitive roads enjoyed lower rates than a city served by only one road. It frequently happened that the charges would be less for a long haul to a city also served by a rival road than for a shorter haul to a city through which the goods would have to pass, but over which the road enjoyed a monopoly.

Sometimes the railroad companies sought to overcome competition by forming agreements to charge uniform rates or to divide the profits be-

tween themselves on a specified proportional basis. Such agreements were known as pools. When the pools had been declared illegal, several other means of overcoming competition were resorted to, such as holding companies, mergers, and interlocking directorates, by which two or more rival companies would be unified under one management so as to avoid further competition.

The Granger Railroad Legislation. The farmers in some of the Middle 

Western states rebelled against the discriminatory practices of the railroads. Meeting in their local lodges, or "granges," they began an agitation for regulatory legislation by the state legislatures. As a result of this agitation, some of the states enacted a series of laws directed against the corrupt practices of the railroads. There was some question, however, about the constitutional right of a state to regulate interstate commerce. 

The constitutionality of the laws was upheld in 1876 by the Supreme Court in the Munn vs. Illinois case; but ten years later, in the case of the Wabash 

Railroad vs. Illinois, the court reversed its earlier view and denied the states the right to fix rates on shipments to other states. 

Federal Regulation of the Railroads. State regulation having broken down, the question now was strictly up to the Federal government. In 

1887 Congress passed the famous Interstate Commerce Act, which declared pools and the discriminatory practices of the railroads illegal and required the publication of all freight and passenger rates. A commission of five members was appointed to see that the provisions of the act were enforced. The law, however, had many weaknesses, and the companies found various ways of evading its provisions. During the first decade of the twentieth century Congress made several attempts to strengthen the Interstate Commerce Commission. The Elkins Act in 1903 was directed specifically against rebates, which persisted in spite of the Interstate Commerce Act. Three years later the Hepburn Act was passed, enlarging the membership of the commission to seven, and extending its authority over pipe lines, express companies, and Pullman companies. It also gave the commission power to determine just and reasonable rates, and to pre scribe the form of accounts and records kept by the companies under its supervision. In 1910 the authority of the commission was still further increased by the Mann-Elkins Act, and its jurisdiction was extended to telephone, telegraph, and cable companies. Later acts which firmly established the principle of regulation by the Federal government were the Newlands Act of 1913, providing for voluntary settlement of railroad disputes, and the Adamson Act in 1916, regulating the hours of labor on railroads engaged in interstate commerce.

Government Operation of the Railroads during the World War. The necessity for the quick movement of war materials and supplies, as well as soldiers, to the eastern ports placed a burden upon the railroads which they were unable to carry unless they co-operated, and co-operation was prohibited by the antitrust laws. To overcome these obstacles and secure consideration and effective service quickly, President Wilson on December 26, 1917, resorting to his war powers, issued a proclamation providing for government operation and appointed William G. McAdoo Director General of the Railroads. His action was later confirmed by Congress. This was a new activity for the government, but it was believed to be necessary, for the railway terminals near the ports from which troops and war supplies were being rushed to France were in a paralyzed condition. The government secured efficiency, for the railroads were managed as if they belonged to one great company. In order to relieve the congested terminals, some goods were routed over longer routes to other ports. The one object was to move the goods as rapidly as possible, for European nations were calling for our immediate assistance. The government accomplished its purpose in the operation of the railroads during the war. After the war was over Congress passed the Esch-Cummins bill (Transportation Act of 1920), by which the railroads were returned to their owners. 

Recent Attitude of the Government toward the Railroads. Since the 

World War the Federal government has departed from its policy of opposing all efforts of the railroads to overcome competition, and in many other ways has changed its attitude toward corporations in general. Some of these changes may be seen in the Transportation Act of 1920, frequently known as the Esch-Cummins Act. The following are some of the most important provisions of the act: (1) The membership of the Interstate 

Commerce Commission was increased to eleven. (2) The powers of the commission were greatly increased by giving it the power to fix minimum as well as maximum rates and to control the issuance of railroad stocks and bonds. (3) Pooling and charging more for a short haul than a long haul was permitted, if it had the approval of the commission. (4) Combinations and consolidations were not only permitted but even encouraged, and the commission was directed to propose a scheme of consolidation. (5) The law also contained a “recapture" clause, which directed that half of all earnings in excess of a fair return should be returned to the commission. 

This money was to be placed in a sinking fund for distribution to the weaker roads which were unable to attain a reasonable earning. 

The depression which came upon the nation in 1929 made it necessary for the railroads to ask the government for special assistance. In answer

to this request, rates were increased, and a ten per cent wage reduction was ordered. In January, 1932, Congress, acting upon the recommendation of 

President Hoover, created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, with authority to make needed loans to railroads and other business enterprises. 

On June 16, 1933, the Emergency Railroad Transportation Act was passed, providing for a greater co-ordination of the transportation agencies of the nation. A system of railroad control was designed to avoid duplication of service and unnecessary competition, to prevent waste, to improve credit, and to encourage the financial reorganization of the railroads. 

Joseph B. Eastman was appointed to fill the office of Federal Co-ordinator, which was created by the act, and continued until June, 1936. 

Transportation by Express. Closely connected with the growth of the railroads was the rise and development of express service. Our modern civilization demands the rapid transportation of many small commodities, the value of which is great in comparison with their bulk. The regular freight service of the railroads did not meet this need. In the colonial days the stagecoach drivers frequently were called upon to deliver small parcels and even to pay or collect bills along their routes. For this service they charged small fees. When the railroads supplanted the stagecoaches, the conductors made an effort to continue this service. William F. Harnden, a conductor on the Boston and Worcester Railroad, saw the need of a regularly organized express service, and in 1839 he contracted with the Boston and Providence Railroad, and the John W. Richmond, a steamer between Providence and New York, to handle their express business. At

first he acted as his own messenger, but the business expanded so rapidly that it soon became necessary for him to establish offices with corps of assistants in both New York and Boston. Harnden even extended the business into an international service. 

In the meantime, other express companies had entered the field, chief of which was Adams and Company, which had been established the next year after Harnden entered the business. Early in the 1850's this company had extended beyond its original field in New York and New England into the Atlantic and Gulf states and even to San Francisco. In 1854 it bought out all of its principal rivals, and reorganized under the name Adams Express Company. Two other important express companies that had come into existence by 1860 were the American Express Company, with its chief field of operations around the Great Lakes; and the Wells- 

Fargo Company, of the Pacific coast. A voluntary division in the Adams 

Express Company during the War between the States brought into existence the Southern Express Company, which continued a separate existence until all express companies were merged during the World War. 

The merger of express companies so far as the handling of express business in the United States is concerned―gave it all to the newly created Railway Express Agency. But a large part of the work originally done by the express companies had already been taken over instead by the Parcel Post service which was begun by the national government in 1912. 

The Automobile. The invention of the steam engine was followed almost immediately by efforts to apply steam power to vehicles. As early as 1769 Nicholas Joseph Cugnot, a French military officer, invented a gun carriage which was driven by steam. He was followed by a host of English and American mechanics who invented steam wagons or steam coaches, some of which attained a speed of from fifteen to twenty miles per hour; but the inventions were not practicable because of the heavy weight of the steam engine which propelled them, and because of the poor roads. 

When the steam locomotive had proved its value on the railroad, interest in the steam coach lagged. Invention of the light but powerful gasoline engine revived interest in the "horseless carriage." In 1879 George B. 

Selden applied for a patent on an automobile propelled by an internal combustion engine, but for a number of years he was unable to get the financial support necessary for the manufacture of his automobile, and the patent was not granted until 1895. Meanwhile three other men had produced successful automobiles-Charles Duryea, Elwood Haynes, and Henry Ford. For a while electric automobiles deriving their power from storage batteries were popular, and some steam automobiles were used,
