A very early automobile race but it was not long until the gasoline-driven car was almost universally adopted.

Since the Duryea machine was invented in 1892, many improvements in automobiles have been made. Two of the most important of these are the pneumatic tire and the self-starter. With the improvements for safety and comfort there was a corresponding increase in speed; the Duryea machine could go only seven or eight miles an hour, while in 1938 G. E. 

T. Eyston, in a racing automobile at Bonneville, Utah, attained a record speed of 357.5 miles an hour. For a time the automobile was merely a plaything for the rich. It is estimated that in 1900 there were only 8,000 automobiles in the United States, but as their cost was reduced, they came to be regarded almost as a necessity; and today there are enough automobiles in the United States to permit our entire population to ride at one time.*

Motor Trucks and Busses. Motor trucks began to come into use about 

1904. Their cheap operation gave them an advantage in their competition with the railroads, and for a time it seemed that the truck might ruin the freight business of the railroads; but it has been discovered that the truck is most profitable for short hauls, while the railroad can give better service on through freight traffic. Consequently, there is a field for both; in fact, in many instances the trucks serve as feeders to the railroads. 

The motor bus began about 1910 with the "jitney," or pleasure car used to carry passengers for pay. It soon gave way to the much larger bus, and by 1933 there were more than 100,000 motor busses in the United States. Today there are regular bus lines operating between most of the more important cities, and some of them do a transcontinental business. 

Influence of the Automobile on American Life. Perhaps no other invention has had so great an effect upon American life as the automobile. 

No longer must many farmers live in isolation, for a trip to town which *In the year 1937 the number of motor vehicles that were registered in the United States was 29,705,220.

formerly required a whole day may now be a matter of only an hour or two. School busses have caused many little one-teacher schools to give way to splendid consolidated schools which compare favorably with those in the cities. The cities, too, are undergoing a great change. Since the automobile has solved the problem of transportation, more and more families are making their homes in suburbs where they are free from many of the unpleasant features of city life, and yet are in a position to enjoy all of its benefits.

Improved Highways. The rapid development of the automobile just described would have been impossible but for a corresponding improvement in the roads. Roads had been neglected for a half century before 1890. The bicycle craze early in the 90's, and the establishment of the Rural Free Delivery mail service in 1896, revived to some extent the interest in better highways; but the automobile made good roads a necessity. Good Roads clubs were formed; legislatures were urged to undertake the construction of highways; and many states organized highway departments. In 1916 

Congress passed the Good Roads Bill, which provided for an appropriation by the Federal government of $85,000,000 to be distributed among the states on the basis of area, population, and post-road mileage, on condition that the states should pay equal amounts for the construction of good roads. Three years later the appropriations were increased by $200,000,ooo. It is estimated that by 1933 a total amount of from $2,500,000,000 to $3,000,000,000 was being spent annually by national, state, and local governmental units on the construction of highways. 

In 1930 the total highway mileage (rural) in the United States was estimated to be about 3,000,000 miles. Of this amount 23 per cent, or about 690,000 miles, were surfaced. High-type surfaced (concrete, brick, macadam, or asphalt) rural roads were almost unknown before the invention of the automobile; but by 1930 more than 125,000 miles of this type had been constructed. 

Improvements in Ocean Transportation. Since 1860 many improve ments have been made in overseas transportation. The screw propeller had come into use before 1860, and soon the twin-screw, and then the multiple-screw, vessels appeared. Now nearly all ocean-going vessels are of the multiple-screw type. A ship with only one screw propeller was helpless if anything happened to its one means of motive power or to its rudder; but a twin- or multiple-screw vessel can still proceed even if one of the propellers is disabled; and if the rudder is broken, the ship can be guided by the propellers in much the same way that a rowboat is guided with oars. Iron ships were coming into use in 1860, but about a decade

later it was discovered that the carrying capacity of the ships could be increased by the use of steel, which was much stronger than iron. By 1890 most of the new vessels were of steel. 

Some of the greatest improvements in modern ships have been in the engines. Multiple-expansion engines took the place of the early engines, which used only one expansion of the steam at low pressure. Turbine engines were the next improvement. In 1902 oil began to supplant coal as 

NORMANDIE 

Courtesy French Line

A modern ocean liner-The Normandie fuel, and today oil is used as fuel on nearly all American vessels. It was discovered about 1910 that oil might be converted into power directly by means of the Diesel type of internal-combustion engine. This elimination of steam boilers meant a considerable saving in space, labor, and equipment. It seems now that the Diesel-motor ship may relegate the steamship to the background in much the same way that the steamship outdid the sailing vessel.

Soon after the World War an interesting experiment was made with a new type of sailing vessel known as the rotor ship. A cylinder revolving at high speed offers much greater resistance to wind than sails having the same area. Instead of masts and sails the rotor ship uses cylinders that are made to revolve at a high rate of speed by electric motors. This type of vessel first made its appearance in Germany and then a few years later it was tried in America, but there is considerable doubt about its future in ocean traffic.

The Modern American Merchant Marine. We have already seen that the War between the States caused a considerable decline in the American merchant marine (p. 537). So great was the decline that by 1900 only 7.1 per cent of our foreign trade was carried in American vessels, as compared

with 66.5 per cent in 1860. The World War, however, stimulated interest in our merchant marine. German ships were driven from the seas, and 

German submarines took a heavy toll of Allied tonnage. In the month of 

April, 1917, the month in which we entered the war, the Allies lost a tonnage of 875,000. In order to meet the resulting shortage in carrying capacity, the United States government spent $4,000,000,000 on the construction of steel, wooden, and concrete ships under the direction of the government agency called the Emergency Fleet Corporation. So rapidly was the work carried on that American tonnage registered in foreign trade increased from 1,066,000 in 1914 to 11,077,000 in 1920; in the latter year, American ships were carrying over 42 per cent of our foreign trade-the best showing of our merchant marine since 1860. 

After the World War, when the emergency which had necessitated the increase in our marine tonnage no longer existed, considerable opposition arose to governmental competition with private shipping. Congress therefore passed the Jones Act (1920), which provided for the lease or sale of the steel ships to private owners; most of the wooden ships were scrapped. 

The result was another decline in the American merchant marine, which in 1933 was carrying only 33.4 per cent of our foreign commerce. It is not likely, however, that our share of the carrying trade will ever again reach the low level of 1900.

The Panama Canal Aids Transportation. The United States had been interested in the construction of a canal across the Isthmus of Panama since the discovery of gold in California in 1848 (see p. 317), but it wavered between the choice of a route across Nicaragua and one across Panama. 

While the United States was hesitating, a French company, headed by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the engineer who had constructed the Suez Canal, secured a franchise for the construction of a canal across Panama in 1879 and began the work of excavation four years later. The company failed, however, because of inefficiency, a lack of funds, and the prevalence of yellow fever and malaria. Interest in the United States was revived in 

1898 by the voyage of our battleship Oregon from the Pacific coast to Cuba by way of the Strait of Magellan. The need of a canal across the isthmus as a means of defense now was apparent to all. Soon after the close of the War with Spain the United States purchased the equipment and franchise of the French company. Failing to reach an agreement with 

Colombia concerning a right of way, our government encouraged the state of Panama to secede from Colombia. We then secured from Panama, in 

1903, the desired grant of control over a Canal Zone including the route of the canal.

Work on the Panama Canal was begun in 1904 and was completed in 1914. Most of the credit for the success of this greatest of all engineering feats belongs to Colonel George W. Goethals, who directed the work of construction, and Dr. William C. Gorgas, who removed the danger of yellow fever and malaria by a successful war upon the mosquitoes of that region. The canal soon became one of the world's busiest highways for trade, both foreign and coastwise, and today the traffic is so great that there is some agitation for the construction of another canal, across Nicaragua.

Experiments with Lighter-than-Air Machines. Man has always dreamed of flying. The first attempts were made with balloons. As early as 1783 two French brothers by the name of Montgolfier made short ascensions with balloons filled with hot air, and a few years later gas was used successfully. Since balloons must be at the mercy of the wind they can have very little value for purposes of transportation, and so scientists. began to experiment with balloons which could be driven through the air with engines. In 1851 such an airship, or dirigible, made a flight under the power of a steam engine, but it was the invention of the internal-combustion gasoline engine that made the dirigible practicable. Count Ferdinand von Zeppelin, of Germany, did more perhaps than any other person to develop the dirigible. He constructed an aluminum frame which enclosed a number of gas bags, instead of one large gas bag, a step which added to the safety of the airship because the escape of the gas from one or even two or three of the bags did not necessitate the descent of the ship. "Zeppelins" were used during the World War in making raids upon Allied cities, and after the war several successful flights were made across the Atlantic. 

The United States has displayed interest in the dirigible, and after purchasing several such ships from foreign nations, constructed the Akron, then the largest airship in the world. It was 785 feet long, 132.9 feet in diameter, and had a gas volume of 6,500,000 cubic feet. It was destroyed in 1933 in a storm off the coast of New Jersey. In 1935 the Macon, a similar airship, was destroyed by a storm. The use of helium, a noninflammable gas, will contribute much to the safety of lighter-than-air transportation if it can be found in sufficient quantities to make its extensive use possible.

The Development of the Airplane. While scientists laughed, Samuel 

P. Langley, secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, experimented with a heavier-than-air flying machine. In 1903 two attempts to make a flight in such a machine driven by a gasoline motor failed, but Langley insisted that the failure was not due to the construction of the plane but to the

Galloway 

Passengers boarding an airplane at the Newark Airport, New Jersey method of launching it, and his opinion was vindicated a few years later when Glenn Curtiss, after installing a more powerful motor, flew it successfully. A few days after the unsuccessful attempts to fly the Langley plane, Orville and Wilbur Wright, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, kept a plane in the air for 59 seconds and flew a distance of 260 yards. Since this beginning was made by the Wright brothers the airplane has been greatly improved. Airplanes have attained a speed of 440 miles per hour, have made continuous flights of more than 7,700 miles, and have, by refueling in the air, remained aloft more than 553 hours. 

One of the most notable flights was that of Charles A. Lindbergh, who left New York alone on the morning of May 20, 1927, and reached Paris 33½ hours later. Among others were the flights to the North Pole in 1926, and to the South Pole in 1929, by Richard E. Byrd; the transcontinental flight across the United States by Roscoe Turner in 1932, in 12 hours and 

33 minutes;* and the first solo flight "around the world," † in 1933, by 

Wiley Post, in 7 days, 18 hours, and 49 minutes. Commercial aviation. has been developed to a remarkable extent. In 1938 passenger planes in the United States carried more than 1,200,000 passengers. The Autogiro. Another invention which may prove to be an important contribution to air transportation is the autogiro, made by a Spaniard, Juan de la Cierva, in 1920. By the use of large rotating wings, this plane can travel at a much slower rate of speed than is necessary to keep the ordinary airplane in the air, and consequently it can land or take off in a much smaller space. It is possible that it will soon be easy to land in the heart of a large city, on specially constructed flat roofs of large buildings. This will remove the inconvenience of having to secure transportation for a number of miles from a city to the nearest airport. 

1. What contributions did James Watt and George Stephenson make to the final success of railroad transportation? List the difficulties confronting railroad transportation in the early years and discuss the progress made in the United 

States by 1835. 

2. State the conditions which demanded a transcontinental system of transportation. What part did the Federal government play in encouraging railroad construction? Why was the joining of the Union Pacific and Central Pacific an event of major importance? 

3. What men were associated with the development of railroad building which followed the War between the States? What improvements in the transportation of man and freight account for the great popularity of trains? What seems to be the future of railroad transportation? 

4. Upon what grounds did the government intervene in private control of railroads? State the provisions and weaknesses of the Interstate Commerce Act, and show why it was a landmark in the history of our country. List the successive laws passed by Congress since 1887 showing the progress made by each toward regulation of transportation. How was the Esch-Cummins Act a reversal of previous acts of 

Congress? How can the government justify itself for the aid it has given railroads since 1928? 

5. Upon what conditions did the success of the automobile as a commercial venture depend? What is the basis of the rivalry between railroads and automotive vehicles? CHAPTER XXIX Means of 

Communication

Methods of Communication in the Colonies. Inasmuch as the earliest methods of communication in America were by direct speech or by written messages, improvements in communication very naturally depended upon the progress in transportation. Before the Revolution, the common method of communication was by means of postriders. Because of the poor roads, this service was very slow, irregular, and expensive. It took as long for a letter to go overland from Charleston to New York as would be required today to send it to Australia, and the charges were greater; in fact, the use of the postal service was a luxury which could be afforded only by the well-to-do. 

Under an Act of Parliament of 1711, fourpence* was the charge for carrying a letter any distance up to sixty miles; from sixty to a hundred miles the charge was sixpence; and for longer distances it was more, but not quite in proportion to the distance. These rates were for letters written. on a single sheet of paper. If two or three sheets were used, the charges were doubled or tripled. Postage was never paid in advance, because of the uncertainty of delivery, but was collected from the person to whom the letter was delivered. It was not until 1847 that our present system of paying postage in advance by means of stamps came into use. Benjamin 

Franklin served as Postmaster General in the colonies for over twenty years, and made many of the early improvements in the service. He traveled over the country in search of better routes for the postriders, and established new post offices; he also admitted newspapers to the mail. About the time of the Revolution, stagecoaches came to be used for carrying mail. They made possible a quicker and much safer service, and because of their ability to carry a heavy load, they could carry the mail more cheaply. *Fourpence in English money is equal to about eight cents in American money; but it should be noted that in the eighteenth century wages and prices were very much lower than now. 

Fourpence in 1711 would buy several times as much food as eight cents would now. 564

WITH 

Courtesy U. S. Dept. of the Treasury 

The Pony Express; painting by Frank Mechau

The Pony Express. When the days of the postriders were long past in the East, the rapid settlement of California caused a temporary return to this method of communication in the Far West. In 1860 the "Pony 

Express" began with weekly service between St. Joseph, the western terminus of the railroad, and Sacramento; later two trips were made each week. Horses were exchanged about every ten miles, and the riders rode in relays of from fifty to seventy-five miles. The trip was completed in from eight to ten days as compared to the twenty-two days required for mail to reach California via Panama. This ride through a wild country inhabited by hostile Indians, and infested with robbers, was attended by many dangers, and was a thorough test of the courage of the brave riders, among whom, for a time, was Buffalo Bill (William F. Cody). Regular scheduled service was continued until late in 1861, when the "Pony Express" had to retire before the more modern telegraph which was extended across the continent that year. Although the "Pony Express" rates were very high-for a time, at first, five dollars for a half-ounce letter -the company lost money and closed business with a large deficit. 

Our Modern Postal System. The foundations of our modern postal system were laid with the passage by Congress of the Act of 1794; and in 

1829 the Postmaster General became a member of the President's cabinet. 

Three features which characterize our postal system are: (1) it is a monopoly of the United States government; (2) it is conducted without any thought of profit; (3) its purpose is to give the greatest possible social service. The people of the United States believe that an efficient postal

service is so conducive to a strong national feeling that this service should be extended to every citizen at the lowest possible cost. This can be accomplished best by letting the government conduct the postal business at cost, and this policy has been closely followed, with few exceptions. In only fifteen years since 1837 has the Post Office Department closed the year with a surplus; in other years it has been necessary for Congress to appropriate money to meet a comparatively small deficit. Among the reasons for the usual deficit have been the low rates charged for newspapers, the large amount of mail sent without any payment of postage by members of Congress and many government officials, and the low rate of two cents or three cents an ounce on letters sent anywhere to any point within the United States or its dependencies, regardless of distance. 

Improvements in our postal service have been many. It has always been the policy of the government to use the fastest agent possible for carrying the mail. The stagecoach was soon abandoned for the faster river steamboats whenever this was possible, and both stagecoach and steamboat had to give way to the railroad, which remained the fastest means of transportation until the invention of the airplane. In 1915, the first airmail service was established between Washington and New York. Today it has expanded into a nation-wide service, reaching nearly all cities of importance, and extending from ocean to ocean. Efforts to improve the postal service have resulted in a tremendous increase in the number of post offices-from 75 in 1790, to 76,688 in 1900. Since 1900, however, the number has been reduced to less than 47,000 because of the more rapid transportation, the Rural Delivery, and other improvements in service. 

In 1863 free delivery was established in the larger towns and cities, and the next year the money-order service was inaugurated. Perhaps the most important improvement was the Rural Delivery, begun in 1896, which today reaches more than thirty million people. Our postal system has been increased in value as a social agent also by the adoption of the postal savings, parcel post, insurance, and C.O.D. (Collect on Delivery) features.

The Telegraph. We have seen that the speed at which messages were delivered in the early history of our country depended upon transportation, but with the dawn of the electrical age a method of communication was discovered in which the element of time was almost completely eliminated. 

This was the telegraph. Early in the 1830's several men were working on the experiment of sending messages over a wire by means of an electromagnet, and more than one of them succeeded in transmitting messages before 1837; but it was in that year that Samuel F. B. Morse applied for a patent for an instrument that proved so superior to the others that he is rightfully known as the inventor of the telegraph. But Morse had considerable difficulty in making practical use of his invention. The construction of lines of wire over considerable distances is expensive, and Morse had no income except the small pittance he received from his work as an artist. 

The public, too, was indifferent. Finally, in 1843, Congress appropriated $30,000 for the construction of a telegraph line between Washington and Baltimore. In 1844 the work was completed, and successful communication was established between the two cities. Soon lines were extended to all parts of the East, and in 1861 a transcontinental line brought an end to the thrilling adventures of the riders on the "Pony Express."

The Atlantic Cable. Builders of telegraph lines were at first perplexed by the problem of spanning large bodies of water. A solution was found in the use of insulated cables laid under the water. In 1850 a cable was laid across the English Channel, and after 1851 telegraphic communication between England and the continent of Europe was unbroken; but the laying of a cable across the Atlantic was more difficult. This project was attempted, in 1857-1858, by Cyrus W. Field, aided by the advice of the great American scientist Matthew Fontaine Maury, superintendent of the Naval Observatory at Washington. After the cable was broken three times in the process of laying it, the task was finally completed and messages were exchanged between Ireland and America for a few weeks, after which the signals became weaker and unintelligible. The attempt was renewed RAFR

An early telephone exchange, and a recent telephone exchange in 1865, with the loss of a thousand miles of cable; but in 1866 Field's persistency was rewarded and the work was successfully completed; in fact, the laying of a second cable across the Atlantic was accomplished in the same year.

The Telephone. At the Centennial Exposition at Philadelphia, in 1876, there was exhibited the first telephone, which had just been invented by 

Alexander Graham Bell, a Scotchman who recently had come to America.

For a time the invention attracted very little notice, and the judges passed it by until their attention was directed to it by accident. It then created a sensation. Bell had been working on the theory that the human voice, or any other sound, could be reproduced by means of electric impulses sent over a wire in much the same way that the dots and dashes were transmitted by the telegraph. On March 7, 1876, he received a patent for the first telephone. The instrument exhibited at Philadelphia was a crude affair, with the transmitter serving also as the receiver. The public was slow to become interested in it, but when its practical use was assured by the installation of a telephone exchange at New Haven, Connecticut, in 1878, it was rapidly adopted by the American people. By 1926, in fact, the company providing most of our telephone service was America's largest corporation, with a capital stock of $1,064,327,800, and an income that year of $116,990,401. In 1930 more than twenty million telephones were

in use in the United States. One of the more recent improvements in the telephone has been the installation of the dial system in many of the large cities. The adoption of this system has made possible prompter service and a reduction in the number of exchange operators. 

Wireless Telegraphy and the Radio. In the latter part of the nineteenth century, new discoveries by scientists led some men to believe that messages might be sent through the ether without the use of wires. In 1896, Guglielmo Marconi, an Italian, secured a British patent for the first wireless telegraph, and three years later the first message was sent across the English Channel. In 1901 faint signals were heard across the Atlantic, and by the next year wireless communication across the Atlantic was an accomplished fact. Since then the wireless telegraph has been extended to all of the nations of the world. It has been especially valuable to ships at sea that could have no other means of communicating with each other or with the mainland. The "SOS" call from ships in distress is always heeded by other vessels within reach, and many lives have been saved through the agency of the wireless telegraph. CHRO

Such "terrors" were more fully realized in our modern radio Just as the ability to reproduce the voice over a wire followed the telegraph, so now the wireless telephone, or radio, followed the wireless telegraph. The radio was developed about the beginning of the World War and by the close of the war it had come into almost general use. In 1920 the results of the presidential election were broadcast. In that year also the Westinghouse Electric and Manufacturing Company, of Pittsburgh, began to transmit entertainment programs on regular schedule. Since then hundreds of broadcasting stations have been set up, with the result that it was necessary to allot each station a definite wave length in order to avoid conflicts. By 1936 their number in the United States had increased to more than 650. Within five years after the first broadcast there were more than 5,000,000 radio sets in the United States, and in 1935 their number was estimated at over 21,000,000. Today because of the

On March 7, 1926, the fiftieth anniversary of Bell's patent, a conversation was held over the radio between New York and London. Today, transatlantic broadcasts by means of short waves are everyday occurrences. The educational possibilities of the radio are almost unlimited.

Recent Improvements in Communication. The telephotograph is a recent development of the telephone. In 1925 a picture was transmitted by telephone from New York to Cleveland, and today the telephotograph is in daily use in newspaper service, and is of inestimable value to police in the identification of criminals. 

Recent inventions of great value are used by the telephone and telegraph companies for sending typewritten messages instantly and automatically. The teletypewriter, or teletype, at one end of a wire types the message just as the sending machine does at the other end; and then it or a similar instrument may be used at once for sending the reply. The teletypewriting services are widely used by the newspapers in gathering their news from the various press agencies; by the United States Weather 

Bureau in transmitting the weather bulletins; and in private business. 

Another recent invention, the possibilities of which have not yet been fully determined, is television. As a result of this invention, it is possible to see objects at a distance either with or without a wire. The first demonstration of television was in 1927, when persons in New York talked to

others in Washington and could see the features of those with whom they talked. A similar demonstration was later conducted successfully between 

New York and London. Television in color also is an accomplished fact.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS Chapter XXX. 

 Chapter XXXI. 

 Chapter XXXII.  Chapter XXXIII.  THE BASIS FOR OUR FOREIGN POLICY in the early days of the Republic was the principle laid down by Washington's cabinet in 1793 that it was to our interest to remain absolutely neutral and to avoid all entanglements with other nations. Perhaps the most important doctrine pronounced by our statesmen as a guide in foreign affairs was the Monroe Doctrine, which suggested that the Western Hemisphere should be for America and that the United States should stay out of European affairs. It was soon found, however, that it is difficult for a nation to remain isolated in its foreign policy, and our country has often been drawn into foreign affairs either by our own interests or by those of our neighbors. 

In the nineteenth century the ideas of nationalism and imperialism were dominant in many parts of the world. The young American nation, whose policy was directed in part by nationalists and imperialists, had a desire for expansion and so acquired additional territory, some of which was obtained from European nations that owned territory on the American 575

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

continent. In 1898 we became involved in a war with Spain. As a result of this war we acquired from Spain the Philippine Islands and, as a condition of peace, a protectorate over Cuba. During the same period we also secured possession of other islands in the West Indies and in the Pacific. 

Because of our interest in the Philippine Islands and in our trade with China, we also manifested interest in the Far East, which later, under the leadership of John Hay, our Secretary of State, led to the announcement of the "open door" policy in regard to China. Since our interests were now in the Pacific as well as in the Atlantic, a canal across the Isthmus of Panama became desirable, and presently was constructed. 

The nations to the south of us have always presented interesting problems; several times internal difficulties in Mexico have been of concern to the United States. In 1914 the United States became involved with Mexico and landed marines at Veracruz. The matter, however, was adjusted to the satisfaction of both governments. 

With the outbreak of the World War (1914) the United States was in a difficult position, because the American people were anxious to continue their trade with European countries. The United States declared itself a neutral; but, because of the German submarine warfare, it was difficult to carry on trade; and finally we became involved in the war. 

Following the World War, the United States participated in the peace conference, at which the Treaty of Versailles, containing a provision for the Covenant of the League of Nations, was adopted. Our government, however, did not ratify this treaty, because of opposition in the Senate. 

Since the World War we have manifested much interest in the problem of world peace. The United States has generally worked in the interest of world peace. We have settled some of our disputes with foreign nations by arbitration treaties. We have entered into negotiations with South 

American countries through the Pan American Union and have maintained friendly relations in the Western Hemisphere. 

The United States took an active part in the Hague Peace Conference in 1899, and again in the second Hague Conference in 1907. During 

Wilson's administration, our Secretary of State, William Jennings Bryan, negotiated a number of so-called "cooling off" treaties with other nations, to provide for the friendly solution of difficulties rather than settlement by war. During Harding's administration European nations met at 

Washington (1921) to arrange for the limitation of navies. The United 

States has later taken an active part in conferences to urge the reduction of armaments; in the framing of the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact; and in other activities for promoting peace.

CHAPTER XXX The Period of Isolation Origin of Isolation as Our Foreign Policy. The foreign policy of the 

United States has been marked by three outstanding characteristicsisolation, imperialism, and international co-operation. At no time in our history have our relations with the rest of the world been dominated by any one of these three characteristics to the entire exclusion of the others, but rather we may say that our foreign policy has been a combination of all three, found in proportions which have varied at different periods of our history. In general, the trend has been from isolation toward international co-operation, with imperialism as an important step. 

Several forces caused the adoption of isolation as the chief characteristic of our foreign policy in the early days of the republic. Geographical conditions made isolation almost imperative. We were too far removed from the 

Old World to play an important diplomatic role in the Eastern Hemisphere, and at the same time our isolated situation insured us against the encroachments of other nations. Furthermore, our country was blessed with rich natural resources which made us an almost self-sufficient people. In our early history it seemed entirely possible for us to work out our own destiny regardless of foreign assistance or influence. Again, our economic interests were largely domestic. Before us was the task of conquering the expanse of a vast continent. Millions of acres of unoccupied but fertile land, and a great variety of untouched mineral resources, offered ample opportunities for lucrative investments. A rapidly growing population which both produced and consumed our agricultural and manufactured products solved the problem of markets. Why then should we not live to ourselves?

Early Difficulties in Maintaining Isolation. Americans soon learned that living alone was not so simple a matter as they had imagined.* The 

Treaty of Paris in 1783 had given us an extent of territory which seemed to be more than was necessary to meet our needs, but the indefinite nature *For an account of our foreign relations, 1789-1815, see pp. 209–216, 231–241, 244–252. 577

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

of our boundaries, and the questions of fishing rights, trade with the British West Indies, and the use of the Mississippi River, were problems which were almost certain to involve us in controversies with other nations. Then, too, the treaty of alliance with France, although it had made possible our victory in the Revolution, now became a source of embarrassment to us. 

Our ally became involved in the wars of the French Revolution, and regarded the United States as obligated to come to her assistance; but 

Washington was determined to maintain neutrality, a course which was made very difficult by the conduct of Citizen Genêt. Relations between the two former allies were so strained by the "XYZ Affair" that a short unofficial war was the result (p. 216). 

Relations with Great Britain were no better, and our efforts to settle the disputed questions with her in Jay's Treaty were a failure. Perhaps the most important result of the treaty was the indirect one of influencing Spain-in the belief that we were about to make an alliance with Great Britain-into accepting the Pinckney Treaty of 1795 (pp. 214-215), by which the parallel of 31° was made the northern boundary of Florida and we were granted temporary use of the Mississippi River. The problem of the free navigation of the Mississippi was definitely settled eight years later by the purchase of Louisiana.

With the outbreak of the Napoleonic Wars, neither Great Britain nor France had respect for our rights as a neutral. Great Britain, especially, vexed the American people by the blockade of European ports, and by the impressment of our seamen. Jefferson, who had formerly favored our intervention during the French Revolution, and had more recently waged war upon the Barbary pirates, now rigidly applied Washington's policy of isolation through the Embargo Act and the nonimportation acts, but his efforts to avoid war were unavailing. The termination of the War of 

1812, by relieving the pressure of foreign problems, and by removing the danger of Indian aggression in the West, opened the way for a great westward migration and the turning of the interest of the Americans to domestic affairs. Isolation then became a more practicable policy. 

The Monroe Doctrine. Soon after the War of 1812, two developments caused a more definite acceptance of the American policy of isolation, or of exclusive attention to affairs in the Western Hemisphere. Russian fur traders had pushed their way down the Pacific coast as far as San Francisco Bay; and in 1821 the czar announced to the world that the 

Pacific coast as far south as the parallel of 51° was Russian territory, and warned all foreign vessels to keep out of the adjacent waters. This was a direct challenge to the territorial aspirations of the American people

Even more alarming was the course of events among our Latin American neighbors. While Portugal and Spain were occupied by French armies during the Napoleonic Wars, Brazil and the Spanish colonies in America enjoyed a period of semi-independence; and with the restoration of the oppressive rule of Ferdinand VII in Spain, by the Congress of Vienna (1815), the Spanish colonies, following the example of the United States, revolted and declared their independence. Brazil also separated from 

Portugal, and by 1823 practically all of the Latin peoples from California to Cape Horn had established their independence and had set up republics with constitutions modeled upon that of the older and larger sister republic to the north.* The United States was in sympathy with its southern neighbors in their struggle for independence, partly because of sentiment, and perhaps even more for commercial reasons. The laws of Spain had X permitted little commercial intercourse between her colonies and foreign powers, but now the independent republics could trade with whom they pleased. The same commercial reasons also prompted Great Britain to support the new republics. 

Austria, France, Prussia, and Russia had formed a league to put down all democratic uprisings, and now they planned to intervene in the revolutionary movement in the New World and restore the colonies to Spain. 

Both Great Britain and the United States were alarmed at this prospect. 

Canning, the British Secretary for Foreign Affairs, influenced France to refuse to participate in the plan, and proposed that the United States and Great Britain act jointly in the protection of the Latin American republics. 

Jefferson and Madison were favorable to Canning's proposal, but John Quincy Adams, the American Secretary of State, believed that the United States should play the role of protector without any kind of co-operative agreement with a European power. Adams's counsel prevailed, and when 

President Monroe sent his annual message to Congress in 1823, it contained an announcement of the policy suggested by Adams, which became known as the Monroe Doctrine. Briefly stated, its provisions were as follows: (1) the Western Hemisphere was no longer open to colonization by European nations; (2) European nations were warned not to interfere with the political affairs of the Western republics; and (3) the United 

States would not interfere with European affairs. 

It should be observed that the Monroe Doctrine was not a law nor a part of international law; it was not even formally endorsed by Congress. 

It was merely an announcement to the world of the policy the United States expected to enforce with respect to Latin America. There was some *Cuba and Puerto Rico, however, remained Spanish colonies.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

doubt as to the willingness of the autocratic European nations to respect such a policy, but when Great Britain with her powerful fleet openly came to the support of the Monroe Doctrine, the European allies dismissed all thought of intervention. The next year Russia signed a treaty with the 

United States, in which she renounced all claims to territory south of 54° 40′ north latitude. The American policy of isolation seemed secure, and, rightly or wrongly, the Monroe Doctrine became the chief basis of our foreign policy.

The French in Mexico. Fortunately, the Monroe Doctrine was not challenged until the United States had grown into a strong nation, thoroughly capable of looking after its own interests. The first violation was by France. Napoleon III, seeing his throne tottering because of the failure of his foreign policy in Europe, conceived the idea of regaining his lost prestige by building up a great empire. Mexico, in the throes of a revolt, offered an inviting field, and the time seemed especially opportune since the United States was involved in the War between the North and the South. Events played into his hands when the Mexican government gave him an excellent excuse for intervention by suspending the payment of debts owed to several of the European powers. Great Britain, Spain, and 

France sent a joint expedition into Mexico, and in a short time they had made a satisfactory settlement of the debt question. The British and 

Spanish troops were withdrawn, but the French forces remained to overthrow the government and set up Maximilian of Austria as a puppet emperor. The United States protested against this flagrant defiance of the Monroe Doctrine, but could take no definite action until after the close of the war. Our government then demanded the immediate withdrawal of the French troops. Napoleon, having no desire to fight the powerful and veteran army of the United States, and because of the rising opposition to him in Europe, promptly ordered the return of the troops to France. Maximilian was soon captured and executed by the Mexicans. This episode added considerably to the prestige of the United 

States in world affairs.

The British in Venezuela. The second incident which involved the enforcement of the Monroe Doctrine occurred in 1895, when Venezuela complained that inhabitants of British Guiana were expanding into Venezuelan territory. If this were true, it would be a violation of the Monroe 

Doctrine; but there was some doubt concerning the exact location of the boundary, and the British government insisted that the territory in question was British territory. Olney, the American Secretary of State, demanded that Great Britain submit the question to arbitration. When the

demand was refused, President Cleveland appointed a commission to study the boundary, and intimated that it was his intention to uphold the findings of the commission. For a time, it seemed that war was inevitable, but Great Britain yielded and signed an arbitration treaty with Venezuela. 

The decision of the arbitration commission was for the most part in favor of Great Britain.

The Second Venezuelan Episode. The third application of the Monroe 

Doctrine against the aggressions of European nations in the New World was in 1902, when Venezuela defaulted in the payment of debts owed to Great Britain, Italy, and Germany. These nations sent a joint expedition to blockade the Venezuelan ports and to force a settlement of the debts. President Theodore Roosevelt, fearing that this action might result in the political control of Venezuela by one or more of the European nations, urged that the nations submit to arbitration. Great Britain and 

Italy agreed, but Germany remained obdurate and threatened to send the German fleet to Venezuela. President Roosevelt then took a firm stand, and, according to his own statement, ordered Admiral George Dewey to hold the entire United States fleet in readiness for action if it should become necessary. Germany then yielded and agreed to arbitrate. It was quite evident, however, that Venezuela was endeavoring to take refuge behind the Monroe Doctrine in order to evade the payment of her debts. Roosevelt had no sympathy for this kind of conduct and brought pressure to bear upon Venezuela to force her to pay her foreign obligations. 

Recent Interpretations of the Monroe Doctrine. Within recent years the scope of the Monroe Doctrine has been extended far beyond its original intention. We have learned that protection implies influence, supervision, and even partial control. Our experience with Venezuela in 1902, and later experiences with other Latin American republics, convinced the United States government of the necessity of playing the role of guardian over our neighboring republics in order that their mismanagement of finances might not be permitted to involve us in serious controversies with their European creditors. The "Roosevelt Corollary," which asserted the right of the United States to intervene and supervise the finances of the smaller republics in case of chronic wrongdoing or mismanagement, was entirely satisfactory to the European nations; they were pleased to use the 

United States as a collection agency; but it was extremely distasteful to the Latin Americans. Interventions in accordance with the policy stated in the "Roosevelt Corollary" will be discussed in Chapter XXXI (pp. 608609). In 1930, our State Department decided that the supervision of the finances of the smaller states was not justified by the terms of the Monroe

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

Doctrine, and for the last few years our policy has been that of nonintervention.

When it was rumored in 1912 that Japan was negotiating with Mexico for the establishment of a naval base at Magdalena Bay, on the Pacific coast (p. 606), the Monroe Doctrine was more broadly interpreted so as to apply to all non-American nations. 

Since many of the Latin American republics are no longer helpless and in need of protection, they can see no good in the Monroe Doctrine, and look upon it merely as a means by which the "Colossus of the North" imposes its will upon its weaker sisters. They can see no justice in a system which, although it affects many nations, is interpreted by only one. 

The Conquest of the Continent Is Begun. The adoption of our policy of isolation made it possible for us to pursue relentlessly our territorial expansion. When we gained our independence in 1783, it was at first believed that we had obtained all the territory that was needed for our future development; but the almost accidental purchase of Louisiana, nearly doubling our area, gave us new visions concerning the ultimate boundaries of our republic. Our "manifest destiny" was to reach to the 

Pacific and, in the eyes of some of the more ambitious expansionists, it was eventually to include the entire continent. The Nashville Clarion, in its issue of April 28, 1812, expressed the sentiments of many Americans when it stated: "Where is it written in the Book of Fate that the American 

Republic shall not spread her limits from the capes of the Chesapeake to Nootka Sound, from the Isthmus of Panama to Hudson Bay?" This belief had no small influence upon our entrance into the war with Great Britain in 1812.

The Acquisition of Florida. Our treaty with Great Britain at the close of the Revolution contained a secret agreement which stated that if Great Britain retained Florida, the boundary should be 32° 28′ north latitude, but if Florida should be given to Spain, the boundary was to be 31°. Spain, however, unwilling to abide by our secret agreement with Great Britain, claimed the former line as the boundary until the Pinckney Treaty of 1795. The settlement of the northern boundary did not remove all of the difficulties with regard to Florida. When Louisiana was purchased, in 

1803, the boundaries of the territory were not clearly defined (see p. 236). 

France had owned a strip of land east of the Mississippi River, but in 1763 she had surrendered to Great Britain all territory east of the Mississippi except the Isle of Orleans, and had given the rest of Louisiana to her ally Spain. It seems that neither Napoleon nor the American negotiators believed in 1803 that any of Florida was included in the purchase.

Nevertheless, Jefferson and his successors in the presidency made a claim to West Florida. Expansion into the Southwest soon brought many 

American settlers into the disputed area, and in 1810 these settlers revolted against the Spanish rule. The district as far east as the Pearl River was promptly annexed by the United States, and in 1812 it was included in 

Ewing Galloway

Old Spanish gate of St. Augustine, the oldest settlement in Florida the newly organized state of Louisiana. It was evident that the Spanish empire in the New World was crumbling. Fearing that this territory might fall into the hands of a stronger power, the United States in 1813 seized the district between the Pearl and the Perdido rivers. 

For six years longer the rest of Florida remained in the hands of Spain. 

During that time it was a haven for runaway American slaves and a base of operations for Indians and pirates. Spain seemed powerless to enforce even a semblance of order in the district. In 1818 General Andrew Jackson pursued some hostile Indians across the border into Florida, captured two Spanish forts, and executed two British subjects whom he accused of arousing and aiding the Indians. For a time it seemed that Jackson's conduct might involve us in serious difficulty with both Great Britain and Spain, but the affair was settled without serious difficulty. Spain had learned from the events of 1810 and 1813 that all of Florida would eventually fall into the hands of the United States. Good judgment prompted her to sell it rather than to see it taken without any remuneration; so in 1819 she negotiated a treaty in which she ceded Florida to the United States and withdrew her claims from all territory on the Pacific coast north of the parallel of 42°. In return for these concessions

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

the United States undertook the payment of claims of American citizens against Spain, amounting to about $5,000,000, and withdrew her doubtful claim to Texas. The acquisition of Florida was a geographical necessity because it controlled the outlet of three of our Southern states, but the methods by which it was obtained are subject to criticism. 

Settlement of Our Northern Boundary. The American "War Hawks" 

who had entered the War of 1812 with the expectation that it would result in the annexation of Canada by the United States were disappointed, but the war did lead to a more accurate definition of the boundaries between the two countries. The Treaty of Ghent (1814) provided for the appointment of commissions which were instructed to settle the disputed boundaries. 

One commission made a satisfactory settlement of the end of the boundary line around Passamaquoddy Bay, in the easternmost part of Maine. 

Another commission reached a satisfactory agreement concerning the boundary from the parallel of 45° up the St. Lawrence River and the 

Great Lakes to the western end of Lake Huron. In 1818 the northern boundary of the Louisiana Territory was fixed as the parallel of 49° from the Lake of the Woods to the "Great Stony Mountains," as the Rocky Mountains were then called. This left three sections of the boundary still unsettled-the northern Maine boundary, the line from Lake Huron to the Lake of the Woods, and the boundary west of the Rocky 

Mountains (map, p. 234).

The settlement of the Maine boundary seemed especially difficult. 

The commission to which this task had been assigned in the Treaty of Ghent reported that it was unable to reach a decision. The question was then referred to the king of the Netherlands, but he was unable to make a settlement which was acceptable to both parties. For years the line remained unsettled, and the relations between the two nations became more and more strained until in 1842 it seemed that the militias of Maine and New Brunswick would come to blows in the fertile Aroostook Valley. 

The seriousness of the situation gave impetus to the diplomatic negotiations then in progress. The Webster-Ashburton Treaty, which was completed in 1842, gave to the United States seven thousand of the twelve thousand square miles in dispute, including the Aroostook Valley. The boundary line from Lake Huron to the Lake of the Woods also was settled in this treaty.

Since 1818, the United States and Great Britain had jointly occupied the Oregon Territory (p. 319). Several times the United States had suggested a compromise with the parallel of 49° north latitude as the boundary, only to be refused by Great Britain. Soon after the election of President

Fairchild Aerial Service 

Peace Bridge across the Niagara River between Canada and the United States Polk, in 1844, notice was given to the British government of our desire to terminate the agreement for joint occupation. In the negotiations which followed, Great Britain offered to accept the forty-ninth parallel if the United States would permit her to have all of Vancouver Island. This arrangement was agreed upon and our northern boundary was definitely fixed. It is significant that all of our boundary disputes with Great Britain were settled by peaceful negotiations. 

The Acquisition of Mexican Territory. The withdrawal of our claim to 

Texas in 1819 (p. 312) did not prevent many American settlers from moving into that Mexican state to take advantage of the cheap land. In the course of time these settlers led a revolt against Mexico, won their independence, and applied for admission into the United States. After several years of sharp debate over the slavery question, Texas was annexed in 1845. The Mexican government had never recognized the independence of Texas, and consequently it regarded the annexation by the United States as an unfriendly act. This finally led to war with Mexico and acquisition of a large area of Mexican territory (see pp. 315-318).

CHAPTER XXXI 

An Imperialistic Foreign Policy Bases of Imperialism. A series of developments during the last half of the nineteenth century caused a partial withdrawal of our policy of isolation, and brought the rise of imperialism as the dominant factor in our foreign policy. America began to turn her attention overseas in search of political and economic advantages. Soon after the War between the North and the South, the Industrial Revolution caused a gradual change from an agricultural to an industrial economic system. Unoccupied land suitable for farming was rapidly becoming unattainable, and before the close of the century the frontier had disappeared. This condition produced an increasing cost of agricultural land, and a consequent decline in returns from agricultural investments. Capital naturally sought more immediate and lucrative dividends through industrial investments. The resulting increase in production created a demand for new markets, for our growing population could not keep pace with our more rapidly increasing production. 

Improved transportation and communication made potential customers of the inhabitants of every industrially retarded country in the world. 

Fabulous profits awaited those who developed trade with them. 

The capitalists were forced to look to other lands not only for markets, but also for larger sources of raw materials to meet the requirements of the rapidly increasing production, and for opportunities for more profitable investments of the rapidly accumulating capital. Soon millions of dollars were invested abroad in mines, oil wells, factories, railroads, and banks. 

Enormous corporations with powerful political influence demanded that the government open the way for the influx of American goods into the prospective markets. The demand for new possessions, protectorates, or "spheres of influence" was urgently pressed upon the government by "big business," and it was also strongly seconded by the masses of citizens who would profit in no material way from the expansion, but who wished to see the enhancement of the national power and prestige. 588

The Methods of the Imperialists. Imperialism, which became the keynote of the foreign policies of all of the leading powers of the world during the half century preceding the outbreak of the World War, was to be found in two different forms, both of which were founded upon commercial interests. First, there was the desire for more territory, and many nations attempted to extend their rule, by purchase, annexation, or conquest, over other lands. Second, there was the economic imperialism, or imperialism of dollars and goods, by which the nations did not actually extend their dominion over the retarded areas, but merely satisfied their commercial needs by "economic penetration," by getting control of trade or of natural resources. Friction with the natives, growing out of commercial concessions, and loans which could not be repaid, were two of the most common excuses for intervention, which almost invariably resulted in the administration of the finances of the smaller state by the "protector," or the forcing of other commercial concessions. 190 10 

The Purchase of Alaska. 

Russia had been on very friendly terms with the United States during the War between the 

North and the South. Soon after the war, William H. Seward, the 

American Secretary of State, began negotiations for concessions to American fur traders who sought the right to engage in the fur traffic in Alaska. When approached by the American minister on the question of concessions, the Russian government offered to sell the entire district to the United States. 

Seward, who was a genuine imperialist, was pleased by the Russian offer, in 1867, to sell Alaska for $7,200,000, and ordered the treaty drawn at once. (See map, page 606.)

Evidently the American public was not yet won to the policy of imperialism, upon which the United States, perhaps unconsciously, was entering. 

American Interests in Cuba. Even before the middle of the nineteenth century, Americans had dreamed of the acquisition of Cuba. Most of the agitation for such a move came from the slaveholders, who hoped to maintain their power in Congress by the admission of another slave state. In 

1848 President Polk offered Spain $100,000,000 for the island, but the offer was declined. In 1854 a scheme to gain Cuba by force, if necessary, was unsuccessful (p. 365). With the collapse of the slave power in 1865, American interest in Cuba lagged. It was not long, however, until the rising industrialism in the United States, seeking new markets and opportunities for investments, caused America again to turn her attention to her island 

Ewing Galloway

Havana, Cuba, with Morro Castle in the distance neighbor. The sugar and tobacco industries were especially inviting. By 1896 American investments in Cuba amounted to more than $50,000,000, and the Cuban-American commerce in 1893 exceeded $100,000,000. 

There were also other reasons why the United States was interested in Cuba. Its close proximity to our shores made it imperative from the standpoint of our own protection that it should not fall into the hands of a strong power which might use it as a base of military operations against us. And

Cuba was a source of annoy- ance and danger to the United

States through the failure of the Spanish officials to take the necessary precautions to prevent the spread of yellow fever to our shores. 

The Cubans Revolt against Spain. By 1860, the last remnants of the once proud Spanish empire in the New World-Cuba, Puerto Rico, and a few other small islands in the West Indies-were seething with unrest and discontent because of misgovernment. The Cubans were burdened with

very heavy taxes. Even more oppressive was the fact that they were given no voice in their own government, but were ruled by Spanish governors who, as a rule, were corrupt and had little concern for the welfare of the island. In 1868 a revolt broke out against the Spanish administration. 

For ten years it continued, and ended only when Spain freed the slaves and promised liberal political reforms. The promises were not kept. The discontent was increased by an economic depression which was caused by the American tariff of 1890 on tobacco, and that of 1894 on sugar. 

With the outbreak of another revolt in 1895 the Cuban insurrectionists hoped to force intervention by the United States by stopping the grinding of sugar cane, thus paralyzing an industry in which Americans had invested heavily. The Spanish government resorted to violent methods in an attempt to put down the revolt. Cuban revolutionists were forced into "reconcentration" camps, where many of them died because of the crowded and insanitary conditions that existed. Both sides were guilty of atrocities and destruction of property, but the Cubans and the Americans who had commercial interests at stake kept up an effective system of propaganda in the United States which gave publicity only to the Spanish cruelties. 

The American public soon became openly sympathetic with the Cubans in their struggle for independence. 

Failure of Diplomatic Negotiations. With public opinion overwhelmingly marshaled on the side of the Cubans, it was difficult for the United States government to maintain a neutral policy. In February, 1896, Congress passed a joint resolution recognizing the existence of a state of war in Cuba and offering the services of the United States in negotiations for the independence of the island. The resolutions were ignored by President 

Cleveland, who was making a sincere effort to enforce neutrality, but they indicated the temper of Congress, which in turn reflected the will of the American people. Soon after the inauguration of President McKinley, a note was sent to Spain again offering the services of the United States, and mildly protesting against the failure of the Spanish government to protect American lives and property in Cuba. The Spanish government promptly recalled the obnoxious Governor Weyler from Cuba and promised to grant autonomy; but the Cubans would accept nothing short of independence. 

On February 9, 1898, another incident still further aroused the American public against Spain. On that date there was published in the New 

York Journal a facsimile of a letter written by Señor de Lome, the Spanish ambassador to the United States, which had been stolen from a Cuban post office by an agent of the press. In this private letter De Lome severely criticized McKinley and spoke of him as a weak politician who was trying

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

to keep on good terms with the "jingoes" of his party. The American public was so aroused by the contents of the letter that it apparently gave little thought to the methods by which the letter was obtained. De Lome was promptly recalled by the Spanish government. 

Less than a week after this incident, the world was shocked by the sinking of the American battleship Maine in the harbor of Havana. This 

Ewing Galloway ship had been sent to Cuba a few weeks earlier to protect American lives and property. On the night of February 15, 1898, it was blown up, with the loss of 260 officers and men. An American court of inquiry reported that the explosion was due to a submarine mine, but Spanish authorities reported that the Maine was wrecked by an internal explosion in a powder magazine, and that the Spanish government was in no way responsible for the accident. Later investigations substantiated the American report, but we do not know today whether the Spanish government had any knowledge of the laying of the mine. 

Excitement in the United States was at fever heat. "Remember the 

Maine" was the watchword of the American people who fixed the blame for the disaster upon Spain and demanded war. When a final demand upon Spain was not fully complied with, McKinley announced his intention of submitting the question to Congress. In view of the temper of that body, there could be no doubt about the outcome of that move. Immediately after this announcement, several European countries appealed to both nations in an attempt to prevent war. The Spanish government sent a message to McKinley, agreeing to a cessation of hostilities and to the granting to the Cubans of "all the liberty they could expect. 

The American minister in Spain twice cabled that the Spanish government, if given time, would go as far as the United States demanded, even to the extent of granting independence to Cuba, or of annexation by the 

United States. 

William McKinley 

War Is Declared. For some reason, McKinley failed to inform the 

American public or Congress of the change in Spain's attitude. On April

11, 1898, the President sent a message to Congress in which he recommended intervention. On April 19, the anniversary of the battle of Lexington, and of the first bloodshed of the War between the North and the South, Congress adopted resolutions which recognized the independence of Cuba, disclaimed the intention of the United States to control the island, and empowered the President to use the armed forces of the United States to force the withdrawal of Spain. Four days later, Spain declared war upon the United States.

Never was a war more popular in the United States. About 200,000 men responded to the call for volunteers. The regular army, however, was poorly prepared, and consisted of only about 28,000 men, a number which was soon increased to about 60,000. The Department of War proved to be woefully inefficient. The clothing and food of the army were much better adapted to a campaign in a frigid zone than in the tropics, and camp conditions were so insanitary that far more American soldiers died from disease than from Spanish bullets. Conditions were very different in the navy, which was most efficiently managed. Spain was not a formidable antagonist, and the war lasted only 110 days. 

The Battle of Manila Bay. Before war had been declared, Commodore 

George Dewey, in command of an American naval squadron, had been sent to Hong Kong, China, with orders that, in the event of war, he was to hold the fleet in readiness for an immediate attack upon the Spanish fleet which was stationed in the Philippines. On the night of April 30 Dewey reached 

Manila Bay, where the Spanish fleet had sought the shelter of the forts. 

Under the cover of darkness, the American squadron succeeded in slipping by the forts which guarded the entrance to the harbor, and made its way well into the bay before being discovered by the Spanish sentinels. The battle which followed was short but decisive. So superior were the American marksmanship and the general efficiency of the fleet that the entire Spanish fleet was destroyed, and all of the forts were silenced. Since Dewey had no army to support him, he was unable to occupy the city and had to wait about two months for the arrival of an American army. In the meantime, he blockaded the Spanish harbor.

The Fall of Santiago. Soon after the declaration of war a Spanish fleet under the command of Admiral Cervera began its journey across the Atlantic. In view of the fact that the destination of the fleet was unknown, many Americans were alarmed by the wild reports that the fleet might attack the cities along the Atlantic coast. Great was the relief when it became known that it had entered the harbor of Santiago de Cuba (in the southeastern part of the island), and had been blockaded there by the

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

American Atlantic squadron under the command of Rear Admiral William 

T. Sampson.

About two weeks later, an American army of 17,000 men, under the command of General William R. Shafter, landed a few miles east of Santiago. On June 24 it began the attack upon the forts which defended the city, most important of which were El Caney and San Juan Hill. Special gallantry was shown by the regiment of volunteers known as the "Rough Riders," under the command of Colonel Leonard Wood and Lieutenant Colonel Theodore Roosevelt, who had resigned from the office of Assistant Secretary of the Navy in order to see more active service in the war. In eight days the American army had advanced to within a mile and a half of Santiago. It was only a matter of time until the city would be forced to surrender.

The commanders of the Spanish fleet knew that its position in the harbor would place it at the mercy of the forts if the city should fall into the hands of the Americans, and therefore they determined to make a dash for freedom. On Sunday morning, July 3, the Spanish ships, one at a time, made their way out of the harbor and turned toward the west. As each 

Spanish ship appeared, it was engaged by a single American vessel. The battle thus became a series of naval duels, and the fact that in every case the Spanish ship was destroyed is evidence of the superiority of the American vessels. On July 17 the campaign in Cuba ended with the surrender of Santiago. The Oregon, one of our battleships in the War with Spain. At the outbreak of the war this ship was on the 

Pacific coast, and in order to reach Cuba it had to make the long voyage by way of the Strait of Magellan.

The End of the War. A few days after the capture of Santiago, an army under the command of General Nelson A. Miles began the invasion of Puerto Rico. Meeting with little resistance, the Americans pushed their way farther and farther into the interior, and had acquired possession of almost all of the island when their advance was stopped by the news that the protocol, or preliminary treaty of peace, had been signed, August 12. 

The news of the protocol did not reach the Philippines in time to prevent the capture of Manila one day later. For several weeks an American army of 10,000 troops, supported by a force of Filipinos under their leader, Aguinaldo, had been completing the conquest of the islands. The campaign ended with the fall of Manila, August 13.

The Treaty of Peace. Soon after the surrender of Santiago, Spain began negotiations through the French ambassador at Washington for preliminary terms of peace. In the protocol of August 12, Spain agreed to the following demands: (1) the recognition of the independence of Cuba and the immediate withdrawal of all Spanish forces from the island; (2) the cession of Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States; (3) the occupation by the United States of the city and harbor of Manila until the final disposition of the islands was determined in the permanent treaty of peace. 

The treaty, which was negotiated at Paris, was strictly an imperialistic one. 

Not only did the United States obtain Puerto Rico and Guam, as was provided for in the protocol, but it also demanded that the Philippines be ceded to the United States for the sum of $20,000,000. Regarding this demand as an ultimatum, Spain consented to the cession only under protest. When the treaty was submitted to our Senate for ratification, considerable opposition arose to the acquisition of the Philippines, because it seemed contrary to the spirit of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution to bring under the American flag the inhabitants of distant lands who could not be granted citizenship. It was only after a debate lasting over a month that the treaty was finally ratified. Isolation as a foreign policy was now out of the question. The United States had definitely launched upon a policy of imperialism. 

American Rule in the Philippines. While the Senate was debating the treaty of peace, weight was added to the arguments of the anti-imperialists by the outbreak of a revolt by the Filipinos who objected to American rule. Claiming that Dewey had promised them independence in return for their assistance in the campaign in the Philippines, they felt that they had been betrayed when the islands were retained by the United States. It was a strange experience for Americans to be forced to put down a revolt of their own subjects fighting for "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." For
