Natives of the Philippines before 1898 

Courtesy Museum of Natural History more than three years the Filipinos, under their intrepid leader, Aguinaldo, resisted a force of 60,000 American troops. The suppression of the insurrection cost more lives than the war with Spain, while the financial cost was about $175,000,000, or nearly nine times the amount paid to Spain for the islands.

The Spooner Amendment, adopted by Congress in 1901, placed the government of the Philippines, temporarily, in the hands of such persons as the President might appoint. A commission of five men, headed by 

Judge William H. Taft, who acted as civil governor, immediately set up a provisional government. The next year Congress passed the Philippine 

Act, which set up a regular government for the islands. The act provided 

Women of the Philippines today making embroidery much used in the United States 

Ewing Galloway

for a governor appointed by the President, for executive departments, and for a legislature of two houses. At first the Filipinos were given little voice in their government except in the lower house, which they controlled, and in the senate, in which they had a minority membership. Later, the extent of local participation in the government was greatly increased. By the 

Jones Act, of 1916, the Filipinos were given control of the senate and all of the executive departments except one, but the governor's right of veto fully protected American interests.

The islanders prospered under American rule. In a period of thirtyfive years the population doubled. Highways, railroads, telephone and telegraph lines were built; agriculture was improved; foreign trade increased about sixfold; and public health was improved by the introduction of better means of sanitation. Perhaps the most remarkable progress was in the field of education. An excellent school system was set up, which by 1935 included more than a million students. The University of the 

Philippines then had an enrollment of over five thousand students. 

The Question of Philippine Independence. In spite of the improvements under American rule, the Filipinos were not satisfied. Since the overthrow of Spanish rule, they had dreamed of complete independencea dream that was encouraged by the repeated declarations of the Democratic party in the United States committing it to the support of Philippine independence as soon as the Filipinos were capable of self-government. In 

1934 Congress passed the Tydings-McDuffie Act, which provided for independence in about ten years. The Filipinos were authorized to hold a constitutional convention and take such steps as were necessary toward setting up a transitional government which would function until the time of complete separation from the United States. This act was promptly accepted by the Filipinos, who soon adopted a constitution for the Commonwealth of the Philippines. In September, 1935, Manuel Quezon was elected president, and on November 15 of the same year he was inaugurated and the new government became effective. Prior to the time of complete independence ten years later, the Philippine government is under the guidance of the United States in matters where foreign affairs are concerned.

The Republic of Cuba. The United States kept its promise to recognize the independence of Cuba. For three years after the withdrawal of the Spanish troops and government officials, the United States maintained a military government, under the direction of General Leonard Wood, while order was being restored and the Cuban government was being set up. During this period of American supervision, many improvements

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

were made. Besides the restoration of order, yellow fever was stamped out, a public school system was organized, city and provincial governments were set up, a census was taken, and extensive public works were conducted. The United States, however, was unwilling to withdraw from control until its own welfare was fully safeguarded. In 1901 Congress passed an army appropriation bill with the Platt Amendment, which provided: (1) that Cuba should enter into no treaties with foreign powers which would impair its independence or extend to them any naval or military concessions; (2) that it should not contract any debts which it could not repay with the ordinary revenues of the island; (3) that the 

United States should have the right to intervene for the protection of life and property and to preserve the stability of the government; (4) that 

Cuba should continue the work of sanitation begun by the Americans; and (5) that it should sell or lease to the United States coaling or naval stations on the Cuban coast. The United States demanded that these provisions be included in the Cuban constitution and refused to withdraw until this was done. Cuba very reluctantly complied with the demands. 

The Platt Amendment really reduced Cuba to the status of a protectorate. We have intervened four times (1906, 1912, 1917, and 1920) for the restoration of order and the protection of American property, but even more effective has been the constant and decisive American influence in domestic and political affairs. Many of the Cuban industries are controlled by American capitalists. The Cubans, although grateful for the assistance of the United States in securing their independence, have not been satisfied with the restrictions imposed upon them by the Platt Amendment. Early in 1934, in keeping with the policy of improving our relations with Latin America, President Franklin D. Roosevelt persuaded the

Senate to ratify a new treaty with Cuba, by which the amendment has been dropped and the right of intervention has been abandoned. 

Puerto Rico. The island of Puerto Rico, with a population of almost a million in 1898, accepted the rule of the United States willingly. By the Foraker Act of 1900 the Puerto Ricans were given a government very similar to that of the Philippines. Many improvements have been made under American administration, and in 1917 the Puerto Ricans were made citizens of the United States. They have not been contented, however, and in 1928 they petitioned President Coolidge for complete home rule. 

The petition was denied. Most of the discontent of the Puerto Ricans has been caused by economic conditions. Americans have purchased much of the farm land, and have specialized in the production of the two most profitable crops-tobacco and sugar. Most of the native inhabitants are

tenants and agricultural workers. The conditions in Puerto Rico-absentee landlordship, a limited crop system, and government by Americans instead of home rule are not unlike conditions that prevailed in Ireland a half century ago.

Hawaii Acquired by the United States. American interest in the Hawaiian Islands a very important group in the Pacific antedated the War between the North and the South, but it was not until we began to emerge from isolation to imperialism that our actual penetration there was begun. In 1884 we secured the right to establish a naval base at Pearl 

Harbor. Capitalists were quick to see the opportunities for investment offered by the Hawaiian sugar industry, and soon American settlers began to move into the islands. When Queen Liliuokalani endeavored to rule with a firmer hand, the American residents, aided by a body of United States marines, led a revolt which overthrew the monarchy and led to the establishment of an independent republic. The successful revolutionists promptly appealed to the United States for annexation. President Cleveland, who felt that the methods used by the Americans were questionable, refused to consider the question of annexation, and ordered the withdrawal of the marines. In 1897 President McKinley revived the question when he submitted a treaty of annexation to the Senate, but again it failed when the necessary two-thirds majority could not be obtained. After Dewey had won his victory at Manila, and American interests in the Far East were, as a result, greatly increased, annexation was consummated by the Airplane view of Honolulu, the capital of the Hawaiian Islands

passage of a joint resolution. The Hawaiians now have a territorial form of government.

Other American Possessions in the Pacific. In 1878 the United States was given the use of the splendid harbor of Pago Pago, on the island of Tutuila, in the Samoan group. Germany and Great Britain obtained similar concessions in other islands of the group, and the three nations were rivals for the control of the islands until 1899, when Great Britain retired. The United States held the island of Tutuila and near-by islets, and the others were controlled by Germany until the World War, when they became a mandate of New Zealand. 

In 1899 the United States also obtained Wake Island, which is about two thousand miles west of Hawaii. In addition to these islands and 

Guam, other American possessions in the Pacific are the Midway, Howland, Baker, and other small islands, which have their chief value as coaling stations.

The inhabitants of these possessions are not entrusted with the responsibilities of self-government, but are governed by United States naval officers.

Early American Interests in the Far East. American interest in the 

Far East dates back to the close of the Revolution. Finding our trade with the British Empire restricted as a result of our separation from Great Britain, American shippers turned their attention to China. After the voyage of the Empress of China, in 1784 (p. 535), there was built up a thriving trade with that ancient empire. When Great Britain, as a result of the Opium War, 1840-1842, secured the use of several Chinese ports and other commercial concessions, our country was quick to demand similar rights. Commodore Kearney, who commanded a squadron of 

American vessels which had been in Chinese waters during the Opium War, secured a promise from the Chinese authorities that American citizens would have the same commercial privileges as the merchants of the 'most favored nation." In 1844 the most-favored-nation clause was incorporated into a treaty negotiated with China by the American minister Caleb Cushing. The treaty also granted to Americans the right of "extraterritoriality," by which citizens of the United States in China who violated Chinese laws were to be tried according to the laws of the United 

States rather than those of China.

Commercial relations with Japan began through the efforts of Commodore Matthew C. Perry, 1853-1854. With a strong American squadron, he boldly entered the Bay of Yedo (modern Tokyo) and delivered to the Japanese government demands for commercial concessions. He did not

Commodore Matthew C. Perry in Japan; from Perry's Narratives press them for an immediate answer, but returned the next year with a much stronger fleet and persuaded the Shogun to sign a treaty opening two Japanese ports to American trade, and granting other privileges. Friendly relations with the Japanese were maintained during the rest of the century. 

The Open Door. The acquisition of our Pacific possessions in 1898 and 1899 intensified our interests in the Far East. We were alarmed to discover, however, that some of the European nations, almost unnoticed in the United States in the excitement of the war with Spain, had inaugurated a policy which not only threatened to lead to the dismemberment of China, but also jeopardized the Chinese markets of other nations. John 

Hay, our Secretary of State, having a sincere desire to preserve the territorial integrity of China, and also to protect our commercial interests, addressed a note to each European power, asking it to subscribe to the following principles: (1) that it would not close any treaty port nor interfere with the vested interests of other nations in its "sphere of influence"; (2) that it would permit the Chinese tariff to be collected by the Chinese government and to apply equally to all nations; and (3) that it would not discriminate against the citizens of other nations in the matter of railroad rates and port dues. Great Britain promptly agreed to the proposal, but it was with the greatest reluctance that some of the other nations did so. 

As the Monroe Doctrine had been a statement of our policy with regard to the Western Hemisphere, so the "Open Door" policy was an announce-

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

ment of our attitude toward the Far East. By it the United States committed itself to the maintenance of freedom of trade in the Orient. 

The Boxer Rebellion. Aroused by the foreign aggressions, the Chinese organized antialien societies known as the orders of "Literary Patriotic Harmonious Fists," or "Boxers." Secretly supported by the troops of the empress of China, they began a series of outrages which culminated in the siege of the British legation at Peking (now Peiping), to which many of the foreign residents had fled for protection. For about two months the besieged party held its own against the "Boxers," while a joint force composed of American, Japanese, British, French, German, and Russian troops fought their way to the city. Fearing that the powers would seize the opportunity to proceed with the partition of China, Secretary Hay hastened to announce to the world that it was the purpose of the United States to uphold the territorial integrity of China. This principle now became a part of our Far Eastern policy. The announcement had the desired effect, and the only penalties imposed upon China were the punishment of the leaders of the rebellion and the payment of an indemnity of $334,000,000. 

Our share of the indemnity was $24,000,000; but when it was discovered that the losses sustained by American citizens and the cost of the expedition amounted to only $11,000,000, the difference was returned to China. 

This was a friendly gesture which did much toward furthering cordial relations between the two nations. China set the money aside as an educational fund to educate Chinese students in American colleges and universities.

Friction with the Japanese. A series of events early in the twentieth century tended to cool the friendship of the Japanese for the United States. 

At the close of the Russo-Japanese War in 1905, the Japanese were disappointed because the terms of the treaty of peace were not as favorable as they had expected. They blamed this diplomatic defeat upon President 

Roosevelt, upon whose invitation the peace conference was held. The 

Japanese irritation which resulted from this affair was increased the next year when the school authorities of San Francisco excluded Japanese subjects from the schools attended by Americans and Europeans. The Japanese were insulted by this racial discrimination, and although the matter was adjusted by President Roosevelt, the affair served to intensify the bitterness of the Japanese toward America. 

The most serious of the problems that involved the two nations was that of immigration. Since 1882, Chinese immigrants had been excluded from the United States, and there was a strong sentiment in this country for the extension of this policy to include all Oriental laborers. In 1907

Japan entered into an agreement with the United States not to grant passports to laborers who wished to come to this country. This "gentlemen's agreement" was observed for nearly two decades; but when the Immigration Act of 1924 was passed, instead of assigning a quota to Japan, as was done to most other nations, the act excluded all members of the yellow or Mongolian race, including the Japanese as well as the Chinese. The proud 

Japanese people were incensed by what they regarded as a deliberate insult, and an open break between the two powers was narrowly averted. (Later 

American-Japanese relations are discussed on pages 640-642.) 

The Panama Canal; Early Interest. Sailors and engineers dreamed of constructing a canal across the Isthmus of Panama almost from the time it was discovered that this narrow strip of land was blocking a direct route from Western Europe to the Indies; but it was not until the middle of the nineteenth century that definite steps were taken toward launching the project. Experts were unable to agree upon the route. Some favored the short but difficult route across Panama, then a province or "department of Colombia, while others believed that a more feasible route was one across Nicaragua. Many Americans favored the latter because of its greater proximity to the United States. In 1846 the United States showed its interest in the isthmian canal by negotiating a treaty with Colombia (then called New Granada). According to the terms of this treaty, the United States was granted the right of way or free transit by any means of transportation, in return for the guarantee of the neutrality of the zone and Colombia's sovereignty over the property. 

Later attempts to modify this treaty in such a way as to give the United States greater concessions were unsuccessful. This treaty was in force at the time of the Panama revolution in 1903. American interest in the canal was greatly increased in 1848 by the discovery of gold in California (p. 317). 

Two years later, by the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty, the United States and Great Britain agreed that any canal connecting the two oceans, and constructed by either, should be jointly controlled by the two powers, should not be fortified, and should be open to the use of all nations. Conflicting interpretations of this treaty, and the outbreak of the War between the North and the South, prevented the launching of the project at that time. In 

1867, however, the United States showed that its interest had not waned, by negotiating with Nicaragua for a right of way across that country. The provisions of this treaty were very similar to those of the treaty of 1846 with Colombia.

Revival of American Interest. In the closing years of the century, several forces caused a revival and an intensification of the interest of Americans in an isthmian canal. Now that the United States had definitely committed itself to imperialism, commercial interests raised their voices in behalf of a shorter water route between our eastern and western coasts. 

Furthermore, the acquisition of Pacific possessions in 1898 necessitated that steps be taken for their defense. The Oregon incident during the 

Spanish-American War (p. 594) convinced many people that the United 

States should choose between two courses: either the construction of a canal to facilitate the movement of the fleet from one ocean to another, or the doubling of the size of our navy, in order that one fleet might be maintained in the Atlantic sufficient for the protection of our interests there, and another in the Pacific. The military leaders insisted that if the former should be adopted, the protection of our interests would be insured only if the canal should be entirely under our control, and should be properly fortified. This, however, was impossible as long as the Clayton-Bulwer Treaty remained in force. That obstacle was removed in 1901 by the ratification of the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, which expressly abrogated the Clayton- Bulwer Treaty, gave the United States the right to build a canal under its exclusive management, and omitted the restriction concerning fortifications. The United States agreed that the canal should be open to the use of all nations on equal terms. The way was further cleared for the canal by the purchase of the rights and the equipment of the French Panama Company in 1902 for $40,000,000. course

The Revolution in Panama. The next step was to secure the right of way across Panama. Negotiations with Colombia culminated in the drafting of the Hay-Herran Treaty, by which the United States agreed to pay Colombia $10,000,000 in cash and an annuity of $250,000 in return for the lease of a strip of land across the isthmus, six miles in width. The treaty was approved by the United States Senate, but it was rejected by the Colombian Senate, probably because the Colombians hoped to make a better bargain after the expiration, in 1904, of the rights of the Panama Company. The cupidity of the Colombian government aroused the ire of

the United States, but it hardly justified our part in the events which followed. The people of Panama, disappointed by what they regarded as a sacrifice of their interests by the Colombian Senate, planned to strike for their independence. They were secretly encouraged and aided by American officials, and President Roosevelt ordered several warships to Panama, with instructions to prevent the landing of an armed force there. The execution of this order would, of course, prevent the Colombian government from putting down the anticipated revolution. As soon as the American vessels arrived, a bloodless revolution was conducted on November 3, 1903. Three days later, the United States extended unprecedentedly hasty recognition to the Republic of Panama. 

The conduct of the United

States in this affair won for her the ill will, not only of Colombia, but also of nearly all of the other Latin American countries. After refusing Colombia's repeated proposals for arbitration, the United States in 1921 made amends, or attempted to make amends, for its conduct by paying Colombia the sum of $25,000,000. 

The Canal Is Completed.

Almost immediately after November 3 negotiations were begun with Panama, and on 

November 18 a treaty was drafted, by which the United States secured a perpetual lease of a zone ten miles wide across the isthmus, in return for which we guaranteed the independence of Panama, and agreed to pay the sum of

Building the Miraflores lock on the Panama Canal $10,000,000 in cash, and an annual rental of $250,000, beginning nine years after the ratification of the treaty. Work began in May, 1904, and was efficiently prosecuted (p. 558). On August 15, 1914, the canal was informally opened to the commerce of the world by the passage of the 

United States steamer Ancon.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

Our Caribbean Interests. The construction of the Panama Canal gave the United States an increased interest in Central America and the Caribbean, for both economic and military reasons. States with unstable governments and demoralized finances were in danger of being invaded at any time by European powers in order to protect their interests. Such a move could not be tolerated by the United States, even if we should be willing to abandon the Monroe Doctrine, because the proximity of a strong power would make the defense of the canal more difficult. We have already seen (p. 581) how President Theodore Roosevelt asserted the right of the United

States to intervene in the internal affairs of the weak Latin American states when their stability was threatened. This was a new interpretation of the 

Monroe Doctrine but it was in keeping with our policy of imperialism. 

Several times during the administrations of Roosevelt and Taft, the United States intervened in Latin America. The policy was continued by Wilson, but the fears of the Latin states were quieted to some extent by his declaration that "the United States will never again seek one additional foot of territory by conquest." He also tried to discourage revolutions by withholding recognition from governments which had been established by force. 

The Dominican Republic. During the administrations of President 

Johnson and President Grant, efforts were made to annex the Dominican Republic, but the move was blocked by Congress. By 1904 the finances of the little island republic had been so badly mismanaged, and the foreign debt had reached such proportions, that the annual revenues were not sufficient to meet the current expenses of the government and to pay the interest on the debt. The European creditors threatened to intervene. 

President Theodore Roosevelt decided to put his "Corollary" (p. 581) into effect by taking charge of the financial administration of the republic. The 

Dominican president agreed to the collection by the United States of all customs receipts, 45 per cent of which was to be turned over to the local government for its regular expenses, and the remainder to be applied to the debt. Conditions improved under American administration, but the natives tired of our protection. In 1916 American marines were landed to put down a revolt, and for the next eight years the Dominican Republic was under an American military dictatorship. The marines were withdrawn in 1924, but not until the Dominican Republic had agreed to the continuation of our supervision of her finances and had recognized our right to intervene. Thus the Dominican Republic became in reality a protectorate of the United States.

Haiti. The republic of Haiti has had a similar experience. In a period of disorder in December, 1914, marines landed and seized the government

funds in the National Bank of Haiti. This was followed in 1915 by another intervention, in which marines forced the election of a president who was acceptable to the United States, and forced the Haitian congress to accept a virtual American dictatorship, which lasted many years. About eighteen hundred natives were killed in the fighting. The overawed Haitians submitted to a treaty which recognized the right of intervention by the United States and placed the financial administration in our hands for a period of ten years. In 1926 the agreement was extended for another ten years. 

Under American supervision the debt has been reduced, roads have been constructed, sanitation has been improved, and commerce has increased. 

In 1934 the American government agreed to withdraw all of its marines. 

Nicaragua. The United States has been especially interested in Nicaragua, not only because of its proximity to the Panama Canal, but also because it offers an alternative route which may eventually be used for another interoceanic canal. During a revolution in 1909 two American citizens were illegally executed by the Nicaraguan government. This led to the intervention of the United States on the side of the revolutionists, and the election of a president who was acceptable to us. In 1912 marines were landed to keep in power the president we favored, and with the exception of a few months in 1925 they remained in Nicaragua until 1933. During this time Nicaraguan finances were administered by the United States. 

In 1916 the Bryan-Chamorro Treaty was ratified by the two nations. In this treaty the United States was granted in perpetuity the exclusive right to construct a canal across Nicaragua, and Nicaragua leased to us, for a period of ninety-nine years, a naval base on the Gulf of Fonseca, and also the Great Corn and Little Corn Islands as coaling stations. In return for these concessions, the United States agreed to pay Nicaragua the sum of $3,000,000, most of which was to be applied to the public debt. 

Guatemala, Salvador, Costa Rica, and Honduras, while not exactly in the status of protectorates of the United States, are under our influence because of their financial complications. President Coolidge significantly stated that the United States had, toward all of the Central American republics, responsibilities which we did not have toward other states. 

The Virgin Islands. The latest territorial acquisition of the United 

States was the Danish West Indies, or Virgin Islands (1917). Fifty years earlier, Secretary Seward had attempted to purchase the islands for use as a coaling station, but the proposal had been defeated in the Senate. Since these islands are on the main trade route between Europe and the Panama Canal, the United States became even more interested in them when it was certain that the canal would be constructed. In 1902 President Roosevelt's

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

attempt to purchase the islands was defeated by the Danish parliament, but during the World War the fear that Germany might seize them caused us to renew negotiations. The purchase was made by treaty in 1917, for the sum of $25,000,000. The transfer of allegiance did not prove fortunate for the inhabitants of the islands. The American prohibition laws ruined the rum industry, which had been their chief source of income; and the use of oil as fuel on most modern vessels reduced the importance of the islands as a coaling station. Many of the inhabitants became almost povertystricken. But with the repeal of prohibition the economic condition of the islands began to improve. 

The Mexican Problem. Our relations with Mexico present a more difficult problem than is found in our dealings with any other Latin American country. Because of its greater population and more highly developed national spirit, it is not feasible for us to follow the same plan of intervention and financial administration that we have used in the other countries near us on the south, and yet the proximity of Mexico to the United States, and her failure to maintain a stable government, have made it necessary for us to be deeply concerned about her political affairs. Mexico's history has very largely been one of revolutions, except for the period from 1877 to 1911, when the country was under the dictatorship of Porfirio Diaz. 

Maintaining his power by force, this strong ruler courted the favor of foreign nations by making valuable concessions to alien capitalists. By 

1910 American investments in Mexico amounted to almost a billion dollars. 

Americans owned 80 per cent of the railroad and mining property, and 70 per cent of the oil property. Diaz, however, gave little thought to the welfare of the masses of his own subjects, 85 per cent of whom were reduced to the status of landless peons. The autocracy of Diaz, the unrest of the peons, and the fear of the growing foreign influence, led to a successful revolution under the leadership of Francisco Madero, in 1911. The United 

States was in sympathy with the revolutionists because during the last years of Diaz's dictatorship he had extended many favors to the British oil companies. But after a short administration of a year and a half, Madero was the victim of a revolution led by Victoriano de la Huerta. 

Wilson's Policy of "Watchful Waiting." Although the Huerta government was recognized by most of the nations of the world, President Wilson adopted the rather novel policy of refusing to extend recognition to a government which had come into power by force and assassination. He did not want to intervene in the domestic affairs of Mexico, and decided to wait for further developments. He called his policy "watchful waiting." 

Contrary to Wilson's desire, intervention soon became necessary. The

3 arrest of two American marines at Tampico in 1914 led to a demand that Huerta apologize for the act by saluting the American flag. When he failed to comply with the demand, Wilson ordered the marines to seize the customhouse at Veracruz. This was done, but at the cost of nineteen Americans killed and seventy wounded.

Wilson also aided a revolutionary movement against Huerta by lifting an embargo on the shipment of arms into Mexico. The revolution was successful, and Venustiano Carranza succeeded to the presidency. In 

1915 the Carranza government was recognized by the United States in spite of the fact that it was faced with a revolt by Francisco Villa, Carranza's former lieutenant. Villa attempted to force the intervention of the 

United States by making raids across the American border.

Again Wilson's policy of "watchful waiting" had to be temporarily abandoned, and General Gendreau

One of Villa's raids, as shown in a moving picture Pershing was sent into Mexico on a punitive expedition against Villa. 

Many Americans demanded that war be declared upon Mexico, but Wilson wisely turned a deaf ear to the demands and accepted the offer of mediation by the ABC powers (Argentina, Brazil, and Chile). 

In 1920 the Carranza government was overthrown by General Alvaro Obregón, but the new government was not recognized by the United States until three years later. Obregón was succeeded in 1924 by his friend 

Plutarco Elías Calles, who brought about extensive changes in his four-year term. In 1928 Obregón was elected again to the presidency but was assassinated before he could be inaugurated. His term of office was completed by three men and in 1934 General Lazaro Cardenas was elected president for a six-year term.

The Mexican Land Laws. In 1917 a new constitution was adopted by 

Mexico. One article of this document gave to the national government the title to all mineral properties, and specified that such properties could be acquired only by residents who were Mexicans by birth or naturalization.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

This was an old principle which had been observed from the beginning of Spanish rule until 1877, when it was ignored by Diaz. The United States protested against this article of the constitution and withheld recognition of the Obregón government until 1923, when Obregón agreed that the provision should not apply to concessions which had been granted before the ratification of the constitution. This agreement was violated during the next administration by the enactment, by the Mexican congress, of a law which provided that: (1) owners of subsoil property had to apply to the 

Mexican government before January 1, 1927, for confirmation of their titles; (2) aliens who owned stocks in Mexican corporations holding land had to dispose of all stock in excess of forty-nine per cent, within ten years; and (3) alien ownership of land was restricted in districts along the coast and near international boundaries. Americans protested vigorously against the law because it was retroactive and also because American capitalists were not satisfied with the right to lease the land but wanted absolute ownership. Through the skillful diplomacy of Ambassador Dwight W. 

Morrow, the Mexican officials were brought to accept the American view with regard to the first point, and the Mexican Supreme Court rendered an opinion favorable to our views. President Calles agreed to confirm the rights of Americans to oil lands in Mexico if the concessions had been secured before 1917, and if the holders were actually developing the property. In 1938, however, the Mexican government seized many oil lands belonging to Americans or to other owners.

CHAPTER XXXII 

The United States and the 

World War 

The Spirit of Peace. At the end of the nineteenth century and near the beginning of the twentieth, earnest efforts were made by many interested people to make war a thing of the past. At the Hague Conference in 1899 plans were made for a permanent court of arbitration. Writers pointed out that because of the invention of deadly weapons and powerful machines of destruction, wars had become so expensive, deadly, and destructive that the nations of the world could no longer afford them. 

The Outbreak of the World War. While the world was still dreaming about lasting international peace we were shocked by the sudden outbreak in 1914 of what proved to be the greatest war in history. The World War was brought about by an orgy of nationalism, imperialism, and militarism in which many great nations of the world had indulged for a number of years. Each government attempted to instill in its citizens a spirit of supernationalism which led them to believe that their nation was vastly superior to all others and that their civilization was far in advance of that found among all the "lesser breeds without the law." It was the ambition of each group of these supernationalists that their nation should acquire greater power and wealth in order that it might definitely establish itself as the leader among world powers. The economic imperialists entered enthusiastically into this spirit because new markets and opportunities for investment were dependent upon the efforts of their government; the greater its power, the greater would be the concessions it could secure. 

The nations entered into a race for new colonies, new markets, and new commercial concessions. Such rivalry could not be friendly; the commercial races led to races in the construction of armaments. Europe became an armed camp. Only a spark was needed to kindle a conflagration. W.40 615

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

In July, 1914, the heir to the throne of Austria-Hungary was assassinated as the result of a plot in which prominent Serbian officials were implicated. After about a month Austria-Hungary declared war upon 

Serbia. In rapid succession, Germany, Russia, France, Belgium, and 

Wm. Thompson

Front-line trenches of the World War in France Great Britain entered the war. 

Within a few months Germany, Austria-Hungary, Bulgaria, and 

Turkey-known as the Central

Powers were faced by a group of Allied Powers composed mainly of all the other European nations except the Scandinavian countries, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and

Spain, but including many nations outside of Europe. 

American Neutrality. Immediately after the outbreak of hostilities in Europe President Wilson issued a proclamation of neutrality. 

But there was quite a difference between the purely legal neutrality enforced by the government and actual neutrality in the attitude of the American public. With a large population of foreign birth or foreign parentage it was only natural that many of our people would sympathize with one of the belligerents and be hostile to its enemies. Neutrality in sympathies became even more difficult because of a campaign of propaganda waged in America by both sides; but the propaganda of the Allies was perhaps more skillfully conducted and it was not long before public opinion in the United States was definitely enlisted against the Central Powers. 

The government, too, had difficulty in maintaining its rights as a neutral. Soon after the declaration of war Great Britain blockaded the 

German ports and Germany retaliated by attempting to prevent all neutral trade with Great Britain by means of a submarine campaign. We soon found ourselves in a situation similar to that which confronted us during the Napoleonic Wars (see p. 240). Both sides violated the rights of neutrals which had been guaranteed by international law. The list of goods which were to be regarded as contraband of war had been agreed upon by the nations, but Great Britain extended this list to include articles which had

3 always been regarded as noncontraband, such as leather, cotton, wool, rubber, chemicals, and even foodstuffs. She also seized American goods bound for neutral countries on the ground that they were intended for ultimate German consumption. She rifled our mail in search of information concerning the plans of her enemies which might be of value to her; also, in exercising her right of search, she forced American merchant vessels to enter British ports and remain there for days before being permitted to proceed. Our government protested against these violations of our neutral rights, but for the most part our protests were unheeded. 

Submarine Warfare. German violations of our neutrality were even more serious because they involved not only vexations to travelers and a loss of property, but a loss of lives as well. In retaliation for the Allied blockade and the extension of the contraband list, Germany decided to extend the submarine campaign to all trade with the Allies. The use of the submarine for this purpose was contrary to international law. Because of its small size and light gunnery the submarine could not comply with the international requirement that ships should be warned and searched before being sunk, and that the crews and passengers should be rescued. 

Announcement was made by Germany that beginning February 18, 1915, all of the waters around Great Britain would be a war zone in which every ship belonging to an enemy would be destroyed at sight, and the warning was given to neutral countries that, in view of the fact that British ships had begun the practice of flying neutral flags when in danger, neutral vessels would be in danger if found in the war zone. President Wilson 

A submarine. Before being submerged, of course, the awnings etc. shown on top are taken inside. Gendreau V-I

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

replied with the announcement that the United States would hold the German government to "strict accountability" for all damage to American commerce or the loss of American lives. In spite of Wilson's note, several American vessels were sunk and several American citizens lost their lives on Allied ships which were victims of the submarines. 

On May 7, 1915, the civilized world was shocked to hear of the sinking, by a German submarine, of the British liner Lusitania, which resulted in the death of 1195 men, women, and children, 124 of whom were American citizens. The American public was almost as aroused as it had been after the sinking of the Maine in 1898. There seems to be some evidence, however, for the German contention that the Lusitania, although a passenger ship, was also an auxiliary of the British navy and was carrying war materials, and that American officials were at fault in permitting passengers, in violation of Federal laws, to take passage on a public carrier which had explosives as part of its cargo.

President Wilson sent a sharp note to Germany protesting against the sinking of the Lusitania and threatening war if the offense was repeated. 

In reply to the protest the German government agreed to stop the unrestricted sinking of vessels without warning and without making provision for the safety of the crews and passengers, and even agreed to discontinue the submarine warfare entirely if the United States would prevent Great Britain from treating food supplies as contraband of war. Great Britain, however, was unwilling to discontinue a practice which gave promise either of starving the German nation into submission or of inducing Germany to continue the submarine warfare and thus making probable the entrance of the United States into the war. On February 1, 1917, Germany resumed the unrestricted submarine warfare, and President Wilson replied by severing diplomatic relations. In February and March several American ships were sunk by German submarines. 

The United States Enters the War. Although Germany's submarine policy was the chief cause of our entrance into the war on the side of the Allies, there were other causes. After the outbreak of the war in Europe 

American manufacturers built up an enormous munitions industry. Since these munitions could be sold only to the Allies because of the blockade, German agents attempted to destroy this legal source of aid to the enemy by blowing up our munitions plants. German diplomatic officials also attempted to arouse Mexico to a war against our country. Another influence upon our decision to join the Allies was the fact that the Central Powers were under the nearly absolute rule of monarchs, while the leading Allied Powers had governments more nearly like our own.

Soon after the second inauguration of President Wilson he issued a call for a special session of Congress, and on April 2 he delivered to Congress his memorable message in which he asked for a declaration of war upon the "irresponsible" German government in order that the world might be made "safe for democracy." His recommendation was followed. On April 6 the

House of Representatives approved, by the vote of 373 to 50, the resolution which declared a state of war, after the Senate had taken similar action by an even more decisive majority. 

Mobilizing Our Man Power. Many people, both in Europe and in 

America, had believed that if the United States entered the war our participation would be restricted to the furnishing of supplies and money; but in the spring of 1917 the Allies found themselves in desperate need of additional man power. Russia had just withdrawn from the war, releasing many additional German troops for service against France. Immediately after the declaration of war, the United States, therefore, took steps toward raising a large army for service in France. Profiting from the experience of the nations engaged in the war, the United States abandoned its traditional policy of depending upon the volunteer system, and on May 18 Congress passed the Selective Service Act. Every man in the United States between the ages of twenty-one and thirty-one years was required to register. These men were then classified for military service according to their physical fitness and the ease with which they could be spared from the war industries and the support of dependents. Many of those who had been classified as eligible for immediate service were then drafted by lot for actual service. Later the age limits were extended to from eighteen to 

One of the World War training camps 10:0

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

forty-five years. The next month after the passage of the act, 10,000,000 men registered; and by September 500,000 men had been called and were being trained in thirty-two training camps. During the war over 24,000,ooo men registered and more than 4,000,000 were called to the colors, about half of whom actually reached France. By the close of the war American troops were being rushed to Europe at the rate of nearly 300,000 a month. 

The danger from submarines was overcome by placing the transports under the convoy of American and British warships. The effectiveness of the submarines was still further reduced by the construction of "submarine chasers" equipped with depth bombs, and by the laying of barrages of mines across the North Sea and the English Channel. 

Financing the War. When we entered the war the financial resources of the Allies were almost exhausted and many of the nations looked to us for loans to enable them to continue the war. The wealth of the United 

States, therefore, became a decisive factor. The total direct cost of the war to the United States, including our loans to the Allies, has been estimated at about $35,500,000,000. This was a sum nearly three times the amount of the expenditures of the Federal government during the first century of its existence, and it represented an expenditure of nearly $50,day for the duration of the war. The United States used two methods of raising this vast sum of money-taxation and loans. 000,000

Income taxes were greatly increased; an excess profits tax of from 15 to 60 per cent was levied upon the incomes of corporations, partnerships, and individuals; heavy taxes were levied upon luxuries, amusements, and documents of various kinds; and the taxes on tobacco and beverages were increased. As a result of these taxes the income of the government increased from $735,000,000 for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1914, to $4,648,000,000 in 1919. 

By far the greater part of the money needed to conduct the war was raised by bond issues. Four bond issues, called Liberty Loans, were floated during the war, and a Victory Liberty Loan was floated after the signing of the armistice. These loans totaled nearly $22,000,000,000. The fact that every issue was oversubscribed is a good indication of the war enthusiasm of the American people. In addition to the Liberty Loans the 

American public also subscribed about $1,000,000,000 by the purchase of 5-dollar war certificates and 25-cent war saving stamps. The national debt of the United States increased from about $1,000,000,000 before the war to about $26,000,000,000 in 1919. 

Co-ordination of Industry. In order to use our resources and industries to the best advantage, government control was carried to a hitherto un-

dreamed-of extent. In order to facilitate transportation by co-ordination, the railroads were operated directly by the government (p. 551). The government also carried out a vast shipbuilding program under the supervision of the Emergency Fleet Corporation (p. 557) in order to replace the tonnage lost by the United States and Great Britain in the submarine warfare. For the co-ordination of our industry, Congress in 1916 had authorized the President to appoint a Council of National Defense, composed of six members of the cabinet and seven civilian advisers on raw materials, finished products, munitions, transportation, labor, engineering, and medicine; but after our entrance into the war the Council's powers were enlarged by the creation of subsidiary boards known as the War 

Industries Board, the War Trade Board, and the War Finance Corpora tion. Early in 1918 the government organized a War Labor Board for the settlement of disputes between employers and employees. 

The President also was given unprecedented powers. By the Food 

Control Act (Lever Act) of August 10, 1917, he was empowered to requisition foods, fuel, and other supplies which were needed for the support of the army and the Allies. In order to encourage the farmers to plant a larger acreage of wheat, the President guaranteed a price of $2.26 a bushel for the prospective crop. The President also appointed Herbert Hoover as Food Administrator of the United States, with control over the conservation of, and economy in, food and fuel. The public was asked to observe meatless, wheatless, sweetless, and even heatless days. The response of the American people was magnificent. While the sacrifices called for by the government were not compulsory, the people almost without exception complied with the government's requests; if any person were not inclined to comply with the program of conservation and economy, public sentiment practically forced him to do so. Probably never in our history has our nation been so completely unified in support of a common cause.

The American Navy in the War. The work of our navy in the World 

War was fully up to the high standard of efficiency established in the Spanish-American War. Soon after war was declared, a squadron of vessels under the command of Rear Admiral William S. Sims was sent to join the Allied fleets in the blockade of Germany and to assist in the war against the submarines. In view of the fact that the German fleet did not venture out on the high seas after our entrance into the war, our fleet was engaged in no naval battles, but it rendered valuable service in convoying transports across the Atlantic, in laying a barrage of mines across the North Sea, and in other operations against the German submarines. American soldiers in a French village successful was the war upon the submarines that in transporting over 2,000,000 troops to France, only a few hundred were lost. Before the war ended more than three hundred American ships were operating in European waters. The American Army in Action. Because of the small size of our standing army, we could be of little assistance to the armies in France until our civilian soldiers were trained. But we sent a small contingent of our regular troops to France soon after the declaration of war and they marched through the streets of Paris largely for the psychological effect their arrival would have upon the French population. This effect, according to Allied and German historians alike, was a very great one. Germany, realizing that America had entered the war in earnest, planned a series of tremendous drives on the French front in the spring of 1918, hoping they would bring the Allies to terms before the Americans could participate in sufficient numbers to be of very great assistance to the Allies. During the winter of 1917-1918 the Americans arrived in steadily increasing numbers. 

When the German drives began in March, 1918, they swept everything before them, and for a time it seemed that they would be successful. Each day, however, the Allied resistance stiffened. American forces were rushed

to the front, where they served at first with British and French units. On 

May 28 they engaged in their first important independent action, when they drove the Germans from the village of Cantigny, on the war front in France.

The role of the Americans now became more important. At Château- 

Thierry they held their ground when other forces around them were retiring before the German advance. Again at Belleau Wood a force of 

American marines and French troops, after a fierce struggle, succeeded in dislodging the enemy. Finally, in the second battle of the Marne, the tide of the war definitely turned against the Germans. About 400,000 

Americans took part in this smashing Allied victory. 

St. Mihiel and Argonne Forest. The American army was now organized as a separate unit and was entrusted with the defense of the southern sector of the battle line which stretched for nearly six hundred miles from the North Sea to Switzerland. On September 12, under the command of

General John J. Pershing, who had been placed in charge of all the American expeditionary forces in France soon after the declaration of war, over 500,000 American and nearly 70,000 French troops attacked the Germans in the St. Mihiel salient. After four days of fighting the Germans were driven from the salient with heavy losses, including 16,000 men who were taken prisoners.

Later in September the Americans became engaged in a terrific battle in the Argonne Forest-the greatest battle in which an American army, fighting as an independent unit, has ever been engaged. This rough sector, which nature had made easily defensible, the Germans had made almost impregnable by a network of trenches seven miles in width, protected by barbed wire entanglements and concrete machine gun implacements. For forty-seven days the battle raged with heavy losses on both sides. Gradually the enemy was forced back a distance of about thirty miles. The battle ended with the capture of Sedan, a most important German base. 

When the hostilities ended in November, General Pershing was planning to carry the war into the enemy's territory with a drive against Metz, the strongest of all German forts. All fighting ceased with the signing of the armistice on November 11, 1918.

Wilson Strives for Peace. Near the close of 1916, when the United 

States was still a neutral, President Wilson took steps toward the establishment of peace in Europe. As a basis upon which to work he asked the contending forces to state their war aims. In view of the fact that at that time the German arms enjoyed a decided advantage over their adversaries, Germany was unwilling to make many concessions in order to end the war,

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

"Over the Top"; from a drawing by Kerr Eby, a U. S. Army artist in France and her reply was very indefinite. The Allies, too, had secret territorial aspirations which they were unwilling to entrust to the mediation of such an idealist as Wilson; their replies also were evasive, and the effort to secure peace was a failure.

After our entrance into the war, Wilson, in a series of addresses, made it clear that no peace could be negotiated with the German kaiser; but that the German people, against whom he declared we held no enmity, must take the power into their own hands. On January 8, 1918, in a speech before Congress, Wilson stated the famous Fourteen Points which he proposed as the war aims of the Allies and Associated Powers (the United States refused to enter into an alliance with the European powers). Eight of the points dealt with the adjustment of the territorial boundaries in Europe largely in accordance with the principle of self-determination of nationalities. The other points were as follows: open treaties of peace, openly arrived at; freedom of the seas; removal of economic barriers; reduction of armaments; adjustment of colonial claims with due regard to the welfare of the populations concerned; and, most important of all, in the mind of Wilson, a league of the nations of the world to enforce peace. 

This statement of war aims, accepted in a general way by the Allied governments, created a profound impression upon the national minorities of Europe and solidified the resistance to Germany at a most critical period

of the war. After the abdication of the German kaiser in an uprising early in November, the agents of the provisional German Republic agreed to the armistice with the understanding that the treaty of peace would be based upon the Fourteen Points outlined by Wilson, with two reservations by the Allies, dealing with reparations and the interpretation of the "freedom of the seas" clause. 

The Treaty of Versailles. The peace conference met at Paris on January 18, 1919. The victorious Allied and Associated Powers were represented there, but the defeated Central Powers and Russia were not. 

Since the treaty of peace was to be based upon the Fourteen Points, Wilson decided to break all precedents by heading the American delegation to the peace conference. Most of the important decisions of the conference were made by the "Big Three": Wilson, Lloyd George of Great Britain, and Clemenceau of France. The great difficulties in the way of a peace treaty in accordance with the Fourteen Points consisted of the secret. treaties by which some European nations had agreed to divide the spoils of the war, and also a feeling of revenge on the part of some victorious Europeans. The first of Wilson's points was violated when the decisions of the conference were made in secret meetings instead of being "openly arrived at." Entire responsibility for the war was imposed upon Germany and there was much talk of hanging the kaiser and making Germany pay for the war. Wilson had no sympathy for these demands, but in order to achieve his chief objective—the organization of the League of Nations he was forced to make concessions. The treaty which Germany was compelled to sign at Versailles—a suburb of Paris-was in many respects a departure from the letter and the spirit of the Fourteen Points, and it could hardly be expected to bring a lasting peace to the world. 

When the Treaty of Versailles was submitted to the United States for ratification, considerable opposition arose, chiefly because of objection to our entrance into the League of Nations. Supporters of the treaty failed to muster the necessary two-thirds majority in the Senate, so that the United States did not become a party to it. The United States did not resume normal diplomatic relations with the Central Powers until 1921, when separate treaties, which did little more than declare the end of the war, were signed with Germany, Austria, and Hungary.

CHAPTER XXXIII The United States and World 

Peace

International Arbitration. A most encouraging development in international relations has been the trend toward the peaceful settlement of disputes. The growth of imperialism made necessary contacts of nation with nation and the breakdown of isolation. Too frequently these contacts were of a hostile nature, necessitating heavy armaments and continual preparations for war. Many statesmen became convinced that just as domestic commerce was most profitable when free from cutthroat competition, so would the intercourse between nations yield the best returns if conducted without constant friction and bitterness. More and more the nations of the world became willing to submit their international disputes to settlement by arbitration through the offices of other nations, or by decisions of an international court. 

In spite of our desire to avoid, as far as possible, dealings with European nations, no government has shown a greater willingness to submit its disputes to arbitration; and several times, through our efforts to enforce the 

Monroe Doctrine, we have urged the arbitration of disputes by other nations. As early as 1795, in the Jay Treaty, the United States and Great 

Britain agreed to the settlement by arbitration of several of the points in dispute. We have already considered the use of arbitration in the settlement of the boundaries between the United States and Canada (p. 585). 

This method was used also in the settlement of claims against Mexico in the 1840's, and in the question of the Newfoundland fisheries. Before 

1907, our country had been a party to the settlement by arbitration of sixty disputes, several of which might easily have led to war. 

The Treaty of Washington. The most important treaty of arbitration the world had seen was the Treaty of Washington, in 1871, in which several 628

serious disputes between the United States and Great Britain were adjusted. The most serious of these was the question of the Alabama claims. 

During the War between the North and the South, the Alabama and the Florida, two vessels which had been built in British ports and delivered to the Confederacy, had inflicted serious losses upon Northern commerce. 

Senator Charles Sumner, the chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, estimated that the direct damages amounted to $15,000,000, but he also insisted that Great Britain was responsible for indirect damages amounting to $110,000,000 sustained as a result of the increased insurance rates and the driving of American commerce from the seas. To these direct and indirect losses Sumner wished to add several billion dollars, the cost of the prolongation of the war, which he said had been due to British interference. Of course these claims were extravagant. Great Britain was willing to pay reasonable damages, for by so doing she would establish the international principle that a neutral nation has no right to deliver ships to another nation at war—a principle from which she might profit in future naval wars in which she might be involved. Other questions that were also in dispute then were the Newfoundland fisheries; the boundary between the United States and Canada, in Puget Sound, between Vancouver Island and the mainland; and financial claims of British and American citizens. 

During President Johnson's administration, the United States refused Great Britain's offer to arbitrate, but in 1871 our Secretary of State, Hamilton Fish, negotiated the Treaty of Washington, by which these questions were submitted to courts of arbitration. The fisheries question was merely patched up for a period of ten years; the boundary line through 

Puget Sound was settled by the German emperor in favor of the American claims; and British citizens were awarded $1,929,819./The Alabama claims were submitted to a commission of five members appointed in the following manner: one by the President of the United States, one by the queen of 

Great Britain, one by the king of Italy, one by the emperor of Brazil, and one by the president of Switzerland. The arbitrators met at Geneva, Switzerland, in December, 1871. They threw out all claims for indirect damages, but decided that the British government, because of its failure to observe its obligations as a neutral, should pay the United States direct damages amounting to $15,500,000. Great Britain promptly paid the award. 

Pan-American Co-operation. The Pan-American movement was an outgrowth of the Monroe Doctrine. As early as the year 1826 Simon 

Bolivar, dreaming of a confederacy of all American republics for protection against European interference, called a conference of all the nations of the

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

Western Continent, at Panama. Henry Clay was in sympathy with 

Bolivar's plan, but our delegates were delayed by the debate in the Senate over their confirmation, and did not reach Panama until the conference had adjourned without any important accomplishments. Little more was done toward bringing the American republics more closely together until over half a century later, when the question was revived by James G. Blaine, our Secretary of State (1881). His plans for a Pan- 

American conference during the administration of President Garfield were thwarted by the outbreak of war between Peru and Chile; but in 1889 the nations assembled at Washington at the invitation of our Congress. 

Blaine, who again was Secretary of State (1880-1892), presided. Not much was accomplished in regard to agreements concerning arbitration and economic reciprocity; but under Blaine's able leadership the conference made a permanent contribution to better relations between the American republics by the creation of the Bureau of American Republics in Washington, later known as the Pan American Union. 

Pan-American Building, Washington, D. C.

The Pan American Union. The headquarters of the Pan American 

Union are at Washington, in a beautiful building given by Andrew Carnegie. The expenses are shared by the member states in proportion to their population. The chief officer is the Director General, but the most important agency of the Union is the Governing Board. Originally, this

board was composed of the diplomatic representatives of the states stationed at Washington, with the American Secretary of State acting as chairman; but some of the states objected to this arrangement because they thought it gave too much influence to the United States. At the sixth Pan-American Conference, at Havana, in 1928, the organization was altered by giving each state the right to appoint a member of the Governing Board, who was not a diplomatic representative at Washington. The chairman is elected by the members of this board. The Director General can no longer act as the delegate of his government at the Pan-American Conferences.

The policies of the Union are determined by the conferences, in which each state is entitled to representation. Since the first conference at Washington, in 1889, others have been held as follows: at Mexico city, 1901; at Rio de Janeiro, 1906; at Buenos Aires, 1910; at Santiago, Chile, 1923; at Havana, 1928; at Montevideo, 1933 and at Lima, 1938. Perhaps the most important of these conferences was the one at Havana. In addition to the revision of the organization of the Pan American Union mentioned above, this conference also provided for an arbitration conference to meet at Washington. It met the same year (1928), and drew up an arbitration treaty similar to the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact (pp. 639-640), and a conciliation treaty providing for the peaceful settlement of all inter-American disputes. All of the republics in the Western Hemisphere have subscribed to these treaties. 

Improvement in Pan-American Relations. President Wilson in 1916 

proposed the formation of an American league of nations, guaranteeing mutual political independence and territorial integrity, and providing for the settlement of disputes by arbitration. The plan was blocked, however, because of the distrust of the United States felt by the Latin-American nations, which have interpreted all proposals of our government as being prompted by our imperialistic ambitions. This distrust has also been the main reason for the failure of the Pan-American Conferences to do more constructive work. Much has been done in recent years to regain the favor and confidence of our smaller neighbors. Soon after President 

Herbert Hoover's election in 1928, and before his inauguration, he broke the ice for better relations by making a good-will tour through South America; and much more was accomplished in and after 1933 under the leadership of President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Secretary of State 

Cordell Hull. In 1933 Hull, in a frank speech before the Pan-American 

Conference at Montevideo, gave convincing assurance of a change in the attitude of the United States toward the American republics. The Lima W-41

Our increased prestige in world affairs, as a result of the Spanish-American War, caused the United States to be included in the invitation of the czar of Russia to the leading powers to attend a conference at the Hague, in the Netherlands, for the consideration methods of preventing war. In 1907 the czar called for a second conference to meet at the Hague. 

The United States was one of the forty-four nations which attended. 

Efforts to reduce armaments failed, but the conference resulted in a codification of international law and the adoption of resolutions looking toward the more humane conduct of war. Of special interest to the nations of the 

Western Hemisphere was the adoption of the Drago Doctrine, supplementing the Monroe Doctrine, to the effect that nations could not use force to collect debts unless the debtor nation refused to submit to arbitration, or to abide by the award. The United States endorsed the doctrine. 

Attempts to Outlaw War. The submission of cases to the Hague Court for arbitration was purely voluntary. In order to add to the effectiveness of the peace machinery, various nations entered into treaties binding themselves to arbitrate all disputes of a legal nature except those involving "national honor" or "vital interests." By these qualifications the treaties were robbed of much of their effectiveness, but they were a step in the right direction. The United States, in 1908, under the leadership of Secretary of State Elihu Root, entered into such arbitration agreements as these with more than a score of nations. 

During the first administration of President Wilson, the Secretary of State, William Jennings Bryan, entered into "cooling-off" treaties with a
