By these treaties the contracting nations agreed to submit all international disputes which could not be settled by friendly discussion to a commission of inquiry, and bound themselves not to begin hostilities for at least a year while the investigation was in progress. 

The Organization of the League of Nations. The League of Nations probably represents the greatest step that has ever been taken toward the promotion of international co-operation. It was organized in 1920, with twenty-four nations as members; by March, 1935, the membership had increased to fifty-nine. The chief object of the League is the prevention of war. Several means were devised for the accomplishment of this object: compulsory arbitration, reduction of armaments, elimination of secret treaties, removal of the causes of economic friction, and the mobilization of public opinion against war. Provision was made for enforcement in the form of military intervention, or an economic boycott by the member nations against an offender. The efforts of the League have not been limited to the prevention of war. It has rendered other services by regulating the traffic in harmful drugs; by improving labor conditions, especially with respect to women and children; by preventing the spread of epidemic diseases; by rendering aid to bankrupt states; by supervising the

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

The new Peace Palace at Geneva, headquarters of the League of Nations government of mandates-the former German colonies; and by caring for the refugees of war. 

The work of the League is conducted through an Assembly in which all member nations are entitled to equal representation; a Council composed of representatives of fifteen member nations, five of which are permanent and the others elected by the Assembly for a term of three years; and the Secretariat, composed of the Secretary-General and a large staff of officials. Most of the policies of the League are determined by the Council, which is by far the most important of the bodies. The expenses of the administration of the League are shared by the member nations in proportion to their wealth and population. The seat of the permanent Secretariat of the League is at Geneva, Switzerland. Other bodies associated with the League but not a part of it are the World Court and the International Labor Office. 

Why the United States Has Not Joined the League. As soon as it became evident that the League would be provided for in the Treaty of Versailles, Senators Lodge and Borah began to mobilize opposition to it in the United States. Some of the criticism of the League was prompted by party politics, but many people were impartial and their objections were prompted by sincere though perhaps misguided patriotism. At first the objection was made that the League would conflict with the Monroe Doctrine in the Western Hemisphere. President Wilson, however, met this criticism by having a clause inserted into the Covenant of the League giving assurance that "regional understandings" would not be infringed upon. 

Perhaps the most serious of the objections urged against our entrance into the League was the claim that it would involve the loss of our national

sovereignty and might result in the violation of our Constitution. It was claimed that the requirement in the Covenant that member nations must, if called upon, place military forces at the disposal of the League to be used against offending members, would automatically lead us into wars; while according to our Constitution, the power of declaring war belongs to Congress. Some objected to our entrance into the League on the ground that it would be a departure from our traditional policy of isolation, which, as a matter of fact, we had long since abandoned; and that it would draw us into European politics. Others believed that the Treaty of Versailles was unjust and that the nations which had gained most in the division of the spoils would use the League as the means of preserving the favorable status quo. Still others feared that the League of Nations might attempt to interfere with such problems as the tariff, immigration, and naturalization, questions which they considered as purely domestic although they involved the citizens of other nations. And, finally, some Americans were alarmed at the fact that the Covenant of the League gave each of the dominions of the British Empire representation in the Assembly, and professed to see in that arrangement the domination of the League by the British Empire. This argument was weakened, however, by the fact that few important questions were settled by the Assembly, and that each nation's interest was safeguarded by the requirement of a unanimous vote on all vital questions.

Those who favored our entrance into the League believed that the United States, claiming to be interested in any measure to prevent war, could not afford to be indifferent to this most forward step toward the promotion of peace. The entrance of the United States into the League became the chief issue in the presidential election of 1920. The overwhelming victory of the Republican party, which claimed that the desired results might be achieved without our entrance into the League, indicated that the American public was definitely opposed to such a move. 

Co-operation without Admission. We must not be deceived into believing that our refusal to become a member of the League of Nations marked a return to our former policy of isolation. Our rapidly increasing investments in foreign states, growing from $2,625,000,000 in 1914 to $18,000,000,000 in 1932, gave us an increased interest in the stability of foreign governments. Isolation was impossible. President Harding soon realized that the United States could not remain indifferent to the activities of the League, and adopted the practice of sending "unofficial observers" who attended the meetings of the League and international conferences without direct participation. American citizens were encouraged by our

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

government to accept positions as judges in the World Court and to assist in the settlement of difficult economic questions. Since 1928 our participation in movements led by the League has been greatly extended. We sent representatives to all of the important conferences on armaments and economic and humanitarian questions. In 1930 we appointed a Consul 

General to the League with offices at Geneva. During the recent Chino- 

Japanese dispute, the United States co-operated with the League to a greater extent than ever before, the policies adopted by the League following closely the suggestions of Secretary of State Stimson. A fuller discussion of these activities will be given in the following pages. 

The World Court. The Covenant of the League of Nations contained an article which provided for the establishment of a "Permanent Court of International Justice." At the second meeting of the Council, in 1920, a committee of prominent jurists, including Elihu Root, former American Secretary of State, was appointed to draft a statute for the organization of the court. In September, 1921, the necessary number of ratifications had been secured and a court of eleven justices, later increased to fifteen, was instituted. This court, usually known as the World Court, is independent The World Court in session 

Wide World of the League of Nations, and nations which have not joined the League may become members. The jurisdiction of the court may be either voluntary or compulsory, but by 1934 fifty-two states had obligated themselves to submit to the court all questions relating to the interpretation of a treaty or of international law, a violation of an international obligation,

or the nature and extent of the reparations for such a violation, and to abide by the decisions. The meetings are held at the Hague. 

The relations of the United States with the World Court have been similar to those with the League of Nations. Elihu Root was very active in the organization of the court, and three Americans, John Bassett Moore, Charles Evans Hughes, and Frank B. Kellogg, have served as judges; but the United States has refrained from accepting membership. In the presidential election of 1924 both parties advocated that we join the World Court, and in 1926 the Senate voted to accept membership, but only on condition that the member nations would agree to five reservations. Four of the reservations were accepted, but the fifth was rejected because it would have given us a position as a specially favored member. President 

Coolidge pressed the question no further and the matter was dropped. In 

1929 the statute of the World Court was revised by the adoption of the "Root Formula" in such a way as to meet the previous objections. President F. D. Roosevelt, in a message to the Senate, recommended our adherence to the World Court. He wrote, "The movement to make international justice practicable and serviceable is not subject to partisan considerations." In February, 1935, after a long and spirited debate, the 

Senate voted not to accept the recommendation of the President. 

Disarmament: the Washington Conference. Almost a century before the outbreak of the World War the United States and Great Britain set a splendid example for the rest of the world by an agreement not to fortify the boundaries between the United States and Canada, and not to maintain a fleet on the Great Lakes except for police purposes. Unfortunately this example of disarmament was merely an exception to the general rule of heavy armaments which was adopted by most of the nations and which had much to do with the outbreak of the war in 1914. One of the outstanding lessons of the World War was that the maintenance of large armies and navies was not conducive to peace. The postwar era, therefore, has been marked by several efforts among the nations of the world to restrict their armaments. 

In 1921 President Harding invited Great Britain, Japan, France, and Italy to join with the United States in a conference at Washington for the purpose of bringing about a limitation of their navies, and other nations having interests in the Far East were invited to attend for the consideration of the problems of that section of the world. When the conference convened in November, Secretary of State Hughes presented a program which called for a holiday in the construction of capital ships; the scrapping of many battleships of older types; and the limitation of the tonnage of

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

cruisers, destroyers, submarines, and airplane carriers to the same proportion as the capital ships. Under this plan the strengths of the navies of Great Britain, the United States, and Japan would be in the ratio of 5 to 5 to 3, with less than 2 each for France and Italy. The three larger powers accepted this plan with a few minor changes, but France refused to accept a limitation of the submarines and other auxiliary vessels, and consequently the proposed limitation was restricted to capital ships-and these were already being largely replaced by the swifter and more effective cruisers.

The Geneva and London Naval Conferences. The world soon realized that the naval disarmament accomplishments of the Washington Conference were rather insignificant. Since there was no restriction upon the construction of lighter vessels, the nations actually increased their naval building programs. In 1927 President Coolidge invited the naval powers to attend another conference at Geneva. The rejection of the invitation by France and Italy, and the failure of the United States, Great Britain, and Japan to reach an agreement relative to the cruisers, caused the conference to end in failure.

Three years later the powers resumed their discussions at the London Naval Conference. At this conference the naval strengths of the United 

States, Great Britain, and Japan were fixed at the ratio of 10 to 10 to 7. 

In December, 1935, delegates from Great Britain, the United States, Japan, France, and Italy again met in London for further consideration of naval limitations. The conference failed when Japan withdrew because she was denied the concession of "naval parity" with the United States and 

Great Britain. 

Failure of Disarmament. The first general disarmament conference was called by the League of Nations to meet at Geneva in February, 1932. 

About sixty nations, including the United States, were represented. Among the questions brought up for consideration were the limitation of appropriations for armaments; the limitation of the length of the terms of military service; the limitation of military, naval, and air forces; and the appointment of a permanent disarmament commission to report to the League concerning the efforts of the nations to comply with the agreements of the conference. France's fear of Germany precluded any important accomplishments. President Hoover submitted a plan providing for the reduction of the world's armaments by about one third. He favored the complete abolition of all tanks, bombing planes, large mobile guns, gas, and other implements of offensive warfare, and reductions in the land, naval, and air forces. The plan was promptly approved by Russia, Italy,

and Germany, but France was unwilling to reduce her forces, and Great Britain and Japan opposed the abolition of tanks, bombing planes, and large mobile guns. Unable to reach a decision, the conference adjourned to meet again a year later. The rise of Hitler to power in Germany and his demand for German equality in armaments with the other nations doomed to failure the next meeting of the conference, which again adjourned without any important results.

Meanwhile the race in armaments continued with increased bitterness. 

Whereas the fourteen greatest powers had organized forces of about 29,000,000 men in 1913, by 1935 they had nearly 48,000,000; and the nations which spent about $1,300,000,000 for armaments in the year 1913, spent over $4,654,000,000 in 1935, and over $10,000,000,000 in 1937. 

The Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact. The chief obstacle to disarmament has been the problem of security against the anticipated aggressions of other nations. One effort to give the nations the wanted security was the 

Geneva Protocol, which was approved by the Assembly of the League in 1924. This proposed agreement provided for the settlement of disputes of all kinds either by arbitration or by the World Court. Each state that accepted the Protocol was to agree to make war upon any aggressor. England objected and the Protocol did not go into effect. The next year a number of the European nations reached the so-called Locarno Agreements, in which each nation agreed not to resort to war against the other signatories of the seven treaties which were concluded. 

In 1928 the United States had a prominent part in promoting the most advanced step that had been taken toward the establishment of national security. Aristide Briand, the French foreign minister, suggested that the 

United States join France in a treaty to outlaw war between the two nations. Secretary of State Kellogg was favorable to the idea, but suggested that it be extended to include as many nations as were willing to sign it with France and the United States. After an exchange of notes fifteen nations signed the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact, or Pact of Paris. It was approved by the United States Senate by a vote of 85 to 1, and at the present time most of the nations of the world are signatories. The provisions of the Pact are as follows:

ARTICLE I 

The High Contracting Parties solemnly declare in the names of their respective peoples that they condemn recourse to war for the solution of international controversies, and renounce it as an instrument of national policy in their relations with one another.

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

ARTICLE II 

The High Contracting Parties agree that the settlement or solution of all disputes or conflicts of whatever nature or of whatever origin they may be, which may arise among them, shall never be sought except by pacific means. 

Proclamation of the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact, at Washington, 1929. The three men standing are ex- 

President Coolidge, President Hoover, and ex-Secretary of State Kellogg. The others are diplomatic representatives There has been some criticism of this pact because it makes no provision for penalties to be imposed upon a nation that violates it. Others reply that in placing dependence upon public opinion for the enforcement of the pact, the signing nations have laid the only true foundation for international peace. In 1933 the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact was strengthened somewhat by the signing of the Pacts of Rome and London by the leading European powers, declaring that the Kellogg-Briand Pact applied to all "aggressor nations" and defining the term "aggressor nation."

The Far Eastern Question. We have already seen the growing interest of the United States in the Far East after the Spanish-American War, and the developments which caused our adoption of a Far Eastern policy stressing the "Open Door" and the territorial integrity of China. These two principles were challenged by a series of events in the twentieth century which brought Japan to the front as one of the great world powers and as the dominant power in the Orient. Her prestige having been increased as a result of a defensive alliance with Great Britain, a smashing victory in the Russo-Japanese War, with its consequent territorial gains, and the 

---

annexation of Korea (renamed Chosen) in 1911, Japan entered upon a policy which established her in a position of supremacy in the Far East similar to that of the United States in the Western Hemisphere. In 1914 

Japan entered the World War as the ally of Great Britain, and immediately seized the Shantung peninsula in China, a German sphere of influence. 

Taking advantage of the preoccupation of the Western powers with the World War, Japan forced the Chinese in 1915 to agree to the "Twentyone Demands," by which China was virtually reduced to the position of a Japanese dependency. By the Treaty of Versailles, the Japanese, in spite of the strenuous protests of China, were permitted to continue their occupation of Shantung, and some of the "Twenty-one Demands" were allowed to remain in force. 

In an effort to bring about a fairer adjustment of the question in dispute, the United States invited all of the nations concerned to consider the Far Eastern problems at the Washington Conference in 1921–1922 (p. 637). 

The outcome of the conference was a series of treaties which, besides the limitation of navies (p. 638), contained the following provisions: (1) the termination of the Anglo-Japanese alliance; (2) the agreement by the 

United States, Great Britain, France, and Japan to respect each other's rights in their Pacific possessions, and to submit any controversies over them to joint conferences; (3) the guaranty of the territorial integrity of 

China; (4) the extension of the "Open Door" policy to industry as well as to commerce; and (5) the withdrawal of Japan from Shantung. 

Japan and China. For many years the Japanese government had looked upon Manchuria as a likely field for territorial and economic expansion. The impotence of the Chinese government and its inability to maintain order gave the Japanese a pretext for intervention in 1931, when the murder of a Japanese captain and the blowing up of a portion of the South Manchurian Railway caused the Japanese military machine to go into operation. While the Chinese officials were appealing to the world for help, the Japanese completed their conquest of Manchuria and set up there the puppet state of Manchukuo. In December, 1931, the League of 

Nations appointed the Lytton Commission to study the situation, and a year later it gave a report which was unfavorable to Japan. Still another commission was appointed, and while it was making its investigation, Japan pushed her forces in Jehol, a Chinese province which was claimed as a part of Manchukuo. The report of the second commission, which was broadcast by radio to the whole world, was a severe indictment of the Japanese policy. Never before in history had the conduct of a great nation been brought up so thoroughly and clearly for justice before the bar of

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

world-wide public opinion. Japan replied to the action of the League by withdrawing from membership therein.

The United States co-operated fully with the League in the Manchurian crisis. Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson proposed that all nations withhold recognition of Manchukuo. This proposal, accepted in theory, has not been followed in practice by the Great Powers. Japan's successful defiance of the League lessened the prestige of that body; and of like effect was her violation of the Kellogg-Briand Peace Pact and the treaties negotiated at the Washington Conference. With Germany and 

Italy, Japan made treaties of co-operation ostensibly intended for combating the spread of communism in Asia. Encouraged by the impunity with which she had taken away from China the Manchurian provinces, and emboldened by the diplomatic support received from Germany and Italy, Japanese imperialists were further stimulated by the military unpreparedness of Great Britain, and by internal political difficulties of France and Russia. The Japanese militarists thought they could acquire control over the whole of China, and to this end undertook in 1937 an "unofficial war." 

The Chinese defense was unexpectedly strong, and losses on both sides were heavy. In 1939, the probable outcome was still doubtful. 

The Problem of War Debts. Soon after the close of the World War the European nations owed to the United States a debt of about $11,000,- 000,000, about 70 per cent of which had been loaned by our government during the war, and the remainder shortly thereafter. No actual money was sent to the borrowing nations; all advances to the debtors were made in American goods, our government assuming the responsibility of paying the producers of the goods. Because of the disturbed financial condition of the European nations, many people, both in Europe and America, felt that the United States should cancel the debts and give that amount as part of our contribution to the war. Another argument in favor of cancellation or reduction was that payments could be made only in goods, and if this were allowed it would have a disastrous effect upon our industries. 

Others said it was an honest debt and should be paid in full. In 1923 agreements were reached with the debtor nations by which the amount of the debts was greatly reduced, and the payments were to extend over a long period of years, small installments to be paid every half year, with a very low rate of interest. 

The leading Allied nations expected to meet their debt payments with the money received from Germany in making her reparations payments. 

Charles G. Dawes and Owen D. Young, American financial experts, co-operated with European experts in an attempt to find some plan by

which Germany would be able to meet her payments, but during the depression which began in 1929 it became apparent that Germany could not continue them. In 1931 President Hoover proposed a moratorium, or postponement, of all payments on international debts for a period of one year. The next year, in a conference of nineteen nations, held at 

Lausanne, Switzerland, the Allied nations agreed to reduce greatly the German reparations, upon condition of a "satisfactory settlement of war debts owed to the United States."

Great Britain and France in November, 1932, asked for an extension of the moratorium and for a new conference to discuss the debt problem, but President Hoover, after a conference with President-elect Roosevelt, denied the request. On December 15, 1932, payments were due from eleven countries. Of these, six, including Great Britain, paid; while five, including France, defaulted. On June 15, 1933, payments from thirteen countries, about $144,000,000, were due. This time only Finland paid in full, while Great Britain made a "token," or part, payment of about $10,000,000. Four other nations likewise made "token" payments, while 

France and seven other nations defaulted entirely. On December 15, 1933, again Finland paid in full, six offered "token" payments, and five defaulted entirely. 

The Debt Default Act. The next payments were due June 15, 1934, but in April, 1934, the President approved an act which prohibited additional financial transactions with foreign governments in default in the payment of their obligations to the government of the United States. 

The act did not consider the token payments as satisfactory fulfillment of obligations. Public sentiment in the United States seemed to be against a revision or cancellation of the debts, because some of the defaulting nations were spending vast sums on armaments. 

on As payments became due at the end of each six-month period December 15 and on June 15-all European governments in debt to the United States, except Finland, continued to default. In March, 1936, Greece paid 35 per cent of her back interest. By June 30, 1938, the past due balances amounted to more than a billion dollars, while the total amount of the debt, together with the unpaid interest, was more than thirteen billion. 

Recognition of Soviet Russia. When the Bolshevik revolution in 

Russia in 1917 brought about the overthrow of the existing government and the establishment of the Communist Soviet government, American recognition of the new government was withheld. This attitude was inconsistent with our well-established policy of recognizing de facto (actu-

THE DEVELOPMENT OF OUR INTERNATIONAL RELATIONS 

ally functioning) governments. The chief reason for our refusal to have diplomatic relations with Russia was the fact that the Soviet government refused to assume the debt of the former Russian government to the United States or to meet the claims of American citizens for losses caused by the revolution. The fact that the Russian Communists were conducting a world-wide campaign of communistic propaganda against the capitalistic system was another reason for our attitude. 

After sixteen years of nonrecognition, our government began to waver in its Russian policy. Most of the other nations had already extended recognition, and as a result some of them were enjoying a profitable Soviet trade. On account of the industrial depression American businessmen were especially anxious to share in this trade. The mutual alarm of Russia and the United States because of the Japanese policy in Manchuria was another factor which helped bring the two nations together. Recognition was extended in November, 1933. 

World Economic Co-operation. In June, 1933, the representatives of sixty-six nations met at London in the World Economic Conference to consider the questions of stabilization of currencies and the removal of trade barriers. The fact that the United States had abandoned the gold standard shortly before the conference and refused to consider stabilization of our currency until there had been a sufficient rise in prices, made a settlement of the monetary question almost impossible. Other difficulties arose with regard to tariff policies. A high light of the conference was a speech by Secretary of State Cordell Hull, in which he denounced extreme economic nationalism and made a strong plea for international co-operation. 

The achievements of the conference were disappointing. It adjourned on 

July 27, with the understanding that it would probably be called together again at some future date.

While the eyes of the world were focused upon the World Economic Conference, the less conspicuous, but more successful, Wheat Conference was in session in the same city. About a month after the adjournment of the Economic Conference, twenty-one nations signed a document pledging themselves to a reduction of the world's wheat surplus, the consequent raising of the price of wheat, improved living conditions for the farmers, and the eventual revision of the tariff schedules. Canada, the United 

States, Argentina, and Australia, the chief wheat-exporting countries, agreed to reduce their wheat exports for the following two years; other countries agreed to encourage a greater consumption of wheat, increase their imports and reduce their tariffs on wheat. A Wheat Advisory Committee was appointed to supervise the enforcement of the agreement.

Neutrality Laws. In 1935 war was begun between Italy and Ethiopia, and many Americans began to ask the question whether the United States would be drawn into another world war. 

In August, 1935, the United States Congress passed a joint resolution authorizing the President of the United States, during the progress of a war between foreign states, to prohibit the exportation of arms, munitions, or implements of war from the United States or its possessions, and to restrict United States citizens from traveling on vessels of a state at war. 

It will be recalled that with the sinking of the British liner Lusitania, on May 7, 1915, one hundred twenty-four American citizens lost their lives and much war feeling was aroused (see p. 618). 

In accordance with this resolution President Franklin D. Roosevelt, on October 5, 1935, issued a proclamation admonishing our citizens to abstain from traveling in belligerent nations except at their own risk, and on the same day issued a proclamation prohibiting the exportation of arms, munitions, or other implements of war to Italy or to Ethiopia. 

The joint resolution expired in February, 1936, but in that month, and also on May 1, 1937, Congress renewed and amended it. Therefore, on the outbreak of the European war in September, 1939, President Roosevelt issued the required proclamation prohibiting the exportation of arms, munitions, and other implements of war to the belligerents; namely, Germany, Poland, France, Great Britain, and British Dominions. In a special session of Congress, however, a new neutrality law was passed early in November. This repealed the existing embargo and permitted the sale of arms and munitions to belligerents on a "cash-and-carry" basis; barred 

American shipping and passengers from combat areas; and contained other provisions designed to keep the United States from becoming involved in the war. In accordance with this Neutrality Act of 1939, President Roosevelt promptly decreed as combat areas the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, all waters surrounding the British Isles and Ireland, and the Bay of Biscay.

Preview for Unit Eleven  IN THE NINETEENTH AND TWENTIETH CENTURIES Chapter XXXIV. THE AMERICAN PEOPLE IN THE EARLY NINE- TEENTH CENTURY (1800-1860) Chapter XXXV. THE CULTURAL DEVELOPMENT OF AMERICA 1865 

TO 1900 

Chapter XXXVI. AMERICAN LIFE  

IN THIS UNIT We shall become acquainted with the everyday life of the American people. We shall learn how the early Americans dressed, what kind of houses they lived in, and how their homes were furnished. We shall see how inventions changed their ways of living, and how the development of public education affected the lives of the people. We shall note also the interests of the American people in literature, art, and religion. 

We have already learned of the westward expansion and the territorial growth of the United States. But the development which came in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries meant spiritual as well as material growth. In the early nineteenth century many social reforms were taking place. During this period we find increased interest in the temperance movement, in the struggle for women's rights, and in prison reform. 

In the period following the War between the States, the population of the United States continued to increase rapidly. American life underwent profound changes because of the industrialization of the country, the rise 651

of cities, and the disappearance of free land on the frontier. With the passing of the frontier, an important problem in the assimilation of immigrants arose, for the frontier had long served as a means of Americanizing our foreign population. The Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia brought to the attention of the American people some of their deficiencies in cultural achievement. There was a renewed interest in education, and the public school system developed rapidly. Many social reforms took place, and progress was made in art and literature. 

The period since 1900 is interesting because of the rapid expansion of metropolitan areas, the continued growth of population, and the restrictions placed on immigration. The first attempts to regulate the influx of foreigners were through laws which did not greatly limit the numbers; but laws passed after 1920 set definite limits on the number of immigrants from each nation of the Old World, based on the percentage of each nationality already a part of our population. 

Because of the longer hours for leisure, considerable interest was aroused in recreational activities. Athletic sports attracted large numbers of our people, both as active participants and as spectators. More attention was given to reading, and millions of books on art, poetry, literature, history, and biography came off the press, while thousands of libraries were established throughout the country. Our government extended its recreational facilities through its national parks and forests. The coming of the automobile enabled people to travel more widely, and thus to enjoy more of the natural scenery of the North American continent. CHAPTER XXXIV 

The American People in the Early Nineteenth Century (1800-1860) The American People Their Growth in Population. In 1790 there were about 4,000,000 people in the United States, but by 1860 the population had grown to about 31,500,000, of whom about 4,500,000 were negroes. This increase was due largely to natural causes (increase of births over deaths), though immigration added about 5,500,000. During this period the area of the United States increased from 892,000 square miles to more than 3,000,000 square miles. 

Immigration to America, which was going on at a rapid rate from 1720 to 1763 (see p. 88), declined during the period from 1763 to 1815. This was due to the French and Indian War, the War for Independence, the Napoleonic Wars in Europe, the War of 1812, and European restrictions. 

However, after 1815 foreigners again came in large numbers. 

Accurate statistics on immigration before 1820 are not available; but according to reliable estimates about a quarter of a million immigrants came to the United States in the three decades prior to 1820. During the period from 1820 to 1860 more than 5,000,000 came (see graph, p. 684). 

Immigrants came to America in the hope of improving their living conditions. Political revolutions, religious oppression, wars, and hard times in 

Europe brought many to the United States, which they considered a land of opportunity.

Settlement of the West. In the West population increased rapidly after the War of 1812. Soldiers returning from the war, men unemployed because of the closing of factories, and plantation owners whose soil had been exhausted, turned westward. The successful Indian fighting of 

Jackson in the Southwest and of Harrison in the Northwest lessened the danger from Indians, and stimulated immigration to those sections of the 653

Fort Dearborn, the beginning of the great city of Chicago country. Many of the European immigrants, especially those from Germany, were interested in agriculture and settled where good farming lands 

Ewing Galloway 

Skyscrapers of Chicago today were plentiful. Due to this settlement of the West, the center of population, which in 1790 was 23 miles east of Baltimore, Maryland, had moved by 1860 to a point 20 miles south of Chillicothe, Ohio (see map, p. 328). By 1860 nearly half of the people of the United States lived west of the Appalachian Mountains.

The Growth of Cities. With the expansion of industry after 1820, population in the East began to shift from farms to towns. The urban population had increased from less than 250,000 in 1800 to over 2,000,000 in 1850, and New

York City had become the metropolis of America. Whereas in 

1815 the only towns or cities in

America with a population over 

10,000 were New York, Philadelphia, New Orleans, Boston, Charleston, Salem, and Providence, by 1830 five had a population of over 

30,000. St. Louis, Cincinnati, Louisville, Pittsburgh, and Memphis, on rivers of the West, and Detroit, Cleveland, Buffalo, and Chicago on the

Great Lakes, were flourishing towns, while in the North streams were dotted with numerous other towns which had grown up around factories. 

Manners and Character. The first generation of Americans born after the formation of the Union entered national politics during the War of 1812. The seemingly limitless opportunities for advancement in the West and in industry had broken down class barriers and created a spirit of optimism and self-confidence which impressed Europeans unfavorably. 

The typical American seemed always in a hurry. The quick business lunch dates from this period, and in the home food was eaten hastily and in silence. Culture seemed to be on the decline. 

Because the spirit of equality was strong in the West, the new states gave the right to vote to adult males without any restriction based on taxpaying or ownership of property; and the older states followed their example. By 1828 the suffrage had been so extended that Jackson was said to be the first President to be elected by the people. In the East, particularly among Southern planters and New England merchants, the aristocrat remained entrenched; and in the capital at Washington, society became highly organized. Elsewhere, however, social barriers were breaking, and advancement depended upon a man's own efforts. 

Food. Food was abundant but not attractively served. Only in the more cultured homes was the dessert served separately from the other dinner. 

Knives frequently did the duty of forks. Among the very poor whites, salt pork, corn bread, and molasses were the staple foods. The tomato, or the "love apple," as it was commonly called, was generally regarded as poisonous until after 1830, but nearly all the other vegetables commonly known today were served. 

In aristocratic homes the men sometimes remained at the table to drink wine or beer after the ladies had withdrawn, but after 1815 coffee began to take the place of stronger beverages. Ice cream became a popular dessert with those who could afford the ice, but most homes were not provided with ice in the summer. 

Dress. The wars with Great Britain had resulted in such strained relations that the United States copied France in fashions of dress and accent. For a short period tight-laced dresses gave place to simpler ones with flowing skirts and low necks. Soft, heelless slippers and long gloves were worn; the hair was elaborately dressed; and the face was powdered with pulverized starch. Men's clothing became more conservative. Kneebreeches were replaced by long trousers, and wigs were discarded in favor of the natural hair, cut long and parted in the middle. Less desirable was the custom of wearing detachable collars and shirt fronts to avoid the need

Street scene in a large city about 1860. Notice the costumes worn, and the store front with windows that were large for that period. of laundering the entire shirt-at a time when, among both men and women, a weekly bath was regarded as sufficient. 

Architecture. Architecture in the period 1800-1860 showed little originality, because the architects were usually merely skilled carpenters and were better copyists than designers. The Capitol and other buildings rising on the Potomac were the pride of the nation, but the architect, L'Enfant, was a Frenchman who followed foreign plans. Banks followed old Greek styles, and Gothic architecture was being introduced in church construction. Stores were awakening to the need of attractive display windows and were widening their window spaces and introducing show cases. In private homes colonial styles changed little. Middle-class families expected to have a living room, dining room, and kitchen in addition to a bedroom for every two members. In the Middle Atlantic cities, such as New York, houses of brick were built close to the street, though one frequently saw houses of brown stone with marble steps and doorposts. 

The interior of the homes underwent greater changes than the exterior. 

Wallpaper, which was now made in the United States, was widely used; rag rugs gave place to rugs covering the entire floor; and restless rocking chairs replaced many of the old straight chairs. The wide kitchen fireplaces were giving place to iron stoves, and in some homes there were bathrooms.

Inventions which Affected our Ways of Living. In a restless striving for advancement, Americans made rapid progress in science and invention before the War between the States. Labor in the home was lightened by the substitution of friction matches for the flint, and of whale-oil lamps for candles. The sewing machine, patented in 1846 by Elias Howe, and the substitution of light tin vessels for the heavier iron ones, lessened the burden still further. On the farm, Cyrus H. McCormick's reaper was releasing laborers for the new factories; and in the towns, house pumps and cisterns were gradually replaced by a public water supply, and streets in the larger towns were lighted by gas. The omnibus, forerunner of the streetcar, was introduced in New York City in 1828 with a 12½ cent fare, and began to make possible the growth of large cities. 

Samuel F. B. Morse's telegraph made practicable the rapid distribution of news, and the running of trains by schedule. Newspapers were greatly multiplied by the general use of Richard Hoe's rotary printing press. 

Goodyear's vulcanizing process, which was invented in 1839, made possible rubber coats and overshoes, while the introduction of the French daguerreotype, named after its inventor, Daguerre, was the forerunner of the photograph. 

Professional Training. The most popular of all professions was that of politics, which was entered by many lawyers who had no professional training except the reading of a few lawbooks or study in the office of another lawyer. Medicine had made considerable progress but was still largely a mixture of science, quackery, and tradition. Fear of "evening damp" and "twilight chill" prevented enjoyment of the night air; newly plowed lands were thought to cause fevers; and the common custom of bleeding patients usually sapped their remaining strength. Calomel and 

Peruvian bark (quinine) had come into use, and by 1815 the use of whisky as a medicine was being questioned. Anesthesia, by means of ether, was first used by the Georgia physician Crawford W. Long in the 1840's. 

Doctors trained at the University of Edinburgh were found in the large Eastern towns. In the Sheffield Scientific School at Yale and the Lawrence 

Scientific School at Harvard, scientific research was in progress. Already, West Point was making a name for itself in engineering, and Harvard and the University of Virginia were offering courses in law. The ministry remained one of the honored professions and was now attracting a group of devoted young men in training for missionary work in many lands. 

In the study of geology, Louis Agassiz had revealed unknown secrets of the Lake Superior region, and J. J. Audubon, through his study of American birds, had created a widespread interest in nature.

EDUCATION 

Schools and Education. During the closing years of the eighteenth century the new American nation had undergone important changes. Many people were then still skeptical about the success of the new government. 

Religious intolerance, and traditional influences and conservatism, coupled with the exacting conditions of the economic life, tended to lower the intellectual and educational standards of the people rather than to lift them to a higher plane. Free education, open to all the children, was considered largely a dream of the theorist, but there was considerable interest in matters of education. The struggle for educational advancement was slow and strenuous but already by the turn of the century definite signs appeared which pointed to success along the lines of educational progress. 

The United States Constitution did not suggest a definite educational policy for the entire country, but the state constitutions declared vaguely in favor of systems of free public schools. Leaders in government frequently expressed themselves as being in favor of free education as a means of perpetuating the new democracy so recently established. The 

Northwest Ordinance passed in 1787 provided that schools be encouraged, and the new states admitted to the Union made provision for school systems. The earlier view that education was the duty of the churches, the family, or the individual was slowly giving way to the view that education was a function of the state and that it should be provided at public expense free and open to all. 

Early Leaders in the Public School Movement. Chief among early educational leaders was Thomas Jefferson, who urged education as a means of securing successful self-government. He worked out an elaborate system of education for the state of Virginia, based upon his political theory of self-government. He urged education for the training of leaders and with that in view succeeded in founding the University of Virginia. Other leaders whose influence was thrown to the side of public education during the early national period were Benjamin Franklin, Benjamin Rush, James 

Sullivan, Nathaniel Chipman, Du Pont de Nemours, Noah Webster,

DeWitt Clinton, and two English schoolmen-Joseph Lancaster and 

Andrew Bell.

Educational Awakening. After the War of 1812 definite factors appeared which stimulated an interest in education, the like of which had not been realized before. This awakened interest was in the direction of better education as a function of government. School societies, infant schools, monitorial schools, the growth of cities, improved methods of

transportation, particularly better highways and later the railroad, better communication, the factory system, the labor movement, and new conceptions of democracy as sponsored by the Jacksonian Democrats, appeared to give impetus to the movement for better education. Political leaders, industrial executives, and social workers viewed education as an important and worth-while activity. 

Effective Leadership. In the second quarter of the nineteenth century there appeared simultaneously many distinguished American educators. whose activities represent the history of educational progress of the period. 

These men published journals, wrote letters, made surveys and reports, studied systems of education abroad, studied local conditions, appeared before state legislatures, and in many other ways endeavored to promote public education in the several states. Among these leaders was Henry 

Barnard of Connecticut, whose monumental work was the American Journal of Education, consisting of thirty-two large volumes. This journal is one of the best works on education ever published. Another outstanding leader was Archibald D. Murphy, who has been called the father of the common schools of North Carolina. He wrote a report on European schools and submitted it to the state legislature in 1817. In addition to describing the educational systems of Europe he set up a rather detailed scheme for a state system of education, including a state board to control the funds and supervise the elementary and secondary schools. His plan also provided reasonable support for the state university.

Horace Mann. One of the most influential educational leaders was Horace Mann, who was largely responsible for the founding of the first public normal school (1839). His report to the State Board of Education of Massachusetts in 1843 covered educational conditions in England, Scotland, France, Germany, Belgium, and Hol- 

Horace Mann land. It dealt with such matters as instructional material, methods of teaching, grading of pupils, discipline, and teacher training. This report was widely read and led to many permanent educational improvements in this country.

Other Educational Leaders. Other distinguished leaders of the period were James G. Carter of Massachusetts, Calvin H. Wiley of North Carolina, Calvin E. Stowe of Ohio, Caleb Mills of Indiana, John D. Pierce and 

Isaac E. Crary of Michigan, Samuel Lewis and Samuel Galloway of Ohio, Robert J. Breckinridge of Kentucky, John Swett of California, and Ninian 

Edwards of Illinois. These leaders in educational thought urged the legislatures and people of influence in their respective states to make provision for suitable educational facilities for all of the children of the state. They pleaded for a real democracy in education which would mean equal opportunities for all who would accept them. Their contribution to the cause of public education cannot be too highly praised. 

In addition to the personal efforts of outstanding leaders, other factors were at the same time contributing to the cause of education in the middle period of the nineteenth century. These factors were educational conventions, teachers' societies, memorials, surveys and reports, and the lyceum. 

All of these social forces contributed directly to the establishment of a new philosophy of public education and also to the creation of a favorable attitude toward the public support of a system of free schools. Thus the movement for free schools was begun on the principle that a free nation must be governed by men free from ignorance.

LITERATURE OF THE NEW NATION, 1790-1830 

After the formation of the new government, the nation set to work to establish itself economically. The northern states became partly industrial. Factories were built. Attention was paid to improving methods of communication. The nation slowly became conscious of its meaning and destiny. With a semblance of maturity there came a new interest in culture. Social conditions for the first time permitted literature as a profession. Scarcely had an English critic asked the question "Who reads an American book?" when an intellectual awakening occurred.

The first American professional man of letters was Charles Brockden Brown, the child of Quaker parents who planned for him a career as a lawyer. Having abandoned law because of his health, he became attracted by the ideas of an English romantic philosopher, William Godwin, and, like him, set forth his ideas in the form of fiction. 

Irving, Cooper, and Bryant. Washington Irving was the first American to achieve a purely literary reputation abroad. His first important work was A History of New York, by Diedrich Knickerbocker, a comic history of the Dutch occupation of New York. The appearance of this book in 1809 may be said to mark the birth of American literature as art. It was followed in 1819-1820 by The Sketch Book, a collection of over thirty papers, among which are the short stories "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow." Irving's fame was made secure by the publication of 

The Life and Voyages of Columbus, 1828; The Conquest of Granada, 1829; and The Alhambra, 1832. In 1859 he completed A Life of Washington in five volumes.

Another writer who advanced the standing of American literature in the eyes of both his countrymen and foreigners was James Fenimore Cooper, also of New York. He lives as a romantic interpreter of the forest, the Indian, and the explorer. The Leather-Stocking Tales are his best work. For these he created one character, Natty Bumpo, or Leather- 

Stocking, the hunter and scout, whose achievements are traced throughout the five volumes of the series. 

William Cullen Bryant won the world's respect for American poetry as Irving and Cooper won it for American prose. Although Bryant continued writing until his eighty-third year, he never surpassed his two early poems, "Thanatopsis" and "To a Waterfowl." The appearance of the first of the above two poems is considered as the birth of American poetry as art. As editor of the Evening Post for forty-nine years, Bryant made an important contribution to American journalism. His translations of the Iliad, 1870,

and the Odyssey, 1872, are generally rated among the best of the English versions of Homer.

Drake and Halleck. Two other New York poets contemporary with 

Bryant are Joseph Rodman Drake and Fitz-Greene Halleck. They collaborated in the Croaker Papers, a series of satires on New York celebrities. 

Drake wrote one volume independently, The Culprit Fay and Other Poems, 1835, including the well-known poem "The American Flag." Halleck is remembered for two poems: "Marco Bozzaris," in imitation of Byron, and an elegy "On the Death of Joseph Rodman Drake."

LITERATURE OF THE MID-NINETEENTH CENTURY, 1830-1870 

The period from 1830 to 1870 is represented in American literature by the transcendentalism of Emerson and his followers, by the antislavery writers, by the scholar poets of Cambridge, and by the aestheticism of Poe.

The Transcendentalists. Ralph Waldo Emerson, the greatest of the 

American Transcendentalists, was a descendant of eight generations of ministers. His chief ideas are summarized in the essay "Nature," published in 1836; "The American Scholar," an address delivered in 1837; and "The 

Divinity School Address," given in 1838. "Nature" embodies all the fundamental ideas of transcendentalism. "The American Scholar" is a plea for the writers of America to free themselves from slavish imitation of Europe. In "The Divinity School Address" Emerson champions inde pendence in religious matters. 

Among Emerson's poems, "Each and All," "The Rhodora," "The 

Humble-Bee," "The Snow-Storm," "Forbearance," "Woodnotes," "Fable," and "Concord Hymn" are easy and well worth remembering. "Threnody," written in memory of his little son who died at the age of six, is probably the greatest poem in American literature on the death of a child.

A friend of Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, put into practice some of the theories of transcendentalism. A Week on the Concord and Merrimack 

Rivers, 1849, is a record of a boat trip taken in 1839 by Thoreau and his brother John. It is the first American specimen of nature writing in prose to attain to the rank of genuine literature. A still more beautiful expression of Thoreau's poetic approach to the study of nature is found in Walden, 1854, a record of his residence for two years in a hut which he himself built on Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts.

Other important members of the Transcendental group were Margaret 

Fuller, Amos Bronson Alcott, George Ripley, Nathaniel Hawthorne, and

Herman Melville. Margaret Fuller was a forerunner of the feminist movement in America. She was the first editor of the Dial, the organ of the Transcendental group. Alcott attempted to apply the doctrines of transcendentalism to the education of children. Ripley was the chief promoter of Brook Farm, the Transcendentalists' experiment in communism. 

Nathaniel Hawthorne. Hawthorne began his career as a man of letters by writing short stories. His best collections of stories are Twice-Told 

Tales, Mosses from an Old Manse, and The Snow Image and Other Twice- 

Told Tales. The first of Hawthorne's four great romances was The Scarlet 

Letter, 1850, usually classed among the world's great novels. It is a revelation of the unnaturalness of Puritanism. The theme is the effect of a great sin upon four persons. The House of the Seven Gables is based upon a legend of the witchcraft trials in old Salem, in which a victim pronounced a curse upon the magistrate. The Blithedale Romance, 1852, grew out of 

Hawthorne's experience in the Brook Farm colony. The theme of The 

Marble Faun is the effect of murder on the man and woman who commit the crime and upon a girl who happens to witness it. The scene is in Rome. 

Herman Melville. Melville's first romances Typee and Omoo grew out of his experience in the South Seas. Moby Dick, 1851, his masterpiece, one of the greatest of sea stories, is a tale of whaling in the days when whaling was one of the most thrilling of adventures. 

John Greenleaf Whittier. Whittier was the principal antislavery poet, having become interested in the movement through William Lloyd Garrison. Every phase of the conflict over slavery is reflected in his poetry. 

The two poems on slavery that will probably endure are "Ichabod,” an attack on Daniel Webster for defending the Compromise of 1850 with its 

Fugitive Slave Law, and "Laus Deo," a song of praise that the strife had ended. Perhaps Whittier's chief contribution is his poetry on New England country life. "Maud Muller," "The Barefoot Boy," "Telling the

Bees," and "In School-Days" belong to this group, but the best is "Snow- Bound," an imperishable picture of Whittier's own boyhood. Songs of 

Labor, published in 1850, is devoted to various kinds of workingmen. 

Whittier's religious verse is represented by Our Master, 1866, from which five well-known church hymns have been taken. 

Another important antislavery writer was Harriet Beecher Stowe.

Her novel Uncle Tom's Cabin, 1852, did much to increase the antagonism between the North and the South (see pp. 364-365). 

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. Of the three men, Henry Wadsworth 

Longfellow, Oliver Wendell Holmes, and James Russell Lowell, usually classed as the Cambridge scholar poets, Longfellow was the one most

closely associated with Cambridge. He is probably the most widely read and loved of all American poets. Besides his short lyrics, such as "A 

Psalm of Life," and "Hymn to the Night," he produced numerous descriptive pieces on simple life and on children, as "The Village Blacksmith,' "The Old Clock on the Stairs," and "The Children's Hour"; ballads, such as "The Wreck of the Hesperus," and "The Skeleton in Armor"; and poems on slavery, of which "The Slave's Dream" is the best. 

Longfellow wrote three long narrative poems. They are Evangeline, based on the expulsion of the French from Acadia; The Song of Hiawatha, his masterpiece; The Courtship of Miles Standish, which introduced in the story of John and Priscilla Alden some of the history of Longfellow's ancestors. He is famous also for Tales of a Wayside Inn, which includes "The Birds of Killingworth" and "Paul Revere's Ride."

Although Longfellow translated into verse many poems from European literatures, his most valuable work is his blank-verse translation of the Divina Commedia, one of the best complete translations of that great poem. 

Oliver Wendell Holmes. Holmes was a physician, novelist, poet, and essayist. His first poem to attract attention was "Old Ironsides," a plea for the preservation of the frigate Constitution which had played an important part in the War of 1812. A year later, 1831, appeared "The Last 

Leaf," written about Herman Melville's grandfather. His best-known poem is "The Deacon's Masterpiece," a satire on the downfall of Calvinism. "The Chambered Nautilus" shows his interest in science. 

In 1857 when the Atlantic Monthly was established, Holmes began to publish in it a series of personal essays which were collected into a book, The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table, and published in 1859. Two years later 

The Professor at the Breakfast Table appeared, and in 1872, The Poet at the Breakfast Table. Over the Teacups, a similar book, was published in 1891. 

Holmes's interest in medicine and science is shown in his novels which he described as "medicated." His three novels, each of which deals with the problem of heredity, are Elsie Venner, The Guardian Angel, and A 

Mortal Antipathy.

James Russell Lowell. Lowell was a poet, a critic, and a reformer. In 

1848 he published The Vision of Sir Launfal, valuable because of its nature poetry; The Biglow Papers, First Series, satires, in dialect verse, on slavery in general, the annexation of Texas, and the Mexican War; and A Fable for Critics, witty comments on prominent contemporary authors. The 

Biglow Papers, Second Series, satires on the Civil War, appeared in book form in 1867.

Besides three volumes of literary essays, Lowell wrote a number of odes. "Ode Recited at the Harvard Commemoration," 1865, is a tribute to the Harvard men who had fallen in the Civil War, while "Under the Old Elm" is in commemoration of Washington's taking command of the 

Revolutionary army.

Southern Writers. In this period capable writers appeared in the 

South. William Gilmore Simms of Charleston, both poet and novelist, in 

1834 published Guy Rivers and in 1835 brought out The Yemassee and The Partisan. John Pendleton Kennedy in 1832 published Swallow Barn and in 1835 Horse-Shoe Robinson. In 1853 Joseph G. Baldwin of Alabama published Flush Times of Alabama and Mississippi. Among the Southern poets was Richard Henry Wilde, who wrote "My Life Is Like the Summer

Rose." Henry Timrod became famous for his "The Cotton Bolls" and "The Lily Confidante." Paul Hamilton Hayne wrote several volumes and was known by English critics as the "Laureate of the South." 

Edgar Allan Poe is important in American literature as a poet, a critic, and a writer of short stories. He stands for the birth in America of an artistic conscience. That he is concerned with craftsmanship instead of ideas is shown in all of his work. Of his tales of physical horror, The Pit and the Pendulum and The Cask of Amontillado are probably his greatest achievements. Poe is the originator of the modern detective story. The 

Gold Bug and The Purloined Letter are examples of this type of story. 

Poe's best known poems are "The Bells," "The Raven," "To Helen," "Ulalume," and "Annabel Lee." He was editor of The Southern Literary 

Messenger in Richmond, 1835-1837.

Newspapers. When in 1833 Benjamin H. Day conceived the plan of offering his paper to the public at one cent a copy and of financing it through paid advertisements, a new era in the newspaper business was begun. Rival newspapers were established, each trying to surpass the others in getting "scoops" and in portraying news in a vivid fashion which often sacrificed truth to sales. With the advent of the telegraph, newspapers were revolutionized, and each part of the nation became intimately acquainted with what the others were doing. Corner stores and courthouses became centers of animated discussions of current events. 

PROGRESS IN OTHER FIELDS, 1800-1860 

Art. Although no great music was produced in America before 1850, river sides echoed to the songs of boatmen, and at country inn and store there was no more popular figure than the fiddler. While the parlors of the wealthy echoed to the notes of the pianoforte and harp, the plantation

negroes were singing their folk songs. "The Star-Spangled Banner," written by Francis Scott Key during the War of 1812, John Howard 

Payne's "Home, Sweet Home," and Samuel Smith's "America" won the hearts of all Americans. Lowell Mason, by adapting the masterpieces of great musicians to psalms and poetry, and by original composition, gave music a prominent place in the churches. 

The restless striving of the period was not suited to the development of great artists. In sculpture and portrait painting, little originality was evident, though in landscape painting some skill was shown. On the whole, however, America-though lacking in original artists-had become "art conscious" and appreciated the productions of Europe. 

Religion. The first half of the nineteenth century was characterized by a religious enthusiasm which evidenced itself in revivals and camp meetings and in humanitarian reform. Though the last religious tax was abolished in 1833, churches were better supported than ever before. The rise of various new denominations such as the Unitarians, Adventists, Mormons, and New Lights was evidence of a spirit of tolerance. Revolutions in Catholic Europe, particularly Ireland, had driven thousands of Catholics to America. Sabbath observance was strictly enforced in the 

East. Chains were stretched across the streets and trains ceased to run on that day. To attend church was the respectable thing to do on Sunday. Reports of the work of the great frontier preacher, Peter Cartwright, and of Adoniram Judson, missionary to Asia, lent an air of romance to missions; and as a result of the work of Samuel Mills in the West, the 

American Bible Society was formed in 1816 to distribute Bibles along the frontier. Missionary activities in the West were handled largely by the earnest and faithful itinerant preachers, whose regular monthly visits were eagerly awaited. 

Recreation. Recreation in the early nineteenth century, in many parts of the country, differed little from that of the colonial period. In the rural regions the swapping of yarns and playing of practical jokes had become a great vogue, while in the West house-raisings and cornhuskings offered all too infrequent sources of pleasure. Public condemnation of theaters. had lessened, and few large towns failed to have a playhouse for traveling actors. In 1849 Edwin Booth began his career as an actor, and thereafter the stage assumed greater importance. Dancing was popular among the fashionable set. Public disapproval of lotteries had not yet awakened, and through the sale of lottery tickets money was raised for such projects as road making and the construction of public buildings. Museums were found in all large towns, and the Smithsonian Institution at the capital

In the home. the reading of Cooper and Scott was a never-ending source of pleasure. 

Social Reforms. Europeans were critical of America after the War of 1812, and America was also critical of herself. In her strivings for material pleasure she did not forget the spiritual. The same generation that loved bearbaiting, cockfighting, and eye-gouging, also organized temperance societies, fought for women's rights, and agitated for the abolition of slavery. Most of the reform movements met a favorable response, and the 1830's and 1840's constituted an era of social reform. Under the direction of Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Lucy Stone, an attempt was made to secure for women the control of their own property after marriage, and the right to vote. Although opposed by churches, politicians, and many women themselves, the movement gained force until by 1850 seven states had given women equal civil rights with men. 

The American Peace Society, formed in 1828 to encourage peaceful settlement of international difficulties, failed because neither Europe nor America was ready for such a step. Nevertheless, it was a move in the direction of creating public sentiment against war. 

The Temperance Movement. During this period, along with other reforms, came a crusade against liquor. As early as the year 1673 Reverend

Increase Mather had preached against the sin of drunkenness. One hundred years later a noted physician wrote essays against the use of strong drink. The College of Physicians of New York in 1790 presented Con gress with a pamphlet deploring the use of strong drink. After 1800 many churches took up the crusade, and so great was the interest in the movement that by 1833 it was estimated that there were 5,000 local temperance societies, with a total membership of 1,250,000. In that year the United States Temperance Union was formed at a convention of delegates from twenty-one states. Three years later it was renamed the 

American Temperance Union.

The argument that alcohol is detrimental to the human system had been used for a long time, but about 1830 it was pointed out that it reduced industrial efficiency, and finally temperance became a moral issue. The agitation led to the passage of prohibition laws, the first of which was that enacted by the territorial legislature of Oregon in 1843. In 1846 the legislature of Maine passed a law providing for prohibition throughout the state. It was difficult to enforce and in 1851, mainly through the work of 

Neal Dow, a new prohibition law was passed in Maine which, except during the years 1856-1858, continued in force until the adoption of the Eighteenth Amendment (1919). By 1856 similar laws had been passed by thirteen other states.

Treatment of Criminals. Few evils in American life needed correction more than the treatment of criminals. The colonial practice of humiliating an offender by placing him in stocks or branding his body had been replaced by imprisonment. The purpose of the imprisonment, however, was at first for punishment without regard to the reform of the criminal. 

In the early prisons criminals were placed together in large rooms without regard to their crimes-young and old, hardened criminals and first offenders. The rooms had little if any furniture, no beds, and scant provision for ventilation or sanitation, and were dens of vice and disease. 

Men imprisoned for debt were placed in separate rooms, but the conditions of imprisonment were little better. 

Pennsylvania took the lead in reform by putting each criminal in a separate cell, but the horror of solitary confinement was so great that New York began the practice of prison labor by day. When Edward Livingston began agitation for reform rather than punishment of criminals, a new day in prison history was begun. Because of the expense, states were slow to copy New York's and Pennsylvania's example. Nevertheless, the prison systems of the United States have been in general better planned and better managed than those of Europe.

CHAPTER XXXV The Cultural Development of 

America 1865 to 1900 Growth of Population. The population of the United States increased from 31,500,000 in 1860 to about 76,000,000 in 1900. Many foreigners continued to come to America during this period and were welcomed by the government and by industry. In 1864 the Federal government set up the Immigration Bureau in Washington for the purpose of assisting those coming from other countries to America. Some of the Western states also maintained immigration bureaus and sent agents to foreign countries for the purpose of stimulating immigration. Due largely to this encouragement, about 14,000,000 foreigners came to America during the last forty years of the nineteenth century. In the latter part of this period most of them went to the cities, whereas a majority of the earlier immigrants had become farmers. 

Changed Character of Immigration. During the 80's a fundamental change took place in the character of the immigration. Before that time three fourths of the immigrants had come from northern and western Europe, while from that decade on they were mainly from southeastern Europe and the Near East. While the earlier immigrants sought farms, the newer arrivals supplied labor for factories and mines during a period when America was rapidly becoming industrialized. It was during the 

80's that the movement to restrict immigration began. Many citizens felt that since this "new" immigration was of racial stock different from the native American, it would be more difficult to assimilate, and impossible to Americanize. The immigrants often settled in foreign quarters of the cities, where they retained their own languages and their native customs. 

Because thousands of these immigrants were laborers who were able to exist at a comparatively low standard of living, they accepted lower wages 671

Culver Service 

Immigrants arriving at New York in 1875 than the American workmen. Soon considerable opposition to immigration. began to develop on the part of organized labor. 

The disappearance of the frontier also brought problems of labor and of immigration into prominence. As long as Western lands remained, the dissatisfied people in the East were able to seek homes in the West, where the frontier aided the Americanization process, but by 1890 this had become almost impossible. As the frontier gradually disappeared, labor unrest became more widespread and labor organizations became more hostile to the increasing number of foreigners. 

As early as 1882 Chinese laborers were excluded by an act of Congress. 

In 1885 a law was passed prohibiting laborers under contract from coming into the United States, and in 1891 Congress passed a law which prohibited the advertising for immigrants by American factory owners. In 1881 the office of Superintendent of Immigration was created, and a tax of fifty cents was levied on each immigrant. Before the end of the century there was agitation for a literacy test. A bill was introduced in Congress in 

1896, providing for the exclusion of all immigrants between the ages of fourteen and sixty who could not read English or some other language. It did not become a law because of the President's veto.* In the twentieth century more rigid immigration laws were enacted and enforced, as we shall see in the following chapter (p. 684). *On May 1, 1917, however, a law went into effect, excluding aliens over sixteen years of age who are physically capable but who cannot read.

673

Social Organization and Customs. By the end of the War between the 

North and the South, great social, political, and economic changes were appearing in the United States. The intermingling of all classes and groups on the battlefield had broken down many of the old social barriers, and with the development of industry a new aristocracy based on wealth was arising.

Among all classes society was more showy and artificial than cultured. 

Nevertheless, women continued to be treated chivalrously and to live sheltered lives until, with the advent of the typewriter, many began to enter occupations outside the home. The modesty of the period before 

1900 is amazing to the generation of today. All styles of dresses included very long skirts (see pp. 396, 656), and the sight of a woman's ankle was shocking, while women who ventured to swim did so clothed in dresses reaching below the knees, and wearing hose. Until the long gored skirts and choker-necked waists displaced the full dresses of the 70's and 80's, ten yards of cloth were required for the average dress. Moreover, in order to conform to fashion, women sacrificed their comfort by wearing tight corsets and small shoes. Fashions for men, too, were overdone. Heavy mustaches and sideburns were special marks of a well-dressed man, while scarfpins, cuff buttons, and watch chains were all too conspicuous. 

View of a bathing beach in the late nineteenth century. Notice the bathing suits worn by men and women of that time.
