Food. When glass jars with rubbers for sealing made their appearance in the home after 1860, a greater variety of foods was made possible for the winter. Dried fruits and vegetables suddenly lost much of their popularity. No less revolutionary was the coming of the refrigerator car in 

1880. Thereafter, tropical fruits and fresh vegetables during the winter became common, and large meat-packing industries displaced the local slaughterhouses. With the application of refrigeration to boats, the 

American market was rapidly extended to Europe. It was not until tin cans were used for preserving, that great canning factories were established, releasing women from the necessity of long hours in the kitchen in preparation for winter months.

Homes. The dignified simplicity of the homes of the previous generation was replaced by overdecoration. This was evidenced by the use of colored windows, balconies, and cupolas, in the construction of the houses; and by bright wallpaper, gaudy pictures, and brilliant rugs within. Unusual pieces of furniture, as the whatnot, and chairs upholstered in deep red or green plush, revealed the love of display, as did the iron deer, dogs, and other statuary placed in the yards. 

Cultural Progress. Indications of better taste came slowly into evidence after the Centennial Exposition of 1876 (at Philadelphia), to which thirty-nine nations sent exhibits. The opportunity afforded for the comparison of the culture of the Old World with the New awakened, in the more than three million American people who attended the exposition, a sense of their own deficiencies in cultural achievements. But the Americans were also interested in more practical displays. Many for the first time saw the new floor covering called linoleum; and an early form of the typewriter was now in evidence. Among the agricultural displays, the incubator for hatching eggs created great interest, while the exhibits showing the natural resources and industrial development of each state aroused a sense of national pride.

The years after 1876 were startling in their achievements. In 1879 

James Ritty, of Dayton, Ohio, patented his cash register, only two years after the first practical typewriter had been developed. These two inventions were destined to revolutionize business. The Bell exchange system soon made the telephone so practical that business could not afford to do without it; and with Marconi's perfecting of wireless telegraphy in 1896, communication was even further developed. In the realm of recreation, Edison's phonograph, 1877, and Eastman's portable camera, 1888, were much used, while Edison's incandescent electric light, 1879, made home life more attractive and comfortable.

675

Renewed Interest in Education. The struggle for a free, state-supported system of public education had been won by the middle of the nineteenth century, but the system needed further extension and development. From the close of the War between the States to the end of the century, many changes were made to improve the school system. The school population was increasing very rapidly. The public high school, which had its beginning in the first half of the nineteenth century, experienced a boom and became an integral part of the public school system. The celebrated Kalamazoo case in the courts of Michigan, 1870-1872, established the legality of public taxation for the support of the high school. After this date the high school became the people's college. The total publicschool enrollment increased from about 7,000,000 in 1870 to about 15,500,000 in 1900. The number of public high schools increased from 300 in 1860 to over 6,000 in 1900. The number of normal schools for the training of teachers increased from 12 in 1860 to 175 in 1900. The cost of all public education increased over 400 per cent during the last forty years of the nineteenth century.

Educational Progress. Much progress was made in the construction of school buildings to meet more adequately the needs of the expanding program of education that was carried on within them. New methods were adopted as well as new divisions of administration such as the kindergarten, the vocational departments, and physical education. Colleges and universities increased in number and efficiency. Whereas there were but 

246 colleges founded by 1860, there were nearly 500 by 1900. Federal aid to education reached a new high level with the passage of the first and second Morrill Acts in 1862 and 1890 respectively. Large grants of land and annual money grants were made by the Federal government to a college of agriculture and mechanic arts in each state. These grants have been well administered and have promoted great advancement in scientific knowledge which has contributed to the wealth and to the general welfare of the nation. Colleges and universities enriched their curricula and gained more complete freedom from the religious domination of an earlier day. 

A few institutions were established solely for graduate study and research. 

European instructors were employed in many of the American institutions, and very many American scholars took advanced degrees in European universities preparatory to teaching in the home institutions. 

Administrative Officers. During the postwar period the office of State 

Superintendent of Public Instruction became generally established as a permanent office in most of the states. At first, in most states, this was a political office to which men without professional training were appointed

or elected. Better methods of appointment, however, were gradually adopted, and greater authority was granted in the administration of the state system of public education. 

The city superintendency assumed a separate and significant role in city school administration. In 1870 there were less than 30 city superintendents in the entire country, and these were found in only 13 of the 37 states; but by 1876 the number had increased to 142. In 1890 there were 

380 superintendents in cities of over 5,000 inhabitants, and by 1920 there were 15,892 executive school officers in incorporated places. County and larger community systems of education made noteworthy progress during this period.

Leaders had been working quietly but effectively to enlighten the people as to the necessity of a more adequate system of education in promising to all people a richer life, with liberty and an unhampered pursuit of happiness.

Libraries Established. By 1860 there were a large number of public libraries making books available to the reading public. Librarians were being trained for the special duties of their office. Toward the close of the century, Andrew Carnegie made numerous gifts in the form of attractive and serviceable library buildings and books to communities that would obligate themselves to maintain this service for the public. Carnegie gave upwards of $60,000,000 and established about 3000 libraries throughout the land.

Medicine and Science. With the development of science came a widespread interest in medicine, an interest which resulted in the lengthening of life and the gradual elimination of epidemics. Pasteur's treatment for rabies and his method of heating milk to kill germs were introduced from France, while the use of fresh-air treatment for tuberculosis replaced that of bleeding the patient. Moreover, sanitation had become one of the major problems of municipal government, and through sanitary commissions the cities were rapidly eliminating sources of disease. Perhaps the greatest 

American contribution to the field of medical science at this time was the proof by Dr. Walter Reed that yellow fever was transmitted by the bite of a mosquito. With this information, Dr. William Gorgas, through a cleanup campaign in which the breeding places of the mosquito were removed, was able to free Cuba and the Panama Canal Zone of the dread disease. When 

John D. Rockefeller created the International Health Board, Gorgas accepted the task of eliminating yellow fever throughout Latin America, and proved so successful that the disease is almost unknown in the Western world today.

Because of the rapid industrialization of the country, chemistry soon became of major importance and yielded many new products. From coal were derived gas, dyes, crude oils, medicines, perfumes, tar, cleaning agents, etc. Agents for preserving food were discovered, while drugs became purer and their properties better known. 

Newspapers and Magazines. Reflecting the spirit of the times, the newspapers also exercised a powerful influence in molding public opinion. 

In the closing decades of the century, two men appeared in newspaper circles in New York who were destined to exercise wide influence; namely, Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst. Their papers were intended to attract public attention, and by means of pictures, feature articles, and stories of crime and romance written in a startling style, these men gained for their papers a wide circulation. 

Among the many magazines that were read at this time, none were more popular in the home than The Youth's Companion and the Ladies' Home Journal. The latter, under Edward Bok's direction, became a leader in exposing the false claims of patent medicines and in introducing artistic taste in the furnishing and building of homes, while such magazines as the Atlantic Monthly, Harper's Magazine, Scribner's Magazine, and the Review of Reviews appealed to a more scholarly taste. 

Literature in 1870-1900. A new and distinctively American type of literature appeared in the writings of Mark Twain (the pen name of Samuel L. Clemens) and Walt Whitman. Whitman became a prophet of a new era and profoundly influenced not only the later American poets, but poets in all countries. He began the use of free verse in America. In his poetry he attempted to reflect what he interpreted as the ideals upon which the nation was founded. "A Song of Myself," "Crossing Brooklyn 

Ferry," "O, Captain! My Captain!" and "When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd" are a few of his best poems. 

Mark Twain represented the wild, carefree spirit of the West with its contempt for tradition. The Innocents Abroad, the result of a journey to 

Europe and the Holy Land, is an example of rough Western humor applied to the sentimental traditions of the Old World. Mark Twain's greatest books are The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, 1876, based on his own boyhood, and its sequel The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, which is conceded a place among the greatest of American novels. 

With the waning of sectional feeling and greater opportunities for publication, literary activities were no longer confined mainly to New England. From the West came Bret Harte, known for his stories of the goldmining camps of California; Edward Eggleston, author of The Hoosier

Schoolmaster, a good picture of rural life in Indiana; William Dean Howells, one of the most prolific of our writers; Eugene Field and James Whitcomb 

Riley, writers of juvenile verse and other poems, and Joaquin Miller, who wrote the well-known poem "Columbus." 

The South contributed its share. Sidney Lanier had both musical and poetical genius. His masterpiece is "The Marshes of Glynn." Other writers include George W. Cable, who did for New Orleans what Bret 

Harte did for California; O. Henry (the pen name of William Sidney

Porter), master of the anecdote type of short story; Charles Egbert 

Craddock, recorder of local color in the Tennessee mountains; Joel 

Chandler Harris and Thomas Nelson Page, both interpreters of the 

Southern negro.

Typical of the historical novel that fascinated the country about 1900 are Janice Meredith, a story of the American Revolution by Paul Leicester 

Ford; Richard Carvel and The Crisis by Winston Churchill; When Knight hood Was in Flower by Charles Major; and To Have and to Hold by Mary Johnston.

One of the most gifted of modern realists was Stephen Crane. The Red 

Badge of Courage, setting forth the emotions of a private in a battle of the War between the States, is one of the most intense of American novels. 

Hamlin Garland revealed the West of the pioneer in an unflattering light. The two volumes of short stories that established his reputation are 

Main-Travelled Roads, 1891, and Prairie Folks, 1893.

Art and Architecture. With few exceptions, public buildings were characterized by a gaudy display and lack of harmony that reflected the postwar spirit. Yet there were evidences of a new era. Here and there in large cities one of H. H. Richardson's buildings, such as Trinity Church in Boston, stood out as an oasis in a desert, while Louis Sullivan, through his steel skyscrapers, proved the superiority of that metal over masonry. 

Among the American painters, John Singer Sargent achieved fame through his portraits, while Thomas Eakins and Winslow Homer preserved on canvas scenes from American life and nature. Albert P. Ryder, through his mystical paintings, and John La Farge, through his work in glass, added to the artistic achievements of America. In sculpture, Augustus 

Saint-Gaudens, Daniel Chester French, and George Grey Barnard made

It possible for America to produce statues commemorating great men and events without seeking European aid. 

Music. Although Americans, with the exception of George Whitefield 

Chadwick, Victor Herbert, and Edward McDowell, composed but little classical music, their musical appreciation was evidenced by the acclaim

awarded Paderewski on his annual tours of the country, and by the enormous sales of pianos and organs, and of sheet music. "Old Folks at 

Home" and other songs by Stephen Foster, and such songs as "The 

Rosary" and "When You and I Were Young, Maggie" enjoyed wide popularity. The demand for music teachers offered a new occupation to women, among the many afforded them since the advent of the typewriter. 

Religion. A very strong influence of this period was religion, as exemplified in the leadership of the Congregationalist Henry Ward Beecher, the 

Episcopal Bishop Phillips Brooks, the Catholic Cardinal James Gibbons, and others. The new organizations Y.M.C.A. and Y.M.H.A. afforded religious, recreational, and educational opportunities to the young, while the Salvation Army carried a message of hope to the poor. The fraternal order Knights of Columbus promoted education, charities, and social security among Catholics. Dwight L. Moody and his song leader, Ira D.

Sankey, traveled throughout the land, converting thousands. The 

Christian Science movement was organized by Mary Baker Eddy in 1876. 

Amusements. Before the latter part of the century, there were few sports in which young men and women might participate except skating and horseback riding, but in this period lawn tennis, croquet, and bicycling were introduced and achieved rapid popularity. Mumble-the-peg, hideand-seek, and hopscotch continued to be the favorites of school children, Skating in the late nineteenth century. Note the woman's small waist line and the men's mustaches.

and in the cities trolley-car rides were the joy of all. For adults, the Chautauqua assemblies afforded opportunities of hearing the best musical artists and the finest lecturers, whereas many men took never-failing pleasure in meetings of their "lodges" or secret fraternities.

CHAPTER XXXVI 

American Life in the Twentieth Century

Concentration of Population. From 1900 to 1930 the population of the 

United States increased from about 76,000,000 to about 123,000,000. During this period there was a continued drift toward the city, so that by 1930 about 56 per cent of our population was classified as urban, that is, living in cities, towns, or villages of 2,500 or more, including one third of our total population living in cities of 100,000 or more. During this period metropolitan areas developed, for large cities usually were surrounded by a number of smaller cities. According to the United States Census Bureau there were in the United States in 1930 ninety-three metropolitan districts, each having an aggregate population of 100,000 or more, and containing one or more central cities of 50,000 or more inhabitants. The Chicago metropolitan district, an area of 1,119 square miles, had a population of 4,364,000, a density of 3,900 per square mile. The New York metropolitan district, an area of 2,514 square miles, had a population of more than 10,900,000, a density of about 4,340 per square mile. This recent development was made possible by rapid transportation, and has extended the influence of the city to larger areas. 

Immigration Restriction. During the period from 1900 to 1910 the number of immigrants to the United States was 8,795,000; from 1911 to 

1915 there were 4,460,000; but from 1916 to 1920, during the period of the war, the number dropped to 1,276,000. In 1921 the United States decided upon a radical change in its immigration policy, looking toward a more rigid restriction. It was felt that the disturbed conditions in Europe as a result of the World War, and the high taxes resulting therefrom, would cause too many poverty-stricken Europeans to come to this country.

1926 to 1930 the total was 1,468,000. This decrease was due largely to the several laws discussed in the following paragraph. 

In 1921 the Emergency Quota Act was passed and remained in effect for one year. It provided that the number of immigrants of a particular nationality should not exceed three per cent of the number of persons of that nationality living in the United States in 1910. In 1922 the Emergency 

Quota Law was extended for two years more. However, it was considered unsatisfactory, and in May, 1924, a new Quota Law was enacted which admitted annually, from July 1, 1924, to June 30, 1927, two per cent of the number of a given nationality resident in the United States in 1890. 

After July 1, 1927, the quota was to be "that proportion of 150,000 which the number of persons of a given national origin residing in the United States in 1920 bears to the country's total population in 1920." In 1929 a new immigration law likewise limited the number of quota immigrants to 150,000 annually. Native people from Canada, Mexico, and Central

and South America, however, may be admitted to the United States without regard to any quota.

The Influence of the Machine Age. The invention of more and more labor-saving machinery destroyed the demand for immigrant labor. It made possible the production of more goods, and by increasing the efficiency in production, shortened working hours, thus affording more leisure time to our working population. The Machine Age produced social changes which affected almost every phase of American life. 

While the coming of the automobile provided additional means of transportation, it also served to draw people away from their homes. In many cases homes were neglected in order that cars might be purchased. 

Manufacturers devoted millions of dollars to the employment of artists and engineers whose task was the production of a beautiful car within the means of the average person. While the automobile tended to take many people away from the home, the radio attracted them to it until the automobile manufacturers met the situation by putting radios in the automobile. Although the principle of the radio had been known, it was not until 

1920 that the first broadcasting station was established in the United States. Immediately, the radio surpassed other forms of entertainment in popularity and friends boasted to friends about the stations they had "picked up" the night before. As the radio established itself as a permanent feature of American life, producing companies entered upon a competitive business which resulted in the clear transmission of sound and the production of ornamental radio cabinets. 

Meanwhile, the airplane was introducing a new element into transpor tation. The efforts of S. P. Langley and of Wilbur and Orville Wright had borne fruit in 1903 in producing a heavier-than-air craft. Though it was largely in an experimental stage until the close of the World War, the airplane has since become an important element in transportation. Through its mail and passenger service, the nation has been drawn closer together than had been possible before. 

In addition to the automobile, the radio, and the airplane, other inventions have altered American life. Electricity has revolutionized the home, has made cities by night fairylands of beauty, and has helped to solve the traffic problem by its automatic lights. Gas stoves have lessened the labors of the cook, and the tractor has displaced older methods of farm labor, while the dictaphone has simplified the duties of the business office. 

American Women. The changed order of society has had a greater influence upon women than upon men. The fact that there were few professions open to women, except those of teaching and stenography, was

A kitchen provided with many electrical appliances not very evident until the World War, when many women were called from their homes to industry to take the places of men who were serving in the army. Thereafter, houses became smaller and more convenient, or the family moved into apartments so that the wife could be free from exacting duties. Electrical appliances such as the vacuum cleaner, the refrigerator, the washing machine, and the pressing iron were as revolutionary in the twentieth century as the telephone and electric lights were in the nineteenth. Released from home responsibilities, many women. entered business or devoted their time to cultural or philanthropic interests. 

Literary, music, and art clubs flourished, and women's patriotic organizations gained in membership. Through the Junior League, young women. not only sought diversion, but also engaged in activities for social welfare. 

The greater freedom of women was shown in the changing style of dress, the increasing frequency of smoking, and extensive participation in sports. 

More women entered professions such as law and medicine, or became authors, while as owners of tearooms, buyers for large concerns, and reporters for newspapers, women soon held a recognized place in the business world.

However, with the change in the status of women there came a decline in the importance of home life. Many children, left without parental direction during the day, spent their hours outside of school in attending the movies, in automobile riding, and in other outside means of entertainment.

Leisure and Recreation. The shorter working day made available more time for leisure, and the nervous strain caused by our complex social and economic system with its keen competition not only made recreation desirable but made occasional relaxation necessary. Within one year's time the people of the United States spent more than $10,000,000,000 for recreation. Much of their leisure time was devoted to travel, camping, hunting, fishing, picnicking, hiking, horseback riding, swimming, golf, baseball, tennis, and other sports. Many who did not care for active participation in sports spent their leisure hours in attending the movies or other theaters, in listening to the radio, or in reading. So great was the interest in reading that in 1929 more than 1,000,000 books on art, 4,000,000 books of poetry, about 18,000,000 volumes on religion and philosophy, and 46,000,000 copies of novels were published in the United States. Books of biography, history, and travel also proved to be popular recreational reading, and in 1929 more than 8,000,000 books on these subjects were published. The total for all books published in the United States in 1929 was in excess of 235,000,000. There were in 1929 about 6,000 public and school libraries, which circulated over 230,000,000 volumes, while numerous rental libraries, according to estimates, rented an additional 10,000,000. 

Courtesy Pennsylvania Dept. of Forestry

Camping in a state recreation park Automobile travel has in recent years become a very popular form of recreation. Many an American family looks forward to vacation days, which often mean an auto tour of several thousand miles, during which time national parks, points of historic interest, summer resorts, and

bathing beaches are visited, with perhaps a few days spent in camping. Our national government offers recreational facilities through its national parks and forests with an area of more than 190,000,000 acres, in which are maintained about 2,000 campgrounds for the enjoyment and convenience of the public. During 1930 about 35,000,000 people visited these parks and forests. The American Automobile Association estimated that in 1930 the tourists in the United States spent more than $3,000,000,000. 

Outdoor sports have assumed an important place in American life. 

Hundreds of cities (about 900, or nearly half of those with population over 5,000) have provided thousands (nearly 12,000) of parks and playgrounds where hundreds of thousands take part in baseball, football, lawn tennis, and golf. Many high schools are provided with playgrounds and athletic fields and take an active part in athletic contests with other schools. College football has attracted wide attention. Many colleges and universities are equipped with huge concrete stadiums, some of which have a seating capacity of more than 70,000. In 1930 the estimated total attendance at university football games was more than 10,000,000, who paid approximately $20,000,000 in admission fees. During the same year an equally large number of people were interested in professional baseball and

689' attended games played by the two major leagues. It may be said that for participation in sports in recent years businessmen have turned chiefly to the golf course; college men and high school boys to the football field, basket ball court, and track; and many men and women to tennis and volley ball courts; while millions of other Americans enjoyed their leisure hours by watching the sports.

A popular form of recreation is the motion picture, which within recent years has changed from a silent film to the "talkie." In 1931 there were more than 22,000 motion picture theaters in the United States, and according to Will Hays, the president of the Motion Picture Producers and Distributors of America, about 115,000,000 people attend motion picture theaters each week.

Innovations. The twentieth century is a period of many innovations. 

New industries, based on temporary demands, rose and fell with alarming rapidity. While the bobbed-hair craze caused an increase in the barber business, it threw out of work multitudes of girls in the hairpin and hair net business. Likewise, the demand for rayon clothing created despair among cotton farmers and caused thousands of laborers in cotton mills to be without work. Changes also took place in the food industry. The question as to whether there were sufficient calories in the diet was the worry of the housewife until it was found that not only calories but vitamins must be considered. Thereupon, foods that had hitherto been considered not particularly desirable came into demand, and the producers of such vitamin-bearing foods as spinach and milk reaped greater profits. While the Eighteenth Amendment was in effect (1919-1933), fortunes were made from nonalcoholic beverages, and the cold-drink stand took the place of the old saloon.

The Typical American. Under the influence of the radio, newspaper syndicate, and moving pictures, individualism in dress, speech, and customs in America has largely disappeared. The popular songs and slang of 

New York are familiar on the streets of the Western and Southern towns, while the poorest shopgirl copies the clothing and manners of the wealthy as she has seen them portrayed in the movies. In many, many places the local newspaper, which once molded the thought of the community, now contains regular syndicated columns, "funny" sheets, and news reports which are found in similar papers throughout the nation. By means of the automobile, people move rapidly from place to place, mixing the culture of the sections, and producing the typical American who is more or less at home in any part of the nation. Books of etiquette have shared in shaping this typical American who knows exactly how to meet all social require-

ments. But all this has been done at the cost of the "rugged individualism" of Americans, and it is doubtful that the gain has overbalanced the loss.

Newspapers and Magazines. In no phase of American life has the spirit of change been more evident than in the newspapers, and in none has organization been carried to a greater extreme. The newspapers of the country bear a remarkable similarity because of their dependence upon the same sources such as the Associated Press and Universal News Service. The Scripps-Howard and Hearst newspaper combinations are so extensive and have been so widely copied by other companies that the locally-owned newspaper is becoming something of a rarity. Never before have newspapers appealed to such a wide variety of classes and interests. 

The masses are reached through a great variety of news, the socially inclined through the social columns, the mother through child-care columns, the sentimental through serial stories, and children through the comic sheets. Cartoons have become more popular than editorials because they are more easily understood. With rare exceptions, newspapers appeal chiefly to man's love of the unusual and startling, and they therefore magnify events of passing interest and neglect more important items which have less sensational qualities. 

Much the same may be said of the magazines. Those which appeal to the intelligence are neglected in favor of the sensational. Some have built large circulations by combining elements of both, and it is these which have the largest circulations. 

Literature; the Muckrakers. Near the opening of the century, a group of realists interested in political and social reform produced sensational literature. Theodore Roosevelt compared them to the man with the muckrake in Pilgrim's Progress, and the group came to be called the "Muckrakers." One of these realists was Ida M. Tarbell, who in 1902 began a series of articles in McClure's Magazine, the "History of the

Norris in The Octopus revealed the struggle of the farmers against railroad domination, and in 1902 in The Pit described the activities of grain speculation on the wheat exchange. In 1904 and 1905 Thomas W. Lawson in a series of articles entitled "Frenzied Finance" in Everybody's Magazine described the working of the stock market and its effect on political and economic life. In 1905 Upton 

Sinclair published The Jungle, a novel which revealed the insanitary conditions in packing houses. This led to the passage of the Pure Food and Drugs Act. David 

Graham Phillips wrote articles on "The Treason of the Senate," and

Lincoln Steffens wrote The Shame of the Cities. These writings led to the correction of some of the worst abuses and produced a moral awakening of the people, so that many gave their support to leaders interested in social and political reform.

Modern Prose. Thornton Wilder came into prominence with the publication of The Bridge of San Luis Rey, 1927. Du Bose Heyward wrote of life in Catfish Row in Charleston in Porgy and Mamba's Daughters. 

Two important women novelists of recent times are Edith Wharton, author of Ethan Frome, a novelette, and of several novels of New York dress, 1900-1936

Ornately decorated parlors of the late nineteenth century society life, and Willa Cather, whose two best books are One of Ours, 1922, and Death Comes for the Archbishop. The last is a tale of Catholic missionary work in the old Southwest. 

Booth Tarkington and Sinclair Lewis must be included in any study of modern American literature. Tarkington's reputation rests on his novels and his stories about boys. Sinclair Lewis became famous through the publication of his seventh book, Main Street, 1920. It is a satire on the provincial mediocrity of a small town. Babbitt gives a characterization of the average businessman, but it is also a satire on life in a city. 

Modern Poets. Numerous poets have arisen since Walt Whitman. A few of the most important are Edwin Markham, who came into prominence with "The Man with the Hoe," based on Millet's famous painting; 

William Vaughn Moody, who was also a dramatist; Edwin Arlington 

Robinson, who shows the tragedy in modern life; Robert Frost, poet of the present-day New England; Amy Lowell, leader of the movement to push further the boundaries of poetic diction; Edgar Lee Masters, author of Spoon River Anthology; and Edna St. Vincent Millay, who belongs in the front rank of our lyric poets. 

The Drama. American drama as a part of literature hardly existed before 1900. Since that time many dramatists have appeared. Clyde

Fitch came near to producing real drama in his comedies of manners called The Climbers, 1901, and The Truth, 1906. Percy Mackaye attempted to mingle the literary and the popular in several plays, among which is The Scarecrow. The Witching Hour is the best play by Augustus Thomas. 

An outstanding figure in the new American drama is Eugene O'Neill, author of The Emperor Jones and Strange Interlude. 

Architecture. The realistic spirit was evident not only in literature, but also in architecture. The ornately decorated homes of the late nineteenth century were followed by homes characterized by simplicity. Unlike the earlier houses, the new ones contain little unused space, and closets make unnecessary the old unwieldy wardrobes and china cabinets. The compact bungalow, suited to American life, is popular among those of modest means, while among the wealthy there is a return to colonial styles. Modernistic living room used also as a dining room. Compare with the picture of the earlier period on the opposite page. 

Within the houses the furniture combines beauty with comfort, but secures the beauty through graceful lines rather than excessive carving. The same simplicity found in private architecture has become evident in public buildings, and a distinct American style is replacing European types (picture, p. 654). As architect of the tallest New York building opened in 

1913, Cass Gilbert popularized the skyscraper, but created the problem of securing light in the streets between the skyscrapers. New York solved the problem by requiring tall buildings to be constructed in "stair-step" arrangement, and thus unintentionally added to their beauty. 

Art. Accompanying the development of an American type of architecture came a new development in art. Commercial artists were demanded

in making designs for industry, in preparing attractive book covers, and in fashioning new styles for clothing. But the greatest demand for commercial artists lay in the field of advertising. Art schools sprang up over the country, specializing in preparing advertisements for magazines and billboards, and in drawing covers for magazines. Moreover, art courses were introduced into public high schools to meet the demand for commercial artists. 

Recent Development in Education. With the turn of the twentieth century public education in all of its branches was moving forward at an encouraging rate. School attendance increased at a rapid pace. This called for bigger and better school plants. The greater interest in school training resulted in a greater number of literate people, that is, people who could read and write. This number was about 89 per cent of the population in 1900; by 1910 it had grown to 92 per cent, in the next decade it rose to 

94 per cent, and by 1930 it had grown to nearly 96 per cent. 

Increased College Attendance; Extension. College and university education became more readily available to a greater number of young men and women than ever before in our history. The physical plants of many colleges and universities were expanded to take care of this increasing number of students. Extension education sponsored by these institutions was begun in 1906. This idea of taking the college to the people through correspondence study, extension lecture classes, educational tours, slides and films, newspaper and magazine clipping libraries, all represented an attempt to give the people more extended service for the support they had given the institutions of higher learning. By 1920 over 120,000 students, some of whom were old men and women, were working in some branch of the university extension service. The number steadily increased in the following decade until the number of students studying in this method reached over 344,000 in 1930.

Public Health. Doctors, nurses, and public health officials were teaching the people how to live in a more healthful way. The prevention of diseases was receiving attention from the professional workers and from the public. Health surveys which revealed shocking conditions served to stimulate interest in public health work. The remedial work necessary to clear up some of the bad conditions called for health legislation in the different cities and states. Many of these laws were passed early in the new century.

The Boy Scout and Girl Scout Movements. Perhaps one of the greatest educational movements of the new century was the Boy Scout movement. 

This organization was started in England by Sir Robert Baden-Powell in

695  1908. It spread immediately to other countries and was established in 

America by Daniel Carter Beard. Today over 2,000,000 boys in more than thirty nations form the membership of this organization. The 

Girl Scout organization was founded in 1912 by Mrs. Juliette Low of 

Savannah, Georgia. By means of the training received and the attitudes developed, boy and girl Scouts are more likely than other boys and girls to become the future leaders of their countries. Besides this, scouting affords to thousands of boys and girls an opportunity to hike, camp, swim, learn woodcraft, prevent and fight fires, make trails, establish bird and game sanctuaries, and otherwise to enjoy life together in the great out-of-doors. 

Educational Reorganization. The organization of the units of the public school system has undergone some important changes in the twentieth century. In keeping with the industrial changes in the country, progressive educators urged the reorganization of the public school system in order to meet the needs of the time more effectively. The result was an enriched curriculum in the various school systems. Practical subjects were introduced into the high school. With the feeling that the individual differences of young boys and girls could not be met adequately in the oldtype high school, the junior high school was organized and became an outstanding part of our educational system. 

The junior high school, consisting usually of grades 7, 8, and 9, was formed by including two years below the older four-year high school, while the junior college was created by including two years above the high school. Its purpose is twofold: first, to relieve the over-crowded college and university classes in the lower division and at the same time offer two years of college work at home; and second, to give courses for the benefit 

A modern high school in a city of about 100,000 population; cost of construction about $1,500,000. 

Ewing Galloway

of those students who can go no farther in their educational work. The junior colleges are both publicly and privately supported. They have increased in number to more than 150. In both the junior high school and the junior college the idea of guidance has been accepted as an essential part of the course, and excellent advisory programs have been worked out.

The responsibility of the schools to give a complete education to the young people is constantly increasing. Within recent years many parents, because of social and industrial changes, have not been able or willing to offer as much training at home as was given years ago in the old-type home. 

Consequently the school has been called upon to assume many of these responsibilities, such as the training in health habits, moral training, and direction of social and recreational activities. In some communities religion is directed in co-operation with the schools. Medical and dental inspection, with nursing service, may also be found in many school programs. Because of better training in psychology and scientific education, teachers today are able to render important service to the mental health of the children as well as to train the mind in purely academic subject matter. 

Visual education has become important in many of our modern schools. 

The radio as well as the motion picture is employed to assist in teaching. 

There were in 1935 more than 21,000,000 radio receiving sets in the country, and in many school auditoriums and other rooms sets are placed and the programs are used for instructional purposes. Particularly effective has been the work in music appreciation by radio directed by Dr. Walter 

Damrosch, a distinguished orchestral and choral conductor. Even the schools which are hundreds of miles from the large cities may share with the nation the best that is available in music, lectures, dramatics, and other forms of instruction and inspiration. 

Humanitarian Activities. While the twentieth century saw the accumulation of vast fortunes, it saw also a spread of private benevolence. The 

Rockefeller Foundation, capitalized at $147,000,000, dotted the country with hospitals and supported experts engaged in medical research; by means of the Carnegie Foundation, communities were able to provide themselves with libraries; while the Julius Rosenwald Fund was devoted largely to negro education. Local community chests were created to provide for the poor, and churches, as always, engaged in charitable activities. The General Education Board created by the generosity of 

John D. Rockefeller was incorporated in 1903. Its general object was "the promotion of education within the United States of America, without distinction of race, sex, or creed." Mr. Rockefeller's original gift made in

1902 was $1,000,000. Later additional gifts brought the total of the 

General Education Board fund by 1934 to more than $150,000,000. 

The Temperance Movement. One of the important social problems of the twentieth century was that of the control of the liquor industry. 

This was not a new problem in American history, for temperance societies were organized in the 1830's and carried on a lively and effective crusade (p. 668). The organized temperance movements before 1869 were both nonpartisan and nonpolitical, but in the summer of 1869, at Mansfield, Ohio, there was formed a state Prohibition party, and on September 1, 1869, through the work of the Independent Order of Good Templars, the national Prohibition party was organized. Although destined to be in the field in every presidential election for the next half century, the Prohibition party was never an important political factor, but the crusade against strong drink continued.

In 1873 a health reformer of Boston, Doctor Dio Lewis, in a series of temperance addresses urged the women of Jamestown and Fredonia, New York, and of Hillsboro, Ohio, to begin a praying crusade to close the saloons. The movement in Hillsboro succeeded in a remarkable way. Before very long the women in city after city were singing hymns before the saloons and even entering to hold prayer at the bar. In the late summer of 1874, at a national convention at Cleveland, the temperance women organized the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which proved to be a moral force in social reform. Under the leadership of Mrs. Mary H. 

Hunt it was largely responsible for securing "scientific temperance instruction in the public schools of nearly all the states." 

During the nineteenth century no less than eighteen states had adopted prohibition laws, but in eleven of these the law was repealed or declared unconstitutional, while one state permitted the people in any political subdivision (as a county or a city) to suspend the law by majority vote. 

In the remaining six the laws were not well enforced, and "speak-easies" and other "joints" evaded the law. 

Perhaps the most popular method of dealing with the liquor problem in the early twentieth century was that of local option, by which any town or city or county could by the vote of its citizens become "wet" or "dry." 

This method was first used by Indiana in 1832. In 1907 it was in force in over thirty states. Its advantage lay in its adaptability to local circumstances and opinions, but the perpetually renewed struggle between the advocates and the opponents of prohibition was a constant source of social and political strife, and the alternate opening and closing of public houses stood in the way of steady improvement.

The increase of local option was due largely to the work of the Anti- Saloon League founded in 1893 by Doctor Howard H. Russell, a Congregational minister, at Oberlin, Ohio. It pledged itself "to avoid affiliation with any political party as such and to maintain an attitude of neutrality upon questions of public policy not directly concerned with the traffic in strong drink." It soon learned how to meet the powerful liquor lobbies and to play the game of politics. It became, in the words of one of its leaders, "a giant politician reaching from the Atlantic to the Pacific. . . . 

It had a powerful lobby at Washington and an enormous house at Westerville, Ohio. It literally turned out newspapers and publications by tons weekly. What it realized was that vote getting is a trade of experts; that votes are made back home in the pleasant summertime. There in the corner grocery store or the Bible Class it silently, year after year, built up the Congress and legislature that gave us national prohibition." 

The Anti-Saloon League became a national organization in 1895. By 

1906 it had been so successful that it decided to attempt state-wide legislation. The crusade was begun when Oklahoma applied for statehood in 

1907. The people in the proposed new state adopted state-wide prohibition by a majority of over 18,000. Other states adopted prohibition in rapid succession. By 1914 state-wide prohibition existed in eleven states and during the World War others were added so that by the end of 1918 the number had grown to twenty-nine. 

National Prohibition. Considerable progress was also made in temperance legislation by the United States Congress. The Jones-Works Law providing for numerous restrictions on the sale of intoxicating liquors in the District of Columbia was enacted in 1912. The Webb-Kenyon Law was passed in March, 1913. It eliminated from the protection of interstate commerce regulations all shipments of intoxicating liquors intended for use in violation of state laws. Other restrictions due to the entrance of the 

United States in the World War limited the liquor traffic. In 1917 Congress restricted the use of foodstuffs in liquor manufacture and in 1918 prohibited altogether the war-time sale or manufacture of intoxicants. On 

August 1, 1917, the Senate adopted the resolution incorporating the 

Eighteenth Amendment by a vote of 65 to 20; on December 17, the House followed, with a vote of 282 to 128.

The proposed Amendment forbade "the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors... for beverage purposes," and gave both to Congress and to the states the right to enact enforcement laws. 

The legislatures of all the states except Rhode Island and Connecticut voted for ratification. In January, 1919, it became a part of the Constitu-

tion, and a year later, January 16, 1920, nation-wide prohibition went into effect, under the Volstead Act. 

Enforcement Machinery. The enforcement of prohibition presented a grave problem. The task was first assigned to the Commissioner of the 

Bureau of Internal Revenue of the Treasury Department. In 1925 a 

Director of Prohibition was appointed to assist the Commissioner, and the two offices were consolidated in 1927. In 1927 the enforcement staff was brought under civil service regulations, and three years later all prohibition activities were transferred to the Department of Justice. 

The enforcement machinery never operated very effectively. From 

1920 to 1932 nearly anyone could obtain readily all the liquor he desired. 

By 1926 the illicit still and illicit brewery were quite beyond the control of the enforcement offices. So great were the sources of illegal supply that ten years after the experiment began the Bureau of Prohibition was prepared to admit that the amount of liquor in circulation was 40 per cent as great as in the year 1917.

The bootlegging industry became thoroughly organized, with bribery necessary in many stages of the game. There were "respectable" bootleggers who catered to the wealthy, and disreputable "moonshiners" who sold cheap corn whisky from the mountains. Women were often employed as retail smugglers.

In order to put a stop to the importation of liquor by "rum fleets," a demand arose for the jurisdiction of the United States to be extended Liquor destroyed in the enforcement of prohibition, by pouring it into the sewer 7545 7543 

Keystone View Co.

beyond the three-mile limit for the purpose of searching and seizing foreign vessels engaged in the traffic. On April 23, 1923, the Supreme Court decided that under the Eighteenth Amendment and Volstead Act American ships could carry liquor outside the three-mile limit, but that no ships American or foreign could bring liquor within the territorial waters of the United States. When the prohibition agents, in accordance with this decision, seized sealed liquors on board foreign ships in American ports, the foreign governments protested. This question was settled with the 

British government by a treaty October 31, 1923, permitting the United States agents to seize ships within a zone of approximately twelve miles if carrying liquor illegally.

On January 15, 1931, President Hoover's Commission of Law Enforce ment and Observance submitted its findings on prohibition. This body, made up of eleven distinguished citizens and headed by George W. Wickersham, had been created on May 20, 1929, to make a general study of the processes and defects of law enforcement. The Commission as a whole declared itself as opposed to the return of the saloon, to the Federal or state governments going into the liquor business, and to the relegation of the liquor question to the several states. Two of the commissioners demanded outright repeal of prohibition, four favored modification, and five were for further continuance of prohibition. 

The facts presented by the Commission showed that enforcement of prohibition was almost impossible because public opinion would not support it, because the illicit liquor traffic was profitable, and because the states refused to use efficient methods of enforcement. 

Repeal of Prohibition. The Republican party platforms of 1920, 1924, and 1928 endorsed strict enforcement of prohibition, but the Democratic national convention of 1924 brought into the open the conflict between the prohibitionist forces headed by William G. McAdoo and those favoring a modification, who supported Governor Alfred E. Smith of New York. In 

1928 Smith received the nomination for President and made his campaign to a large extent on the issue of restoring state control in the regulation of the liquor trade. He carried only eight states, among them Republican 

Massachusetts and Rhode Island, but carried many of the larger cities. 

In 1932 the Republican party platform favored transferring to the states the control over the liquor traffic, but retaining in the Federal government the power of preserving the gains already made. The Democratic platform demanded unconditional repeal and favored the immediate modification of the Volstead Act to legalize the manufacture and sale of beer and other beverages of small alcoholic content.

701

In March, 1933, Congress passed the Cullen Bill which was to end the Federal prohibition of beer, wine, and other "non-intoxicating" beverages containing not more than 3.2 per cent of alcohol by weight; the bill also levied on their manufacture and on their sale a tax of $5 per barrel of 31 gallons, and imposed a license tax of $1,000 on brewers. This bill became law when signed by the President, and went into effect fifteen days later, on April 7. On that date the sale of beer and other mild alcoholic beverages was permitted in nineteen states and in the District of Columbia. 

The Blaine resolution proposing the repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment passed the Senate on February 16, 1933, by a vote of 63 to 23; on 

February 20 it passed the House by 289 to 121. It became the Twentyfirst Amendment to the Constitution, after its ratification by conventions called for that purpose. The legislatures of forty states then in session took prompt action and between April 3 and November 7, 1933, thirtynine States voted. Thirty-six favored repeal and two opposed it. The 

Amendment went into effect December 5, 1933. The responsibility that was taken by the Federal government in 1920 was thus thrown back upon the states.

 Chapter XXXVII. LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES 1868–1896 Chapter XXXVIII. LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES 1896-1932 Chapter XXXIX.  POLITICAL CONDITIONS in the United States, the government of which is carried on by means of parties, have always been affected by the major problems of American life. Industrialism, which was responsible for the development of big business, for the organization of labor, and for the changes in agriculture, created many problems. The protective tariff, favored by industry, became a political issue, and many times throughout the period since 1868 has been prominent in both presidential and congressional elections. In general the Republican party has favored a high protective tariff, while during most of the period the Democratic party has stood for a tariff for revenue only. 

Many issues were raised by big business, with its organized trusts, the regulation of which occasioned much political concern. Our financial system likewise has engaged the attention of political leaders; in the election of 1892, and again in 1896, it was the main subject of controversy. 

In 1896 the Democrats favored the free and unlimited coinage of silver, while the Republicans insisted that gold should remain the standard. 

The agricultural problem has again and again been drawn into politics, as was demonstrated by the Granger movement in the 1870's, and by 707

the Populist revolt of the 1890's, when aid was sought for distressed farmers. The question of farm relief persisted, and after the World War, during the Harding administration, became of paramount importance. 

It continued during the Coolidge and Hoover administrations, and again appeared in that of Franklin D. Roosevelt, when, as a part of the New 

Deal, the Agricultural Adjustment Act and later acts were passed. 

The problems which arose because of the changes in transportation and communication, resulting in the appointment of the Interstate Commerce Commission, also challenged the attention of political leaders. Our relations with foreign countries, especially after the war with Spain, caused the question of imperialism and anti-imperialism to become another point of political debate. During the Taft administration the Republican party was divided, and the Progressive party was organized in the interest of reform. As Presidents, Theodore Roosevelt, William Howard Taft, and

Woodrow Wilson struggled with the problem of regulating trusts and other types of big business. 

Soon after 1868 the question of the civil service reform and the merit system arose, and during the administration of President Hayes, made considerable progress. Theodore Roosevelt and Woodrow Wilson also were interested in extending civil service reform. 

Minor parties, or third parties, of considerable strength appeared again during this period. The Greenback party in 1876 sought the extension of the use of greenbacks as currency. In 1884 the Anti-Monopoly party was organized as a protest against big business. In 1892 the Populists appeared in an effort to help farmers obtain relief. In 1912 the Progressive party sought reform, as did also the Farmer-Labor party in 1920. 

These minor political parties endeavored to solve the numerous problems of the period, but the Republican and Democratic parties continued to direct the affairs of the American people. CHAPTER XXXVII 

Leaders, Parties, and Policies 1868-1896 The Election of 1868. Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 and was succeeded in office by Andrew Johnson, who was a Unionist rather than a Republican. The radical Republicans thought for a time that he would support their policies and make reconstruction difficult for the South, but they soon discovered that Johnson's views on reconstruction were similar to those of Lincoln. Disagreement followed and, as friction developed, the rift between Congress and the President widened, while the popularity of the victorious Union general, Ulysses S. Grant, increased. Grant had taken no active part in politics before the War between the North and the South, but after the war was over he showed himself not averse to political honors. He had no special training to fit him for the presidency, but because of his popularity due to military success the Republican party felt certain that he could be elected. Many people, too, felt that a successful soldier would be a capable President. For a long time after the end of the war many politicians, in electoral campaigns, called 1905 1909 1913 1917 1921 1925 1929 1933 1937 1941 1945

attention to the record of the party which claimed the credit for winning the war.

In May, 1868, the Republican convention was held in Chicago. Grant was nominated, and with him, as the candidate for the vice-presidency, was Schuyler Colfax, the Speaker of the House, who had been in favor of the radical reconstruction measures which had been forced upon the South (pp. 409-411). The platform adopted gave hearty approval to the plan of reconstruction which the radicals had passed in Congress. On the question of negro suffrage, the platform held that Congress should enfranchise the negro in the states which had seceded from the Union; but that in other states the question should be decided by the people of those states. 

In July the Democratic convention met in New York. The Democrats were in an embarrassing position, for many of their former leaders had come from the South, and most of the Southerners had been discredited in the eyes of the North, where the term "Copperhead" was still applied to those who had been sympathetic toward the South. New leaders and new issues had to be found before a Democratic victory could be attained. 

The Democrats nominated Horatio Seymour, of New York, and in their platform favored "Immediate restoration of all the states to their rights in the Union, amnesty for all political offenses, . . ." It urged reform in taxation and finance, and economy in administration. The radical reconstruction program was condemned. The election which followed was a Republican victory, with 214 electoral votes for Grant and 80 for Seymour. While more than 5,000,000 popular votes were cast, Grant's majority was only slightly over 300,000. 

Grant's First Term. Grant's brief inaugural address gave little evidence that he understood the complex problems of government. Not only was he lacking in the experience and training necessary for a great statesman, but he was lacking also in the ability to choose good officialsand many of his friends took advantage of this weakness. The cabinet selected by him contained only a few men of outstanding ability. 

However, in one respect Grant showed true statesmanship. One of the important problems that came to his attention during his first term was that of civil service reform. He was sincere in his preference for honest and efficient public servants. He was interested in securing reform of the civil service, in which thousands of government employees such as clerks, revenue collectors, and postal employees served the government. 

Appointment to these positions had long been considered the spoils of the victors, and party workers had been rewarded for their party loyalty by appointment to office. This, however, had made for inefficiency in the

civil service; and Grant asked Congress to pass a law requiring that certain appointments be based on fitness, that competitive examinations be given, and that the tenure of office for these positions should not depend on political affiliations, but that efficient people should be kept in office regardless of their political views. 

Liberals in Congress, notably 

Thomas A. Jencken and Carl

Schurz, were greatly interested in civil service reform, and in 1871 Congress passed an act which they had sponsored. A commission was appointed, and the work of securing better public servants began. A system of competitive examinations was instituted and continued until 1873, when Congress refused to appropriate money for the commission. Effective civil service reform, therefore, had to wait another decade, when the assassination of 

President Garfield by a disappointed 

Ulysses S. Grant office seeker aroused the people, and the Pendleton Act of 1883 was passed by Congress.

Grant Re-elected in 1872. Opposition to Grant developed even within the Republican party as early as 1870, and a group known as the Liberal Republicans, led by Carl Schurz, of Missouri, urged that the government should be more liberal in dealing with the political problems of the South, and that it reform the civil service and revise the tariff. In 1872 the 

Liberal Republicans, in their convention at Cincinnati, nominated Horace Greeley, editor of the New York Tribune, for President, and B. Gratz 

Brown, of Missouri, for Vice-President. The Democrats realized that their only opportunity to defeat Grant and the Republicans would be by endorsing the Liberal Republican candidates and platform. This was difficult, for Greeley had seriously denounced the Southern Democrats. 

Yet even though the choice was a hard one, it seemed to be the only way to success, and the Democratic party, therefore, joined in the nomination of Greeley for President. It was evident, however, that there was strong opposition to Greeley.

The Republicans renominated Grant and pointed with pride to the achievements of their party. They favored a high protective tariff and

payment of war pensions. Besides the Liberal Republican, Democratic, and Republican parties, there were two other parties in the field-the Labor Reform party and the National Prohibition party. The latter party's chief interest was in the prohibition of alcoholic liquors, but its platform also advocated the direct election of United States senators, an income tax, and woman suffrage. It is interesting to note that these three demands were later included in amendments to the Constitution. 

The campaign was full of interest and enthusiasm. The cartoonist

Grant received 272 electoral votes, while Greeley electors numbered 66. The effort to reform the Republican party had failed. 

Scandals and Corruption in High Places. Following the war came a period during which public morals were at a low ebb. Corruption, fraud, and general political dishonesty were to be found in the national government, and some startling and sensational scandals came to light during Grant's second administration. Local governments, as well as the national government, were suffering because of political dishonesty. The country received its first shock with the exposure of the infamous Tweed Ring. Boss Tweed and his associates had gained control of the offices of

the city government of New York through which the finances were administered. By means of fraudulent contracts and ingenious bookkeeping, these men had feathered their own nests at the expense of the taxpayers. 

The city paid $11,000,000 for a courthouse, the construction of which cost only $3,000,000. A plasterer was given credit on the books for $138,187 for two days' work. Men working for the city were encouraged to present bills for many times the amount due them so that those connected with the ring could collect and pocket the difference. 

In 1871 the ring was broken up and Boss Tweed was brought to justice largely through the efforts of Samuel J. Tilden, but it was not until the debt of New York City had increased $70,- 000,000 in the space of two and one half years.

Cartoon on the Tweed Ring, by Thomas Nast. Tweed (the largest man) and others are shown as each trying to clear himself of blame by saying ""Twas him." 

Credit Mobilier. Equally scandalous were the activities of the Credit Mobilier, a railroad construction company composed of the controlling stockholders of the Union Pacific Railroad. Through control of the railroad company, these grafters secured for their construction company the contract for the construction of the railroad at a tremendous profit. In order to prevent congressional investigation or interference with the company, some shares of stock were distributed by Oakes Ames, a member of Congress and an official of the construction company, to other members of Congress. These shares of stock, which paid high dividends, were either distributed free or sold at a very low price. Many government officials, including chairmen of leading committees and prominent party leaders, were involved in the scandal. The most disgraceful part of the affair was the way in which a House committee "whitewashed" the guilty members. 

The Salary Grab Act. With corruption in the air, Congress passed the "Salary Grab Act," which provided for an increase in the salaries of all congressmen, the President of the United States, the Vice-President, and the justices of the Supreme Court. Moreover, the increase was made retroactive, in that it declared that "these salaries shall be in effect for the preceding two years." Public sentiment, however, was aroused, and its effect became evident in the congressional election of 1874, with the result that at the next session Congress repealed the act.

The Whisky Ring. Other scandals followed and involved some of the closest advisers of the President. President Grant's private secretary was found to be affiliated with the so-called "Whisky Ring." This ring during a period of ten months had defrauded the government of taxes amounting to more than $1,500,000. It was charged that the Secretary of the Treasury, William A. Richardson, had employed someone to collect revenue due the government at a 50 per cent commission. Richardson resigned in order to avoid censure. Other high officials were implicated. It was charged that the Secretary of War, W. W. Belknap, had taken money for appointing an 

Indian Territory trader at Fort Sill. The House voted to impeach him a few hours after he had resigned; but his trial ended in acquittal. 

The causes of corruption are difficult to ascertain with any degree of certainty. Perhaps they were the result of a moral reaction which followed the war. In a period during which quick profits and huge fortunes developed, no great emphasis was placed on honest toil. The economic expansion in the 1870's was rapid and was accompanied by the concentration BEG TO REPEAT THAT

The Disputed Election of 1876. As the political parties looked for standard-bearers for the coming election, the friends of President Grant, and perhaps Grant himself, looked toward a third term. But in 1875 the 

House of Representatives passed a resolution declaring itself against a third term. The President's supporters then turned to Roscoe Conkling, of New York, and to O. P. Morton, of Indiana. James G. Blaine, a former

Speaker of the House, was another possible candidate but was opposed by

the supporters of civil service reform. The Republican convention met in 

Cincinnati. After several ballots were taken, during which votes were cast for Blaine, O. P. Morton, Bristow, Conkling, and others, it became evident that none of the leading contenders would be chosen, and the drift was toward a "dark horse," Rutherford B. Hayes, a favorite son and former governor of Ohio, who was nominated for President on the seventh ballot. 

The Democrats realized that the country was tired of scandals and they chose for their candidate Samuel J. Tilden, who was well known as a reformer. He had prosecuted the Tweed Ring in New York and had served as a reform governor of New York.

A third party, known as the National Greenback party, was also in the field, stressing a proposed monetary reform (see p. 507).

Throughout the campaign it was evident to both Democrats and Republicans that the election would be won by a narrow margin.* The number of electoral votes necessary for making a choice was 185, a majority of the electoral college. On the day following the election it was evident that 

Tilden had secured 184 votes and Hayes 165, with twenty votes in doubt. 

The leading Democratic newspapers claimed a victory, while many of the Republican papers admitted that the Republicans had lost. It was evident that for winning the election Tilden needed only one of the twenty contested electoral votes, while Hayes needed all twenty. 

Among the twenty disputed votes was one from Oregon, where a postmaster served as elector. His selection was in violation of Article II, Section I, of the United States Constitution, which provides that "no... person holding an office of trust or profit under the United States shall be appointed an elector." From three Southern states-Florida, Louisiana, and South Carolina-two conflicting sets of returns were sent to the president of the Senate, who, according to the Constitution, opens the certified lists of votes in the presence of both houses of Congress. However, the 

Constitution does not tell how to decide which set of votes shall be counted in case two conflicting lists are presented from any state. 

The Electoral Commission. In that emergency it became necessary for Congress to act. The majority of the House of Representatives was *The number of states in the Union in 1876 was only 38, as Arizona, Idaho, Montana, New Mexico, the Dakotas, Oklahoma, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming had not yet been admitted. 

The four most populous states, casting more than one fourth of the electoral votes, were New York, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Illinois, as they have continued to be since then (see map, p. 755). 

The eight next most populous states in 1876, together casting more than one fourth of the electoral votes, were Missouri, Indiana, Massachusetts, Kentucky, Tennessee, Virginia, Iowa, and Georgia (the five last named being then more populous than New Jersey, Michigan, North Carolina, Texas, or California, which have since then grown faster in population; see map, p. 755).
