Democratic, and of the Senate Republican, and only a compromise measure could pass both houses. A bill was passed providing for an Electoral 

Commission to settle all questions pertaining to the conflicting returns. 

The commission was made up of five representatives, of whom three were Democrats and two Republicans; five senators, of whom three were Republicans and two Democrats; and five justices of the Supreme Court, two 

Democrats, two Republicans, and one to be selected by these four justices. 

It was expected that the fifth justice to be chosen would be David Davis, of Illinois, who was considered independent in politics; but the state legislature had elected him to the United States Senate before the commission could decide. He therefore was no longer eligible, and Justice Bradley, who had voted with the Republicans, was chosen as the fifteenth member of the commission, which therefore seemed to be composed of eight Republicans and seven Democrats. In deciding the various disputes the members of the commission voted along party lines, and by a vote of eight to seven the Electoral Commission decided that all twenty disputed votes should be cast for Hayes, who then had 185 votes to Tilden's 184, and was declared elected President. 

The Administration of President Hayes. Hayes was a capable, honest, and conscientious President; but his administration began with a serious handicap, because his enemies charged that he was elected through fraud, and he was referred to as "Old Eight to Seven." He was thoroughly interested in civil service reform and was therefore not popular with the oldline politicians, who referred to him as a "goody-goody," and as "Granny Hayes." Some of the old-line party leaders tried to ridicule him by calling him "the Old Woman." In spite of these handicaps and criticisms, he pursued a straightforward policy. He was charged with ruining the party because he did not make the political appointments asked of him. He replied, however, that the President of the United States should strive to be always mindful of the fact that he serves his party best who serves his country best.

President Hayes manifested a friendly attitude toward the South. He withdrew the military forces from the Southern states and permitted the "carpetbag” governments to collapse, thus giving the Southern people an opportunity to set up their own governments. To the office of Postmaster 

General, he appointed David M. Key, of Tennessee, who was an ex-Confederate soldier and a Democrat. During Hayes's administration the financial question came to the front with the passage of the Bland-Allison Act in 1878 (see p. 483). The Resumption Act became effective in 1879 (see p. 488).

In an attempt to carry out civil service reforms President Hayes issued a communication to the Secretary of the Treasury, in which he said, "It is my wish that the collection of revenue should be free from party control and organized on a strictly business basis. . . . Party leaders should have 

NTS ALLER 

Ewing Galloway

Customs officers examining baggage of passengers from abroad, to prevent smuggling no more influence in appointments than other equally respectable citizens. No assessments for political purposes on officers or subordinates should be allowed." It soon came to the President's attention that the customs officers of the port of New York, through which three fourths of our imports from foreign countries came, ignored his order concerning party control. He discovered that many officials there had been replaced for political reasons. Therefore, after careful investigation, he asked the resignation of the leading customs official, Chester A. Arthur, collector of the port of New 

York. This brought on a bitter fight between the powerful New

York machine which supported the new customs officials, and the President. Hayes succeeded in removing these customs officials and appointed new men, though it cost him the support of many party leaders, with the result that Hayes was not considered as the party candidate for re-election. 

The Election of 1880. In the Republican convention, the opponents of Hayes, who were called the "Stalwarts," preferred Grant, but the opposition to making anyone President for a third term ruled him out. Roscoe 

Conkling, of New York, and James G. Blaine, of Maine, were also considered; but finally, after more than thirty ballots had been taken, James 

A. Garfield, of Ohio, a "dark horse," was nominated for President. Chester

A. Arthur, a friend of Conkling and a Stalwart, was nominated for the vice-presidency. The Democrats nominated Winfield Scott Hancock, of

Pennsylvania, for President, and the Greenback party nominated James B. 

Weaver, of Iowa. The Democrats in their platform advocated a "tariff for revenue only" and the "free coinage of silver." The Republicans in their platform urged the continuation of the high tariff. In the campaign important issues were submerged, and the personalities of the candidates loomed large. The Republicans won by a majority of 59 electoral votes. 

Garfield's Administra- 

MAINE 

tion. President Garfield was an able man and had been associated with the better element of the party. He came from humble circumstances and, like many earlier Presidents, had been born in a log cabin. He had worked on the farm, taught school, had been a minister and a college president, had studied law, and had served as a member of the United

States Senate. When he took office, John Hay said to him, "You go to the presidency with the best equipment possible. Besides the qualities that are personal to you, you know more of the past and present of government, more history and politics, than any man since the younger Adams." He had been a careful student, was an effective speaker and had a knowledge of public affairs; but as John Sherman said of him, "His will power was not equal to his personal magnetism. . . . He changed his mind and honestly veered from one opinion to another." 

Scene in the Republican convention in Chicago in 1880, when many of the delegates were cheering for Blaine; from a contemporary drawing

Garfield soon fell out with some of the Stalwarts of the Republican party. He appointed as Secretary of State, James G. Blaine, who was an opponent of the Stalwart leader, Roscoe Conkling. He further antagonized 

Conkling by not consulting with him in the appointment of a customs collector for the port of New York. For this office Garfield selected William 

H. Robertson, who was a friend of Blaine and a political enemy of Conkling. Conkling and his colleague, T. C. Platt, also senator from New York, opposed the appointment of Robertson on the basis of senatorial courtesy.

When the Senate confirmed the appointment, both Conkling and Platt resigned from the United States Senate in protest, expecting to be reelected by the New York state legislature. To their surprise, however, the legislature of New York did not re-elect them. 

On July 2, 1881, about four months after President Garfield had assumed office, while he was at the railway station in Washington, accompanied by Secretary of State Blaine, he was assassinated by a disappointed office seeker. As the assassin fired the fatal shot, he said, "I am a Stalwart.

Arthur is now President of the United States." Garfield, however, lingered on in serious illness until September 19, when he died. He was succeeded in office by Chester A. Arthur, who at the time of the assassination was in Albany, working with the legislature of New York in the unsuccessful attempt to secure the re-election of his friend Roscoe Conkling. Garfield's assassination brought the spoils system to the attention of the people. 

Arthur's Administration. Many remembered that Chester A. Arthur was the man whom Hayes had removed from the office of collector at the port of New York (p. 718) and were therefore greatly disturbed when he became President. However, when Arthur sent his first message to Congress, he surprised the reformers by recommending civil service reform, and stated that he would support any reform bill enacted. The responsibility of the presidential office had brought to the front Arthur's best qualities. He was capable and possessed dignity and common sense, and he gave the country an administration which was free from corruption. 

In his inaugural address he promised to "correct abuses, to enforce economy, to advance prosperity, and to promote the general welfare." He lived up to these promises. He broke with Conkling, and refused to submit to partisan politics. It was during his administration that the Pendleton 

Act of 1883 was passed, which substituted the "merit system" for the spoils system. The act provided for a bipartisan commission of three, which was empowered to prohibit all political assessments of government employees. It provided for competitive examinations with the view of determining fitness for office. It provided for a classified list of positions to which appointments were to be made only on the basis of examinations. 

It prohibited removal for political reasons. A beginning was thus made to improve the civil service. Of the total of 135,000 positions to be filled, about 12 per cent, or 15,600, were placed on the classified list by President Arthur. This list was steadily extended until during President Hoover's administration, out of the total of 563,000, about 83 per cent were on the classified list—a total of 467,000. In the following administration, under 

President Franklin D. Roosevelt, however, when many new positions were

added to the civil service, few of them were put in the classified list. Out of the total service, the percentage of the classified list was reduced to less than 60 per cent.

The Election of 1884. As the campaign of 1884 approached, a demand for economic reform was presented by the Anti-Monopoly party. As the name indicates, this party was opposed to the increasing concentration of business and urged that the public give more attention to the regulation of industry and also to the fostering of agriculture. It opposed land grants to corporations, advocated tax reforms, and worked for an interstate commerce law. General Benjamin F. Butler was nominated by this party, and was endorsed by the Greenback Labor party as well. 

President Arthur, who had made an excellent record, desired the Republican nomination. However, he failed to satisfy the party leaders, who were not united. He had lost the sympathy of the Stalwarts and did not have the full support of the "Half-Breeds." In the Republican convention which met in Chicago, the party platform again endorsed the protective tariff, with the promise to reward both labor and capital. The money question was coming to the front, but the delegates were so divided that the party merely announced itself as favoring "the best money known to the civilized world." James G.

Blaine was nominated for 

President, with General John 

A. Logan as his running mate.

The reform element in the Republican party was dissatisfied and disappointed, and many of that group deserted the party to join the Democrats. They were called "Mugwumps." Theodore 

Culver Service

Democratic convention at Chicago in 1884, cheering the nomination of Cleveland Roosevelt and Henry Cabot Lodge, both new in politics, were disappointed in Blaine's nomination, but they did not desert the party. 

The Democrats held their national convention in Chicago and nominated Grover Cleveland and Thomas A. Hendricks. Grover Cleveland had

entered politics as a county sheriff, had served as mayor of Buffalo, and later as governor of New York, where he had made an excellent record. 

He had opposed Tammany Hall, the Democratic organization usually in power in New York City, and had vetoed legislation which he considered unfair. The Democratic platform promised to revise the tariff "in a spirit of fairness to all interests," and asserted its belief in "honest money." 

The campaign proved to be one in which the real issues were ignored, while the personal records of the candidates were attacked. Cleveland's record in private life was criticized by his enemies, while the enemies of Blaine found fault with his public record. The contest has been designated as a "mud-slinging" affair and was said to be "the vilest political campaign ever waged." As Blaine came to the city of New York to deliver an address near the end of the campaign, he was introduced by a partisan clergyman, Dr. Burchard, who referred to the Democrats as the party of "rum, Romanism, and rebellion." Blaine did not comment on this introductory remark, and some considered his silence as approval of what was interpreted as an insult to the Catholic Church and the Democratic party. 

The Democratic newspapers featured this incident, and many considered it responsible for Blaine's defeat, because Cleveland carried New York state by a plurality of only 1,149, and had a total electoral vote of 219, against 182 for Blaine (map, p. 716). A change of less than 600 popular votes in New York would have carried that state, with its 35 electoral votes, and would have given Blaine the presidency.

Cleveland's First Administration. In 1884 the people also elected a Democratic majority to the House of Representatives, but the Senate retained a Republican majority. The legislation of the Cleveland administration of necessity was therefore of a nonpartisan character. A new 

Presidential Succession Act was passed, which provided that in case of the death of both the President and the Vice-President, the office of President should be filled by the Secretary of State, if eligible, and if not, then by another, the first one eligible, in the list of seven cabinet members named in the act in the order in which their offices had been created. This act, still in effect, practically prevents the possibility of changing the political complexion of the administration, as would have been possible under the earlier law, which gave the succession to the president pro tempore of the Senate, or to the Speaker of the House, following the death of both President and Vice-President. An Electoral Count Act, passed in 1887, provides that the certificates of the state electoral authorities shall be accepted as final - thus preventing any such contest as that of 1876. 

In 1887 there was passed also the Interstate Commerce Act (see p. 550).

LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES, 1868–1896 

723 Cleveland stood out as an able and honest President. He pointed out that "public office is a public trust," and believed that the President should exert leadership above partisan politics. He soon became unpopular, however, because he vetoed many bills, including a Rivers and Harbors Bill which carried appropriations for many sections of the country. Moreover, he vetoed a Dependent Pension Bill, which provided that every Union soldier who depended upon his own labor for support, and who had served three months in the army, should be paid a pension of $12 a month. 

Cleveland, after a careful study of the bill, vetoed it and thereby incurred the hostility of the Grand Army of the Republic, an organization made up of Union veterans. During his first term Cleveland vetoed no less than 

301 bills, which was twice as many as had been vetoed by all previous administrations. His act in vetoing these bills is sometimes referred to as a victory for executive independence, because the President did not hesitate to oppose Congress when bills which he did not approve were passed.

In 1887 Cleveland's entire annual message to Congress dealt with the tariff. He urged the immediate reduction of the tariff because there was a surplus in the treasury. It was his contention that labor was not benefited by high tariff, because of the small percentage of wage earners in the protected industries. The Mills Bill, providing for lower tariff rates, was passed by the House but was rejected by the Senate. The issue, therefore, went before the people in the election of 1888. 

The Election of 1888. In 1888 the Republicans held their convention in Chicago and nominated Benjamin Harrison, of Indiana, for President, and Levi P. Morton, of New York, for Vice-President.

In this election appeared the Union Labor party, which was composed of the old Greenbackers, Knights of Labor, the Grangers, and Anti- Monopolists. This party adopted in its platform a program of reform, and among other reforms advocated the single tax-a tax on land only-the idea of which had been set forth by Henry George in his book, Progress and Poverty, published in 1880. 

Cleveland was nominated again by the Democrats, and made tariff reduction the main campaign issue. In the election Harrison received 233 electoral votes to 168 for Cleveland (map, p. 716). It is interesting to note, however, that Cleveland had nearly 100,000 more popular votes than did Harrison.

The Republicans Return to Power, 1889. With the election of President 

Benjamin Harrison, the grandson of William Henry Harrison, the ninth

President of the United States, the Republicans again assumed control of

the government. Since the campaign had been fought largely on the tariff, the Republicans, with William McKinley of Ohio as chairman of the Ways and Means Committee, passed a bill providing for high tariff (see p. 471). 

Republicans came into power not only in the presidency, but also in the House and in the Senate, under the leadership of such men as Reed, McKinley, and Platt, and the great influence of Secretary of State Blaine. 

Thomas B. Reed, of Maine, became Speaker of the House, and ruled with an iron hand. Reed has been referred to as the greatest Speaker the country has produced. Joseph G. Cannon said that in Reed was "combined the greatest intellect with the greatest courage, the keenest appreciation of humor, and the greatest command of sarcasm." Reed, because of his control of the House, was referred to as "Czar." He believed that it was the duty of the successful party to see that its policies were carried out. Before 1889 it had been the custom of the minority at times to prevent the majority party from carrying on business by refusing to answer the roll call, even though they were present, when by so doing they could prevent a quorum. Speaker Reed, however, would not permit the minority thus to obstruct the business of the House, and so ordered the clerk to record the names of some of the opposition as present but not voting. To this there was objection, for the opponents charged that he was "upsetting the precedent of a hundred years." Reed replied, "Yes, and I am establishing precedents for the next one hundred years. A member of Congress denied the right of the Speaker to count him as present, but Reed replied by saying, "The chair is making a statement of fact that the gentleman is present. Does he deny it?" This produced laughter and enabled the Speaker to carry his point. With the House in control by means of autocratic rule, "Czar Reed" directed the legislation. 

A Billion-Dollar Country. The treasury then had an annual surplus of $100,000,000, and Congress proceeded to the Dependent Pensions Bill, which increased the appropriation for pensions from $89,000,000 in 1889 to $159,000,000 four years later. Further appropriations were made for the improvement of rivers and harbors and also for the construction of public buildings. It was during this period of vast expenditures that the term "pork barrel" legislation was applied to appropriations for public buildings. Expenditures were so great that for the first time in the history of the United States a single Congress made appropriations in excess of a billion dollars. This caused the Democrats to criticize the Republicans for extravagance. However, Speaker Reed replied to their criticism by saying, "This is a billion-dollar country." The silver question again came to the attention of Congress, and the Sherman Silver Act of 1890 was passed

(see p. 484). The question of big business engaged the attention of Congress and the Sherman Antitrust Law was passed (see p. 434). Dissatisfaction in the agricultural region of the West brought on a movement known as Populism (see p. 509).

The Return of the Democrats. By the election of 1892 the Democrats were returned to power for another four years. The Republicans under 

Harrison had become extravagant, raised the tariff, and increased the cost of living. To this came a reaction which was expressed by Western farmers in their organization of the People's party. This movement, known as the 

Populist revolt, was a protest against the acts of the party in power. 

In the coming election the Democrats nominated Grover Cleveland, and in their platform denounced the protective tariff as a fraud and "a robbery of the great majority of the American people for the benefit of the few." 

The Republicans nominated President Harrison again and in their platform emphatically endorsed the principle of the protective tariff. 

Because of the rise of Populism, attention was again called to the currency question, and a demand arose for the free coinage of silver. The political leaders of both the Republican and Democratic parties were cautious in expressing themselves on the silver question. Cleveland, however, made the statement that he believed the attempt to establish free coinage to be "dangerous and reckless." The position of both the Democratic and Republican parties on the currency question was practically the same. Both favored gold and silver on a parity; that is, keeping the value of the gold dollar and the silver dollar equal, by "appropriate legislation.' 

The Populists selected for their candidate, James B. Weaver, of Iowa. 

The result of the election was a victory for Cleveland and the Democrats. 

Cleveland received 277 electoral votes, while Harrison received 145, and Weaver 22 (map, p. 716). The Populists polled more than a million votes and increased their strength in Congress. 

The Panic of 1893. Business conditions during the Harrison administration were becoming unsatisfactory. In 1890 the banking house of 

Baring Brothers in London collapsed, and during the next two years many bank failures occurred in the British colonies. Austria-Hungary established the gold standard in 1892 and began the purchase of gold. The Bank of France added to its supply of gold, and European bankers generally began to add to their gold reserves. American gold was sent abroad to be used for the settlement of trade balances, with the result that the supply of gold in the treasury, which on March 4, 1889, when Cleveland left office, was $196,689,000, was diminished until, when he took office four years later, the supply of gold was only $103,500,000.

In February, 1893, the month before Cleveland took office, the Philadelphia and Reading Railway Company, with a capital of $40,000,000, went into bankruptcy, and in May of the same year the National Cordage, with a capital of $20,000,000, collapsed. Thus, as a result of the business failures and the decline of the gold reserve, uncertainty developed which finally led to panic and serious depression. During 1893, 600 banks and more than 15,000 commercial firms failed, while 30,000 miles of railroad passed into the hands of receivers. 

Cleveland's Second Administration. As is usually the case, the party in power was charged with responsibility for the depression, and it became clear that Cleveland and the Democratic party would have difficulty in remaining in power in the coming election. During the course of the administration Cleveland insisted on the repeal of the Silver Purchase Act, which he maintained was responsible for depleting the gold reserve (see p. 484). During the year 1894 the Wilson-Gorman Tariff Law was passed, which was a downward revision; but because conditions in the country were not prosperous, the Republicans blamed the Democrats and the tariff for the depression.

Along with the depression of 1893 came labor difficulties, which were increased by the large number of unemployed. The unrest of the times was dramatically portrayed by a group of unemployed who in 1894, under the leadership of Jacob Coxey, marched to Washington. There was wide discontent, and Coxey's army was merely an incident which called attention to the unrest of the times. Not much resulted from this army of unemployed, for at the capital the leaders of Coxey's army were arrested on a technical charge of walking on the grass, and the group was scattered. 

However, the common man was turning to his political leaders to find solutions for his difficult problems. Among the many causes which contributed to the unrest, were the increase in population and the disappearance of free lands in the West, which made adjustment more difficult. 

No longer did the safety valve of going west to take up land exist; and the social and economic problems which in the earlier days were easily solved because of the westward movement, were now turned back on society. 

With the disappearance of the frontier, it became more difficult to settle the social and economic problems which arose in our complex society. In 

1892 the Populist group, coming from the agricultural sections, insisted that low prices and hard financial conditions were due to a scarcity of money. Many of their number were urging the use of silver in larger quantities. Unrest and the demand for more money brought the currency question to the front as the election of 1896 approached.

CHAPTER XXXVIII Leaders, Parties, and Policies 

1896-1932 

The Election of 1896; the Battle of the Standards. The Democratic party had lost confidence in President Cleveland and was torn by a struggle between the Western and Eastern factions. Most of the Westerners were in favor of silver, while most Easterners advocated the gold standard. 

Among the leaders of the silver Democrats was an ardent worker, William Jennings Bryan, of Nebraska, who had been characterized by Cleveland as a "Populist pure and simple." Bryan became a powerful influence in the 

Democratic party. He had been educated in Illinois, where he began the practice of law before moving to Nebraska. He was talented in oratory and took an early interest in politics. In 1890, at the age of thirty, he was elected to Congress, and was re-elected two years later. In Congress he served on the Ways and Means Committee, opposed the rule of "Czar" Reed, and objected to Cleveland's method of building up the gold reserve. 

He favored the income tax and took an active part in securing tariff reductions. At the Democratic convention the silver Democrats, mostly from the West, urged the free and unlimited coinage of silver at the ratio of 16 to 1 (see p. 482). When the convention met in Chicago, on July 7, it was soon evident that the silver faction was in the majority. In the course of the debate on the money question, Bryan delivered the famous "Cross of Gold speech," which electrified the convention (see p. 485). In this speech he not only set forth his ideas on silver, but demonstrated his ability as an orator and won for himself the nomination of the Democratic party. 

He was also the nominee of the Populist party (p. 511). 

The Republican convention was less exciting. One of the leading spirits in it was "Mark" Hanna, a wealthy business man who had taken an active part in politics and was a devoted follower of William McKinley. 731

He was able to hold the different factions together and unite them behind a plank calling for a single gold standard. William McKinley, who had been an advocate of the high tariff and the author of the famous McKinley Bill, was nominated on the first ballot. His support of a high protective tariff helped to make him popular, because the panic of 1893 had come during an administration which had reduced the tariff. 

The campaign of 1896 was one of great enthusiasm. There were many speeches and torchlight processions. The people in general took an active part in the campaign and tried to inform themselves on its issues. The campaign revealed that there was a close relation between the Republican party and big business. Mark Hanna, as campaign manager, collected large sums from bankers, manufacturers, and moneyed interests generally. 

The Republican party sent out many speakers, and printed pamphlets and posters in many languages, in an attempt to reach all the voters. 

McKinley, however, did not travel through the country, but delivered speeches from his front porch at Canton, Ohio, to which delegations came 

Culver Service

McKinley delivering a speech on his front porch at Canton, Ohio by train to hear his addresses. The campaign was referred to as "the front porch" campaign. The Republicans urged the return of better times, promised "a full dinner pail," and hailed McKinley as "the advance agent of prosperity."

While McKinley was addressing delegations from his front porch, Bryan made a whirlwind campaign throughout the nation, in which he traveled 18,000 miles, and addressed 5,000,000 persons, in no less than

six hundred speeches. He referred to the delegations going to Canton as "worshiping at the shrine of the golden calf."

The Administration of McKinley. When the votes were counted, it was found that Bryan had 176 electoral votes and McKinley 271. Both houses of Congress had Republi- can majorities. McKinley, in his inaugural address, referred to the tariff as the most pressing issue, and later called a special session of Congress, at which the Dingley Tariff Act was passed (p. 472). 

Shortly after the inauguration of McKinley, as we have seen, new sources of gold were found in 

Alaska and in Australia. Furthermore, the cyanide process for extracting a larger percentage of gold from ore was discovered.

These discoveries tended to make more money available, and along with other factors, helped to bring the return of prosperity.

McKinley had a magnetic personality and became a popular President. He appointed to his cabinet capable men, including John Hay and Elihu Root. 

Culver Service 

Bryan delivering a campaign speech. He was called "the golden-voiced orator"

The Re-election of McKinley, 1900. As the time for another presidential election came, the Republicans renominated William McKinley for President, with Theodore Roosevelt of New York for Vice-President; and the Democrats again called on William Jennings Bryan for leadership. 

The currency question, which attracted so much attention during the preceding campaign, was no longer an issue. A new issue arose as a result of our war with Spain, fought during the administration of McKinley (see p. 592). As a result of the war the United States acquired the Philippine Islands and Puerto Rico, and obtained a protectorate over Cuba. In the election of 1900, therefore, the parties differed on the question of imperialism. The Democrats opposed the acquisition of new territory, and in their platform said, "We declare again that all governments instituted among men derive their just powers from the consent of the governed; that any government not based upon the consent of the governed is a tyranny; and that to impose upon any people a government of force is to substitute the methods of imperialism for those of a republic." The

Republicans, on the other hand, maintained that it was the duty of the United States to extend the benefits of our government to the less fortunate people of those islands. In their platform they said, "The largest measure of self-government consistent with their welfare and our duty shall be secured to them by law."

In this election there were a number of minor political parties in the field. Among them were the Social Democratic party, the Socialist Labor, the Prohibition party, the Mid-Road Populists, the Union Reform, and the United Christian. McKinley received 292 electoral votes, while Bryan received 155. The American people thus expressed their approval of the idea of imperialism. They were willing that our government should embark on "untried paths" and undertake to govern territories far distant from the United States and inhabited by alien races. 

Assassination of President McKinley. Within six months after his second inauguration, while President McKinley was attending the Pan- American Exposition at Buffalo, he was shot by a fanatic, and after lingering between life and death for eight days, he died on September 14, 1901. 

With the death of McKinley, Theodore Roosevelt, the Vice-President, assumed the office of President. Active, broad-visioned, varied in experience, and only forty-three years of age, he became one of our most beloved Presidents. He was a Harvard graduate, had lived on a ranch in the West, led a regiment in the Spanish-American War, had been a member of the New York legislature, had been head of the New York City police force, had served as a member of the Civil Service Commission, had been Assistant Secretary of the Navy, and had served as governor of the state of New York. All of these offices he filled with such success that he brought credit to himself as a public servant. He had always been a loyal Republican, but was feared by the party bosses because of his ability and his popularity. William Allen White, in a book called Masks in a 

Pageant, speaks very highly of Theodore Roosevelt, and says of him: "He kept himself well-trained physically; an electric energy seemed to exude from his body and emphasize his personality. His walk was a shoulder-shaking, sturdy, heel-clicking, straightaway gait, rather conspicuously rapid as one who is habitually about his Master's business." 

Roosevelt was an advocate of the strenuous life. He was active in outdoor sports and interested in hunting, read widely, and was the author of many volumes on history and politics, and on outdoor life. He was interested in meeting outstanding people, and invited to the White House men of wealth, as well as poor men, writers, editors, explorers, prize fighters, laborers, and farmers. His principal contribution was perhaps his un-

selfish interest in reform. At a period in our history when many reform movements were considered unpopular, Theodore Roosevelt gave his full support to reform and worked in the interest of better government. 

The Election of Roosevelt, 1904. In 1904 the Republican party nominated Theodore Roosevelt for the presidency, while the Democrats nominated Judge Alton B. Parker, of New York. In the campaign which followed, the Republicans emphasized the protective tariff and the national expansion which had begun during the McKinley administration. The 

Democrats, on the other hand, again opposed the tariff and also emphasized their opposition to imperialism. Roosevelt won the election, receiving 

336 electoral votes, while Parker received only 140. 

Roosevelt's Administration. During the next four years Roosevelt continued in the progressive way in which he began his administration. 

He led the fight against the abuses of corporations and big business (see p. 438). He became an advocate of the "square deal," and opposed all forms of corruption. It was during his administration that the construction of the Panama Canal was begun (see p. 605). When Russia and Japan were at war, Roosevelt proceeded to work for peace and invited delegates from Russia and Japan to the United States, where the Treaty of 

Portsmouth (New Hampshire) was signed, ending the war between those two nations. For this service he was awarded the Nobel Peace

Prize. 

The Election of 1908. In 1908 

the Republican party nominated 

William Howard Taft, of Ohio, for 

President (with James S. Sherman of New York for Vice-President), while the Democrats nominated 

William Jennings Bryan for the third time. The Republican party centered its interest on the tariff as the main issue, and again won the election by a large majority. Taft received 321 electoral votes, while Bryan had only 162. Taft had a majority of more than 1,200,000 popular votes. He was a highly educated man, trained in law, and considered one of the outstanding constitutional lawyers in the country. Moreover, he had had wide experience in public 

Theodore Roosevelt

The White House-a recent view 

Ewing Galloway office. At the age of twenty-one he was an assistant prosecuting attorney. 

He became judge of the Superior Court of Ohio before he was thirty. 

Later he became in turn solicitor general of the United States and judge of the Federal Circuit Court. He served as governor general of the Philippine Islands, and then as Secretary of War in President Roosevelt's cabinet.

Taft's Administration. Roosevelt and Taft were very close personal friends. They had long been associated together in public office and had formed a strong attachment for each other. Roosevelt, indeed, was largely responsible for securing the Republican nomination for Taft; and, before the election, he made the statement that with the exception of Washington and Lincoln, "Taft as President will rank with any other man who has ever been in the White House." In this prediction, however, Roosevelt was mistaken, for it soon became evident that, even though Taft had political and administrative experience, and though he was well trained as a lawyer, he was conservative and overcautious and was slow to take action on important matters. Moreover, he was not in sympathy with the wide reform movement that was in the air during his administration. Yet with all his shortcomings, Taft was looked upon as a capable President. 

He was good-natured and honest. He brought before the courts many cases against the trusts, and was active in adding a long list of offices to the classified civil service list. During his administration the Postal 

Savings Bank was established and the Parcel Post system was inaugurated. 

Also during his administration the Constitution was amended so as to provide for an income tax, and the Seventeenth Amendment was proposed,

providing for the direct election of United States senators. This Amendment went into effect during Wilson's administration. 

During the campaign of 1908 the Republicans had promised a revision of the tariff, which Taft said meant a downward revision. Soon after his inauguration Taft called a special session of Congress, at which a tariff bill was introduced by Representative Sereno E. Payne. In the Senate this bill, under the guidance of the "standpat" Nelson W. Aldrich, was amended 847 times. Three fourths of these amendments called for increased rates of the tariff. During the discussion of the tariff bill Senators 

A. J. Beveridge of Indiana, A. B. Cummins and Jonathan Dolliver of

Iowa, J. L. Bristow of Kansas, and Robert M. La Follette of Wisconsin, together with other progressives, fought against this increase in the tariff. 

Their opposition, however, was not strong enough to prevent the enactment of the Payne-Aldrich Bill. The Republican members of Congress who had opposed the bill were termed "insurgents." Many of the Republicans considered that this new tariff act, which provided for higher rates than previous acts, was not in keeping with the campaign promises of a downward revision of the tariff. In an attempt to check the growing hostility to the administration, President Taft made a speaking tour in which he defended the tariff act; he said it was "the best tariff law the Republicans had ever made and, therefore, the best the country. ever had."

In addition to the disagreement over the tariff, the Republican party was further torn asunder over the Ballinger-Pinchot controversy. During 

Roosevelt's administration the government took a decided step in the direction of the conservation of our natural resources. This included the withdrawal from public sale of certain lands on which were located waterpower sites. These lands were placed under the supervision of the Department of the Interior. During Taft's administration the Secretary of the 

Interior, Ballinger, reversed the policy of President Roosevelt and permitted the sale of some of these lands to private individuals. The chief forester of the United States, Gifford Pinchot, who was a personal friend of Roosevelt and in his official position subordinate to Secretary Ballinger, protested against this sale. He criticized his superior officer, the Secretary of the Interior, and was removed from office by President Taft. 

The Progressive Movement. The "Progressive" element in Congress opposed the administration of the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Joseph G. Cannon, who exercised much power through his appointment of the committees. This opposition to the rule of Cannon, together with the Ballinger-Pinchot controversy and the split over the tariff, led ulti-

mately to the organization of the Progressive party. The progressive 

Republicans, together with the Democrats, succeeded in forcing the adoption of a resolution introduced by George W. Norris of Nebraska, increasing the membership of the Committee on Rules from five to ten, all of the members to be elected by the House. With the election of the 

Committee on Rules by the House, the power of the Speaker was cut down and the Republican power in Congress weakened. 

Taft and Roosevelt, who had been firm personal friends for many years, became less friendly after Taft became President. In fact, soon after the election it appeared that the friendship between the two men was cooling; and with the announcement of cabinet appointees, in which the friends of Roosevelt were ignored, it became evident that before long a break was inevitable. After the inauguration Roosevelt and his son Kermit left for a hunting trip in Africa. The American public eagerly followed the newspaper accounts of the adventure. On his way home Roosevelt stopped in 

Europe, where he was entertained by many crowned heads. He delivered addresses at and received degrees from some of Europe's finest universities. 

He returned after an absence of fifteen months, more popular than ever. 

On his return to the United States, Roosevelt, who had been progressive, saw how Taft in his conservatism had failed to keep the Republican party united behind him. Soon the rift between Roosevelt and Taft became an open secret. Roosevelt openly criticized Taft, and many of the divergent elements of the Republican party began to flock to him. Among them were reformers, idealists, college professors, and leaders in industry. As the time for the presidential campaign of 1912 approached, it became evident that in both parties there were strong progressive elements that were interested in popular government. Their opposition to special privilege, their efforts to secure governmental regulation of big business, and their interest in reform, tended to bring these different elements into one party.

In January, 1911, the insurgent Republicans in Congress organized the National Progressive Republican League. They declared that "popular government in America had been thwarted and progressive legislation strangled." In April a conference of the progressives decided to support 

Senator La Follette of Wisconsin as a candidate for the Republican nomination against Taft. However, with the return of Roosevelt, many progressives who were not attracted by La Follette because of his extreme radicalism looked toward Roosevelt, and in February, after Roosevelt had been approached by many party leaders he announced that he would accept the nomination "if it is tendered to me, and I will adhere to this

decision until the convention has expressed its preference." When the national Republican convention met in Chicago, it soon became evident that the "Old Guard," as the conservatives were called, was in control. 

This group ignored the wishes of the Progressives and renominated Taft for President and Sherman for Vice-President.

Roosevelt Heads the Progressive Party. Immediately after the nomination of Taft the Roosevelt delegates withdrew, held a meeting, and asked Roosevelt to head a new party-the Progressive party. Roosevelt urged the delegates to wait, to go back home and get the approval of the voters, and to return later to nominate a candidate for President who would appeal to all sections of the country. Organization went on rapidly through the summer; and in August the delegates of the Progressive party assembled again in Chicago and held their convention, at which time Roosevelt delivered his famous speech known as his "Confession of Faith." 

Roosevelt was nominated by acclamation, and Hiram Johnson of California received the nomination for Vice-President. 

The platform adopted by the Progressives was interesting from both the political and the economic standpoints. It advocated a tariff which would make the cost of imported goods equal to the cost of those produced at home. It advocated a system whereby the farmer could secure credit more easily, and recommended stricter antitrust laws. The Progressives favored social insurance, laws to protect workers against sickness, old age, and unemployment. They advocated minimum wages for women, laws to prevent or control child labor, and the creation of a Department of Labor in the cabinet. Politically, the platform stood for more direct legislation, direct primaries by means of which the voters might express a preference for presidential nominees, the direct election of United States senators, woman suffrage, greater publicity concerning campaign expenditures, a simpler method of amending the Constitution, the registration of lobbyists, and the wider use of the recall, including the recall of certain types of judicial decisions. The party chose the bull moose as its emblem and is often called the Bull Moose party. Roosevelt in 1904 had made a statement that he would not again be a candidate for the presidency, as he did not favor a third term. This statement now confronted him; but he explained it by saying that the third term meant a third consecutive term.

The Democrats Elect Woodrow Wilson, 1912. With the division of the Republicans into these two factions the Democrats looked hopefully to a victory. Within the Democratic party, as well as in the Republican party, there were conservative and progressive elements, but they were

able to unite, and in the Democratic convention which met in Baltimore, they selected Governor Woodrow Wilson of New Jersey as their candidate for President. Other candidates under consideration were Governor Harmon of Ohio, Senator Underwood of Alabama, and Champ Clark of Missouri.

One of the most powerful leaders in the Democratic convention was William Jennings Bryan, who had been three times a candidate for President on the Democratic ticket. This time he was not a candidate, but he still had an important following. The platform which the party adopted was largely his work. He urged a tariff for revenue only, a presidential preferential primary, an amendment of the Constitution limiting the President to one term, direct election of United States senators, improved banking laws, and further antitrust and railroad legislation. William Jennings Bryan supported Woodrow Wilson, who was nominated on the forty-sixth ballot. 

Thomas Marshall, who was said to be "a progressive with the brakes on," was nominated for the vice-presidency. 

In the campaign which followed, the factions of the Republican party wasted much effort in attacking each other. This reacted in favor of 

Wilson, the Democratic nominee, who received 435 electoral votes. 

Roosevelt received 88, and Taft 8 (map, p. 730). A Democratic House and Senate also were chosen. 

Woodrow Wilson and His Program. Woodrow Wilson, the son of a Presbyterian minister, was born at Staunton, Virginia. He attended

Davidson College, Princeton University, the University of Virginia, and later did graduate work at 

Johns Hopkins University. He studied law, and after graduating from Princeton began the practice of law in Atlanta, Georgia. This, however, was not to his liking, and he took up the study of history and government. He taught the social sciences at Bryn Mawr College, at 

Wesleyan University, and at Princeton, where he was chosen president of the university in 1902. While president of Princeton he led a movement to make college life more democratic; and in 1910 he was elected governor of New Jersey on the Democratic ticket. 

Woodrow Wilson

LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES, 1896–1932 

741 Woodrow Wilson had been brought to the attention of the political leaders of New Jersey by George Harvey, editor of the North American Review, who felt that unless some outstanding man appeared in the Democratic party, Bryan's influence would be too great. As soon as Wilson became governor of New Jersey, however, it was evident that he was a liberal, an independent thinker, and that he would not be subject to control by the machine politicians. He understood the masses and was their champion without being one of them. His brilliant mind and keen understanding and his high idealism removed him somewhat from the people. 

He lacked the personal magnetism of Jackson or Roosevelt. His political theories were the result of years of study. His conception of the presidency was that the President should be a leader of his party, a leader of the people, and the one whose duty it was even to lead Congress. His talent and ability in the use of language, both in speaking and in writing, especially fitted him to put into operation his theories of government. 

A short time before his inauguration as President, he announced his program in a booklet called The New Freedom. He accused the old leaders of acting for the people but being unwilling to act through the people, and charged that our wealth and credit were concentrated in the hands of a few. In his inaugural address, he proposed industrial legislation, the revision of the tariff, and also revision of currency and banking laws. 

Tariff Reform. Soon after Wilson's inauguration he called a special session of Congress, which at once took up the question of revising the tariff downward. The result was the Underwood Tariff Act of 1913, which received the President's signature in October of that year (see p. 474).

Because of the lower tariff rates, it was estimated that the revenue from the new tariff would be from $38,000,000 to $57,000,000 less than before. 

To make up this deficit Congress provided for an income tax, which was now possible after the ratification of the Sixteenth Amendment. With the income tax and the corporation tax, together with the tariff and other taxes, the government was able to balance its budget for 1913-1914. 

Other Legislation. The second important reform in the Wilson administration was directed toward banking and currency. In 1913 the Federal 

Reserve Act was passed, which provided for twelve districts, with a Federal Reserve Bank in each district (see p. 491).

In order to curb the activities of large-scale industry, the Clayton Antitrust Act was passed, which strengthened the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890 by prohibiting interlocking directorates (see p. 439). 

Congress also passed the Seamen's Act of 1915, providing for better living conditions for American sailors. In 1916 the Adamson Eight-Hour-

Day Act was passed by Congress at the request of President Wilson to prevent a threatened railroad strike. This act provided for an eight-hour working day for trainmen, with overtime payment equivalent to one and a half times the regular rate. 

In 1914 the World War broke out in Europe; and, while the United 

States did not take an active part until April 7, 1917, yet many problems arising out of that conflict demanded the attention of the administration (see pp. 616-618). 

The Election of 1916. Early in June, 1916, the Republicans held their convention in Chicago. The Progressives also held a convention and asked 

Theodore Roosevelt to accept the nomination, but he withheld his answer until the Republicans had made their selection. Charles Evans Hughes of 

New York, who was justice of the Supreme Court, was nominated by the Republican party, with Charles W. Fairbanks as his running mate. Hughes immediately resigned from the Supreme Court and accepted the nomination. Theodore Roosevelt then announced that he would support Hughes, and most of the Progressives returned to the ranks of the Republican party. The Republican platform concerned itself largely with criticism of the Democratic administration, and denounced President Wilson's foreign policies as especially bad. The platform condemned Wilson's policy of 'watchful waiting" in regard to Mexico (see p. 610). The Republicans declared that the President had not protected the honor or the lives of our citizens in Mexico. As usual, too, the Republicans favored a high protective tariff and condemned the tariff legislation of the Democratic party. 

On June 14 the Democratic convention met in St. Louis. President

Wilson and Vice-President Marshall were renominated by acclamation. 

The platform praised Wilson and his administration and urged a policy of national defense by more adequate "preparedness."

As the campaign got under way domestic issues received less attention than foreign policies. The Republican nominee, Hughes, accused President 

Wilson of not being firm enough with England and Germany in protecting our shipping interests. He also attacked the President for the support he had given to the Adamson Eight-Hour-Day Law. During the campaign a supporter of Wilson referred to the fact that "he kept us out of war." 

This soon became a campaign slogan which was widely used. The election was close, and for several days after the voting had taken place the result was in doubt. Indeed, many believed Wilson had been defeated; but when the count was completed, Hughes had received 254 electoral votes while

Wilson had 277. President Wilson carried all the states in the South. Ohio,

LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES, 1896–1932 

743 New Hampshire, and every state west of the Mississippi River except Oregon, Minnesota, and South Dakota. Hughes carried the states in the 

North and in the East except those mentioned above. In this election 

California's vote was important. Because the election was so close, the electoral votes of California would have been sufficient to elect the Republican nominee. However, Wilson carried that state by the small majority of 3,000 votes. In the congressional elections also there was a close race. For the lower house 217 Republicans and 213 Democrats were chosen, while in the Senate there were 54 Democrats and 42 Republicans. 

The World War. Shortly after Wilson's inauguration for the second term, the United States entered the World War, and all energies were bent toward bringing it to a successful and early close. Domestic issues were relegated to the background, and politics was not considered an important factor for the next two years. Both Republicans and Democrats worked together in the common task of winning the war (see pp. 618–625). 

Wilson and the League of Nations. At the close of the war President 

Wilson went to Europe as head of the American delegation to the Peace Conference. He took a very active part in the deliberations and was responsible for having the Covenant of the League of Nations embodied in the Versailles treaty of peace. When the treaty was presented to the 

United States Senate for ratification, the Republicans refused to accept it, and Wilson attempted to bring the matter before the people by a speaking tour through the West, hoping to overcome the opposition of the Senate by a direct appeal to the voters. However, he was unable to carry on the fight and was forced to return to Washington, due to a physical breakdown, and the treaty was not ratified by the Senate. 

The Election of 1920. During the latter part of the Wilson administration it became evident that his foreign policy was being defeated. The 

Republicans then looked forward with high hopes to the coming election. 

In June they held their convention in Chicago, where General Leonard 

Wood, Governor Frank O. Lowden of Illinois, and Senator Hiram Johnson of California were important contenders for the nomination. It soon became evident, however, that none of these had sufficient strength to obtain the nomination. A compromise was reached, and Senator Warren G. 

Harding of Ohio was nominated. Governor Calvin Coolidge of Massachusetts was nominated as the Republican candidate for the vice-presidency. 

The platform promised legislation necessary for the return of prosperity, farm relief, and economy in governmental expenditures. 

The Democratic convention met on June 28 in San Francisco. The 

Democratic platform praised Wilson's policies, both foreign and domestic,

promised farm relief, and advocated the ratification of the Versailles treaty. When the convention opened, the most active candidates for the nomination were Attorney General Palmer and William G. McAdoo, the son-in-law of President Wilson. As the balloting proceeded it became

evident that neither could secure the two-thirds vote required by the rules of the Democratic convention, and on the forty-fourth ballot Governor James M. Cox of Ohio was nominated for President. Franklin D. Roosevelt, 

Assistant Secretary of the Navy, was nominated for Vice-President. 

Two minor parties were very active in the contest. The Socialists nominated Eugene V. Debs for the fifth time. The Farmer-Labor party appeared with Parley T. Christensen of Utah as its candidate for President.

The main issue in the campaign centered around the League of Nations, which the Democratic National Committee maintained was the leading issue, urging that the election was in the nature of a referendum on the question whether the United States should join the League. The Republicans denounced the Versailles treaty which provided for membership in the League of Nations, but indicated that they favored participation in an "association of nations." The issue, therefore, was somewhat confused. 

Many Republicans who favored American participation in the settlement of world problems felt they could support the Republican party, which favored an "association of nations." 

Shortly before the election, the Nineteenth Amendment to the Federal Constitution, granting women the right to vote, was ratified, so that now for the first time women in all the states participated in a presidential election. Harding's popular vote was 16,152,000, while Cox received 9,147,000. ENEMIES LEAGUE

The Socialist candidate, Eugene V. Debs, received 919,800, and Christensen, the Farmer-Labor candidate, 265,400. In the electoral college the Republican candidate received 404 votes, while the Democratic nominee received only 127 (map, p. 730). In Congress both Senate and House had an overwhelming Republican majority.

Harding's Administration. Harding had been a newspaper owner and editor in Marion, Ohio, and had taken an active part in politics. He served as state senator for four years, from 1900 to 1904, and as lieutenant governor of Ohio from 1904 to 1906. In 1914 he was elected to the United 

States Senate, and two years later became the permanent chairman of the Republican National Committee. His record as a senator was not impressive, and as President he considered himself as the spokesman for those who determined the policies of the government, but did not feel called upon to outline or direct those policies. His administration in some respects bore a marked resemblance to the Grant administration, in that it was marred by several scandals. The director of the Veterans' Bureau, Charles 

R. Forbes, was found guilty of misconduct and dishonesty, by a Senate investigating committee. According to this committee, one fourth of the billion dollars appropriated for rehabilitation and care of the sick and disabled veterans was either stolen or squandered during a period of two years. A Senate investigating committee found irregularities in the work of the Department of Justice, and the Attorney General, Harry M. 

Daugherty, was charged with criminal neglect of duty and was later asked to resign. A friend of his, Thomas W. Miller, who held the position of alien property custodian, was found guilty of conspiring to defraud the government and was sentenced to eighteen months' imprisonment and a fine of $5,000.

Startling disclosures of fraud and corruption in the leasing of naval oil reserves attracted wide attention. Oil reserves which had been set aside for naval purposes by Presidents Taft and Wilson, and which had been in charge of the Navy, were transferred during Harding's administration to the Department of the Interior, headed by Albert B. Fall. Soon after these lands were transferred, Fall leased some of them to his friends, E. M. 

Doheny and Harry F. Sinclair. Suspicion aroused by these transfers led to an investigation by a Senate committee which found that E. M. Doheny had made a loan of $100,000 to Secretary Fall without security or interest. 

As a result of the investigations, Secretary of the Navy Denby and Secretary of the Interior Fall resigned their offices, and in 1927 the Supreme Court ordered the return to the government of the oil reserves, and branded those connected with the leases as guilty of "fraud, dishonesty, and cor-

ruption." Secretary Fall in 1929 was convicted of accepting a bribe and was sentenced to serve one year in jail and to pay a fine of $100,000. 

It seems that some of the friends of President Harding had betrayed him. In June, 1923, at a time when there was much talk of corruption in the government, he left for a trip to 

Alaska. Returning from Alaska, President Harding died in San 

Francisco August 2, and was succeeded in office by Calvin Coolidge. 

President Coolidge. Calvin 

Coolidge was born in Plymouth,

Vermont. After having received his education he began the practice of law in Northampton, Massachusetts. This led to politics, first in the capacity of councilman in the city government, then as state legislator, later as mayor of Northampton, and still later as a member of the state senate. In 

1916 he became lieutenant governor of Massachusetts, and in 1919 governor. He came into prominence during a strike by Boston policemen in 1919, when he sent a telegram to the president of the American Federation of Labor, in which he said, "There is no right to strike against the public safety by anybody, anywhere, any time." As President of the United States he helped to restore the reputation of the party, for his honesty was not questioned. He was conservative and cautious, though not a great leader; and as he held office at a time of prosperity, his administration was considered successful. 

Calvin Coolidge

The Election of 1924. When the Republican convention met June 10, 

1924, in Cleveland, Coolidge was nominated for President without opposition. General Charles G. Dawes of Chicago was nominated for the vicepresidency. The Republican platform promised rigid economy in government, reduction of taxes, membership in the World Court, and opposition to the League of Nations. Furthermore, it urged the principles of high protection and restriction of immigration. 

The Democratic convention assembled in New York on June 24. The platform stressed tax reduction and declared itself in favor of a scientific tariff. It emphasized the need of honesty in government, and suggested farm relief and readjusted railroad rates for the benefit of farmers and

certain other shippers. The Democrats also declared themselves in favor of immediate independence of the Philippine Islands, while the Republicans had declared themselves in favor of the independence of the Philippine Islands when they were ready for it. The Democrats suggested that the question of joining the League of Nations be submitted to a vote of the people. The leading contestants for the Democratic nomination were 

William G. McAdoo of California and Alfred E. Smith of New York. In the main, McAdoo had the support of the dry, rural element, while Smith was considered wet and had the support of large city machines. McAdoo was Protestant, while Smith was Catholic. It became evident, however, that neither of these candidates could be selected, and on the 103rd ballot John W. Davis of New York was nominated for President and Governor 

Charles W. Bryan of Nebraska, brother of William J. Bryan, was selected as the candidate for the vice-presidency. 

A third party played an important part in the election. The Farmer- 

Labor party of 1920 was greatly weakened because many Communists had taken an important part in its deliberations. Conservative labor leaders therefore withdrew from it and gave their support to a new organization known as the Conference for Progressive Political Action. This body met in St. Louis in February, 1924, adopted resolutions and called a nominating convention to meet in July. This Progressive convention nominated 

Senator Robert La Follette of Wisconsin for President and Senator Burton 

K. Wheeler of Montana, a Democrat, for Vice-President. The convention accepted La Follette's platform, which was directed against monopoly and presented an agrarian program. The platform stated that "The great issue before the American people today is control of government and industry by private monopoly." It further stated that "monopoly has crushed competition, stifled private initiative and independent enterprise, and, without fear of punishment, now exacts extortionate profits upon every necessity of life consumed by the public." 

In the election that followed, Coolidge received 15,725,000 popular votes; Davis, 8,386,500; and La Follette, 4,822,900. In the electoral college 

Coolidge had 382 votes; Davis, 136; and La Follette, 13 (from the state of Wisconsin).

Coolidge's Administration. In 1925-1929 prosperity continued, and no radical economic reforms were proposed by the President. In his inaugural address he urged economy in government and the reduction of taxes. 

While prosperity reigned in many parts of the country, it failed to reach the farmer. Europe had ceased buying American foodstuffs in large quantities, and the farmer was producing a surplus which he could not hope to

sell in the world market at a reasonable profit. To aid the farmer, Congress passed the McNary-Haugen bill in 1927. This bill, however, was vetoed by the President because he maintained that, if passed, it would put the government into business and encourage speculation. The following year Congress again passed the bill, and President Coolidge again vetoed it.

The Election of 1928. As political leaders were looking forward to the next election, the friends of Coolidge urged his re-election; but on August 

2, 1927, he put an end to that question by saying, "I do not choose to run for President in 1928." The Republican party held its convention at 

Kansas City on June 12 and nominated Herbert Hoover on the first ballot, with Senator Charles Curtis of Kansas for Vice-President. The Democrats met in Houston, Texas, June 27. Governor Alfred E. Smith of New York, who had been an active candidate for the nomination four years before, now succeeded in getting the nomination without much opposition; and 

Senator Joseph T. Robinson of Arkansas was nominated for Vice-President.

The campaign of 1928 proved to be one of great interest. The Republicans endorsed the administration of Coolidge, and approved the principle of protection, as well as the administration's foreign policies. The 

Democrats, on the other hand, criticized the administration, especially its handling of the agricultural situation, but did not themselves promise any definite program. On the tariff question the party platform was vague. It declared for a tariff program that would "maintain legitimate business and a high standard of wages."

This was by many interpreted as favoring a high protective tariff.

A careful analysis of the two party platforms showed that there were few fundamental differences between them. However, the two candidates, Hoover and Smith, represented different philosophies. Hoover was born on an Iowa farm, while Smith came from a poor East-Side home in New York City. Hoover was trained as an engineer at Stanford University and had acquired a considerable fortune. 

He had traveled extensively, for his engineering projects took him to 

Herbert Hoover

LEADERS, PARTIES, AND POLICIES, 1896–1932 

749 different parts of the world. He had served as head of the Belgian Relief during the World War, and had shown considerable ability as food administrator and as chairman of the American Relief Administration. 

Even before the interesting and exciting campaign was over it became evident that the Democratic nominees would be defeated. They lost not only the usual Republican states and the doubtful ones, but also the Southern states of Virginia, North Carolina, Tennessee, Florida, and Texas (see map, p. 730). Hoover, on the other hand, gathered a large popular vote, 21,392,000, and 444 electoral votes. Smith's popular vote was 

15,016,000 with an electoral vote of 87. Norman Thomas, Socialist, had 

267,000 votes, while Foster, the Communist, had less than 49,000. 

President Hoover was thoroughly in accord with the laissez-faire theory of government. He felt that the government should permit big business enterprise to develop without hindrance, that under the theory of individualism America had made great progress and what business needed was the aid of the government in the form of information concerning markets and business conditions. He felt that continued prosperity depended on free reins for big business and that its prosperity would benefit all forms of society. He could foresee a condition when, because of the individual initiative, poverty would be banished entirely. 

The Stock Market Crash of 1929. However, by October, 1929, it seemed that many of Hoover's theories were being severely tested, if not wholly disproved. People had been urged by some forecasters and economists to believe that business was as usual and that production should continue without interruption. Yet there was an uneasiness in business circles caused by other advisers, who warned that we were facing a period of readjustment, and that a decline in prices of securities might be expected. 

On Thursday, October 24, 1929, came the crash which started a rapid decline of security values, and also a wild scramble on the floor of the Stock Exchange to sell large blocks of stock. When the exchange closed at 3 o'clock, its regular closing time, a new record for volume of trading had been attained. The number of shares sold there that day was 12,894,650.

President Hoover pointed out that "the fundamental business of the country, that is, production and distribution of commodities, is on a sound and prosperous basis." Yet the drift continued to be downward, industries curtailed production, millions of workers joined the ranks of the unemployed, and President Hoover throughout most of his administration was forced to struggle with problems brought by the depression and with methods of recovery,

Soon after his inauguration he called a special session of Congress for the consideration of the tariff (see p. 475).

Hydroelectric Power. Another important matter which came to the front during Hoover's administration was the government's policy toward the generation of electric power. During the three decades prior to 

Hoover's administration the output of electric power had been increased twentyfold, and in the year 1929, 97,352,000,000 kilowatt hours were produced, more than a third of it by water power. Many people had advocated the government's operation of such plants as Muscle Shoals, in Alabama, on the Tennessee River; but Hoover was opposed to the government's taking any part in the operation of such a plant. 

Farm Relief. Like President Coolidge, Hoover was forced to grapple with the question of farm relief (see pp. 514-515). 

The Moratorium on Reparations and War Debts. President Hoover maintained that the depression which followed the stock-market crash was in part caused by conditions in Europe; and in order to enable European countries, especially Germany, to get back on their feet, he proposed in June, 1931, a moratorium; that is, a postponement, for one year, of payment on reparations and war debts. This measure he urged was necessary in order to prevent the collapse of Germany. 

As the depression wore on, President Hoover and the Republican party tried to encourage business by insisting that prosperity was "just around the corner," and that what was needed were confidence and a continuation of business as usual. To that end he urged business enterprises not to cut wages. 

Reconstruction Finance Corporation. In February, 1932, Congress, at the request of President Hoover, passed an act creating the Reconstruction Finance Corporation, which was provided with a fund of $500,000,000 and the power to borrow more, for the purpose of relieving frozen credit of financial institutions, and for the purpose of making loans to railroads, banks, insurance companies, trust companies, and other industries. In the following administration, under Franklin D. Roosevelt, the life of the 

Reconstruction Finance Corporation as a government lending body was greatly extended.

CHAPTER XXXIX Franklin D. Roosevelt and the New Deal 

The Election of 1932. In the latter part of the Hoover administration the depression had become severe, more people were out of employment, and the measures suggested by President Hoover and his advisers had failed to bring relief. Since the American people had never returned to power an administration that held office during a major depression, the prospects for success in the coming election were not bright for the Republican party, and the Democrats felt certain of victory. The Republicans renominated President Hoover and also Vice-President Curtis. In their platform the Republicans pledged themselves to continue the gold standard; they favored a high tariff, and agreed to raise prices of agricultural products by any scheme that was economically sound and workable. They pledged themselves to the task of economic recovery and maintained that the depression was due largely to events in Europe over which they had no control. Their platform urged that prohibition should not be a political question, and proposed to submit to the people an amendment which would allow the states to deal with this problem according to the wishes of the people,―provided that the Federal government should have the power to protect the dry states and everywhere prevent the return of the saloon. 

The Democrats, in their convention in Chicago, nominated Governor 

Franklin D. Roosevelt of New York for President, and Speaker John N. 

Garner, of Texas, for Vice-President. Their platform favored the reduction of governmental expenditures, a tariff for revenue, and a sound currency. They urged the restoration of agriculture through the increase of the price of farm products, and demanded the repeal of the Eighteenth Amendment, but also suggested that the states take measures to prevent the return of the saloon. In foreign affairs they proposed the 753

independence of the Philippines and the entrance of the United States into the World Court.

In the spirited campaign that followed, President Hoover pointed with pride to the Reconstruction Finance Corporation and to the efforts of the administration in fighting the depression. He also pointed to the beneficial effects of the tariff, to the economy of his administration, and to its public works program. He maintained that the Republican tariff had protected the American market against European goods produced by sweated labor. 

Roosevelt made a vigorous campaign, traveling thousands of miles throughout the country and discussing the leading economic questions in his numerous speeches. In the preparation of his addresses he was assisted by a group of college professors and other experts who were soon called the "Brain Trust." One important difference between the contentions of the two candidates was that Mr. Hoover placed the responsibility for the depression chiefly on international causes beyond his control, while Mr. Roosevelt contended that the depression was of domestic origin and that proper measures could be taken to bring the nation back to prosperity. 

Many million voters heard the campaign speeches by radio. 

The election was a decisive Democratic victory. The popular vote was 

22,821,857 for Roosevelt, while President Hoover received 15,761,841. 

The Socialist candidate, Norman Thomas, had 884,781 votes; and Foster, the Communist, received 102,991. Of the electoral votes Roosevelt received 472, while Hoover had only 59. The Democrats also received large majorities in both houses of the Seventy-third Congress. The Senate was composed of 59 Democrats, 36 Republicans, and one Farmer-Labor member. In the House there were 313 Democrats, 117 Republicans, and five 

Farmer-Labor members. Thus with a large majority in both houses and an apparent approval by the voters of the party platform, the Democratic party, under the leadership of Franklin D. Roosevelt, looked forward to 

March 4 to inaugurate the program to which the party had pledged itself. 

President Roosevelt. The new President was an experienced leader in politics and in government. He was a distant cousin of former President 

Theodore Roosevelt, and had been brought up in an atmosphere of wealth, which offered him the best opportunities for a broad education. He was a graduate of Harvard University and the Columbia Law School. In 1911, before he had reached the age of thirty, he entered the state legislature in New York. He was re-elected in 1912, and having been a supporter of 

President Woodrow Wilson, was appointed by him as Assistant Secretary of the Navy. In 1920 he became the Democratic candidate for the vice-presidency. In the following year he was stricken with infantile
